UN votes overwhelmingly against U.S. embargo on Cuba
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:46 CST
06:26:46 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The UN General Assembly on Wednesday adopted a resolution calling for an end to the decades-old U.S. embargo on Cuba.
The resolution was adopted with 130 votes in favor, 17 against and 25 abstentions.
It expresses concern about the continued promulgation and application of laws and regulations, including the Helms-Burton Act enacted by the United States in 1996, whose extraterritorial effects undermine the sovereignty of other states, the legitimate interests of individuals and entities under their jurisdiction, and the freedom of trade and navigation.
The resolution calls on all states to refrain from promulgating and applying such laws and measures, and urges states that have applied and continue to apply such laws and measures to take necessary steps to repeal or invalidate them as soon as possible.
The resolution also requests the UN secretary-general to prepare a report on the implementation of this resolution and to submit it to the General Assembly at its next annual session.
Wednesday's resolution marked the 34th consecutive adoption of a resolution on the necessity of ending the economic, commercial and financial embargo imposed by the United States on Cuba. ■

ROME, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet on Wednesday approved a draft budget worth about 26 billion euros (29 billion U.S. dollars) for 2027, featuring tax cuts and social support measures.
The package expands the 33-percent income tax bracket to cover annual earnings of up to 55,000 euros, up from the current threshold of 50,000 euros. It also raises the income ceiling for self-employed workers to qualify for a flat-tax regime from 85,000 to 100,000 euros.
Other measures include a 5-percent flat tax rate for new hires under the age of 35 and an annual state contribution of 100 euros for each newborn until the child turns 18.
Meloni said a new levy on the profits of major banks, other lenders and insurance companies was expected to generate about 5 billion euros in revenue.
The budget is the government's final spending plan before general elections scheduled for 2027. The administration faces mounting pressure to tackle the rising cost of living, as trade unions, social organizations and student groups have staged protests in recent weeks.
Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti cited rising raw material costs and borrowing rates as key challenges. However, he said an agreement with European Union authorities allowing a temporary increase in next year's fiscal deficit would provide the government with additional room for spending.
The draft budget will now be submitted to parliament for approval by both chambers before being sent to EU authorities by the end of the year for assessment under the bloc's fiscal rules. Enditem (1 euro = 1.11 U.S. dollar)

European natural gas prices top 100 euros for first time in nearly four years
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:41 CST
06:26:41 KST

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- European natural gas prices surged above 100 euros (about 111.50 U.S. dollars) per megawatt-hour on Wednesday for the first time since December 2022, amid concerns over disruptions to liquefied natural gas (LNG) supplies from the Middle East and tightening inventories ahead of winter.
Dutch Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural gas futures for November delivery, the European benchmark, climbed to an intraday high of 100.75 euros per megawatt-hour. Prices have risen by about 40 percent so far this month.
According to Gas Infrastructure Europe, EU gas storage facilities were about 74.9 percent full as of Oct. 26, well below typical levels for this time of year. Storage levels in Germany and the Netherlands stood at approximately 61.7 percent and 65.5 percent, respectively, adding to supply pressures as the winter heating season begins.
Market analysts attributed the price surge to continued disruptions to LNG shipments from the Gulf region and growing concerns that the conflict between the United States and Iran could escalate following the U.S. midterm elections, further tightening global supplies.
According to Trading Economics, forecasts of colder-than-usual weather in parts of Europe and Asia could boost heating demand and intensify competition for LNG cargoes between the two regions, putting further upward pressure on natural gas prices. ■

====================================================================================================

Explainer: Two deadly crashes in nine months: What's happening to Spain's high-speed rail?
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:35 CST
06:26:35 KST

MADRID, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Just nine months after a deadly railway accident near Adamuz in southern Spain, another high-speed train collision occurred on Wednesday on the same Madrid-Seville railway line, raising renewed concerns about the safety of Spain's high-speed rail network.
The collision between two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, central Spain, has killed at least 68 people and injured 180 more.
WHAT HAPPENED AND WHY?
At around 8:54 a.m. local time (0754 GMT) on Wednesday, a Renfe-operated AVE train carrying 378 passengers struck the rear of a stationary Iryo train with 147 passengers aboard near Urda station. Both trains were heading from Madrid to Seville, according to Spain's Ministry of Transport and railway operator Renfe.
At least 68 were killed, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha. More than 180 people were reported injured, with some in critical condition.
Spanish Transport Minister Oscar Puente said at a press conference on Wednesday afternoon that the LZB train safety system had failed at around 8:30 a.m. due to a communication problem involving three computers, affecting a 63-km section of the railway and automatically bringing several trains to a halt.
According to Puente, Adif's control center subsequently authorized the AVE train to resume normal operations at around 8:36 a.m., despite a red signal and the presence of the stationary Iryo train ahead. The AVE traveled approximately 25 km before crashing into the Iryo at around 8:53 a.m..
Under Spanish railway safety regulations, trains must remain stopped when the LZB system fails and the track ahead is occupied. Any authorized movement must follow restricted operating procedures requiring drivers to maintain a speed that allows them to stop upon detecting an obstacle ahead.
Puente described the control center's decision as "inexplicable," while railway engineering expert Ramiro Aurin told Spanish news agency EFE that human error was the most likely explanation for the collision. However, the exact circumstances and responsibilities remain under investigation.
GOVERNMENT RESPONSE AND PUBLIC SCRUTINY
The tragedy prompted the Spanish government and several major political parties to suspend their scheduled activities on Wednesday.
During a visit to the accident site in Urda, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez stressed that rescuing victims and supporting their families remained the government's top priority. He pledged a thorough investigation into the collision, saying that any negligence or failures in railway safety systems would be addressed. "We will get to the bottom of this," Sanchez said.
The government also declared three days of national mourning from Oct. 29 to Oct. 31, while the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha activated an emergency response plan and mobilized additional rescue and medical resources. Several hospitals suspended scheduled activities to accommodate the injured, while psychological support teams were deployed to assist victims and their families.
The accident also triggered calls for accountability. Opposition People's Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo said Spain had the right to know what was happening with its railway infrastructure. He called for immediate government and judicial investigations, as well as a comprehensive and independent review of the country's entire railway network.
In Madrid, hundreds of demonstrators gathered outside the Ministry of Transport on Wednesday evening, demanding the resignation of the Transport Minister Puente.
Railway unions also called for stronger safety safeguards. The Independent Trade Union and Civil Servants' Central (CSIF) demanded an urgent explanation of the accident, accountability for those responsible, and greater investment in railway infrastructure and maintenance.
The Spanish train drivers' union Semaf said it would proceed with a strike scheduled for Thursday, calling for stronger railway safety guarantees and structural reforms. The union also said it was considering further action following the latest tragedy.
GROWING CONCERNS OVER RAIL SAFETY
The collision marks Spain's second major fatal high-speed rail accident this year, with a crash near Adamuz, in the southern province of Cordoba, claiming 46 lives on Jan. 18.
While investigations into both accidents remain ongoing, experts have pointed to different possible causes. Jordi Vinolas Prat, a mechanical engineering professor at Francisco de Vitoria University, told Europa Press that the Adamuz disaster appeared to be linked to railway infrastructure problems, while the latest collision raised questions about signaling systems.
Jose Trigueros, president of the Association of Civil Engineers, told Spanish national broadcaster RTVE that the latest collision was particularly concerning because high-speed rail safety systems were designed to prevent two trains from occupying the same section of track. He questioned the reliability of automated safety protections and the extent to which railway operations depended on human intervention.
Concerns over railway safety had already been raised following the Adamuz disaster. Rafael Escudero, secretary-general of the Sindicato Ferroviario railway union, told Spanish radio station Onda Cero that the union had called for an audit of renovation works on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line after the January accident. He urged a review of how the more than 700 million euros (770 million U.S. dollars) allocated to upgrading the line had been spent, while stressing that the cause of Wednesday's collision remained under investigation.
The latest tragedy has also unsettled some railway passengers. Daniel, a frequent traveler between Malaga and Madrid, told Spanish radio station Cadena SER that the accident had left him feeling angry and insecure, saying recent railway incidents had undermined his confidence in train travel.
Civil engineer Martin Perea, a transport specialist and master's program director at Universidad Europea, also warned of serious damage to the reputation of Spain's railway system, calling for a thorough investigation, support for victims and their families, and a broader reassessment of the country's high-speed rail operations. ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Fed holds interest rate steady ahead of midterm elections
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:26:08 CST
06:26:08 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. Federal Reserve on Wednesday kept its target range for the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.75 to 4 percent, less than a week ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.
"Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little," said the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) in a statement.
Nevertheless, inflation remains elevated. In support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate, "the Committee decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 3-3/4 to 4 percent," the FOMC said.
The committee reaffirmed "its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system" and "price stability," saying the accumulation of more information will help the committee "determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal."
Of the 12 FOMC members, 10 voted to keep the rate unchanged, while two favored a rate hike.
"Since our policy action in September, we have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions. They have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said at a press conference after the FOMC meeting. "Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations."
Financial conditions broadly are helping create a path toward price stability. But with the near-term inflation picture still too high, "it's our responsibility to get inflation down," Warsh said, adding that the Fed's discussion over recent days "focused mainly on the price stability side of our remit."
Warsh announced that the Fed will change its meeting schedule in coming years. The FOMC will still meet eight times a year.
"But in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," he said, adding that he expects there will be two strategy sessions in 2028.
The change in the meeting schedule will allow the Fed time to think about "big questions," Warsh said.
Responding to a question about U.S. President Donald Trump's assertion that other board members want to see the country "do badly," Warsh said he will not respond to quotes from public officials.
Following the Fed's decision to keep the rate unchanged, major U.S. stock indexes kept steady, while U.S. bond yields and the U.S. dollar index rose slightly.
The Fed's pause is within market expectations after its first rate hike in three years in September. Chris Hodge, chief U.S. economist at Natixis, said in a research note earlier in the week that pausing would allow more time to determine whether recent high inflation readings were part of a larger trend.
"Inflation is still the No. 1 problem in the U.S. economy, and there are a lot of signs it is getting more broad-based," Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, told CNBC. However, "given that it's right before an election, they won't hike in October."
U.S. midterm elections fall on Nov. 3. To avoid impacting the power held by each political party, the Fed has mostly maintained its charted course in previous election cycles, except in 1978, 1982, 2018 and 2022, when inflation ran high.
The Federal Reserve's decision to hold rates steady at the October meeting suggests its prior hawkish stance was a matter of empty showmanship, Cem Karsan, founder and CIO at Kai Wealth, told CNBC. "At the end of the day, they're trying to gain credibility." Karsan said the only way to respond to what is important is through more dovishness from the Fed.
Nevertheless, it is widely expected that a hike in December is still in the cards. ■

06:26:03 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- UN humanitarians on Wednesday voiced deep concern about the intercommunal violence in the Ethiopian town of Moyale on the border with Kenya that has displaced thousands of people.
Casualties have been reported, along with disruptions to transport, markets and cross-border trade, limiting access to essential goods and services, said the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).
On the Ethiopian side, the violence that erupted on Oct. 18 has reportedly displaced thousands of people in Oromia and Somali regions. This is in addition to the thousands of people who have reportedly crossed into Kenya, it said.
Local authorities in Kenya estimate that up to 50,000 people have crossed into the country since Thursday, amid reports of further crossings, it said.
Many of those fleeing are women and children. While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations, such as schools and churches. Food remains the most urgent need, alongside safe drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and health care, said the office.
"Continued insecurity has forced several partners to suspend activities," OCHA said. "The UN and its partners are preparing a joint assessment mission to areas affected by the violence as soon as security conditions permit."
It is critical to ensure the safety of the population, as well as safe, sustained and unimpeded humanitarian access to all people in need, said the office.
The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has deployed an emergency team to Moyale and is working closely with the Kenyan government, UN agencies, the Kenya Red Cross Society and other humanitarian partners to support the national and local response, said OCHA.
The Kenya Red Cross Society is operating six health service points, screening for malnutrition and distributing relief items. Local communities have shared food and water, though their stocks are limited, said OCHA.
The UN and its humanitarian partners are working to scale up the response. UN agencies have deployed staff and are mobilizing additional supplies, including to prepare for potential further displacement. UNHCR is mobilizing emergency relief supplies, including essential household items and temporary shelter materials, to support nearly 12,000 people, with efforts under way to scale up assistance as needs grow, said OCHA. ■

Carvalho framed the announcement in the context of Portugal's ongoing energy crisis, saying that "freeing Portugal from dependence on fossil fuels is not a chimera: it is an essential condition for a better future and less dependence on third parties." ■

News Analysis: Britain's budget targets breathing space for households, businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
05:25:54 CST
06:25:54 KST

LONDON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on Wednesday unveiled the Budget 2026, aiming to give families and firms breathing space from rising costs through supporting measures in the fields including energy, income, housing, spending and business tax.
The government will provide 100 pounds (about 133 U.S. dollars) household energy payment for up to 20 million qualified households in England, with funding for similar support provided to the rest of the UK. Meanwhile, it will extend the value-added-tax cut on electricity bills to July 1, 2027, according to the budget.
The budget supports drivers by extending the cut to fuel duty for a further six months, while cutting prices at local, lower-powered public chargers to reduce costs for electric vehicle drivers who rely on them.
Earlier Wednesday, the Chancellor also abolished standing charges on household gas bills, a fixed daily fee added on top of a household gas bill regardless of how much gas has been used.
In response to the rising inflation, the government will remove tariffs from more than 100 products to lower import costs for everyday family spending such as baked beans and chocolate, and cut tariffs on kerosene and fertilizer to support households and farmers facing higher costs.
At the same time, the budget plans to increase the National Living Wage by 3.9 percent per hour on April 1, 2027.
Moreover, the budget provides a further 1.5 billion pounds (about 2 billion dollars) in funding for social and affordable housing, taking total capital investment over the next 10 years above 40 billion pounds (about 53 billion dollars).
On the front of business support, the budget backs England's high streets with a package that means all retail, hospitality and leisure properties in England will see their business rates either frozen in real terms, reduced or cut to zero.
On top of the extra 20 percent business rates cut for pubs and all but the largest live music venues, announced in July, this package will take around 70,000 more retail, hospitality and leisure businesses out of business rates by increasing the Small Business Rates Relief threshold.
To deal with the energy price hikes faced by enterprises, measures will be taken to support over 10,000 eligible businesses in electricity intensive Industrial Strategy sectors and the foundational sectors in their supply chains to cut electricity bills by up to 25 percent and bring electricity costs closer to other economies in Europe from April 2027.
However, due to the limited momentum of change brought by the budget, analysts believe there should be more ambitious plans from the government to increase living standard and boost business investment in the country.
"For this budget, the outcome for UK residents is really one in which Healey tinkers around the edges," John Bryson, a professor at the University of Birmingham, told Xinhua.
Since forecasts anticipate energy bills will rise again by as much as 27 percent in January, the government also needs to be thinking more long-term about how to protect households from rising energy bills not just in the short term but over a sustained period, said Caitlin Robinson, a professor at the University of Bristol.
This will require more ambitious investment in energy efficiency, low carbon heating and renewable electricity, Robinson added.
"This was a 'steady as you go' budget, sending the right signals to business, but lacking big calls that would really shift the economic dial," Shevaun Haviland, director general of the British Chambers of Commerce, said.
"Our key tests for the Chancellor were whether his plans would boost growth and ease costs for business. Many firms will have been hoping for a greater impact," she noted.
Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, hoped the increase in Small Business Rates Relief should have covered more businesses, such as manufacturers, small exporters, nurseries and office-based businesses which are not just on the high streets.
Eamonn O'Brien, chair of the Local Government Association, argued that no overall funding increase for local government means councils will continue to struggle to meet demand and provide services to their communities. ■

The fare cuts were introduced as part of a series of government measures to cushion the impact of rising fuel prices on households. A 50-percent discount on second-class rail tickets was initially introduced on Oct. 1 for 30 days, while half-price bus fares took effect on Oct. 12 for the same period.
Slovak Transport Ministry, which proposed the extension, said the measures had proved effective.
The Finance Ministry will allocate 5.3 million euros (about 5.9 million U.S. dollars) to the Transport Ministry to cover the extended rail fare discounts. It will also release more than 8.5 million euros (9.4 million dollars) to regional authorities and regional capitals to subsidize bus services. ■

EU backs away from offer to Canada to start ‘associate member’ talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:06:28 UTC
06:06:28 KST

The EU has backed away from its offer to Canada to start talks on becoming an “associate member” after disagreements between members states just as an EU-Canada summit was set to begin in Montreal.
A draft of a joint statement to be issued after the end of the summit, which runs Thursday and Friday, showed a watered-down version offering “an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself”.
The issue was triggered after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, surprised nearly everyone by announcing in last month’s state of the union address that the EU would consider “associate membership” for Canada.
The declaration had been hailed as a landmark in EU history, offering a non-EU country such close ties to the bloc, which has not allowed any state membership since Croatia joined in 2013.
It was also seen as a sign that the call by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, at the Davos summit in January for “middle powers” to work together was paying off.
But instead of announcing a work programme on developing “associate membership”, the draft communique, seen by the Guardian, states the two sides would “work to define by the 2027 EU-Canada summit the concept of an ever closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself, to reflect, through this even closer association, our common endeavour and cooperation towards our shared goals of prosperity, economic security and strategic autonomy”.
Associate membership had been mooted, and rejected, previously for countries such as Ukraine.
Von der Leyen’s declaration caught EU capitals by surprise and led to pushback politically and legally. Given “associate status” has no definition, diplomats wondered about such issues as whether Canada could join the European Council, legislative bodies or decision-making processes without a vote.
At a meeting on Monday, ambassadors in the EU raised concerns about the dramatic offer, but vowed to make efforts to seek a diplomatic path to rescinding the offer of “associate” membership without embarrassing Von der Leyen. It is understood that Italy suggested “associate membership as proposed by the commission”, with the definition to be thrashed out later by member states.
Germany walked back further, suggesting the wording “an ever closer association of Canada” to the EU.
“Nobody was consulted about associate membership apart from [Von der Leyen’s] closest staff, it would seem. Many member states, including Germany, were not happy. This is all about fixing the plane while it is flying,” said one diplomat.
Germany had argued that “associate membership” should be reserved as an interim step for prospective candidate countries, such as Ukraine or Montenegro, noting that the status has no formal grounding in current EU treaties.
Donald Trump, the US president, previously called the EU’s proposal to make Canada an associate member “laughable”, and said if he interpreted the move as a “hostile act” the US might stop trading with Europe “on many things”.
A bitter trade war with the US, a longtime ally, has seen Carney seek out new trading partnerships around the world. Ahead of the summit in Montreal, one of Canada’s largest banks released a report suggesting there was “meaningful” upside for Canada if it were to deepen economic ties with Europe. Tens of billions of dollars in additional trade would be possible if barriers were removed in areas of overlapping interest such as defence, energy, critical minerals and digital markets, TD Economics said.
Carney has spoken specifically about the need to lessen reliance on Elon Musk‘s Starlink satellite network, following a decision to throttle its usage over Ukraine.
Earlier this week, Carney posted on social media that Canada would join the popular music competition Eurovision. But despite fears raised by political rivals, Carney has said Canada has no interest in formally joining the EU. Changing Canadian laws to bring it in line with European nations would probably prove unpopular, despite public support for stronger ties.
Carney told reporters on Tuesday that the summit this week was the launch of further formal negotiations that will take place another year.
“The good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature,” Carney said. “What matters is the difference it will make to the lives of Canadians.”
A previous draft statement had included at least two references to Canada as an “associate member”, including an acknowledgment that defining the term would take another year.

Qatar is awaiting a response from Tehran to a new proposal that could see Iran take a limited step on its nuclear program in exchange for sanctions relief and potentially the release of frozen funds, two regional diplomats told The Jerusalem Post. The response could come as early as Thursday.
The measure under consideration would involve allowing inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to return to Iran’s nuclear sites in return for sanctions relief.
On Tuesday, IAEA Director-General Rafael Grossi briefed members of the UN Security Council, saying that only the return of inspectors to the ground could provide an accurate picture of the current state of Iran’s nuclear program.
"I invite Iran to work with the IAEA without any further delay to clarify outstanding safeguards questions and to give the IAEA the information and access the agency requires, so that it can verify all relevant facilities and material, as is Iran's legal obligation," Grossi said.
The proposal comes amid continued difficulties in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. Iran has demanded that the US lift its blockade and provide some sanctions relief before discussions on its nuclear program can begin. The Trump administration, however, has insisted that Iran take an initial step on the nuclear issue from the outset of any agreement.
Potentially last opportunity for Iran to make a deal before Trump decides to strike
The return of IAEA inspectors could offer a potential starting point for bridging the gap between the two sides, while allowing the international community to assess the status of Iran’s nuclear activities.
Senior officials from the mediating countries told Iranian officials that this deal might be "the last chance before President Trump might decide to launch a military operation against Iran".
“As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait.

Israel election results: Netanyahu bloc holds lead with double envelopes to be counted overnight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:05:14 UTC
06:05:14 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead and was projected to win 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc was projected to win 48 seats, the Central Elections Committee reported Wednesday evening.
More than five million votes had been counted in Tuesday’s election, it said.
Both blocs fell short of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority without the support of the Arab parties, which at last count had won a record-breaking combined total of 19 seats.
The official vote count reached about 88% on Wednesday evening and only excluded double-envelope ballots, which were set to be counted throughout the night.
Double-envelope ballots could still affect final election results
Those ballots allow eligible Israelis, including soldiers, hospital patients, prisoners, and certain election workers, to vote outside their designated polling stations. They could have a significant effect on the final election results.
Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to have 26 seats, making it once again the largest party in the Knesset, according to the official vote count. United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Otzma Yehudit were expected to have seven seats, and the Religious Zionist Party was expected to have six seats.
Most TV channel polling before the election had Likud receiving significantly fewer seats, while the other parties in Netanayhu’s bloc had been projected to gain more.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and The Democrats, was projected to have 48 seats, according to Central Elections Committee data.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar was projected to have 21 seats. B’Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, was projected to have 12 seats. Yair Golan’s The Democrats was projected to have eight seats, and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu was projected to have seven seats.
Most TV channel polling before the elections had shown the opposition bloc in the lead, and Yashar was projected to be the largest party in the Knesset.
Ofer Winter’s People of Israel and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party, were both projected to fall short of the required 3.25% threshold, potentially further complicating efforts by Netanyahu’s bloc to secure a majority.
The Joint List was projected to have 12 seats, while Ra’am was projected to have seven seats.
Amid the high Arab voter turnout, the Likud on Wednesday accused the Arab parties of allegedly stealing the election through widespread election fraud, bribery, intimidation, and ballot manipulation. It demanded an immediate investigation by law-enforcement authorities.
Despite the election results, the prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot has appeared unlikely. Eisenkot has rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a coalition led by Netanyahu.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Herzog calls on politicians to keep open minds during coalition negotiations
President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday called on political leaders to approach coalition negotiations with open minds, warning that Israel must do everything possible to avoid another election.
“One thing must be understood, and I said this even before the elections: We must do everything, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said. “Therefore, I expect everyone who comes here to arrive with an open mind.”
He was referring to consultations expected to take place at the President’s Residence.
Golan on Wednesday confirmed he would be meeting with “three opposition leaders” on Thursday. In a Channel 12 interview, he declined to name which leaders he would be meeting.
Earlier on Wednesday morning, Golan called on the opposition bloc to form a government with the Arab parties. He said Netanyahu had lost the election with some 55 seats, compared with the opposition’s 65, including the Arab parties.
“Netanyahu lost,” Golan posted on social media. “I know how to count to 120. Sixty-five is more than 55. That’s how Israeli democracy works. Period.”
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid... We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he added.
Golan said the opposition had won a Zionist majority, saying Netanyahu “should subtract 16 seats” belonging to the haredi parties.
All the other opposition party leaders have said Arab parties being part of the government would be a redline for them, following the October 7 massacre in 2023.
Eisenkot has called for the leader of the largest party in the opposition bloc to become its candidate for prime minister, although no agreement on the arrangement has been announced within the bloc.
He declared victory for the opposition bloc on Tuesday night after exit polls showed Yashar in the lead. Later that night, Netanyahu also delivered a victory speech after polling began showing his bloc with a clear lead.
The political deadlock also raised the possibility of a minority government being formed that could win a Knesset confidence vote without holding an absolute majority of 61 seats. In that scenario, Arab parties could agree to support the opposition bloc. Members of the Arab parties have said anything possible should be done to prevent Netanyahu from remaining in office.
Objection within the opposition bloc to relying on Arab parties could complicate such an arrangement. Liberman openly rejected such an option ahead of the election.
Joint List prepared to 'pave the way,' for Netanyahu ouster, Jabareen says
On Wednesday, Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen said his party was ready to “pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government.” He had previously expressed his willingness to support a minority government if a series of demands were met.
Later, in an interview with Army Radio, Joint List faction chairman MK Ahmad Tibi (Hadash-Ta’al) hinted at his willingness to sit with the opposition.
“The opposition bloc will be able to form a government if it has the courage,” he said. “We are extending a hand and are ready to help.”
The Bennett-Yair Lapid government formed in 2021 was the first in Israel’s history to include an Arab party, Ra’am, in the coalition. It was a highly controversial move. Bennett has since taken a firm stance against including any Arab faction in a future coalition.
Ra’am has sought to be seen as a viable coalition partner. Its chairman, Monsour Abbas, in August said former Yesh Atid MK Yoav Segalovitz would be No. 2 on his list.
The move was unprecedented, as he was the first Jewish candidate to join the Islamist political party. The addition of a Jewish, Zionist candidate to the Arab party’s list has been widely seen as a way for Ra’am to be viewed as a more viable coalition partner.
Shir Perets and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

21:01:16 UTC
06:01:16 KST

DETROIT — Ford Motor expects earnings next year will be roughly in line with the automaker's anticipated results this year, the company said Wednesday as it reported mixed results for the third quarter.
The Detroit automaker beat Wall Street's third-quarter earnings expectations but slightly missed revenue estimates. The company has been working to stabilize production of its F-Series pickup trucks after dealing with supplier issues for much of the past year.
"This quarter's results reflect deliberate actions to improve profitability and deliver consistent financial returns," Ford CFO Sherry House told reporters during a call Wednesday.
Here's how Ford performed in the third quarter, compared with average estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: 49 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected
- Automotive revenue: $46.08 billion vs. $46.24 billion expected
The Detroit automaker also narrowed its 2026 guidance to adjusted earnings before interest and taxes of between $10.5 billion and $11 billion, compared with a previous outlook of $10 billion to $11 billion. Ford maintained its adjusted free cash flow guidance for this year of between $6 billion and $7 billion.
House said the company expects 2027 earnings to be roughly in line with this year's results, citing several offsetting factors in production issues this year as well as rising commodity costs.
House noted a $1.3 billion tariff refund during the first quarter of this year was largely offset by additional costs from alternative aluminum sourcing that the company does not expect to have next year, leveling out the year-over-year comparison.
She also said production of its F-Series Super Duty trucks in Canada in 2027 will make up for lost production it's expecting at its F-150 factories to retool for new models.
"Next year will be the third year on our journey of increasing and improving our warranty and material cost savings, and that's getting extended to structural costs throughout the company as well in terms of savings," House said.
Ford CEO Jim Farley called 2027 a "foundational year" for the company on its way to a previously announced target of an 8% adjusted EBIT margin by 2029. The company reported a 5.4% margin during the third quarter.
Ahead of the results, Wall Street analysts were mixed about whether Ford would be able to maintain profits in 2027.
The company has multiple efforts that will add to costs next year: It's rolling out several new or redesigned models, including its next-generation EV and Canada-produced pickups, and is enhancing its energy business that it announced earlier this year.
The missed revenue for the third quarter was a result of each of the automaker's main business units – which are broken into Blue traditional operations, Pro fleet and Model e electric vehicle segments – underperforming compared with Wall Street's expectations, according to StreetAccount.
As part of its modified guidance, Ford said it now expects pre-tax earnings of its Ford Blue unit to be $5.5 billion, which is at the high end of a previous guidance.
It's also anticipating EBIT of about $7 billion for the year for Ford Pro and Ford Model e losses of about $4 billion. Its Ford Credit unit is expected to record about $2.8 billion in EBIT for 2026.
Ford's overall revenue, which includes its credit segment, was off roughly 2% compared with the third quarter of last year, to $49.5 billion.
Its net income also was off $400 million from a year earlier to $2 billion, while adjusted earnings before interest and taxes were up slightly year-over-year to $2.7 billion.
Ford's 2025 third-quarter results included $47.19 billion in automotive revenue, net income of $2.4 billion and earnings per share of 45 cents adjusted.

Saab launches space command and control platform
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:56 GMT
06:00:56 KST

Saab has launched the Allied Mission System, a cloud-based platform that brings space domain awareness, mission management and command and control together so that operators can watch and respond to activity in orbit, according to the company.
The system fuses data from integrated sensors and third party assets, runs automated analysis to produce decision support, and gives operators the means to coordinate assets, task systems and manage missions. Its modular architecture lets data services, mission services and applications evolve separately, and it is built to integrate later with wider multi-domain operations.
Andy Keough, managing director of Saab Australia, said: “Almost everything we do relies on space in some way and we have designed our new AMS platform to give the user the capability to act in this highly congested and contested domain. This innovative and purpose driven technology leverages Saab’s experience delivering trusted multi-domain command and control systems and exemplifies our commitment to ongoing sovereign capability development.”
Chris Picton, the South Australian Minister for Defence and Space Industries, said: “South Australia is the home of the nation’s space industry and Saab’s AMS demonstrates the advanced technologies being developed right here in SA. As space becomes an increasingly important domain for national security, South Australian based companies like Saab are helping develop the sovereign capabilities Australia needs while creating high-skilled jobs and strengthening our defence industry.”
The platform was designed and built in Australia for deployment worldwide and will be sold as software as a service, with customers able to tailor and extend it. Saab already supplies command and control systems for sea, land and air forces across a range of countries.

British stratospheric spy flight planned for next year
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:21 GMT
06:00:21 KST

Project AETHER is planning a multi-payload, long endurance flight in the 2027-28 financial year to demonstrate a broader range of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance collection from stratospheric altitudes, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress has been made in delivering the project, following up an answer given in October last year.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Project AETHER capability development is progressing under the sponsorship of the Cyber and Specialist Operations Command. Planning is currently ongoing for the delivery of a multi-payload, long endurance flight in financial year 2027-28. This will seek to build upon the previous trial events by demonstrating a broader range of Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance collection techniques from stratospheric altitudes.”
AETHER covers uncrewed aircraft operating in the stratosphere, above conventional air traffic and below orbit, where solar powered platforms can stay aloft for weeks or months and provide persistent coverage of an area at a fraction of the cost of a satellite. Earlier trials have flown from the Hebrides range, and the Ministry of Defence has worked with several manufacturers of high altitude platforms.
Cyber and Specialist Operations Command was created under the restructuring that followed the Strategic Defence Review, bringing together cyber, electromagnetic activities, intelligence and specialist capabilities under a single command.

This Is What the GOP’s Final Midterms Push Looks Like
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Republicans are spending the final week ahead of the midterm elections defending historically red Senate seats that have suddenly become competitive, according to federal filings and sources familiar with the matter.
A significant focus is now on four Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina, Nebraska, and even Mississippi, all traditionally red seats, in what’s an ominous development for Republicans in their effort to at least keep control of the upper chamber.
Trump operatives tell Inner Loop that they do not expect Democrats to win those Senate seats and that they have mainly directed GOP outside groups to spend there to help boost incumbents that only have a narrow lead.
But the operatives also concede that they are having to divert an increasing amount of resources to those states—states that president Donald Trump carried by double digits in 2024 and where Republicans never dreamed of having to spend tens of millions of dollars.
In total, in the penultimate week of the campaign, the Senate Republican–aligned Senate Leadership Fund spent $14 million across those four states, according to a WIRED review of federal filings. The biggest spend has been in Kansas, where SLF has abruptly dumped more than $5 million.
Trump operatives say Kansas has been a major headache since the start of October, when Trafalgar Group, a GOP pollster, found Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton one point ahead of incumbent GOP senator Roger Marshall.
Marshall, a doctor, has had an unusually tough race following a slew of negative stories about how he pursued legal action against his patients with unpaid bills and how much time he spends in Florida. Some political operatives have also complained that he has not taken his race seriously, sources say.
But the last-minute spending is also coming in places like South Carolina, where SLF spent another roughly $5 million to help incumbent Darline Graham, who has struggled to galvanize Trump's base despite having the president’s endorsement that propelled her to victory in the primary.
SLF also spent nearly $3 million in Nebraska to help Republican incumbent senator Pete Ricketts, who has been behind in some polls, and in Mississippi, the fund put just under $1 million toward Republican incumbent senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.
The final sprint has highlighted the fraught predicament for Republicans, who are having to patch a seemingly ever-growing number of vulnerabilities.
Trump's campaign schedule has also added several deep-red states that are flashing warning signs, in addition to the expected campaign stops in battleground states. Last week, Trump went to Kansas and South Carolina. This week, he has been in Mississippi and will return to Kansas and South Carolina, as well.
Still, several Trump operatives tell Inner Loop they have been encouraged by the fact that Democratic candidates lately have not expanded their leads in several key Senate races—a concern that has cropped up among some Senate Democratic leadership aides.
Chief among their concerns is Michigan, the best GOP pickup opportunity. Many of the most viable paths to Democrats taking the Senate majority pass through the state, but Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed has suffered lingering issues with key voting blocs.
Black voters turned out in droves to help Barack Obama carry the state in 2008 and 2012, and the conventional wisdom in Washington is that El-Sayed will need similar support in order to keep the seat blue, one of the Democratic aides tells Inner Loop.
But the trouble for El-Sayed, they add, has been the decades-long animosity between Arab and Black communities in Michigan, a divide that was further strained during the primary when supporters of his challenger, Haley Stevens, ran ads featuring Barack Obama praising her earlier work during the financial crisis.
In an effort to rebuild at least part of that coalition, Obama held a joint rally with El-Sayed in Detroit over the weekend, which aides are hoping could persuade some voters. Operatives aren’t sure if it’ll be enough.
We will have to see how it pans out. See you next week, on the other side!

US technology firm Microsoft reported Wednesday that its revenue rose 19% year-on-year to $92.3 billion in the July-September quarter, driven by strong growth in its cloud computing business. 
The company said in its financial results for the first quarter of fiscal year 2027, which ended Sept. 30, that net income increased 32% to $36.6 billion from $27.7 billion a year earlier.
Diluted earnings per share rose 32% to $4.92, compared with $3.72 in the same period last year, according to the company's statement.
Operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion from approximately $38 billion a year earlier.
Excluding the impact of investments in OpenAI, Microsoft's adjusted net income rose 18% to $36.4 billion, while adjusted earnings per share increased 18% to $4.89.
The company said its Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9 billion, up 30% year-on-year, while revenue from its Azure cloud computing platform surged 48%.
Revenue from its Agents and Infra segment increased 25% to $76.8 billion, while commercial remaining performance obligations jumped 73% to $677 billion.
Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17% on a reported basis, while consumer cloud revenue rose 17%.
Meanwhile, revenue from the Devices and Consumer segment declined 3% to $15.5 billion.
Windows OEM and Devices revenue fell 22%, while Xbox content and services revenue decreased 2%. Search and advertising revenue, excluding traffic acquisition costs, increased 12%.
"We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack," Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella said.
"By helping organizations build and own their own intelligence, and earning trust through agent safety and security, we are translating our innovation into growing adoption and real-world impact across every industry," he added.
Microsoft Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said the company's cloud business maintained strong momentum.
"We delivered a strong start to the fiscal year with Microsoft Cloud revenue of $63.9 billion, with growth accelerating to 30% (up 31% in constant currency) year-over-year," Hood said.
"Results exceeded expectations across revenue, operating income, and earnings per share," she added.
Microsoft also said it returned $10.2 billion to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases during the quarter.
The company said it would provide its financial outlook during its quarterly earnings conference call.

Microsoft stock jumps 4% as cloud growth drives earnings and revenue beat

2026-10-28

05:57:21 KST

Microsoft shares rose 4% in extended trading on Wednesday after the company reported better-than-expected quarterly results, driven by 48% growth in its Azure cloud infrastructure business.
Here's how the company fared relative to LSEG consensus:
- Earnings per share: $4.89 adjusted vs. $4.73 expected
- Revenue: $92.28 billion vs. $90.69 billion expected
Microsoft's revenue grew 19% year over year in the quarter, which ended on Sept. 30, according to a statement, with Azure now its biggest single business.
The software giant has been rapidly building out data center infrastructure to meet artificial intelligence demand, while also maintaining positive free cash flow unlike its fellow hyperscalers. Microsoft reported $45.2 billion worth of capital expenditures and finance leases during the quarter, up about 30% from a year earlier. Analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected $50.67 billion.
Microsoft flagged a higher growth rate for cash paid for property and equipment than overall capital expenditures, which include finance leases, because of "timing differences between receipt of goods and payment and a lower mix of finance leases."
Around 75% of capital expenditures are now tied to short-lived assets such as Intel chips and Nvidia graphics processing units, up from about 66% in the past three quarters and half in the year-ago quarter. The shift indicates Microsoft's prioritization of infrastructure it can can quickly turn into revenue.
Free cash flow declined 27% to $18.63 billion. Cloud rival Alphabet reported more than $9 billion in negative free cash flow in the quarter after Meta said last week its cash flow turned negative for the first time.
Microsoft's net income increased to $36.63 billion, or $4.92 per share, from $27.75 billion, or $3.72 per share, a year ago. Adjusted earnings exclude a roughly $200 million loss on its investment in OpenAI.
For the first time, Microsoft disclosed revenue from its Azure cloud in dollars, at $33.17 billion in the quarter. Analysts polled by StreetAccount expected $32.32 billion. The growth rate in the June quarter was 42%.
Microsoft reported results under two operating segments — Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. For the past 11 years, the company had three segments that divided up its Azure, Office and Windows businesses.
In Agents and Infra, revenue rose almost 25% to $76.8 billion, more than the $75.63 billion consensus among analysts polled by StreetAccount. The segment contains Azure, along with Microsoft 365 cloud products, productivity and server licensing, industry solutions and frontier and support services.
The number of people using the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant is up 50% from last quarter, CEO Satya Nadella said on a conference call with analysts. The company did not disclose the number of paid seats.
Revenue in the Devices and Consumer business slipped 3% to $15.48 billion, beating the StreetAccount consensus of $15.05 billion. The unit includes search and advertising, Xbox, devices and Windows operating system licenses sold to device makers.
Sales of devices and Windows licenses declined 22%, as higher memory and storage costs elevated prices. The company pointed to the end of support for Windows 10 last year and weak PC demand.
As of Wednesday's close, Microsoft shares were up about 10% year to date, trailing the S&P 500 index, which has gained 13% over the same period.
During the fiscal first quarter, Microsoft said it would cut 4,800 jobs, and followed up by announcing on Monday that it's offering buyouts to up to 60,000 employees, as it strives to balance a costly AI build-out with capital efficiency. Microsoft also established, during the quarter, an AI implementation unit and revealed a Copilot AI "super app" with coding abilities.
Executives will discuss the results with analysts and issue guidance on a conference call starting at 5:30 p.m. ET.

US Democrats allegedly recruited 'spoiler' candidates to undermine Republican senator in Alaska
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:56:04 UTC
05:56:04 KST

Democratic operatives working with US Senate candidate Mary Peltola's campaign sought to recruit spoiler candidates to undermine Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's closely contested Senate race, according to a New York Times investigation published Wednesday, which uncovered an extensive operation involving campaign aides, national Democratic officials, and a political consultant operating under a false identity.
The operation, internally dubbed the "ballot composition project," sought to exploit Alaska's unusual election system by recruiting candidates who could draw votes away from the Republican incumbent, including another candidate named Dan Sullivan.
The findings emerged less than a week after the Trump administration filed a federal lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska's Senate election results if confusion between the two candidates named Sullivan affects the outcome.
Double Dan Sullivan
According to the Times, the effort began in the summer of 2025, when a Peltola campaign staffer was instructed to search Alaska voter records for individuals sharing the Republican senator's name.
The search eventually led to Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher from Petersburg, a small fishing community in southeastern Alaska, who entered the Senate race in May. He has maintained that he decided to run independently.
Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) both denied involvement in recruiting candidates.
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race," the campaign told the Times.
The DSCC similarly denied recruiting Sullivan or any other Republican candidate.
Democratic operative allegedly used false identity to recruit candidates
The investigation identified Jerid Kurtz, an Ohio-based Democratic operative, as a central figure in the recruitment effort.
According to former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios, Kurtz was introduced to senior campaign aides by DSCC officials in 2025 and subsequently participated in discussions about potential spoiler candidates.
Rios, who was dismissed during an August campaign shake-up, told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved in the operation but was "definitely aware."
The report described Kurtz traveling throughout Alaska using the name "Zane" while approaching potential candidates in bars, restaurants, and private meetings.
One prospective candidate, Matthew Salisbury of Anchorage, said an individual identifying himself as Zane repeatedly encouraged him to enter the race, offering potential financial support through outside political spending.
After receiving a photograph of Kurtz from the Times, Salisbury identified him as the individual who had approached him.
The operation also allegedly involved efforts to recruit Gerald Heikes, a Republican drywall contractor who ultimately secured a place on the November ballot.
Heikes told the Times that a man from the Midwest had encouraged him to run and promised outside support. He did not identify that individual as Kurtz.
Federal Election Commission records cited by the Times showed that a pro-Peltola super PAC paid approximately $87,000 to Wingspan Strategies, a firm co-owned by Kurtz. The PAC denied hiring or paying Kurtz personally for services.
Kurtz did not respond to the newspaper's requests for comment.
Secret messages reveal discussions about manipulating ballots
Text messages reviewed by the Times indicated that senior Peltola campaign aides and DSCC officials discussed the recruitment operation over several months.
Among those involved in the communications were Anton McParland, Peltola's former chief of staff, and Andrew Piatt, the DSCC's director of campaigns.
In January, McParland raised the possibility of establishing a new right-wing political party to attract conservative voters who might otherwise support the incumbent senator.
"Imagine if there was a MAGA party!" McParland wrote.
"Smart," Piatt replied. "Let's see."
The idea was reportedly abandoned in May.
The investigation also described efforts to persuade Democrat David Leslie to withdraw after he advanced through Alaska's August primary. His departure allowed Heikes to claim the fourth position on the general election ballot.
According to the Times, Kurtz contacted Leslie before his withdrawal and later congratulated him.
The August primary resulted in both candidates named Sullivan advancing alongside Peltola, with the eventual four-person ballot containing three candidates other than the Democrat.
Former campaign manager retracts statements
Rios provided extensive interviews about the alleged operation over two months, according to the Times, but later attempted to withdraw her statements.
The newspaper reported that she contacted its journalists shortly before publication and said she no longer wanted to serve as a source.
The Times said its reporting was corroborated by other interviews and documentary evidence, including text messages and records connected to the campaign.
Rios had reportedly been considering a wrongful termination lawsuit against Peltola's campaign but had not filed one.
The Times also reported that political consultant Jim Lottsfeldt had discussed supporting long-shot candidates through outside spending during a dinner with campaign employees.
Lottsfeldt denied knowledge of the operation and disputed Rios's account.
Justice Department lawsuit adds pressure before election
The revelations come as Alaska's Senate race attracts growing national attention, with Democrats seeking to capture Republican-held Senate seats in the November midterms.
The Justice Department's lawsuit argues that the presence of two candidates named Sullivan could mislead voters and improperly influence the results.
The Republican incumbent appears on the ballot as Dan S. Sullivan, identified as the incumbent and a registered Republican, while his namesake appears as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., without a party affiliation.
The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the second Sullivan could remain on the ballot, rejecting attempts to disqualify him.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, under which voters can rank candidates by preference, with subsequent preferences counted if no candidate initially secures a majority.
Election law experts have questioned the federal government's legal basis for challenging certification over potential voter confusion.

European Hypersonic Interceptor HYDEF Advances to Prototype Development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:53:05 UTC
05:53:05 KST

Europe has completed the first phase of the HYDEF project, which aims to protect the region against hypersonic missiles.
Over three years of work, specialists developed a concept for the future missile defense system and tested its key technologies, the European defense procurement agency OCCAR reported.
HYDEF (European Hypersonic Defence Interceptor) is a joint European project to develop a system capable of intercepting hypersonic and ballistic targets within the atmosphere.
The program is funded by the European Union through the European Defence Fund, as well as by Belgium, Germany, Norway, Poland and Spain.
OCCAR oversees the program’s organizational arrangements and contracts. Its main objective is to develop an indigenous defense system against high-speed missiles and reduce dependence on foreign technology.
During the first phase, developers established the overall concept for the future interceptor missile. All planned analytical and engineering work was completed on schedule.
All key technologies for the project reached at least Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 3, which involves initial laboratory validation of a concept. This was achieved through computer simulations, calculations and a series of preliminary tests.
Some key components and solutions have already been tested under realistic conditions, reaching TRL 4–6. This helps reduce technical risks in subsequent design stages.
Specialists have drawn up a roadmap for further development of the system. It calls for a technology demonstrator to reach TRL 6 by 2030.
Following the first phase, participating countries established a joint scientific and industrial base, enabling them to proceed with the design and manufacture of prototype systems.
Completion of this phase lays the groundwork for the next stage of the program, which will involve assembling and testing the first components of the hypersonic interceptor.
Militarnyi previously reported that in August, the HYDEF program successfully passed its requirements review.

Lawsuit seeks to block Trump administration effort to find noncitizen voters
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
21:52:29 CET
05:52:29 KST

By Tom Hals
WILMINGTON, Delaware, Oct 28 (Reuters) - A Trump administration initiative to deploy hundreds of investigators to hunt for noncitizen voters is illegally intimidating naturalized US citizens and subjecting them to possible disenfranchisement, according to a lawsuit filed by civil rights groups that seeks to end the practice.
The lawsuit filed on Wednesday in California federal court by the American Civil Liberties Union and affiliates also alleges that the administration is demanding state election officials deny ballots to certain voters based on flawed eligibility data, potentially undermining confidence in next week’s midterm elections.
President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party is locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress, has repeatedly asserted that noncitizen voting is widespread in US elections, a claim that has been widely debunked.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that the administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas for records on tens of thousands of voters in at least a dozen states as part of the effort to uncover noncitizen voting.
“The administration can’t keep creating political stunts to sow distrust in our elections and lay the groundwork to question results they don’t like,” said Theresa Lee, an attorney with the ACLU’s Voting Rights Project, in a statement.
HOMELAND SECURITY AMONG DEFENDANTS
The lawsuit names as defendants the Department of Homeland Security and Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and US Citizenship and Immigration Services and Director Joseph Edlow. DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In August, DHS launched the Unlawful Voter Initiative, which directed US Citizenship and Immigration Services personnel to generate lists of individuals to investigate for possibly voting without being a US citizen, as is legally required.
In the months since, the Justice Department has brought more than 100 cases accusing individuals of noncitizen voting. It has also launched a legal effort to prevent California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters that the administration alleges are noncitizens.
The ACLU lawsuit said the initiative has led to thousands of fully naturalized American citizens being subjected to improper investigations, door-to-door interrogations and potential disenfranchisement.
The groups alleged the initiative violates the Civil Rights Act and laws governing privacy and administrative procedures. The lawsuit seeks to vacate the Unlawful Voter Initiative and asks for the destruction of records that were created and maintained as part of the initiative.
Last week, a federal judge in California placed limits on the Unlawful Voter Initiative in nine states, but the plaintiffs said those restrictions expire at the end of Election Day on November 3, allowing the initiative to be used in future federal elections.
(Reporting by Tom Hals in Wilmington, Delaware; Editing by Rod Nickel)

Bolsonaro lands in Miami with his family after fleeing Brazil: 'He is in a safe location'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:49:25 UTC
05:49:25 KST

Flavio Bolsonaro, the right-wing candidate who lost Brazil's presidential election this week to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, landed in Miami, Florida, on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil despite a court order prohibiting him from leaving the country.
Bolsonaro arrived in the United States with his wife and two daughters after an escape route that took them through Argentina and Ecuador. AFP and Reuters reported his arrival, with the first footage showing the Brazilian politician stepping off a private jet at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.
AFP footage showed Bolsonaro emerging from the aircraft with his family after its door opened. Reuters cameras also captured the family disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 jet and heading into the airport.
According to a report by NPR, uniformed security personnel escorted the family to a waiting vehicle while holding large umbrellas to shield them from journalists gathered at the scene. Bolsonaro made no statement and did not answer reporters' questions.
His arrival in the United States followed a day of widespread speculation about his whereabouts. According to flight-tracking website FlightAware, the private jet carrying Bolsonaro and his family departed Wednesday morning from Guayaquil, Ecuador, where it had stopped to refuel, and landed in Miami at approximately 9:25 a.m. local time.
The journey began Tuesday evening, when Bolsonaro and his family crossed the land border from Brazil into Argentina before boarding a private plane to Ecuador. Brazilian media also revealed that Bolsonaro used his Italian passport to enter Argentina, even though Brazil's Supreme Court had ordered him to surrender all his passports, including foreign travel documents.
According to Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo, his wife, Fernanda, and their two daughters presented Brazilian documents. Argentine authorities confirmed that the family entered the country with valid travel documents and that there was no legal impediment to their entry.
Trump backs Bolsonaro's arrival as tensions with Brazil rise
Bolsonaro's entry into the United States was made possible after the State Department announced that it would grant visas to him and his family. President Donald Trump, a longtime ally of the Bolsonaro family, expressed support for their arrival.
The move could further strain relations between Washington and Brasília after Lula accused the U.S. administration of cooperating with the Bolsonaro family in an effort to return it to power.
Bolsonaro is expected to break his silence Thursday and publicly address his escape for the first time.
Paulo Figueiredo, a close associate of the Bolsonaro family, announced that the politician would hold a news conference in Miami during the afternoon. According to Figueiredo, Bolsonaro is currently in a "safe location" and is "resting with his family."
Figueiredo claimed that false and contradictory reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts had circulated in the media in recent hours, some of them attributed to officials in other countries.
Election defeat, corruption investigations and a disputed escape
The younger Bolsonaro, 45, fled Brazil just two days after losing the presidential runoff to Lula, receiving 48.21% of the vote compared with 51.79% for the incumbent left-wing president. He refused to recognize the results and alleged voting irregularities, without presenting evidence to substantiate claims that the outcome had been falsified.
Meanwhile, Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports amid ongoing investigations into suspected corruption and money laundering. He failed to comply, and authorities revoked the validity of his passport.
On Wednesday, Brazil's Supreme Court also denied reports that federal police had raided Bolsonaro's mansion in the upscale Lago Sul neighborhood of Brasília.
Despite the travel ban, no arrest warrant had been issued for Bolsonaro when he fled the country. According to Folha de S.Paulo, federal police did not monitor his movements after he left his home in Brasília.
The four family members also did not undergo federal police border checks when leaving Brazil, because Brazilian citizens are not required to complete that procedure when crossing the land border into Argentina.
As recently as Monday, after being ordered to surrender his passports, Bolsonaro declared that he had no intention of leaving Brazil and planned to defend himself against the allegations, which he denies. Now that he has arrived in the United States, it remains unclear how long he intends to stay.
His term in Brazil's Senate is expected to end in February, when he will also lose his parliamentary immunity from prosecution.
Argentina investigates possible assistance in Bolsonaro's escape
Bolsonaro's flight has also sparked controversy in Argentina, where a criminal complaint has been filed demanding an investigation into the circumstances of his passage through the country. 
Lawmaker Marcela Pagano called for authorities to examine whether government officials helped Bolsonaro travel onward despite the restrictions imposed by a Brazilian court. She requested the preservation of security camera footage from the border crossing and airport, passenger manifests and documents related to the chartering of the private jet.
"The Argentine border is not anyone's VIP corridor," she declared.
Meanwhile, Argentine news website Infobae reported, citing government sources, that President Javier Milei's administration helped coordinate the operation that enabled Bolsonaro's departure. According to the report, government officials were involved in examining logistical and legal options in an effort to prevent Argentine authorities from becoming entangled in legal complications.
Following in his father's footsteps
Bolsonaro's escape echoes the actions of his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who also left Brazil for the United States after losing to Lula in the 2022 presidential election and refusing to acknowledge the result. The elder Bolsonaro later returned to Brazil, where he was convicted of involvement in an attempted coup and sentenced to 27 years in prison.
Flavio's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, already lives in the United States and said before the election that he would support his brother leaving Brazil if he lost.

Five ways out of Israel's political deadlock, and one that keeps every promise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
20:45:15 UTC
05:45:15 KST

The inevitable conclusion from the near-final results of the 2026 election is clear: There is no decisive winner, and for a government to be formed after the election for the 26th Knesset, someone will have to break one or more campaign promises.
For now, and probably even after the remaining absentee and special ballots are counted, neither bloc is close to securing the 61 seats needed to form a stable government on its own. Without relying on the Arab parties, which achieved a record 19 seats, the opposition's bloc for change remains far from being able to form a government to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
So, with the emerging results giving Netanyahu's bloc a slight advantage over the bloc for change led by Gadi Eisenkot, is there a way to avoid another election? The answer is yes, but in every such scenario, political players on both sides would have to break several campaign promises.
These are the possible scenarios for forming a government, based on the actual election results that defied pollsters' predictions:
Unity government under Netanyahu
In light of the election results, this has become one of the most plausible scenarios, but also the one that would require the most broken promises across the political spectrum.
Under such an arrangement, Netanyahu could break his pledge to form a government with all the parties in his existing coalition, a promise he repeated several times in recent weeks. On the other side, Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman, the potential partners in such a government, would break their promises to voters not to serve under Netanyahu, whose Likud party finished far ahead of its rivals as the largest party.
ynet reported before the election that this was the scenario President Isaac Herzog had sought from the outset. On Wednesday, Herzog commented for the first time on the emerging results, saying everything possible must be done to avoid another election, another indication of his efforts to bring about a unity government amid the political deadlock.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who made no secret of his willingness to intervene in Israel's election before Oct. 27, could also become involved afterward to help bring about such an arrangement. A unity government could make it easier for him to advance diplomatic initiatives, including expanding the Abraham Accords, the normalization agreements between Israel and several Arab countries.
Unity government with Netanyahu first in a rotation
Given Netanyahu's double victory in the election, both in leading the largest party and in heading the larger political bloc, excluding the Arab parties, it is doubtful he would agree to a power-sharing rotation. Still, the possibility cannot be ruled out entirely.
Under this scenario, the leaders of the change bloc would also break their promises to voters, having pledged not to serve under Netanyahu. Some even argued that Netanyahu was unfit to serve as a minister after the failures of Oct. 7 and therefore should have no place in any government, even one he did not lead.
Netanyahu government with defectors from the change bloc
In this scenario, the politicians breaking their promises would be members of the change bloc who chose to join a Netanyahu-led government.
All the bloc's party leaders, and apparently members of all four parties, promised not to serve under Netanyahu. Most also pledged not to cooperate with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which have traditionally been Netanyahu's natural coalition partners.
Even before the election, ynet reported that if Netanyahu emerged closer to the 61-seat threshold, as now appears to be the case, Likud was counting on the possibility of defections, particularly from Eisenkot's Yashar! party.
As ynet previously revealed, Likud even established a special team tasked with persuading lawmakers from Eisenkot's party to cross over to Netanyahu's bloc after the election.
Temporary minority government or caretaker government led by Eisenkot
Under this scenario, every leader of the change bloc except Yair Golan would break a campaign promise.
Throughout the campaign, Golan said Arab parties were legitimate partners in a future government. Senior figures in his Democrats party reiterated that position Tuesday night, saying political leaders must "show political courage" and form a government with Ra'am, the Islamist-leaning Arab party led by Mansour Abbas.
Eisenkot, too, did not rule out such a move during the election campaign, particularly when asked about Ra'am. However, he faced opposition from his main partners in the bloc, Bennett and Liberman.
All three parties, Yashar!, Beyachad and Yisrael Beytenu, have figures who are firmly opposed to such an arrangement.
Meanwhile, in statements over the past 24 hours, the Arab parties have not ruled out the possibility and have said they would help remove Netanyahu from power.
Netanyahu has already launched a campaign to delegitimize the Arab parties, even claiming they "stole the election in Israel" following their dramatic electoral gains.
Another possibility is that the change bloc, together with the Arab parties, could seek to take control of the Knesset. That would mean replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana and, at a minimum, advancing the establishment of an official state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 massacre.
In such a scenario, the Knesset could be dissolved immediately after those measures are carried out, sending Israel to another election.
Another election
That leads directly to the scenario that appeared most likely before Oct. 27: another election.
If no one breaks the many promises made over the past several months, Israel, once again caught in a political deadlock, could find itself heading back to the polls within a matter of months.
The election results revealed something most polls failed to predict: Likud's enduring support. Although the party lost some ground, it remains by far the largest in the Knesset.
According to most assessments within the political establishment, another election could primarily benefit Netanyahu.
Disillusionment within the change bloc could depress turnout in center-left strongholds and perhaps also among Arab voters, who turned out in unprecedented numbers in this election, effectively fulfilling the familiar political refrain about voters "flocking to the polls in droves."
