“Homos‑masturbators” strike back.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:58:08 UTC
04:58:08 KST

Art: Maria Tolstova / Mediazona
What unites a Catholic priest from Kirov, a pensioner from Kurgan, and the author of a poem about a Porsche Cayenne? They all cheered Russia’s ban on the LGBTQ+ community—and then faced prosecution for posting rainbows.
“Right decision,” Vera Makeeva, a pensioner from Kurgan, commented on VK when the Justice Ministry first demanded the “LGBT movement” be banned as an “extremist organisation”.
Half a year later, a local court fined Makeeva 1,500 rubles ($18): a rainbow flag she had posted to her social media was now considered an “extremist symbol.” The administrative protocol was triggered by her repost of homophobic entries featuring the hashtag #YourFavoriteUnicorn and a photo captioned: “Welcome to the LGBT kindergarten! Who is QUEER? Maybe I should join LGBT too? Lesbians are so cool! Let’s draw a rainbow!”
“It’s my own fault—I hadn’t cleaned up my photo albums for 13 years, and people found it who were interested in checking,” Makeeva told Mediazona. “As for the photo, I took it from a Telegram channel and didn’t notice the trail of links. Why did I publish it at all? Because I am fiercely against this filth, and they were in Kurgan too.”
Following the Supreme Court ruling, LGBTQ+ mentions were completely outlawed in Russia. Books, films, and series face total censorship; at least 32 people across 14 regions are facing criminal charges for “LGBT extremism,” and administrative cases for “propaganda” or “extremist symbols” run into the hundreds.
Law enforcement operates on a well-worn track, and Makeeva’s case is far from unique: authorities are regularly charging the authors of overtly homophobic statements under laws meant to suppress the LGBTQ+ community.
Pyotr Voronin, a resident of Pyatigorsk, received one day of arrest for an image that featured both a swastika and a rainbow flag—both of which are considered “extremist symbolism” in Russia.
“I reposted a picture where Zelensky, Macron, and several other European leaders are shown with a fascist swastika and a rainbow. The FSB’s AI decided I was spreading propaganda,” he told Mediazona.
“In court, I asked the judge about patriotic films where actors do the Nazi salute and wear swastikas on their sleeves without being sent to prison,” Voronin said. “But they locked me up for a day, explaining that I considered Zelensky and Macron to be fascist and gay, which is openly advertised in the media. I asked if I should officially apologise to Zelensky. In short, the AI that reads our messages is a complete moron, and we mean nothing to it.”
Voronin’s outrage echoes the 2000s and 2010s, when Russians were routinely punished for publishing swastikas in historical or satirical contexts—from 1945 WWII Victory Parade photos to movie parodies. Only in 2019 was the law amended to allow extremist symbols, provided there is a “negative attitude” and no “propaganda”.
In some cases,courts are now applying this logic to homophobic statements in the context of prosecution for “LGBT extremism.”
Alimardan Ruziev,a host on Yamal’s Nashe Radio (apparently known there under the pseudonym Uncle Alik), published a post with a poem on his VK page in January 2023:
Three years later, an administrative case was opened against him.
Uncle Alik got lucky. He had originally added a disclaimer, so the court noted the illustrations were “placed precisely in a negative light”—and closed the case.
Vladimir Sugakov, a pensioner from Kuzbass, tried a similar defense. He was charged with “LGBT propaganda” for a slideshow of Pride photographs edited to a derogatory song by Sergei Trofimov.
“I created a video criticizing LGBT, but [the police officer] took screenshots and sent them without explanation. The court didn’t bother to figure it out and fined me,” Sugakov complained.
He was fined 100,000 rubles ($1240). According to his VK page, the pensioner is a committed homophobe who regularly uses the slur evropediki—something like “Eurofags”. But Russian courts rarely look into the specific brand of humour used by authors who subsequently claim they meant the exact opposite.
Georgy Rezankov, a 21-year-old teacher of history, social studies, and “fundamentals of homeland security” in Veliky Novgorod, was fined 1,500 rubles ($18) for demonstrating the rainbow flag.
One of his images featured German communists Clara Zetkin and Rosa Luxemburg next to a rainbow with the caption: “Aunt Clara and Aunt Rosa congratulate you on International Women’s Day. Kosher! Fashionable! Youthful!” Another image showed Honkler, a dogwhistling Pepe the Frog variety, wearing a rainbow wig. Following the police’s lead, the court deemed the wig an “extremist” symbol.
Rezankov asked Mediazona not to publish his comments, emphasising his “sincere negative attitude” toward “sodomites.” “And how did you even find me on Tel-agram?” the schoolteacher asked, further showing his antisemitism.
In St. Petersburg, a court blocked a poem titled “It’s Cool to Be Gay” by an anonymous author, despite its aggressively homophobic lyrics: “Let’s hit balls / Like billiard players / But we aren’t athletes / We are homos-masturbators.”
A Moscow resident was fined 100,000 rubles for a video equally homophobic and contemptuous of neo-Nazis. The two-minute clip, titled “Initiation into Nazis (boneheads),” showed a young man shaving his head, putting on skinhead clothing, and having sex with two similar-looking men, ending with a swastika and the phrase “Join our ranks!!!” The court considered this “LGBT propaganda.”
Other recent cases included a student in Karachay-Cherkessia fined 1,000 rubles for an image of Hitler with a rainbow flag, and a Kurgan man investigated for an image of Putin against a rainbow (the latter case was closed for lack of intent).
The court dealt most harshly with Father Grigory (Grzegorz Zwoliński), a Polish Catholic priest living in Kirov.
Father Grigory told Mediazona he has a long-standing public conflict with Paolo Pezzi, the metropolitan of the Moscow Catholic Archdiocese, whom the Polish priest criticizes for supporting the LGBTQ+ community. In February, he published a post about Pezzi, attaching a photo of the bishop next to a rainbow flag to “attract attention”.
“I was summoned to the migration service. It turns out there is a KGB office on the fourth floor,” Father Grigory recalled. “They immediately drew up a protocol saying I published an article. It was actually against LGBT, but there was a photo of Bishop Pezzi and a rainbow flag next to it.”
In court, he drew an analogy to swastikas: “Imagine I published a book about fascism, and on the cover is Hitler or a swastika, but it is against fascism!”
The court ignored the plea, fining him 1,000 rubles.
The priest’s problems did not end there. Because of the court-confirmed violation, Russian authorities annulled his residence permit and issued him a 50-year ban on entering the country. Having lived in Russia for 24 years, he is now unsuccessfully attempting to appeal his deportation from Poland, where he writes online about the revenge of the “rainbow church”.

Quick hits: Green survives Rorschach test as Aussies put Cape Town to sleep
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:57:53 UTC
04:57:53 KST

Cam Green has fallen on the right side of a line-ball call and "that annoying number three" has collected another unwanted record as the Aussies sent Cape Town to sleep on a dominant second day.
Here are the quick hits from the third Test at Newlands.
1. Unwanted record for 'annoying number three'
The Aussies were cruising.
Starting their innings at the beginning of day two, the tourists raced out of the blocks in glorious mid-morning sun, just as South Africa's openers had done 24 hours earlier.
But things changed with Simon Harmer's entrance into the attack, with the off spinner promptly removing Travis Head for 41 and exposing the under-pressure Marnus Labuschagne.
The South Africans had been clearly looking forward to welcoming Labuschagne to the middle all morning, with the stump mic having earlier picked up an unknown fielder encouraging his bowler to "get that annoying number three in here".
Loading Instagram content
But the hosts did not get much of an opportunity to enjoy Labuschagne's company, with the Queenslander spending four deliveries trying to work a single before edging to slip to be out for a five-ball duck.
Harmer wheeled away in celebration, joined by a horde of ravenous teammates, as Labuschagne's career crisis continued.
The Queenslander's latest failure was his 48th Test innings without a century, making it the longest run without a ton for a top-four batter in Australia's history.
2. Green survives third umpire's Rorschach test
The Proteas were convinced they had their man.
Cam Green had made his way to 22 when he pushed tentatively to a Gerald Coetzee length ball, with his thick edge flying to a stooping Harmer at second slip.
At first glance, it looked to be a regulation grab, with the off-spinner rising then roaring in celebration, but Green was not going anywhere.
After a brief consultation, the umpires decided to send the decision upstairs, where the footage was combed over frame-by-frame.
It was close, with the two camera angles telling two different stories.
Straight on, it could be argued the ball had kissed turf as it nestled into Harmer's hands, but side on, the ball looked to have been collected cleanly.
It was something of a Rorschach Test for the third umpire, and unfortunately for the hosts, he saw the image that kept Green out in the middle.
Only a matter of moments later, it was Renshaw's turn to survive a very close call, with a line-ball LBW decision going the Aussies' way.
3. Sandpaper in the stands
The only remaining member of the trio that was punished for the Sandpapergate scandal in 2018, Steve Smith's 11th hour withdrawal robbed cricket fans of one of the most eagerly anticipated returns in Test history.
But if the Australians thought that meant they wouldn't be reminded of one of their darkest days, some in the Cape Town crowd have ensured they were mistaken.
Video emerged of Nathan Lyon taking his place on the boundary at fine leg on day one, with a cackling spectator leaning forward while holding out a sheet of what looked to be sandpaper.
Loading Twitter content
Lyon declined the offer.
Another fan, wearing a shirt with Smith's sobbing face emblazoned across it, told the Herald Sun he was disappointed the batter wasn't playing, and that he had been looking forward to some "banter".
Loading Twitter content
4. Magic Marco joins rare air
With both Renshaw and Green set and with the luck appearing to go their way, South Africa was in need of something special.
Marco Jansen provided it.
The world's number one ranked bowler provided a fearsome spell in the shadows of tea, dismissing both batters to swing the momentum once again.
Renshaw stood his ground as he just about middled one through to Ryan Rickelton behind the stumps, but was rightly given out for 74 on review, and Green (65) was caught — this time fairly — by Harmer at second slip.
With neither the ball nor pitch appearing to offer very much, it was a seriously impressive five-over spell, and one that saw the 26-year-old take his 100th Test wicket.
In terms of balls bowled, Jansen's 3,864 deliveries saw him become the fifth-fastest bowler to claim a century of scalps, and the third fastest since the 19th century.
5. Carey and Inglis put Cape Town to sleep
Coming together after that Jansen double strike and with Australia's innings at a crossroads at 4-185, Alex Carey and Josh Inglis were composed and circumspect in building their partnership.
The pair were for the most part untroubled in pushing their stand past 100, playing only the shots that were presented to them and offering up few opportunities to the increasingly desperate South Africans.
Not even the second new ball could interrupt their rhythm, with Jansen and Kagiso Rabada unable to emulate Mitchell Starc's stunning spell from late on day one.
But where Starc had low clouds and fading light, the South African spearheads had a placid pitch and still sparkling evening sun.
And in the dying embers of a taxing, 90-over day, some in the Newlands crowd couldn't help but nod off.
Carey (51*) and Inglis (85*) will resume on day three having batted the entire final session and with Australia one run in front.

Amid uncertainty over EU aid, Vitalii Kim insists Ukraine has no choice but to fight for motherland

François Picard is pleased to welcome Vitalii Kim, Minister for Veterans Affairs of Ukraine. “If Europe will not support us, we also will fight because it's our motherland,” says Kim, insisting that Ukraine's determination to resist Russian aggression will endure regardless of the outcome of negotiations over European financial assistance. Yet behind this assertion of national resolve lies a more complex reality: a country confronting not only the immediate pressures of war, but also its mounting psychological, social and institutional consequences.
Speaking to FRANCE 24's François Picard during a visit to Paris for discussions with French defence officials, Kim describes a conflict increasingly defined by attrition. In the southern city of Kherson, civilians face relentless bombardment and attacks by inexpensive, short-range drones, while repeated Russian strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure are taking a cumulative toll. “People just get tired,” he acknowledges, offering a rare glimpse into the tensions between public resilience and the exhaustion generated by prolonged warfare.
The interview also highlights the formidable challenge of reintegrating Ukraine's growing veteran population. With an estimated 1.5 million veterans already requiring support and projections of substantially higher numbers in the coming years, Kim outlines plans to simplify administrative procedures, expand mental healthcare and draw on French expertise. The implications extend beyond individual rehabilitation to the future capacity of the Ukrainian state to meet the needs of a society profoundly transformed by war.
Against the backdrop of uncertainty over a €90 billion European aid package and renewed diplomatic speculation surrounding Donald Trump's efforts to bring the Russian and Ukrainian presidents together, Kim remains unequivocal about Ukraine's commitment to its own defence. Asked about the prospect of presidential talks, however, he offers a notably restrained response: “I need to be politically correct to answer this question. I have no reaction. I have only my job to do.”
His remarks reveal the central paradox of Ukraine's prolonged resistance: a determination to continue fighting, even as the human and material resources required to sustain that resistance come under growing strain.

Russia Equips Geran Drones With Magnetometers for Improved Navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:57:32 UTC
04:57:32 KST

Russia has equipped its Geran strike drones with magnetometers to improve navigation.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s commissioner for sanctions policy, reported this in a Facebook post, but did not specify the type of magnetometer.
The sensors were found in the drones’ tail sections and vertical stabilizers.
Vlasiuk also said specialists were examining the operating parameters of a new electronic jamming system found on the drones.
As is typical, all the new components and electronic modules are based on Western-made parts.
A magnetometer is an instrument used to measure the characteristics of a magnetic field and changes in that field across space. The device detects small variations in the magnetic background as it moves within Earth’s magnetic field or near large metal objects.
In military applications on drones, the sensor serves as an additional navigation aid. It measures the strength and direction of the natural magnetic field, functioning like an electronic compass.
The device’s primary purpose is to enable autonomous navigation when satellite navigation systems are being actively jammed. A magnetometer can help determine a drone’s heading and spatial orientation without relying on GPS or GLONASS signals.
In addition to magnetometers, Russian developers are equipping strike drones with new electronic jamming systems designed to counter Ukrainian electronic warfare measures.
Ukrainian specialists are already examining the operating parameters of the electronic equipment discovered on the drones.
Militarnyi previously reported that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology supplies Russia with equipment for Geran and Gerbera drones, including mesh modems that allow the drones to maintain communications and be controlled during flight.
Journalists found that the manufacturer’s products had been shipped to Russia through the companies Atlant-Engineering and LT Global Forwarding. Customs declarations listed the equipment as antennas and remote-control devices.

Knifeman on LNER train ‘caused terror and fear on unimaginable scale’, court hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:54:19 UTC
04:54:19 KST

A knifeman “caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale” to passengers when he stabbed 10 people on board a London-bound train, a court has heard.
Anthony Williams, 33, is accused of attempting to murder 10 passengers and staff on board an LNER train on 1 November last year and stabbing four people in the 24 hours before.
Christopher Paxton KC told jurors at Cambridge crown court on Wednesday: “The defendant, Mr Williams, armed with a knife, caused terror and fear on an unimaginable scale, moving up and down a busy train from which there was no escape, stabbing several people as he did so.”
During his opening statement, Paxton showed a CCTV clip of a passenger, Stephen Crean, attempting to wrestle a knife from Williams. He said Williams told Crean: “Do you want to die?”
“We say, clear evidence of the defendant’s intention to kill, as was the use of the knife to stab so many, and to stab and cut Mr Crean in his hand, head and lower back,” Paxton said.
Paxton described the “terror” of the attack, which led some train passengers to run “for their lives” and hide away in toilets, store cabinets and under seats.
The prosecutor also praised the “extraordinary bravery” of the passengers who tried to wrestle the knife off Williams.
This included Scott Green, who was stabbed while he attempted to grab the knife from Williams. A member of the train crew, Samir Zitouni, was also stabbed multiple times as he tried to use a frying pan to stop Williams, jurors heard.
“In the face of that threat and the defendant’s sheer brutality some stood tall to protect others trying to de-escalate his rampage, defending themselves and putting themselves in harm’s way to protect strangers,” Paxton said.
Paxton also praised the train driver for his decision to make an emergency stop in Huntingdon.
Williams, of no fixed abode, previously admitted a series of offences, including the wounding of 12 people, but denies 14 counts of attempted murder.
Paxton told the court Williams posed a “dangerous threat” to the people he encountered before the train attack on the evening of 1 November.
Jurors heard Williams had approached a 17-year-old boy on the Docklands Light Railway in London in the early hours of 1 November and asked him if he was “beefing the devil” before he knifed him in the face and hand.
Williams also attacked three people in Peterborough on the evening of 31 October, the court heard, including a 14-year-old boy.
“Across the Halloween weekend last year, to the many people he encountered, the defendant, Anthony Williams, posed a dangerous threat, marauding through towns and cities, on streets and trains alike, armed with a knife,” he said.
“He stabbed many, seeking to end their lives with deadly intention, striking out at them when they were defenceless and in fear.”
The trial continues on Thursday.

US and Japan Finalize Agreement for AMRAAM Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:53:39 UTC
04:53:39 KST

At a high-profile meeting of defense ministers in the Philippines this week, U.S. and Japan leaders finalized an agreement to establish a production facility in Japan for the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, following a massive $20.7 billion Pentagon contract to expand production of the missile over the next seven years.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi announced the agreement in an Oct. 28 press conference after meeting with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Defense Ministers’ Meeting.
The agreement is the culmination of an effort that began in July 2024 under both men’s predecessors.
“We finally reached an agreement on the establishment of a final assembly and inspection facility in Japan for the AMRAAM air-to-air missile, which is essential for the F-35,” Koizumi said, according to a translation of his remarks. “This is a groundbreaking agreement that will not only ensure the acquisition of equipment needed by both Japan and the United States, but will also strengthen Japan’s defense industry base.”
In a readout of the two leaders’ meeting, the Pentagon did not mention the AMRAAM facility but said Hegseth “welcomed Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense industrial capacity, and both leaders committed to continue close coordination on critical munitions production.”
The location for the facility has not yet been announced.
The approval process took more than two years in part because Japan has severe constitutional restrictions on exporting lethal weapons or even coproducing offensive weaponry with allies, which date back to its peace-focused foreign policy following its devastating losses in World War II.
The AMRAAM also contains classified guidance systems and intellectual property that require key safeguards to prevent leaks of crucial information about the weapon.
U.S. and Japanese officials have said the agreement will diversify the AMRAAM industrial base and build regional stockpiles for both the U.S. and its allies at a time when President Donald Trump, and Hegseth and his leadership team at the Pentagon have urged allies to invest more in their own defenses.
AMRAAM has long been the U.S. military’s main dogfighting weapon—the first missiles were delivered in 1988. The latest variant is the AIM-120D, which features GPS guidance and improved range, lethality, and jam-resistance over its predecessors.
All legacy fighters, as well as fifth-generation fighters such as the F-22 Raptor and F-35 Lightning II, can carry the AMRAAM.
In late September, the Pentagon and contractor RTX announced a five-year production contract for AMRAAM with two additional option years valued at up to $20.7 billion. The two sides had previously agreed to a framework agreement in February for AMRAAM and other key munitions.
While the contract award—officially published by the Air Force on Oct. 23—does not specify quantities of missiles, the February framework agreement calls for RTX to increase production “to at least 1,900” per year.
Both the length and size of the new contract are far greater than previous deals. Those usually covered a single year, and demand could whipsaw depending on budgetary pressures or service priorities.
As recently as fiscal 2022, the Air Force budget request called for buying just 186 AMRAAMs and the Navy requested none. Those totals wound up changing through reprogramming requests and congressional adds, but generally speaking, procurement stayed at or below 400 missiles between the services from fiscal 2017 to 2022.
AMRAAM Procurement
Source: Department of Defense Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System reports. 2026 totals not finalized.
This new award expands the Pentagon’s multiyear procurement authorities, covering Lots 41-47. Those lots include fifth-generation technology in AIM-120D-3 variants, such as modernized processors and software-defined measures for the electronic warfare threat.
The deal is part of a broader effort by President Donald Trump’s administration to secure multiyear deals for munitions and aircraft, aiming to break the stop-and-start funding cycles of the past few decades.
The contract also increases output to other countries, with foreign military sales to 16 international partners for additional procurement pipelines included.
“We are accelerating output to record levels to deliver this critical capability for the U.S. services and more than 40 allied nations,” an RTX spokesman told Air & Space Forces Magazine in an email.
“We have invested heavily over the past several years to expand capacity, modernize manufacturing, and strengthen our supply chain,” the spokesman wrote. “RTX proactively sourced $80 million in test equipment before any award. These investments will ramp annual production over the coming years to at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles.”
The company is currently delivering previously contracted AMRAAMs, but the new multiyear contract helps avoid delivery interruptions, the spokesman wrote.
AMRAAM production has faced bottlenecks from a variety of issues, including subcontractor component supply chain problems and solid rocket motor production lag times.
“Like many advanced defense systems, AMRAAM relies on complex components that have long lead times,” the spokesman wrote. “Through sustained investment, supplier partnerships, and efforts such as new U.S. rocket motor production lines coming online in 2027, we are building faster than ever before.”

Peltola campaign aides, DSCC officials helped recruit second Dan Sullivan in Alaska race: NYT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:52:06 UTC
04:52:06 KST

People working with Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee participated in efforts to recruit a man named Daniel J. Sullivan to enter the Alaska Senate contest, in a bid to draw votes away from incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, The New York Times reported Wednesday.
The Times — citing interviews, texts and documents prepared for a potential lawsuit against Peltola's campaign — reported that "not only did Ms. Peltola's team work with people trying to recruit Mr. Sullivan to run for Senate, but the effort was much broader."
"The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent's support and help catapult the Democrat to victory," the newspaper reported.
Peltola's former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved in the project, but she was "definitely aware," according to the report.
The Times noted Rios last week tried to retract comments she made confirming the effort to recruit spoilers.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC "denied participating in efforts to recruit spoilers to the ballot in Alaska," The Times said.
The newspaper's report noted ballot-stacking tactics are "common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska."
The report comes days after the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit allegingthe campaign by the non-incumbent Sullivan was geared toward him acting as a spoiler for the incumbent Sullivan because of voter confusion.
The DOJ has asked a federal judge in Alaska to block certification of any Senate race result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
The winner of the election could determine whether Democrats regain a majority in the Senate, or if Republicans retain their current majority.
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ's lawsuit.
After the Times published its report, Trump demanded that Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan both be removed from Alaska's election ballot.
Trump, in a Truth Social post, claimed the report showed Democrats "illegally" sought out the same-named man "in order to defraud, confuse, and obfuscate the Election, thereby taking votes away from the REAL Senator, Dan Sullivan."
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on The Times article, said, "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC."
A DSCC spokesperson in a statement to CNBC said, "The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan."
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," the spokesperson said.
The spokesperson pointed to several examples of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.
Peltola's campaign and DSCC, as well as Alaska's election officials, have asked the judge overseeing the DOJ's lawsuit, Sharon Gleason, to dismiss the suit before Election Day, Nov. 3. The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the advocacy group Common Cause have also sought to intervene in the case to oppose the DOJ's efforts.
Alaska officials said the DOJ "lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate," and that the lawsuit and "requested relief cast a cloud over Alaska's election."
State officials said in a court filing that Alaska's Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
Gleason on Monday evening fast-tracked the case, increasing the chance she will decide whether to dismiss the case in U.S. District Court in Anchorage before Election Day.
Daniel J. Sullivan prevailed in a legal fight that ended with the Alaska Supreme Court allowing him on the nonpartisan primary ballot over the opposition of state election officials who argued his presence would confuse voters.
He won enough votes in that contest to win a place as one of four candidates on the general election ballot.
On that ballot, his name is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as Sullivan, Dan. S. with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Peltola, a former U.S. House member, is the only Democrat on the ballot.
Alaska uses ranked-choice voting, which allows voters to rank candidates by preference. That method could allow voters to rank both Sullivans as choices, allowing a vote for the non-incumbent to be transferred to the incumbent senator if the non-incumbent is eliminated in the first round of counting.
The Times quoted Peltola's former campaign manager Rios, who the newspaper reported was fired in August, as saying, "Alaskan voters need to know" about the effort to recruit others into the race.
"There was a lot of speculation, and voters should get the full picture when making their decisions," Rios was quoted as saying.
Rios told The Times last week that she wanted to retract her prior statements.
"As discussed on our call earlier today, I am confirming that I have retracted all statements made regarding the 2026 Alaska Senate Race in connection with any article you may or may not be writing," Rios wrote, according to The Times. "I am not willing to be a source for any story in any capacity."
The newspaper said it told Rios she would be part of its article, and noted her interviews "were consistent with The Times's other reporting."

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:51:00 UTC
04:51:00 KST

Alliance response must be credible if Russia uses nuclear weapons, former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy says
Jim Stokes, a GLOBSEC expert and former NATO Director of Nuclear Policy (2023–2025), made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform.
“In this hypothetical situation, if Russia uses nuclear weapons, NATO will have to respond... The response must be credible,” Stokes said.
He recalled NATO’s stated readiness to inflict damage far exceeding any potential gains. The response could involve nuclear weapons, conventional weapons, or a combination of both. The decision would be made at a later stage, as it would be unwise to reveal to an adversary where these red lines lie or exactly how a response might be formulated and carried out, the former NATO official emphasized.
Stokes said that in an emergency or during a crisis, the Alliance could make political decisions and implement them very quickly. He added that member states were also capable of acting independently and swiftly. The United States, the United Kingdom, and France could each independently employ their nuclear forces to deter aggression against the Alliance, not just a nuclear attack. Stokes described this as a major advantage for NATO.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and NATO’s designation of Russia as a threat to the Alliance, NATO has been adapting its nuclear deterrence posture, including by modernizing its nuclear forces. Exercises and preparations for a potential NATO nuclear operation demonstrate that the Alliance is capable of carrying one out effectively with its current capabilities and force posture, the former official said.
He noted that NATO aircraft could deliver free-fall nuclear bombs. Some advocate the option of launching missiles from sea-, land-, or air-based platforms. In Stokes’s view, all options should remain on the table.
As previously reported, British and French fighter jets conducted joint exercises over the Mediterranean for the first time in October, involving French nuclear forces and demonstrating deeper defense cooperation between the two countries amid tensions with Russia. In July 2025, the two countries agreed to deepen their cooperation on nuclear deterrence in response to growing threats to Europe and uncertainty over the role of the United States as an ally.

Ukraine Rolls Out Amphibious UGVs to Brave1 Market After 40-Km Combat Mission
Ukraine has added a new category of amphibious unmanned ground vehicles to the Brave1 Market , allowing military units to order robotic systems capable of moving across both land and water, Ukraine’s Defence Ministry reported on October 28.
The ministry stated that three amphibious UGV models are already available on the platform, with additional systems expected to be added later. Military units will eventually be able to order them through Ukraine’s ePoints program .
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The deployment forms part of Ukraine’s growing use of unmanned ground systems for frontline logistics and other high-risk missions. By mid-August, Ukrainian UGVs had completed more than 100,000 missions in place of soldiers since the beginning of 2026.
Amphibious UGVs are designed for frontline logistics in areas where rivers, canals, wetlands, or damaged terrain can block conventional ground routes. The systems retain high mobility on land and can switch within seconds to moving through water, according to Ukraine’s Defence Ministry.
The ministry noted that Brave1 and the Defence Ministry have been developing the amphibious systems market to accelerate their deployment to Ukrainian units. Brave1 launched a dedicated grant program for amphibious UGVs in June 2026, while developers have continued refining the systems using feedback from frontline troops.
The technology has already been tested in combat. Soldiers from the Alter Ego unit of Ukraine’s 93rd Separate Mechanized Brigade recently completed what the ministry described as the world’s first combat logistics mission using an amphibious ground robot.
The vehicle traveled more than 40 kilometers across land and water before successfully delivering food and ammunition to Ukrainian positions.
Ukraine is also expanding unmanned aerial systems into battlefield casualty evacuation. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Ukrainian troops used the StarGate aerial CASEVAC drone to evacuate two seriously wounded soldiers in one week, including one mission covering nearly 60 kilometers round trip despite Russian GPS jamming.

Israel deadlocked: Do the Arabs hold the key to defeating Netanyahu?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:48:26 UTC
04:48:26 KST

Netanyahu’s Israel deadlocked: were the elections ‘stolen by the Arabs’?
Israel’s parliamentary elections are over, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been wounded, but not defeated. His battle to form a government and stay in power is just beginning.
The final results of the Israeli election won’t be known until Thursday, when Israel’s Central Election Committee (CEC) finishes tallying so-called ‘double envelope’ ballots cast by soldiers, diplomats living abroad, prisoners, and other voters unable to make it to polling stations on election day.
However, with more than 85% of votes counted as of Wednesday evening, a picture of political deadlock is becoming clearer, and neither Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc, nor the center-left to center-right bloc of his opponents, are on track to win a majority in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset. Either bloc must secure 61 out of 120 Knesset seats to form a government.
What are the results of the Israeli election?
Netanyahu’s Likud remains Israel’s largest political party, and is projected to win 26 seats, down from 32 in 2022.
Yashar, led by Netanyahu’s chief rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is in second place with 21 seats.
Both politicians lead large and potentially fractious blocs. Together with four far-right and religious parties – Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism, Shas, and Religious Zionism, Netanyahu’s bloc controls 53 seats, ten short of a majority.
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc comprises Yashar, former Prime Ministers’ Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid’s B’Yachad party, Yair Golan’s Democrats, and Yisrael Beytenu, a right-wing party led by former Defense Minister Avigdor Liberman. Together, this bloc controls 48 seats.
What about the Arabs?
Israel’s two main Arab parties, Yousef Jabareen’s Joint List and Mansour Abbas’ Ra’am, have almost doubled their representation in the Knesset. Driven by anger over Netanyahu’s war on Gaza and his appointment of overt Jewish supremacists to cabinet positions, voters in Arab-majority districts turned out in record numbers to award the Joint List and Ra’am 12 and seven seats respectively, up from a combined ten seats in 2022.
With a combined 19 seats, the Arab parties could play the role of kingmakers when coalition talks begin. However, they would likely find few allies within either Jewish-led bloc.
Will Netanyahu work with the Arabs?
Netanyahu has explicitly ruled out cooperation with either Arab party, both of which have condemned his war on Gaza. “It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel and to establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties,” he said after polls closed on Tuesday.
In the run up to the vote, the Israeli prime minister framed the election as a choice between “Me and [US President Donald] Trump, or Eisenkot and Abbas,” and accused his opponents of plotting to recognize a Palestinian state after entering a government with the Arabs.
In a statement on Wednesday, Netanyahu claimed that “the elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties,” and that Likud had uncovered evidence of vote-buying, “threats and violence against polling station members,” and repeat voting in Arab districts. The PM called on police and Israel’s Shin Bet intelligence agency to conduct a “thorough investigation” into his claims.
Eisenkot’s party warned on Tuesday that Netanyahu would attempt to delegitimize the election. “Netanyahu is panicking and has begun making up stories and claiming that the election is being stolen,” Yashar said in a statement. “This is no accident. He is already laying the groundwork to challenge the election results.”
What about the opposition?
Eisenkot, Liberman, and Bennett have all ruled out cooperation with the Arabs, with Eisenkot declaring on election night that he intends to form “a Zionist government.” Democrats leader Yair Golan, on the other hand, has called on the anti-Netanyahu bloc to reach out to Ra’am and the Joint List for the sake of ousting Netanyau. Partnership with the two Arab parties would give the bloc 65 seats – a clear majority.
“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid,” he wrote on social media on Wednesday morning. “We have a majority. We have responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel’s Arab citizens.”
Abbas has said that he is willing to enter government with the anti-Netanyahu bloc, while Jabareen has said that his Joint List lawmakers would “pave the way for the ousting of the Netanyahu government” by refusing to oppose a minority government in exchange for some concessions on Palestine and funding for Arab communities.
Who will form a government in Israel?
Israeli President Isaac Herzog will ultimately decide which political leader stands the best chance of forming a stable government, and task them with forming a coalition. Herzog has called on all parties to enter negotiations “with an open mind.” As the political horse-trading begins, three potential outcomes are laid out below:
Netanyahu wins back the right
Netanyahu could secure a majority by striking a deal with Bennett and Liberman to peel B’Yachad away from the opposition bloc. Both are right-wingers, but both campaigned on ousting Netanyahu and forcing military conscription on Israel’s ultra-Orthodox Haredi communities. In this case,, Netanyahu would likely lose the backing of the two ultra-Orthodox parties in his coalition, United Torah Judaism and Shas.
Swapping these parties for B’Yachad would leave Netanyahu’s bloc even further away from a majority, meaning one side would have to compromise on their core campaign promises to make this arrangement work.
Eisenkot joins the Arabs
Eisenkot’s opposition bloc could quickly secure a majority and form a government, but only if he, Bennett, and Liberman decide that taking power is worth cooperating with, or securing the abstention of, the Arab parties.
Doing so would carry political consequences for everyone involved. At a time when public support for a two-state solution has collapsed and fewer Israelis than ever believe that they “cannot coexist peacefully” with their Palestinian neighbors, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Liberman would risk alienating their right-wing voters.
Likewise, Arab voters could see any partnership with the Israeli-right as a betrayal by the Joint List and Ra’am. Earlier this week, Joint List parliamentary leader Ahmad Tibi alluded to this fear, telling Türkiye’s Anadolu news agency that he does not want his party “to be responsible for incursions into Al-Aqsa Mosque, a war in Gaza, the continuation of Jewish terrorism and settlement activity, or house demolitions.”
Entering a government with Eisenkot and the right-wing opposition would make the Joint List “collectively responsible” for these crimes, he explained.
Could a grand Zionist coalition emerge in Israel?
A unity government – in which Netanyahu and Eisenkot rotate the premiership with the support of Bennett and Liberman – may seem like an obvious solution for everyone involved. Likud, Yashar, B’Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu are all aligned on security matters, and entering a grand coalition would allow Netanyahu to cast off his ultra-Orthodox and far-right partners, while Eisenkot could sever ties with the Democrats and Arabs.
Such an arrangement is not without precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz – a centrist ex-general – reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
However, the Netanyahu/Gantz coalition fell apart in less than a year, at a less polarized time in Israeli politics. This time around, all of Netanyahu’s opponents have focused their campaigns around deposing the prime minister, with Eisenkot accusing him of corruption, incompetence, and ignoring “dozens of warnings” prior to Hamas’ attack on Israel in 2023.
“I unequivocally pledge that I will not serve under Netanyahu in a rotation agreement. Period,” Eisenkot told Radio 103 last week. “If that were to happen, you would see me resign an hour later.” Eisenkot did not explicitly rule out working with Likud, if Netanyahu were to retire.
The alternative for Israel: deadlock and elections
Should none of these arrangements work, Israel could be thrust into another election cycle. Repeat elections and failed coalition talks were a leitmotif in Israeli politics until the October 7 attack and subsequent wars ushered in a period of relative stability: in the four years before 2022, Israel went through five elections.
Herzog has made it clear that he wants to avoid such an outcome. “We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections,” he said on Tuesday. However, unless Israel’s main parties can find some kind of compromise, another election may be inevitable.

Colombia's lower house rejects changes to pension reform articles
BOGOTA, Oct 28 - Colombia's lower house on Wednesday rejected changes to a package of specific articles from a pension reform bill that had been returned to the legislature by the Constitutional Court, which ordered lawmakers to remedy a procedural flaw in the bill.
In August, the Constitutional Court approved most of the 2024 pension system reform, championed by former President Gustavo Petro.
The rejection means the version of the bill approved by the Senate will stand and the court will now need to decide if the procedural flaw has been corrected.
The pension reform aims to strengthen the state-run pension administrator Colpensiones, reduce subsidies for high pensions, provide benefits to women with children, and expand coverage to protect older adults living in poverty.
The bill maintains the retirement age at 62 for men and 57 for women. The law requires all Colombians earning up to 2.3 times the monthly minimum wage — approximately 4 million pesos (about $1,300) — to make contributions to Colpensiones.
Those earning above that amount can choose a private pension fund for the surplus portion of their income.
The measure also stipulates that workers who failed to accumulate enough contribution weeks to qualify for a pension will receive aid, while those in poverty who did not contribute will receive a monthly payment of around $75.
The Petro government estimated more than 2.6 million older adults will benefit from the measures.
Men with 900 weeks of contributions and women with 750 will remain in the current system and will not be required to contribute to the state fund.
Some economic and social initiatives championed by Petro were rejected or faced difficulties gaining approval in Congress, where he lacked solid support. He left office in August and was replaced by right-wing President Abelardo De La Espriella, who has pledged to maintain some of Petro's popular social reforms.
The reform is one of Colombia’s most significant social policy reforms in years, according to analysts, who note that it would expand the state’s role in the pension system while preserving a role for private funds—an issue that has long divided lawmakers, businesses, and unions. REUTERS

Fed holds rates steady despite concerns over inflation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:43:48 UTC
04:43:48 KST

The Federal Reserve voted Wednesday to keep benchmark interest rates on hold, opting to take a patient approach in its fight against inflation despite mounting evidence that price pressures are proving more nettlesome than policymakers had hoped.
In a widely expected decision, the Federal Open Market Committee kept the overnight funds rate in a range between 3.75%-4%, where it has been since the central bank approved a quarter percentage point increase in September.
"Inflation remains elevated," the post-meeting statement said. "The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."
Two voters dissented
Two of the 12 FOMC voters dissented from the decision – Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, both of whom wanted the committee to raise rates by a quarter percentage point.
Cook has been at the center of a continuing controversy in which President Donald Trump has tried to remove her from office over allegations concerning information she provided on home loan applications. While the Supreme Court stopped the president's attempts, the administration has restarted the move, with a hearing scheduled for early November.
This was Cook's first dissent since joining the Fed in 2022 as an appointee of President Joe Biden.
Dallas President Lorie Logan and Minneapolis President Neel Kashkari both joined Hammack in voting no the last time the committee held, in July, and both have expressed the need for higher rates. However, they fell in with the majority Wednesday.
The midterm elections have lingered over the decision. Pivotal votes take place nationwide on Nov. 3, with control of Congress at stake. Fed officials consider political independence to be a cornerstone of the central bank, but some observers have speculated that officials won't want to raise rates this close to an election.
Trump, who nominated Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to the position, has been at odds with the Fed for years. Trump has charged that the funds rate should be much lower.
The dissents reflected underlying conflict on the committee over how aggressively it needs to raise rates to combat rising prices. Inflation has been above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, and the pace of price increases has only picked up since the September meeting.
Statements over the past several weeks, though, have reflected a desire to wait for additional data to come in before tightening policy further. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams both said current economic conditions allow policymakers time to evaluate their next move.
The statement characterized economic activity as "expanding at a strong pace," a seeming upgrade from "solid" in September. There were no other substantial changes to the statement other than the removal of a sentence that explained the September increase.
The decision came as little surprise as markets had been pricing in a less than 10% chance of a hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Following the decision, the S&P 500 held on to its gains.
However, it raises fresh questions about how long policymakers are willing to wait before tightening again. Futures market pricing indicates a strong possibility of another hike at the next FOMC meeting in December, and perhaps another increase or two in 2027.
Separately, Warsh unveiled at a news conference changes to the FOMC meetings next year that could reduce the number of rate-setting meetings each year.
"We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated," Warsh said. "The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in 2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for setting policy."
Complicated economic picture
The Fed is up against a complicated economic and political picture. Inflation as measured by the Fed's preferred gauge is expected to be above 3% for September, even when excluding volatile food and energy prices. Economists are concerned that inflation has broadened beyond the energy sector and the impact from the Iran war.
At the same time, the unemployment rate has remained low and economic growth has been strong. The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker is pointing to 3.4% annualized growth in the third quarter, which would be the strongest in a year. Consumer spending also has been solid, and investment tied to the artificial intelligence boom has helped keep the U.S. economic engine running.
The combination, though, has added to debate about how much restriction the Fed's current interest rate is actually exerting on the economy, and whether policymakers will need to move more aggressively if the price data doesn't improve.
While markets expect additional hikes, Warsh has avoided providing so-called forward guidance about the FOMC's intentions. In June, his fellow committee members, through the "dot plot" grid, indicated the likelihood of another increase this year.
"The Fed is taking a wait-and-see approach, and I think that makes sense given where we are in the cycle," said Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust and a former BLS analyst. "The economy is slowing, but slowing and breaking are two different things. Holding rates steady gives policymakers more time to assess how the economy is responding to September's hike and the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs."

Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Abiy has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to the country’s economic and security interests.

The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later fought alongside Ethiopian government forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray conflict, but relations have since deteriorated.

RFK, Jr.,  loosens restrictions for six popular peptides, bypassing the FDA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:40:43 UTC
04:40:43 KST

The Department of Health and Human Services announced a loosening of restrictions on six unproven peptides on Wednesday. These substances have long been touted by biohackers as a means to hack people’s bodies and brains for the better, but they often have had scant scientific evidence behind them. In the past, HHS chief Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., has voiced support for peptides, such as the so-called Wolverine stack, a combination of two such substances—BPC-157 and TB-500—that is meant to promote healing. Both of these peptides are included in the list of those that are now available to dispense.
The new policy allows some licensed pharmacists to produce compounds made up of multiple peptides—provided that those peptides are made by registered manufacturers. Users must also have a valid prescription to receive the compounds.
In a document outlining the new policy, the agency acknowledged that compounded drugs carry risks: they are not regulated in the same way as a name-brand or generic medication by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, leading to concerns over their safety and efficacy. But the agency said that the level of public interest and available data had led it to expand access to some combinations of peptides and that doing so would discourage the growing gray and black markets for peptides.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Peptides are small chains of amino acids, which are the building blocks of proteins. Humans produce a large number of peptides naturally, but taking them as supplements has become a major trend among health influencers, tech executives and the “Make America Healthy Again” movement. Depending on the peptide, the substances are marketed as helping with everything from extending lifespan to healing from injuries and workouts to improving one’s complexion. Perhaps the best-known peptide products on the market are glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) drugs, such as Ozempic and Mounjaro.
The peptides included under the new policy are: BPC-157 and TB-500; Epitalon, which is promoted as a sleep and longevity aid; KPV, which is used as an anti-inflammatory; MOTS-c, which is used for obesity and osteoporosis; and Semax, a supplement for migraine and chronic pain.
Willie Underwood III, president of the American Medical Association, criticized the policy shift in a statement, saying the peptides have "not undergone the rigorous testing required of FDA-approved drugs."
"“Allowing pharmacies to compound unapproved synthetic peptide substances without sufficient evidence of their safety and efficacy puts patients at risk," he said. "Expanding access without adequate safeguards and oversight could expose patients to serious, preventable harm.”
The affected peptides are also rarely taken alone, and in some cases, there is very little research as to what so-called stacks of two or more peptides might do to health. Despite that lack of evidence, the loosening of restrictions has come after the FDA began analyzing how to make the substances more accessible and convened a panel to discuss allowing compounding pharmacies to manufacture them.
HHS appeared to acknowledge the lack of data in its announcement, saying it may revisit the issue if safety or product quality issues arise as the compounded peptides become more available.
Editor’s Note (10/28/26): This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

Spain high-speed train crash kills 68
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:40:43 UTC
04:40:43 KST

Spain high-speed train crash kills 68
A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 68 people and injured scores more on Wednesday, with the toll likely to rise, authorities said, in one of Europe's deadliest such disasters this century.
The second such accident to strike Spain this year will raise fresh questions about the country's rail safety, with the transport minister speaking of an "error" and "inexplicable circumstances" that led to the collision.
AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.
Dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.
Castilla-La Mancha's leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene that 68 people had died, raising an earlier toll of 64 and having already warned of more victims being found.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.
State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
Pablo Mejia, 42, with blood staining his grey jumper, told AFP that he had miraculously survived after changing his seat, as he awaited a transfer to the southern city of Seville.
He recounted "a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos."
A visibly shaken Manuel Ortiz who lives in the village of Urda close to the site of the accident, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid, told AFP he had been transporting survivors all morning in his car.
Ortiz, 49, described a "horrific, horrible" scene that "smelled of an accident, of metal".
Transport Minister Oscar Puente told reporters that the collision came after a train was ordered to go in "error" despite a technical failure affecting the automatic control system that halted all services on a 69-kilometre stretch of track.
"The decision to resume traffic, while that system had not been restored, belongs to the control centre," which resumed traffic "in circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable", Puente said.
The Renfe train restarted and travelled 25 kilometres until it collided with the stationary Iryo, at a speed that could have reached "up to 200 kilometres per hour", Puente added.
The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it", Puente said.
The accident comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for this year's first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership in an early general election on November 29.
He said Spain would observe three days of mourning from Thursday, conceding it was "not acceptable" that two high-speed collisions could happen within months. His Socialists halted campaign activities.
The leader of the main opposition conservative Popular Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who leads in most polls, also suspended campaigning but said: "Spain has the right to know what is going on with its infrastructure."
Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
Spain's high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the second-largest in the world after China's and a source of national pride.
But Wednesday's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country's railways.
That crash was Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.

'Reverse course while there's still time' — US senator tells ships carrying Russian diesel to turn around
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:40:00 UTC
04:40:00 KST

'Reverse course while there's still time' — US senator tells ships carrying Russian diesel to turn around
U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, issued a warning to the shipping company transporting a cargo of Russian diesel to the United States: turn back, or risk violating U.S. sanctions law.
The senator's demand comes a few days after Reuters reported that the Malta-flagged tanker Agioi Fanendes was heading to New York with 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel — the first delivery under a recent deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Blumenthal penned a letter to Athanasios Martinos, managing director of the shipping service Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited, urging him to confirm the reports and recall the vessel.
"I'm sending a sledgehammer message to shipping companies whose tankers are transporting illegal Russian diesel to our ports," Blumenthal said in a social media message accompanying the letter. "Reverse course while there's still time."
The letter points out that diesel shipments are banned under the 2022 Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, signed into law by former President Joe Biden following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Should the Agioi Fanendes port and discharge its cargo, you would be engaged in an illegal transaction or aiding and abetting it," he warns.
Trump's diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin —announced Oct. 9, with the stated goal of bringing down domestic fuel prices — does not "supersede clear, unambiguous law," the letter argues.
"The Administration's conflicting directives on Russian energy in the past weeks should not be used as an excuse to ignore legal prohibitions," Blumenthal writes. "The President may have given a license to facilitate this transaction, but only Congress can make it legally valid."
read also
Blumenthal's letter is part of a wave of legislative action against Trump's diesel deal, which has provoked strong bipartisan backlash.
Previously, the Kyiv Independent reported that Democratic officials have been contacting U.S. industries involved in facilitating the deal to ensure they understood the potential legal and investigative risks.
U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced the Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, a bill designed to block imports of Russian diesel and mandate further sanctions against Moscow.
But as Congress looks to block the deal, the Agioi Fanendes is making its way to the U.S. East Coast. The ship loaded its cargo in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is set to arrive in the U.S. on Nov. 7.
When announcing the deal, Trump claimed Russia would "immediately supply over 300,000" metric tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets, delivering 500,000 metric tons in November and 1 million metric tons "immediately thereafter."
Soon after the announcement, Moscow partially lifted restrictions on its diesel exports, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons.
The deal shocked Kyiv, European partners, and U.S. lawmakers, who argued the move would help Putin finance the war in Ukraine without having to make any substantial concessions. Russian diesel imports are also unlikely to do much to offset domestic gas prices, which have primarily been driven up by the war against Iran.

28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
A group of countries including the US, the UK, Japan as well as the EU on Wednesday reiterated their demand for North Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs and urged all UN member states to fully implement sanctions.

"The MSMT and EU reaffirm our commitment to the complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization of the DPRK, calling on it to abandon its unlawful WMD and ballistic missile programs, and taking action to counter DPRK attempts to violate and evade UN sanctions."
It added: "We continue to strongly support the implementation of all DPRK-related UN Security Council resolutions."
The signatories also urged all UN member states, especially permanent members of the Security Council, to fully implement the resolutions.

Which way will Israel break? Netanyahu still in it after election night surprises
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
In Israel, the surprises only start with election night: they're still counting ballots in a vote that featured the highest turnout in decades, historic inroads by Arab parties, Benjamin Netanyahu’s worst result since 1999 and yet Israel’s longest-serving prime minister still has a path to staying in power. As we await the definitive makeup of the next parliament, our panel breaks out the calculators and pie charts: in what scenario does Netanyahu survive? Is the issue with the right-wing Likud leader or his policies?
Horse trading ahead between the 11 parties that will make up the next 120-seat Knesset. In the mix, there's nationalists on both sides of the Bibi divide, the bitter battles over religion, the nature of Israel's democracy and over whether a coalition can include the 20-percent of Arab Israelis who this time turned out in droves. Can they enter government or even strike a deal to support the opposition? After years of hardline rhetoric against Palestinians, is that even possible? Otherwise put, is Israel about to get a lot more polarized or forge a whole new path?

Putin says trade turnover with Egypt ‘growing steadily’ despite regional tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:34:12 UTC
04:34:12 KST

Burç Eruygur
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
President Vladimir Putin said Wednesday that Russia’s trade turnover with Egypt is “growing steadily” despite regional tensions, as he met Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi in Moscow.
In opening remarks during the talks, held on the sidelines of the two-day Russia-Africa summit that began in Moscow earlier Wednesday, Putin said joint efforts have accomplished a great deal since the first summit in 2019, as shown by the growth in trade between Russia and Africa.
“Since 2022, the total volume has increased by 50%, surpassing $27 billion. Egypt accounts for a significant portion of this trade turnover,” said Putin, noting that there is much “common ground” between Russia and the continent on development priorities.
Noting that, together with their colleagues, they will discuss the state and future prospects of Russia-Africa engagement and outline new areas for cooperation during plenary sessions Thursday, Putin noted their engagement on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month.
“The historic relationship between our two countries is rooted in the principles of mutual respect, consideration for each other’s interests and mutual assistance. These relations are developing successfully in accordance with the Treaty on Comprehensive Partnership and Strategic Cooperation,” he said.
Putin noted that trade turnover between Russia and Egypt continues to grow steadily “despite regional tensions,” stating that it has already increased 14% in the first eight months of 2026.
“In 2025, it reached record levels, exceeding $10 billion for the first time,” he said, praising the joint intergovernmental commission between the two countries.
“The flagship project, the construction of the El Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant in Egypt, is proceeding according to schedule. On July 9, a formal ceremony was held to mark the installation of the reactor pressure vessel for the second power unit,” he added.
Sisi said Egypt is working to develop the strategic partnership and hopes to expand cooperation, primarily in the economy and trade, as well as in areas related to grain supplies.
“Furthermore, the El Dabaa project remains the most significant initiative in our bilateral engagement,” said Sisi, noting they are committed to completing the projects according to the established timelines, and are making “every effort” to meet payment obligations.
He said he is counting on the Russian president's support to ensure they can deliver the El Dabaa project on schedule.
“We look forward to strengthening and broadening our cooperation. This includes the potential for installing new power units beyond 2030, as well as the development of a research reactor and a testing center,” he said.
Sisi added that they are also interested in collaborating with Russia on small-scale nuclear reactors, including floating nuclear power units, and in deepening their partnership within specialized industrial sectors, such as the extraction of uranium and rare metals.

Netanyahu opens coalition talks as opposition weighs bid to oust Knesset speaker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:33:25 UTC
04:33:25 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began talks with his political allies Wednesday following an inconclusive parliamentary election, speaking with far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir as rival opposition leaders prepared their own consultations over the formation of the next government.
Netanyahu held his first post-election conversations with Finance Minister Smotrich, who leads the Religious Zionist Party, and National Security Minister Ben-Gvir, chairman of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party. Talks with leaders of the ultra-Orthodox parties are expected to follow.
The discussions marked the first steps toward coalition negotiations after Tuesday's election left neither Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc nor the rival pro-change alliance with enough seats to command a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
According to the Central Elections Committee, 88.6% of votes had been counted as of the latest update, with no change in the projected distribution of seats among the main political blocs.
Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53 seats, compared with 48 for the pro-change bloc and 19 for the predominantly Arab parties. A governing majority requires at least 61 seats.
The figures remain preliminary, with hundreds of thousands of ballots still outstanding.
The Central Elections Committee estimated that between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called double-envelope ballots had yet to be counted. These include votes cast by soldiers and other eligible voters outside their regular polling stations. Counting of those ballots had not yet begun.
"The processing work is in full swing, and not all the outer envelopes have yet been received," the committee said.
An analysis of the latest results also showed that the joint Reservists-Economic Party list, led by former minister Yoaz Hendel and economist Yaron Zelekha, remained 30,910 votes short of the electoral threshold required to enter parliament.
If the list crosses the threshold, it could alter the distribution of seats and further complicate efforts to form a government.
Opposition leaders prepare talks after day of silence
After nearly 24 hours without contact among leaders of the pro-change bloc, Democrats Chairman Yair Golan is expected to hold separate meetings Thursday with Yashar! leader Gadi Eisenkot and Yair Lapid of the Beyachad party.
No meeting has yet been scheduled between Golan and former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who also leads Beyachad.
The consultations are expected to focus on the opposition's options following an election that left the bloc short of a parliamentary majority despite its efforts to unseat Netanyahu.
One of the first proposals likely to be discussed is replacing Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, when the newly elected parliament convenes.
Although no concrete negotiations have begun, opposition figures are considering whether to move against Ohana as early as the Knesset's swearing-in ceremony, expected on Nov. 10.
The initiative would likely require support from predominantly Arab parties, whose combined parliamentary representation is projected to increase to 19 seats.
Opposition leaders view replacing the speaker as a parliamentary maneuver rather than a formal political alliance with Arab parties. Nevertheless, they recognize that relying on Arab lawmakers could carry a political cost.
Likud, for its part, is expected to portray any such effort as evidence that the pro-change bloc is joining forces with the Joint List, an alliance of predominantly Arab political factions.
There are also disagreements within the opposition over potential cooperation with Golan's leftist Democrats party, adding another complication to efforts to coordinate a common strategy.
Ultra-Orthodox party weighs abstention on speaker vote
United Torah Judaism, an ultra-Orthodox party traditionally aligned with Netanyahu, is considering abstaining if a vote to remove Ohana is brought before the new Knesset.
Such a move could affect the parliamentary arithmetic surrounding the opposition's initiative.
Tensions between Ohana and some ultra-Orthodox lawmakers are not new.
During the election campaign, United Torah Judaism lawmaker Yitzhak Pindrus criticized Ohana in an interview with the ultra-Orthodox newspaper Mishpacha.
Ohana's sexual orientation has drawn objections from some ultra-Orthodox politicians, who oppose homosexuality on religious grounds.
"The government failed because Amir Ohana was Knesset speaker. It was a desecration of God's name," Pindrus said.
Despite the possibility of abstaining on the speaker vote, United Torah Judaism has not announced any intention to leave Netanyahu's political bloc.
Party chairman Yaakov Asher said there had been no contacts between United Torah Judaism and the pro-change parties.
"We wish to clarify that there have been no approaches from party leaders, apart from a message conveyed by people close to Prime Minister Netanyahu indicating that he intends to keep the coalition parties together," Asher's office said.
Shas rules out abandoning Netanyahu
Another key ultra-Orthodox party, Shas, signaled that it would remain loyal to Netanyahu.
A Shas official told ynet that party chairman Aryeh Deri had no intention of abandoning the alliance he helped build or opening negotiations with Eisenkot.
"Anyone who thinks that Deri, the day after the election, will leave the bloc he established and start courting Eisenkot is very much mistaken," the official said.
The statement appeared intended to dispel speculation that Netanyahu's traditional religious allies might consider joining an alternative coalition.
With Netanyahu's bloc projected to hold 53 seats, the prime minister would need support from lawmakers outside his existing alliance to reach the 61-seat threshold.
Bennett urges supporters to remain hopeful
Bennett, whose Beyachad party was projected to win 12 seats before the counting of double-envelope ballots, acknowledged the disappointing results for the pro-change bloc but sought to encourage his supporters.
"My brothers and sisters, keep your heads up," Bennett wrote on X. "We have only one home, and we are here to stay. With God's help, things will be good here!"
He accompanied the post with a video thanking members of his party's election campaign staff.
The former prime minister has not publicly outlined a new coalition strategy, and no meeting with Golan has been arranged.
