Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:31:40 UTC
04:31:40 KST

Israeli firm turned Starlink traffic into espionage tool across 105 countries
Netanyahu loses his majority, Eisenkot cannot win one, and the wars go on
TEHRAN — Recent disclosures from digital defense watchdogs have exposed an obscure Tel Aviv-registered advertising company, Discover-Tech, running aggressive online ad campaigns designed to geolocate and track users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet network across more than 100 countries.
Investigative research by TrendAI, a division of Tokyo-based Trend Micro, revealed that Discover-Tech became the dominant global bidder for ad space displayed to Starlink terminals, according to a Reuters report on Oct. 27.
Operating under the internal threat codenamed "Shadow-Earth-79," the Israeli firm captured an implausibly high share of ad auctions in restricted or conflict-heavy jurisdictions including Syria, Libya, Yemen, South Sudan, and Venezuela.
By harvesting the metadata embedded in real-time bidding requests, Discover-Tech systematically turned routine browser traffic into an active intelligence pipeline.
From ad impressions to silent infiltration
Programmatic ad auctions rely on instant exchanges of telemetry. Every time an advertisement loads on a web page or mobile application, a bid request transmits the user's IP address, device model, software configuration, autonomous system number, and exact location parameters to participating ad networks.
Discover-Tech leveraged this routine infrastructure to build a comprehensive tracking map.
TrendAI concluded that the firm’s bidding behavior reflected a dedicated tracking operation rather than commercial marketing, noting that legitimate Western advertising demand in heavily sanctioned states is virtually non-existent.
On observed Starlink connections, Discover-Tech accounted for nearly 13 percent of winning ad bids worldwide.
The surveillance mechanism went far beyond passive location mapping. Concurrent technical investigations by Canada’s Citizen Lab and ad-security firm Confiant exposed a sophisticated exploitation vector named "AdFection."
Discover-Tech's proprietary ad platform served as a conduit, connecting mainstream advertising exchanges directly to mercenary spyware operators. When a targeted device loaded a background advertisement, Discover-Tech servers screened the incoming telemetry.
High-value targets were served malicious JavaScript that delivered zero-click attack payloads without requiring any user interaction, while ordinary users received empty responses.
Citizen Lab confirmed with high confidence that at least 45 devices belonging to news personnel at Al Jazeera were targeted with Candiru spyware through this ad-driven vector.
Starlink and the military-industrial infrastructure
The focus on Starlink underscores how low-Earth-orbit satellite constellations have become central to Western military strategy and intelligence operations.
SpaceX's Starlink network bypasses land-based telecommunications gateways, routing data through satellite links to circumvent national regulatory frameworks and local internet blocks.
The U.S. Department of "War" and NATO forces have integrated Starlink and its military-grade derivative, Starshield, into frontline combat operations. In Ukraine, the technology provides primary battlefield command architecture, directing artillery, facilitating real-time satellite coordination, and guiding long-range combat drones.
This deep integration into Western military operations makes Starlink terminals prime targets for intelligence agencies.
Intelligence outfits seek to identify, geolocate, and compromise satellite terminals operating inside sensitive sovereign territory.
Israeli-owned firms were already pitching commercial clients on specialized methodologies to map and deanonymize Starlink subscribers by exploiting commercial ad data.
The Discover-Tech operation confirms that these theoretical pitches were already operationalized at a global scale, turning satellite terminals into beacons for military intelligence gathering.
The broader ecosystem of Israeli cyber warfare
Discover-Tech represents the latest evolution of a commercial cyber-arms ecosystem cultivated by the Israeli regime.
For decades, intelligence entities such as Unit 8200 and Mossad have maintained an institutional pipeline into private surveillance vendors, enabling former Israeli operatives to commercialize state-funded hacking techniques.
Discover-Tech’s corporate history shows direct ties to veteran surveillance executives, including past directors associated with Circles, an affiliate of NSO Group, and Senpai Technologies, linked to the Intellexa consortium.
This ecosystem includes a wide network of offensive vendors. NSO Group gained global infamy through its Pegasus software, which infected the phones of diplomats, political opponents, and human rights defenders.
Candiru, operating under various corporate names such as Saito Tech and Integrity Labs, specialized in zero-click desktop compromises. Paragon Solutions markets its Graphite interception software, while Intellexa and Cytrox developed the Predator spyware suite.
Other key players include Cognyte, Cytrox, Cellebrite, and Black Cube, the private intelligence agency staffed by former Israeli operatives specializing in deception and corporate espionage.
These entities routinely establish international shell companies across Europe to bypass nominal export restrictions and maintain access to global markets.
Industry self-censorship and structural vulnerability
Despite the scale of Discover-Tech’s operations, accountability remains hindered by self-censorship within the commercial security sector.
TrendAI initially omitted Discover-Tech’s name from its public report, opting instead for the "Shadow-Earth-79" alias after corporate executives raised legal concerns.
This practice allows offensive operators to evade immediate platform bans and legal scrutiny.
Following the public identification by Citizen Lab and news outlets, major tech platforms including Google, Comcast's Beeswax, Vungle, and Eskimi cut off Discover-Tech’s access, while IAB Europe suspended the firm from its approved vendor list.
Internal inquiries were also launched by a major U.S. technology corporation and an international organization to evaluate potential employee targeting.
These platform removals disrupt specific operational routes, but the underlying vulnerability remains unaddressed.
Discover-Tech operated inside approved industry registries for years, utilizing standard European data privacy frameworks to collect targeting parameters.
As long as commercial advertising exchanges permit real-time data harvesting, state-aligned surveillance contractors will continue to use programmatic ad bidding as an unregulated, low-cost vector for global espionage.

Tokayev says Türkiye among Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners
The meeting between the Presidents of Kazakhstan and Türkiye continued with the participation of members of the official delegations of the two countries, Qazinform News Agency cites Akorda.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described the meeting as deeply symbolic, as it was being held on the eve of the Republic Day of Türkiye, and congratulated President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and the brotherly Turkish people on this significant national holiday.
“Under your wise leadership, Türkiye is successfully implementing large-scale reforms. The country is developing dynamically, pursuing political and economic modernization. Türkiye’s position on the international stage continues to grow stronger year by year. You are recognized as one of the world’s most influential leaders. Your principled and resolute political course, as well as your tireless efforts to uphold peace and justice, have earned global recognition. I am confident that the standing of the Turkish people will continue to grow. Kazakhstan unwaveringly supports Türkiye and sincerely rejoices in all the achievements of the brotherly Turkish people,” the President of Kazakhstan said.
Kassym-Jomart Tokayev emphasized that he attaches particular importance to expanding cooperation with Türkiye.
“Relations between Kazakhstan and Türkiye have deep historical roots. We are united by our shared history and language, as well as similar traditions. Political interaction between our states rests on a solid foundation of mutual trust and enduring friendship. There are no contradictions or disagreements between us. Our countries consistently support each other both bilaterally and within international organizations. Trade and economic ties continue to expand steadily. Türkiye is one of Kazakhstan’s five largest trading partners. Furthermore, Türkiye ranks among the ten largest investors in our country, having made substantial investments in Kazakhstan’s economy. Many major Turkish companies operate successfully in Kazakhstan. We stand ready to provide comprehensive support to our Turkish partners and create favorable conditions for their businesses,” the Head of State said.
According to Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s state visit to Kazakhstan in May this year was highly productive and resulted in a number of important agreements. The sixth meeting of the High-Level Strategic Cooperation Council between the two countries was held. Major projects were launched in trade and economic cooperation, investment, and cultural and humanitarian affairs. Kazakhstan-Türkiye relations have reached the level of eternal friendship and enhanced strategic partnership.
“The steady development of our bilateral partnership serves our common interests. Tomorrow, we will attend the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States together. The COP31 Climate Summit will be held in Antalya in the near future, and I intend to participate. These events will undoubtedly give fresh impetus to strengthening our bilateral and multifaceted ties,” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted.
In turn, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan congratulated the Head of State and the brotherly people of Kazakhstan on the recent Republic Day.
The Turkish President noted that a presentation of the book The Phenomenon of a Qurultay, dedicated to the history of Kazakh statehood, had recently been held in Ankara. In addition, the book Nauryz – A Common Heritage of the Turkic World, which comprehensively explores the history and significance of the holiday, has been translated into Kazakh.
“During my visit to Astana in May this year, we signed a number of important documents, including the Declaration on Eternal Friendship and Enhanced Strategic Partnership. We intend to reinforce our cooperation with practical steps at the next meeting of the Strategic Cooperation Council. We aim to increase bilateral trade to 15 billion US dollars and intensify the investment dimension of our relations,” the Turkish president said.
During the talks, the two sides also discussed prospects for cooperation in transport and logistics, energy, artificial intelligence, agriculture, and the defense industry, as well as ways to strengthen cultural and humanitarian ties.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Recep Tayyip Erdoğan had held restricted-format talks.

92-year-old US judge handling Nicolas Maduro case dies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:29:59 UTC
04:29:59 KST

92-year-old US judge handling Nicolas Maduro case dies
NEW YORK - Alvin Hellerstein, the US judge overseeing the case against deposed Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro, has died aged 92, an official confirmed on Oct 28.
As one of the oldest US federal judges, questions had been raised about whether he was the right justice to preside over what could be a prolonged trial for Maduro on drug trafficking charges.
Hellerstein’s lengthy career included overseeing the civil cases arising from Al-Qaeda’s Sept 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on New York and Washington, often rejecting deals he saw as unfair to complainants.
His death was confirmed to AFP by an official at the United States District Court, Southern District of New York, where he presided.
Hellerstein also tangled with Donald Trump, rejecting a request by the US president to have his New York hush money case moved to federal court.
In 2025, he blocked the Trump administration from deporting alleged Venezuelan gang members without a court hearing.
In a noteworthy 2015 ruling, Hellerstein ordered the US government to release a trove of photos depicting abuse of detainees in Iraq and Afghanistan.
He also presided over a trial in 2025 in which a jury found French banking giant BNP Paribas’ work in Sudan had helped prop up the regime of former ruler Omar al-Bashir, awarding US$20.75 million (S$26 million) in damages to three plaintiffs from Sudan.
Hellerstein handled the sprawling drug trafficking case linked to Maduro for over a decade, which has already seen the conviction of Venezuela’s former intelligence chief, Hugo Armando Carvajal.
Maduro was seized by US forces in January, in a military raid on his compound in Venezuela.
A graduate of Columbia University law school, Hellerstein served as a lawyer in the US Army from 1957 to 1960 before entering private practice.
He was nominated by then president Bill Clinton in 1998 to be a district court judge for the Southern District of New York. AFP

Fed holds interest rates steady in last decision before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:26:41 UTC
04:26:41 KST

The US Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last board meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.
Two out of 12 board members voted against the pause, preferring to raise rates by a quarter point this meeting, the Fed board said in a statement.
Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation, bringing rates to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, the pause signals the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
During a press conference on Wednesday afternoon, the Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, told reporters that the upcoming election played no role in deliberations.
“Politics played no role in the decision,” he said. “I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.”
The central bank is still focused on price stability, he said, but emphasized that “the information that we receive over the coming period will help us determine where want policy to be”.
“The period right in front of us is information rich, there’s a lot that’s happening in the world, my colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it,” he said.
September’s rate hike infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Warsh declined to comment on a remark from Donald Trump that, besides Warsh, the Fed board is full of Democratic-appointed members who “would like to see the country do badly”, but said that the latest meeting was “a heck of a family fight”.
“I’m honored to be here, and I’m honored to be chairman of this group,” he said.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” the Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.
The proximity of the election also made it more likely that the Fed will “not take any radical action”, said Nicholas Economides, a professor of economics at the NYU Stern Business School.
“Even if the Fed were to do something radically different, the economy would not have time to adjust before the elections,” he said.
Rising prices this year have largely been driven by war in the Middle East with Iran. Oil prices have soared with the closure of the strait of Hormuz, a crucial passageway for trade. Inflation rose last month to its highest level since the spring, while oil traded briefly above $117 a barrel earlier this week, its highest price in more than six months.
The higher cost of living is expected to play a crucial role in the upcoming midterm elections that will determine which party will control Congress. Across multiple polls, the economy has been cited as the top issue for voters.
By itself, hiking interest rates cannot solely address inflation caused by supply shocks, Economides said. Raising rates is helpful for when the economy is too hot, or when demand outpaces supply, but can be counterproductive otherwise.
“If inflation is caused by supply factors, it doesn’t make sense to try to cure it by increasing interest rates because it won’t work,” he said. “It will slow down the economy at a time in which you don’t want it to slow down.
On Wednesday, Warsh also announced upcoming changes to the Fed’s eight board meetings it conducts annually. Starting in fall 2027, only seven of those meetings will be convened to set interest rates. That number will go down to six in 2028, with the other meetings dedicated to “broad monetary policy” when the change is implemented.

19:24:53 UTC
04:24:53 KST

Ukrainian company Robotic Complexes is developing a specialized CASEEVAK module for the Murakha unmanned ground vehicle (UGV).
The project is designed to protect wounded military personnel during transport and provide communications and monitoring of their condition, the company told Militarnyi.
Unlike conventional cargo UGVs, the new system features an armored capsule made of 3.5 mm Armox 500T steel with an internal HDPE 1000 lining.
The capsule is equipped with ventilation, heating and lighting systems, as well as a first-aid kit. Side and rear doors allow the wounded to be loaded from any side and provide access to them during evacuation.
A camera with day and night channels and two-way audio communication are installed inside to monitor the occupant’s condition.
The system is controlled through ELRS, LTE, Starlink or fiber-optic communication links. If the capsule is detached from the main platform, it retains two independent communication channels.
The developers are currently working to integrate vital-sign monitoring systems. This will allow medical personnel to receive information about the casualty’s condition while the vehicle is moving.
The platform’s protection is supplemented by passive counter-drone measures, net launchers and electronic warfare systems. An electric powertrain has been installed to reduce the vehicle’s signature.
The platform has two electric motors with a combined torque of 1,600 N·m and a 35 kWh battery pack. Its range is up to 80 km.
Company specialists have already conducted ballistic tests of the armor steel at a distance of 50 meters using various calibers. Development of a slat armor system to protect against FPV drones is also underway.
Militarnyi previously reported that in October 2025, Ukrainian forces began using Murakha-Mini ground drones to support logistics near the front line.
The UGVs help deliver equipment, food and other supplies.

inside the parisian hotel renovation where british club culture meets haussmannian architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:24:01 UTC
04:24:01 KST

inside the parisian hotel renovation where british club culture meets haussmannian architecture
at paris’ historic hotel westminster, laurent maugoust renovates the historic interiors while helen stephens reimagines the restaurant, preserving two centuries of architectural heritage.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
FROM NAPOLEON’S PARIS TO A BRITISH HOTEL
In a city with no shortage of historic hotels, Hotel Westminster has had more than two centuries to develop its identity. Located at 13 rue de la Paix, between Place Vendôme and the Palais Garnier, the Parisian address has undergone an extensive restoration led by interior architect Laurent Maugoust, with British designer Helen Stephens reimagining its restaurant, Le Céladon. The project, completed one year ago, preserves architectural elements accumulated throughout the building’s history while introducing contemporary interiors. Awarded its fifth star in 2025, the Westminster enters its latest chapter with a rather unusual distinction: a distinctly British character in one of the most recognizably French corners of Paris.
The story begins in 1802, when Napoleon Bonaparte ordered the sale of land belonging to a former Capuchin convent and commissioned architects Percier and Fontaine to develop a new district. The street, originally named rue Napoléon before becoming rue de la Paix in 1814, welcomed the Hôtel Wagram in 1807, the predecessor of today’s Westminster. As British travelers increasingly settled in the neighborhood, the area acquired the reputation of being a small piece of London in Paris, an identity reflected in the hotel’s eventual name. The building itself continued to evolve through successive extensions and renovations, most notably between 1905 and 1907, when architect Jacques Marcel Aubertin gave it the Haussmannian silhouette it retains today.
LAURENT MAUGOUST RESTORES HAUSSMANNIAN INTERIORS
For Laurent Maugoust, the restoration involved working with architectural elements belonging to different periods rather than recreating a single historical moment. Across the hotel’s 102 rooms, including 20 suites, the intervention preserves marble fireplaces, decorative mouldings and herringbone oak parquet floors, combining them with contemporary furnishings and textiles in shades of beige, green and violet. The designer’s approach draws on his experience with Haussmannian interiors, where proportions, materials and craftsmanship establish a continuity between past and present. ‘I set out to reinterpret its style by bringing different eras into dialogue,’ Maugoust explains, describing a project that builds on the existing architecture rather than attempting to replace it.
Other details reveal how the Westminster has accumulated its own collection of objects and decorative elements over the decades. Antique clocks, some dating from the 19th century, remain scattered throughout the rooms and suites, alongside paintings, historical photographs and furnishings associated with the property’s past. Some suites overlook rue de la Paix, while others face a flower-filled inner courtyard, offering two rather different perspectives on central Paris. These surviving features also reflect the building’s long history of transformation, from its early extensions to the reconstruction that established its present appearance. At the Westminster, even the supposedly timeless Haussmannian setting has undergone more than a few changes.
DUKE’S BAR PRESERVES THE HOTEL’S BRITISH HERITAGE
The hotel’s most recognizable connection to Britain survives at Duke’s Bar, an English-club-inspired interior defined by dark wood panelling, deep armchairs, subdued lighting and an original fireplace. During the 1920s, the bar became a gathering place for British aristocrats and political figures, later attracting writers and personalities from Parisian cultural life. According to the hotel’s historical account, Winston Churchill was among its regular visitors, while Coco Chanel, Agatha Christie, Arthur Conan Doyle and Françoise Sagan also frequented the address. Black-and-white portraits of Churchill, Chanel, Rudyard Kipling and the Duke of Westminster now line the walls, preserving something of the atmosphere that once made the bar a meeting point between British and French society.
A different interpretation of the hotel’s history unfolds at Le Céladon, redesigned by Helen Stephens to establish a visual connection with Duke’s Bar. Shades of green reference both the bronze of the Vendôme Column and the foliage of the nearby Tuileries Garden, bringing elements of the surrounding city into the restaurant’s interiors. Beyond the dining spaces, the Westminster continues its relationship with Parisian cultural life through musical evenings and literary events organized in collaboration with Galignani, the city’s historic English-language bookshop. More than two centuries after the first hotel opened on rue de la Paix, the Westminster remains a curious meeting point between Parisian architecture and British tradition, two identities that have become difficult to separate.

Each of the three options facing US in confrontation with Iran carries strategic losses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:23:09 UTC
04:23:09 KST

Each of the three options facing US in confrontation with Iran carries strategic losses
LONDON - America's available options in the West Asia region are constrained by substantial strategic costs, meaning that none appears to be free of losses. These options can be summarized in three main scenarios: maintaining a state of neither war nor peace, withdrawing without an agreement, or withdrawing under an agreement.
Maintaining a state of neither war nor peace involves maintaining the current situation without reaching a final settlement and without returning to open warfare at the same intensity.
The first option of maintaining a state of “neither war nor peace” does not mean that Iran’s instruments of pressure will cease to operate. If Iran continues working to break its blockade and retains the ability to target vessels or assets connected to the confrontation, Washington will find itself facing a prolonged war of attrition rather than a stable situation that can be managed without cost.
Maintaining the situation in this form may not be sustainable for more than two years, that is, until the end of Trump’s term, although this timeframe remains a political estimate rather than an established certainty.
The second option is “withdrawal without an agreement”. The United States may withdraw without reaching a comprehensive agreement, while maintaining its policy of sanctions against Iran.
In such a situation Iran will retain its right to respond effectively to the instruments of blockade. Its response could go beyond the methods used before the war.
Iran would continue working to break the naval blockade and impose costs on the countries maintaining it. This could include economic and political pressure and extend to military action if circumstances will warrant it.
This would leave the region in an unstable condition and force the U.S. to pull out of the region without a settlement, a step that postpones the conflict, rather than addressing its underlying causes. Iran would then gain additional strategic advantages on top of those it had already acquired through the war, including experience and the ability to shift the confrontation to another level, one in which the balance would be more favorable to Iran.
However, the consequences of a prolonged state of “neither war nor peace” for the global economy, commercial activity, financial markets and fertilizer supplies would create intense pressure to end the war. Such an outcome would not serve American interests, given that the United States would be regarded as responsible for initiating the illegitimate war on Iran.
This would significantly weaken American influence and international standing, as the country would be seen as a source of instability and negative repercussions, having drawn dozens of countries and entangled them in the consequences of a reckless war.
The third option of “withdrawal under an agreement” would allow the United States to end the confrontation on the basis of the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that contains 14 clauses. An agreement would pose a dilemma for the U.S. since the issue is not simply about money, but about the changes that an agreement could bring to the nature of Iran’s relationship with the wider region.
If Iran were integrated into regional political and economic relationships, the effectiveness of the terminology and policies used to isolate it could diminish. 
 
Furthermore, the normalization of economic and political relations could give Iran’s allies greater room to operate within recognized regional arrangements, rather than remaining under pressure and confrontation.
This could strengthen Iran’s regional position, consolidate the position of Ansarallah in Yemen and strengthen the Lebanese resistance's position. At the same time, the Israeli occupation entity could withdraw from the areas it entered following the war that began on February 28 in accordance with the first clause of the memorandum of understanding. If this outcome is materialized as described, it would represent more than a ceasefire. It would amount to a restructuring of the regional balance of power and political relationships.
Withdrawal without an agreement could leave Iran under naval blockade but it would fail to bring Iran under American control, yet withdrawal under an agreement could provide Iran with extensive economic and political opportunities. Maintaining the current situation would also leave America facing continuous attrition. This leads to the argument that all three options, despite their differences, carry strategic losses for the United States.

South Korea Boosts Russian Coal Purchases in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:20:04 UTC
04:20:04 KST

South Korea raised coal imports from Russia in the first eight months of 2026, Finland-based energy think tank Centre for Research on Energy and Clear Air (CREA) said.
CREA’s September report on Russian fossil fuels, initially published on Oct. 16, said Seoul’s Russian coal purchases reached 18 million metric tons from January to August, up 34% from the same period in 2025 and 19% from 2021, based on South Korean customs data.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
It added that Suek, a Russian coal company under sanctions, appears to be a major supplier.
The think tank said Russia overtook Indonesia as South Korea’s second-largest coal supplier, behind Australia, which supplied 34% of the country’s coal needs.
“Most of it is burned in power stations run by state-owned KEPCO and its generating companies, which bought 73% of South Korea’s Russian thermal coal between February 2022 and May 2026,” CREA analyst Luke Wickenden told Kyiv Post.
South Korea ranks fourth in Russian coal purchases based on 2026 data, after China, India, and Turkey, the CREA report shows.
More coal to make up losses in nuclear generation
CREA attributed the increase to South Korea’s reduced nuclear energy production, along with the expiry of its 40-year reactor operating licenses.
“Coal-fired power generation in South Korea rose 18% between January and July 2026 compared with the same period in 2025 (from 87 TWh [terawatt hours] to 102 TWh), while nuclear generation fell 14% over the same period (from 114 TWh to 98 TWh), according to Ember data,” the report says.
Zelensky Says Ukraine-Russia-US Peace Talks Could Take Place on Nov. 10
The think tank added that the drop in nuclear power output roughly matched the increase in coal-fired generation.
“Total electricity generation was unchanged, and the 15 TWh increase in coal generation is close to the 16.5 TWh fall in nuclear,” CREA wrote.
How much did Russia earn from South Korea’s coal purchases?
South Korea paid €299 million ($333 million) to Russian coal suppliers in August 2026, according the latest available monthly data, Wickenden told Kyiv Post.
From January to August, the amount also jumped 44% from €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) to €1.7 billion ($1.9 billion) compared to the same period in 2025, though he added that the fees also include shipping, and not everything went to Russian suppliers.
“According to customs data, South Korea paid an average of €109 ($121) per ton for Russian coal in July 2026, up from €86 ($96) in January 2026. Benchmark prices support this,” Wickenden said.
But he also noted that Asian coal prices jumped throughout 2026, and South Korea’s Russian coal purchases have also increased since mid-2025.
He said the price rose 7% while the volume jumped 34% when comparing the same months in 2026 and 2025.
“Newcastle, the main Asian coal benchmark, rose from an average of €92 ($102) a ton in January 2026 to €114 ($127) in July and €127 ($141) in September,” he said.
“Much of that rise came after the strikes on Iran in early March, when Newcastle jumped 16% in two trading days, but South Korea’s imports of Russian coal had already been climbing since mid-2025, as coal replaced nuclear power,” he added.
CREA said Russia earned around €58 million ($65 million) per day in September from overall coal exports, down 12% month on month.
Major drop in South Korea fuel exports to Russia
South Korea’s seaborne oil product exports to Russia also fell from the peak of 95,000 tons in August to only 8,000 tons in September.
The 95,000-ton CREA figure differs from the 112,000 tons in August previously reported by The Guardian. Wickenden attributed the difference to revised data from monitoring platform Kpler.
Kyiv Post previously reported on questions over South Korea’s fuel shipments. Seoul later said the shipments were not prohibited, while it investigated the trade.
Seaborne fuel exports from India to Russia also dropped significantly the same month, with Turkey and Morocco taking the lead as Russia also reduced its seaborne oil products by 44% compared to August.
Russia introduced an oil products export ban in mid-2026 after repeated Ukrainian strikes knocked out much of its major refinery capacity, with Kyiv claiming that 43% was offline by July.
Russia also introduced nationwide fuel rationing during the crisis and importing fuel, some of it refined overseas from Russian crude, to meet demand that exceeded domestic production.
But despite the production drop, Moscow struck a deal with Washington in October to supply diesel to the US and global markets, promising to release up to 3.5 million tons of diesel by year-end in exchange for sanction relief.
Kyiv Post has examined the proposed supplies against fuel consumption.

Lula’s victory once again showed Latin America is not US backyard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:17:21 UTC
04:17:21 KST

Lula’s victory once again showed Latin America is not US backyard
TEHRAN — History has a peculiar way of embarrassing those who believe political opponents can simply be imprisoned, exiled or erased. Nelson Mandela walked out of prison after 27 years and became South Africa’s first Black president. Juan Perón returned to Argentina after nearly two decades in exile and reclaimed the presidency.
In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has written his own chapter in this tradition. A former factory worker and trade unionist who rose to the presidency, endured imprisonment and returned to power, Lula represents something that political establishments have repeatedly underestimated: the resilience of popular movements.
His political journey carries significance beyond Brazil’s borders. At a time when Washington seeks to consolidate its influence across Latin America and Israel faces growing international opposition over its treatment of Palestinians, Lula has refused to surrender Brazil’s independent political voice. His solidarity with Palestine is particularly significant.
Wearing a Palestinian keffiyeh, Lula publicly identified himself with the Palestinian people, turning a familiar symbol of resistance into a statement of political defiance. His criticism of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza has likewise challenged the Western assumption that solidarity with Palestinians must remain subordinate to Washington’s strategic preferences. For Lula, the Palestinian question is not separate from the broader struggle over sovereignty, dignity and the right of nations to determine their own future.
The October 25 presidential election demonstrated that this independence still commands substantial support at home. Brazil entered the final weeks of campaigning deeply polarized. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, led the first round by approximately 2.22 million votes. Most electoral calculations favored the challenger. Lula faced a deficit no candidate had previously overturned in 
 
Brazil’s modern presidential runoffs. Yet elections are not decided by opinion polls alone. 
Between October 4 and October 25, Lula's campaign transformed an apparent mathematical disadvantage into a nationwide mobilization. Workers, students, rural communities and social movements returned to the streets.
The Landless Rural Workers' Movement (MST) helped sustain the grassroots offensive, while an energetic digital campaign challenged the right's political narrative. The result was historic. Lula secured 51.79 percent of valid votes against Bolsonaro's 48.21 percent, winning by more than 4.43 million ballots.
The overall electoral margin shifted by approximately 6.66 million votes between the two rounds. For the first time in Brazil's modern presidential history, a candidate who finished second in the opening round emerged victorious in the runoff.
The victory also exposed the limitations of treating working-class voters as an electoral constituency to be courted every four years rather than an organized political force. Lula's achievements, including Bolsa Família, minimum-wage increases, expanded university access and support for family farming, established that poverty was not an unavoidable national condition.
Public policy could change millions of lives. But Brazil's economic contradictions remain unresolved. Wealth, land and financial power are still concentrated in relatively few hands. Conservative parliamentary forces, expensive credit and fiscal restrictions continue to constrain the government's ability to deliver deeper reforms.
Lula's fourth mandate will therefore demand more than preserving previous social achievements. Agrarian reform, industrial development, public investment and greater economic participation by ordinary Brazilians must become central priorities. The movements that rescued his electoral campaign must also have a meaningful role in shaping his government's direction.
Beyond Brazil, however, the election delivered an uncomfortable message to Washington. Donald Trump had considerable political reasons to prefer a Bolsonaro presidency. A right-wing government in Brasília would have strengthened his administration's attempt to consolidate a sympathetic regional bloc through the Shield of the Americas initiative, launched in Miami in March 2026.
Brazil is not an insignificant prize. It is Latin America's largest economy, a founding BRICS member and a country possessing enormous agricultural, energy and mineral resources. Its strategic independence complicates Washington's ambition to maintain the Western Hemisphere as an exclusive American sphere of influence.
Trump's reaction to the election was revealing. Rather than welcoming Brazil's democratic verdict, he publicly questioned the legitimacy of Lula's victory without substantiating his allegations. Bolsonaro initially challenged the outcome before his party acknowledged the result. There is a familiar contradiction here. Washington celebrates democracy when elections produce governments compatible with American interests, yet becomes considerably less enthusiastic when voters choose an independent political direction.
For Iran, this contradiction requires little explanation. From the 1953 Anglo-American coup against Mohammad Mossadegh to decades of sanctions and coercive diplomacy, Tehran has experienced the consequences of Washington's determination to shape other nations' political choices. Brazil and Iran have different political systems and national priorities, but both recognize the importance of a multipolar international order in which sovereignty is not conditional upon American approval. Their participation in BRICS provides an institutional platform for strengthening South-South cooperation and reducing excessive dependence on Western dominated economic structures.
Lula's position on Palestine gives this broader political argument an unmistakable moral dimension. In February 2026, he wore a Palestinian keffiyeh presented by Palestinian Ambassador Marwan Jebril during a diplomatic ceremony in Brasília. The image captured something that Western governments have increasingly attempted to suppress: public identification with Palestinians as a people entitled to dignity, freedom and statehood.
Lula has also challenged Israel's conduct in Gaza, refusing to accept that Palestinians’ suffering should be treated as an unfortunate footnote to Israeli security. His position exposes the double standards of a Western political establishment that invokes international law against its adversaries while repeatedly accommodating Israeli aggression. This does not make Lula an ideological counterpart of Iran, nor does it erase differences between their governments. It demonstrates something more important: opposition to Israeli policies and American unilateralism extends far beyond West Asia. It is increasingly part of a wider international demand for political independence and equal application of international law.
Brazil's election has not dismantled American influence in Latin America, nor has it eliminated the far right. Bolsonaro received nearly 60 million votes, demonstrating that the political forces behind his campaign remain formidable. Nevertheless, Lula's victory has disrupted Washington's preferred regional trajectory and given progressive movements across Latin America renewed political confidence.
Mandela's freedom did not automatically dismantle South Africa's economic inequalities. Perón's return did not resolve Argentina's political divisions. Lula's reelection will not, by itself, transform Brazil's entrenched economic structures. But history offers another lesson through these extraordinary political returns: powerful establishments may imprison leaders, manufacture political isolation and declare popular movements defeated. What they cannot always control is whether the people accept that verdict. On October 25, Brazil refused to accept it. And Washington was reminded, once again Latin America is not its backyard, the Strait of Hormuz is not its playground, and neither Brazil nor Iran needs America’s permission to defend their sovereignty.

Erdogan, Trump discuss regional tensions, Ukraine war and bilateral ties in phone call

Ex-Unmanned Systems Forces commander Sukharevskyi to lead Ukraine's Marines, media reports
Colonel Vadym Sukharevskyi, ex-commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, have been chosen as the new head of the country's Marines, several Ukrainian media reported on Oct. 28 citing sources familiar with the matter.
Sukharevskyi will replace Major General Dmytro Deliatytskyi in the job, sources confirmed independently to Ukrainska Pravda and Interfax-Ukraine.
The popular commander had been assigned to lead the pioneering new drone branch of Ukraine's military back in 2024, but was dismissed after less than a year in the job, amid reported disagreements with then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi.
Since then, Sukharevskyi has spent over a year in de facto wilderness as deputy commander of Ukraine's Eastern Group of Forces, a temporary command umbrella covering most of the eastern front line.
His return is part of a larger ongoing reshuffle of Ukraine's high command launched by Syrskyi's replacement, Mykhailo Drapatyi, in an effort to distance the military leadership from his predecessor's Soviet-style leadership culture.
Sukharevskyi etched his name in the history of Ukraine's resistance to Russian aggression in April 2014, when, as a senior lieutenant in the 80th Airborne Brigade, he ordered his troops to open fire on Russian proxy forces in Sloviansk, the first shots fired in Ukraine's effort to quash Moscow's fake "separatist" uprising in Donbas.
In the first years of the full-scale war, Sukharevskyi commanded the 59th Motorized Brigade, one of the key units which liberated the city of Kherson from Russian occupation.
Ukraine's Marine Corps — officially part of the country's navy — has traditionally specialized in amphibious warfare, similar to the Russian and U.S. equivalents.
Since the full-scale invasion, Ukrainian Marine brigades have fought in some of the most intense hotspots of the front line, from Mariupol, Pokrovsk, and Kostiantynivka in Donetsk Oblast, to the daring but costly Krynky offensive across the Dnipro River over 2023 and 2024.

US Fed Chair Warsh warns inflation remains too high as energy prices climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:13:30 UTC
04:13:30 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh warned on Wednesday that inflation remains too high after running above the central bank's 2% target for nearly six years, pledging readiness to act as needed to restore price stability.
Speaking at a news conference after the Federal Open Market Committee voted to keep the benchmark interest rate at 3.75% to 4%, Warsh said policymakers focused their two-day discussions mainly on curbing price pressures.
"Real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction; that's good news, but inflation is too high," Warsh said.
"Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks, and our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored," he added.
Warsh noted that US economic growth has strengthened, with gross domestic product expansion in the first half of 2026 revised up to 2.4% from an earlier estimate of 1.8%.
Third-quarter growth appears to have accelerated further, driven by consumer spending running above 3% and business investment rising at a double-digit pace, he said.
Capital expenditures have reached a historically high share of gross domestic product, led by high-tech investment alongside broader gains across other sectors, he added.
On the labor market, Warsh described employment conditions as "quite positive," pointing to a lower jobless rate compared to a year ago, faster payroll growth and a four-week moving average of unemployment claims near multi-decade lows.
Following the Fed's policy action in September, financial and credit conditions have tightened for some businesses and households as market participants become more selective in capital allocation, Warsh said.
"And while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said, adding that the shift supports longer, more durable economic growth and price stability.
Warsh also announced an institutional overhaul of the Federal Open Market Committee's meeting schedule starting in the fall of 2027.
While the committee will continue to hold eight meetings per year, one meeting in 2027 will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy without an interest rate vote or a policy statement, leaving seven regular rate-setting meetings.
In 2028, the central bank expects to dedicate two meetings to long-term strategy discussions and six to setting monetary policy, Warsh said.
"It's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations — for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons," he added.

====================================================================================================

Labour is still searching for an energy fix for a new world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:11:36 UTC
04:11:36 KST

Amid the myriad of small measures, virtually everything in John Healey’s budget came back to the cost of energy. The higher energy prices that have resulted from the Iran war have pushed up inflation, are eating into households’ incomes, are a drag on businesses – and are the main reason why the forecast for GDP growth next year was cut from 1.6% to just 1%.
And energy was the focus of Healey’s sole surprise in his consumer-facing policies – the £100 payment to 20m households in A-D council tax bands to help with fuel bills this winter. It will be funded, in effect, by tapping the banks for a few quid for 15 months via the bank surcharge.
But the chancellor will know that £100 won’t look generous when the bills land. Gas prices are still rising, and leading supplier EDF’s latest prediction is that the regulator’s price cap will be hiked by £466 in January, pushing the annual rate for an average household to £2,189. When Labour took office in July 2024, talking naively about taking £300 off bills over the life of the parliament, the cap was £1,568.
No surprise, then, that the messaging on energy is shifting. Here is the passage in Healey’s speech that hinted at big changes ahead: “Today I’m setting a new course on energy: to get UK energy costs down in line with Europe. From this point, our Labour government’s priority is first and foremost cheaper energy, with clean power key to achieving this.”
Thank goodness for the reset towards affordability. It is long overdue. The biggest impediment to economic growth, including the prime minister’s longed-for “reindustrialisation”, is the cost of energy in the UK. There is little Healey can do about international gas prices, but he can do “deep reform of our energy system”, as he put it. So what’s the plan?
That, unfortunately, is where the “new course” turned blurry. Take the promise to introduce “a new cost control framework to drive down all aspects of energy bills”. The ambition is laudable, because energy bills have become littered with levies and charges – everything from socialising unpaid consumer energy debt to funding Sizewell C – that should more naturally be funded from general taxation. It’s about time the Treasury took an interest in such hidden taxes.
But the costs don’t disappear just because they are placed within a new framework. The tough question is how much a chancellor is willing to fund from Treasury coffers in the interest of lower upfront bills for consumers and business. It is not a small question, because wide-ranging definitions of levies can produce figures as high as £15bn.
It’s good that Healey is demanding no new levies (unless they bring down bills), but that’s not the same as hacking into the existing thicket. Funding for green hydrogen projects is being taken on by the Treasury, which is a start. But come back in next year’s spending review, it seems, to discover the size of Healey’s scythe. More urgency is needed.
There was a bit more clarity on the electricity generation side. “This government will only buy and build new projects when they lower bills and when they can connect to the grid,” said Healey. That reads as a strong hint that offshore wind commissions will be slowed until prices fall (which probably requires a fall in borrowing costs for developers) and the upgrade of the grid is more advanced. Very sensible: sequencing matters, as the alarming costs of “wasted wind” demonstrate regularly.
But Healey’s ambition to “break the grip of international gas prices” by switching older renewables projects on to lower fixed-price contracts is not new. Ed Miliband, when energy secretary, said the same. The test is how hard ministers are willing to twist the arms of renewables owners, who are very attached to arrangements that give them jackpot revenues when gas prices are high. The basic tension remains: for consumers to win, somebody has to be paid less than they were expecting.
So, yes, one can applaud the change of tone and direction. A reset in energy policy to prioritise affordability was bound to arrive eventually. The drive to clean power also had to be a drive to cheap power. But one cannot yet say the new approach is joined-up. Policies to drive the electrification of homes and transport were not turbo-charged, which they need to be to reduce long-term dependency on gas and oil. And “deep reforms” to the electricity market are, to put it gently, a work in progress. More urgency needed.

US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:06:56 UTC
04:06:56 KST

US-Iran war bill reaches $47.1 billion
TEHRAN — The cost of the US war against Iran reached an estimated $47.1 billion by October 16, with bombs, missiles and other munitions accounting for more than 60% of the total, according to figures the Pentagon provided to US lawmakers, The New York Times reported.
The estimate, disclosed to congressional national security committees last week, highlights the mounting financial burden of the military campaign launched by the United States and Israel against Iran on February 28, as well as the pressure on American weapons inventories and military resources.
Despite US President Donald Trump holding back, at least for the time being, from resuming major combat operations, the Pentagon incurred an additional $3.5 billion in costs over approximately six weeks, compared with the estimates previously shared with Congress.
The figures provide an unusual, unclassified breakdown of the expenses incurred by the US armed services, including the costs of deploying forces, maintaining military operations, replacing damaged equipment and transporting supplies.
However, congressional officials cautioned that the $47.1 billion estimate does not represent the full financial cost of the war, with several significant expenditures still excluded from the Pentagon’s accounting.
Munitions account for $29 billion
According to the figures cited by The New York Times, the US military has spent approximately $29 billion on munitions since the war began, making bombs, missiles and other weapons the largest component of the reported expenditure.
The extensive use of ammunition has depleted global inventories of several critical weapons, including Patriot air-defense interceptors, while supplies have also been diverted from US military commands in Europe and Asia to support operations related to the war.
The scale of the expenditure raises questions about the sustainability of prolonged high-intensity military operations and the resources required to replenish depleted stockpiles.
The Pentagon has also spent $6.1 billion replacing dozens of damaged or destroyed combat aircraft, weapons systems, and other military equipment.
These replacement costs illustrate how the financial burden extends beyond the direct expenditure on weapons used in combat to include the loss of valuable military assets.
Air Force, Navy and Army face mounting costs
The Pentagon’s breakdown shows that the US Air Force has spent approximately $7.6 billion operating dozens of fighter and bomber squadrons involved in the military mission.
The Navy has incurred around $1.5 billion in costs associated with deploying more than two dozen warships, including several aircraft carriers, while maintaining Army forces in the region has cost approximately $2.1 billion.
According to US Central Command, more than 50,000 American troops are assigned to the war mission.
The figures also reveal additional expenditures on specialized military operations and logistical support. The Pentagon has spent $645 million to deploy and sustain several thousand Special Operations personnel in the region.
US Transportation Command has incurred $92.2 million in costs for moving supplies and equipment, while US Cyber Command has spent $14 million on cyber support operations.
A congressional official, speaking anonymously to discuss information provided to lawmakers, also disclosed that $24.5 million had been spent on internal medical support for US service members.
The Pentagon has reported that 18 American service members have been killed and more than 860 injured in the war.
Official estimate excludes major expenses
Despite the scale of the reported spending, congressional officials said the actual cost of the war was almost certainly higher than the Pentagon’s estimate.
According to The New York Times, the administration’s calculations excluded $1.5 billion in fuel and other expenses that the Trump administration had requested through a supplemental funding proposal intended to cover the war’s costs.
The estimate also did not include the cost of repairing or rebuilding US military facilities damaged or destroyed by Iranian attacks, including the US Navy’s base in Manama, Bahrain.
The Pentagon has indicated that some damaged facilities could be closed permanently or left unreconstructed. However, if the US military or host countries decide to rebuild them, congressional officials estimate that the bill could reach tens of billions of dollars.
Such expenses could substantially increase the overall financial burden, particularly if Washington decides to restore damaged infrastructure while simultaneously replenishing weapons inventories and maintaining its regional military presence.
The extent of the additional costs remains uncertain, and the figures disclosed so far should therefore be treated as a partial accounting rather than a final assessment of the war’s financial consequences.
Washington seeks up to $70 billion in additional military funding
The disclosure comes as US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Trump administration seek as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the war against Iran and finance additional weapons and personnel.
The request underscores the growing financial demands associated with the campaign, particularly as the Pentagon faces the dual challenge of sustaining military operations and replacing equipment and ammunition already expended or lost.
The unclassified figures provided to Congress offer a rare glimpse into the financial accounting of a war whose costs have largely remained undisclosed by the Pentagon’s senior leadership.
The reported $47.1 billion in spending, combined with excluded fuel costs, potential reconstruction expenses and the administration’s request for additional funding, indicates that the final bill could rise substantially beyond the amount currently acknowledged.
For Washington, the financial consequences extend beyond the immediate costs of military operations to the long-term task of replenishing strategic weapons reserves, restoring damaged facilities and maintaining military readiness across other regions.
The Pentagon has not immediately responded to The New York Times’ request for comment on the figures.
While the final cost of the war remains undetermined, the disclosed estimates highlight the considerable financial resources consumed by the US military campaign and the additional expenditures Washington may face as it addresses the consequences of the conflict.

Spanish town rallies to help victims of deadly train crash
URDA, Spain, Oct 28 - Shocked residents of Urda swung into action to help as soon as they heard of Wednesday's deadly train crash on the railway line a few kilometres from the normally sleepy Spanish town.
Urda's 78-year-old pharmacist said he was one of the first on the scene, jumping into his car to try to help after his daughter told him of the crash involving two high-speed trains.
Antonio Garcia said that as he approached, the scale of the accident that has so far left at least 68 people dead became clear, with one carriage wedged inside another and scores of bodies.
"Just imagine what was inside," said Garcia, who brought first aid materials, painkillers and tranquillisers from his pharmacy as well as blankets to help treat the injured.
Garcia described how one passenger who had lost an arm in the crash was calmly asking for an ambulance, while another was saying his final goodbyes to his family.
"His last words were 'God is good'. For those of us who are believers, these are very beautiful words," said Garcia.
Other locals brought bottles of water to give to passengers who were evacuated from the two trains.
'DEVASTATING'
A few hours later, Urda was brimming with police, firefighters and emergency workers from across the region and its local sports hall was converted into a centre for survivors.
The local primary school was reserved for relatives of the victims, where a volunteer psychologist from Madrid called Carmen said she had been helping out since the morning.
"There were many mothers who found out their children had been killed. That was the worst of today. Telling a mother that her child has died in a train crash is devastating," she said.
Some relatives made the two-hour trip from the Spanish capital Madrid to search for family members.
A woman who gave her name as Ana said she had travelled to Urda after a call from environmental police who had found their dog, Trece, who was on board a train with her husband Pepe.
Ana fought back tears as she described searching for her husband at the crash site, Urda's sports hall and the primary school, adding that his name was not on any list. REUTERS

Knesset stalemate plunges Israel into political paralysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:05:47 UTC
04:05:47 KST

Knesset stalemate plunges Israel into political paralysis
Netanyahu loses his majority, Eisenkot cannot win one, and the wars go on
TEHRAN — Israel voted in record numbers on October 27 and produced a parliament nobody can run.
With more than 85 percent of ballots counted as of writing this, Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc held 53 seats, down from the 68 his coalition controlled. Former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc had 48. Arab parties had 19. A government needs 61, and nobody is close.
Double-envelope ballots from soldiers, diplomats, and others away from home, more than half a million, are still being counted, and certified results are due by November 4.
This was Israel's sixth election since 2019, and like the other five, it delivered a verdict on Netanyahu and nothing else.
Turnout reached 77.7 percent, the highest since 1999, and more than seven points above 2022. Likud fell to roughly 27 seats from 32.
Eisenkot's Yashar took 21, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid's joint list about 12, Yair Golan's Democrats 8, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beiteinu 7.
On the other side, Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit kept seven and Bezalel Smotrich's Religious Zionism six. Three years into the war, millions queued to pick its next manager.
Arab voters sink the right's majority
Palestinian "citizens" inside the Israeli regime, a fifth of the population, voted at an estimated 75 to 80 percent.
The Joint List and Ra'am nearly doubled their combined strength from 10 seats in 2022 to 19, the best "Arab" showing in Israeli history.
Netanyahu helped them along. All day Tuesday, he and Ben-Gvir warned followers about Arab turnout, and Likud paid crews to film Arab voters outside polling stations.
The legal center Adalah described stalled admissions and missing Arabic ballot slips. Joint List chair Yousef Jabareen said his voters had sent the fascist government "to the dustbin of history."
The arithmetic that sinks Netanyahu does nothing for his rival. Add the Arab seats to Eisenkot's 48, and the anti-Netanyahu side reaches 67.
But Eisenkot promised a "Zionist government," and Bennett, Lapid, and Liberman have ruled out the Arab parties outright. Eisenkot has said he would consider them only if they recognize Israel as "a Jewish state" and condemn Hamas. Golan alone broke ranks.
Four ways out, none of them open
After certification, President Isaac Herzog will pick a nominee. He is not obliged to choose the biggest party's leader.
That person gets 28 days, extendable by 14. If he fails, a second nominee gets a turn, and after that the Knesset heads for dissolution. Herzog has urged parties to keep an "open mind."
A Netanyahu coalition is the longest shot. He is eight seats short. Even if three of Eisenkot's lawmakers defected, he would reach 56 against 64.
Bennett and Liberman have both served in Netanyahu’s governments and walked out, and both campaigned on ousting him. Liberman also refuses to sit with the ultra-Orthodox parties over conscription.
A unity government is the option Washington has floated. The Washington Post reports Netanyahu's allies are pushing it, that Trump's envoys are receptive, and that it would let Netanyahu shed Ben-Gvir.
Eisenkot refuses to serve under him, rotation included. The only version that works on paper is Likud without Netanyahu, plus Yashar, Bennett, and Liberman: about 67 seats. Likud would have to dump its longtime leader.
Trump, who endorsed Netanyahu twice, claimed credit Wednesday for a "come-from-behind stalemate."
An Eisenkot minority government is the realistic alternative and the riskiest. He trails the Netanyahu bloc by five seats and needs at least six votes from outside his camp.
Jabareen says the Joint List will help remove Netanyahu, and Ra'am sat in the Bennett-Lapid government in 2021. But Eisenkot's own partners recoil from relying on Arab votes, and a handful of defections to Likud would sink it. Expect Netanyahu's operatives to work the phones.
A seventh election, likely in spring 2027, may suit both leaders better than compromise. Netanyahu would stay caretaker throughout, with a wartime premier's full powers.
On election night, he called this a "historic, one-time opportunity" to "finish Iran" alongside Trump. A new phase of hot war may freeze the political calendar in his favor.
Same wars, new cabinet
No outcome touches Israel's wars of aggression. Eisenkot, who laid out the Dahiyeh Doctrine of punishing civilian areas in 2008, promises to "destroy Hamas" within 18 months. Bennett calls a change of government in Iran "a must." Lapid wants Iranian energy facilities bombed.
Liberman has said Gaza holds no innocents. When five opposition leaders signed a September pact for a "Zionist, statesmanlike government," none of them even got close to accepting that the war on Gaza is a genocide, a conclusion a UN commission reached in 2025.
Israel holds about two-thirds of Gaza, and 1,493 Palestinians have been killed there since the ceasefire, by one count. Settlers beat a man in Burqa, near Nablus, as Israelis voted, while the army sealed every West Bank crossing.
Netanyahu enters the coming weeks as caretaker, under indictment, with his war powers intact. His possible successors have offered Palestinians, Lebanese, and Iranians the same wars with some changes in appearance.

Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US
Rates will remain 3.75-4 percent even as inflation continues to rise.
The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.
The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.
CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
The Fed noted how inflation continues to rise.
It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September, up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.
There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.
“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”
The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.
Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.
Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

Naval Drones Strike Ship Off Bulgaria as Three NATO Defense Ministers Meet
Three naval drones struck a Liberian-flagged container ship approximately 21 miles off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast on October 28, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov confirmed.
Stoyanov announced the attack during a meeting with his counterparts from Romania and Türkiye in Sofia, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) reported on October 28.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"While this meeting was taking place, a container ship was struck by three naval drones in the adjacent waters. The distance is approximately 21 miles from Shabla," Stoyanov stated.
The vessel, identified as CONTSHIP JET, was traveling from Haifa, Israel, toward Constanța, Romania, when it was attacked near Cape Kaliakra, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The ship sustained extensive damage to its starboard side, while fishermen in the area reported that it was burning. Crew members evacuated onto life rafts, and a nearby tanker was directed toward the vessel to provide assistance.
Stoyanov emphasized that Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye unanimously condemned drone attacks against commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
"These tragic incidents represent a dangerous escalation of tensions and create serious risks to the safety of navigation," the minister warned.
The three NATO members also agreed to establish a trilateral coordination mechanism for Black Sea security. The initiative will involve regular consultations, improved intelligence sharing, enhanced maritime surveillance, and stronger early-warning capabilities.
Stoyanov confirmed that the countries had adopted a joint statement and planned further political-level talks in Bucharest and military expert consultations in Ankara.
The strike on CONTSHIP JET follows a string of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria's coast earlier in October. On October 13, three aerial drones hit the Maltese-flagged, Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 roughly 18 nautical miles east of Byala, forcing all 15 crew members to evacuate.
The same night, the cargo ship Azov Concord sank after being struck 17 nautical miles east of Krapets. Before that, two other commercial vessels were hit in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone, killing at least two people.
Sofia moved to summon the Russian ambassador, arguing that the attacks benefited Moscow while acknowledging it lacked conclusive evidence of responsibility.

US jury convicts Rwandan American of lying about role in genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:02:38 UTC
04:02:38 KST

US jury convicts Rwandan American of lying about role in genocide
Jurors heard competing witness testimony on where Eric Nshimiye was and what he was doing in April 1994.
A federal jury in Boston, Massachusetts, has convicted a Rwandan American man of perjury and obstruction of justice for lying about his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Eric Nshimiye, a 55-year-old father of four and a United States citizen, was accused of lying in his testimony in a 2019 trial, also in Boston, for Jean Leonard Teganya, a former medical school roommate who was later convicted of helping to perpetrate the genocide. At the time, Nshimiye told the court neither he nor his friend had taken part in the killing and rape of Tutsis in Butare, where the pair were studying at a medical university.
Investigators from the US Department of Homeland Security arrested Nshimiye at his home in Ohio in 2024, alleging he had lied to them in an interview about his time in Rwanda during the genocide.
Nshimiye was originally charged with multiple counts of perjury, obstruction of justice and committing fraud on his immigration paperwork because prosecutors said he had told immigration officials he did not take part in the genocide when he moved to the US several years after the violence. He became a US citizen in 2009.
The immigration charge was dropped by prosecutors before the trial began. On Tuesday, the jury convicted Nshimiye on four counts of perjury and one count of obstruction of justice.
“For nearly three decades, this defendant concealed his involvement in the 1994 Rwandan genocide and the heinous acts of violence he committed, including clubbing people to death,” Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva in the Department of Justice’s Criminal Division said in a statement on Wednesday. “Then, he lied to immigration officials in order to become a US citizen, and he lied to a federal jury to protect himself and a fellow perpetrator of the Rwandan genocide.”
After the verdict, Nshimiye’s attorneys filed a request with the court to count the time he had already spent in prison before the trial towards any sentence. In a court filing, the attorneys argued Nshimiye should be set free because the two and a half years he had already spent in custody were longer than the usual sentence for the charges he was convicted of.
Nshimiye’s family, including his US-born children, were in attendance when the verdict was announced in court.
“It was quite shocking, difficult to process at first because we were expecting a different outcome. We were expecting to bring him home,” his son Tresor Nshimiye, told Al Jazeera.
Prosecutors brought a series of experts to help the jury understand the scope of the crimes in Rwanda, starting with academics who pointed out where the country was on a map of Africa.
Witnesses from Rwanda told jurors they recalled Nshimiye taking part in killings and other violence in Butare directed at minority Tutsis in 1994. They were part of a nationwide outbreak of genocidal violence by hardline majority Hutus that killed more than 800,000 people over about 100 days. Others said Nshimiye was part of the pro-Hutu National Revolutionary Movement for Development and the Interahamwe, the paramilitary group blamed for most of the killings during the genocide.
The defence argued Nshimiye had never been implicated in domestic and international tribunals after the genocide, including the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda as well as an informal transitional justice system inside Rwanda, called gacaca, which tried more than a million people for their roles in the atrocities.
Defence lawyers pointed out apparent inconsistencies in government witnesses’ testimonies and brought other witnesses who said Nshimiye was with them in the capital, Kigali, and other parts of the country during the genocide.
Nshimiye’s attorneys also argued in court that Rwandan authorities had interfered with the investigation because they had met with some witnesses before they testified in Boston.
“At the end of the day, it was just two competing stories, and so much is lost with this all happening 30 years or so ago. … I guess the jury was more convinced of the prosecutor’s witnesses because they victimised themselves in their stories,” Tresor Nshimiye said.
Nshimiye’s case is one of several currently under way in the US related to the Rwandan genocide.
In April 2025, prosecutors charged Faustin Nsabumukunzi, a 65-year-old beekeeper in Long Island, New York, who had applied for US citizenship, with similarly concealing his role in the violence. And in June 2025, authorities charged 65-year-old Vincent Nzigiyimfura of Dayton, Ohio, who had also applied for US citizenship, with concealing his role in the genocide.
Both men were previously listed publicly as fugitives by Rwandan authorities.

Ukraine, Russia Reportedly Agree on Monthly Kherson Aid

Ukraine and Russia have agreed to conduct humanitarian operations in the Kherson region at least once a month after the Oleshky mission ends, Fox News reported on Wednesday, Oct. 28.
The arrangement calls for regular aid deliveries and repatriation efforts, with assistance and coordination from US First Lady Melania Trump, the outlet said.
