Unregulated peptides contributed to actor's death, coroner finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Coroner recommends TGA review peptide restrictions after Australian actor's death
In short:
Actor Richard Norton's death last year is believed to be the first in Australia known to have been triggered by unapproved peptide use.
A coroner found he suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting CJC1295 and Impamorelin, which had been prescribed to him by a doctor.
The coroner has recommended the TGA consider tougher restrictions on the use of unapproved peptides.
A coroner has found the death of Australian actor Richard Norton was "triggered by" his injection of unapproved peptides, and has recommended the medicines regulator consider tougher restrictions.
Norton's death is believed to be the first confirmed fatality in Australia from unapproved peptide use.
Norton, 75, was an experienced martial artist who worked in the film and television industry as an actor, stuntman, and instructor.
Coroner David Ryan found Norton's death in March last year was a result of complications that arose from his use of unapproved peptide products CJC1295 and Impamorelin.
He collapsed and suffered a cardiac arrest after injecting the products, which a doctor had prescribed to him.
In findings delivered on Wednesday, Mr Ryan said Norton "had been taking amounts of the medication in excess of the dose prescribed by his medical practitioner".
The coroner recommended the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) review the therapeutic benefits and safety risks of peptides such as CJC1295 and Ipamorelin and "consider whether further restrictions ought to be imposed on their use".
Doctor prescribed unapproved peptides
Norton was "interested in peptide therapy" and he approached medical practitioner Jerzy Muchnicki, according to the coroner's report.
Norton, who had asthma, osteoarthritis and previous bilateral shoulder reconstructions, told Dr Muchnicki he had been previously prescribed peptides by another practitioner to treat symptoms relating to fatigue, reduced physical recovery, shoulder pain and the loss of lean muscle mass.
The coronial findings noted Dr Muchnicki reviewed Norton's medical history and "discussed in detail what was involved with peptide therapy, including the experimental nature of the treatment".
"They also discussed the potential risks and the lack of other alternative treatment options currently approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA)," the coroner wrote.
Norton also signed an "Informed Consent Form for Peptide Therapy" outlining the treatment, benefits and risks.
"Dr Muchnicki also arranged a series of blood tests 'to confirm baseline health parameters and assess for any contraindications or underlying conditions that may influence treatment decisions'," the report stated.
Norton was prescribed unapproved peptide products CJC1295 and Ipamorelin in injection form which were compounded for him by a licensed compounding pharmacy in Queensland.
The ABC has contacted Dr Muchnicki for comment.
Martial artist taking 'double the dose' of unapproved peptides
In the days before his death Norton reported to Dr Muchnicki that he was "feeling good and the peptide therapy was improving his symptoms".
The coroner noted Norton disclosed to a nurse at Dr Muchnicki's clinic that he had been administering double the prescribed dose of CJC1295 & Ipamorelin.
"The nurse advised Richard that from the following week he ought to only administer the prescribed dose."
Hours after that conversation, Norton became unresponsive after injecting a dose of CJC-1295 and Ipamorelin.
Norton died at Melbourne's Alfred Hospital on March 30, 2025.
Medical board investigation
The coroner's report said the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency received a notification "raising concerns" about Dr Muchnicki's treatment of Norton.
The Medical Board of Australia (MBA) then conducted an investigation which included a report from clinical professor Alistair Vickery.
Professor Vickery stated: "There is insufficient evidence that CJC1295/Ipamorelin is safe, effective or beneficial for human use."
He said taking into account Dr Muchnicki's training and experience and the history of written consent obtained from Norton, including his prior use of peptides without adverse effects, "the clinical care provided by Dr Muchnicki was at a standard reasonably expected".
However, he considered that the notes taken by Dr Muchnicki were "sparse, inadequate and perfunctory" and that his "performance as a medical practitioner was below the standard expected in regards to this issue".
The board's investigation noted that Dr Muchnicki acknowledged these criticisms, accepted accountability for his actions and apologised for his errors in judgement and lapses in record keeping.
"And [he] expressed sorrow for the impact on Richard and his family," the report stated.
He said he had reflected on the circumstances and was committed to improving his practice and professional standards and had engaged an educator to provide one-on-one education in clinical record keeping and management.
In its decision in July this year the MBA found Dr Muchnicki's practice, "is or may be unsatisfactory" however regulatory action was not warranted. He received a caution and conditions were imposed.
The coroner's report noted the TGA said various pathways existed which enabled medical practitioners to access unapproved peptides.
In a statement after the coronial finding was handed down, the TGA said it "continues to warn consumers about the risks of unapproved peptides which have not been assessed by the TGA for safety, quality or effectiveness".
The medicines regulator said it had also communicated those risks to health practitioners.
"We are continuing to assess the risks associated with these products and considering whether further regulatory or other measures may be appropriate," the statement said.

CSIRO criticised for lack of transparency over gas leak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

CSIRO staff questioned how 'fulsome' to be in response to concerns over Santos Darwin LNG methane tank leak, documents show
In short:
Internal emails and messages obtained under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws reveal CSIRO staffers were uncomfortable about scrutiny of the agency.
The correspondence followed reporting by the ABC about a secret 18-year leak from Santos's Darwin LNG plant.
What's next?
CSIRO has been called on to open its books on the scale and impact of the leak for public consideration.
Australia's national science agency scrambled to spin its role in helping fossil fuel giant Santos investigate a secret 18-year leak from its Darwin LNG plant, internal CSIRO messages have revealed.
The ABC exposed the leak and government agencies' knowledge of it last year.
CSIRO was engaged by Santos for a range of services in 2021 and 2024 including to advise on methods used to monitor emissions at the Darwin site.
The science agency staffers sent emails and internal messages revealing how uncomfortable they were with scrutiny of the agency, following the ABC's reporting, noting it made things "difficult and tricky" with the minister, documents released to the Environment Centre NT (ECNT) under Freedom of Information (FOI) laws show.
The staffers openly discussed how some of their responses to questions could be more "fulsome" and went to lengths to note the agency's work did not include direct monitoring of the leak — while also acknowledging internally CSIRO's contract with Santos allowed for direct monitoring.
"These documents suggest to us an ongoing and frankly unacceptable reluctance on behalf of CSIRO to be transparent with the public," said Bree Ahrens, acting Executive Director of the ECNT.
Former NSW Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy said there was a "distinct impression given that CSIRO have not been entirely frank and open in relation to their dealings in this matter".
"They are a public agency and we should expect them to be open with us. I think the public expect that and the media expect that as well," he said.
The leak that helped scuttle Australia's biggest-ever foreign takeover bid
In September 2025, the ABC revealed the LNG storage tank at Santos' Darwin LNG plant had been leaking methane into the atmosphere following damage it incurred during commissioning in 2006.
The amount of methane released was estimated to be nearly 100kg per hour — just shy of what would count as a "super-emmitter" under US regulations.
The revelations were widely reported as contributing to the collapse of a $36 billion takeover bid for Santos.
The reporting also revealed a number of state and federal agencies had knowledge of the leak, including CSIRO, which was engaged by Santos to help validate emissions measurement methods.
None of those agencies made the leak public, or informed other government agencies that were considering approving Santos's application to use the damaged LNG tank for decades beyond its planned life.
Santos has since been approved to continue using the tank for another 20 years — an outcome that played a crucial role in the company's development of the controversial Barossa gas field off the north coast of Australia.
'Your mate': Draft CSIRO statement shared with Santos
The documents show how scrutiny played out inside the agency, and between CSIRO, the minister and the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR), which oversees it.
In one explanation about CSIRO's work to DISR, CSIRO said: "In 2024, CSIRO was engaged by Santos to undertake monitoring of the Darwin LNG project site."
Across multiple messages, CSIRO staffers explained the agency also assessed methodology used by Santos to measure the leak, and assessed options for ongoing monitoring.
But internal discussions show the agency was at pains to minimise any impression CSIRO was involved in monitoring of the tank leak. At one point a draft response was edited, with a staffer noting: "I suggest adding wording to reinforce it was 3rd party methods we reviewed to be crystal clear we didn't do any monitoring."
As staff drafted a public statement responding to the ABC story, one staffer shared the agency's contract with Santos. A reply read: "perfect — that's pretty clear… says we can do monitoring… but we didn't."
One staffer then asked the other if they had checked the draft public statement about the ABC report with Santos, saying: "are you going to send our statement to your mate?"
A staffer responds, "All good — I sent to their media chap this morning", noting that Santos would be busy with another story about the leak that day in the Australian Financial Review.
A spokesperson for CSIRO told the ABC: "CSIRO developed and approved its own media response. A copy of the statement was provided to Santos as a courtesy."
In the published statement, CSIRO said the work "did not involve monitoring, prevention or remediation advice related to the leak".
CSIRO staff squirm following ABC investigation
As questions mounted, one staffer working on a response to the ABC said in an internal message; "difficult and tricky — for us too with the minister. god damn it."
The final CSIRO published response said it was correcting "errors" in the ABC report, but no errors were identified in the statement.
The reporting from September last year focused on revelations CSIRO knew about the leak and did not tell other agencies or the public. The FOI documents confirmed the agency knew the size of the leak, with staffers noting it was estimated to be 97.6kg per hour.
The CSIRO spokesperson said the agency's concern was, "that the article conflated CSIRO's work assessing background methane concentrations and a desktop review of third-party methane measurement methods with advice relating to management of the reported leak. CSIRO did not provide monitoring, remediation or leak-management advice".
Ms Ahrens called on CSIRO to open its books on the issue.
"We've had various claims about what the volume of the leak from the Santos facility is, and little to substantiate claims that there is no reason to be concerned about its impact on air quality," she said.
"The only way to resolve these unanswered questions is to put the full set of data and the review on the table for the public to consider."
The possibility of making the data available was raised when CSIRO staffers discussed how to respond to questions from then-Greens leader Senator Larissa Waters.
"Do we take the opportunity to be a bit more fulsome and include the work?" one staffer asked.
The CSIRO spokesperson said: "As is normal when developing responses, different levels of detail and draft formulations were considered. The final statement reflected the information considered necessary to accurately explain the nature and scope of CSIRO's work."
A Santos spokesperson told the ABC the company developed a "leak detection and repair program” in 2025.
"This program is aimed at finding and mitigating any potential fugitives within the facility. This measurement and monitoring will further enhance reporting of fugitive emissions."

Switzerland adopts new climate adaptation plan as temperatures rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:59:23 UTC
02:59:23 KST

Beyza Binnur Dönmez
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Switzerland has adopted a revised climate adaptation strategy and action plan, the Federal Council announced Wednesday, as temperatures continue to rise across the country.
According to the council, Switzerland's average annual temperature has risen by around 3 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, making the country particularly vulnerable to climate change.
The council said heat waves, summer droughts and heavy rainfall have become more frequent and intense.
The strategy for 2026-2031 identifies 30 areas for action aimed at protecting the population, infrastructure and natural resources from worsening climate impacts.
According to the council, key priorities include reducing heat exposure in urban areas, safeguarding water supplies, strengthening protection against natural hazards and improving the resilience of agriculture, forests, ecosystems and transport infrastructure.
The plan also outlines measures to improve workplace safety during extreme heat, protect water quality, develop climate-resilient forests and adapt navigation on the Rhine River to increasingly dry summers, the council said.
The government said the strategy draws on Switzerland's 2025 climate risk assessment and updated national climate scenarios, including the possibility of continued increases in greenhouse gas emissions.
The action plan also includes 12 cross-sector measures aimed at improving scientific knowledge, coordination and implementation, according to the council.
The Federal Council said the strategy seeks to minimize climate-related risks, strengthen society's ability to adapt and take advantage of potential opportunities arising from changing climatic conditions.

The Climate Change Committee has shown that the investment needed is manageable and the cost of inaction far greater.
Net zero and adaptation are not alternatives. Mr Burnham should say what he will deliver, and when.

He continued: "Were it not for the resistance and the sacrifices of our people and our families, and the offering of the righteous martyrs, foremost among them the master of the nation's martyrs, Sayyid Hassan (may God be pleased with him) and Al-Hashimi, and the wounded and the captives, and bearing the burdens of displacement and the destruction of homes and crops, and were it not for this great steadfastness, the Israeli enemy would have begun establishing settlements, and would have controlled all of Lebanon politically, administratively, and territorially, and would not have stopped at the limit it is at now."
He added: "Our steadfastness and the continuation of our resistance are our only path to liberating our entire land, even if after a while."

He said that "the tyrannical America's condition is no better," noting that Iran and its great people stood firm, and Iran offered martyrs, foremost among them the Sayyid, the leader of its march and the march of the Ummah, the martyr Imam Ali Khamenei and his family, and martyrs from the leadership and the people, but it foiled America's and Israel's objectives of overthrowing the Islamic system and dividing the country.

The BBC’s education editor role should not be scrapped | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:58:56 UTC
02:58:56 KST

Can I add my voice to the expression of considerable disquiet at the BBC’s proposal to eliminate the post of education editor, instead combining responsibility with that of social affairs (BBC News to axe education editor role in cost-cutting move, 22 October). These two distinct areas of public life are critical to our understanding – under the remit of the BBC charter – to educate and inform, as well as entertain.
The requirement to take education seriously surely requires someone with deep understanding of this complex area, which affects every single person in the country: from the moment they’re born, all the way through lifelong learning and the current challenges of artificial intelligence and robotics.
Some readers will remember the great Mike Baker, who was a practitioner as well as an informer; an experienced and extremely erudite broadcaster who brought alive the elements of the education debate which, when I was the education and employment secretary, were described as the then-government’s top three priorities: “Education, education, education.”
The proposition to downgrade the standing and the acquired experience necessary to present to the public speaks volumes not only about BBC priorities, but about the state of our public dialogue.
 
David Blunkett
 
Labour, House of Lords
It is retrograde of the BBC to downgrade its education coverage. Educational changes and debates are news. They need nuanced analysis. While it is true that they fit into a wider spectrum of social issues, all electors deserve journalists devoted to this coverage.
When I was the Guardian’s education correspondent from 1968 to 1972, when debates raged on comprehensive schools and there were student sit-ins and a teachers’ strike, it would have been inconceivable if there had not been a full-time BBC education correspondent.
People as different as Margaret Thatcher, then education minister, and Jack Straw, then a student leader, became household names thanks to TV, radio and journalism. The BBC should think again.
 
Richard Bourne
 
London

Reporter's notebook: Visiting a POW camp is the best possible antidote to sympathy for Russian soldiers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:57:43 UTC
02:57:43 KST

Reporter's notebook: Visiting a POW camp is the best possible antidote to sympathy for Russian soldiers
Russian soldiers, enticed by lucrative payouts, continue to sign up voluntarily in droves to attack and kill in Ukraine.
Captive soldiers of the Russian military eating lunch at a Ukrainian prisoner of war camp in western Ukraine on June 25, 2026. (Francis Farrell / The Kyiv Independent)
Once our eyes adjusted to the aggressive glare of the freshly painted white walls around the yard, we began to make out figures, dozens of them dressed in navy blue, clinging to the inner walls of this surreal space.
It was a scorching June day in western Ukraine, and we had just been released, like kids in a petting zoo, into a courtyard full of prisoners of war from the Russian military.
Who we decided to walk up to and talk to, and what we wanted to talk about, was up to us.
Whether these men, captives of the country they had attacked with rifle in hand, wanted to speak to us was up to them.
And so we began our work.
Looking one's enemy in the eye and trying one's best to see their human face is a strange place to put oneself in.
Standing opposite a man who, in some ways, is the living embodiment of all the suffering and death brought to your home and the people living in it, and trying to have a normal, civilized conversation is especially strange.
That was my goal when I signed up this summer to visit one of the Ukrainian prisoner-of-war camps where Russian soldiers were being held captive.
This wasn't exclusive access. Trips like this for the press are organized by Ukrainian authorities at the same facility every month.
But I wasn't there just for the shock and awe of seeing Russian POWs and asking them gotcha questions.
In the fifth year of full-scale war, Vladimir Putin is still doing his best to continue his quest to destroy independent Ukraine without needing to announce large-scale forced mobilization at home.
But Russia's offensives continue, with hundreds — often upwards of a thousand — Russian single-use soldiers killed or badly wounded on the battlefield every day.
Moscow can sustain this because, somewhere, all across the depths of that huge country, tens of thousands of men every month continue to sign up voluntarily to fight in Ukraine.
For there to be any chance of Putin considering winding his war down, this flow of warm bodies needs to dry up. But for now, they just keep coming.
I wanted to understand why. I wanted to understand who these people are, and why they decide to leave their civilian lives and join a war of aggression.
Fast forward four months, and not only is this basic fact about Russia's wartime military still not understood, but the question of whether or not one should have sympathy for these invaders has once again become a popular topic of discussion.
Deep into autumn, the weather has turned, the first blackouts have begun, and a nation of tens of millions is bracing itself for a winter humanitarian crisis unlike anything seen before, all thanks to Russia's escalating strike campaign against critical infrastructure.
But as if this time wasn't going to be difficult enough as it is, openly showing contempt for Ukraine and directly assisting Russia's war effort through waived sanctions, diesel deals and the throttling of Starlink is now in vogue among two of the most powerful men in the world, Donald Trump and Elon Musk.
Reading it from Kyiv, Musk's post on X about feeling sympathy for the poor young Russian soldiers forced to fight crosses into the domain of the absurd.
And yet here we are.
More than anything, this moment in time back to that summer day at the POW camp and what I heard from the Russian soldiers themselves about why they ended up in Ukraine, fighting for the aggressor's army.
This was my second time speaking to Russian prisoners of war.
The first time, ironically, was probably the only scenario in which Musk's comment really applied: when Ukrainian forces captured hundreds of young Russians doing mandatory military service as they broke across the border in Kursk Oblast in the summer of 2024.
This time, all four Russians were, unsurprisingly, contract soldiers. And, by coincidence, they all happened to hail from the depths of Siberia, from the regions around Lake Baikal.
This is what they had to say.
Pavel Malikov was the first man I approached in the yard. He seemed aloof at first, but after I asked him if we could speak, he replied, “Well, we're already speaking, aren't we?” At which point, we pressed the record button.
A factory worker from the remote Altai Krai, Malikov had joined Russia's Spetsnaz, Moscow's once-feared special forces.
But by the time he first saw the battlefield in Ukraine, his mission barely differed from that of the average assault infantryman: move forward to his designated point, dig in and wait for orders.
He was captured on his second mission.
Looking me in the eye, Malikov spoke confidently with an air of pride, the basis of which I couldn't quite understand.
"I signed the contract because… well, you know… there was seemingly nothing bad in my life, but not much good either, I was kind of stuck. My decision wasn't so much about changing my life as it was about changing myself.
"I went and signed the contract. Many people regret it after they sign it, they think, 'why the hell did I do this,' and so on. I don't have any such thoughts. I signed the contract, that means it was meant to be.
"I had an idea of what was going on here, but I only gained a full understanding after I came here. Yes, war is bad, but nonetheless, I am a patriot of my country, my Russia, and I still stand by my country, no matter what."
Next was 41-year-old Oleg Krasikov from Buryatia, captured that summer after suffering light wounds to his leg, who told a commonplace story of being deceived and forced into the assault infantry.
Now a prisoner, his position on the war had suddenly been imbued with a performative moral clarity.
"It's not clear yet when it will all end. I hope that Moscow will come up with something, because as I understand it, comrade Zelensky is ready to negotiate."
But beyond the facade of remorse lay Krasikov's real story, and his motivations for joining up in the first place couldn't have been more banal.
"I had an ordinary life, home work, traveling for work.
"At one point, work stopped, and I stayed at home for half a year, doing odd jobs. I saw the advertisement, and honestly, I had financial problems, I needed to do renovations (to my home). Maybe that's what pushed me, the urgent need for money. So I signed the contract.
"They offered something different, not the front line, not shooting, nothing like that. I had a picture of what it might be, but it wasn't like that.
"I went to a recruitment center, they explained everything there, and gave me a contract to sign.
"I signed the contract, got the money, and did the renovation."
At a conference in Europe last year, I had a rare conversation with an exiled journalist from Russia's Arctic region.
In his grim appraisal of Russia's manpower situation, he predicted that Putin would not have to announce forced mobilization.
After years of war, the pervasive militarization and wholesale brainwashing in Russia's school system, he argued, would ensure a consistent flow of young voluntary recruits joining up after school for years to come.
After a bland but nutritious lunch shared with the POWs, we had time for two more interviews. I specifically requested to speak with younger soldiers who had been captured this year.
The first was 21-year-old Dmitry Nefedov, who had spent the entirety of Ukraine's most recent brutal winter in a basement in the gray zone, surrounded by Ukrainian soldiers and abandoned by his commanders, until he was finally captured.
Nefedov spoke with a blankness in his eyes and a passive naivety that I still think about to this day.
Nothing in his words or mannerisms suggested that any part of this ordeal had been a lesson to him.
"I didn't have enough money, and I wanted to hang out, have fun. First my friends signed up, for a while I thought about it, and I signed a contract."
I asked if he didn't think that this war and the deaths of so many countrymen was pointless.
"I don't even know what to say… I know that only presidents can solve this.
"If I'm released and all of this is over, I don't know what I will do. If I don't find a normal job, I'll sign another contract. Otherwise, I might try to become a welder or a builder."
The last Russian soldier was even younger. Eighteen-year-old Maksim Alechko, had barely started school when Russia first invaded Ukraine.
He seemed more mentally proactive and switched on than any of the other POWs I spoke to.
But even then, Alechko's worldview seemed defined by a complete disconnect from the reality of the war, let alone any moral framework for understanding what his country was doing when he volunteered to join.
In his hometown, the industrial city of Chita, the Russian military and service in it carried only positive associations, he said.
"I liked the army, I joined the army, and stayed there. That's it, an order is an order.
"I only ever saw myself in this field. It's prestigious, it's beautiful, something to be proud of, to be a soldier.
"I wasn't interested in the war in Ukraine, I was interested in being a soldier. For my country.
"I didn't think anything bad about Ukraine, but when the war started, this whole information war began. Future generations are being turned against each other.
"What they are saying in Russia now, the reasons to join the military… The last time I watched, they were saying 'We are winning, come join the ranks of the victorious!' or something like that.
"People think the war will end soon, so they can sign up, earn some money, and that will be it."
Note from the author:
Hi, this is Francis Farrell, the author of this piece. We are entering a new phase of the war, where once again the daily, brutal fight on the front line to hold Russia back is drowned out by geopolitical noise. Despite the difficult winter ahead of us and the effect that will have on the work of our newsroom, we will continue to report from the field wherever necessary. Allison Pearson said to be negotiating exit from Daily Telegraph amid job cull
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:56:50 UTC
02:56:50 KST

The controversial Daily Telegraph columnist Allison Pearson is understood to be in negotiations about leaving the broadsheet as the newspaper’s new owner makes significant newsroom cuts.
Sources told the Guardian that Pearson – firmly on the right of the Telegraph’s roster – is preparing to announce her exit imminently and is crafting a statement about her future plans.
The news comes after the German media company Axel Springer, which completed a £575m takeover in June, warned that as many as 100 journalists’ roles were at risk of redundancy as it transitioned into being “a global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”.
One insider said the Brexit-backing columnist had been “in some sort of negotiation to make an elegant departure” after discussions with management about her future at the title.
But they said rumours of her expected exit had been circulating within the newsroom for a number of days, and were not a surprise after a column she wrote in September had raised some eyebrows internally, particularly among senior management.
Pearson wrote in an opinion piece that the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, had “the rough-diamond charisma to pull a large, enthusiastic crowd”.
She also wrote: “Every single person who marched in the rain to Unite the Kingdom, every decent person hanging our beautiful flags from lamp-posts and motorway bridges and on village greens, is making patriotism respectable again. Step by step, inch by inch, we are taking our country back from those who hate it.”
Pearson has been the Telegraph’s chief interviewer and a columnist since 2010. But her relations with some senior editorial figures were said to be strained over a number of subjects she raised in her columns, particularly around immigration.
Other managers did not welcome the attention she brought to the title when she was investigated by police in Essex in 2024 for allegedly stirring up racial hatred with a social media post.
The force was criticised by Pearson and her supporters when officers knocked on her door on Remembrance Sunday over a photograph she retweeted amid heightened tensions over the policing of Gaza protests. Pearson deleted the post and the police investigation was dropped, but a review concluded the force was right to look into the allegations.
When the Telegraph’s purchase was announced – ending three years of uncertainty over its future – Mathias Döpfner, Axel Springer’s chief executive and controlling shareholder, said he planned to invest in the title as he wanted to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.
The Telegraph will also focus on increasing its audience globally, “particularly in foreign affairs, defence and business”, according to an email to staff from the chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol.
She added: “To deliver on this ambition, we need to change how we are organised, how decisions are made, where we focus our resources and create efficiencies. We need clearer accountability, faster decision-making and a simpler, more effective organisation.”
Some staff at the Telegraph said that in the difficult period since the cuts were announced, the newsroom had felt like “a morgue”.
Proposed changes include folding separate departments such as health and travel into one features department.
A spokesperson for the Telegraph declined to comment, saying they could not discuss the employment status of individual staff members.
Pearson has been approached for comment.

China Tests Trimaran Submarine Designed to Carry Missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:56:42 UTC
02:56:42 KST

China is developing a trimaran submarine that combines the concept of a semi-submersible missile carrier with an uncrewed platform.
The vessel is undergoing tests in Huludao, in the Bohai Bay area. It was transported there from the southern city of Guangzhou via the port of Dalian, according to Naval News.
The vessel is designed to carry a large number of missiles and launch them using targeting data from other ships, aircraft or satellites.
The central hull houses two missile compartments containing launch canisters. The total number of missile launch cells is estimated at 16 to 18.
To launch its weapons, the submarine must surface, open the compartment doors and raise the launchers into a vertical position.
The vessel may carry anti-ship missiles or land-attack cruise missiles. Possible options include YJ-20 missiles, which are used on Type 055 destroyers.
The hull design, with additional side floats at the stern, provides stability while underway and when stationary on the surface. These elements compensate for shifts in the center of gravity as the missile canisters are raised.
The vessel is equipped with a snorkel to allow its diesel engines to operate while submerged. Its propulsion system consists of main propellers or waterjets for diesel-powered operation, along with electric propellers on the side floats.
The trimaran has a submerged displacement of approximately 900 metric tons. The weapons compartment occupies most of the vessel’s internal space.
Due to the lack of available interior space, the vessel is believed to be uncrewed. The bridge at the top is intended only for control during port entry and maneuvering in roadsteads.
Its operating concept resembles that of diesel-powered submarines from the Cold War era, which surfaced to launch missiles.
Militarnyi previously reported that Russia had transferred technical documentation and materials to China for submarine testing.

New Delhi: Govt is targeting to mobilise $220 billion in investment in the renewable energy sector by 2030 to expand manufacturing, transmission infrastructure and green hydrogen production, as it prepares to host the four-day Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo (BRESE) in the capital from Nov 2 to 5.While solar energy projects would require an investment of nearly $70 billion, wind projects would need $25-30 billion, energy storage deployment $20 billion, transmission networks $40-45 billion, hydropower $12-15 billion and green hydrogen offtake $20-25 billion. India aims to achieve 500 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity by 2030.The summit will be inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi at Bharat Mandapam on Nov 2 and is likely to be attended by energy ministers from 30 countries, including Australia, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, as well as representatives of the European Union, with the aim of exploring cooperation in renewable energy financing, green hydrogen, energy storage, clean energy manufacturing and technology development.Santosh Sarangi, secretary in Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE), said India had secured $64 billion in private investment between June 2024, when the previous RE-Invest Summit was held, and June 2026, including $6.2 billion in foreign direct investment (FDI).“With 308 GW of installed non-fossil fuel capacity, we are firmly on course to reach our 500 GW target by 2030. Realising this ambition will require approximately $220 billion in investment between 2027 and 2030, alongside accelerated deployment of energy storage, stronger transmission networks and expanded domestic manufacturing capabilities,” Sarangi said, adding that financial investors, private equity firms, pension funds and mutual funds were expected to play a key role in it.
Ministry is also developing a framework to assign exploration rights for geothermal energy, similar to the guidelines on petroleum exploration, which is expected to be ready within a month or two.BRESE 2026 will be held alongside the 9th Session of International Solar Alliance (ISA) Assembly and 4th International Conference on Green Hydrogen (ICGH).
Sarangi said Indian green hydrogen developers have so far secured orders for about 5.5 lakh tonnes per annum (MTPA), including 4.5 lakh MTPA secured in 2026 alone. Japan, South Korea and the EU were looking at greater sourcing of green ammonia and green methanol.He said green hydrogen had huge potential, with several pilot projects already under way in the direct reduced iron (DRI) steel and transportation sectors. India is also conducting an experiment across 10,000 acres in six states, covering 10 different crops, to inject ammonia directly into the soil instead of applying urea, a move that could improve efficiency and reduce costs and losses due to volatilisation and irrigation, Sarangi said.

Atul is known for investigative depth and strong human-interest narratives as he strives to bring clarity and context to complex issues. He currently tracks the energy sector, writing on power, renewable energy, coal and mines.

Unknown

Andrew Wasike 
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed announced Wednesday that Ethiopia has received 12 advanced Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets and plans to acquire four S-400 air defense systems.
The announcement comes as tensions with neighboring Eritrea and renewed fighting in the northern Tigray region raise fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa.
"Ethiopia's newly deployed military jets will remain more ready than ever to defend the airspace!" Abiy wrote on US social media platform X.
He said the fighter jets were delivered under an earlier agreement with Moscow, and the S-400 air defense systems are expected to arrive later.
"I would like to express my gratitude to my friend, Russian President Vladimir Putin, for his dedication in ensuring we received these warplanes a year ahead of our agreed schedule," said Abiy.
He described the acquisitions as a major step toward strengthening Ethiopia's military capabilities and protecting its sovereignty.
The Russian multirole combat aircraft is designed for air superiority and ground attack missions. The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system that can engage aircraft and other aerial threats.
Tensions have heightened between Ethiopia and Eritrea, former allies whose relations have deteriorated because of Addis Ababa's demand for access to the Red Sea and disagreements on security in northern Ethiopia.
Ethiopia has been landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Abiy has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to the country's economic and security interests.
Renewed fighting in Tigray, where Ethiopian federal forces and rival Tigrayan factions have been engaged in hostilities, has also raised concerns about instability along the Ethiopian-Eritrean border.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later fought alongside Ethiopian government forces during the 2020-2022 Tigray conflict, but relations have since deteriorated.

Balad leader blasts ‘racist’ exclusion of Arab parties in Israel
Elections have yielded no clear winner but opposition bloc refuses to ally with Arab parties.
The leader of Israel’s Balad party has condemned the country’s main political leaders for refusing to form a coalition with Arab parties, even after a record showing in polls could make them kingmakers for the next parliament after no clear winner emerged.
Sami Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about a fifth of the population, are being treated as illegitimate partners despite their turnout.
“This is racism,” he said. “We are a legitimate elected leadership of the national minority. The vast majority of our people decided that we are their leadership.”
Arab parties are on course to win a record 19 seats, giving them potentially decisive leverage over the main political blocs. With 85 percent of the vote counted, Israel’s Central Elections Committee has Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc ahead with at least 53 seats, and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot on 48.
Both are short of the 61 needed to govern. Netanyahu says Israelis chose a strong right-wing government, while Eisenkot says they voted for change.
Abu Shehadeh, who leads Balad, one of the Joint List’s three parties, was not a candidate.
Israel’s elections committee voted to disqualify him at the request of far-right Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who accused him of supporting the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack due to an article issued the following day in which Abu Shehadeh called it an “important historical event”.
Abu Shehadeh subsequently told the Supreme Court he did not support “armed struggle” but acknowledged that a paragraph in the article had been incorrectly worded. He said his intention was to call for moving the conflict towards a political process.
He withdrew in October after a majority of the Supreme Court panel appeared willing to approve the disqualification. He rejects the grounds and said the court had made clear that Israel has “two different judicial systems, one for the Jews and one for the Arabs”.
“We are very proud of the Arab Palestinian minority in Israel that went in this very high percentage of voting,” he told Al Jazeera. The community’s first promise to voters, he said, was to prevent “this gang of criminals” from returning to power, naming Netanyahu and far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Ben-Gvir. “So our first promise, we can keep it from now .”
Numbers point to Arab parties but opposition bloc resistant
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu “has scared off everybody from talking to the Palestinian Israeli parties”, leaving him best placed to “call the shots”. She said that Eisenkot and his allies have indicated that they want a Zionist government and “do not want to form a government” with the Arab parties, leaving them few options.
Danny Ayalon, a former Israeli ambassador to the United States, told Al Jazeera that turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel came in “really unprecedented numbers” and that the parties “are going to have some significant clout”.
Mathematically, he said, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the two Arab parties and pass the threshold, though it would take “political wizardry”. Yousef Jabareen, who leads the Joint List, has said his alliance’s “hands are extended” to oust Netanyahu.
Abu Shehadeh set out what Palestinian citizens want from the next government.
“We are against genocide and we are against apartheid. We want to promote a different political alternative, one which is based on the values of freedom, justice and equality for both people who are living between the river and the sea.”
Of Netanyahu, he said: “Our problem … is that he is a war criminal.”
A UN commission said in a report published on Monday that Israel has continued to commit genocide in Gaza after last October’s US-brokered ceasefire in the enclave.
The Hague-based International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in 2024 for war crimes during the Gaza war.

Support unpaid carers so they aren’t pushed to the brink of suicide | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:54:16 UTC
02:54:16 KST

Reading the report on Matilda Davis’s death was heartbreaking (Burnham backs mandatory suicide prevention training for social workers after parent-carer Matilda Davis’s death, 21 October). That someone already under immense pressure could leave a meeting with social workers feeling so distressed, and that the professionals had received no suicide-prevention training, is an indictment of the system. It is reassuring to hear Andy Burnham’s support for mandatory training for social workers. But there is an even more troubling issue at the heart of this story – the finding that 41% of parent-carers have contemplated suicide should prompt outrage and immediate action.
Campaigning by Ed Davey, alongside the Guardian’s investigation into the carer’s allowance scandal, have exposed the extent to which unpaid carers have been failed by the state. For years they have been described as inspirational and selfless. They give up careers, sacrifice income and provide care that saves the state billions of pounds. Yet the reality revealed by this figure is that many feel so overwhelmed and unsupported that they have contemplated ending their lives.
Mandatory suicide-prevention training may help professionals identify those in crisis. But the real scandal is that so many are being pushed to this point in the first place. It is time for the government to provide the practical, emotional and financial support that unpaid carers desperately need.
 
Dr Louise Lawson
 
Lecturer in social policy, University of Glasgow

Ensuring prisoners can’t refuse to attend court | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:54:12 UTC
02:54:12 KST

The report on judges being given powers to punish prisoners who refuse to attend court raises a question about why we appear to have abandoned a straightforward approach that once worked (Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules, 22 October).
When I joined the Prison Service as an officer more than 30 years ago, prisoners were not permitted to decide whether they would attend court. If they refused to go voluntarily, they could be escorted under restraint where necessary.
The result was predictable: few prisoners refused, because they knew their refusal would not prevent them from appearing.
There is a wider lesson here for the administration of justice. When noncompliance becomes a means of delaying or obstructing the system, introducing additional punishments may be less effective than ensuring that lawful instructions are carried out in the first place. Prisoners have rights, and the use of restraint must always be lawful, proportionate and justified. But those rights do not extend to exercising a veto over the judicial process.
After more than three decades, I find it difficult to understand why a principle that was once routine now appears to require a fresh solution. Sometimes, effective public administration is not about creating new sanctions but about having the resolve and resources to enforce existing rules.

Burnham’s budget blasts British baked beans

02:54:10 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham’s love affair with beans is well documented.
Asked what items he would stockpile in case of an emergency, the prime minister picked the store-cupboard staple, together with soup and Twiglets.
Now bean makers are screaming betrayal.
Advertisement
As part of a stream of “everyday fixes” aimed at easing the cost of living, Chancellor John Healey said the government would suspend tariffs on more than 100 products, including imported chocolate, marmalade and Burnham’s beloved baked beans.
An analysis of the list — published in full today — reveals that tariffs of 16% will be removed on an array of finished bean products imported from around the world, many of which are also manufactured in the U.K.
While the raw beans used to make products like baked beans are mostly imported, the U.K. boasts a major bean processing industry which food executives fear could now be undermined by exporters such as China and the U.S.
Karen Betts, chief executive of the Food and Drink Federation, said the budget did “nothing to ease the pressures food and drink manufacturers are under.”
“Instead, one of the chancellor’s flagship announcements, removing tariffs from some food and drink products, will have no meaningful impact on consumer prices,” Betts said. “But it will undermine British factories and their workers, grappling with much higher costs, producing the same products.
“The Treasury in particular has persistently failed to recognise the importance of food and drink manufacturing to jobs and prosperity the length and breadth of the U.K.,” Betts added.
Advertisement
Instead of making it easier to import rival products, Betts said the government should be addressing the “acute pressures” the sector is facing, including high energy costs and “overly complex” regulation.
A spokesperson for Princes Group, which produces Branston Baked Beans in the U.K., said removing tariffs on imported finished baked beans was “unlikely to have a meaningful impact on prices, particularly as there are currently no tariffs on the imported haricot beans used by U.K. manufacturers and no tariffs on EU imports.”
“We believe measures that help address the higher costs of manufacturing food in the UK, particularly energy costs, would have a greater impact for both consumers and British businesses.”
According to the government, the move, together with existing tariff suspensions announced earlier this year, will reduce consumer costs by between £245 million and £595 million a year, saving households up to £21 on their food shop annually.
In response to a consultation on the changes, the government said it had taken the decision to exclude several products from the initial list “due to concerns about the impact on domestic production, developing countries, international considerations and other government policies.”
“The government recognises that for some remaining products, there may be some limited impacts on domestic producers of goods which will be able to be imported tariff-free for the specified period. However, the government considers the benefits of this to consumers, through reduced costs, outweigh those risks.”
The U.K. government did not respond to a request for comment.

Activist Dolores Huerta Dies at 96. Here's What To Know About Her Trailblazing Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:52:43 UTC
02:52:43 KST

Dolores Huerta, an internationally renowned activist, community organizer, and political force who co-founded what is now known as the United Farm Workers of America (UFW) alongside Cesar Chavez, died Wednesday at her home in Bakersfield, California. She was 96.
News of Huerta’s death was shared by family members through her Instagram account, though the post did not disclose a cause of death. The New York Times reported that the cause of death was cancer, citing a spokesperson for Huerta.
"We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy," the post said.
Huerta dedicated her career to fighting a variety of causes, including labor rights, women's rights and immigrants’ rights. She is also credited with coining the phrase "Yes we can"—"Sí se puede"—which was later adopted by Barack Obama.
In March 2026, Huerta publicly accused Chavez of sexually abusing her decades earlier, breaking a silence she said she had maintained to protect the farmworker movement. Her disclosure accompanied a New York Times investigation into allegations that Chavez sexually abused women and girls.
"I think she kind of radiates empowerment not only for herself, but for others," Mario Garcia, a professor of Chicano Studies and History at the University of California, Santa Barbara, told TIME in an interview before Huerta's death. "She's really quite an electrifying person."
Indeed, when Huerta received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012, Obama noted that she "does not play."
"Without any negotiating experience, Dolores helped lead a worldwide grape boycott that forced growers to agree to some of the country's first farmworker contracts," Obama said during the ceremony. "And ever since she has fought to give more people a seat at the table. 'Don't wait to be invited,' she says. 'Step in there.'"
"On a personal note, Dolores was very gracious when I told her I had stolen her slogan, Sí se puede, Yes we can," Obama added. "Knowing her, I'm pleased that she let me off easy."
How Huerta's early life shaped her activism
Huerta was born on April 10, 1930, in Dawson, New Mexico, to Alicia Chávez and Juan Fernández, who both played a major role in her views on justice.
Her father was a miner and farmworker who went on to join the New Mexico state legislature. After her parents' divorce, her mother opened up her own hotel in Stockton, California, and often offered affordable or free rooms to low-wage workers, according to a biography by the Dolores Huerta Foundation (DHF). Huerta often said she became a feminist because of her mother. As a girl, Huerta was a high-achieving student, an active member of several school clubs, and a member of the Girl Scouts. Huerta now has a Scouts patch dedicated to her.
In 1945, one of her two brothers was beaten for wearing a zoot suit, an ensemble then popular with Black and Mexican-American men who were often unfairly labeled as delinquents. She has said that her brother's beating further influenced her activism.
After Huerta graduated from high school, she obtained a provisional teaching credential at the University of the Pacific’s Stockton College, which later became San Joaquin Delta College, and began teaching at an area elementary school. She also got married and had two children with her husband at the time, Ralph Head. She has repeatedly said that her students, many of whom were children of farmworkers, inspired her activism.
"I think the one thing that really kind of hooked me for life was going to the homes of some workers who did not have linoleum or wood on their floor, only dirt," Huerta told MAKERS, a documentary project featuring influential women, in 2012. "And yet, these are people who are working, they're working very hard and you know that this is wrong."
Huerta decided to pursue a career in community organizing in 1955 when she met Fred Ross Sr., founder of the Community Service Organization (CSO) and a nationally influential community organizer who began his career fighting for the rights of Dust Bowl-era farmworkers.
Dolores Huerta accepts TIME100 Impact Award
Finding her voice
At a November 2018 TED Talk, Huerta told an audience she found her voice while volunteering at the Stockton chapter of CSO, which she co-founded.
She described a day she was volunteering there when she was 25 years old and a disabled farmworker walked in asking if someone could help him apply for disability benefits. She went to a welfare office with the man, but she was not allowed to submit an application on his behalf. Defeated, she returned to CSO, where Ross told her to go back and demand that a supervisor allow the man to submit an application.
"I kind of overcame my anxieties and my fears. I went down to the welfare office and I demanded to see the supervisor," Huerta said. "That taught me a lesson. That taught me that I had a voice."
Ross taught Huerta to make demands of people, she said, especially public officials. He also instilled the importance of voting.
While at CSO, Huerta founded the Agricultural Workers Association, led voter registration drives and met Cesar Chavez in 1955, while he was an organizer with CSO. Chavez would later become CSO's executive director in 1959.
Ross died in 1992, but Huerta described Ross as her "spiritual father" for the rest of her life, and the first person to teach her and Chavez community-organizing techniques.
Founding the United Farm Workers
In 1962, Huerta and Chavez left CSO to found the National Farm Workers Association, which would later become UFW, a union that continues to advocate for the rights of agricultural workers.
They were motivated to found the association after hearing from scores of California farmworkers working under harsh conditions: no benefits, low wages, and no access to bathrooms or water while in the fields. The Bracero Program, established through a 1942 agreement between the U.S. and Mexico, recruited Mexican workers to address wartime agricultural labor shortages and continued until 1964.
Chavez and Huerta believed the Bracero Program allowed for farmworker abuses and lobbied to end it. They lobbied against the program, which ended in 1964.
Huerta and Chavez continued their fight for workers' rights, including leading protests, worker strikes, hunger strikes, and arguably their most famous tactic, national boycotts. Huerta helped organize the nationwide grape boycott that supported the Delano grape strike of 1965-1970. The strike began with Filipino farmworkers affiliated with the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee; Huerta and Chavez’s National Farm Workers Association subsequently joined them. The Delano Grape Strike and Boycott convinced grocery store chains to stop selling the fruit until industry labor standards were set.
Huerta’s boycotts were effective in forcing industries to guarantee better working conditions for their employees.
"I think one of the things about when people are oppressed is that they start accepting their condition and they often kind of blame themselves," Huerta said during a 2015 Q&A with the National Portrait Gallery. "Our job was to convince them again that they could make a difference and that they had the power to do it."
In 1975, California passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act, which gave farmworkers the right to unionize. The state credited Huerta as instrumental in establishing those rights. Though Chavez often receives national accolades for the achievements of the farmworker movement, historians say Huerta played an equally essential role through every success—but historically received far less credit.
"[Chavez] didn't win you over with his rhetoric, [Chavez] was always soft spoken, but he also radiated strong internal leadership qualities," Garcia said. "[Huerta], by contrast, was always much more verbal, a much better speaker than [Chavez]."
In a 2018 interview with TIME, Huerta said she didn't expect recognition.
"I think that’s very typical of women," she said. "I had been acculturated to be supportive, to be accommodating, to support men in the work they do. We never think of getting credit or recognition or even taking the power. We didn’t think in those terms."
She added that she believed times were changing. "That could make an incredible amount of difference in our world,” she said. “We will never have peace in the world until feminists take power."
In March 2026, Huerta disclosed that Chavez had sexually abused her in the 1960s. She alleged that he pressured her into sex on one occasion and raped her on another. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, she said, and she arranged for the children to be raised by other families. She said she later developed close relationships with them.
Huerta said she had remained silent for decades because she feared damaging the movement to which she had devoted her life. Coming forward after a New York Times investigation into allegations that Chavez abused other women and girls, she emphasized that the movement’s achievements belonged to thousands of people.
Balancing activism and motherhood
Huerta was a change-maker while also raising 11 children, which gave her kids a front-row seat to her activism.
During the five-year Delano grape boycott, Huerta said she and her family encountered violence.
"There were times when my home was terrorized in the middle of the night, my windows broken when I'm there alone with my children," she told MAKERS. "We had shotguns and rifles aimed at us."
In order to start the farmworkers union, Huerta had to move most of her family—by then she had seven children—to Delano, while leaving two of her children behind in Stockton, California. Huerta credited the women of the movement, including Cesar Chavez's wife, Helen Chavez, and his sisters-in-law, for organizing childcare in Delano.
"I had a lot of criticism from family and friends for years until huelga [the strike] became famous and now they all like me," Huerta jokingly said during the 2015 National Portrait Gallery Q&A. "But it was difficult. We were pretty much living like the farmworkers."
Huerta's family and Chavez's family relied on assistance from a food bank and were organizing the union without a steady source of income of their own.
"In the strike, women were always on the picket lines with the children," Huerta said.
It was also not lost on Huerta that Chavez and other male activists were not asked about how they managed their important work with their parental duties.
"The thing about that is that every single mother in every single working family has that question every single day. Who am I going to leave my children with? Are they going to be safe? Are they going to be protected? That’s something women have to deal with all the time," she told TIME in 2018.
Huerta had 14 children, 24 grandchildren, 23 great-grandchildren, and seven great-great-grandchildren, a spokesperson tells TIME.
“Dolores was a deeply private person when it came to her family, and while all 14 of her children were part of her life, some parts of that story were never shared publicly,” according to the spokesperson.
Her lasting legacy
Over the course of her career, Huerta was arrested more than 20 times. In 1988, she was severely beaten by a police officer in San Francisco at a rally against presidential candidate George H. W. Bush. She was 58 years old at the time, and suffered broken ribs and a ruptured spleen.
Despite those types of encounters, Huerta continued to mobilize and fight for causes through her Dolores Huerta Foundation. She established her foundation in 2003 after receiving a $100,000 prize from the Puffin/Nation Prize for Creative Citizenship in 2002. Her youngest daughter, Camila Chávez, helped run the foundation as the executive director.
In the course of her career, Huerta was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the Eleanor Roosevelt Human Rights Award, and the Mexican Government's Ohtli Award. She also received at least nine honorary doctorates from universities across the country. In 2026, TIME named Huerta one of the world’s 100 most influential people, with a tribute by Gloria Steinem recognizing her decades of organizing and her courage in speaking publicly about Chavez. She received the TIME100 Impact Award at the TIME100 Gala in New York City on April 23, 2026.
Huerta endorsed presidential candidates, including speaking at the 2016 Democratic National Convention in support of Hillary Clinton. She was also the subject of a PBS documentary, Dolores, which won a Peabody Award in 2018.
"She was not afraid to speak truth to power," Clinton said of her in the Dolores documentary.
In July 2018, California Governor Jerry Brown signed a bill declaring April 10 Dolores Huerta Day. "Dolores Huerta deserves proper recognition for her numerous sacrifices in the name of justice and the amelioration of severely inadequate working conditions," the bill’s text said.
"Change comes from the bottom," Huerta said during a May 2012 interview. "But you've got to be able to organize those folks at the bottom to be able to get out there and make the changes that they need. And of course, if you don't have organization, then you don't have a democracy."

Sahin Demir

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Iran is in contact with mediators to review proposals to implement a seven-day plan with the US.
Araghchi wrote on US social media company X that Tehran continues to give diplomacy a chance despite tensions with Washington.
“While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed,” he said. “We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week.”
Iran’s seven-day plan, presented to Washington through Qatari mediators in September, proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming negotiations with the US within a week if Washington meets Tehran’s conditions.
The US would take agreed steps during the first five days, including ending hostilities, lifting its naval blockade on Iranian ports, easing restrictions on Iranian oil exports and releasing frozen Iranian assets.
On the sixth day, Iran would reopen the strait to normal commercial shipping, while negotiations between Tehran and Washington toward a comprehensive agreement would resume on the seventh day.
The proposed measures remain subject to agreement.
On Oct. 8, Araghchi said Tehran was reviewing Washington’s response to the proposal, with messages continuing to be exchanged through mediators.
The latest remarks come amid diplomatic efforts to maintain a fragile ceasefire between Iran and the US following months of military confrontation.
The two countries signed the Islamabad Memorandum on June 18 following negotiations mediated by Pakistan and Oman.
That agreement addressed several disputed issues, including maritime security in the strait, sanctions relief and the withdrawal of US naval restrictions.
Oman, Pakistan and Qatar have maintained diplomatic contacts aimed at resolving differences between Tehran and Washington.

Apple unveiled the MacBook Pro with a touch-sensitive OLED display
Kyiv • UNN
The new MacBook Pro features a touch-sensitive OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and up to 24 hours of battery life. Sales begin on November 6.
Apple unveiled a new MacBook Pro with a touch OLED display, M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, and support for Dynamic Island. The laptop features a display with a refresh rate of up to 120 Hz, up to 24 hours of battery life, and the ability to connect up to four external displays. Preorders are already available, and sales will begin on November 6. The Verge reports, writes UNN.
Details
The presentation took place on Wednesday during the “Pro and tell” event. The new MacBook Pro is equipped with a PROLED XDR display featuring a tandem OLED structure. It supports peak SDR brightness of up to 2,000 nits and has a contrast ratio of 10,000,000:1.
The screen features Dynamic Island, which can display Live Activities—interactive notifications similar to those available on the iPhone. In addition, Apple has brought back the illuminated logo on the laptop lid.
According to the company, the touch sensor is built directly into the display panel rather than placed on top of it. This design is intended to reduce latency when interacting with the screen.
Touch controls can be used to scroll through web pages, zoom in on photos, test apps for iOS and iPadOS, and work with software musical instruments. Apple also said that its apps are optimized for touch input, while an updated API will allow third-party developers to add touch support to their own applications.
The laptop is available in two sizes. The 14-inch model weighs approximately 1.36 kg, while the 16-inch model weighs 1.81 kg. The displays’ actual diagonals are 14.2 and 16.3 inches, respectively. Both models are thinner thanks to a redesigned construction.
According to Apple, the MacBook Pro provides up to 24 hours of battery life. The ports include MagSafe 3, a headphone jack, an SD card reader, HDMI, and three Thunderbolt 5 ports. The laptop supports connecting up to three external displays simultaneously, while the M5 Max version supports up to four.
Apple also highlights a six-speaker audio system that, according to the company, delivers 50% deeper bass and clear sound. In addition, the device features a newly designed hinge for improved stability.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch model starts at $3,399. Preorders can be placed now, and official sales are scheduled to begin on November 6.
Apple did not support the idea of touchscreens in laptops for a long time. In 2016, the company began equipping the MacBook Pro with a Touch Bar instead of traditional function keys. However, in 2021 it brought back physical keys, and in 2023 it completely discontinued the Touch Bar.

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:50:35 UTC
02:50:35 KST

Europe must finally hold Russia accountable for hybrid attacks
A soldier patrols outside the building hosting the NATO summit of heads of state and government in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 24, 2025. (John Thys/AFP via Getty Images)
Marek Zenisek
Czech politician and academic
Europe has already learned to better recognize hybrid threats, which is definitely a good thing, but recognition alone is not enough and doesn't serve as sufficient deterrence.
European officials have grown accustomed to scenarios where a cyberattack disrupts public services and critical infrastructure, drones appear over sensitive sites, and a flood of misinformation on social media exploits societal uncertainty.
European governments then investigate, share information, release statements, and sometimes announce new security measures until another incident elsewhere grabs the headlines again.
This approach is obviously not enough. Up until today, it appears that Russia is pretty confident that the cost of these hybrid attacks is a bargain — it costs little, and consequences look spectacular in Russian intelligence reports.
And this is exactly where Europe still has a problem. Resilience and deterrence are not the same thing. Europe must become a harder and, above all, much more expensive target for Russia.
Europeans must ensure that deterrence is a priority, as resilience is an unlikely tool to actually change the cost of a Russian attack.
Let's stop treating every incident as an isolated case and add them all up
A single attack may seem too small to justify a major response.
We've seen it many times.
In July 2024, an incendiary package caught fire at Leipzig airport on July 20, followed by similar incidents in Poland and the U.K. over the next two days.
German security authorities did not issue a wider warning to the aviation and logistics sectors until Aug. 28, more than five weeks after the first incident.
The subsequent investigation established links between the incidents and a broader Russian sabotage campaign. The response eventually came, but the delay illustrates the advantage Russia gains when individual incidents are treated separately rather than as parts of a broader campaign.
Determining responsibility can take weeks, and governments may differ in their assessment of the available evidence as well as their opinion on the appropriate reaction. Before responsibility is confirmed, political attention may shift elsewhere, giving Russia a strategic advantage in this gray zone.
This creates an asymmetry that favors the aggressor. Moscow can carry out a long-term campaign while European states deal with individual incidents one by one.
European governments, therefore, need to evaluate individual incidents in a broader context and together.
A cyberattack, sabotage, or an attempt to infiltrate an intelligence network is a full-blown hybrid campaign targeted against European countries.
Repeated operations also consume European resources, reveal weaknesses, create uncertainty, and above all, test how far Europe is willing to go.
So every new investigation shouldn't start from scratch, and instead should take into account what came before it.
Deterrence can't start only after an attack
The central objective of Europe's deterrence strategy should be to change Moscow's calculus and make further aggression an unacceptable gamble. European governments can rise above the Kremlin's dirty tricks by pursuing a constructive, systemic approach that addresses the threat at its roots.
To develop that, European governments should prepare a credible set of possible consequences before another serious incident occurs. Russia doesn't need to know exactly what Europe will do in every situation; strategic ambiguity has its value, but Moscow must believe that Europe will respond and that the consequences will matter.
That's the foundation of credible deterrence.
There's also a broader reason why this is important. If we add up the various forms of pressure Russia has exerted on European countries in recent years, future generations could rightfully ask why Europe tolerated so many things without developing a more systematic response.
It will be especially hard to explain to our children and grandchildren why a group of countries with much greater economic resources than Russia repeatedly allowed Moscow to set the pace of the confrontation.
Europe needs to be much better prepared. European countries should have a set of possible responses ready that can be adapted to specific cases, instead of having to come up with a reaction from scratch after every new attack.
That way, deterrence becomes more than just a statement made after the damage has already been done.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent so far?
and it may appear in our Letters section.
Europe needs to change the calculation
Everyone understands that Europe cannot prevent every hostile operation. It can't know where the next test will come from, just like it can't rule out the possibility that Russia or another adversary will take advantage of Europe's openness. It can, however, make such operations more difficult.
Europe can better protect its societies. It can improve the ability of its intelligence and security services to identify hostile networks. It can coordinate accountability better. It can remove unnecessary legal and institutional obstacles. And it can make it clear that repeated aggression will not go unpunished.
The main goal, as mentioned before, has to be to change the adversary's calculation.
Russia must not only ask whether a certain operation can be carried out successfully. It also has to ask how much it will cost if Europe uncovers it and holds Moscow responsible.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Herzog urges Israeli parties to avert fresh election as neither bloc secures majority

Israeli President Isaac Herzog has urged political parties to make every effort to avoid another election after preliminary results left neither main bloc with a parliamentary majority.
“Everything must be done, especially after yesterday, to avoid repeating another election,” Herzog told reporters on Wednesday in remarks carried by Israeli public broadcaster KAN.
He said he would begin consultations with parliamentary factions next week after receiving the official election results from the Central Elections Committee.
“I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind,” Herzog said.
He said he would listen to each faction, ask questions and hold discussions before deciding which lawmaker to task with forming a government.
Under Israel's basic law governing government formation, the president must consult parliamentary factions and assign a Knesset member the task of forming a government within seven days of the official publication of election results.
The selected lawmaker receives 28 days to form a government, with the possibility of extensions totalling up to 14 additional days.
If the first candidate fails, the president may appoint another lawmaker. At a later stage, at least 61 lawmakers can nominate a candidate to form a government.
Failure to establish a government could ultimately trigger another election.
Although coalitions generally seek support from at least 61 lawmakers, Israeli law allows minority governments to take office if more lawmakers vote in favour than against in a parliamentary confidence vote.
Until a new government wins the Knesset's confidence and takes office, Netanyahu's outgoing government will continue performing its duties.
According to Israeli Channel 12, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset after all regular ballots were counted on Wednesday.
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win 19 seats, the broadcaster reported.
More than 500,000 special ballots remained to be counted.
Neither main bloc has been projected to reach the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.

Israeli exit polls show deadlock in apparent setback for Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
