Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.
In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this.
Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.
A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards.
“The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.”
The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options.
“It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.”
It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility.
The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.
“I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
“We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit.
“Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.”
Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.”
Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum.
In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”

Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:44:44 UTC
01:44:44 KST

Bank of Canada raises interest rates for the first time in three years
The central bank increased key rate by a quarter point as soaring energy prices push up inflation.
The Bank of Canada (BoC) has raised its key interest rate for the first time in more than three years and warned that further increases might be needed to prevent soaring energy costs from fueling broader inflation.
Wednesday’s quarter-point hike to 2.5 percent was widely expected, while the bank also ramped up its inflation forecast for 2027 to 3.1 percent from the 2 percent it had predicted in July. Growth this year is set to be 1 percent, higher than the 0.7 percent seen in July.
“With the outlook for inflation substantially higher and the economy showing resilience, an increase in the policy rate is needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalised inflation,” BoC governor Tiff Macklem said.
“There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, we will proceed carefully,” he added.
The annual inflation rate hit 3.2 percent in September, above the bank’s 1 to 3 percent target range, and was driven almost solely by higher energy and energy-related transportation costs.
Macklem said inflation was expected to end the year at 3.5 percent and stay at around 3 percent for most of 2027, before returning close to the 2 percent target by the middle of 2028.
“Governing Council agreed that risks to inflation had increased and there was less scope for monetary accommodation,” Macklem said.
The rate hike was the first since July 2023.
“We don’t expect that core measures of inflation will accelerate as much as the bank fears, particularly if global energy prices ease a little, and as a result we don’t think that the policy rate will need to move above 2.75 percent,” said Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC Capital Markets.
Money markets are pricing in another 25 basis point rate cut in January and see the benchmark rate going up to 3.25 percent by December next year.
Past experience suggests that businesses will increase the cost of products and services in line with changing costs over the next year, increasing overall inflation, Macklem said.
“The combination of higher energy prices and pass-through increases the persistence of inflation,” he said, although he added that there are lingering uncertainties such as the trade rift with the United States and a faster resolution of the conflict in the Middle East.
Economists who opposed a rise said core inflation, which strips out the cost of volatile items, is still hovering at about 2 percent. They also say a rate hike could impede modest economic recovery, given US trade tensions and a weak job market.
Macklem said new US tariffs would slow the economy in the fourth quarter, but expressed confidence that growth should pick up again in 2027 as consumer spending continues, exports pick up and business investment strengthens.
After a robust annualised growth of 3.3 percent in the second quarter, the economy is likely to slow to 2 percent in the third quarter and further down to 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter, the BoC’s new monetary policy report projected.
The report, however, upgraded its gross domestic product (GDP) forecast for next year and the year after to 2 percent from 1.8 percent for both 2027 and 2028, as predicted in July.
Macklem said this additional growth would help absorb the slack, or its unused capacity, in the economy.
The BoC’s next rate decision is on December 9.

The death toll from a collision between two high-speed trains in central Spain rose to at least 68 on Wednesday, as Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged a thorough investigation into the disaster.
Speaking at the crash site in Urda, Toledo, Sanchez said authorities would determine the cause of the accident and take action if wrongdoing was uncovered, Spanish news agency EFE reported.
"We will get to the bottom of this. If there has been negligence, it will be known," he said.
Sanchez announced three days of national mourning from Oct. 29 to 31, saying it was "unacceptable for a country like Spain" to experience two high-speed rail accidents in a single year.
He referred to another train crash in Adamuz, Cordoba, in January.
The prime minister said preliminary indications suggested the two accidents had different causes, but stressed that determining this was the responsibility of independent investigators and judicial authorities.
He pledged decisive measures to restore public confidence in Spain's railway system if safety shortcomings were identified.
Meanwhile, opposition People's Party leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo demanded "immediate" government and judicial investigations, insisting they be conducted "with all available resources and without interference."
Feijoo said Spain "has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," calling for a comprehensive, independent review of the country's entire railway network.
He declined to discuss political responsibility for the disaster, saying it was not the day to do so.
A minute of silence will be held at 8 pm local time (1900GMT) on Wednesday at town halls across Spain to honor the victims, according to the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces, which organized the tribute.

Likud claims election ‘stolen,’ demands probe into alleged voting fraud
Party says it is submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to police, Shin Bet and election officials over alleged irregularities at Arab polling stations.
Likud has alleged widespread fraud at Arab polling stations in Israel’s election, claiming the vote was “stolen” and demanding an immediate investigation by law enforcement and electoral authorities.
In a statement, the party accused Arab parties of bribery, intimidation, violence, forgery and the use of prohibited voter-mobilization software.
Likud said it was submitting hundreds of testimonies and pieces of evidence to the Israel Police, the Shin Bet security agency and the Central Elections Committee.
Among its allegations, the party claimed that thousands of envelopes contained cash alongside ballots for the Ra’am party. It also alleged threats against polling station officials, multiple voters entering voting booths together, voting under false identities and discrepancies between the number of ballot envelopes and recorded voters.
The statement did not identify the polling stations involved or specify how many votes were allegedly affected.
Likud called on police and the Shin Bet to investigate and bring anyone responsible for criminal offenses to justice. It also demanded that the Central Elections Committee urgently examine the allegations, arguing that the purported violations had compromised the integrity of the vote and its outcome.
The party described the alleged misconduct as a “grave assault on Israeli democracy” and citizens’ voting rights.

Ethiopia clashes drive 50,000 people into Kenya: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

Nearly 50,000 people have fled southern Ethiopia into neighboring Kenya amid fighting that erupted last week, the United Nations said Wednesday, citing figures provided by local authorities.
The figure represents a sharp jump from the 36,000 recorded on Tuesday by UNHCR, the U.N. refugee agency, in the wake of clashes between the armies of southern Ethiopia's Somali and Oromia regions.
"According to local authorities, up to an estimated 50,000 people have crossed into Kenya," said Fatima Mohammed-Cole, the UNHCR representative for Kenya.
That number could quickly change given the situation on the ground, with fresh crossings being recorded, Mohammed-Cole warned.
The unrest was sparked on Oct. 20 after a Somali regional flag was hoisted in Moyale, a city jointly administered between Somali and Oromia. Several people have died in clashes, sources told AFP on Saturday.
Many of those who had fled were women and children, Mohammed-Cole said.
"While some are staying with relatives and host communities, others have sought shelter in temporary locations like schools and churches," she added.
UNHCR has sent an emergency team to the region and is working with the Kenyan government, alongside other humanitarian organisations such as the Red Cross, to provide aid to those displaced.
Ethiopia, Africa's second most populous country at some 130 million people, is the scene of various armed conflicts across its vast territory.
The borderlands of its various regions, whose tracing dates back to 1991, are often the source of clashes.
For several years, the federal government has been locked in conflict with rebel movements in the Oromia and Amhara regions, the country's most populous.
After months of tensions, fighting has also broken out again in the northern Tigray region, already the scene of a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
Diplomatic disagreements with neighbouring Eritrea have likewise led to fears of another conflict between the fractious Horn of Africa neighbors.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:06 UTC
01:42:06 KST

Ethiopian online influencers are pushing for their government to invade neighboring Eritrea and seize access to the sea, following its success against rebel and Eritrean forces in the past few weeks.
The Ethiopian army has advanced right up to the border after repelling an offensive by rebels in the northern Tigray State who were supported by Eritrean troops.
Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has repeatedly said that securing a base on the Red Sea is a vital national objective for Ethiopia, which lost its coastline when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.
Photo: EPA
Some online influencers say that the opportunity to invade has arrived.
“The time for military action to secure access to the sea and end the Eritrean regime security threat is now for Ethiopia,” said Jawar Mohammed, a political activist who recently launched the “Now or Never” campaign on social media.
Jawar has more than 3.5 million Facebook followers and 1.3 million on TikTok, and thousands of Ethiopians have amplified his campaign, some sharing artificial intelligence (AI)-generated images of themselves in Ethiopian military uniforms as a mark of support.
Jawar, 40, was once the leader of a protest movement that helped propel Abiy to power in 2018, but fell out with the prime minister over what he sees as an increasing shift to “one-man rule,” and was jailed for two years before fleeing the country.
Despite years of criticizing Abiy’s government from an undisclosed new location in Europe, the fighting has brought Jawar back to the government’s side.
“The Ethiopian government currently holds a military and technological advantage, supported by a highly motivated force capable of advancing its strategic goal of securing sea access,” Jawar said, adding that delays could give Eritrea time to improve its defenses.
Eliyas Kebede, 25, from Addis Ababa, also spends hours every day online, posting and creating AI-generated content to support the idea of invading Eritrea, including altered maps that show the Eritrean port of Assab as part of Ethiopia.
“I see myself as someone who tries to defend his country’s narrative,” Kebede told reporters.
He said he would like to see the “Ethiopian army advance to Asmara, oust the Eritrean government, and negotiate access to Assab.”
Not everyone agrees with his approach.
“You are a warmonger, recklessly paving the way for mass deaths,” one Facebook commenter said under an image Eliyas created of a large crowd of Eritreans warmly welcoming the Ethiopian army to Assab.
Eliyas says he does not feel guilty “at all.”
“I believe my use of AI has been somewhat successful in boosting the morale of Ethiopian army supporters,” he said.
With Ethiopia and Eritrea reinforcing troop deployments along their border, the international community has expressed mounting concern about the risk of a new war.
Ethiopia has one of the harshest media climates in the world — ranked 148th out of 180 countries and regions in the Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders — so many young Ethiopians rely heavily on social media for news.
Kjetil Tronvoll, a Horn of Africa specialist at Oslo New University College, said the online campaign would not sway the government’s decision on whether to invade.
However, it can “rally the diaspora and local communities around the need for regime change in Eritrea,” Tronvoll told reporters.
Yaya Beshir, a prominent online activist who has backed the campaign from Australia, posts regularly about invading Eritrea to more than 740,000 Facebook followers.
Beshir said that forcibly seizing Eritrea’s Assab port could trigger a regional security crisis, but is unconcerned.
“Ethiopia initially prioritized a peaceful solution, but after those efforts failed, it has now turned to military means,” Yaya said.

Lai outlines goals to European group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:04 UTC
01:42:04 KST

Taiwan will continue to counter sabotage targeting undersea Internet cables, as well as China-directed transnational repression in collaboration with the democratic world, President William Lai (賴清德) told European lawmakers at the Presidential Office in Taipei yesterday.
The nation is a trustworthy partner to the world’s alliance of democracies and will stand steadfast in the global fight against transnational repression, Lai told a meeting with a Formosa Club delegation headed by Latvian member of the European Parliament Rihards Kols.
The Formosa Club is an inter-parliamentary group of pro-Taiwan European legislators.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan thanks the Formosa Club’s members for their support in words and action that have aided the nation and improved solidarity among liberal democracies, Lai said.
The club has repeatedly issued statements urging greater cooperation between the Legislative Yuan and the European Parliament, and support for Taiwan’s quest to participate in international frameworks, Lai said.
The European lawmakers have also expressed concern over China’s hegemonic expansion, as well as emphasized the importance of peace in the Taiwan Strait to the Indo-Pacific region and Europe, he said.
Peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific region are crucial to the European economy, Lai said.
The Russian invasion of Ukraine and tensions in the Taiwan Strait are reminders that democracies must build partnerships with like-minded countries to safeguard peace, he said.
Taiwan remains committed to bolstering its defense industrial base and self-defense capabilities, and cooperating with Europe to forge secure supply chains for artificial intelligence, semiconductors and drones, he said.
The Formosa Club’s members, who represent a diverse political spectrum, are united in their support of Taiwan, said Kols, who handed Lai the club’s joint annual resolution.
The statement was signed by more than 30 lawmakers from across Europe and issued at the annual meeting of the Formosa Club in Taipei on Saturday last week.
Europe’s support for Taiwan is a consensus that transcends party divides and will endure changes in government, Kols said.
While Taiwan and other democratic societies might have different histories and responsibilities, they nonetheless “share an interest in a world where threats do not decide whom we meet, how we trade or how our people choose their future,” he said.
The resolution was offered in this spirit, reflecting a “friendship built over time” and a “clear understanding that Europe and Taiwan have much to contribute to each other’s security,” he said.
The Baltic countries and Taiwan share a determination to control their destinies and be free of interference from hegemonic powers on their doorsteps, he said.
The resolution this year emphasizes cooperation between Taiwan and Europe to establish trustworthy supply chains in strategic industries, secure undersea cables from malicious attacks and oppose unilateral changes to the cross-strait “status quo,” he said.
The club reaffirms its support for Taipei’s bid to meaningfully participate in the proceedings of international organizations and furthering the mutually beneficial friendship between Taiwan and Europe, he said.

Chances ahead in asset guidance: PwC Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:03 UTC
01:42:03 KST

The Asia-Pacific region’s expanding asset management market offers Taiwan’s financial firms an opportunity to attract more wealthy clients and regional capital, but stronger investment expertise and service capabilities would be essential to compete, PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) Taiwan said in a report yesterday.
Assets under management in the region are projected to rise to US$34.5 trillion by 2030 from US$23.2 trillion in 2024, while industry revenue is expected to increase by US$47 billion, the report said.
Total client assets are forecast to reach US$154.3 trillion by 2030, up from US$107.2 trillion in 2024, and assets of high-net-worth people and mass-affluent clients are projected to reach US$52.4 trillion and US$70.1 trillion respectively, the report said.
Photo: Ge You-hao, Taipei Times
As Taiwan aims to capitalize on the opportunity by developing its capital markets and financial services into a regional wealth management hub, the government’s Asian asset management center initiative has helped increase assets under management across Taiwan’s financial industry by NT$15.24 trillion to NT$47.8 trillion (US$470.1 billion to US$1.474 trillion), exceeding its original four-year growth target of NT$14 trillion ahead of schedule, PwC Taiwan said.
As of the end of August, 26 banks had been approved to provide wealth management services to high-net-worth clients, managing NT$3.11 trillion in assets, the Financial Supervisory Commission (FSC) said.
The asset management special zone in Kaohsiung, which allows financial institutions to test new services, had attracted 58 institutions by the end of June. Participating banks served 6,214 wealthy clients and managed NT$728.1 billion, with pilot programs covering family offices and cross-border services, the commission’s data showed.
Taiwan’s asset management market is forecast to grow at a compound annual rate of 15.9 percent through 2030, said Jassie Chen (陳麗媛), cohead of PwC Taiwan’s Asian asset management center office.
The FSC has opened the door to private equity and private credit, and is considering easing restrictions on some offshore funds. It is also planning to overhaul real-estate investment trusts, shifting toward a fund-based structure and allowing for potential investments in infrastructure, data centers, renewable energy and healthcare facilities.
The government is also promoting exchange-traded funds and Taiwan Individual Savings Accounts to deepen capital market participation.
However, a larger market will not guarantee regional competitiveness, said Kuo Po-ju (郭柏如), financial services operations leader at PwC Taiwan.
“Market growth does not mean all players will benefit equally,” Kuo said.
Firms must improve their investment expertise, technology, talent and compliance capabilities to compete on service quality rather than price, she said.

Titled The Beast, which is also Lin’s nickname, the film follows Lin’s career with Taiwan Beer, China’s Zhejiang Guangsha Lions, the Taiwanese national team and the Taipei Fubon Braves, while exploring the change in his approach to the game.
Widely considered the greatest Taiwanese basketball player, Lin retired in June following the Braves’ 107-81 defeat to the Taoyuan Pauian Pilots in Game 7 of the P.League+ Finals, drawing to a close an illustrious career that spanned more than two decades.
Photo: CNA
No other Taiwanese player has matched the longevity of Lin’s career, sports broadcaster Marc Tien says in the documentary.
That was not always easy to foresee.
The film recounted how Lin left the sport in high school and again in college before finding his way back to the game.
During his early years with Taiwan Beer in the semi-professional Super Basketball League (SBL), there was a period when he rarely turned up at the court before noon, sports journalist Huang Chi-jen says in the film.
Former Taiwan Beer captain Hsu Hao-cheng, who was responsible for driving Lin to the court, describes having a “love-hate relationship” with his teammate.
Lin says in the documentary that his move to China’s professional league was a turning point.
In unfamiliar surroundings and with few outlets for his emotions, he turned to training, he said.
When he returned to Taiwan during the offseason a year later, former Taiwan Beer teammates said he had become a different person.
Lin joined Taiwan Beer in 2003, moved to Zhejiang Guangsha in 2009 and returned to Taiwan to play for the Braves in 2019.
A member of Taiwan’s “Golden Generation,” Lin won two SBL titles with Taiwan Beer in 2007 and 2008, and three consecutive P.League+ championships with the Braves from 2021 to 2023.
Lin said the film brought back memories of teammates and different stages of his career.
“There are difficult times and low points, but you have to believe in yourself and be willing to face challenges,” he said.
Planning for the documentary began in late 2024 and the production team interviewed more than 50 people, including family members, coaches and former teammates, the Braves said.
The documentary is to debut on streaming platform MyVideo early next month before becoming available on the Braves’ YouTube channel after the team’s home-opening week. Lin’s No. 12 jersey is to be retired at a ceremony on Nov. 14.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who was defeated in Brazil’s presidential election at the weekend, was on his way to Ecuador after fleeing Brazil, Argentina’s government said yesterday.
Bolsonaro, who lost the runoff election to Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, entered Argentina on Tuesday night before boarding a flight to Ecuador, the Argentine National Directorate of Migration said on X.
The 45-year-old entered Argentina “with valid travel documents and no legal impediment,” the agency said, despite a court order banning his exit.
Photo: AFP
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters boarded “a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador,” it said.
Data from the Flightradar24 Web site showed that the flight took off just after midnight yesterday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country’s northeast.
Baires Fly did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US media citing anonymous sources had earlier reported that Bolsonaro had arrived in the US on Tuesday.
The US Department of State and US President Donald Trump said that they backed issuing visas to Bolsonaro and his family, but did not confirm their travel plans.
The Brazilian Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports.
He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and with his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity.
Bolsonaro has not acknowledged his electoral defeat, citing a decision by the court to extend polling hours.
Trump said that he approved of Bolsonaro entering the US.
“Well, I would approve,” Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on his return from a campaign trip to Texas, adding that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.
“I think they’re fine people,” Trump said. “The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It’s gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market.”
“I think it’s so terrible to see it,” he said.
“I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well,” he said, referring to former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, whom he has previously said was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
“The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn’t involved,” Trump added. “That’s Brazil. It’s a different country.”

Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan’s efforts to create a ‘Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:42:01 UTC
01:42:01 KST

Much attention is being paid to increasing security ties between Taiwan and the Philippines, and rightfully so. The stakes are potentially existential, as explored in “ Donovan’s Deep Dives: Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines need to face the common threat from Beijing” (Sept. 12, page 12).
Getting less attention is that across the board the relationship is growing stronger, and both sides appear to be planning to put more of their eggs in each other’s baskets.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) in August last year confirmed plans to open a second Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) representative office in Cebu Province.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
Meanwhile, the Philippines representative office, Manila Economic and Cultural Office (MECO), earlier this month opened its largest overseas Filipino worker (OFW) service center in Taipei, with plans for establishing two more in central and southern Taiwan over the next two years. It is only the third such overseas service center the Philippines has opened. MECO has maintained a strong presence in Taiwan for years with representative offices in Taipei, Taichung and Kaohsiung.
These are just the latest significant moves, but they are part of a pattern of rapidly increasing ties and mutually reinforcing interest that could have long-lasting positive implications.
GOING SOUTH
In the democratic era, Taiwanese interest in the Philippines as a way to reduce reliance on China is not new. In the 1990s, President Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) launched the “go south” policy, encouraging investment in Southeast Asia, but with only modest success in the Philippines. In 2016, one of Lee’s top trade advisors, Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), was elected president and launched a similar New Southbound Policy, with similar results.
The election of Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr as president in 2022 brought a positive change on the Philippines side towards relations with Taiwan, which has since been matched by a similar eagerness on the Taiwanese side under Foreign Minister Lin after he was appointed in 2024 by President William Lai (賴清德).
Marcos issued a memorandum in April last year easing decades-old restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan. This quietly opened the door for higher-level, though still unofficial, contacts between the two sides.
This change quickly bore fruit; in August, Lin led a delegation of investors to the Philippines in a “private capacity” on his regular, non-diplomatic passport. Since the two sides severed diplomatic ties in 1975, this is only the second known trip by a Taiwanese foreign minister after then-minister Chang Hsiao-yen (章孝嚴) took a “vacation” to the Philippines in 1997.
This is part of a larger context. Reportedly, American investors were also in the delegation. Just the month prior to this trip, Lin had also visited Japan. Improved relations between Taiwan and the Philippines is part of a broader integration push in the region that includes the US and Japan into a more cohesive grouping of mutually supported interests.
Lin explicitly tied his efforts to those nations, saying on Facebook: “we are actively promoting the ‘Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor,’ linking it with the US-Japan-Philippines ‘Luzon Economic Corridor’ to build more resilient supply chains together.”
In the same post he added: “I have also taken note of the recent announcement by the US and the Philippines that they will work together to establish a 4,000-acre ‘Economic Security Zone’ to strengthen supply chain security and industrial development. In my view, the US possesses world-leading technological capabilities, Taiwan has a comprehensive manufacturing base and the Philippines has abundant land and a high-quality workforce.”
That development is part of the US-led Pax Silica initiative which, according to the State Department, “hails a new economic security consensus ensuring aligned partners build the AI ecosystem of tomorrow — from energy and critical minerals to high-end manufacturing and models.”
That statement lists 25 signatories, which of course does not include China, and rather forlornly Taiwan sits at the bottom listed as a “Non-Signatory Participant” with an asterisk noting that “Taiwan has endorsed the Pax Silica declaration principles via the Joint Statement on the Pax Silica Declaration and US-Taiwan Economic Security Cooperation.”
Such is Taiwan’s international standing that, despite being a key player in the “AI ecosystem of tomorrow,” it participates only through a separate endorsement rather than as a signatory.
DESTINATION: PHILIPPINES
Lin’s “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor” remains ill-defined, but two things jump out. One is the addition of a Cebu office, and the other is his comment about “abundant land and a high-quality workforce.”
Cebu is far from Luzon geographically, but its central location makes it a major hub for domestic shipping and inter-island logistics. It is possible that Lin’s strategic calculation is to use his economic corridor plan to extend the US-Japan-Philippines efforts geographically in a way that is both complementary, but separate enough that it highlights Taiwan’s importance.
Taiwan lacks land and is increasingly desperate for a “high-quality workforce,” so, unsurprisingly, Lin sees the opportunities.
Quietly, but increasingly, Taiwan’s entire manufacturing ecosystem has grown reliant on Filipino talent. Contrary to expectations, this is happening at every level, from the lowest-tech to the highest.
The National Immigration Agency’s August report lists 214,806 Filipinos in Taiwan. The majority work in manufacturing, often starting at low-level positions. However, over time they become essential skilled technicians and managers, able to communicate in Mandarin, English and Tagalog.
Lin is likely counting on this for his “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor.” Many Taiwanese investors already have a solid base of well-trained Filipino experts who know how to run their factory floors and manage the business.
Though exact numbers are not available, older estimates put the number of Filipinos working in white-collar high-tech positions in the low thousands, but this number is likely higher today. When I used to live near the Central Taiwan Science Park, it was not uncommon to run into Filipino engineers and technicians.
Crucially, more are being trained and prepared for just such roles. According to a July press release from the Ministry of Education, the number of Filipino students in Taiwan rose 78.7 percent between 2022 and last year, reaching 5,536. They are primarily studying engineering, information and communication technology (ICT), manufacturing, business management and medical and health sciences.
The AI ecosystem and supply chains stretch across the planet. A Filipino engineer or ICT expert trained in Taiwan, with Mandarin skills and excellent English is worth their weight in gold both locally, and even more so if they want to expand into the Philippines or English-speaking nations such as the US.
Much of China’s manufacturing dominance was originally built on Taiwanese expertise and capital, but once trained and capitalized, China favored local competitors over the Taiwanese investors. Taiwanese investment helped Malaysia develop into a significant mid-tier player in the semiconductor industry, and continues to fuel Vietnam’s growth in manufacturing.
Lin’s “Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor” has potential. Taiwan has the know-how, abundant capital, a desperate need for cheap land, energy and water and access to significant Filipino human capital to make it all work. With a presence in Manila in Luzon and future presence in the key logistics node of Cebu, Taiwan will be well positioned to facilitate investment expansion.
However, much depends on the Philippines making itself a desirable investment destination. Reviews vary widely in their assessment. In 2018 the US News & World Report named the Philippines as the “best country to invest in,” and CEO Magazineranked it seventh out of the top 10 best countries in 2020. Less positively, the Philippines ranked 95th out of 190 countries in the 2020 World Bank Report on Doing Business, though that was a jump of 29 spots from the year prior.
Ramped up interest by the US and Japan in investing in the Philippines could help smooth the way. Their financial and diplomatic muscle could pressure the Philippines to continue to make positive changes in its investment environment.

Donovan is also the central Taiwan correspondent at ICRT FM100 Radio News, co-publisher of Compass Magazine, co-founder Taiwan Report (report.tw) and former chair of the Taichung American Chamber of Commerce. Follow him on X: @donovan_smith.

Arsenal on Tuesday suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood Town in an EFL League Cup penalty shoot-out.
Mikel Arteta’s side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time.
Arsenal’s Bruno Guimaraes’s penalty was saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood’s winner.
Photo: Reuters
Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalized after the interval.
Arsenal’s 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages.
Arteta paid the price for prioritizing Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly.
No one would have predicted Arsenal’s embarrassment regardless of Arteta’s selection gamble.
They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday, but instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club’s glittering history.
The Gunners boss conceded Arsenal could have no complaints, admitting it was a painful moment in his reign.
“First of all, congratulations to Fleetwood for going through the next round. The manner that they have done it, and for us a very sad day,” Arteta said.
“There is nothing to criticize the players for their attitude, their application,” he said. “The determination, you could see that was there from the start, even with 10 men, but we conceded a really poor goal to start with that gave them some momentum.”
Fleetwood made a mockery of the 84 places between the clubs in the English soccer system with a defiant display that stopped Arsenal establishing any momentum.
Their refusal to be overawed by Arsenal’s star power was a tribute to Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor, who won the tactical battle with Arteta by sitting deep and attacking on the counter.
“I just can’t believe it. The biggest night in the club’s history in terms of opposition coming to town and we’ve managed to beat the champions,” Lawlor said.
“We’re not stupid enough and not egotistical enough that you think we’re going to outplay the best team in the country and the most organized team in the country,” he said. “So we had to ride our luck, we had to deny space, we had to deny options for them, and I think we did that really, really well in terms of the majority of the game.”

Ministry, school sign MOU on smart forest governance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:58 UTC
01:41:58 KST

The Ministry of Environment and the National Taipei University of Technology yesterday signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) on smart urban forest governance, with a demonstration site set up near the university.
Minister of Environment Peng Chi-ming (彭啟明) said trees are part of climate resilience infrastructure and require scientific methods to develop.
The cooperation between the ministry and the university focuses on smart energy saving and climate resilience governance, and is expected to set an example for smart urban forest governance, he said.
Photo: Wu Po-hsuan, Taipei Times
It can be divided into four main aspects: using scientific data, and light detection and ranging technology for sustainable governance; promoting circular reuse of critical process waste from semiconductor manufacturing; adopting in-depth energy saving powered by artificial intelligence; and developing climate resilience professionals through interdisciplinary exchanges, Peng said.
The key to urban forest governance lies in respect for life and cultural foundation, he said.
A simulation driven by a digital twin system would be introduced to demonstrate the benefits of lower temperatures for urban pedestrians, Peng said.
University president Jen Yi-jun (任貽均) said the school has long been dedicated to microclimate monitoring, environmental engineering, smart power grid and research on energy conservation in air-conditioning systems.
The university would use scientific research capabilities, and capitalize on its alumni and experience in revitalizing Chienkuo Brewery (建國啤酒廠) — a historical heritage building in Taipei — to develop the demonstration site, he said.
Minister of Culture Li Yuan (李遠) said his ministry would help include the city’s Air Force Command Headquarters National Cultural Base in the demonstration site for urban forest development.
Each tree carries the history, cultures and memories of locals, he said, adding that the urban forest project is expected to restore trees and cultures.
Meanwhile, a recent rise in the number of trees removed across Taipei has sparked public outrage and raised questions about the city government.
Asked about the issue, Peng said he protested the felling of old camphor trees when he was young.
The environment ministry’s proposed specialized urban forestry act would treat urban trees as vital public infrastructure and living entities, he said.
Public notification would be required before their removal, and treatment for diseased trees would be mandatory instead of immediately felling trees, Peng said, adding that it aimed to curb arbitrary tree felling nationwide.
Additional reporting by Wu Po-hsuan

India vows ‘swift action’ after rare cheetah shot dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

India has vowed “swift action” after a cheetah was shot dead, the first such killing since the country began reintroducing the animals in 2022, the Indian government said yesterday.
The Indian Ministry of Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change said that it had ordered a “high-level team for an on-ground investigation” into the shooting of the 19-month-old male, treating the incident with “utmost gravity.”
The India-born cheetah — whose mother was among those introduced to India from Botswana, Namibia and South Africa as part of efforts to restore the planet’s fastest land animal — was shot as it prowled in forests outside a protected national park.
Photo: Reuters
Asiatic cheetahs were declared extinct in India in 1952. The critically endangered subspecies, once found across the Middle East, Central Asia and India, now survives in very small numbers in Iran.
Their African cousins were first reintroduced in September 2022 to India, to the Kuno National Park, 300km south of New Delhi.
The wounded cheetah was picked up on Sunday in forests in Madhya Pradesh state, outside Kuno’s boundaries, and taken for veterinary care.
“During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body,” the ministry said.
Despite efforts, the cheetah died on Tuesday, it said.
“Medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the recovered firearm pellets,” it added.
The high-profile project, championed by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, has been dogged by criticism over the deaths of several of the cats.
However, experts in animal reintroductions say they often result in more than 50 percent mortality, especially in the initial phases.
The National Tiger Conservation Authority, which oversees the cheetah project, said that survival rates and hunting successes are “comparable to other international cheetah reintroduction efforts, with recorded wild prey kills confirming successful adaptation to the Indian landscape.”
The total cheetah population in the wild in India is about 60, including about 40 Indian-born cheetahs.

Taiwan’s representative in Geneva, Greg Lee (李冠德), has been removed from his post after an investigation found that he had engaged in workplace bullying, while Taiwan’s ambassador to the Marshall Islands, Hsu Wei-ming (徐蔚民), has returned home and is to leave his post, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) said yesterday.
Lee has returned to Taiwan and is working at the ministry’s Taipei headquarters, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry’s comments came after local media reported earlier yesterday that the Cabinet had approved its recommendation to recall Lee to Taipei, and that he began working at the Department of Treaty and Legal Affairs on Monday.
Photo: Lo Pei-de, Taipei Times
Lee’s removal from his post in Geneva followed a determination by an ad hoc investigative team formed by the ministry that he had engaged in workplace bullying.
According to the team’s findings, released on Oct. 7, Lee was found to have frequently “shouted and yelled” during meetings and repeatedly criticized or obstructed some of his subordinates in the office.
The team concluded that Lee had abused his position of power, exceeded the necessary and reasonable scope of his duties, and continuously created a hostile work environment through threats, offenses, insults or other means, thereby harming the physical and mental health of office staff who filed complaints.
Lee was also accused of misusing public resources for personal purposes in late July.
The ministry did not say if those allegations were being investigated.
Meanwhile, amid controversy over a proposed Double Ten National Day drag show, the ministry yesterday confirmed that Hsu had returned and would leave his post.
Local media reported earlier this month that the ministry had rejected Hsu’s suggestion for the Oct. 10 performance as “inappropriate.”
Hsu later came under bipartisan criticism when a video of a rehearsal for the event emerged, showing him lying astride a wooden bed carried aloft by eight Marshallese men acting as litter bearers.
Asked about the incident during a legislative session yesterday, Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs Director-General Michael Lin (林昭宏) said he and Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs Baushuan Ger (葛葆萱) had informed Hsu that, as an ambassador, he was expected to wear formal attire and maintain a solemn demeanor when addressing attendees and hosting the National Day celebrations.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) told the same session that the ministry had managed to “avert a major controversy.”
Lin said that the ministry had recalled Hsu to clarify the incident and held reviews to ensure that a similar incident would not happen again, adding that Taiwan had remained in close contact with the Marshall Islands government over the incident.
“It was purely the personal behavior of the ambassador — and the Marshall Islands, once apprised of the situation, expressed full support for how Taiwan handled the matter,” he said.
The incident would not affect bilateral ties, Lin added.
Hsu took up the ambassadorial post in December last year.
The Taiwanese embassy in the Marshall Islands is currently headed by its second-in-command, minister Hank Liu (劉漢清), the ministry said.

Runners swap streets for malls in Singapore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

The pounding of shoes echoed through a Singapore shopping mall as runners desperate to train take refuge from choking haze.
Smoke from wildfires in neighboring Indonesia has sent air quality in the city-state plummeting to its worst levels in more than a decade in the past few weeks, canceling outdoor activities.
Those seeking exercise, including runners training for international events, have found an unconventional alternative: air-conditioned shopping malls.
Photo: AFP
On Saturday, more than 80 runners turned the corridors of the Marina Square shopping center into makeshift running tracks, clocking laps past storefronts on two floors before shops opened for business.
There are strict rules.
“No sprinting, no overtaking, no shouting or yelling,” Eugene Beh, 52, founder of Singapore Runners Club, told about 60 members before their run.
Spitting and wiping sweat on the floor are also banned.
Beh said they had to cancel several runs outdoors because of the haze, blown in by the wind from forest and peatland fires in Borneo and Sumatra.
Angeline Zeng, 57, who works in banking, completed 10 loops at the mall, or about 10km.
With a half-marathon in Taipei in less than a week and a full marathon in December, Zeng needs to clock as much mileage as she can.
As treadmills at her neighborhood gym are often full, she and her fellow runners were excited when they heard about the mall runs.
“We were like, wow, we didn’t expect that at all,” she said.
“I love it because the air-con makes you feel like you’re running overseas where there’s cold temperatures, so it’s really great,” Zeng added.
However, circling inside the mall becomes “boring” after a while, she said.
“Maybe for shorter runs this is OK, but if you need to do long runs, maybe not so suitable,” she said.
Singapore Runners Club member Doris Tan, 42, said she thought running indoors would be a bit suffocating.
“I didn’t expect it to be so cool ... but if you have to ask me, I still prefer outdoors,” she said.
Paul Wong, a 54-year-old retiree from a club called X-Run, completed 21 loops inside the mall, or about 21km.
With just more than a month until the Singapore International Marathon — which many other fellow runners are also training for — Wong would have to run up to 80km per week, but the haze has forced him indoors.
“For the last two weeks I’ve been running close to 100km on the treadmill. The longest I’ve run is 28km for two-and-a-half hours; it’s very mental,” Wong said.
“The mall run is definitely better because the treadmill feels like a hamster run. You just keep repeating the routine,” he said.
Eddie Chang, lead coach for X-Run, said they had to present a carefully laid-out plan to get approval from the mall for the runs.
They had to consider factors like walkway width, tight corners and holding the run early in the morning before the shops open.
“The biggest challenge for outdoor training is the weather. Humidity is very high, plus the haze now, the impact is doubled and tripled, so it’s very hard to manage,” Chang said. “By converting to indoors, you definitely reduce all the impact from the outdoor experience and continue running.”
The air quality improved this week, but yesterday, Singapore remained one of the 20 most polluted major cities in the world, according to Swiss-based air quality monitor IQAir.
The two running clubs are likely to extend the mall runs if poor air quality persists, and plan to ask more malls to open their doors to them.
“I believe there will be opportunities. This is something new in the sports scene,” Beh said. “Hopefully, with the permission of building management, this can spread out to other sports groups.”

China’s BRI crisis in South Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:54 UTC
01:41:54 KST

China Merchants Port Holdings, a state-owned Chinese port operator, withdrew from a proposed US$392 million joint venture to develop a logistics hub in Sri Lanka’s Port of Colombo this month, renewing questions about the viability of China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in South Asia. The development recalls the controversy surrounding Hambantota port, which Sri Lanka leased to a Chinese company for 99 years in 2017 amid mounting financial pressures.
However, the difficulties extend beyond Sri Lanka in South Asia and point to a common problem: the gap between the BRI’s promise of economic transformation and the conditions required to realize it. Pakistan provides the clearest illustration of this dilemma. The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) was designed to connect China’s Xinjiang region with Pakistan’s Arabian Sea coast through transport infrastructure, energy projects and the strategic Port of Gwadar. However, persistent economic instability, energy-sector liabilities and financing difficulties have complicated its implementation.
Security poses an additional obstacle. Attacks on Chinese nationals and projects, particularly in Balochistan, have increased the costs and risks of protecting Chinese investments. The broader lesson is that infrastructure investment does not automatically generate sufficient revenue to service debt or produce sustainable development. Although Pakistan remains strategically important to Beijing, close political relations have proved insufficient to guarantee the economic success of major infrastructure commitments.
Bangladesh illustrates the importance of domestic political change. Chinese investment has supported infrastructure and industrial development, making Beijing an important economic partner. However, the removal of Sheikh Hasina’s government in August 2024 created a new political environment for Dhaka’s external relationships. The implications for China’s position should not be overstated: Political change does not automatically mean that a country would abandon existing investments or partnerships. Nevertheless, it demonstrates that agreements reached under one government do not guarantee continuity of strategic priorities under its successors.
Bangladesh’s challenge is to retain the economic benefits of Chinese investment while diversifying its external partnerships and preserving diplomatic autonomy. Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s trip to Japan on Monday has added a new dimension to the evolving Bangladesh-China ties. For Beijing, the lesson is that access to political elites and strong relations with an incumbent government cannot substitute for broader political legitimacy or guarantee that its long-term interests would remain unaffected by domestic transitions.
Nepal reveals a different limitation: the difficulty of translating geographical proximity into practical connectivity. Its engagement with the BRI reflects an ambition to diversify transport and trade links beyond traditional routes through India. However, difficult Himalayan terrain, high infrastructure costs, financing questions and the practical challenges of cross-border transport have complicated this ambition. Nepal’s dependence on transit access through India also limits the extent to which Chinese connectivity projects can transform its economic geography in the short term.
Therefore the central challenge is not simply whether Nepal and China can reach political agreements, but whether those commitments can produce commercially viable, financially sustainable and operationally viable infrastructure. Announced projects and signed agreements should not be confused with completed transport links or economically productive connectivity. Nepal demonstrates that geography, costs and implementation capacity can constrain the strategic value of infrastructure even when political intentions are aligned.
The Maldives highlights the interaction between infrastructure investment, domestic politics and regional strategic competition. Chinese-backed infrastructure and closer diplomatic relations have become part of the country’s wider debate over foreign influence, economic dependence and national sovereignty. Changes in domestic political priorities can alter the emphasis of the Maldives’ external partnerships without necessarily producing a complete break with Beijing.
As a small island state situated in a strategically important part of the Indian Ocean, the Maldives must balance economic opportunities with the need to preserve its decisionmaking autonomy and maintain relations with competing regional powers, particularly India and China. Chinese investment can generate commercial opportunities and diplomatic access, but neither guarantees an uncontested sphere of influence. The Maldivian experience underlines the importance of local political choices in determining the durability of Beijing’s regional partnerships.
These cases reveal the limits of treating the BRI as a uniform model of regional development. Pakistan illustrates the interaction of economic vulnerability and insecurity; Sri Lanka highlights financial exposure and questions of commercial viability; Bangladesh demonstrates the significance of political transitions; Nepal exposes geographical and implementation constraints; and the Maldives shows how domestic politics and strategic balancing shape the influence that China can exercise. These differences matter as much as the similarities. They suggest that the BRI’s outcomes depend not only on the resources China commits, but also on recipient countries’ economic conditions, institutional capacities and political choices.
India’s opposition adds another dimension to Beijing’s difficulties. New Delhi rejects the CPEC because it traverses territories claimed by India and remains concerned about China’s expanding presence in its neighborhood and the Indian Ocean. India has sought to strengthen regional connectivity and economic partnerships, including through the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, announced in 2023. The BRI’s predicament in South Asia is best understood, hence, as a crisis of conversion: the difficulty of translating infrastructure investment into sustainable development and durable geopolitical influence. China remains a major regional actor, and not all of its projects have failed.
Moreover, the future of the BRI would depend less on the scale of Beijing’s commitments than on the value those commitments ultimately deliver.
Sumit Kumar is a Ministry of Foreign Affairs visiting fellow at National Chengchi University and an assistant professor in Delhi University’s Department of Political Science.

Rays stun Brewers to force Game 5
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:41:53 UTC
01:41:53 KST

Milwaukee was three outs from its first World Series title in a game that stretched well past midnight yesterday when Junior Caminero started the bottom of the 12th inning with a grounder to third. Thousands of Brewers fans who trekked to Tropicana Field to witness the long-awaited moment started to cheer.
Not so fast.
Third baseman Joey Ortiz bounced the throw, and the ball glanced off first baseman Jake Bauers’ mitt for an error.
Photo: AP
One of the most stunning rallies in World Series history started to unfold.
Liam Hicks, Jonny DeLuca, Chandler Simpson and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson followed with consecutive singles in a 15-pitch span against rookie Shane Drohan, and the Tampa Bay Rays staved off elimination with a 4-3 win that forced Game 5.
“Sometimes the game tests you. Sometimes the game makes you want to dig deep,” Brewers captain Christian Yelich said. “It’s all part of the journey, all part of the experience, and that’s part of our story.”
Milwaukee rookie Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th for a 3-2 lead, sending the Brewers sprinting out of the dugout in excitement as they sensed completing the first Series sweep since 2012.
Milwaukee’s bullpen, led by seven outs from Aaron Ashby, had combined for seven straight scoreless innings, before Caminero reached against Antonio Senzatela.
Ortiz grimaced.
“I’ve got to make that play,” he said. “Just no excuse about it.”
Caminero appeared to hurt his left foot, but stayed in the game.
Brewers manager Pat Murphy brought in Drohan, a 27-year-old left-hander who had not pitched since a one-inning start in Game 4 of the National League Championship Series on Oct. 15.
With Pratt shifted toward second for the left-handed batter, Hicks hit an opposite-field grounder through the vacated shortstop hole and into left field as Caminero slid headfirst into third.
“For just regular D, that’s right at Coop,” Drohan said of the defensive alignment.
Pinch-runner Cedric Mullins replaced Caminero before DeLuca, who had made sparkling catches to deny Yelich in the third and William Contreras in the fourth, hit a grounder past the mound as Drohan tried in vain to make a behind-the-back snag. The ball bounced into center as Mullins tied the score at three.
Nick Fortes ran at second for the slower Hicks. After missing a bunt attempt and pulling back another while taking a called strike, Simpson lined a single into center, loading the bases.
Sal Frelick moved in from left to form a five-man infield, with three defenders on the left side and everyone playing in.
Williamson, who had been 1 for 15 in the post-season, batted for Victor Mesa Jr.
“It’s what you dream of as a player to be in that spot,” Williamson said.
On the game’s 367th pitch, he hit a chopper that kicked up chalk from the foul line 2m from home plate. The ball bounded high over Bauers and onto the grass in short right field. Fortes sprinted across the plate with the winning run, then headed toward first to join his jumping teammates in foul territory.
“That was totally what I told him to do,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said, drawing laughs.
Drohan walked off, his head bowed.
“Definitely hard. I’m human,” he said softly. “I knew what I was walking into. I just didn’t do the job there.”
Tampa Bay became the fourth team in World Series history to avoid elimination with an extra-inning comeback, according to OptaSTATS, joining the 1912 Boston Red Sox, 1986 New York Mets and 2011 St Louis Cardinals — who all went on to win titles.
“We’ve got a lot of fight in us. We’re never going to shy away,” Simpson said. “We were going to keep fighting until the end — the last inning, the last out, the last play, the last pitch.”
Tampa Bay became just the fifth of 26 teams that fell behind 3-0 in the World Series to win Game 4. The previous four lost Game 5.
Of 43 teams to trail 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason matchup, the only one that rebounded to win was the Boston Red Sox against the New York Yankees in the 2004 American League Championship Series.
“It just shows the resiliency of this group,” Williamson said. “We continue to fight, and that’s been the motto this series and this full season, is just fight.”

====================================================================================================

Principle of neutrality not a ban on free speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

The Chiayi-based troupe Our Theatre (阮劇團) earlier this month performed the play Louder! (噪音風暴) at Taipei’s Wellspring Theater. The troupe set up a public bulletin at the venue, where an audience member posted a campaign sticker of Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋). Taipei Department of Cultural Affairs Commissioner Tsai Shih-ping (蔡詩萍) asked the troupe to remove the sticker, saying that municipal regulations forbid partisan messages in publicly owned venues.
While this might appear as a dispute over venue management, it raises a fundamental question for democratic societies: Is administrative neutrality a principle designed to constrain the exercise of public power, or a pretext for interfering with citizens’ right to political expression?
The legislative purpose of the Act Governing the Administrative Impartiality of Public Officials (公務人員行政中立法) is to ensure that civil servants maintain political neutrality in the performance of their official duties and prevent them from using their authority or public resources to support specific candidates. It was never intended to require citizens to give up their right to political expression. How, then, can members of the public posting stickers on a theater troupe’s bulletin board to express their political views be equated with government agencies using public authority or funds to campaign for a candidate? Conflating the two obscures the law’s original intent, turning a principle designed to prevent the abuse of power into justification for restricting people’s rights.
Public cultural venues certainly need rules governing their use, but the authorities responsible for managing them must have a clear legal basis for exercising that authority. If a venue has established clear and lawful regulations, they should be applied consistently. However, if the Department of Cultural Affairs ordered the removal of the sticker simply because am audience member expressed their political views, it should explain the legal basis for the order, venue management rules and the necessity of such restrictions.
What is particularly concerning is that the Department of Cultural Affairs controls access to public venues and cultural funding. Even a seemingly friendly “reminder” might exert pressure on independent arts groups that rely on public-sector resources to operate, given the power imbalance between the two parties. Even without an explicit ban, authorities’ actions might lead theater companies to avoid politically sensitive topics out of concern that their access to future funding might be affected. When creators begin to restrict themselves to protect their own interests, a chilling effect can quietly take hold. The department should publicly explain the basis for asking the troupe to remove the sticker and subject its actions to public scrutiny, rather than simply dismissing the matter as a well-intentioned reminder.
The cultural essence of a democratic city lies in respecting differences and embracing diverse voices, not categorically forbidding political symbols. If the Department of Cultural Affairs truly seeks to uphold the principle of administrative neutrality, it should administer clear regulations and consistent standards rather than acting solely on assumptions. Rules governing the use of public venues are undoubtedly necessary, but such rules must not become a rationale for restricting political expression.
Yeh Yu-cheng is a secretary at the Pingtung County Public Health Bureau.

In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

People riding light electric two-wheelers under the influence of drugs would soon face tougher sanctions under an amendment to the Road Traffic Management and Penalty Act (道路交通管理處罰條例) proposed by the Ministry of Transportation and Communications.
The changes aim to address a rise in drug-impaired driving cases and related issues, the ministry said in a report to the legislature’s Transportation Committee.
The stricter penalties include confiscating the vehicle and license plate of light electric two-wheeler riders if they refuse to stop for inspection or undergo a drug test, the ministry said.
Photo: Huang Liang-chieh, Taipei Times
Drunk-driving cases involving light electric two-wheelers increased by 270 in the first nine months of the year, up 17 percent from the same period last year, it said.
Drug-impaired riding cases surged from 71 to 580, with the number of riders who refused to undergo drug tests also rising by 334, the ministry said, citing data collected by the National Police Agency.
Drug-impaired cases involving light electric two-wheelers have increased significantly since on-the-spot saliva drug screening kits became available last year, greatly enhancing efficiency in cracking down on drug-impaired riders, it said.
The ministry plans to submit the proposal to the Executive Yuan for further review next month, it said.
The police agency said the notification period to claim confiscated vehicles would be shortened from three months to one month, which would take effect on Saturday.
Some owners of confiscated vehicles failed to claim them before the notification period ended, while others had no intention of taking them back, it said.
This has affected the efficiency of vehicle impound lots, limited their capacity and increased their management and maintenance costs, it added.

Hualien Radar Weather Station to hold open house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:48 UTC
01:41:48 KST

The Hualien Radar Weather Station is holding an open house on Saturday to mark its 60th anniversary, with interactive exhibits to introduce the technology it uses to track weather and protect Taiwan from natural disasters.
The open house, called “2026 Kiss Science” and organized by the Central Weather Administration (CWA) and the National Science and Technology Council, will run from 9am to 5pm, with guided tours scheduled throughout the day.
People do not need to register in advance and can freely explore exhibitions and participate in activities, the organizers said, inviting the public to seize the rare opportunity to explore the famous weather facility, also known as “the eye of the east.”
Photo: Wang Ching-yi, Taipei Times
The station is along Hualien City’s coastline and features a 30m radar tower and a white dome. It has become one of the city’s landmarks.
Hualien is on the front lines of typhoons making landfall in Taiwan and is prone to natural disasters such as earthquakes and floods, station director Yu Jui-ching (余瑞清) said.
The station’s fourth-generation dual-polarization Doppler weather radar, the METEOR 1700SDP, can transmit horizontal and vertical electromagnetic waves, Yu said.
It can conduct precise, high-resolution observations when a typhoon comes within 460km of Taiwan’s east coast, tracking the movement of precipitation to provide disaster response agencies with timely, accurate rainfall data for flood warnings, they said.
Since the station opened in 1966, it has been one of the CWA’s most restricted facilities, the agency’s event Web site said.
More than 40 specialists from the agency’s headquarters have designed the guided tours and interactive activities for the open house, the CWA said.
Visitors can take part in science experiments, including demonstrations of radar remote sensing and atmospheric pressure, and get a close-up look at a mobile weather radar that is expected to begin monitoring the Mataian River (馬太鞍溪) next year to fill gaps in rainfall observation data in eastern Taiwan, it said.
People can also play a weather-themed board game that introduces meteorological technology and earthquake monitoring through hands-on activities, it added.
The station is a key part of Taiwan’s nationwide weather radar network, and would continue monitoring weather and threats in eastern Taiwan to protect the public and their property, Yu said.
Opened in 1966 after Typhoon Gloria exposed gaps in radar coverage off eastern Taiwan, the radar station is the first of its kind in Taiwan.
Its construction received substantial funding from the UN Special Fund and a plaque bearing the words “United Nations” remains at the station, preserving a rare piece of Taiwan’s diplomatic and meteorological history.
The station also preserves a collection of vintage observation equipment and historical records from times when early meteorologists relied on their expertise and determination to protect Taiwan in the absence of automated equipment, computers and the Internet.
The open house would display several historical records for the first time, including the earliest hand-drawn radar echo map, dated Aug. 19, 1966, the first hand-drawn record of a typhoon observation, documenting Typhoon Cora on Sept. 4 that year; and the oldest black-and-white radar photograph, taken during Typhoon Clara on July 10, 1967.

EDITORIAL: A second shot at preparedness
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:45 UTC
01:41:45 KST

The military has introduced a new combat training framework this year to improve readiness against the threat from China, the Central News Agency reported on Sunday.
Combat Training Center 2.0 (CTC 2.0) replaces scripted exercises with unscripted scenarios that require troops to respond to unexpected enemy movement and coordinate with other units. The nine-week program includes live-fire exercises, laser engagement systems to simulate combat outcomes, digital tools for sharing battlefield information and reviews.
The approach brings Taiwan closer to the realistic, adaptive training methods used by advanced Western militaries. It could significantly improve combat readiness by teaching troops to adapt when plans break down, coordinate across units and make decisions under pressure. Digital tracking and realistic engagement simulations could also expose weaknesses that scripted demonstrations might miss, allowing the military to address them before a conflict.
However, the extent of the improvement would depend on how rigorously the exercises are conducted, whether lessons lead to changes in tactics and equipment, and how well the training translates into operational performance. CTC 2.0 is not necessarily the nation’s biggest advance in military preparedness, but it represents a meaningful shift toward testing how forces perform under realistic conditions.
The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in military operations adds another dimension to this challenge. AI can help commanders process intelligence, identify emerging threats, assess potential courses of action and coordinate forces more quickly. Taiwan is well positioned to benefit from these advances, because it plays a central role in manufacturing the world’s most advanced AI chips. However, access to advanced chips and AI models alone does not guarantee battlefield superiority; the key is integrating them effectively into military operations.
That technological advantage also creates vulnerabilities. Disruptions to Taiwan’s undersea communications cables, including incidents involving China-linked vessels, have highlighted the risks to the infrastructure supporting its digital economy and military communications.
In a conflict, attacks on undersea cables, power supplies, data centers and communications networks could cut military units off from AI tools. Many advanced AI applications rely on cloud services, remote servers and distributed computing, all of which could become inaccessible if networks are damaged or power supplies fail. AI systems designed to operate locally on military hardware could reduce this dependence, but they would not eliminate the risks posed by damaged equipment, depleted power supplies or lost sensor data.
Officers and troops must be able to fight effectively without advanced technology. AI-assisted systems could provide a significant advantage when available, but personnel must still be able to assess threats, interpret incomplete information, coordinate with nearby units and act on their commanders’ intent without digital support. Unscripted exercises such as CTC 2.0 could help develop these skills if they deliberately simulate communications blackouts, disrupted intelligence feeds and the loss of AI assistance. The objective should be a military that combines AI’s speed and analytical power with the adaptability, initiative and judgement of its people.
The US remains a crucial military partner for Taiwan, providing arms, training and advice to help bolster the nation’s defenses. Although it is unclear whether US input directly influenced the adoption of CTC 2.0, the shift creates an opportunity for the two sides to deepen their cooperation in developing increasingly realistic, unscripted exercises. Combining Taiwan’s knowledge of its own operating environment with US expertise in large-scale combat training could help develop approaches tailored to the challenges of a conflict in the Taiwan Strait.
Ultimately, advanced weapons, AI and digital battlefield systems would remain important to the nation’s defense, but technology alone cannot guarantee success. Equipment can be destroyed, communications disrupted and AI systems rendered inaccessible. Well-trained personnel who can think independently, adapt to changing circumstances and continue operating under pressure are indispensable.
By moving away from scripted demonstrations toward realistic, unpredictable combat training, Taiwan acknowledges that its military readiness depends not only on the technology it possesses, but also on its ability to use that technology effectively — and to fight when it is no longer available. CTC 2.0 represents a promising step in that direction, provided the nation sustains the approach, learns from its shortcomings and continues refining its training in cooperation with experienced partners such as the US.
Taiwan heads to the polls next month for local elections. Beneath the campaign ads lies a deeper question: What do we call this place and who gets to decide? In the pages of the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), that question has been playing out across three centuries. The entries for “Formosa” and “Taiwan” chart an island’s journey from colonial fantasy to self-named reality. Names are rarely neutral; they are the first act of possession. Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.
There are two space races that the democracies must win: one to deter military campaigns near Earth, and the other to secure positional deterrence on the Moon and beyond. The good news is that the US is engaged in both races, which will also benefit US allies and partners in Asia, including Taiwan. On Sept. 14, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink disclosed, “...the US now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action.” No details about these “space control weapons” have yet been disclosed. Taiwan inflation could rise if energy subsidies end: Central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:45 UTC
