The new ‘Sense and Sensibility’ channels our money anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:11 UTC
01:41:11 KST

“What have wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?” teenaged Marianne Dashwood rhetorically asks in Jane Austen’s 1811 novel Sense and Sensibility.
Her prudent sister Elinor replies: “Grandeur has but little, but wealth has much to do with it.”
Elinor’s wise answer seems to have served as the north star for a new film adaptation, directed by Georgia Oakley and written by Diana Reid. Austen is a regular source material for filmmakers, but the most resonant retellings of her work tend to reflect their era. This latest one, released in US theaters last week, does more to highlight the Dashwood sisters’ financial precarity — a smart creative choice that shows an understanding of what moviegoing audiences are especially attuned to now.
It is clear from the get-go that the girls are extremely short of funds following the death of their father. There are bills they cannot pay. They have been all but evicted from their stately home by its new owners: their half-brother and his odious wife. Elinor writes letter after letter to try and find an affordable cottage. When she finally does secure one, it is dim and cramped — a familiar fate for many a modern renter.
To underline their fall from the 1 to the 99 percent, we subsequently see the Dashwoods growing their own crops, cooking their own food, doing their own laundry and even — unless my eyes deceived me — chopping their own wood. Perhaps it should be mandatory viewing for the tradwife-curious.
It is a harder fate than Austen herself devised for her heroines. However, dialing up the Dashwoods’ money troubles resonates at a time when many moviegoers are feeling the pinch of higher prices for essentials.
Women, always the primary audience for Austen films, feel this acutely. A Pew poll found US women are 11 points less likely than men to say they can pay all their bills; a different survey shows women 13 points more pessimistic about the labor market. Experts suggest women are overrepresented in jobs that could be automated by artificial intelligence.
So, the central problem of so many of Austen’s novels — what does a woman have to do to get a little financial security around here? — hits close to home.
The prosperous 1990s were a different story. The successful Austen adaptations of that era tended to be marketed as Regency rom-coms. Some even gave rise to other rom-coms: 1995’s Pride and Prejudice, which famously shows Colin Firth as Mr Darcy in a wet shirt, inspired the screwball Bridget Jones’ Diary books and films (which, of course, featured Firth again).
For the most part, these adaptations were also explicitly escapist, greeted by critics as nostalgic comfort-viewing for audiences nervously awaiting the turn of the millennium. Adaptations that reached for more gravitas or grappled explicitly with difficult topics — such as 1999’s Mansfield Park, which explicitly included the slave trade as a major theme — struggled to reach audiences of that era.
However, times change, and so do viewer expectations. By the 2005 adaptation of Pride and Prejudice, starring Keira Knightley, viewers were getting a different type of heroine — rather shouty and slightly tomboyish. That was the era of so-called girlboss feminism, when women were encouraged to overcome the odds through pluck, grit and power poses.
That version came out post-dot-com bust, but pre-Great Recession. It was a time when filmmakers were starting to have Austen’s women be more explicit about their financial fears.
“I’m 27 years old,” Charlotte Lucas says in that adaptation, justifying her decision to marry the odious — but financially stable — Mr Collins. “I’ve no money and no prospects. I’m already a burden to my parents, and I’m frightened.”
Those lines were improvised by British film icon Emma Thompson, who consulted on that script — and who won an Oscar for her screenplay for the 1995 version of Sense and Sensibility, in which she also co-starred. That adaptation, directed by Ang Lee (李安), does show the girls’ change in status, but as a much gentler comedown. Their sun-filled cottage is filled with art and knickknacks. They must economize on beef (relatable), but they still have live-in servants (not).
One scene that would have injected a frisson of real danger was eliminated before production began. Thompson had wanted to emphasize the Dashwoods’ vulnerability by showing a fox hunt — with a desperate vixen searching for an escape — but the idea was scrapped.
The 2026 version, by contrast, is crammed with such metaphors. A caged canary rides with the Dashwoods to their dank little cottage; we also get several close-ups of dead birds shot for dinner. Whether it is a grouse or a spouse, everyone is on the hunt for something.
Yet as dire as the Dashwoods’ straits are, it is clear that the answer is not to marry for money. The story is filled with cautionary characters who dug for gold and lived to regret it. Perhaps the film should also be mandatory viewing for TikTok girlies looking to become stay-at-home girlfriends.
Spoiler alert: In the end, Elinor gets her man. However, as punishment for choosing the penniless Elinor, his wealthy mother cuts him out of his inheritance. Grandeur he will not have, but he does find a stable job. In 2026, that is swoon-worthy.
Sarah Green Carmichael is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist and editor. Previously, she was an executive editor at Harvard Business Review. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Nowhere is this more evident than in the OED, where the two entries serve as a linguistic seismograph for one of the world’s most enduring geopolitical fault lines.

AI boom: ‘one Taiwan, two worlds’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:09 UTC
01:41:09 KST

Taiwan is experiencing an unprecedented economic boom on the surface. Despite surging GDP, stock market and artificial intelligence (AI) exports, why do more people feel they have not become wealthier? This contradictory issue cannot be avoided, and the answer lies in the “K-shaped economy.”
According to data from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, the economic growth rate reached 14.5 percent in the first half of this year, and is forecast to rise 11.05 percent for the full year. However, the income gap between the top and bottom 20 percent of households grew by 6.17 times last year. In other words, while the overall economy is surging, income distribution has not, and AI dividends are enjoyed by a select few.
The K-shaped economy is creating a phenomenon in which Taiwan experiences an economic polarization. At the top of the “K,” there is a minority dominated by AI, semiconductors, servers and high-tech exports. At the bottom, there lies a vast workforce in traditional manufacturing, small and medium-sized enterprises, and the massive service industry.
The nation is not facing an economic downturn, but rather a reshaping of key production factors amid an economic boom — including capital centralizing in high-return AI industries, more talent shifting to high-paying tech sectors, and a crowding-out effect in energy resources, such as electricity and green power. The Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research and industry studies warned that this structural polarization is widening.
This year’s World Inequality Report estimates that the top 10 percent in Taiwan hold approximately 61 percent of the nation’s wealth, while the top 1 percent hold 27 percent. This can explain the surreal disconnect between the booming stock market and grassroots public sentiment.
While the stock market is about capital returns and future profits, ordinary families focus on housing prices, rent, living costs, children’s education and monthly salaries — practical realities of what they can afford and spend. The wealthy with great assets can accumulate more wealth through reinvestment as asset values grow, but those without assets can only rely on wages to keep up with price hikes. The same economic growth figure tells different stories for different people.
The issue Taiwan faces is the lack of social mobility caused by the K-shaped economy. The wealthy are running ahead faster through the accumulation of capital, technology and assets, while the workers are struggling to make a living.
At a time when economic growth is primarily driven by a few industries, enterprises and asset holders, the more impressive the GDP becomes, the more divided society might feel. Therefore, a policy challenge is the only way to transform AI dividends from the “K-peak” of a few sectors into a “K-slope” for the overall economy.
How can the nation enable traditional industries to access transformation capital, allow small-and-medium enterprises to integrate into AI supply chains, boost productivity and wages in the service sector, and equip workers with genuine skills to transition careers? More importantly, how can it provide those without assets an opportunity to accumulate wealth or share the dividends of economic growth driven by the whole public?
While AI has boosted GDP, it has failed to deliver the fruits of such growth to every household. At the top of the “K,” Taiwan is finally riding the wave of today’s AI boom after years of hard work. At the bottom, it should pragmatically confront the pressing issue: resolving the contradictory polarization of “one Taiwan, two worlds.”
Jeff Wu is an economic observer.

Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:41:08 UTC
01:41:08 KST

This weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second-largest city, Novi Sad. The tragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-led protests across the country.
Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.
On Sunday, that was more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundingly defeated former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.
For well over a decade Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observers confirmed on Monday, the Serbian government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings would have been noted across a continent in which youth protest is challenging political priorities.
As in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition to unseat former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?” they put forward a student list of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70 percent — the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 — delivered them a comfortable majority.
What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public — including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vucic support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbia plunge toward the bottom of European corruption rankings.
Politically, the priority would be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. However, in the longer term there would be less straightforward debates to be had. Vucic’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. However, on foreign policy issues such as joining the EU and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.
As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Vucic’s Serbia, like Orban’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. However, now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.

Guardian and ITN have ‘duty to public and sources’ to publish sexual allegations against well-known figure, court hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:40:36 UTC
01:40:36 KST

Two news organisations have a duty to the public and their sources to publish allegations of exploitative sexual behaviour by a well-known figure despite claims he is “highly likely” to attempt suicide, the high court has heard.
The anonymous individual, known in court simply as PPT, is seeking an injunction against the Guardian and ITN to stop them publishing the allegations, which he denies.
His legal team have argued that publishing would be likely to lead to his death, after two previous attempts to take his own life.
However, the legal team for the media groups told the high court there were powerful “countervailing” considerations compelling them to publish the claims.
Gavin Millar KC, the lead barrister for the media outlets, said they had “not just the responsibility, but the duty to publish information we believe to be in the public interest”.
He argued the claimant had not taken the impact on the sources involved in the investigation “sufficiently into account”.
“They have made a substantial commitment to being contributors, and were extremely anxious for the publication and the broadcast to go ahead as soon as possible,” Millar said.
Many of the women making the allegations have been traumatised by PPT’s alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result, according to a written submission from the media groups.
It states: “They believe that it is important that their allegations are publicly aired so that other women are protected and the full nature of his conduct is disclosed, and in order to assist the sources to recover from their own experiences.”
It said the media outlets had credible evidence of seriously improper conduct “towards a large number of women over a prolonged period”, including potential criminal conduct.
Millar said if publication of the allegations were blocked, “our women contributors and others we are aware of” were likely to find “other ways to make their stories known publicly”.
He added that proceeding with publication through the Guardian and ITN would be the “best way to put the information into the public domain”.
The well-known figure is seeking to block publication of the allegations by citing article two of the European convention on human rights (ECHR), which relates to the right to life; article three, relating to “inhuman or degrading treatment”; and article eight, which protects the right to respect for private and family life.
However, the media companies argue that the European court of human rights, which enforces the ECHR, has never ruled in such a way that would cause these articles to apply in this case. They also argue countervailing rights under article 10, which protects the right to freedom of expression.
Millar said the investigation into PPT had spoken to more than 100 people, including 30 who gave first-hand accounts.
He told that court that since the Guardian and ITN first contacted PPT in May so he could respond to the allegations, deadlines had been repeatedly extended and unusual measures put in place in order to act responsibly, given PPT’s medical issues.
Millar said that “recognising the difficult and unusual nature of the case”, the media companies had then agreed to delay publication so that PPT could seek an injunction and have his case heard before a judge.
PPT’s legal team has previously told that court there was evidence his life would be endangered should the allegations be published.
A summary of an assessment of the claimant’s current wellbeing by an independent expert stated that he could not conclude either that suicide was inevitable if publication went ahead, or that psychiatric treatment could eliminate all risk.
The expert said that the risks could be lowered should the allegations be published while PPT was in an inpatient psychiatric setting.
The trial has now concluded, with Mr Justice Nicklin retiring to come to a ruling.

In the US, you can call or text the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline on 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor. In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found at befrienders.org

Dolores Huerta, Labor Leader and Civil Rights Icon, Dies at 96
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:40:11 UTC
01:40:11 KST

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded what became known as the United Farm Workers union to help secure better pay for laborers, has died at age 96.
Huerta’s team, in a statement shared through her foundation, said she passed away on Wednesday at home in Bakersfield, California, “surrounded by her close family.”
In a separate statement, Huerta's family remarked on the "incredible loss" and said they will "share plans to recognize and celebrate" her legacy at a future date. While a cause of death was not shared, the New York Times, citing family spokesperson Erik Olvera, said cancer was behind her passing.
Huerta, who campaigned for the rights of migrant laborers throughout the 1960s and '70s, is credited with coining the rallying cry “Sí, se puede”—“Yes, we can.” The phrase inspired generations and was famously adopted by former President Barack Obama, who presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012.
Upon receiving the award, Huerta credited the advice her mother had once given her: "If you see people that need help, you have an obligation to help them, and you shouldn't wait for people to ask." Huerta said that once she had acquired the necessary skills, she honored that obligation by teaching people "how to come together and be able to fight" for their rights.
“One of the few women lobbyists of her era, [Dolores] became a formidable advocate for people who could not afford one,” reads the obituary shared by Huerta’s foundation. “Her legislative victories included a California measure allowing driver’s license examinations in Spanish, the extension of Aid to Families with Dependent Children to California farmworker families, and disability insurance protections for agricultural workers.”
Huerta founded United Farm workers with Cesar Chavez in 1962 and served as its vice president for almost four decades. She worked closely with Chavez until his death in 1993. Earlier this year, Huerta came forward with allegations against Chavez, accusing him of having sexually abused her in the 1960s. “I have kept this secret long enough. My silence ends here,” said Huerta in a statement in March.
The abuse led to two pregnancies, Huerta said, explaining that she "chose to keep [the] pregnancies secret and, after the children were born, arranged for them to be raised by other families that could give them stable lives."
Huerta said she was driven to share her experiences after an investigation released by the New York Times revealed accusations that Chavez, a long-celebrated icon of the labor movement, groomed and sexually abused multiple girls and women who worked in the movement.
Huerta said she had "carried this secret" for so long because she feared speaking out would compromise her life’s work and risk all the progress made for laborers.
“The formation of a union was the only vehicle to accomplish and secure those rights and I wasn’t going to let Cesar or anyone else get in the way. I channeled everything I had into advocating on behalf of millions of farmworkers and others who were suffering and deserved equal rights," she explained.
In April, Huerta was named on TIME's list of the "100 Most Influential People of 2026." Her long-time friend and fellow activist, Gloria Steinem, who died in September, wrote a tribute acknowledging the recognition.
Celebrating Huerta for stepping forward, Steinem said: "We can all learn from the courage and conscience Dolores and others have modeled. The truth about Chavez reminds us to look honestly at the behavior of everyone, including our leaders, and to lend support to those who may be hurt by misused power... Dolores’ impact, like that of many other activists, will continue to guide us, regardless of the hurtful behavior of any one individual."
Family, recognition, and legacy
Dolores Clara Huerta (née Fernández) was born on April 10, 1930, in Dawson, New Mexico. She was the only daughter of Juan Fernández and Alicia Chávez. Her parents divorced when she was 3 and she later moved to Stockton, California, with her mother. She went on to study at the University of Pacific’s Delta College in Stockton, now known as San Joaquin Delta College.
Huerta married Ralph Head when she was in college. The marriage, out of which came two children, ended in divorce. She had five children with her second husband Ventura Huerta, whose surname she kept after they divorced. When Huerta was in her early 40s, she embarked upon a relationship with Richard Chavez, a brother of Cesar Chavez’s, and they were "life partners" until his passing in 2011. They had four children together, according to the New York Times.
In her decades spent campaigning on behalf of laborers, as well as her work supporting the rights of immigrants and women, Huerta was arrested more than 25 times for participating in, what her foundation describes as, "non-violent civil disobedience activities and strikes."
In 1988, when she was 58 years old, Huerta suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen after being beaten by baton-wielding members of the San Francisco police force during a protest against the policies of presidential candidate George H.W. Bush. Huerta and others filed a civil rights lawsuit in the U.S. District Court in San Francisco after they were injured.
Huerta's activism continued, and her foundation notes that "even in her 90s, Dolores could still be found at rallies, walking precincts, speaking to young organizers, and urging people to vote."
She has been honored numerous times over the years on account of her contributions to marginalized communities. In 1993, Huerta was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame. In the late '90s, former President Bill Clinton presented her with the Eleanor Roosevelt Award for Human Rights. In 2022, she won the Clinton Global Citizen Award, in recognition of her "trailblazing lifetime of public service advocating for the dignity and fundamental human rights of women, children, and working class people worldwide."
Huerta is survived by her family and also the foundation that bears her name. In 2003, Huerta returned to California’s Central Valley and started the Dolores Huerta Foundation, which cites its mission as "inspiring and organizing communities to build volunteer organizations empowered to pursue social justice.”
The foundation has said it plans to open the "Dolores Huerta Peace and Justice Cultural Center in the Central Valley" in 2027.
Tributes pour in for civil rights icon
In a moving statement, former President Obama remembered Huerta as one of his heroes.
Dolores spent "her life fighting for marginalized communities, even as she herself faced sexism and abuse—including, as she revealed earlier this year, from Cesar Chavez and others within her own movement," Obama said. "She also came up with a pretty good slogan, 'sí, se puede'—yes, we can—that I too often get credit for. But as usual, Dolores got there first."
The Congressional Hispanic Caucus remembered Huerta as someone who "defied definition." Referring to her as a "national and international icon," the group said: "Her legacy is woven into the fabric of our history. Her fight for justice will continue to inspire generations. Rest in power, hermana."
María Teresa Kumar, the co-founder and president of Voto Latino, an advocacy organization that aims to empower the next generation of Latino voters, celebrated Huerta's influence. “Dolores always saw the value and spirit in young people before the rest of the world was ready to," she said. "Because of her, our community has been empowered to be our own advocates.”
Fellow co-founder Rosario Dawson said that Huerta had "centered her life around doing good in this world and around the deep-rooted belief in leaving it better than we found it. It is now up to us to carry her legacy forward."
Championing Huerta's community work, California's Gov. Gavin Newsom said: "California—and the United States—would not be what we are today without her resolute spirit, her passion for justice and fairness, and her commitment to those overlooked and forgotten."
He recognized Huerta as having "represented the best of us" and said her "fight for gender equity, workers' rights, and civil rights paved the way for generations to come."
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi referred to Huerta as a "dear friend" and noted how her rallying cry had inspired "generations of Americans to believe in the power of collective action."
Alongside pictures of herself and Huerta, former Vice President Kamala Harris posted a personal tribute to social media.
"I was blessed to know Dolores for many years and proud to organize alongside my dear friend to champion working families and immigrant rights. I will always be grateful for her support and friendship," said Harris. "We will honor her legacy by continuing the fight for the dignity of every person."

Turkish investors ready to buy stake in $25B Akkuyu nuclear plant: Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:36:24 UTC
01:36:24 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said that Turkish investors were ready to acquire a stake in the Akkuyu nuclear power plant in southern Türkiye, as Moscow seeks partners for the multibillion-dollar project.
“We are building, operating and owning the plant. Some Turkish companies ... are ready to acquire a stake. We would welcome that,” Putin said on Wednesday, according to Interfax news agency, valuing the project at around $25 billion.
The plant is being developed by Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom and is financed by Russia.
Rosatom seeks partners to share investment burden
Russia and Türkiye signed an agreement in 2010 to build the plant, which will feature four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors. Construction began in 2018.
Rosatom, the plant’s sole owner, can sell up to a 49 percent stake to a partner, potentially helping distribute the substantial investment costs.
In April, Rosatom said it had opened new talks with Turkish companies on joint ownership of Akkuyu.
Earlier in October, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev said the negotiations were making progress.
First reactor target remains in focus
The project’s original commissioning target was 2023, but the schedule has been pushed back several times.
Rosatom now expects the first reactor to achieve its first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction before the end of this year, marking a key milestone towards bringing the plant into operation.
Akkuyu is a major element of Turkish-Russian energy cooperation, and potential Turkish investment would give local companies an opportunity to take part in a project currently financed by Russia.

Trump expands hunt for noncitizen voters with broad subpoena campaign before midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:36:06 UTC
01:36:06 KST

Trump expands hunt for non-citizen voters with broad subpoena campaign before midterms
Oct 28 - The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, part of an escalating effort ahead of next week’s midterm elections to uncover evidence of unlawful voting by people who aren’t US citizens.
Most of the subpoenas documented by Reuters were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known. It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest results in close midterm races, despite scant evidence that voting by noncitizens is widespread.
Reuters identified the subpoenas through public-records requests and interviews with local and state officials. Many were issued in Democratic strongholds, including Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Los Angeles and other California cities. But they also reach into Republican-leaning states with competitive races, including Texas, Kansas and Georgia.
At least 49 of the subpoenas were issued under the authority of grand juries, indicating they are tied to criminal investigations and making them generally harder to challenge in court than administrative subpoenas issued directly by federal agencies.
The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem that warrants the sweeping federal effort to identify and prosecute such cases, including through the deployment of hundreds of federal law enforcement agents. It has vowed to keep the effort a top priority. “The Trump administration is sending a clear message that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Reuters. “Only Americans should be electing America’s leaders.”
Multiple studies and a Reuters analysis have found that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare.
The subpoenas are one piece of an expansive campaign targeting noncitizen voting. Armed Homeland Security agents have questioned residents in several states about their immigration status and voting, while the Justice Department has sued 30 states that refused to provide voter rolls containing sensitive personal information such as driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. A federal judge largely halted Homeland Security’s field operations in nine states on October 21, and courts have ruled against the Justice Department in every voter-roll case so far. Many of those cases remain under appeal.
The subpoenas issued by the Justice Department and Homeland Security offer another way to obtain the same voter information, which legal experts say could figure in disputes over midterm election results. Elections are administered primarily by the states, with the federal government playing a limited role. Under most state laws, only losing candidates or voters can challenge election results, but the Justice Department could still take legal action to delay or block certification of winners.
Heavily Democratic California offers a glimpse of how such a fight could unfold. Its congressional seats could decide who controls the US House of Representatives. The Justice Department alleged this month that more than 20,000 “likely” noncitizens in California had received mail ballots and demanded any ballots cast by them not be counted until their citizenship was verified. California officials refused and called the list unreliable, saying a review of 200 registrations found nearly 40% appeared to be US-born.
The Justice Department declined to confirm or deny its use of subpoenas in noncitizen voter investigations, but said it “will enforce the law wherever the evidence leads.” The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions.
Some election officials and lawyers told Reuters the noncitizen voting investigations could bolster a false narrative that American elections are vulnerable to widespread fraud. In a closely divided country, Trump and his allies could use those claims to attack the legitimacy of narrow defeats, particularly in tightly contested races, they said.
The subpoenas issued by the administration are “clearly a distraction” for local and state election officials, said Paul Charlton, a former US attorney for Arizona in the Republican administration of George W. Bush. “In my time as a federal prosecutor, we prosecuted people who shouldn’t have voted, but it was so infrequent as to never even come close to altering the outcome of an election.”
Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting under a federal “voting by aliens” statute, including 102 since the start of September, according to a Reuters analysis of court filings and federal records. The cases – most of which remain unresolved – amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024.
The investigations are “setting up” post-election challenges that, while legally weak, could sow chaos, said Ben Berwick, a former Justice Department attorney who served in the Obama and Trump administrations and now leads the election law and litigation team at Protect Democracy, an advocacy group. Trump-aligned candidates who lose could argue that suspected noncitizen votes made it impossible to determine the rightful winner and seek to have ballots or even the election result thrown out, Berwick said.
The stakes are high. Democrats need to gain four Senate seats and five House seats to take control of Congress. Winning either chamber would give them power to launch investigations into the Trump administration and Trump family business dealings.
A BROADENING SEARCH
The subpoenas identified by Reuters varied widely in scope, from records on individual voters to demands for entire local voter rolls containing tens of thousands of names. None of the jurisdictions contacted said they were resisting the subpoenas.
In the US, subpoenas are legally binding orders requiring recipients to testify or produce documents or other evidence.
In Minnesota, a traditionally Democratic state with an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race, the Trump administration issued subpoenas for voting records on dozens of people in the Minneapolis-area counties of Anoka and Hennepin, where the administration has carried out a major federal immigration crackdown. To date, the Justice Department has charged at least eight people from the two counties with voting as noncitizens. All the cases are ongoing and no one has been convicted.
In California, the Justice Department has issued at least 17 subpoenas to governments in Democratic-leaning jurisdictions, including Los Angeles and San Diego counties. The state is home to at least two districts with competitive US House races and is typically slow to count ballots, with final results sometimes taking weeks.
Some voting experts said the Trump administration and its allies could use the period before California finishes counting ballots to amplify allegations of noncitizen voting and challenge the legitimacy of close races. Reuters also identified previously unreported subpoenas seeking voter records that were issued to Marin County and Fresno County. Fresno lies within California's 22nd Congressional District, a closely watched midterm battleground.
In Philadelphia, a Democratic stronghold, local officials confirmed receiving at least four subpoenas for voting records. In reliably Democratic Massachusetts, one of the states where federal courts blocked the administration’s voter roll demands, a Trump-backed US attorney has targeted at least eight cities and towns with grand jury subpoenas, six of them not previously reported, Reuters found.
At least three of the Massachusetts subpoenas required officials to provide a list of all registered voters, including names, addresses, party affiliations, birth dates, voting status and voter identification numbers. An accompanying letter, obtained from one city through a public records request, urged recipients “not to disclose the existence of this subpoena or the fact of your compliance therewith, to anyone,” but said the request for secrecy was not mandatory.
In Lynn, Massachusetts, a city with a large Hispanic population, federal prosecutors subpoenaed records for 25 to 30 people. “Up until now, they’ve found one instance of someone voting in an election that shouldn’t have been voting,” James Lamanna, the city’s clerk and election chief, told Reuters. “This doesn’t reach the level of something serious and pervasive that it would jeopardize the integrity of an election.”
Other states where subpoenas have been issued include Arizona, Washington, New York, Connecticut, Utah and Michigan.
CLAIMS UNDER SCRUTINY
Trump has repeatedly portrayed noncitizen voting as a grave threat to election integrity. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank that has raised similar concerns for years, argues that weak verification procedures create opportunities for illegal voting and that voter fraud could affect the outcome of a close election.
Voting-rights groups counter that repeated reviews have found no evidence of noncitizen voting on a scale that has changed an election outcome. Thousands of noncitizens have been mistakenly registered to vote because of clerical errors or software glitches, often while obtaining driver’s licenses, but state and local officials say only a small fraction actually cast ballots.
In a nationally televised address in July, Trump said his administration had identified more than 275,000 noncitizen voters, which the White House said were in four Democratic-leaning states. State officials disputed those assertions. In Nevada, federal officials initially claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls before revising the figure to fewer than 200. Nevada officials later concluded those remaining individuals were all citizens.
Federal prosecutors are continuing to report suspected new cases. In Washington state this week, they said they had identified more than 400 noncitizens who appear to be registered to vote. They asked state election officials to set aside any current ballots from those individuals until their citizenship could be verified. The Washington secretary of state's office told Reuters it has received about 60 federal subpoenas in recent weeks seeking information on individual voters.
The administration has also intensified its enforcement efforts. On October 19, the Justice Department said it had charged 28 people in California, all legal permanent residents, with voting as noncitizens or making false statements on voting or naturalization paperwork. California election officials have called the campaign a politically motivated distraction, noting that the cases uncovered so far amount to a tiny fraction of the state’s more than 23 million registered voters.
The administration has also threatened legal consequences for election officials who resist its demands. California officials objected after federal authorities threatened to prosecute election officials who did not act on the list of 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters. Acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, who spearheaded the administration’s claims in California, acknowledged last week that the list could include US citizens.
“We’re not perfect,” he said. REUTERS

Ethiopia receives 12 Russian Su-35 jets, plans S-400 acquisition
PM Abiy Ahmed makes the announcement during a Moscow summit as Ethiopia battles armed groups in Tigray and Amhara.
Ethiopia has received 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also acquire four S-400 air defence batteries, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced.
Abiy made the announcement on X on Wednesday during a visit to Moscow for the two-day Russia-Africa Summit, where Russia is seeking closer security and economic ties with African countries.
The acquisition comes as Ethiopian forces fight renewed battles with rebels in northern Tigray and a separate rebellion in the neighbouring Amhara region.
The prime minister said the warplanes had arrived a year earlier than expected under an existing agreement with Moscow, thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin for helping speed up the delivery.
He gave no date for the arrival of the S-400 batteries, designed to shoot down aircraft and missiles.
Abiy said on Wednesday that the new equipment would strengthen Ethiopia’s ability to “preemptively deter aggression”.
In a second X post later that day, he described the jets as newly deployed and said they would defend Ethiopian airspace.
Military cooperation
The announcement is the latest sign of Russia‘s growing military partnership with Ethiopia, following a series of agreements in recent years.
The two governments signed a military cooperation agreement in Addis Ababa in July 2021 aimed at improving the Ethiopian armed forces’ training and technology.
In January, defence publication Janes reported that Ethiopia had displayed newly acquired Russian Yak-130 advanced jet trainers during celebrations marking its air force’s 90th anniversary.
Russia supplied 15 percent of Africa’s imports of major weapons between 2021 and 2025, making it the continent’s third-largest supplier, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Moscow has sought closer military and economic ties with African countries while facing Western sanctions over its war in Ukraine.
The Russia-Africa Summit, which began on Wednesday, brings African leaders together for talks on trade, investment and security.
Tigray war
The announcement follows a major shift in the fighting in Tigray, where government troops and allied forces entered the regional capital Mekelle on October 4 after fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) withdrew.
The TPLF, an armed group that previously governed the region, has suffered further territorial losses as government forces advanced into other towns.
Addis Ababa has since appointed a six-month caretaker administration for Tigray, but the fighting has not stopped.
A TPLF commander called for continued resistance in a television broadcast last week, while the group has also claimed attacks against government-aligned troops in northwestern Tigray on Wednesday.
The renewed war has effectively undone a peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 that ended two years of fighting, which researchers at Belgium’s Ghent University estimate killed about 500,000 civilians.
Government forces are also battling Fano, an Amhara armed group that has been fighting federal troops since 2023.

Puerto Rican boxing champion Amanda Serrano will retire after defending her unified featherweight world titles against Australia's Skye Falzon on Jan. 9, her promoter Most Valuable Promotions announced Wednesday.
The fight, dubbed “The Last Walk,” will take place at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan, where Serrano, 38, will defend her World Boxing Organization (WBO) and World Boxing Association (WBA) featherweight titles.

Serrano made history alongside Ireland's Katie Taylor in 2022 when they became the first women boxers to headline Madison Square Garden.
Their rivalry became one of the most prominent in women's boxing, culminating in a trilogy of fights that Taylor swept with a majority decision in their third encounter in 2025.
Serrano, Puerto Rico's only undisputed boxing champion, has won world titles in seven weight divisions.

For Israel’s Arabs, record turnout may bring political clout
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:31:29 CET
01:31:29 KST

By Pesha Magid
NAZARETH, Israel, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Israel’s Palestinian citizens appear set to secure a record number of seats in parliament and could emerge as kingmakers after strong turnout in Tuesday’s election, galvanized by what they describe as the racist policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
But while they may have helped block an outright win by Netanyahu and his far-right allies, parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority have so far been shunned by the prime minister’s main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, who has no clear path to power without them.
Vote tallies show the two main Arab parties on course to win around 19 of parliament’s 120 seats, nearly double their current representation in the Knesset. Netanyahu’s coalition bloc is on track for 53 seats, short of the 61 needed for a majority, with Eisenkot’s grouping expected to win 48 seats.
‘GETTING RID OF NETANYAHU’S GOVERNMENT’
Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Arab-dominated Joint List, told Reuters his party would seek to use its projected 12 seats “to facilitate getting rid of Netanyahu’s government and hopefully helping to change the political situation in Israel.”
Jabareen said the Joint List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s military campaign in Gaza and occupation of southern Lebanon.
But he left open the possibility of bolstering Eisenkot’s bloc from the outside, propping up a minority government that could survive confidence votes.
“We have our demands to protect our community, to advance the rights of our community and to promote equality for our community,” said Jabareen, speaking from his home in the Arab town of Umm al-Fahm.
He said the priorities were tackling soaring crime, boosting funding and opportunities in Arab communities, and reopening peace talks on a Palestinian state.
The second main Arab party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, who joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time an independent Arab party entered an Israeli coalition. That government collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.
This time, Abbas, a dentist-turned-politician, has sought to make Ra’am a more attractive coalition partner, adding a Jewish former police official to its slate and saying he would join an Eisenkot-led government.
Speaking to Israeli television after voting wrapped on Tuesday night, Ra’am chief Mansour Abbas said: “I believe we can overcome the difficulties … and I think that most voters for the (Eisenkot) bloc do want to see (a) government with the Ra’am party.”
He said senior members of Eisenkot’s bloc had discussed a possible deal with him even before the election.
Eisenkot ruled out forming a government with Arab parties during the campaign, citing what he called a lack of shared values, including recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state.
In remarks to supporters after exit poll results were published on Tuesday night, Eisenkot said he would work to form a “stable Zionist government that serves all Israeli citizens.”
Ameer Fakhoury, a political sociologist at Jerusalem’s Van Leer Institute, said that Arab votes may block Netanyahu and make an alternative government possible.
“But arithmetic is not legitimacy. The Jewish opposition may need Palestinian votes while refusing Palestinian partners. That is the central paradox,” he said.
ARABS FRUSTRATED BY RIGHT-WING RHETORIC
Israel’s Arab minority is mostly descended from Palestinians who lived under Ottoman and British colonial-era rule and who remained inside the borders of what became the modern state of Israel in 1948.
Throughout the elections campaign, Israel’s far-right have demonized Palestinian citizens of Israel and branded Arab political participation as a threat to the state.
Ahead of the vote, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich proposed a plan to “Judaize” areas around Nazareth and in southern Israel where many Arabs live, comparing it to Jewish settlement expansion in the West Bank.
Pollsters had predicted high Arab turnout, and, on election day, Netanyahu, Smotrich and far-right partner Itamar Ben-Gvir repeatedly warned that Arabs were voting in large numbers, appealing to their own supporters to turn out.
Mohamed Abbas, 19, speaking in Nazareth, said he and many others in his generation were driven to vote by what he described as rising racism toward Arab Palestinian citizens.
“We want equality…we do not want displacement laws or preference given to Jewish people,” Abbas said.
(Reporting by Pesha Magid; editing by Rami Ayyub and Ros Russell)

Germany brigade in Lithuania to monitor Kaliningrad, Belarus with electronic warfare
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:31:25 CET
01:31:25 KST

By Andrius Sytas
PALUKNYS AIRFIELD, Lithuania, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Germany’s permanent brigade in Lithuania will use electronic warfare capabilities to provide early warning of military activity in Kaliningrad and Belarus, the military’s cyber chief said.
The brigade, due to be fully deployed next year, will also collect data on Russian and Belarusian military emitters and radar systems to update electronic-warfare databases used by German and allied forces, Vice Admiral Thomas Daum told Reuters.
“If anything happens, these units will identify that”, he said.
“We’ll put (the data) into electronic warfare databases which will then inform all our systems if there is a new radar on the Belarusian side.”
Daum said Russian activities in parts of Europe had reached what he called “phase two, where the intent is to hurt” below the threshold of armed conflict.
“The cyber-information domain is not yet at war, but it’s no longer peace”, he said.
He said an earlier phase had focused on covertly penetrating Western networks through cyber attacks and establishing footholds inside systems.
Germany’s cabinet in August approved measures, which must still be approved in parliament, to grant intelligence services new powers to hack communications and disrupt foreign adversaries’ operations to counter what officials say is a growing threat from cyber and hybrid attacks.
The German army is currently testing electronic-warfare systems in Lithuania, such as drone-detection tools, signal interceptors, jammers and sensors designed to relay battlefield data to remote analysts.
Before the war in Ukraine, the German military could barely convince commercial companies to supply it with such systems, said Patrick Jeschke, who heads the Bundeswehr’s cyber innovation hub.
The challenge has shifted from finding suppliers to selecting the most promising technologies from a flood of proposals, he said.
“Over the last decades, we have not invested too much money into new capabilities. We’ve used what we had because we were focused on missions abroad, in Afghanistan and other places,” said Daum.
“Now… there is a need to improve our capabilities.”
(Reporting by Andrius SytasEditing by Keith Weir)

A timeline of Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s wild journey to the US
SAO PAULO, Oct 28 - Flavio Bolsonaro's sudden departure from Brazil — less than three days after his election defeat — started on Sunday with his refusal to concede in the runoff and culminated in his arrival in Miami via Argentina and Ecuador aboard a private jet on Wednesday.
The right-wing lawmaker left after receiving a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports in connection with a money-laundering investigation, in which he denies wrongdoing.
Below is a timeline of the events. All times are Brasilia time (GMT-3).
SUNDAY — ELECTION DEFEAT AND CHALLENGE
• Bolsonaro loses Brazil's presidential runoff election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, despite having entered the race as the favorite after winning the first-round vote
• Bolsonaro does not concede defeat and says he would seek annulment of the election, arguing that a Supreme Court decision extending voting hours by two hours had affected the outcome
• World leaders quickly recognize Lula's victory, but US President Donald Trump and Argentine President Javier Milei initially remain silent
MONDAY — PASSPORT ORDER
• Trump alleges, without presenting evidence, that the Brazilian election "looked like another rigged election," but Bolsonaro's Liberal Party acknowledges the runoff result
• Bolsonaro posts a video on social media saying federal police had requested he turn in his passports following an order from Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes
• The senator said he would comply with the order and rejected speculation that he planned to flee Brazil after the election
TUESDAY — REPORTS OF DEPARTURE
• 1:00 a.m.: Argentine news site Infobae reports that Bolsonaro had left Brazil for Argentina and planned to continue to the US aboard a private jet waiting at Puerto Iguazu airport near the border
• 11:15 a.m.: Argentine immigration authorities say they have no record of Bolsonaro entering the country, adding that inspectors had checked the aircraft and its crew and found no flight plan listing Bolsonaro or his family
• 11:30 a.m.: A spokesperson for Milei says Argentina had taken note of Lula's victory but did not plan to congratulate him, and declines to comment on whether Argentina would consider an asylum request from Bolsonaro
• 12:00 p.m.: Bolsonaro misses the deadline to surrender his passports; although his whereabouts are unknown, federal police sources tell Reuters the documents have been canceled
• 2:15 p.m.: CNN Brasil reports, citing Bolsonaro allies, that the senator has traveled to the US
• 2:20 p.m.: An ally of Bolsonaro tells Reuters he has already left Brazil and is heading to the US
• 2:30 p.m.: A US official tells Reuters that Bolsonaro is on a plane bound for the US
• 6:05 p.m.: A senior US State Department official says that Bolsonaro and his family would be allowed to enter the country and would receive visas
• 6:25 p.m.: Lula describes Bolsonaro's departure from Brazil after his election defeat as "shameful"
WEDNESDAY — ARRIVAL IN THE UNITED STATES
• 12:22 a.m.: Flight-tracking data shows a Baires Fly Gulfstream G400, registration LV-JQW, departing Puerto Iguazu
• 1:30 a.m.: Trump says he would have approved Bolsonaro's arrival in the US and describes Brazil's election as "very strange"
• 2:00 a.m.: Argentina's migration authority says Bolsonaro and his family had entered the province of Misiones late on October 27 using valid travel documents, adding they crossed the Tancredo Neves Bridge in Puerto Iguazu and later boarded a private Baires Fly flight bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador
• 5:46 a.m.: The aircraft arrives in Guayaquil, according to flight-tracking data
• 6:22 a.m.: The plane departs Guayaquil for Miami's Opa-locka Executive Airport, according to flight-tracking firm FlightAware
• 10:31 a.m.: The aircraft arrives in Miami; Reuters TV images show Bolsonaro disembarking along with his wife and two daughters REUTERS

By Mark Trevelyan
Oct 28 (Reuters) - President Vladimir Putin hailed Elon Musk as a genius on Wednesday, acknowledging Russia is only beginning to roll out its answer to his Starlink satellite internet system.
The admission was all the more striking because a version of Starlink, developed by Musk’s SpaceX, has been used by Ukraine’s military throughout the war with Russia as a key component of drone operations and battlefield communications.
Putin made the remark while listening to a presentation by Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev, who said Russia had launched more than 30 satellites as it builds its own Starlink equivalent.
“Just a second, I want to point out this is just our first step. Elon Musk is a genius, he’s just a real genius,” said Putin, who was accompanied by a group of African leaders attending a summit in Moscow.
PUTIN SAYS RUSSIA IN CONTACT WITH US PARTNERS
Shadayev said in reply to a question from Putin that Musk had more than 5,000 low-orbit satellites up and running — although the actual number is close to 10,000, according to independent tracking site Orbital Radar.
“Over 5,000 — while we are only taking our first steps. But we are proud that we have begun to do this, and started to do it independently,” Putin said, adding that the task now was “to move from quality to quantity”.
“We are in close contact with our American partners — including Mr Musk — because it is very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” he said.
Starlink uses a constellation of satellites that orbit far lower than traditional geostationary communications satellites, reducing signal travel time.
Ukraine has relied heavily on the system and its military version Starshield, but complained earlier this month of speed restrictions that hampered its ability to intercept Russian attack drones and forced the cancellation of some operations.
The problems added to tensions between Kyiv and the US after President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel while pressing Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries and saying it was time for Ukrainians to replace their president.
At the weekend, Ukraine said Starlink and Starshield were again fully functional, but Musk accused the Ukrainian military of violating SpaceX’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, have taken responsibility for imposing the speed curbs.
Russian officials have spoken highly of Musk before. In 2025, Putin’s investment envoy Kirill Dmitriev said Russia would like to work with him on a mission to Mars.

Saudi diplomatic push exposes divisions among Iran hardliners
A diplomatic initiative involving Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan has exposed divisions among Iranian hardliners, with influential conservative figures disagreeing over whether the talks represent recognition of Tehran's regional influence or an attempt to force concessions over Yemen.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistani military chief Asim Munir visited Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior security officials.
The meeting, held amid renewed threats of US and Israeli military action against Iran, concluded with an agreement to continue discussions on regional security.
According to Reuters, citing a Pakistani official, Munir presented Tehran with a proposal to end hostilities that had received US President Donald Trump's approval.
Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Qatar could reportedly act as guarantors of an agreement, although no diplomatic breakthrough was announced.
The initiative has generated contrasting reactions among Iranian political figures, according to Iranian media reports.
Iran's state-run Iran newspaper welcomed the visit, declaring that regional security was impossible without Tehran's participation.
Abdollah Ganji, a former editor of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-affiliated Javan newspaper, similarly portrayed the talks as recognition of Iran's regional importance.
Writing on X, Ganji suggested that Tehran was becoming central to an emerging regional security arrangement opposed to Israel.
However, Hossein Shariatmadari, the influential editor of the hardline Kayhan newspaper, questioned the intentions of the visiting governments.
Shariatmadari argued that Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were too closely aligned with Washington to act as credible mediators.
He also challenged the optimism expressed by Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who had presented the meeting as an opportunity to establish a new regional security framework.
Shariatmadari warned that the initiative could weaken Iran's position by relieving pressure on Washington while encouraging Tehran to distance itself from regional allies.
Former Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif, meanwhile, advocated a broader regional security arrangement based on non-aggression, confidence-building and economic cooperation.
Much of the controversy concerns Yemen's Houthi movement, which has renewed attacks against Saudi Arabia amid continuing tensions over the country's unresolved conflict.
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention in Yemen beginning in 2015, launching a devastating bombing campaign and imposing restrictions on the country's ports and borders that contributed to one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
Although large-scale fighting diminished following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, the conflict remains unresolved, with the Houthis controlling much of northern Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
The movement maintains close political and military ties with Iran but has its own domestic political objectives and decision-making structures.
Shariatmadari warned that the diplomatic initiative could result in pressure on Tehran to abandon the Houthis, something he insisted Iran would not do.
Hardline parliamentarian Mahmoud Nabavian defended the movement, arguing that attacks against Saudi Arabia would continue while restrictions on Yemen remained in place.
Former parliamentary national security committee chairman Heshmatollah Falahatpisheh, however, suggested that resolving the Yemen conflict was a central priority for Saudi Arabia and its regional partners.
The diplomatic initiative comes as Washington reportedly prepares for another military campaign against Iran following the 3 November US midterm elections.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that the Trump administration had warned Gulf governments to prepare for a possible short but intense military operation.
The prospect of renewed fighting has increased the urgency of regional diplomacy, even as Iranian political figures disagree over whether negotiations could protect Tehran's interests or undermine its regional alliances.

Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:30:51 CET
01:30:51 KST

By Bill Trott
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) with Cesar Chavez and fought legislators and powerful growers in the US to improve the lives of a previously powerless constituency, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, her family said in a statement.
Huerta was one of the foremost women in US labor history, serving the UFW as chief negotiator, strike organizer, lobbyist and reformer during its heyday in the 1960s and ’70s in California’s agriculture-rich Central Valley.
Thanks to the contracts the UFW negotiated, farmworkers won job security, healthcare, retirement plans, a credit union and job-specific benefits such as guaranteed rest periods, toilets in the fields, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides.
Huerta was credited with giving the UFW its slogan “Si, se puede,” the loose translation of which, “Yes, we can,” was later used by Barack Obama during his successful 2008 presidential campaign.
She remained a regular on the college lecture circuit into her 90s, speaking out against the immigration policies of President Donald Trump. During elections she traveled the country, endorsing candidates and registering voters.
UFW co-founder Chavez, who died in 1993 and was the face of the organization, was a seventh-grade dropout and former grape picker with a man-of-the-soil appeal who espoused the non-violent philosophies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King, with a nod to Emiliano Zapata, a leader of Mexico’s peasant revolution in the early 20th century.
But Chavez had a dark side. In 2026, Huerta was one of a number of women who came forward with accounts of how they had been sexually assaulted by him, in some cases when they were minors. Huerta said that he had pressured her into having sex one time, and another time raped her. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, and Huerta said she arranged for the babies to be raised by others.
OUT OF THE SPOTLIGHT
While Chavez was recruiting, going on well-publicized hunger strikes and being embraced by liberal lawmakers and celebrities, the diminutive, college-educated Huerta handled negotiating with growers, lobbying legislators and other business for the UFW.
She was arrested more than 20 times, subjected to death threats and other harassment. She suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen when beaten by baton-wielding San Francisco police in a 1988 protest against the policies of George H.W. Bush during his presidential campaign.
In an interview with PBS in 2012, before the assault accusations against Chavez came to light, Huerta said she had been fine with him taking the spotlight as she wanted to focus on helping people rather than gaining fame.
“He said, ‘One of us is going to have to be the spokesperson. Are you all right if I’m the spokesperson?’ Of course, I said yes.”
STANDING UP
Huerta was born in Dawson, New Mexico, to a Mexican immigrant family, and spent much of her youth in Stockton, California, after her parents divorced. Her father was a miner, laborer, union activist and state lawmaker; her mother raised three children while buying and running a hotel for low-income people in Stockton.
Huerta’s mother instilled a spirit of activism in her daughter. Huerta was into her second marriage when she became a schoolteacher, but that career did not last long.
“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”
She registered voters in Stockton and founded the Agricultural Workers Association before meeting Chavez and joining him in starting the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 they began a series of strikes and boycotts that would last five years against various California grape growers and eventually spread to lettuce growers.
During that period the organization evolved into the United Farm Workers and picked up support from King and New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy. Not eating a grape — unless it had a union label — became a political statement in the United States.
The boycotts and strikes sometimes became contentious. In addition to industry opposition, the UFW found itself up against California Governor Ronald Reagan, who denounced the UFW as immoral and made a point of eating grapes on television.
COLLECTIVE BARGAINING
One by one, growers began signing contracts with the UFW and in 1975 Huerta’s work also helped bring about another victory — passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first law in the US that gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.
Huerta said that being a woman gave her an edge at the negotiating table with growers.
“They really didn’t know how to respond because they couldn’t do the usual forceful type of thing,” she told PBS. “And when you would bring up to them and show them the conditions that the workers were working under, and they were kind of embarrassed, actually.”
In 2012, Obama presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country’s highest civilian award.
Her life was the basis of the award-winning film “Dolores” that was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017.
While the UFW’s influence abated, Huerta’s activism did not. In 2002 she established the Dolores Huerta Foundation for community activism with her daughter Camila Chavez as its executive director. She pushed for changes in immigration laws, voter registration, women’s rights and Obama’s healthcare reform.
Huerta, who said she remained close to the two children she had with Chavez, also had two children from her first marriage, five from her second and four from a long-term relationship with Richard Chavez, brother of Cesar and another key UFW figure, who died in 2011.
(Reporting by Bill Trott; Additional reporting by Bhargav Acharya and Daphne Psaledakis; Editing by Patricia Reaney and Rosalba O’Brien)

Budget bill is worth some 26 million euros says Meloni
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
17:30:16 CET
01:30:16 KST

The 2027 budget package is worth a
total of approximately 26 billion euros, Prime Minister Giorgia
Meloni stated during a press conference following the cabinet
meeting at which the package was approved.
                                    
She said that the abolition of road tax for most Italians gas
been made structural; saying that those who dismissed it as an
election-time handout are proven wrong.
                                    
She said it applies to approximately 70% of vehicles currently
on the road.
                                    
In the budget, "we are making the vehicle tax relief structural,
just as we had approved during one of our final cabinet
meetings.
                                    
"This means no road tax for small-to-medium-powered cars—up to
80 kilowatts—or for motorcycles.
                                    
We are talking about roughly 70% of the vehicles currently on
the road.
                                    
"Many tried to downplay this measure, claiming it was merely an
election-time handout—partly because it was initially set to
apply only in 2027—but they will now be proven wrong; they will
see in black and white exactly what we had stated all along: the
measure is structural and permanent.
                                    
"At least for as long as the center-right is in
government—because, as it turns out, the center-left actually
likes road tax."
In the budget, she added, "we are raising the threshold for the
second personal income tax (IRPEF) bracket to 55,000 euros per
year."
"If we could have, we would have done much more," she added.
                                    
Meloni said the IRPEF cuts would provide a benefit of 500 euros
per year.
                                    
With previous measures regarding the personal income tax
(IRPEF), the State has foregone "approximately 21 billion euros.
                                    
Now, we are taking another step forward: we are raising the
threshold for the second tax bracket—taxed at 33%—up to 55,000
euros.
                                    
"The maximum benefit is 500 euros per year. Some might say that
is still not enough—we would have liked to do more—but this must
be considered alongside the steps taken previously."
Meloni also said that the government would provide air
conditioning for all schools, using a portion of energy-related
flexibility funds.
                                    
"We have decided to use a portion of the energy-related
flexibility resources to equip all schools with air conditioning
units and heat pumps, making our classrooms more comfortable. It
would have been better if, in the past, resources had been
invested in this—rather than in desks with wheels."
She also said that the 'agreed-rent' tax rate would drop to 5%,
or 1% if renting to those under 35.
                                    
"The problem of rental housing affects all of Europe, and Italy
is no exception—which is why we have launched a housing plan.
                                    
"As part of the budget, we have included a measure whereby the
flat-rate tax on 'agreed-rent' [regulated-rate] leases will drop
to 5%, and to 1% for those who rent to young people up to the
age of 35."

Middle East energy shock puts upward pressure on inflation, UK chancellor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:27:01 UTC
01:27:01 KST

Gökhan Ergöçün
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Higher energy prices driven by the conflict in the Middle East are putting upward pressure on UK inflation, British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey warned on Wednesday.  
In a letter setting out the annual remit for the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee, Healey told Governor Andrew Bailey that monetary policy remains vital to supporting households and businesses by returning inflation sustainably to its 2% target in the medium term.
"Higher energy prices resulting from the conflict in the Middle East are putting upwards pressure on inflation," Healey wrote.
He noted that while the Monetary Policy Committee holds primary responsibility for returning inflation to target, the government's fiscal plans support the central bank by reducing borrowing over time and easing inflationary pressures.
Healey stated that low and stable inflation is essential for long-term economic growth and rising living standards, reducing uncertainty and easing costs for consumers and businesses.
He also confirmed that the central bank's Asset Purchase Facility will remain in place for the 2027-28 financial year and for as long as needed, in line with the multiyear strategy set out by policymakers on Sept. 17.
Reiterating the government's full support for the committee's operational independence, Healey said the symmetric 2% target, measured by the 12-month increase in the Consumer Prices Index, applies at all times.

Türkiye, Bulgaria, Romania stress importance of Black Sea for int'l trade, supply of grain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
16:24:47 UTC
01:24:47 KST

Esra Tekin
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Turkish, Bulgarian, and Romanian defense ministers on Wednesday reiterated the significance of the Black Sea for international trade and the supply of grain, fertilizers, and energy in a joint statement.
The statement came after the Türkiye-Bulgaria-Romania Meeting of Defense Ministers and Chiefs of General Staff held in Sofia.
Turkish National Defense Minister Yasar Guler, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov, and Romanian Defense Minister Stefan-Radu Oprea attended the meeting.
The ministers “strongly condemned” attacks against commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
“We wish to reaffirm the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security. Disruptions to maritime traffic threaten global supply chains, food and energy security, particularly in vulnerable regions of Africa, the Middle East, and Asia,” the statement said.
“We call on all parties to refrain from any further actions that could endanger commercial vessels, maritime infrastructure and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea.
"We deeply regret the loss of innocent seafarers who have lost their lives in these attacks. We emphasize our full solidarity with the states whose citizens and vessels have been affected by these attacks,” it added.
The statement urged all parties to obey international law, including the Montreux Convention and applicable international humanitarian law, in order to safeguard security in the Black Sea, preserve regional stability, and facilitate safe maritime activities.
The statement noted that Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye, as NATO allies, contribute to meeting the region’s security needs. It also expressed appreciation for NATO’s support in the areas of deterrence and defense.
The three countries agreed to take appropriate measures, in coordination with NATO where necessary, to increase information and intelligence sharing, strengthen maritime situational awareness, and improve early-warning capabilities in pursuit of these objectives.
The statement further noted that cooperation and coordination between the three countries’ armed forces would continue to be strengthened to support security and stability in the Black Sea.
It also stated that consultations, information exchanges and the identification of practical measures contributing to regional security and stability would be facilitated.
The next round of consultations is scheduled to take place in Ankara and Bucharest.
