Bolsonaro crossed the border “with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country,” the agency stated.
It is unclear if Bolsonaro crossed the border using his national identity card, or with his Italian passport, as he has held Italian citizenship since 2023.
Once in Argentina, the Bolsonaro family boarded a private jet bound for Ecuador, the DNM stated. Argentinian President Javier Milei and Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa are both right-wing allies of Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro and his family were seen arriving in Florida on Wednesday, where the State Department has told AP that it will grant visas to him and his family. While the State Department has not admitted any role in helping Bolsonaro flee Brazil, Mexican entrepreneur Simon Levy, who describes himself as “proud to serve President Trump and MAGA,” claimed on Tuesday that the entire operation was “coordinated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.”
Rubio has not commented on Levy’s claims. However, Rubio and Trump are both political allies of Bolsonaro. Rubio’s State Department sanctioned Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year over his role in jailing Bolsonaro’s father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, in 2022, and over his censorship of American social media platforms. Moraes is a close political ally of Lula.
Bolsonaro’s passports were canceled in connection with an ongoing corruption and money laundering probe. Despite Moraes being named in the same investigation, Lula warned Bolsonaro earlier this month that he would “be in a lot of trouble” if he lost the election, threatening him with “plenty of investigations.”
It is unclear how the US intends to respond to Lula’s election win. Trump has suggested that the election “had a very bad look…the way it was tabulated.” After claiming that Rubio aided in Bolsonaro’s flight, Levy made a cryptic post on X, saying “get ready for tomorrow…”

What to Say—and Not Say—to Someone Having Intrusive Thoughts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:10:16 UTC
00:10:16 KST

Have you ever had a disturbing thought pop into your head out of nowhere—something you'd never consider actually doing?
Intrusive thoughts are unwanted thoughts, images, or urges that can feel upsetting, confusing, or wildly out of character. They're more common in people with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) but can happen to anyone, and they can involve everything from violence and sex to religion, relationships, and the fear of having done something wrong.
Many people are able to brush off the occasional intrusive thought and move on quickly. People with OCD, on the other hand, can get stuck trying to figure out what the thought means—and whether they might act on it. “We stop and we treat that thought as super important and meaningful,” says Alissa Jerud, a clinical psychologist and clinical assistant professor of psychiatry at the University of Pennsylvania.
Intrusive thoughts can feel especially disturbing because they often involve someone or something the person cherishes. “We tend to have intrusive thoughts about the things we care most about,” Jerud says.
Some of Jerud’s patients have kept their intrusive thoughts to themselves for 20 years before telling her. They might be thinking: “Why am I having these thoughts? What does it say about me? Maybe I’m a monster,” she says.
A calm, compassionate response can make it easier to keep talking. “It can help them feel like there’s hope,” Jerud says. “Maybe I don’t have to beat myself up for having these thoughts in the first place.”
Here’s what to say if a loved one tells you they’re having intrusive thoughts.
Start with, “I’m so glad you shared this with me”
Start by thanking your friend for trusting you. Skip responses like “How could you think that?” or “Don’t say that,” which can reinforce the shame they’re already feeling.
It’s helpful, too, to make it clear that what they told you won’t affect your relationship: “This doesn’t change how I think about you,” suggests Madeline Thompson Smith, an Atlanta-based licensed professional counselor who specializes in OCD. Then acknowledge how upsetting the thoughts sound: “That sounds really scary to have stuck in your head.”
Pay attention to how you sound and look, too. A warm invitation to explain more can feel like judgment if you’re staring intensely or using a sharp tone. If you look startled, acknowledge it instead of hoping they didn’t notice. Kimberly Leonte, a psychologist in Boston who specializes in OCD, suggests wording it like this: “I guess I wasn’t expecting that, but I want to hear more.”
Offer support without repeatedly reassuring them
When someone you love is distressed by an intrusive thought, reassuring them can feel like the kindest thing to do. But if they keep coming back with the same question, answering it again and again can become part of the OCD cycle.
Say your partner keeps asking whether an unwanted thought means they’re dangerous. You reassure them, they feel better, and you both get back to your evening. Until another question arrives: But what if you’re wrong? What if they didn’t explain the thought accurately enough? Next thing you know, they’re asking for reassurance again.
A single reassuring response isn’t necessarily a problem, Thompson Smith says. The concern is when seeking reassurance becomes a compulsion—a behavior someone feels driven to repeat to relieve their distress. Each answer briefly helps them feel better, but it leaves them needing another answer when the doubt returns.
Instead of debating what the thought means, acknowledge how they’re feeling and express confidence in their ability to get through the discomfort. Thompson Smith suggests: “I know this feels really uncomfortable right now. I’m not going to help you go down the rabbit hole, but I’m happy to sit with you while it’s hard.”
If reassurance has become a routine between you, talk about changing it together, ideally with guidance from their therapist. Abruptly refusing to answer can leave your loved one wondering what happened. “It’s tough if the person’s used to getting reassurance, and you just stop giving it and they don’t know why,” Leonte says. Instead, discuss how you’ll respond the next time they ask—and make sure you both understand why you’re trying something different.
Meanwhile, aim to avoid suggestions like “Just stop thinking about it” or “Replace it with a happy thought.” Besides being considerably easier said than done, trying to force an intrusive thought away can keep someone preoccupied with whether it’s gone yet.
Ask whether they want you to listen or help
Find out what your loved one wants from the conversation. They might be seeking support in taking a step toward getting mental-health help, or they may simply want you to know what they’ve been going through.
“Do you want me to just listen, or do you want help figuring out what to do next?” Thompson Smith suggests asking. If this is the first time they’ve said their intrusive thoughts out loud, they might not be ready to discuss next steps.
If they’re already in therapy, ask how you can support what they’re learning: “What would your therapist recommend trying right now?” Leonte suggests asking. If they’re interested in learning more about intrusive thoughts but feel overwhelmed, you could offer to read about them together.
Sometimes, they simply want someone to listen. Your loved one might be telling you because “they just don’t want to be alone in this, and you can help them hold it,” Thompson Smith says. Or they may need to know “you’re not gonna judge me or people aren’t gonna run away if I start trying to be open and get help.”
Know when intrusive thoughts call for professional help
If unwanted thoughts are causing significant distress or interfering with daily life, offer to help your loved one find a therapist. Keep it low-pressure: “If you ever want me to help you find a therapist, I’d be happy to do so,” Jerud suggests saying.
For OCD, look for a therapist trained in exposure and response prevention, or ERP, Jerud suggests. It helps people learn to tolerate intrusive thoughts without turning to rituals like repeated reassurance. The International OCD Foundation maintains a directory to help people find one.
There’s also an important distinction between an unwanted thought about harm and wanting or intending to act. Don’t assume that every disturbing thought is benign, Thompson Smith says. If you’re unsure what someone means, ask calmly and directly: “Is this a thought that scares you, or something you want to do?” If they describe wanting to act, ask about plans and help them get professional support right away.
Keep being the friend you’ve always been
After someone opens up about their intrusive thoughts, keep treating them like you always have. Send the ridiculous meme, ask whether they’re still coming to dinner, and keep including them in the things you usually do together.
People often fear that sharing their intrusive thoughts will change how others see them, Thompson Smith says. Pulling away—or asking about their mental health every time you talk—can leave them wishing they’d kept quiet.
You might get frustrated or struggle to find the right words, Leonte says. If you react in a way you regret, apologize and let them know you’re still there for them. “No one’s perfect,” she says. “The goal isn’t to be perfect, it’s just to be supportive.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 parliamentary seats Wednesday after all regular ballots were counted, with more than 500,000 special ballots still pending, Channel 12 reported. 
The opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot was projected to secure 48 seats, while predominantly Arab parties were expected to win 19 seats, according to the broadcaster. 
Neither main bloc was projected to reach the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority in the 120-member Knesset. 
According to Israeli news website Ynet, Netanyahu’s Likud was projected to remain the largest party with 26 seats, down from 32 in the 2022 elections, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar with 21 seats. Yashar is contesting its first parliamentary election. 
Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together (Beyachad) alliance was projected to secure 12 seats, also in its first election.   
The predominantly Arab Joint List was projected to win 12 seats, while Ra’am was expected to secure seven, bringing the combined representation of Arab parties to 19 seats, up from 10 in 2022. 
The Democrats were projected to win eight seats, compared with four seats won by their predecessor parties, Labor and Meretz, in the previous election. 
Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu was projected to secure seven seats, up from six in 2022. 
The ultra-Orthodox Shas party was projected to win seven seats, down from 11 in the previous election, while United Torah Judaism was expected to secure seven, unchanged from 2022. 
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit was projected to win seven seats, while the Religious Zionism-Zehut alliance, led by far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, was expected to secure six. 
Ben-Gvir’s and Smotrich’s parties contested the 2022 elections together on a joint list that won 14 seats. Their projected combined representation of 13 seats would mark a decline of one seat. 
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999, Channel 12 reported. 
However, more than 500,000 special double-envelope ballots remained to be counted, potentially affecting the final distribution of parliamentary seats. 
Double-envelope ballots are used by voters casting their votes away from their registered polling stations, including soldiers, diplomats, police officers and displaced residents. 
Under the system, voters place their ballots in an envelope, which is then placed inside a second envelope containing their identification details to prevent duplicate voting. 
Elad Naveh, director of the Central Elections Committee’s control center, said the counting of double-envelope ballots was expected to begin Wednesday evening and finish Thursday evening. 
He said the process could continue until Friday. 
Netanyahu’s Likud party stepped up attacks on Arab parties after preliminary results showed they had won 19 seats. 
In a statement, Likud alleged that “the elections in Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state.” 
It claimed irregularities at polling stations in Arab communities, including bribery, intimidation, violence, fraud and the use of prohibited software to mobilize voters. 
The party also alleged that thousands of envelopes containing cash and ballot slips for the United Arab List, known as Ra’am and led by Mansour Abbas, had been distributed. 
The projected results could change once election officials complete the counting of the remaining ballots. 
More than 7.3 million Israelis were eligible to vote in Tuesday’s election, the first since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

Russell Brand takes the stand at his rape and sexual assault trial
Actor and comedian Russell Brand took the stand in his trial on rape and sexual assault charges in London on Wednesday.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one charge of attempted indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. Brand has pleaded not guilty to the charges.
He started the morning by answering questions on whether he committed each respective charge with a terse "no." Under cross-examination, he said he was innocent.
"My entire life has been consumed by these allegations," Brand said in his initial questioning. Under cross-examination, he said that while he believes he behaved promiscuously during the time period in question, he thinks that "consent is absolutely non-negotiable."
Brand calls consent "more important than sex itself"
One woman alleged she met Brand at a Labour Party conference in 1999. She believed Brand was gay, and invited him to her hotel room to continue a conversation that began after a cabaret show where he performed. She alleged he came out of the bathroom topless before raping her.
Brand said he remembers meeting the victim and chatting with her. When asked if he portrayed himself as gay, he said, "I don't think so." Brand said the victim was the one who suggested returning to her hotel room.
Brand said he believes he would have checked in with the woman during the encounter, and denied raping her. He said he believes "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself."
A woman who was working at MTV in 2001, where Brand was also employed, said she was showing him where the bathrooms were when he grabbed her hard by the forearm and said "come in, go on, come in." Brand said he was only at those offices "between two and five times," does not recall meeting the alleged victim, and does not recall taking her by the arm or attempting to engage in nonconsensual sexual activity.
Another woman alleged Brand grabbed her breasts and orally raped her in a London bar in July 2004, allegations that Brand again denied.
Brand initially told police in 2024 that he "had no memory of meeting" the victim, but he said on the stand that he revisited the alleged location and recalled an encounter. He also said that seeing a video interview between the victim and police helped him recall the encounter. When asked by prosecutors if he waited to give his account until he saw the video interviews from that alleged victim and others to "structure his case" around their comments, he said no.
Brand answers questions about alleged apology
Another victim alleged Brand anally raped her in 2009. She alleged the encounter left blood and feces on bed sheets, which Brand then forced her to clean. Prosecutors say the alleged victim had a threesome with Brand backstage at London's Hammersmith Apollo Theatre before returning to his home for consensual sex.
On the stand, Brand confirmed that he and the woman had anal sex, along with other forms of penetration, and recalled being "excited and enthusiastic" about the "kinky" experience. He said the woman had consented and agreed to the encounter.
Brand said he had no indication that the woman was in pain, and she did not ask him to stop. He said he had a full-time housekeeper who would have cleaned the bed sheets.
Brand said he does not recall texting the victim after the encounter, but she said that she sent Brand a message where she accused him of treating her "like an animal." The woman alleged that Brand texted back "sorry." On the stand, Brand said he did not recall the exchange, but said he would have been apologizing for the "expressed dissatisfaction."
Brand blames documentary for charges
Under cross-examination, Brand blamed a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary program for the allegations against him. He said he believes the media have been unfair to him in the case, and said he was "innocent" of all allegations.
Before the documentary was released, Brand posted a video online denying the allegations. In the video, he noted again that he had been promiscuous during the time period described, but his relationships were "absolutely, always consensual."
He suggested the reports were part of a coordinated attack because of his newfound prominence as an online wellness influencer and political commentator. The women featured in the documentary said they only felt ready to share their stories after being approached by reporters, with some mentioning Brand's online fame as a factor in their decision to speak.
After the allegations, Brand's YouTube channel was demonitized. He was also dropped by his talent agency and had scheduled performances canceled.

World Bank warns of food crisis as war, weather shocks hit supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:02:30 UTC
00:02:30 KST

The World Bank has warned that global commodity prices were set to increase by 23 percent by the end of 2026, with energy prices at four-year highs due to the war on Iran and food prices driven up by global conflicts and El Nino.
"Commodity markets are being hit by several major shocks at once," said Ayhan Kose, the World Bank's deputy chief economist, in a statement accompanying the release of the organisation's Commodity Markets Outlook report on Wednesday.
"Higher energy costs and trade disruptions are driving up prices across a broad range of commodities, threatening to worsen inflation, food insecurity, and economic growth."
Food supplies under pressure
Food prices were expected to rise by 10 percent in 2026 and another seven percent next year, due to conflict-affected grain supply lines, the effects of an extreme El Nino phenomenon and high fuel and fertiliser prices.
El Nino is a naturally occurring weather phenomenon that is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet this year, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
For food producers, it is expected to lead to more flooding, droughts and heat stress across multiple regions.
Higher energy prices
Energy prices are projected to increase by 32 percent this year before moderating in 2027, the World Bank report said, assuming that conflicts in Iran and Ukraine do not intensify.
Global energy and fertiliser prices have skyrocketed since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in late February, plunging the Middle East into violence.
Iran responded with attacks on US allies in the region and virtually choked the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil, natural gas and fertiliser supply route.
The World Bank report warned that an especially strong El Nino, intensifying attacks on Black Sea grain shipments during the Russia-Ukraine war or further energy price spikes from the Iran war could lead to a "food crisis".
"In an adverse scenario in which these risks materialise together, Brent could average $105 a barrel in 2027 and food commodity prices could be 12 percent higher than expected in the baseline forecast, surpassing their level in 2022," the report said.
Since the start of the war on Iran, the World Bank has provided $8.7 billion in emergency support for vulnerable countries.
"The priority must be to protect the poorest people and support low-income countries already struggling with heavy debt burdens," said Kose.
Oil supply set for steep decline
Global oil supply is slated to fall by 5.2 percent in 2026, the largest decline in more than four decades outside of the pandemic, due to the effects of wars in the Middle East and between Russia and Ukraine.
The report noted that global oil price forecasts would be higher still if oil consumption were not forecast to fall by 2.5 percent this year, the third-largest such drop after the Covid pandemic and the 1980 oil crisis.
Still, the forecasts for food, energy and overall commodity prices were sharply higher than the bank's earlier predictions in April.

Researchers Are Challenging AI Consciousness Claims: The Backlash Shows What I Call ‘Silicon Science’ in Action
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:00:59 UTC
00:00:59 KST

A recent article in nature by Anil Seth, Ned Block, and Gulio Tononi argues that AI isn’t conscious. As someone who regularly reads the AI consciousness literature, I think this article was more forthright in its conviction that AI isn’t conscious than is typical for some of these authors.
It presents three core arguments against AI consciousness. First, even if we think of LLMs as intelligent, there is no reason to think that intelligence and consciousness are the same thing. These things do co-occur in humans, thus perhaps pushing us to believe that intelligence and consciousness may co-occur in other entities. But we should resist that intuition in the case of LLMs. While I’m not a fan of this argument, as I don’t believe LLMs are ‘intelligent’, it’s a reasonable one to make in context.
Second, they argue that the belief that AI is conscious depends on computational functionalism, i.e., that certain computational architectures are sufficient for consciousness. The authors reject this view, stating that ‘‘it is impossible to separate what biological brains do — their functional organization — from what they are — their material substrate’’. As I’ve written about before, I think this argument is true, and that we should reject computational functionalism.
Third, they argue that there are plausible non-computational theories of consciousness, which, if true, suggest that AI’s can’t be conscious. I think this argument has some merit, though my own view is that most theories of consciousness right now are very likely incorrect, so to me, this is mostly a moot point.
With that said, I am very glad to see ‘big names’ like Seth, Block and Tononi write in a more fortnight fashion that AI is not conscious. Moreover, I am especially happy to see them admit that functionalism is likely false, especially since at least two of three of these authors have written more modest articles where they are not as explicit in rejecting AI consciousness or functionalist claims, before.
Anil Seth, for instance, has written other papers in which he suggests consciousness is likely rooted in human biology. Ned Block too, has written similar articles with a more modest bent. In this piece however, the authors conclude that:
‘‘the balance of theory and evidence strongly suggests that, no matter how intelligent it is, silicon-based AI is unlikely to be or become conscious. The default position of the research community should therefore be that AI is not conscious and should not be treated as such’’
Perhaps it is just the genre of the writing (I imagine that this article, which appeared in the comments section of Nature, was not peer reviewed) that has the authors making slightly stronger claims than in other writing. Either way, I see this as a positive net development for the AI consciousness debate.
Moreover, either way, the computational functionalist camp —as I will fairly or unfairly call them — predictably clapped back. Amongst the clap
back, there was Chalmers, who claimed that the article, titled, ‘three reasons AI isn’t conscious’, should have been more properly called “three reasons why AI might not be conscious”, essentially dismissing the first argument (I think that’s fine), and suggesting that the second/third argument ‘need to be established’.
This particular claim —that is, responding that computational functionalism is likely false is one that needs to be ‘established’ — is an instance of what I have called in previous work ‘the perversion of the new silicon science’.
As I recently argued, the assumption that those who believe consciousness is biological need to prove this point has the science completely backwards. There are basic methodological precepts that exist in science for a reason: they have proven highly successful. Assuming that natural phenomena arise from organic matter is one of those precepts.
Given the success of this precept, I believe that anyone who wants to reject it needs to present the evidence for why. As Chalmers post on X suggests however, the burden of proof is often on those who accept this highly successful methodological precept rather than the other way around.
Another response to the paper goes even further, likening the authors article to a Monty Python skit and denying that the authors provide any arguments for their view.
Barenholtz’ response offers another instance of silicon science in action. The argument that consciousness requires biology, he writes, is ‘‘the conclusion restated as a premise’’. In other words, Barenholtz is again assuming that one must argue for the highly successful methodological precept that natural phenomena arise from organic matter.
Silicon science wants to reverse a fundamental premise of ordinary science, but to do that, it has to give us real evidence for its view. Claiming that those who believe consciousness isn’t likely in silicon are ‘not offering arguments’ or ‘should be more modest’ in their claims, is not, I think, the evidence that we need.
AIs Without Minds is an independent philosophical research newsletter that relies on paid subscriptions to keep going. If you value this work consider a paid subscription. You’ll get monthly zoom calls with me, monthly literature round-ups, and an AI & mind community chat dedicated to taking about these issues. As always, thanks for reading 📖 ✨

He called for "doubled efforts in work and innovation to add to the strength and authority of beloved Iran," expressing hope that the path toward "the peaks of progress and Islamic-Iranian civilization" would soon be realized.
The message to student groups follows a statement issued Monday by Ayatollah Khamenei addressing Iran's scientific and sports medalists, in which the Leader outlined a comprehensive roadmap for an "ever-stronger Iran."
In that message, Ayatollah Khamenei congratulated Iranians on recent successes in scientific Olympiads, including astronomy, mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, artificial intelligence, and the humanities, as well as on international sporting achievements.
The Leader framed Iran's elite—scientists, students, and athletes—as the engine of national strength. He cited stem cell research, nanotechnology, biotechnology, aerospace, nuclear energy, and defense technologies as evidence that "knowledge and talent can be turned into tools for addressing the real problems facing the people and the country.”
The Leader has also tied scientific advancement directly to Iran's geopolitical standing, stressing that "a strong Iran depends on scientific and technological power" and that this pillar shapes Iran's role in "the emerging global equations and the new world order."

norman foster discusses his first watch with LEBOND and why good design transcends scale
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

norman foster discusses his first watch with LEBOND and why good design transcends scale
from architecture to watchmaking, the british architect discusses how material choices, engineering, and everyday use inform his approach to designing objects across different scales.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
norman foster brings his architectural thinking to the wrist
Norman Foster unveils his first wristwatch, developed in collaboration with Swiss watchmaker LEBOND and the Norman Foster Foundation’s Innovation and Design Unit. The LEBOND Norman Foster applies the architect’s approach to materials, engineering, and function to a precision timepiece, rethinking the relationship between case and strap through an integrated design that prioritizes comfort and customization. For Foster, the shift in scale does not demand a different design philosophy. ‘I have never really thought that scale changes the nature of design,’ he tells designboom. ‘Whether it is a city, a building, a chair or a watch, you are still asking the same questions: how does it work, how is it made and how do all the parts come together?’ The watch offers an opportunity to apply these questions to an object encountered at close range and used repeatedly throughout the day. Unlike a building, it travels with its wearer, moving between professional settings, journeys, and private moments. ‘What is different about a watch is that it is intensely personal,’ Foster says. ‘You wear it, you travel with it and it becomes part of your everyday life.’
removing the boundary between case and strap
The defining decision is the removal of conventional lugs, the components that typically connect a watch case to its strap. Instead, the strap continues the line of the case, giving the watch a unified profile and allowing it to sit more comfortably on the wrist. The interchangeable strap also allows for different combinations of color and material, giving the wearer room to personalize the watch. ‘Normally, you have a watch case and then you attach a strap to it,’ Foster explains. ‘We started to question the obvious. Why should they feel like two separate objects? Once we began thinking of the strap as a continuation of the case, the whole watch started to come together.’ The decision reflects Foster’s approach to design, in which form and function develop together. ‘For me, it always starts with performance,’ he says. ‘I do not really see form, structure, materials and engineering as separate things. The best designs are those where they all reinforce one another.’ The watch takes shape through a process of sketches, prototypes, and successive adjustments, familiar to Foster from his architectural practice. Each stage brings the design closer to its essential idea. ‘You explore options to finally arrive at the essential idea and then you keep refining it until everything seems inevitable,’ the architect observes.
a precision instrument shaped by travel
The practical character of the watch reflects Foster’s longstanding interest in aviation and his experience of international travel. Its bidirectional rotating 12-hour bezel allows the wearer to read a second time zone using the main hour hand, addressing a familiar requirement for those who move frequently between locations. The dial follows the same emphasis on legibility. Restrained typography, clearly defined hands with Super-LumiNova, and a date window keep the information accessible without introducing unnecessary visual elements. ‘A watch has to tell the time clearly, it has to be comfortable and it has to work reliably,’ Norman Foster highlights. ‘The rotating 12-hour bezel, for example, comes directly from travelling and the practical need to read another time zone. The dial is deliberately restrained because the information should be immediate and clear.’ This emphasis on use also informs his understanding of timelessness. In a market where watches can function as status symbols and expressions of changing tastes, Foster frames longevity as a consequence of resolving the fundamentals. ‘I think timelessness is really the opposite of fashion. Fashion is transient. A well-designed object should continue to give satisfaction over time,’ he adds.
The case measures 38.5 mm in diameter, widening to 40 mm where it meets the integrated strap, and is 10 mm thick. Made from Grade 5 titanium, it is available with either a micro-sandblasted natural finish or a matte black diamond-like carbon (DLC) coating. Both editions feature a domed sapphire crystal with anti-reflective coating and water resistance to 50 meters. The Natural Titanium Edition pairs its case with a sunray-brushed dial, polished hands, and a light gray FKM rubber strap. The Black Edition combines a matte black-coated case with a black lacquered dial and hands, matched with a black FKM rubber strap. Both use a Grade 5 titanium deployant clasp. For Foster, these specifications matter insofar as they support the intended use of the timepiece. ‘For me, that comes down to purpose, proportion, materials and clarity,’ he points out. ‘If you resolve those fundamentals properly, then hopefully the object can age well. I would much rather it felt timeless than fashionable.’
making the mechanics part of the design
The mechanical movement of the watch introduces another dimension to Foster’s interest in the relationship between engineering and appearance. Through the sapphire caseback, a customized rotor, finished in blue in the Natural Titanium Edition and red in the Black Edition, becomes visible within the automatic movement. Five precision-machined perforations give the component a distinct geometry, while its color introduces a concentrated accent into the otherwise restrained design.
Inside, the watch uses a Swiss automatic ETA 2892-A2 movement operating at 28,800 vibrations per hour, with 21 jewels and an approximately 50-hour power reserve. Each timepiece is individually numbered. The rotor is more than a technical component presented for inspection. Its treatment brings the movement into the overall visual composition, making the mechanism part of the identity of the object. This reflects that engineering need not be concealed to achieve visual refinement, a principle Foster has applied across his work. ‘I have always believed that engineering can be beautiful when you allow the logic of how something works to be visible,’ he reflects.
a watch for everyday life
The collaboration also extends the work of the Norman Foster Foundation beyond buildings and urban research. Through its Innovation and Design Unit, the foundation explores projects across different scales. The project has an educational dimension, too. All proceeds received by the Norman Foster Foundation through royalties from watch sales support the educational programs of the Norman Foster Institute, which focuses on developing future generations of architects, designers, and urban leaders working toward more sustainable and resilient cities. For Foster, however, the measure of the object remains its ability to function naturally across different contexts. He imagines wearing it while working in the studio, visiting a building site, traveling, or attending a formal occasion. Its design should accommodate these situations without becoming tied to any one of them. ‘Probably that good design should improve everyday life without shouting about itself,’ he says, when asked what idea he hopes people carry with them when wearing the watch.
For Foster, the watch is an extension of the way he approaches design across different scales. Its appeal lies in the details, from the way the strap meets the case to the clarity of the dial and the movement beneath it. These are the elements he hopes the wearer will come to appreciate over time. ‘Hopefully, over time, you appreciate the relationship between all the parts rather than one feature in isolation, the way it feels on the wrist, the clarity of the dial, the space it defines, the engineering and the materials,’ Foster says. ‘For me, that is when an object really succeeds: when it simply becomes part of your life and you continue to appreciate it through use.’

brand: LEBOND Watches | @lebondwatches

Sony Wants You to Forget About Discs With Its Gorgeous Transparent Controllers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Sony has a collection of colorful, translucent cosmetics for its PlayStation consoles and controllers. Announced Wednesday, the Prism collection brings three new, gorgeous color options that conjure a nostalgic, transparent tech feel.
They come in Flare Orange, Emerald Green, and Graphite Gray. (Based on the pictures, the gray looks more like a blue to me.) You can get Sony’s DualSense PlayStation 5 controllers in the Prism design or opt for PS5 console covers. On the controllers, translucent plastic wraps around almost the entire device’s frame, letting you view the components inside. On the console cover version, the transparency is more limited—you can see only the fan and a few other components.
The Prism Collection DualSense wireless controllers cost $85, while the console covers cost $75. Preorders start on November 10, but the collection won’t ship until February 4. Those are roughly the same prices as existing controllers and covers, though on the higher end. Basic color controllers start at $74 on the PlayStation website. Covers start around $59. The more colorful options on both products go up from there.
Apple’s original iMac largely popularized translucent, colorful tech that lets you see inside the machine. The look was en vogue for a while in seminal devices like the PlayStation 2 and Nintendo’s Game Boy Color.
That see-through aesthetic was a signature in the early 2000s. (My first CD player had a translucent top, and you could see the disc spinning around the whole time.) Twenty-some years later, it’s being revived as nostalgia bait in a transparent tech renaissance. You can find the transparent look in everything from gaming handhelds to a Theragun. Sony also has a transparent pair of earbuds.
Reminiscing about the good ol’ days might also remind you that Sony’s old consoles used to have disc drives. In July, Sony made a controversial decision to end production of physical game discs starting in 2028. Ownership advocates have decried the choice, noting that Sony’s own terms of service state that buying a digital copy of a game does not mean the customer owns it. It’s yet another move toward the end of physical media.
Still, the Prism collection sure looks pretty.

Text description provided by the architects. Inhabiting the open landscape of the Córdoba hinterland calls for an act of spatial delimitation and the establishment of a domestic order. Located in La Bolsa, this low-cost residential project adopts the patio as the generative principle of its architectural layout, drawing on a dwelling type deeply rooted in the history of architecture. Its references include Jørn Utzon's celebrated Kingo Houses and Alvar Aalto's Muuratsalo Experimental House, both of which explore the L-shaped house organized around an open space, establishing an articulated relationship between domestic intimacy, landscape, and collective life.

Iraq, Syria discuss oil exports via Baniyas pipeline with capacity of 2M barrels per day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

14:57:48 UTC

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa discussed Wednesday exporting Iraqi oil through the Baniyas pipeline, and efforts to strengthen economic and security cooperation, according to a statement from the Iraqi prime minister’s media office, Anadolu reports.
The discussions took place during expanded talks between delegations from both countries in Damascus.
The talks addressed “exporting Iraqi oil through the Baniyas pipeline with an export capacity of up to 2 million barrels per day,” as well as increasing trade, it said, but provided no details on the project’s technical requirements, financing or implementation timeline.
The two sides also discussed joint efforts to develop the agricultural sector to achieve greater food and economic integration.
Zaidi described Iraqis and Syrians as “one people in two countries,” stressing the importance of expanding cooperation in various fields, particularly economic and social relations.
He also urged strengthening security cooperation, coordinating positions on regional and international issues, and promoting peace and stability in the region.
Sharaa welcomed Zaidi’s visit and reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to strengthening relations and achieving the highest levels of cooperation between the two countries.
Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa welcomed Al-Zaidi, who headed a high-level delegation, on arrival at Damascus International Airport, both the Iraqi News Agency (INA) and the Syrian Arab News Agency reported.
READ: Iraq says no US troops left in the country, not even advisers
Citing al-Zaidi’s office, INA said talks were expected to address bilateral ties, without providing further details.
Earlier, local media said talks were also expected to address border security and counter-terrorism efforts.
On Tuesday, Sharaa said the border between the countries is “completely” secure, adding that Damascus and Baghdad are already coordinating on several issues.
Damascus and Baghdad signed a memorandum of understanding in July to rehabilitate an oil pipeline extending from Haditha in western Iraq to the Syrian Mediterranean port of Baniyas, with US energy company Chevron expected to implement the project.
Earlier that month, the Iraqi government approved technical and financial studies for two proposed oil export routes: Basra-Haditha-Baniyas through Syria and Basra-Haditha-Kirkuk-Ceyhan through Turkiye, as part of efforts to develop alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.
The visit comes amid efforts by both countries to strengthen ties following the establishment of a Sharaa-led administration in Syria in January 2025.
The two leaders met in New York in September on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly, where they discussed political and security coordination and expanding economic and trade cooperation.

Minister Sjoerdsma announces new support package during visit to Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:57:48 UTC
23:57:48 KST

The Dutch government will provide Ukraine with a package of non-military support worth € 1.2 billion over the coming three years. The package will address the country’s most urgent needs and contribute to recovery and reconstruction, and improve opportunities for Dutch companies in Ukraine, especially in areas where they can offer expertise.
The bulk of the package is aimed at the energy and water sectors. Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation Sjoerd Sjoerdsma made this announcement during his visit to Kyiv on Wednesday. ‘Ukraine is under heavy fire and facing a tough winter’, he said. ‘It is essential for the security of us all that we continue to support Ukraine and its people to withstand this war. That is why the government has decided on this new package.’
The Netherlands will make a contribution of € 40 million to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund before the end of this year, to support the most urgent replacement and repairs to the energy system. Russian air strikes are increasingly targeting Ukraine’s energy and water infrastructure and have caused extensive damage and destruction. Dutch support will make it possible to repair damaged installations, stockpile emergency supplies and train specialist personnel for the energy and water sectors. The Netherlands will also provide € 55 million for in-kind energy support, enabling the delivery of energy equipment from Dutch companies to Ukrainian partners via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
Mr Sjoerdsma is visiting Kyiv together with the president of the Confederation of Netherlands Industry and Employers (VNO-NCW), Coen van Oostrom. They will talk with Ukrainian officials and Dutch businesses active in Ukraine about strengthening business relations, forging collaborations and removing obstacles.
The new package increases the government’s private sector support, enabling Dutch companies to play a bigger role in recovery and reconstruction and secure a better position in the Ukrainian market. For instance, € 136 million will go toward initiatives including the Ukraine Partnership Facility. Additionally, the government is enlarging the coverage of the existing export credit insurance in order to reduce risks for businesses aiming to export to Ukraine, with an additional €19.5 million available, on top of the existing €60 million facility.
Foreign trade minister Sjoerdsma: ‘Support for recovery and reconstruction can’t wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now: military support, but also social and economic assistance. However successful you are on the battlefield, it's also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over. This is not possible without the involvement of the private sector. That’s why it’s good to be here today with VNO-NCW. The companies that get involved now will help shape the partnerships, supply chains and opportunities of the future.’
VNO-NCW president Coen van Oostrom: ‘It’s impressive to see how Ukraine is keeping its economy running under very difficult circumstances. But reconstruction will be a huge job, and Dutch companies can play an important role in it. In this, we'll need to work closely with the Ukrainian government and remove obstacles for businesses. That’s what I'll be talking about today.’
Mr Sjoerdsma and Ukraine’s Minister of Economy and Environment Oleksandr Kravchenko will sign a declaration of intent on the Netherlands’ contribution to President Zelenskyy’s Industrial Ramstein initiative (€ 10 million). Its focus is on repairing and modernising the production capacity of Ukrainian businesses by facilitating the delivery of machines, equipment and other goods from other countries, including the Netherlands.
In addition, through the United Nations Development Programme, the Netherlands continues to support efforts to locate and return abducted Ukrainian children. Finally, the package also includes support in the areas of housing, humanitarian assistance, healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, demining, democracy and the rule of law, and the restoration of cultural heritage.
With the package, the government is providing more details about how it will spend the amounts it had already pledged for the coming three years, namely €878 million in non-military support set out in the coalition agreement and an additional €327 million announced on Budget Day. A large part of this support is channeled through the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the World Bank, and the European Investment Bank (EIB)

High-speed train collision in Spain kills 64
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:55:34 UTC
23:55:34 KST

Two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on this morning, leaving dozens dead and prompting a major emergency response.
At least 64 people were killed, according to the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, Reuters reported.
Authorities were continuing to search the damaged trains for victims.
The collision occurred around 9 a.m. near Urda, a town in Toledo province.
Images from the scene showed derailed carriages, including at least one that had fallen down a railway embankment. Several carriages were severely damaged, with wreckage scattered across the area.
An unnamed source briefed on the accident told Reuters that one train had stopped near Toledo because of a signal failure when another train struck it.
According to local authorities, one train was carrying 397 passengers and the other 147.
“We heard a violent noise, a completely enormous bump that lasted for ten seconds,” a passenger named Miguel told Spanish radio station COPE, according to Reuters.
“Through the window we could see a destroyed train. I imagine it was the other one.”
Emergency services deployed firefighters, helicopters and mobile intensive care units. Health Minister Mónica García urged people to donate blood.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed shock at the accident and offered condolences to victims’ families. He also cleared his Wednesday schedule.
The opposition People’s Party (PP) canceled its campaign events ahead of Spain’s November 29 parliamentary election.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” alongside the victims’ families.
The collision follows another high-speed rail accident in January, when 46 people died and more than 120 were injured near Adamuz in Andalusia.
Both accidents occurred on the Madrid-Seville route.

Copenhagen Airport says tighter security checks and staffing shortfalls contributed to long queues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
14:55:22 UTC
23:55:22 KST

An order from the Danish Transport Authority led to additional baggage checks from October 8. Some passengers missed flights, and SAS reported rebooking 352 travelers.
Copenhagen Airport introduced additional security checks following an order from the Danish Transport Authority and underestimated staffing needs on some days in October, the airport said Wednesday after long queues caused passengers to miss flights.
The airport received the order on October 6 and introduced the measures two days later. The changes meant more passengers had their baggage checked manually, it said in a press release.
The airport did not explain why the authority issued the order or give details of its requirements.
There were periods of long waits on October 8, October 22 and October 23, the airport said. Passengers also faced waits of up to an hour early on Saturday, October 24.
Danish media have reported lengthy queues, particularly over the past five days, with some passengers reaching their flights too late to depart as booked.
The airport acknowledged that it had underestimated staffing needs on some days during October. It said “it is naturally not satisfactory” that some passengers had had “a bad experience”.
SAS said on October 23 that it had rebooked 352 passengers because of the long waits. Passengers were also urged to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time for security.
Norwegian also offered affected customers rebooking.

Danish tax agency faces further scrutiny over identity theft cases
Denmark’s Parliamentary Ombudsman has demanded further explanations from the Danish Tax Agency over its handling of cases involving citizens who were wrongly pursued for millions in taxes after becoming victims of identity theft.
Ombudsman Christian Britten Lundblad said the agency’s report, submitted on August 31, did not adequately address concerns raised about the cases.
“After reviewing the report and the complaint that I previously received from a lawyer on behalf of a citizen in the complex of cases, I have found reason to ask the Danish Tax Agency for a statement,” Lundblad wrote.
The investigation concerns 126 people involved in tax cases linked to money transfers through five businesses. The agency began examining the transfers in 2021.
In June, TV 2’s investigative programme Operation X highlighted how citizens had faced incorrect tax claims worth millions following suspected identity theft connected to money laundering cases.
The agency’s own report found that it should have acted in 2023, when police provided information suggesting widespread identity theft.
In August, Danish Tax Agency Director Thomas Hjortenberg acknowledged the mistakes and apologised to those affected.
“Our mistakes have had major personal consequences for the affected citizens,” he said.
Hjortenberg also admitted that the agency should have responded much earlier to the police’s warnings.
The ombudsman now wants to establish what information the agency possessed before issuing its tax assessments.
He has also requested clarification on whether evidence in each case supported the information obtained from the money transfer businesses.
The Danish Tax Agency has until November 7 to provide its response.

Alm. Brand to lay off 55 employees as it reports record insurance result
Danish insurance group Alm. Brand has decided to lay off 55 employees and has eliminated 30 other positions as part of efforts to reduce costs, even as it reported its highest quarterly insurance result to date.
The group’s insurance result reached 755 million DKK in the third quarter, according to financial statements released Wednesday. The measure reflects earnings from its core insurance business, taking account of premium income, claims and operating expenses.
Chief Executive Officer Andreas Ruben Madsen said the job cuts were needed to improve efficiency and support the company’s previously announced strategy.
“It is a difficult decision because it affects colleagues, but it is at the same time a necessary step to realize the efficiencies that support the strategic direction we have already announced,” he said in a stock exchange announcement.
Lower claims costs were the main factor behind the record insurance result. Claims expenses fell by 165 million DKK from the same period last year to approximately 1.7 billion DKK. Insurance income rose slightly to more than 3 billion DKK.
The group reported a third-quarter profit after tax of 397 million DKK.
Madsen attributed the insurance result mainly to fewer major claims, fewer weather-related claims and positive run-off results. Run-off results arise when an insurer adjusts its estimates for claims from previous periods.
He cautioned that those factors might not provide the same boost in future quarters.
“This contributes significantly to earnings in the quarter, but at the same time these are conditions that we cannot expect will contribute at the same level going forward.”

Kirill Dmitriev, a Russian envoy involved in negotiations over the war in Ukraine and an adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin on economic and international affairs, said Tuesday that Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen deserves to lose Greenland.

“She (Mette Frederiksen, ed.) deserves to lose Greenland. The warmongers will lose. Dialogue will prevail,” Dmitriev wrote.
The comments came after Finnish President Alexander Stubb announced Tuesday morning that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre had spoken with Putin by phone.
The call received a mixed response from the countries’ allies. Frederiksen was among those who criticized the decision to speak with the Russian president.
“I am very skeptical of this Norwegian and Finnish own initiative. It is not coordinated with the rest of us,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcaster TV 2 during a meeting of the Nordic Council in Finland.
“I think one should keep Europe together instead of going solo,” she added.
Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson also expressed doubts about the call.
“Holding talks that risk dividing the European voice, that is risky,” he said Tuesday, according to Swedish media.
Støre later rejected the criticism, saying the talks were conducted with other countries’ knowledge.
“We do not speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves, but it has been thoroughly consulted, and all our partners and allies were informed in advance and have also received a thorough summary afterwards,” he told Norwegian media outlet VG on Tuesday.
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy took a more positive view of the talks. In a post on X, he said he was “grateful” for Norway and Finland’s active diplomatic work.
Study finds problematic social media use more common among girls
More than one in five girls aged 15 to 21 in a Danish study show signs of problematic social media use, compared with fewer than one in 10 boys, according to research from the Rockwool Foundation, a Danish research foundation.
The study surveyed 8,239 young people about their use of platforms such as Snapchat, TikTok, Instagram and Facebook. Researchers also asked about their well-being and the amount of time they spend on social media.
Based on their answers, participants were classified using an internationally recognized scale for problematic social media use.
The results show that 22.2 percent of the girls surveyed fell into the category, compared with 9.6 percent of the boys.
Nadja Eifler, a PhD student at the Rockwool Foundation, said part of the difference could be explained by the activities young people choose online.
“In the study, we asked specifically about social media such as Facebook, TikTok, Instagram, and Snapchat, so part of the difference between girls and boys may lie in the fact that many boys spend more time on computer games, which is also for many a social activity where you can be in dialogue with friends,” she said.
The study also found a link between problematic social media use and poor well-being, particularly among girls.
“We can clearly see that poor well-being is most widespread among young people with problematic social media use, especially for the girls, where more than half of these young women have low well-being,” Eifler said.
Among girls who did not have problems with social media use, just under four in 10 reported low well-being.
The report recommends looking beyond the number of hours young people spend on social media when assessing whether their use is problematic.
Other warning signs include difficulty reducing use, feeling restless or uneasy when a phone is out of reach, and social media having a negative effect on school or education.
The findings suggest that how young people use social media, and how it affects their daily lives, may be important factors alongside the time they spend online.
ATP’s investment return falls to 1.5 percent after weak quarter
Danish pension provider ATP recorded a negative investment result in the third quarter, reducing its total return for the first nine months of the year to 1.5 percent.
The company announced the figures in a press release on its website but did not disclose the size of the investment loss during the third quarter alone.
ATP’s return stood at 14.5 percent when it published its half-year report a few months earlier. The latest figures show that much of the return earned during the first half of the year was lost in the following three months.
ATP Chief Executive Officer Martin Præstegaard described the period as difficult, pointing to rising interest rates as a key factor behind the weaker result.
“We have had a challenging third quarter, where rising interest rates have affected the result negatively,” he said.
He added that the company had delivered a good investment return during the first half of the year, leaving the overall return positive for the first nine months.
“The interest rate fluctuations do not change the fact that pensioners can count on receiving the pension they are guaranteed, and a robust bonus capacity allows us to increase pensions for all members,” Præstegaard said.
ATP is Denmark’s statutory supplementary pension scheme. Employees who work at least nine hours a week and their employers pay contributions into the scheme. People receiving certain public benefits also contribute to ATP.
Around 5.8 million people are members of the scheme.
ATP provides a guaranteed, lifelong monthly pension payment that supplements the Danish state pension after people stop working.
The company’s investment portfolio accounts for approximately 20 percent of its total assets.
The latest figures cover the first nine months of the year, including the period from July through September, when rising interest rates weighed on investment performance. Despite the decline in the third quarter, ATP said its overall return for the year remained positive.
Viking-era Danish coin sells for 136,000 DKK at Copenhagen auction
A Danish coin dating back more than 1,000 years has sold for 18,300 euros, approximately 136,000 DKK, at an auction in Copenhagen.
The coin, associated with Viking king Svend Tveskæg, fetched more than twice its estimated price of 6,000 to 8,000 euros, or roughly 45,000 to 60,000 DKK.
Auction house Stack’s Bowers confirmed the sale on its website following Tuesday’s auction.
The coin is considered the first official Danish coin to feature both the name of a Danish ruler and the country’s name.
Svend Tveskæg was the first ruler to have his name appear on a Danish coin.
“This coin type is considered the first official Danish coin and has an exceptionally great historical significance because it was the first Danish coin that bore both the king’s and the country’s name,” the auction house stated.
However, archaeological discoveries indicate that coins were used in Denmark long before this particular type was produced.
The coin weighs just 1.95 grams and had previously been broken into several pieces before being repaired, according to the auction house.
It belonged to a collection assembled by Danish businessman Lars Emil Bruun, who died in 1923.
Bruun made his fortune as a butter wholesaler, exporting canned butter to markets around the world.
In his will, he stipulated that his extensive coin collection could not be sold until 100 years after his death.
Several other coins from Bruun’s collection were also sold during Tuesday’s auction in Copenhagen.
The auction is scheduled to continue Wednesday, October 28.
Electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex recalled over electric shock risk
Danish company Epiq ApS has recalled four electrical products sold at Bilka and Føtex supermarkets because they pose a risk of electric shock.
The recall covers power strips, extension cord sets and a double-socket adapter sold between June 2 and September 18, 2026, the company announced in a press release.
According to Epiq ApS, the affected products lack child safety protection covering the socket openings, creating a potential electric shock hazard.
The company has urged customers to “immediately stop using the products” and return them to the store where they were purchased.
Customers will receive a full refund even if they no longer have their receipt.
The recall covers the following four products:
Scoop ledningssæt med tre stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with three sockets. EAN code: 5713359129661.
Basis ledningssæt med fire stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with four sockets. EAN code: 5713359131749.
Scoop ledningssæt med fem stikdåser: A 1.5-meter extension cord with five sockets. EAN code: 5713359129692.
Scoop dobbeltstik: A double-socket adapter. EAN code: 5713359129685.
An EAN code is a product identification number commonly found on packaging or labels. Epiq ApS says the codes for the recalled items can be found on the back of the products.
Consumers can use these numbers to check whether an electrical product they purchased is affected by the recall.
The company has instructed customers to return affected products to their original Bilka or Føtex store for a refund without requiring proof of purchase.
Veteran Venstre lawmaker expelled over party discipline dispute
Preben Bang Henriksen has been expelled from Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, after refusing to promise that he would follow the party’s position in future parliamentary votes.
The lawmaker confirmed his expulsion Tuesday following a meeting at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing.
“The conclusion of a vote was that I am expelled,” he said.
Henriksen will continue as an independent member of parliament but said he had hoped to remain in Venstre.
The dispute followed a September vote on legislation concerning fertilizer use, when five Venstre lawmakers opposed the party’s position over concerns about its impact on agriculture.
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen subsequently sought stronger party discipline, receiving support from the party’s national executive committee Sunday.
“Once the debate has taken place, and a majority has decided on a direction, the expectation is that the majority backs it, even if one wished for a different result,” Poulsen said Tuesday.
Henriksen refused to make that commitment, arguing that lawmakers should retain their independence.
Under Denmark’s Constitution, members of parliament are bound only by their own convictions.
However, Venstre’s internal rules prevent lawmakers expelled from its parliamentary group from remaining party members.
Henriksen, a former lawyer from Aalborg, entered parliament in 2011 at age 57.
He has served as the party’s justice spokesperson and chaired parliamentary committees overseeing legal affairs and intelligence services.
Known for following his own conviction, he has previously gone against the party line. In 2021, he voted with eight members against launching an impeachment trial against Inger Støjberg, who ended up being convicted. The members were granted a free vote when they voted.
In the 2024 book “Ærlig talt – Borgen indefra”, he described that he was close to leaving Venstre because of Lars Løkke Rasmussen’s purchase of clothes with party money. The book also contains criticism of political conformism and the workflows at Christiansborg.
With Preben Bang Henriksen’s departure, Venstre loses another one of its vote-magnets, as he received the fifth-most votes in Venstre in the election in March 2026.
Danish parties move toward majority support for ban on fast-growing chickens
Several Danish political parties are backing a ban on breeding fast-growing chickens, commonly called “turbo chickens,” amid concerns about animal welfare.
Around 70 million of these chickens are produced annually in Denmark, according to Berlingske.
The Ross 308 breed, widely used in Danish poultry farming, grows from approximately 50 grams to two kilograms in just 33 days.
Their rapid growth can put considerable strain on their legs, leaving many chickens sitting for much of their final weeks before slaughter, Berlingske reports.
The Alternative, the Red-Green Alliance, the Socialist People’s Party, the Social Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance and the Conservative People’s Party support a ban. The Denmark Democrats have also expressed support for its aims.
The Moderates, a centrist party, have changed their position since 2024, when parliament rejected a proposal to ban the production, sale and import of Ross 308 chickens.
At the time, the governing coalition preferred pursuing a European Union-wide solution.
“When you say A regarding the pigs, then I also think you have to say B regarding the chickens,” Moderates animal welfare spokesperson Ellen Emilie Mindegaard-Müllertz told Berlingske.
An EU-wide agreement could take time, while a Danish production ban would not prevent imports from other countries.
Animal welfare organization Anima recently reported that fast-growing chickens account for two-thirds of chicken sales at Salling Group’s Netto, Bilka and Føtex supermarkets.
At Rema 1000, the figure is 15 percent.
Social Democratic animal welfare spokesperson Birgitte Vind also told Berlingske that the chickens’ conditions were unacceptable and should be examined.
Engineering consultancy Rambøll will lay off 400 employees at management level as it seeks to simplify its organization and speed up decisions, the company announced Tuesday.
The layoffs are expected to be completed by the end of November. There will also be voluntary departures, though the company declined to say how many.
CEO Christian Jensby said Rambøll’s growth had made the organization more complex.
“In many areas, the organization has become difficult to navigate, decisions take too long, and areas of responsibility are not sufficiently clear,” he said in a statement.
The company plans to remove unnecessary tasks and internal coordination processes to improve collaboration and decision-making.
Rambøll employs about 18,000 people worldwide, including 4,000 in Denmark. The announcement did not specify how many of the layoffs would affect its Danish workforce.
The company said it would continue examining ways to streamline the organization, which could also affect employees below management level.
Jensby took office May 1 after leading Deloitte Denmark.
Founded in 1945, Rambøll advises clients on construction, transport, the environment, energy and management. The Rambøll Foundation owns 98% of the company, with employees holding the remaining 2%.
Norwegian to cut 123 jobs at Copenhagen Airport as it reduces locally based aircraft
Norwegian will lay off 123 employees at Copenhagen Airport, including 53 pilots and 70 cabin crew members, as it reduces the number of aircraft based in the Danish capital.
The decision follows talks with Flyvebranchens Personale Union, or FPU, the union representing the employees, according to Danish business outlet Finans.
Most affected staff will leave at the end of January next year, with the remaining departures planned 10 months later.
“It is a sad day for Norwegian, and I am incredibly affected on behalf of the affected employees,” Sara Neergaard, the airline’s country manager in Denmark, told Finans.
“But there is no other way. The redundancies are happening out of necessity.”
Norwegian plans to reduce its Copenhagen-based fleet during the summer season from 16 aircraft to 14. The airline says demand varies considerably between seasons, requiring 16 aircraft during the summer peak but only 10 in winter.
The change will not reduce the number of summer departures from Copenhagen. Some summer routes will instead be operated by aircraft based in Spain.
Union challenges the decision
FPU Chair Thilde Waast described the layoffs as an attempt to “undermine Danish working conditions.” In a written response, she accused Norwegian of seeking to replace Danish employees with “cheaper Spanish labor.”
Neergaard said the union had rejected options that could have reduced the number of layoffs, including seasonal contracts under which staff would work more in summer and less in winter, as well as voluntary leave.
Norwegian was Copenhagen Airport’s second-largest airline by passenger share last year, according to the airport’s latest financial report. It carried 15% of passengers, behind SAS at 38% and ahead of Ryanair at 9%.
With 16 aircraft, Copenhagen has been Norwegian’s second-largest base after Oslo. The airline served 77 destinations from Copenhagen last year.
EU Commission proposes expanding Frontex border force to 30,000 and increasing its deportation role
The European Commission proposed Tuesday expanding the personnel available to Frontex, the EU’s border agency, to 30,000 and giving it a larger role in deportations.
The plan would create a reserve of 17,000 personnel who could be deployed when needed. According to AFP, these would be national border guards made available by member states.
Frontex’s own workforce would grow from 3,000 to 6,000, alongside 7,000 personnel already on loan from EU countries. The proposal also includes a rapid reaction force.
“Europe decides who comes to our union – and under what circumstances,” Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.
“Therefore, we are proposing today to strengthen Frontex so that it can support the member states when and where it is needed.”
The proposal follows an incident in July when thousands of migrants entered Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the African continent, within a short period.
Established in 2004, Frontex helps EU countries protect the external borders of Europe’s free-movement area. Its responsibilities expanded in 2016, following the previous year’s refugee and migration crisis, to include broader border management and a greater role in fighting cross-border crime.
The agency frequently faces criticism from migrant rights groups. Melissa Camara, a member of the European Parliament’s Greens group, criticized the direction of EU policy.
“Ever more oppression, dehumanization of displaced people, and an increasing tendency to mimic the rhetoric of the far right,” she said, according to AFP.
The proposal requires approval from the European Parliament and the Council, which represents EU member governments.

The University of Copenhagen says it was not hit by a second cyberattack Monday, reversing its initial assessment after shutting down several administrative systems.
Activity that appeared to signal another attack prompted the shutdown. By Monday evening, the university had determined that no new attack had occurred, it said on its website.

The breach also compromised ID card PINs belonging to about 20,000 employees and students. The university temporarily restricted physical access to selected critical locations following a security assessment.
Those locations have reopened after all affected cardholders received new PINs.
The University of Copenhagen, the Technical University of Denmark and Aarhus University have all faced cyberattacks within a few weeks.
Christina Egelund, Denmark’s minister for research, higher education and digitalization, previously told Ritzau that leaders from the country’s eight universities had been summoned to a meeting Monday to discuss security.

Bank deposits in Denmark fall for two consecutive months
Danes’ bank deposits fell for a second consecutive month in September, reaching 1,309.3 billion kroner, according to figures from Danmarks Nationalbank, Denmark’s central bank.
That was down from 1,317.7 billion kroner in August and 1,323.2 billion kroner in July. Helle Dalsgaard, head of advisory services at pension provider Sampension, said the last decline lasting two consecutive months occurred in January 2023, but cautioned against treating the latest figures as evidence of a broader trend.
Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, Denmark’s main employers’ and business association, said September declines were common, occurring in 16 of the past 20 years. He suggested loan payments and spending on autumn and winter clothing could help explain the fall, while noting that September does not bring large child benefit payments or tax refunds.
Despite the recent declines, deposits remained above the 1,283.1 billion kroner recorded at the beginning of the year. Dalsgaard expects savings to grow again, saying uncertainty about personal finances could encourage Danes to put more money aside.
