Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:17 UTC
21:00:17 KST

Scientists discover a hidden 100-million-year-old volcanic system
- Date:
- October 28, 2026
- Source:
- Istanbul Technical University
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a long-lost volcanic system in Iran that dates back roughly 100 million years, revealing a hidden chapter in Earth's tectonic history. The discovery sheds new light on the disappearance of an ancient ocean and the powerful geological forces that reshaped the Middle East.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered evidence of a previously unknown volcanic system that formed roughly 100 million years ago in what is now northwestern Iran. The discovery reveals a missing chapter in the region's geological history and offers new clues about the powerful tectonic forces that shaped ancient oceans and continents.
Mountain ranges contain valuable records of Earth's distant past, preserving traces of vanished oceans, shifting continents, and the geological processes that transformed the planet over millions of years. However, these records are often difficult to interpret because later tectonic activity, erosion, and layers of buried sediment can conceal evidence of much older events.
An international team led by Istanbul Technical University (ITU) has now identified remnants of an ancient continental magmatic arc that had previously gone unrecognized. Named the Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc, the system formed during the Late Cretaceous period in a region that is now part of the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone.
The research, published in Geoscience Frontiers, indicates that the volcanic system was active approximately 101 to 97 million years ago, when the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean was undergoing major geological changes. Over time, tectonic deformation, erosion, burial beneath sedimentary basins, and a younger episode of volcanic activity during the Eocene obscured much of the evidence of its existence.
Ancient Rocks Reveal a Lost Volcanic System
To reconstruct this overlooked chapter of Earth's history, the researchers examined volcanic and plutonic rocks collected from multiple locations across northwestern Iran. Much of their investigation focused on formations along the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault.
The team used several advanced techniques to determine when the rocks formed and where their original materials came from. These included zircon U-Pb geochronology to establish their ages, Hf isotope analyses to investigate their sources, and whole-rock geochemistry to examine their chemical composition.
Together, the results revealed signatures consistent with continental arc magmatism, a geological process that occurs when one tectonic plate sinks beneath another, generating magma that can rise through the overlying continental crust.
Dr. Ali Mohammadi, the study's corresponding author at Istanbul Technical University, explained: "This study shows that the magmatic history of northwestern Iran is more complex than previously recognized. By integrating geochronological, isotopic, and geochemical evidence, we identified a Late Cretaceous continental arc that was subsequently obscured by later tectonic processes."
The international research effort also involved scientists from the Institute of Tibetan Plateau Research and Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography, Chinese Academy of Sciences; ETH Zurich, Switzerland; Karadeniz Technical University, Türkiye; and Damghan University, Iran.
A Missing Piece of Iran's Geological History
Previous reconstructions of Iran's ancient magmatic activity have largely centered on two major geological features: the Sananda-Sirjan Magmatic Arc and the Urumieh-Dokhtar Magmatic Arc.
The newly identified Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc adds another important piece to that history. Its discovery suggests that northwestern Iran experienced a separate episode of continental arc activity during the Late Cretaceous, expanding scientists' understanding of how the region developed.
The findings also point to a potentially important role for the Siah Cheshmeh-Khoy-Misho-Tabriz Fault. Researchers suggest that this fault may mark a major tectonic boundary connected to changes in the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean system.
Those changes may have included slab rollback, a process in which a descending tectonic plate retreats as it sinks into Earth's interior, as well as the migration of volcanic arcs to new locations. Such movements could help explain why this particular episode of magma formation lasted for a relatively short period.
New Clues About the Disappearance of an Ancient Ocean
Beyond Iran, the discovery provides a broader lesson about how Earth's geological history can become hidden over immense stretches of time.
Ancient magmatic arcs do not always survive as continuous, easily recognizable formations. Tectonic movements can break them apart, erosion can remove exposed rocks, and sedimentation can bury what remains. Later volcanic activity can further complicate the record, making older systems particularly difficult to identify.
By recognizing the surviving fragments of these ancient structures, scientists can better reconstruct how tectonic plates descended beneath one another, how volcanic arcs shifted, how continental crust grew, and how once-vast oceans eventually closed.
The Azerbaijan Continental Magmatic Arc offers new evidence for understanding the Late Cretaceous evolution of northwestern Iran and the larger Neo-Tethyan region. It also helps researchers refine geological models of an area shaped by repeated episodes of ocean closure and continental collision.
The ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean played a major role in the geological development of the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East, and Western Asia. Its eventual disappearance helped shape the modern landscapes of these regions.
By uncovering a volcanic system that had been largely erased from the geological record, researchers have added another piece to the complex story of how Earth's continents and oceans evolved over millions of years.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Istanbul Technical University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Ali Mohammadi, Hadi Shafaii Moghadam, Amaneh Kaveh-Firouz, Anna Lechmann, Fulong Cai, Lin Ding. The missing late Cretaceous magmatic arc in the Arabia-Eurasia collision zone (NW Iran): constraints from zircon geochronology, Hf isotopes, and geochemistry. Ocean’s ability to absorb carbon is weakening as climate change intensifies, UN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Ocean’s ability to absorb carbon is weakening as climate change intensifies, UN warns
The ocean absorbs around 30 per cent of human-caused carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions and 90 per cent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. But climate change has already reduced its capacity to absorb carbon by approximately six per cent, a new UN report warns ahead of the COP31 climate conference in November.
The report was a collaboration between the UN’s environment agency, UNEP, and the UN climate secretariat, UNFCCC, which co-organises COP31.
“For a long time the ocean has been doing us an enormous climate service, but that service is under increasing pressure,” Sara Traerup, lead author of the report, told UN News.
Rising temperatures and changes in ocean chemistry, circulation and ecosystems are weakening its ability to absorb and store carbon, leaving more CO₂ in the atmosphere.
And this process “can definitely accelerate” in the foreseeable future, Ms. Traerup warned.
Bridging our knowledge gap
A major challenge is the lack of reliable ocean monitoring data, particularly in the Southern and Indian Oceans, the Arctic and many coastal regions.
The report therefore calls for stronger “ocean carbon intelligence” – using science, technology, data and local knowledge to better understand and manage ocean carbon systems.
“As of now, we don’t have full information about the ocean, and what we don’t know, we cannot manage and protect,” Ms. Traerup explained.
From sensors to seagrass
UNEP looked at three main types of ocean climate technologies, each offering different opportunities and risks.
The first is ocean monitoring: observation systems, sensors, data systems and modelling. Ms. Traerup called these the most mature technologies and the most immediately needed.
The second is blue carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes. They already sequester around 407 million tonnes of CO₂ a year, and restoring them could add significantly more. They also protect coastlines, support biodiversity and sustain livelihoods.
The third is marine carbon dioxide removal, which aims to extract CO₂ from the atmosphere and store it over the long term. While potentially promising, these approaches remain highly uncertain and require further research, monitoring and regulation.
“We shouldn’t treat ocean-based technologies as a shortcut,” Ms. Traerup cautioned, as they must complement, not replace, emissions reductions and ecosystem protection.
Islands leading the way
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) contribute less than one per cent of global emissions, yet are “on the front line of ocean and climate impacts,” Ms. Traerup noted.
The report called for greater access to finance, technology transfer and capacity-building to enable these countries to develop ocean solutions tailored to their needs. Some islands are already showing how this can work.
In 2015, Seychelles, for instance, benefited from a debt-for-nature swap, which involved restructuring part of its foreign debt in exchange for marine conservation commitments. This enabled the country to set up a trust fund to finance marine conservation, climate resilience and the sustainable blue economy.
In the Pacific, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu received support to map seagrass meadows and mangrove forests, and measure how much carbon they store. As a result, more than 100 people were trained in blue carbon assessment, giving governments data to feed into their national climate plans.
The report also stressed the importance of integrating local and Indigenous knowledge.
“Communities have been coping with climate change for many, many years,” Ms. Traerup said, pointing to their experience in protecting coastlines through natural habitats and in managing fisheries and coastal resources sustainably.

Ending conflict is ‘number one thing’ to reduce world hunger, new WFP chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Ending conflict is ‘number one thing’ to reduce world hunger, new WFP chief says
Reducing conflict is the single most effective way to tackle global hunger, the new head of the UN World Food Programme (WFP), Luke Lindberg, said on Wednesday, noting that conflict drives two thirds of the acute food insecurity affecting 266 million people worldwide.
“Conflict is a man-made situation. It is something that we can solve,” Mr. Lindberg told journalists at UN Headquarters in New York in his first press conference since taking office earlier this week.
“The number one thing we can do to reduce hunger in the world is to reduce the amount of conflict that is happening all around the world.”
On top of that, El Niño is set to push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity, while chokepoints in global supply chains are exacerbating the problem further, he said.
‘Big platitudes’
Mr. Lindberg said WFP did not need “big platitudes or big announcements” but execution, built on three priorities: protecting staff, strengthening donor partnerships and improving operations “a little bit better each and every day”.
More than 700 humanitarians have been killed in the last few years while trying to save lives, he said. “Nobody should lose their life trying to save somebody else’s.”
He also pledged to keep investing in preparedness ahead of disasters, including through tools such as artificial intelligence, and to “go big” on school meals.
First trip to Sudan
Mr. Lindberg said his first trip as Executive Director would be to Sudan in a couple of weeks, to thank frontline staff working in “the most challenging places on Earth”.
Sudan, South Sudan and Somalia are the three operations where WFP is currently focusing, he said. “In the short run, it’s no more famines.”
Asked about Gaza, he said the number of people going hungry there was unacceptable, adding that while WFP has access to deliver food, it is cutting back because of funding shortfalls.
He pledged to stand up for WFP employees wherever they are located. “If anywhere in the world there are people attacking humanitarians, I will absolutely do what I can to protect them,” he said.
‘All-of-the-above approach’
On funding, Mr. Lindberg said the United States remains WFP’s largest funder, while the private sector is now its fifth-largest donor. “There is no one nation, no one entity that can do this alone,” he said.
Asked whether he saw himself as Washington’s representative at the UN, Mr. Lindberg called it “an unfair characterization”, saying his mandate from the Secretary-General is to end hunger and that he would be a “team player” across the UN system.
Mr. Lindberg said US President Donald Trump had personally called him to ask him to be the US nominee for the post, and that he had “a great relationship” with many members of the Trump administration.
People “all the way up the chain to the president” within the US Government want to support humanitarian work around the world, he said, adding that WFP also needs to build deeper donor partnerships with other countries.
Mr. Lindberg succeeds Cindy McCain, who led WFP from April 2023 to May 2026, and Carl Skau, who has served as Acting Executive Director since June.
The new WFP chief previously served as Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs with the US Department of Agriculture.

Protecting the storytellers: Women journalists on the frontline of conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Protecting the storytellers: Women journalists on the frontline of conflict
As online abuse, gender-based attacks and impunity ramp up the threats to women reporting from crisis zones, journalists and UN leaders are calling for urgent action to protect those who document conflict.
“Every woman journalist driven out of a conflict zone is a peace process that loses its witness,” said Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, addressing the United Nations this week.
She urged governments to move beyond promises and take concrete action to protect women media workers in the field.
“When the messenger is a woman, it is sexualized, it's dehumanizing, and it is relentless,” said Ms. Ressa, co-founder of the Philippine news organisation Rappler.
As part of Women, Peace and Security Week, she was speaking at a high-level event organised by the Permanent Mission of Greece, gender equality agency UN Women, and the UN education and culture agency, UNESCO, which champions journalist protection.
‘Fight before it’s too late’
Ms. Ressa, who has faced arrest, legal cases and sustained online attacks, reiterated how intimidation can wear down journalists’ credibility and confidence, threaten their safety and ultimately kill their determination to continue reporting.
At the height of the attacks against her, she received 90 hate messages an hour.
The attacks illustrate how gender-based abuse can be used to discredit women who challenge those in power.
“Kill the messenger to kill the message,” she explained to the event – Every Voice for Peace Counts: New Perspectives on the Women, Peace and Security Agenda.
AI enabler
Artificial intelligence is adding to the threat, enabling deepfakes, fabricated sexual images, cloned voices and coordinated attacks to spread at scale.
According to UN Women data, nearly one in four women human rights defenders, activists and journalists reported experiencing AI-enabled abuse which in time can manifest as physical violence.
Recent research highlights how online attacks - once dismissed as “virtual” problems - are now spilling offline, affecting women’s safety, well-being, and ability to participate freely in public debate.
Ms. Ressa called for online violence to be treated as such, arguing for stronger accountability for perpetrators and technology companies that amplify abuse, sustained funding for women-led journalism, and the inclusion of women journalists in peace and security discussions.
‘This is the moment’
Invoking the words of Mzia Amaglobeli, a Georgian journalist who remains imprisoned, Ms. Ressa described how she had held up a copy of How to Stand Up to a Dictator in court when she was unable to speak freely.
“What she said from her cell is, fight before it's too late,” Ms. Ressa said. “We're getting there. This is it. This is the moment.”
She called on journalists, civil society, governments and international institutions to stand together against a system that allows attacks on women journalists to go unchecked.
“We refuse to be the victim,” she said. “The women here turned the attack into the story, and every time one of us stood up, others stood with us. Courage is contagious. But courage isn't a protection strategy - the nations of the UN are”.
The meeting took place 26 years since the adoption of Security Council resolution 1325, which affirmed the importance of women's full participation in conflict prevention, resolution and peacebuilding.
Keeping Afghan women's voices alive
For Afghan journalist and media entrepreneur Hamida Aman, protecting women journalists means ensuring that millions of women are not shut out of public life altogether.
When she launched Radio Begum in March 2021, her aim was to create a space where Afghan women could share their experiences and access information relevant to their lives. Since the Taliban takeover, restrictions have made that work increasingly difficult.
Citing figures from the International Federation of Journalists, Ms. Aman said the number of women journalists in Afghanistan had fallen from about 2,800 before the takeover to fewer than 700.
“Being allowed to operate doesn't mean being free to operate,” she said, describing the scrutiny and administrative obstacles facing Radio Begum. The organisation has been threatened and temporarily shut down, and some colleagues have been jailed for more than six months.
“If these journalists disappear, who will speak about the lives of Afghan women? Who will make their voices heard?” Ms. Aman asked.
Silencing collective stories
Protecting women journalists is not only about individual safety. It is also about whose experiences of conflict are documented, whose voices shape public understanding and whose contributions to peace are recognised.
“When women journalists are silenced, the women whose stories they are telling is also silenced,” said UN Women Deputy Executive Director for Normative Support, UN System Coordination, and Programme Results, Nyaradzai Gumbonzvanda. “So, it's not just the silencing of the journalists, it's the silencing of our collective story.”
Women in conflict settings are often portrayed as victims, she noted, despite their roles in preventing violence, mediating disputes, sustaining communities and rebuilding societies. When their experiences go unreported, the public sees only part of the reality of war, “half of the picture of peace”.
The scale of the problem is stark. According to a recent study by UN Women and UNESCO, 75 per cent of women journalists surveyed had experienced online violence. Forty-two per cent linked online attacks to abuse or assault in the physical world, up from 20 per cent in 2020.
Meanwhile, between 2013 and 2023, coverage of conflicts grew more than sixfold, yet only 5 per cent of published articles focused on women's experiences of war. Just 0.04 per cent mentioned women leaders in peace processes, according to figures presented at the event. “We are not invisible”, Ms. Ressa told the room of women in New York.
Begoñã Lasagabaster, Director of UNESCO's Division for Gender Equality, recalled the exhibition They Told the World About It, documenting almost 200 women journalists from more than 25 countries who reported on the Spanish Civil War 90 years ago.
“While much of the world counted battles, these women counted lives – they wrote about hunger, displacement, about what war does to a mother, a father, a child, a city, a country,” she said, and with that “they changed the way the world saw war”.
Protection must become action
International frameworks for protecting journalists already exist. Yet women journalists continue to face physical violence, legal harassment, psychological trauma and online campaigns designed to discredit their reporting.
As the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists approaches on 2 November, UNESCO is preparing to launch a new campaign – Threats Evolve, Impunity Endures – alongside new findings on journalist safety and impunity.
“Every voice for peace counts,” said Ms. Ressa, “but a voice only counts if it is heard, if that woman survives being heard.”

Record heat-related deaths in 2023, WHO-partnered report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Record heat-related deaths in 2023, WHO-partnered report finds
Climate inaction continues to harm and kill people in all countries with a record 710,000 estimated deaths globally from heat in 2023, a UN-partnered report warned on Wednesday. For the first time, more than seven in 10 fatalities were attributable to human-caused climate change.
The latest Lancet Countdown report in association with the World Health Organization (WHO), finds that health harms from climate change are accelerating, with expanded fossil fuel extraction holding back progress and threatening “catastrophic” health risks.
“Heat-related deaths, drought and other climate-related risks (are) increasing faster than a decade ago, even as clean energy investments and climate action begin to deliver health benefits,” the report’s authors state.
Key findings:
- Heat exposure caused the loss of 573 billion potential work hours in 2025, costed at $1.07 trillion
- Clean energy jobs grew 2.3 per cent in 2024, almost twice direct fossil fuel employment
- Cleaner air is preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year in 70 countries where air pollution from fossil fuels has fallen
- National laws on climate change and health have risen roughly 50-fold since the year 2000 and most have been since 2016
- Wealthy nations accounted for 55 per cent of climate–health laws in 2025, compared to two per cent in developing countries
Other findings indicate that the global area affected by extreme drought “has grown more than 700 per cent faster than it did in 2006–2015”, with droughts affecting 51.8 per cent of land on earth for at least one month in 2025.
The report also examines the link between rising temperatures and rainfall patterns to dengue transmission, finding that conditions suitable for dengue transmission by Aedes albopictus mosquitoes increased by 24 per cent between 1981-90 and 2016-25, while suitability for transmission by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes rose by seven per cent.
Drilling down
And in a warning that too little is being done to mitigate climate change, the report also notes that the world’s 100 largest oil and gas companies plan to produce “150 per cent more fossil fuels by 2040 than is compatible with keeping warming to 1.5°C [above pre-Industrial Revolution temperature averages], up from 138 per cent a year earlier”.
These and other worrying findings highlight the urgent need to formally recognize climate change as a global health emergency, the authors maintain, in support of stronger, health-centred climate action ahead of the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
Priorities include accelerating reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, increasing support for adaptation and expanding investments that strengthen health system resilience.
Action on climate
WHO responds to climate-related health risks through surveillance, early warning systems, health adaptation planning, technical guidance and emergency response teams.
The agency is also closely following the expected health impacts of the ongoing El Niño event through a global incident management team, mobilizing expertise, health intelligence and support to countries most at risk.
WHO also oversees the work of ATACH (the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health), the only network of health ministries and partners working together to develop climate-resilient, low-carbon and sustainable health systems at the country level.
Scientific approach
The report – produced by researchers and institutions from all over the world and led by University College London – analyses global trends across 54 indicators linking climate change and health.
It shows that heat-related deaths increased by nearly 36 per cent in the years following the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change compared with the previous decade. The report also highlights worsening drought conditions, increasing exposure to water-related extremes and substantial economic losses linked to heat exposure.
Premature deaths protection
In more positive developments, important progress has been made in resisting the health impacts of climate change, the report notes, pointing to a record $2.1 trillion global investment in clean energy last year.
“Many countries that have lowered fossil fuel-related air pollution are estimated to be protecting thousands of people from premature deaths each year,” it adds.
The report also notes advances in climate-resilient health systems, including increased adoption of national health adaptation plans and climate-based early warning systems.
Around one in four countries now have a national plan for adapting health services to climate change, up from just 14 WHO Member States in 2015; 47 have separately completed a vulnerability assessment to underpin plans.
The development follows a warning by the UN World Meteorological Organization (WMO) that levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases accumulating in the atmosphere reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increase for the planet.

DR Congo: WHO urges sustained efforts as Ebola cases top 10,000
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DR Congo: WHO urges sustained efforts as Ebola cases top 10,000
As Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) surpass the 10,000 mark, the World Health Organization (WHO) has underlined the need for continued efforts to contain spread of the disease.
Latest data from the Congolese Ministry of Health indicates there were 10,141 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths as of Monday.
“Sustained efforts are essential to end the outbreak,” WHO said in a tweet.
“This requires continued scale-up of key control measures, greater access to affected areas, and community outreach that builds trust and encourages people to engage with the response.”
Historic outbreak
The UN agency and partners are assisting the DRC authorities in curbing transmission of Ebola disease caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus for which there is currently no vaccine or treatment.
This is the 17th Ebola outbreak in the country’s history, and the largest to date. It is also the second largest in the world after the West Africa outbreak from 2014-2016.
The outbreak began in the vast and volatile eastern region of the DRC amid conflict, hunger and widespread displacement, and has expanded to eight provinces, including areas that are hard to access.
Signs of progress
Yet WHO noted that “progress is being made”, as more than 2,600 people have recovered from Ebola, while capacity for testing and treatment have expanded. Moreover, clinical trials of candidate vaccines are underway.
The TUMAINI trials – Swahili for “hope” – will initially evaluate whether the Evebro vaccine used to treat the Zaire strain of the Ebola virus can provide protection in the current crisis.
Vaccines will be administered through the ring vaccination approach, which involves close contacts of confirmed Ebola patients.
“During the West Africa Ebola outbreak, WHO and partners used this same ring-vaccination approach in Guinea to help establish the efficacy of Ervebo,” said Dr. Meg Moherty, the agency’s technical lead for vaccine trials, who attended the TUMAINI launch in the city of Bunia on Friday.
“Today, scientists are building on that experience to seek answers about Bundibugyo virus,” she added.
WHO recently convened expert groups to evaluate evidence on two other vaccines designed specifically against Bundibugyo and the findings are expected to be published this week.
Support for Kenya
Meanwhile, a UN humanitarian fund has allocated more than $2 million to boost Ebola preparedness and response in Kenya.
The funding will enable aid partners to support Government-led efforts, including enhanced surveillance at border crossing points and training for rapid response teams and front-line responders.
Resources will also be used to strengthen preparedness along high-risk refugee and travel routes in the northwest.
Kenya has recorded nine Ebola cases, including two deaths. All are linked to the country’s first case of the disease – a Kenyan man working in the DRC who flew to Nairobi via Uganda on 3 October and died two days later.
More than 130 contacts were identified who were placed under quarantine, and 20 have since been discharged.

How Israel evades responsibility for Gaza’s flour massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:59:55 UTC
20:59:55 KST

Breadcrumb
How Israel evades responsibility for Gaza’s flour massacre
What led them to him was a trail of blood, and there he was, lifeless and slumping against a wall, still hugging a bag of flour that had turned dark pink. Two bullets had struck him in the back, and he had bled to death, alone, just seventeen years old.
Mutaz was my cousin. He was killed during the flour massacre in February 2024.
That day, thousands of starving Palestinians gathered around humanitarian aid trucks in northern Gaza, desperately seeking food. At least 112 people were killed and hundreds injured amid Israeli gunfire and chaotic scenes around the convoy.
I recently came across an article by pro-Israel advocacy organisation HonestReporting, originally posted in October 2025, disputing accounts of the massacre.
The organisation depicted the massacre as one of 25 alleged media falsehoods about Israel's war in Gaza. It argues that the overwhelming majority of victims were crushed in a stampede or run over by aid trucks, while approximately ten were killed by Israeli gunfire after approaching military positions. It also accuses the media of uncritically repeating Hamas's account and falsely portraying the incident as an Israeli massacre.
I would have let it slide, had it not been for something far more disturbing than the familiar exercise of defending Israel. The article effectively dismissed our lived experience, my family's tragedy, and the grief of Mutaz's mother, who wept over her son's body, cursing all the flour in the world.
One would expect an advocacy group to engage in ideological framing. But behind HonestReporting's account lies a broader mechanism that reduces human catastrophes to isolated technicalities through reframing, omission, and causal attribution. Together, these shape not only which facts enter the account, but also how responsibility for an event is assigned. I call this mechanism "reductive advocacy."
Evading accountability
By claiming that most victims died in a stampede or beneath aid trucks, HonestReporting makes the manner of death the central issue, narrowing the scope of responsibility to the circumstances of their deaths rather than the conditions that brought them there.
The significance of this reduction is heightened when set against the evidence. Alongside field medical reports, there’s been a UN Commission of Inquiry analysis identifying horizontal tracer rounds and gunfire in footage of the incident, and a CNN investigation that examined dozens of videos, 22 eyewitness accounts and forensic evidence.
Nevertheless, for us, the funerals on our street spoke louder than any report or commission. My family's neighbour’s teenage son was also shot dead in the massacre. He was brought home that very day, drenched in fresh blood, unlike Mutaz, whose body lay undiscovered for longer, his blood drying to dark brown.
Israel rejects such findings and has regularly dismissed international criticism as biased or antisemitic.
One need not pull the trigger to cause death. Circumstances can be deliberately engineered to produce it, while obscuring or diluting responsibility for the outcome. The past offers many examples, and Jewish history bears witness.
After sealing the Warsaw Ghetto in November 1940, Nazi authorities confined more than 400,000 Jews to approximately 1.3 square miles, imposing drastically inadequate food rations. Overcrowding, malnutrition and disease became endemic, and approximately 83,000 Jews died between 1940 and 1942.
The Nazis killed those Jews without shooting or gassing them. In Gaza, too, Israel set the stage for the tragedy long before the first truck arrived, turning starvation into the tinder for a deadly scramble for survival.
Deliberate starvation
Two days after 7 October 2023, Defence Minister Yoav Gallant ordered that Gaza be cut off from food, water, electricity and fuel. Aid restrictions and the bombardment of bakeries followed. By November, all five flour mills in Gaza had fallen silent. On 27 February 2024, the UN warned that 576,000 Palestinians — one-quarter of Gaza’s population — stood on the brink of famine.
Around that time, I began hearing a word from my family over the phone that I had never heard from them before: hunger. Desperate, Mutaz set out with two cousins towards Gaza City’s border, hoping to bring food home. He never returned. My uncle would say, "he never told us he was going," only to repeat, "Our hunger sent my son to his death."
Even if gunfire and deliberate starvation were not decisive factors in the massacre, HonestReporting’s reductive advocacy still erases the long-winded structural conditions that made it possible.
Israel occupied Gaza in 1967, extending its control over a population most of whom it had rendered refugees following its establishment in 1948. Although it withdrew its settlements and army from the Strip in 2005 because of unsustainable costs and security concerns, it maintained substantial control over the territory’s crossings, maritime access, population registry, and movement and trade.
Furthermore, the blockade imposed in 2007 placed Gaza under siege within an ongoing occupation, only a year after Tel Aviv effectively put Gaza’s population “on a diet,” by setting the threshold of consumption without triggering a visible humanitarian crisis.
The cumulative effect was a gradual erosion of the productive, economic, and logistical capacity needed to sustain Palestinians and their ability to withstand emergencies.
Such constraints create structural fragility that may remain partly concealed during periods of lower tension, only to escalate catastrophically fast when tensions rise. We have seen it in every major Israeli assault on Gaza since 2008; bombardment rapidly deepened the humanitarian crisis, while Israel’s control over the flow of goods has made basic necessities a parallel weapon against a population it tightly controls.
An unnatural occurrence
Mutaz was born into a besieged Gaza, his life shaped by the cumulative vulnerabilities that decades of occupation and successive Israeli assaults had imposed on his family and society. By the time famine came, those vulnerabilities were already deeply entrenched.
Reductive advocacy obscures this history by treating Gaza’s vulnerability as a natural occurrence. Once that condition is accepted as a given, tragedies appear as isolated crises, and the deaths can be attributed to the immediate conduct of those struggling to survive.
Taken together, the three layers of dismantlement show how fragments of factual truth can assemble into a misleading whole, obscuring the political agency and historical conditions needed to account for suffering.
Yet HonestReporting claims to defend consistent journalistic standards while selectively deciding which criticism of Israel is legitimate and which constitutes delegitimisation.
Like with the flour massacre, it recasts the victims of a system of domination as responsible for their own circumstances. In doing so, it helps normalise the conditions from which it seeks to absolve Israel, making dehumanisation part of the work of exoneration.
The HonestReporting’s broad claims, therefore, must be tested against what it scrutinises, what it omits, and whose accounts it treats as credible.
To my family, Israelis and their allies can reductively dispute the massacre and many others, but none of these fragments can erase the blood of Mutaz and thousands like him. Nor can any rearrangement of facts absolve those who manufactured the conditions that have dispossessed four generations of Palestinians.
We’re constantly grieving, a feeling deepened by the fact that responsibility can even become a matter of debate when one people occupies and controls the lives of another.
Our fifth generation won’t need to be taught that. They are already seeing this firsthand, at least those who have survived so far.
Dr Emad Moussa is a Palestinian-British researcher and writer specialising in the political psychology of intergroup and conflict dynamics, focusing on MENA with a special interest in Israel/Palestine. He has a background in human rights and journalism, and is currently a frequent contributor to multiple academic and media outlets, in addition to being a consultant for a US-based think tank.

Belgium starts building a giant repair center for its army vehicles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:59:28 UTC
20:59:28 KST

- Belgium laid the foundation stone on Oct. 27 for a 30,000 m² army vehicle maintenance center in Rocourt, run by the LS² joint venture.
- LS², formed by FN Herstal, John Cockerill Defense and Thales Belgium, will maintain the army’s vehicles and weapons under a 20-year deal.
Belgium has started building a new maintenance center for its army’s armored vehicles in Rocourt, near Liège, where a joint venture of FN Herstal, John Cockerill Defense and Thales Belgium will repair and service the Belgian Land Component’s vehicles and their weapons under a 20-year deal.
Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken laid the foundation stone on Oct. 27 at the site of the army’s Rolling Stock and Armament Competence Centre, FN Herstal said on social media. The joint venture, called LS², short for Land Systems Logistic Support, will maintain the land forces’ vehicles throughout their service lives, along with the weapons, information and communication systems fitted to them.
The new building will cover about 30,000 m² (323,000 square feet), making it the largest private maintenance center for military vehicles in the country, and LS² expects to hire around 200 people for it, mostly mechanics, technicians and other skilled workers, Belgian broadcaster RTBF reported. Some 400 people already work at the Rocourt site, and construction is due to finish around July 2028, L’Avenir reported.
The three partners split the work by specialty. John Cockerill Defense handles the vehicles and their turrets, FN Herstal covers the weapons, from machine guns such as the recently modernized FN MAG to remote weapon stations, and Thales Belgium supports radios, sensors and onboard computer systems.
Belgium’s Ministry of Defence confirmed the partnership on Jan. 30, 2026, and appointed Thibault Lambrecht, previously a sales executive at John Cockerill Defense, as chief executive. The Belgian business daily L’Echo put the contract’s value at about €700 million (about $779 million), La DH reported at the time.
LS² began work well before the new building. Within weeks of its launch, its staff started taking over maintenance of most army vehicles at the bases in Marche-en-Famenne and Leopoldsburg, home to Belgium’s 7th and 1st brigades, Forces Operations Blog reported in March, and the joint venture also carries out maintenance at other land force bases across Belgium.
The partnership arrives as the Belgian army takes delivery of hundreds of new French-designed armored vehicles under the CaMo program, run jointly with France. Belgium has ordered close to 500 Griffon 6×6 armored personnel carriers and 60 Jaguar reconnaissance vehicles, which are replacing older Piranha IIIC and Dingo 2 vehicles, and it has also ordered French artillery systems under the same program, including CAESAR NG self-propelled howitzers and 24 Griffon MEPAC 120 mm mortar carriers. The new vehicles remain under manufacturer warranty for their first years in service, and LS² will take over their maintenance once those warranties expire and the Rocourt center is fully running. The Belgian Griffons carry remote weapon stations from FN Herstal, which builds its FN DEFENDER stations at its plant in Herstal, a few miles from Rocourt.

Smotrich vows to establish Israeli settlements in Gaza after election
Israel's extreme-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has vowed to establish Jewish settlements in Gaza, as uncertainty surrounds the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition following Tuesday's parliamentary election.
Addressing supporters at his extremist Religious Zionism party's election headquarters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Smotrich dismissed celebrations among opposition parties and Palestinian citizens of Israel over initial exit polls suggesting gains for Palestinian parties and that Netanyahu's bloc could lose its parliamentary majority.
"I see on some of the screens that the Arabs are celebrating, so I am announcing to you and to them: We will not let them celebrate," Smotrich said, according to Israeli media.
"They are celebrating because they think they will succeed in reversing our settlement revolution in Judea and Samaria," he added, using an Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.
"They will not succeed. Jewish settlements will rise in Gaza."
Smotrich's Religious Zionism party, running on a joint electoral list with Moshe Feiglin's Zehut party, was projected to secure six or seven seats in the 120-member Knesset, according to Israeli exit polls.
The result would represent a political lifeline for the extremist minister, whose party had struggled to clear the electoral threshold in several pre-election surveys.
However, neither Netanyahu's right-wing bloc nor the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot appeared to have secured the 61 seats necessary to form a government.
With the final results still pending, the composition of Israel's next coalition remains uncertain, as does Smotrich's ability to pursue his settlement ambitions.
Renewed push to settle Gaza
Israel dismantled its settlements in Gaza in 2005, withdrawing around 8,000 settlers and its permanent ground forces from the territory.
Since Israel launched its devastating war on Gaza in October 2023, Smotrich and other far-right politicians have repeatedly advocated re-establishing settlements in the Palestinian territory.
In September, Smotrich called for Israel to annex territory under Israeli military control up to the ceasefire's so-called "Yellow Line", while also advocating territorial annexation in southern Lebanon.
He has additionally called for dismantling the Palestinian Authority in the occupied West Bank and expanding Israeli settlements across that territory.
His latest remarks came as Israeli settlers intensified their campaign to return to Gaza.
According to a report published by Le Monde on Tuesday, around 20 Israeli families have established an unauthorised encampment known as the "Gaza Pioneers" near the territory's border.
The initiative, supported by the far-right Nachala settler movement, aims to prepare for the eventual re-establishment of settlements inside Gaza.
The establishment of Israeli civilian settlements in occupied Palestinian territory is illegal under international law.
Palestinian voters targeted
Smotrich's remarks also followed a contentious election campaign in which Netanyahu and his far-right allies repeatedly warned supporters about rising turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel.
On election day, Netanyahu highlighted queues at polling stations in Arab communities and suggested that an opposition victory could produce a government dependent on Palestinian parties.
Smotrich similarly urged right-wing voters to abandon smaller parties, claiming unusually high turnout among Arab voters threatened the governing coalition.
Palestinian political leaders condemned the campaign rhetoric as racist, while welcoming increased participation among Arab voters.
The election produced no immediate parliamentary majority for either principal bloc, with Palestinian Arab parties potentially playing an important role in determining whether a new government can be formed.

Russian Billionaire Takes Tiny Norwegian News Outlet to Court in London

Russian tycoon Vitaly Orlov is suing The Barents Observer, a small Norwegian news outlet, over its reporting on sanctions against his fishing company.
The Barents Observer is a six-person non-profit newsroom in Kirkenes, a town of about 7,000 people in Norway’s far north. But the lawsuit isn’t taking place there — or even in Norway. Instead, Orlov has lodged a defamation suit in the High Court of London.
“We don’t even have money for plane tickets to go to the court,” said Editor in Chief Thomas Nilsen.
“It’s just not possible for us to defend ourselves against all of the claims,” he told OCCRP’s Norwegian media partner, NRK, adding that if Orlov is awarded some legal costs, The Barents Observer “will go bankrupt.”
Orlov’s fishing company, Norebo JSC, said in a statement provided to OCCRP that the choice of London as a venue for the lawsuit was related to the fact that The Barents Observer publishes in English.
“The Barents Observer is a Norwegian publication that publishes in English and now complains at being sued in England. This is the very country The Barents Observer has courted,” the company said.
The legal claim by Orlov’s lawyers, from the London firm Devonshires, states that The Barents Observer website received 190,000 hits from the U.K. in 2025, according to a web analytics firm.
But U.K. readers make up only 5 percent of The Barents Observer readers, according to a letter the publication sent to the court.
“It is difficult to understand the logic behind Vitaly Orlov bringing his grievances before a court in England,” The Barents Observer stated in its letter.
The Barents Observer noted that it is based in Norway, and that Norebo is already engaged in a lawsuit against the Norwegian government in response to its ban on company vessels using its territorial waters and ports.
Orlov is claiming damages as a result of “serious harm” to his reputation caused by five news stories published by The Barents Observer between May 2025 and January this year. The news reports covered the E.U. sanctioning of Norebo, but also included information about Orlov himself.
The E.U. sanctions notice does not mention Orlov, and he has not been sanctioned. The sanctions notice alleges that Norebo vessels showed “movement patterns [that] align with malign objectives.”
“The movement patterns have been linked, including by Member States and the authorities of third states, to the Russian state-sponsored surveillance campaign that employs inter alia, civilian fishing trawlers, to conduct espionage missions directed against civilian and military infrastructure in the North and Baltic Sea,” the sanctions notice states.
In the claim brought to the High Court of London on behalf of Orlov, Devonshires lawyers note that “Norebo disputes the designation and has brought annulment proceedings before the General Court of the European Union.”

toyota swaps wheels for snow tracks in five arctic-ready concept vehicles
developed by calty design research for sema 2026, the five concepts combine white snow tracks, arctic camouflage and expedition gear for extreme winter exploration.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
TOYOTA SNOWHUNTER CONCEPTS REPLACE WHEELS WITH WHITE TRACKS
Toyota has unveiled five Snowhunter concept vehicles that trade conventional wheels for snow tracks, turning some of its best-known trucks and SUVs into machines built for extreme winter exploration. Presented ahead of the 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, the collection includes modified versions of the Tundra, Tacoma, 4Runner, Land Cruiser, and Sequoia. Rather than creating five identical vehicles, the Japanese automaker has given each model a different purpose, from navigating narrow snowy trails to serving as a mobile basecamp in remote landscapes.
Developed by CALTY Design Research in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the Snowhunter family shares a distinctive visual identity. White powder-coated snow tracks replace traditional wheels, while custom camouflage graphics, Snowhunter badging, and gloss-black accents give the vehicles a coordinated appearance. All five feature auxiliary lighting by Rigid Industries and suspension lift components from Toyota Genuine Parts and Toyota Racing Development (TRD). The oversized tracks dramatically alter their proportions, transforming familiar automotive silhouettes into something closer to polar expedition machines.
CALTY DESIGN RESEARCH ADAPTS FIVE TOYOTA MODELS FOR WINTER
The Tundra Snowhunter is conceived as a mobile basecamp, with a CALTY-designed TrailLift Pro Rack System that transforms its cargo bed into a configurable storage platform. Its articulating upper rack can be lowered to simplify loading bulky equipment, including bicycles, kayaks, and canoes. The smaller Tacoma Snowhunter takes a more agile approach, incorporating a roof rack, a full-length bed rack with MOLLE panels, an awning, recovery equipment, and additional lighting. Toyota envisions this configuration for narrow trails and self-supported winter expeditions.
Meanwhile, the 4Runner Snowhunter combines Toyota rock rails with a Prinsu roof rack and a Thule Pulse 2 cargo box, providing additional protection and storage for extended journeys. The Land Cruiser Snowhunter takes a similar approach, adding underbody skid plates and a Thule SnowPack ski rack. With its protective equipment and roof-mounted accessories, the SUV is configured for winter sports and travel across remote terrain, where conventional road conditions are something of a distant memory.
SNOWHUNTER CONCEPTS EXPLORE FORMS OF OFF-ROAD TRAVEL
The largest member of the family, the Sequoia Snowhunter, focuses on carrying passengers and equipment during longer journeys. Its modifications include a TRD front skid plate, cast-aluminum running boards, a Prinsu roof rack, and a Thule cargo box. Across the five vehicles, the design strategy goes beyond simply replacing wheels with tracks. Each configuration explores how storage systems, protective components, and outdoor accessories can adapt an existing vehicle to different forms of winter travel.
Toyota will showcase the Snowhunter concepts at the 2026 SEMA Show, taking place from November 3 to 6 in Las Vegas. The automaker has clarified that these are special-project prototypes, modified with components that may not be commercially available or legal for public-road use. No production plans have been announced. For now, the five vehicles remain an exercise in automotive customization, exploring just how far Toyota’s off-road lineup can go when the roads disappear beneath the snow.

Britain to build sub-hunting sensors for AUKUS underwater drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:51:41 UTC
20:51:41 KST

- Britain will lead AUKUS development of three underwater drone payloads: a synthetic aperture sonar, an anti-submarine sensor and a non-kinetic effector.
- The payloads will be available across Australian, British and U.S. uncrewed underwater fleets from 2027, the UK Ministry of Defence said.
Britain will lead development of three new sensor and effects packages for underwater drones under the AUKUS security partnership with the United States and Australia, with the systems due to be available across all three nations’ uncrewed underwater fleets from 2027, the UK Ministry of Defence said on Oct. 27.
The three payloads are a synthetic aperture sonar, a deployable anti-submarine warfare sensor and a deployable non-kinetic effector. The Ministry of Defence said they will let uncrewed underwater vehicles map the seabed in detail, place sensors that detect and classify underwater threats, and generate effects underwater, helping the drones watch large areas of ocean and protect undersea cables and pipelines.
A synthetic aperture sonar combines many sonar pings taken as the vehicle moves to build a much sharper image of the seabed than a conventional sonar of the same size, while the anti-submarine sensor is designed to be dropped or laid by the drone to keep listening for submarines and other threats after the vehicle moves on. The third payload, a non-kinetic effector, acts on a target without explosives or physical destruction, though the ministry did not say what form the British system will take.
The announcement closed a week of testing at Maritime Big Play Pacific, an AUKUS exercise in San Diego where the three countries test autonomous maritime systems in realistic conditions before wider adoption. It advances the first signature project under AUKUS Pillar 2, the part of the partnership covering advanced technologies such as autonomy and undersea warfare, which the three governments announced in May to develop payloads for uncrewed underwater vehicles, while Pillar 1 covers Australia’s acquisition of nuclear-powered attack submarines.
“The UK is all in on AUKUS, and this cutting-edge technology shows why. By leading development of these sensor payloads, we’re putting British innovation at the heart of AUKUS and strengthening our collective undersea capability,” said Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry.
At Maritime Big Play, Australian, British and American crewed and uncrewed systems worked together across four strands: anti-submarine warfare, lethality, contested resupply, and subsea and seabed warfare. The UK led the anti-submarine strand, contributing 13 uncrewed surface vessels, two anti-submarine targets and four underwater gliders from six industry partners. Royal Navy Kraken K3 uncrewed boats also operated during the exercise, and one of them launched three short-range loitering munition quadcopters at Naval Base Point Loma on Oct. 20, showing how a drone boat can carry aircraft closer to an operating area without putting a crew at risk. American companies took part as well, including Saronic Technologies, which fielded three Corsair drone boats with U.S., British and Australian forces for pier resupply runs, some of them carried out with communications denied, and a trilateral sense-decide-effect mission within a mixed uncrewed fleet.
“Maritime Big Play-Pacific gives AUKUS a unique opportunity to turn autonomy into operational advantage,” said Royal Navy Capt. Keith Taylor.
The exercise also featured two of the four winners of the AUKUS Maritime Innovation Challenge, SEA Ltd of Frome and Decision Analysis Services Ltd of Basingstoke. Together with A2i of Dorchester and U.S. company MSI Transducers, they share £3 million (about $4 million) to develop technology for commanding, controlling and coordinating undersea systems.
The payload announcement follows another AUKUS undersea milestone last month. On Sept. 13, the Royal Navy’s extra-large uncrewed underwater vehicle XV Excalibur launched an inert U.S. Mk 48 heavyweight torpedo at the British Underwater Test and Evaluation Centre in Scotland, the first torpedo firing from an uncrewed submarine for either navy. The 12 m (39-foot) Excalibur is an experimental vessel used to test autonomy and new payloads for the Royal Navy’s planned Hybrid Navy, which mixes crewed warships and submarines with uncrewed systems.
Britain is funding the work as part of its Defence Investment Plan, which sets out £298 billion (about $396 billion) in defense spending over the next four years.

U.S. cruise ship suspends around-the-world voyage due to fuel costs

U.S. cruise ship suspends 3-year around-the-world voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs
Sihanoukville, Cambodia — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting at around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
The average price for a gallon of diesel fuel the day before the war started, Feb. 27, 2026, was $3.76, according to AAA, and was $6.52 late last month, an increase of $2.76.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
However, a blogger who has been on the cruise, Randy Cassingham, wrote online that "the company has done absolutely nothing to help: we couldn't even walk out of the port, so there were shuttle buses that dropped us in the middle of town, Sihanoukville, Cambodia."
"They didn't even give us a list of hotels, let alone help us get there or pay for them," Cassingham said on his website. The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being sidelined by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

this horse-shaped headset asks designers to see the world through animal eyes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:50:20 UTC
20:50:20 KST

this horse-shaped headset asks designers to see the world through animal eyes
simulating equine vision, the headset invites humans to reconsider how we design for and interact with other species.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
a speculative approach to interspecies design
Ulster University researcher and designer Alan Hook develops Equine Eyes, a giant horse-shaped headset that allows people to experience an approximation of how horses see the world. The wearable forms part of his wider research into interspecies design, which explores how objects and environments might be designed with other animals in mind. What happens when the animals that share our spaces are considered users too?
With its elongated white muzzle and upright ears, the headset has a peculiar, almost cartoonish appearance. Small cameras sit on either side of the head, where a horse’s eyes would be, while a virtual reality display translates their live footage for the human wearer. The experience is deliberately playful, inviting participants to temporarily step outside their familiar way of seeing.
Equine Eyes recreates a horse’s wide field of vision
Horses have eyes positioned on either side of their heads, giving them a much wider field of vision than humans. To approximate this difference, Hook developed a system using two 180-degree cameras that together create a simulated view of approximately 350 degrees. The images overlap slightly at the front, while the sides of the wearer’s body become visible within their peripheral vision. The footage is also processed to reflect the horse’s dichromatic color perception, shifting the visual range toward blues and yellows.
During testing, one participant compared the disorienting experience to ‘taking your eyes out and sticking them on the sides of your head.‘ Familiar surroundings appear through a different visual arrangement, prompting wearers to reconsider how horses navigate space and respond to activity around them. Of course, the headset can only approximate certain aspects of equine perception. A horse experiences its surroundings through an entirely different body, extending well beyond what its eyes can see.
the horse-shaped mask becomes part of the experiment
Alan Hook began developing Equine Eyes in 2017, initially using low-resolution webcams connected to an Oculus Rift headset. These early prototypes produced heavily pixelated images, making participants conscious of the technology itself.
The researcher began experimenting with a simple cardboard cutout of a horse’s head, placed between the cameras, and found that this addition changed how people responded to the experience. Participants reported feeling more transformed when the equipment resembled the animal they were trying to understand.
The project gradually evolved into the sculptural white mask seen today, with a lightweight shell that extends well beyond the wearer’s face. During earlier testing, Hook also experimented with removing the horse-shaped enclosure to make the equipment easier to transport. Participants felt that something was missing. The physical act of putting on the animal’s head had become an important part of the interaction, encouraging people to engage with the simulation through their own bodies.
an interspecies design toolkit extends the idea beyond horses
The same questions inform Hook’s Interspecies Design Toolkit, a speculative proposal developed through his research at Imagination Lancaster and Ulster University. Drawing from Microsoft’s Inclusive Design Toolkit, the project examines how design processes could account for nonhuman animals. Microsoft’s original framework encourages designers to recognize exclusion among people with different abilities. Hook adapts this thinking to consider the diverse sensory experiences of other species.
The downloadable toolkit includes guidelines and activity cards intended for design workshops. Participants are encouraged to observe how animals interact with their surroundings, identify barriers created by human-centered design, and imagine alternatives based on those observations. One exercise suggests allowing an animal to initiate play, following its behavior instead of directing the interaction.
Another principle encourages designers to begin with an individual animal before considering how their findings might apply more widely. The approach offers a way to think about everything from domestic objects to architecture, where even a seemingly ordinary opening or interface can determine which bodies are accommodated.
from speculative research to public experience
Equine Eyes has since moved into exhibition spaces, allowing visitors to engage directly with the research. In 2024, the headset appeared in the Superpower Design exhibition at the Centre for Innovation and Design at Grand-Hornu, Belgium, where Hook led workshops and invited participants to test the device.
More recently, in July 2026, the National Museum of Racing and Hall of Fame in Saratoga Springs, New York, introduced two Equine Eyes headsets for public use and educational programming. Here, the experiment finds a particularly relevant audience among people who regularly work with horses.
The headset remains an exercise in speculation, with Hook acknowledging the limits of simulating another animal’s subjective experience. Its purpose is to encourage people to consider how differently another species might encounter the same environment. Equine Eyes makes this question physical, while the Interspecies Design Toolkit brings it into the design process itself.
project info:
name: Equine Eyes / Interspecies Design Toolkit
designer: Alan Hook

Ethiopia receives its first Russian-made Su-35 fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:41:56 UTC
20:41:56 KST

- Ethiopia has received its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets, a year ahead of schedule, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on Oct. 28.
- Abiy said Ethiopia will also receive four S-400 air defense batteries but did not disclose the deal’s value or delivery timeline.
Ethiopia has taken delivery of its first 12 Russian Su-35 fighter jets and will also receive four batteries of the S-400 long-range air defense system, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed said on social media on Oct. 28.
Abiy said the jets arrived under an earlier agreement with the Russian government and a year ahead of the agreed schedule, and he thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for the early delivery. He did not disclose the value of the deal, its terms, or when the S-400 batteries will arrive, Addis Standard reported.
“In accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have today taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets,” said Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The announcement came while Abiy was in Russia for the third Russia-Africa Summit, according to Ethiopian state broadcaster Fana Media Corporation, which reported that he witnessed the official handover of the aircraft. Abiy described the purchase as a major boost to the defense forces and said it puts Ethiopia in the lead among Sub-Saharan African nations.
The Su-35 is Russia’s most advanced fighter in export service after the Su-57. It is a single-seat, twin-engine multirole jet built for both air combat and ground attack, with thrust-vectoring engines that let it maneuver sharply and a long-range Irbis-E radar. Sukhoi calls it a “4++ generation” aircraft, meaning a heavily upgraded fourth-generation design that stops short of the stealth features of fifth-generation fighters.
The S-400 is a long-range surface-to-air missile system designed to shoot down aircraft and some missiles. A battery typically includes radars, a command post and several launcher vehicles.
Ethiopia’s interest in the Su-35 first surfaced a year ago. In October 2025, a hacker group called Black Mirror published internal files from Russian state defense conglomerate Rostec that listed Ethiopia as having signed a contract for six Su-35s, alongside larger orders for Iran and Algeria. Neither Rostec nor the Ethiopian government commented at the time. The 12 jets Abiy announced are double the number in the leaked documents, and his description of them as the “first” twelve suggests more could follow, though he did not say how many Ethiopia has ordered in total.
The new jets will join an air force that has flown Russian Sukhoi fighters for more than 25 years. Ethiopia received Su-27s in the late 1990s and used them in its 1998 to 2000 border war with Eritrea. In January 2024, it inducted Su-30K fighters, believed to come from a batch originally built for the Indian Air Force, along with Turkish Akinci drones.
Only a handful of countries have received the Su-35 for export. China took delivery of 24 aircraft between 2016 and 2018, and Algeria received its first units in March 2025, Army Recognition reported. The S-400 is in service with China, India and Turkey, and Turkey’s purchase led the United States to impose sanctions on its defense procurement agency in 2020 under a law targeting significant arms deals with Russia.
Tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have risen this year, and Russia has offered to host talks between the two countries, Addis Standard reported. Abiy said the new equipment would allow Ethiopia to deter aggression and support regional stability.

Italy’s Tommaso Grollero wins ‘World Chocolate Masters’ in Antwerp

At an event held at the Antwerp Stock Exchange, where the price of imported cocoa beans used to be set, Italian Tommaso Grollero won the World Chocolate Masters. This prestigious competition was held in Antwerp for the first time in 20 years. “I think the jury appreciated the personal touch in my creations and the way I’ve made my best desserts ever,” beamed the winning chocolatier.
Becoming a World Chocolate Master is one of the most coveted titles in the world of chocolate. For the past 20 years, the competition has taken place in Paris; this time, organiser and chocolate manufacturer Barry Callebaut chose Antwerp and the historic Antwerp Stock Exchange for the first time.
“If you look at the chocolatiers and pâtissiers here in Antwerp, the city really is one of the hotspots for chocolate. Not just in Belgium, but actually all over the world,” says organiser Dries Roekaerts.
‘Throughout the four challenges, Tommaso Grollero demonstrated just how exceptionally well he combines flavour, technical precision and a distinctively creative vision. He epitomises a chef’s consistent and clear vision of flavour,’ says Amaury Guichon, chair of the World Chocolate Masters judging panel.
The Italian beat 14 other international competitors. Lyu Haoran from China and Keita Koshimizu from Japan completed the top 3.
The port also plays a major role in the development of the chocolate industry in Antwerp. “It is the port in Europe where the largest quantity of cocoa beans is stored,” says Piet De Lombaerde of Antwerpen Koekenstad, the non-profit organisation that promotes the historical heritage of chocolate and biscuits.
“Only the port of Amsterdam handles a greater volume of cocoa beans. The reason for this is that the Dutch company Van Houten invented the process for effectively separating cocoa from the oil – the butter – contained within it. That is why most roasting takes place in the Netherlands.”
Thanks to cocoa imports through the port of Antwerp, the industry soon began to focus on chocolate production. The Felix Archive contains an application from 1852 by an entrepreneur who wished to install a machine for roasting cocoa beans in Antwerp’s Kasteelpleinstraat.
“Antwerp has been a pioneer in many areas. For example, the very first chocolate bar was launched here with the ‘Perrette’,” says De Lombaerde. “Chocolaterie Meurisse, Belgium’s first major chocolate factory, which opened in 1845, launched the bar at the Liège World’s Fair in 1905. The idea arose during a crisis. Chocolate in larger forms had become too expensive, so a smaller bar was developed.”

Bolsonaro touches down in US as legal pressure mounts in Brazil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:38:59 UTC
20:38:59 KST

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami with his family on Wednesday after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, escalating tensions between Brasilia and Washington following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election.
The U.S. government has said it will grant entry visas to Bolsonaro and his family, despite the Brazilian investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering. Bolsonaro denies wrongdoing.
Reuters TV footage showed Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters disembarking from a Gulfstream G400 private jet at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.
Their journey to the United States unfolded across several countries under a cloud of secrecy. Argentina's migration department said the family entered northern Argentina late Tuesday before traveling by private jet to Guayaquil, Ecuador, and then continuing to Miami.
Argentina's presidency, Ecuadorian government ministries and Baires Fly, the private jet operator, did not respond to requests for comment.
The arrival followed conflicting reports about Bolsonaro's whereabouts. CNN and The Washington Post reported Tuesday that he had reached the United States, citing anonymous sources, while a Brazilian police source told AFP there was no formal record of his departure.
The source also said Bolsonaro's Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been canceled. However, the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document reviewed by AFP.
Bolsonaro's departure threatens to further strain relations between the two largest countries in the Americas, as Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of helping the Bolsonaro family regain power.
Reuters reported before Sunday's election on a U.S. State Department campaign aimed at restoring the family to office.
U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Bolsonaro's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, said Wednesday he supported Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States. The State Department had announced a day earlier that it would issue visas to the senator and his family.
Trump has repeatedly portrayed Jair Bolsonaro as a victim of political and judicial persecution in Brazil. He also claimed Monday that Brazil's election was rigged following Flavio Bolsonaro's defeat, without providing evidence.
Jair Bolsonaro traveled to the United States in December 2022 after losing that year's presidential election to Lula and refusing to concede. He returned to Brazil three months later and was eventually sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his supporters' storming of government buildings in Brasilia.
Flavio Bolsonaro, 45, had campaigned on a pledge to secure his father's release. He was widely expected to win Sunday's election after finishing ahead of Lula in the first round, but the incumbent secured 51.8% of the vote in the final round.
The senator rejected the result and said he would seek to have it annulled, citing an extension of polling hours intended to address transportation difficulties that prevented some voters from reaching polling stations. Both campaigns had requested an extension, with Bolsonaro's team citing bad weather in parts of the country.
Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came days after a Supreme Court justice ordered him to surrender his passports. The senator had said Monday he intended to comply and defend himself against what he described as an attempt to intimidate him.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
His defeat also puts his legal position at greater risk. Bolsonaro is expected to lose parliamentary immunity when his Senate term ends in February, potentially exposing him to further legal action.
His campaign manager, Rogerio Marinho, said Tuesday he had been unable to establish the senator's whereabouts.
Marinho told reporters in Brasilia that Bolsonaro had sent him a text message that morning, saying he would wait before speaking to the campaign team. He said he had received no further communication and expressed shock at reports that the senator had left the country.
Lula condemned the reported departure, calling it shameful and suggesting it raised questions about Bolsonaro's intentions.
Separately, Brazil's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered police to investigate alleged foreign financing of Bolsonaro's campaign and possible overseas interference, including the manipulation of social media.
Lula's campaign had accused Meta, the parent company of WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, of algorithmic manipulation that affected the election. Meta denied favoring either candidate, although it acknowledged that some of Lula's campaign advertisements had been mistakenly deactivated because of technical errors.
