Families brace for a fourth winter of wind, rain and floods in Gaza’s camps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:36:04 UTC
20:36:04 KST

Families brace for a fourth winter of wind, rain and floods in Gaza’s camps
Gaza’s impending winter is likely to lead to further devastation for Palestinians.
Gaza City — Mohammed al-Jamal, 60, tries to secure the nylon sheets of his family’s worn-out tent as a storm approaches his displacement camp on a beach in western Gaza City.
He and his sons pull at the tarpaulin, trying to fasten it firmly to the ground for protection from rain and wind coming in from the sea.
This will be the fourth winter that displaced Palestinians in Gaza have faced without adequate shelter. Many still live in tents and makeshift structures that offer little protection against the impending winter weather when temperatures can drop to 7C (below 45F) but can feel much colder due to strong coastal winds and rain.
The family cannot afford to fix their damaged tent with a replacement tarpaulin costing between 120 and 150 shekels ($37-$47) in local markets.
All al-Jamal can do is patch up the damaged shelter and hope it holds through the coming storm.
“We are trying to prepare as much as we can to protect ourselves from the water and the wind,” he said. “We follow the weather reports, and whenever there is a warning of a storm, we start preparing. But once the storm comes, everything gets torn apart, and we have to start all over again. It is continuous suffering throughout the winter.”
Mass displacement
Al-Jamal, originally from Gaza City’s Shujayea neighbourhood, has been displaced several times since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
About 30 members of his extended family live in these difficult living conditions.
“We are just trying to adapt to what we have. This is what is available to us. We need everything,” he said.
When it rains, water enters the tent and floods their living space, risking damage to their meagre belongings.
When temperatures drop, tents offer little protection for the displaced, with al-Jamal and his family having no choice but to put on more layers of clothing.
“We are out in the open. We are living in the street, not in houses that protect us,” he said.
Al-Jamal said he had repeatedly heard promises that shelter materials and caravans would be allowed into Gaza, but none had arrived for his family, and he had not seen any of them enter.
He described these announcements as “false promises and lies” that had left displaced families waiting for help that never came.
“Our demand is to have our lives back the way they were before,” he said.
Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 74,500 Palestinians and destroyed or damaged more than 80 percent of buildings. With homes and infrastructure in Gaza destroyed, about 1.5 million of Gaza’s 2.3 million people are living in tents or makeshift shelters.
Many of the displaced have been forced to move from city to city when Israeli assaults begin on their homes or camps.
At least 294,250 families in Gaza need winter shelter assistance, according to the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), but with current supplies, only 52,000 families, roughly 18 percent of those in need, have access to partial humanitarian assistance.
More than 65 percent of displaced households were living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to a Shelter Cluster survey, with more than half of those shelters in poor or very poor condition.
Israel’s siege on Gaza has also affected supplies reaching the enclave, with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) saying on October 5 that at least 500 truckloads of shelter materials were awaiting entry or procurement.
At the current pace, NRC said, it could take more than seven months for those supplies to enter Gaza. The materials include tents, tarpaulins, ropes and other items needed to repair shelters.
Winter around the corner
For families already living in torn tents, the shortage leaves few options beyond repeatedly repairing the same shelters.
Khitam Salman, 39, originally from Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, has been displaced multiple times over the past two years.
Now living near the beach, she is trying to prepare for winter with tents that have already suffered repeated damage.
“Every time there is a storm, we put up the tarpaulins and tie them down, only to have to do it all over again,” she said. “With every low-pressure system, it is the same.”
Khitam said one of the family’s tents had collapsed four times while they were sleeping inside and was torn, allowing sand to enter and offering little protection from rain and wind.
She is trying to cover the family’s tents and the space where they store their belongings, but the costs are beyond their means.
“We need a tarpaulin for this tent, another for the other one, and one for the room where we keep our belongings,” she said. “But we don’t have the means. We have done what we can.”
Her husband works in the health sector, but she said he receives his salary only once every three months, and it is not enough to cover the family’s needs.
“The tents are not suitable for living in any more,” she said. “They are torn, and sand gets inside. It is exhausting.”
Last winter, after their tent collapsed and their belongings were soaked, Salman said she became so overwhelmed that she walked away and sat by the sea for hours.
“I was so frustrated,” she recalled. “The tent had fallen, everything was flooded, and all our belongings were wet.”
“I’m worried about this winter … that the whole nightmare will repeat itself all over again.”
Damaged roads, drainage and sewage systems also increase the risk that rainwater will mix with wastewater and swamp the camps.
Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for Gaza Municipality, said more than 85 percent of the city’s infrastructure had been damaged and its rainwater drainage system was operating at about 20 percent of its previous capacity.
Rubble, damaged drainage networks and shortages of heavy machinery, fuel and maintenance materials are hampering preparations for winter, Muhanna said.
The municipality has begun emergency cleaning and maintenance work, but its efforts remain constrained by a lack of resources.
Flood risks beyond tents
Yosra Mesleh, 45, was displaced from her home in Gaza City’s Nassr neighbourhood when her home was destroyed and is preparing for her second winter living in a tent.
Preparing for winter means thinking about what to do when water enters their tents and soaks bedding and belongings. When this happens, they often have nowhere dry to sit, cook or eat.
“When it rained last winter, the water came inside and reached the bedding. Everything got wet,” she said. “It was difficult to find somewhere to sit while we waited for everything to dry.”
In summer, the heat and humidity inside the tent were unbearable, she said, with water shortages compounding their dire living situation.
“The place where we are living is not healthy or safe. It is not suitable for summer or winter,” she said.
Her husband has been out of work since the beginning of the war, while her son is struggling to cover his own expenses.
“We need tents and tarpaulins. We need cooking utensils and a proper place to prepare food. We also need a regular supply of gas,” she said.
Without cooking gas, she worries about how the family will prepare meals when rain keeps them inside.
She remembers life before the war, when life was hard but they had an apartment and her husband ran a tea and coffee shop. They have since lost their home and their only source of income.
“We are not asking for towers or anything extravagant,” she said. “We are asking for tarpaulins and tents, for a dignified life.”

Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, but more borrowers still sought savings in riskier loans

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:33:43 UTC
20:33:43 KST

Mortgage rates fell for the second straight week, and that finally brought consumers back to their brokers. A growing share, however, applied for riskier loans at even lower rates.
Total mortgage application volume rose 3.4% last week compared with the previous week, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association's seasonally adjusted index.
The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances, $832,750 or less, decreased to 7.37% from 7.41%, with points increasing to 0.76 from 0.75, including the origination fee, for loans with a 20% down payment.
"The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications," said Joel Kan, vice president and deputy chief economist at the MBA, in a release. "Mortgage rates are still more than a percentage point higher than the same week last year and most homeowners still have rates much lower than prevailing market rates."
And that is why refinance is still running well behind where it was last year. Applications to refinance a home loan climbed 3% for the week but were 61% lower than the same week one year ago. About half of all borrowers today have a mortgage rate below 4%, according to data from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Mortgage Database.
Applications for a mortgage to purchase a home rose 4% for the week but were still 18% lower than the same week one year ago. While mortgage rates have pulled back some in the last few weeks, they are still much higher than they were just a few months ago, and home prices are still rising. Potential homebuyers are also worried about the broader economy, and, anecdotally, some agents say buyers are waiting to see the results of the midterm elections.
As borrowers search for savings, more are opting for adjustable-rate mortgages. The ARM share of applications increased to 11.3% last week, the highest level in more than a year. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs decreased to 6.41% from 6.46%. ARMs are considered riskier because they adjust to whatever the current market rate is at the end of their fixed term.
Mortgage rates haven't moved at all to start this week, according to a separate survey from Mortgage News Daily. That is because there has not been much economic data for the bond market to react to. While the Federal Reserve is not expected to announce any change in its interest rate at Wednesday's meeting, markets could move on any commentary from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh.

Russia-Africa Summit: What is on the agenda, and why does it matter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:33:26 UTC
20:33:26 KST

Russia-Africa Summit: What is on the agenda, and why does it matter?
Moscow aims to strengthen economic and security ties with African leaders during the two-day gathering.
Trade and security are expected to be on the agenda as delegations and leaders from dozens of African countries gather in Moscow for a two-day summit with Russia.
The third instalment of the Russia-Africa Summit will run through October 28–29 and will be chaired by Russian President Vladimir Putin and the current African Union chair, Burundian President Evariste Ndayishimiye.
Russia has boosted security and trade cooperation with African nations as it grapples with Western sanctions imposed in response to its war against Ukraine.
So who will be attending and what is at stake?
Here’s what we know.
What is the Russia-Africa Summit?
The Russia-Africa Summit is a two-day diplomatic and economic meeting being held in Moscow on Wednesday and Thursday.
Leaders and delegations from 48 African countries are meeting to discuss bilateral cooperation spanning politics, defence and technology.
This high-profile forum is the third of its kind. The first summit took place in October 2019 in Sochi, marking an unprecedented turn in Russian-African relations.
What’s on the agenda for the summit?
The event’s official theme is Developing Mutually Beneficial Cooperation and “unlocking the potential of every African country”.
More than 40 sessions and about 100 speakers will cover trade, investment, technology transfer, food and energy security, healthcare, education and youth exchange.
There will also be a business programme, culminating in a plenary session.
Who is attending?
Representatives from 48 African countries will participate, as well as 22 heads of state, according to Kremlin presidential aide Yury Ushakov. Heads of state from 17 countries attended the last summit in 2023.
Fewer leaders came to the last two summits, compared with the first gathering in 2019, when 43 took part, a decline which Moscow blamed on Western pressure.
Russian President Putin is scheduled to meet with his Egyptian counterpart Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and Ethiopia’s Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
The guest list includes leaders closely tied to Russia’s growing security role in Africa, including Burkina Faso’s Ibrahim Traore and Niger’s Abdourahamane Tchiani.
Kenya’s William Ruto, Uganda’s Yoweri Museveni and Namibia’s Netumbo Nandi-Ndatiwah are also expected, as well as Sudan’s Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed al-Menfi, the chairman of the Presidential Council of Libya.
What is the relationship between Russia and Africa like?
Russia has gained far more influence in Africa through security than trade, according to a report by the African Security Analysis group (ASA), a security consultancy.
Russia’s security presence has risen significantly in the region. In 2023, Russian forces, mostly from the Wagner Group, operated in only a few African countries, but the ASA now counts Russian missions or troops in at least nine countries.
Trade between African countries and Russia has exceeded $28bn. It was estimated to be about $16.8bn in 2019, when the first summit was held. But trade is mainly concentrated in a few countries and overshadowed by that of China and the European Union.
Russia’s strongest ties to the continent are in energy, fertilisers, defence and nuclear power, where the state-owned firm Rosatom has signed a string of agreements.
Russia has been an essential supplier of fertilisers and wheat to many countries in the region.
In 2023, Russia exported 200,000 tonnes of grain to Mali, Somalia, the Central African Republic, Burkina Faso, Eritrea and Zimbabwe.
Why does this summit matter?
This is the first summit since 2023, so it will be an indicator of how far the relationship has developed and where it is heading, analysts say.
A final declaration and a Russia-Africa Partnership Forum plan should be adopted by the end of the Summit to cover 2027-2029.
Analysts have said that meetings on the sidelines could be more important than the main event, as talks between African delegations and Russian defence officials can illustrate where Moscow plans to expand its military ties.
The recruitment of Africans to fight in Ukraine could also be a growing problem for Moscow, as it has already caused diplomatic concern in countries such as Kenya.
Amnesty International has used the run-up to the summit to raise the issue of Africans being recruited to fight with Russia.
In an open letter, the directors of Amnesty’s African section urged leaders attending the summit to demand that Moscow end what the group describes as deceptive and coercive recruitment of Africans to fight in its war in Ukraine.

High voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel threatens Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:33:13 UTC
20:33:13 KST

High voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel threatens Netanyahu
A historic voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel could unseat Benjamin Netanyahu and position Arab parties as decisive political kingmakers.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have turned out in unprecedented numbers for Israel’s parliamentary elections, with some towns reporting participation rates exceeding 70 percent.
Historically, however, Arab towns have witnessed lower participation rates in Israeli elections, ranging between 45 and 65 percent in recent years.
This electoral surge from Palestinian citizens of Israel now threatens to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing coalition.
For many from this contingent, who might normally have abstained from voting, this election was perceived as a chance to defeat a government that was totally hostile to Palestinians and Arabs at large.
There have been a number of measures enacted by Israel’s current right-wing government that encouraged high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel in this election. These include attempts by Jewish settlers to establish an outpost on Palestinian land in Majd al-Krum in the Upper Galilee.
“The people who were indifferent to the elections, and who did not want to participate or vote, the matter provoked them,” Hussein Manna, a resident of Majd al-Krum, told Al Jazeera. “They know very well what awaits us if this government returns to power.”
Path to power
Netanyahu and his far-right allies, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, have heavily targeted Arabs in their campaigning. But this appears to have backfired and instead encouraged Palestinian citizens of Israel to go out and vote for Arab parties, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am).
Preliminary reports suggest that these parties could secure up to 17 seats combined, enough to prevent Netanyahu from reaching the required 61-seat majority.
“It is fateful for Netanyahu and for his political future, and it is also fateful for the State of Israel because it will determine its identity later on,” Walid al-Omari, Al Jazeera’s bureau chief in Palestine, said.
He added that if Netanyahu’s coalition remains in power, Israel “will move more towards racism and towards extremism”.
Ahmad Tibi, head of the Arab Movement for Renewal, told Al Jazeera: “The first goal: bringing down the government of Netanyahu, Smotrich, and Ben-Gvir, the government of crimes, the government of failure, and the government of racism and incitement against us.”
But he warned that the leaders of almost all parties opposed to Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties.
“What is the excuse? It is post-October 7, and this is a racist position,” Tibi stated. “We are ready to extend our hands to cooperate with the opposition to bring down the speaker of the Knesset [Amir Ohana] and also to prevent Netanyahu from becoming the head of a transitional government.”
In exchange for this tacit support, the Arab parties have strict demands. “The next alternative government is not our knight in shining armour and will not be a government of peace, but it will not have Ben-Gvir and Smotrich and the racist ministers,” Tibi said.
“Accordingly, we will make room for the establishment of another less bad alternative government that dialogues with us on issues that concern our society as a safety net for our society, such as issues of crime, violence, personal security, home demolitions and racism, as well as an important political horizon on our part because we have a clear political position on the occupation and on the crimes of the occupation and war crimes.”
Al-Omari said if Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, Netanyahu’s main opponent in the election, gets 53 seats, and Ra’am, headed by Mansour Abbas and most acceptable to the Eisenkot-led alliance, wins eight, then a coalition of 61 members could be formed.
‘Voter intimidation’
When the prospect of high Palestinian voter turnout emerged, Netanyahu and the far right launched a frantic campaign, warning supporters about this.
Netanyahu posted AI-generated images of Arab voters to incite his base, a move the Joint List condemned as an attempt to create a “misleading scene”.
Mohannad Mustafa, an academic and expert in Israeli affairs, believes that Netanyahu considers the Arab vote illegitimate. He said racist fearmongering and a hostile environment during the campaigning set a dangerous precedent.
“This is also what led to the assassination of Rabin in 1995 when Netanyahu said Rabin’s government in approving the Oslo Accords relies on the Arab lists in the Knesset,” Mustafa added, referring to former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.
There were also reports of right-wing parties deploying activists to polling stations, which was widely interpreted as a form of intimidation against Palestinian citizens of Israel who were voting.
“I toured the ballot boxes here in Taibe, Tira and Qalansawe; in every box there is [someone] obstructing the electoral process and slowing it down specifically so that long queues form at the boxes,” Tibi stated.
He believes the right hoped such tactics would make Palestinian citizens of Israel tired of waiting in line at the polls and leave without voting. Instead, he saw the community’s “determination to stay until the voting is done”.
The outcome of the election carries significance for the broader Middle East, with Netanyahu launching the genocide in Gaza, killing more than 74,500 Palestinians, and assaults on Syria, Lebanon and Iran during his term.
Tariq Hamoud, a political analyst, noted that an Israeli government without Netanyahu might have implications for these ongoing military engagements.
What could determine the election, though, is that Netanyahu “bears responsibility for the security failure on October 7, which opened the doors” to these wars.

HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season, leaving Britain without an ice patrol ship in the South Atlantic for a second consecutive year while the government looks at how to cover the gap, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what steps are being taken to ensure an ice patrol vessel is available for the coming season.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Due to unforeseen circumstances, HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season. Answering a separate question, Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, confirmed that the ship last went south during the 2024-25 season. Pollard told Parliament last week that Protector could not sail from Teesside to Devonport under her own power this month because of propulsion defects and had to be towed, and that she missed the 2025-26 season because of prolonged essential and mandatory maintenance.
The ship is the Royal Navy’s only ice patrol vessel and carries out Britain’s survey and inspection commitments under the Antarctic Treaty, alongside supporting the British Antarctic Survey and maintaining a presence around the British Antarctic Territory. She was bought in 2011, originally built as the Norwegian vessel Polarbjørn, and was taken on initially as a short-term replacement for HMS Endurance, which was crippled by flooding in 2008 and never returned to service.

‘Human is the master’: labour chief says AI is reshaping jobs, not ending them

Unknown Publisher

Humans should be ‘the master’: labour chief says AI reshaping jobs, not ending them
Chris Sun says employers want staff who pair AI know-how with deep domain expertise and strong soft skills
Soft skills and deep domain knowledge will decide how far young workers go in the age of artificial intelligence, Hong Kong’s labour chief has said, predicting that demand for AI practitioners with both technical capability and professional expertise will grow three- to fourfold.
Rejecting fears that automation will replace the human workforce, Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han dismissed the claim as a “zero-sum game”, stressing that the future lay in close collaboration between humans and machines.
Speaking on the second day of the Global University Presidents and Leaders Summit on Wednesday, Sun said it was clear that AI was destroying some jobs while creating others and that demand for AI practitioners was rising.

Page\Park uses local stone and timber for school wellbeing hub in Edinburgh
Scottish architecture studio Page\Park has completed The Allardice Centre, a health and wellbeing hub for Fettes College in Edinburgh, which is topped with a lantern-like roof.
Named after the independent day and boarding school’s alumnus David Allardice, the 469-square-metre centre brings together medical and pastoral care services in a fully accessible building nestled into a wooded plot.
According to Page\Park, the centre’s design was informed by the late Allardice’s interest in Eastern philosophy, in particular the elemental philosophy of Wuxing, which led to a palette of timber, stone and metal.
The building’s structure is made from Scots-grown timber, while Darney stone quarried nearby forms the external load-bearing cladding, which is contrasted by a bronze roof.
“Allardice spent much of his working life in East Asia, and was drawn to ancient Chinese philosophy and the five essential elements, fire, water, wood, metal and earth,” the studio told Dezeen.
“This narrative directly influenced the design, materiality and construction approach, which can be seen through the strata-like stone cladding, burnt bronze metal roof, and connection to the outside,” it added.
The Allardice Centre is organised across a single storey, with an open wellbeing hub at its centre, wrapped by a series of individual treatment and counselling rooms overlooking the surrounding woodland.
Illuminating the central hub is a mono-pitched, lantern-like roof. This creates a ring of clerestory windows, framed by the exposed glued-laminated timber (glulam) structure designed in collaboration with Scottish engineering firm Will Rudd.
“Fitting the full brief for both medical and pastoral functions into this constrained site, while avoiding level changes to maximise accessibility, forced the plan to be quite deep,” explained the studio.
“Bringing natural light into this deep plan therefore became a challenge. To resolve this, the glulam structure extends and branches out at high level to reveal a triple-glazed clerestory lantern formed of timber curtain walling,” it added.
Inside The Allardice Centre, white walls allow the timber structure to come to the fore. In the treatment rooms, leaf-print and green fabrics create a visual connection to the surrounding site, which was developed by landscape architects Harrison Stevens.
“We were interested in the didactic implications of exposing the glulam timber frame, offering an insight into how the building was crafted, celebrating its sustainability principles and the elemental philosophy underpinning the design,” said the studio.
“The Darney stone chosen for the project was quarried only 75 kilometres away, and had fantastic mineral veins through it which paired neatly with the varying course sizes, leaning into the earth element theme, and giving a sense of permanence,” it added.
Other projects in Edinburgh recently featured on Dezeen include the extension of a Georgian townhouse by Pend, which complemented the existing stone structure with skinny red brickwork.
Elsewhere, Page\Park recently completed a teaching building for the University of Stirling, which was shortlisted for the 2025 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award.

BeeX shows ALPHA mine-killing drone in UK after U.S. Navy win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:29:57 UTC
20:29:57 KST

- BeeX’s ALPHA underwater drone placed and fired charges against a moored mine and a floating steel plate during a UK demonstration on Sept. 17.
- The U.S. Navy named BeeX a winner of its Mine Countermeasure Modernization Prize Challenge, with winning systems set for fleet integration.
Singapore-based BeeX used its ALPHA underwater drone to place explosive charges on a moored sea mine and a swinging steel target and then destroy both during a closed-door mine countermeasures demonstration in the United Kingdom, the company said on Oct. 27.
The one-day event, held on Sept. 17 and hosted by British defense consultancy Copper Turtle, brought together representatives of the UK Ministry of Defence, the Royal Navy, industry and academia. BeeX worked alongside three other firms: Alford Technologies, which supplied the charges, Blueprint Subsea, which supplied the acoustic firing system, and ELWAVE, which supplied an electric sensor for finding mine-like objects.
ALPHA is a hovering autonomous underwater vehicle, a drone that can stop and hold its position in the water instead of cruising past a target like a torpedo-shaped survey vehicle. That ability to hover is what let it do the hands-on part of mine clearance during the demonstration. Operating semi-autonomously from a laptop, ALPHA approached each target, held station close to it, and used its sonar and cameras to inspect and identify it.
It then attached Alford’s Remote EOD Delivery System neutralizers, confirmed the charge was ready, backed away and fired. The first target was a moored mine, the kind anchored to the seabed and floating at a set depth below the surface. The second was a steel plate hung from a buoy, chosen to make the job harder because it rotated unpredictably in the water. BeeX said ALPHA still placed the charge accurately on the moving plate. After each detonation, the drone used its sonar and cameras to check the damage and confirm the targets had been neutralized.
Blueprint Subsea’s through-water fire set sent the detonation command acoustically, through the water, so no cable had to run to the charge. The event also included the successful detonation of an Alford magnetic charge. Alford says its system is operational to a depth of 950 m (3,117 feet) and can produce either a full explosion or a smaller, controlled effect against underwater explosive ordnance.
ELWAVE’s EPULSE sensor demonstrated the search end of the process. It uses electric sensing to detect objects regardless of water visibility or murkiness and can find objects that are exposed, buried or partly buried in the seabed.
BeeX also showed how the drone can be reprogrammed from far away. Its engineers in Singapore accessed ALPHA over Starlink during the event and changed its mission settings remotely. The company says the same connection could eventually let navies send firing commands from anywhere, keeping personnel out of the danger area.
The UK demonstration follows a U.S. win for BeeX. On Oct. 1, the U.S. Navy and the Defense Innovation Unit named BeeX one of three winners of the Mine Countermeasure Modernization Prize Challenge, alongside BlackSea Technologies and Vatn Systems. The challenge drew 80 submissions, and 11 companies were chosen to compete across near-surface mine neutralization, bottom mine detection and bottom mine neutralization. The U.S. Navy said the winning systems will be integrated into the fleet’s autonomous mine countermeasure kits.
Mine clearance has moved up the agenda for both navies this year. The U.S. Navy used underwater drones to help clear Iranian mines from the Strait of Hormuz, while the Royal Navy fitted the support ship RFA Lyme Bay in Gibraltar to act as a mothership for uncrewed mine-hunting systems. Other companies are also bringing new drones to the field, including French firm SEABER, which launched its RAVEN mine-hunting drone this week.
BeeX was spun out of the National University of Singapore in 2018, and in October 2025 Singapore’s Defence Science and Technology Agency awarded it a contract to supply its hovering drones to the Singapore Ministry of Defence. The company says ALPHA can operate untethered, so several units can be deployed at once, and can be launched from autonomous surface vessels.

National call launched to advance Persian medicine, herbal research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:29:33 UTC
20:29:33 KST

National call launched to advance Persian medicine, herbal research
TEHRAN - Iran has launched a national call for scientific, research, and technology-based proposals in Persian medicine, medicinal plants, traditional pharmacy, and natural products, focusing on technological development, artificial intelligence (AI), international cooperation, and commercialization.
The initiative aims to identify and support the country's scientific and technological capacities, facilitate innovation and help translate research findings into marketable products. Projects involving multiple national committees and research centers will receive particular priority.
The call covers education, research, AI applications, international partnerships, pharmaceutical development and industrial production. It seeks to strengthen links among universities, research institutions and industry, supporting projects from initial scientific investigation to the development and commercialization of new products.
Advancing research in Persian medicine
Persian medicine, one of the world's oldest traditional medical systems, has a long history of scholarship associated with prominent physicians such as Rhazes and Avicenna. Its traditional framework places considerable emphasis on maintaining health, preventing disease, and adopting appropriate lifestyles.
According to figures previously reported by the health ministry, the country ranks third globally in traditional medicine clinical trials registered on the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), following China and India. Traditional and complementary medicine trials account for approximately three percent of all clinical trials registered in Iran, while specialists in the field represent around 0.3 percent of the country's healthcare workforce.
The national call seeks to build on this research capacity by supporting clinical trials, cohort studies, molecular research, microbiology, bioinformatics, and other scientific approaches. It also emphasizes preclinical investigations and the evaluation of the safety and effectiveness of traditional medical interventions.
These priorities reflect a broader effort to connect Iran's traditional medical heritage with contemporary research methods and evidence-based healthcare.
Medicinal plant resources
Iran's rich plant diversity offers considerable potential for herbal medicine research and the development of natural products. Around 8,000 plant species are found in the country, according to figures previously cited in reports on Iran's medicinal-plant resources.
A scientific review published in Medicina in 2020 documented 245 plants used in Iranian traditional medical practices and identified scientific studies involving 89 plants collected in Iran. The review highlighted the potential of traditional knowledge to inspire pharmaceutical research, while noting that many herbal remedies still require further scientific investigation and validation.
The national call aims to help researchers and manufacturers explore this potential through the development of herbal medicines, natural pharmaceutical ingredients, functional foods and nutraceuticals. It also supports product standardization, quality assessment, technology transfer and the establishment of pilot production facilities.
The proposed initiative identifies Iranian products such as saffron, Damask rose, rosewater, pomegranate, barberry, pistachio, black seed, licorice, cumin and Shirazi thyme as potential areas for research, product development and branding.
Plans also include strengthening distribution networks, developing domestic and international brands, and helping small-scale manufacturers and knowledge-based companies bring research-based products to market.
Artificial intelligence and health research
Artificial intelligence and digital technologies are central to the initiative. Proposed projects include AI-based healthcare tools, research databases, digital patient records and improved health information systems.
Research priorities include nutrition, sleep, stress management, reproductive health, obesity, diabetes, hypertension, fatty liver disease and digestive disorders. Other areas include cardiovascular disease prevention, respiratory and musculoskeletal conditions, neurological diseases, mental health, addiction treatment and healthy aging.
The program encourages researchers to investigate potential applications of Persian medicine in these areas through appropriate scientific methods. AI and digital infrastructure could also support data analysis and collaboration among research centers.
Education and international cooperation
The call also prioritizes professional education, research networks, reference books, clinical guidelines, and digital learning platforms. These measures are intended to strengthen the skills of healthcare professionals and improve the documentation and scientific assessment of traditional medical knowledge.
International cooperation is another key component, with proposed activities including joint research and development, clinical trials, drug discovery and partnerships with BRICS member states, neighboring countries and Indian Ocean nations. The initiative also encourages technology transfer, international co-branding and cooperation in the production and marketing of traditional medicines and natural products.
By bringing together scientific research, digital innovation and industrial development, the call seeks to strengthen the evidence base of Persian medicine and expand opportunities for Iran's medicinal-plant and natural-product industries.

Analysis-Mbappe’s Mao remarks expose costs of crossing China’s red lines
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
12:28:45 CET
20:28:45 KST

By Casey Hall
SHANGHAI, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappe’s rapid fall from favour in China after remarks about Mao Zedong followed a familiar pattern: online outrage, corporate distancing, platform restrictions and official intervention.
Within 24 hours of a podcast clip surfacing in which the France captain referred to Mao as “some guy - I think he’s a Chinese dictator”, sponsors including Mengniu Dairy, Shanghai Milkground and energy drink-maker Eastroc ended cooperation with the footballer.
State broadcaster CCTV removed Mbappe-related advertising and Chinese social media platforms restricted access to his accounts. Mbappe apologised on Tuesday, describing his remarks as “ill-judged”.
The speed of the fallout will be familiar to companies, brands and celebrities with exposure to China. Analysts say the episode is the latest reminder of a business risk that remains difficult to manage despite years of similar controversies.
Foreign brands have repeatedly faced public backlash in China, from Dolce & Gabbana’s cancelled Shanghai fashion show in 2018 and apologies by Versace, LVMH-owned Dior and Tapestry’s Coach in 2019, to boycotts of H&M, Nike and Adidas over Xinjiang cotton and the NBA’s fallout with CCTV after a Houston Rockets executive expressed support for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement.
The details differ, but the pattern is similar: a remark, image or statement gains traction online, commercial partners come under pressure to respond, and reputational damage quickly outgrows the original offence.
“You don’t need to think like a Chinese person to succeed in China, but you do need to understand how Chinese audiences will react and the cultural implications of not self-policing,” said Michael MacRitchie, founder of MGI Group, which connects global celebrities with Chinese brands.
A MATTER OF RESPECT
A central question in such episodes is how much of the backlash reflects genuine public anger and how much is amplified by state media, online platforms and official actors.
The Mbappe case illustrates how difficult that distinction can be to draw. As the controversy unfolded, the original comments about Mao were largely inaccessible on China’s heavily censored internet. Many consumers were therefore exposed less to what Mbappe said than to reports that sponsors had dropped him and official media were condemning him.
“What we’ve had in this situation is to a certain extent a manufactured outrage,” said Mark Dreyer, a sports analyst and author of “Sporting Superpower”, a book about China’s sporting ambitions.
Even so, Dreyer said it would be unwise for leagues, clubs and athletes to underestimate the reaction such incidents can provoke.
“They can’t be seen to be giving a stated directive to their players not to say anything that could offend China,” he said. “Of course, behind the scenes, I’m sure people are being told, just be careful, be sensible, be aware that these sorts of reactions can happen.”
Zak Dychtwald, founder of BridgeWorks Global, which advises multinational organisations, said that although these controversies remain relatively common, they are preventable.
“If you are participating in this market, the expectation is that you respect China’s self-narrative and you have a basic understanding of what it is. Red line education should come at the foundation of it,” he said.
Another challenge for brands, leagues and celebrities, however, is that while China’s political and cultural red lines are broadly understood, they are rarely clearly defined. That uncertainty can encourage companies and commercial partners to distance themselves from controversial figures before the scale of any offence has been fully established.
“There is no rule in black and white for what crosses a line,” said Wei Kan, founder of consultancy Conduit Asia. The line shifts depending on “how consumers feel, the wider mood in society, and how platforms and media amplify a story,” he said.
For foreign businesses, China’s sensitivities should no longer come as a surprise. Yet analysts say political and cultural risks are still often treated as secondary considerations rather than routine commercial hazards.
MacRitchie said his firm includes behavioural and reputational clauses in endorsement contracts; others point to market-specific briefings, media training and crisis-response planning as increasingly necessary safeguards rather than optional precautions.
“When it goes well, everybody celebrates,” Dychtwald said. “But when you get (China) wrong, it can be extraordinarily painful and swift in its retribution.”
(Reporting by Casey Hall in Shanghai, additional reporting by Josh Arslan in Beijing, editing by Ed Osmond)

Austrian startup shows off APS1 anti-drone turrets in Vienna
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:19:34 UTC
20:19:34 KST

- GuardAero presented its APS1 vehicle drone-defense system to Austrian Defence Ministry Secretary General Arnold Kammel at Vienna’s Heldenplatz on Oct. 26.
- The version shown used two rotating turrets with 12 barrels each and camera blocks to identify and shoot down attacking drones.
Austrian startup GuardAero showed its APS1 drone-defense system for military vehicles to Arnold Kammel, secretary general of Austria’s Ministry of Defence, during the Austrian Armed Forces’ National Day display at Vienna’s Heldenplatz on Oct. 26.
The Graz-based company shared images of the presentation on social media, saying APS1 was shown as part of its research project with the Austrian Armed Forces and that the system is made in and for Austria. APS1 is an active protection system, a self-defense unit fitted to a vehicle that detects an incoming threat and destroys it before impact. GuardAero built it specifically to stop drones attacking vehicles at close range.
Photos from Heldenplatz show the system mounted on the turret of a combat vehicle. It uses two separate rotating turrets, each carrying a block of 12 barrels arranged in three rows of four, and each fitted with its own optical sensor. A cluster of camera blocks at the base of the mount handles visual identification of incoming threats.
Small first-person-view drones, flown by a pilot watching a live video feed and steered straight into their target, have become one of the most common threats to vehicles in the war in Ukraine. APS1 is designed as a last line of defense against those drones when they get past other layers of protection.
The system tracks approaching drones with passive sensors, meaning it watches for threats without emitting signals that could give the vehicle away. GuardAero currently uses a shotgun-based kinetic effector, firing shot to knock the drone out of the air. Because the turrets rotate, each can turn its barrels toward a drone coming from any direction.
GuardAero has also fitted APS1 to an Austrian Armed Forces Mitsubishi L200 pickup and has completed several live-fire tests on a dirt road in eastern Austria, shooting down attacking drones. The company says the system is vehicle-independent, so it can be fitted to different platforms, and its current work focuses on integrating it with other military vehicles.
The startup was founded in 2025 and first drew attention when it won the innovation competition at the Austrian Defence Innovation Conference in Klagenfurt in January 2025. It is funded by private capital in the low seven figures, according to Austrian military magazine Militär Aktuell, and in May 2026 it presented APS1 with the Austrian Armed Forces on a military vehicle at the Europa-Forum Wachau technology day. Earlier this month it won the Protection Award at Defence Innovation Pitch Day 2026 in Munich.
Other companies are working on similar close-range shields built around multi-barrel launchers and passive sensors. In the United States, Picket Defense Systems has developed the Inferno RTC, a rotating turret that sweeps its barrels through a full 360-degree hemisphere and fires shotgun-type and small-caliber rounds after detecting drones with acoustic sensors and cameras. Its barrels sit at fixed angles and spin continuously, so the system fires without first turning toward the target, while APS1 swivels its barrel blocks to face an approaching drone. Germany’s Mehler Protection is pursuing the same goal with SCILT, which fires shotgun-type interceptors cued by optical cameras.
APS1 would sit at the bottom of Austria’s drone-defense layers. Higher up, the Austrian Armed Forces are buying 36 Rheinmetall Skyranger 30 turrets on Pandur 6×6 wheeled armored vehicles, combining a 30 mm cannon and Mistral missiles, with the first systems due to arrive in 2027.

Third child dies in Morocco diphtheria outbreak

Breadcrumb
Third child dies in Morocco diphtheria outbreak
A twelve-year-old boy has died of diphtheria in northern Morocco, prompting parents to demand urgent action against the contagious bacteria infection in schools.
The boy died on Tuesday at Lalla Meryem Provincial Hospital in the northwestern city of Larache after he received intensive treatment for the disease.
The boy was not vaccinated against the disease, Hespress reported. Two other children in northern Morocco have recently died of the disease.
Parents' associations are now calling for an urgent vaccination programme, and health monitoring in schools.
96% of people in Morocco have received three doses of the diphtheria vaccine, according to estimates from the World Health Organisation (WHO).
The WHO now recommend that children are given six doses of the vaccine before adolescence, though they do not record data for vaccinations past the third dose.
The vaccine is often given in combination with vaccines against other diseases like tetanus and polio.
Diptheria is caused by an infection of a bacteria called Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which makes a toxin that kills healthy tissue.
The bacteria can be spread between people through respiratory droplets, often from coughing and sneezing.
Typical symptoms of diptheria include fever, difficulty breathing, swollen glands, and puss-filled blisters on the skin. In rare cases the toxin can enter the blood stream, damaging vital organs.
Diphtheria can usually be treated with antibiotics or other medicines, though it proves fatal in approximately 10% of cases, even with treatment, according to Oxford Vaccine Group.
Morocco's Ministry of Health announced in September that they have identified two clusters of diphtheria involving children who have not been fully vaccinated against the disease.
Before the recent outbreak, Morocco had not reported diphtheria cases in three decades.
The most recent outbreak of Diptheria reported by the WHO was in Guinea in 2023. That outbreak caused 13 confirmed deaths.
The WHO has not yet reported current the outbreak of Diptheria in Morocco

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's stock exchange, Bursa Malaysia's net profit for the first nine months ended Sept. 30, 2026, rose 13.46 percent year on year to 214.81 million ringgit (about 52.68 million U.S. dollars), while revenue increased 19.48 percent to 641.46 million ringgit, driven by stronger market activity and fundraising momentum.
For the third quarter, net profit grew 9.96 percent year on year to 70.21 million ringgit, while revenue rose 20.3 percent to 216.42 million ringgit, according to its bourse filing on Wednesday.
Chief executive officer Fad'l Mohamed said the exchange recorded continued momentum across its markets during the nine-month period, supported by stronger trading activity, fundraising and investor participation.
Bursa Malaysia recorded 47 initial public offerings during the period, while average daily volume in the securities market increased 27.6 percent and average daily contracts in the derivatives market grew 19.3 percent.
"These point to healthy participation across our markets," he said. ■

Malaysia's producer price inflation accelerates to 10.8 pct in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:59 CST
20:14:59 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Malaysia's producer price index (PPI) for local production rose 10.8 percent year on year in the third quarter of 2026, accelerating from a 7.4 percent increase in the previous quarter, official data showed on Wednesday.
The increase was driven by growth across all sectors, particularly mining, which rose 41.9 percent, and manufacturing, which increased 8.8 percent, the Department of Statistics Malaysia said in a statement.
On a quarter-on-quarter basis, the PPI rose 2.8 percent in the third quarter, slowing from a 6.8 percent increase in the second quarter, supported mainly by a 3.6 percent rise in the manufacturing sector.
Meanwhile, the PPI for local production increased 12 percent year on year in September 2026, up from 10.7 percent in August. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's Canton Fair opens a wider door to shared gains
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:58 CST
20:14:58 KST

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- When German businessman Can Yildirim first walked into the Canton Fair 23 years ago, he was young and unsure how to find the right business partners. As luck would have it, a stranger named Jimmy Chen noticed that he seemed a bit lost and offered to help him navigate the fair.
That first meeting really stuck with him. Yildirim and Chen have kept in touch, and Yildirim has been connected to the Canton Fair ever since.
"It's about being open-minded and making friends," said Yildirim, who now keeps a long list of suppliers he has met through the fair. "When we have to cope with a difficult period, none of my Chinese suppliers has ever left me on my own," he said.
The China Import and Export Fair, better known as the Canton Fair, has grown and thrived through openness for 70 years. Now, it's back in Guangzhou, Guangdong Province, for its 140th edition. Running in three phases from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4, the fair has grown into China's largest and longest-running international trade event, with buyers coming from more than 220 countries and regions and cumulative transactions reaching 1.6 trillion U.S. dollars.
Often seen as a barometer for China's foreign trade, the fair has enjoyed enduring success that underlines China's unwavering commitment to expanding high-level opening-up and the practical need for economies to draw on each other's strengths and work together for mutual benefit.
Official data showed that China's foreign trade maintained solid momentum in the first three quarters of this year, with total imports and exports rising 18.8 percent year on year during the nine-month period, the highest level for the same period in five years.
Smarter and greener products are helping drive China's export growth, a trend on full display at the Canton Fair. The first phase of the fair drew more than 12,000 exhibiting companies, about half of which were high-quality firms such as specialized or innovative enterprises. The number of new products, AI products and green products on display were up 6.7 percent, 20.5 percent and 13.5 percent respectively over the same period of the previous edition.
For international buyers, the expanding range of products and technologies offers fresh opportunities for growth.
"China is like a gold mine. The deeper you dig, the more you get," said Anis Sajan, a buyer from the United Arab Emirates. His company imports more than 500 containers of goods from China every month, helping his business grow 30 percent this year.
Such trade is increasingly about more than importing finished goods. More countries are relying on China's products, technology and capital to improve their own industrial systems and lift their high-end export capacity, accelerating industrial upgrading and steadily climbing the global value chain.
At the booth of Bodor, a Shandong-based company specializing in laser cutting and welding, several buyers from Southeast Asia watched closely as a machine sliced cleanly through aluminum alloy. "We don't just need cutting equipment," said one buyer from the sheet metal industry. "We want equipment that can help drive digital upgrading across our whole industry. A complete digital solution like this is exactly what our current transformation needs."
China's push for more balanced trade is also creating opportunities for exhibitors to tap further into the Chinese market. The Canton Fair has hosted an import section since 2007, giving foreign companies a direct channel to Chinese and global buyers.
During the second phase of the fair, which had just concluded, the import section brought together 213 companies from 27 countries and regions, including national pavilions from nine countries, such as Egypt, Thailand and Pakistan, showcasing kitchenware, household goods and gifts.
Dominik Bledzki, general director of the Polish-Chinese Chamber of Commerce, comes to the Canton Fair twice a year and finds something new each time -- new buildings, new suppliers and new products, all of which help him expand his business.
"China is a global buyer, but it's also a global seller," Bledzki said. "If you look for your products, if you want to do business, you have to be here. China is not only manufacturing goods; it is manufacturing ideas, new technology and new designs," he said. ■

Vietnam's capital approves plan to expand its administrative boundary
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:47 CST
20:14:47 KST

HANOI, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The 17th People's Council of Vietnam's capital Hanoi approved a plan to adjust the administrative boundary between the city and the northern midland province of Phu Tho at its seventh session on Wednesday, the Vietnam News Agency reported.
The plan covers the transfer of more than 4,000 hectares of land and 1,057 residents from Phu Tho to the capital, incorporating the areas into Ba Vi and Yen Xuan communes, according to the report.
The boundary adjustment comprises over 2,500 hectares of Ba Vi National Park and 1,477 hectares of its buffer zone, aiming to align territorial administration with park management, improve forest protection and biodiversity conservation, and strengthen forest fire prevention and control, water resource protection and ecological conservation.
According to the municipal people's committee, more than 2.4 million households, or 94.97 percent of the total consulted across 126 communes and wards, supported the proposal, which will take effect after approval by the National Assembly. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: Flavio Bolsonaro's reported departure for U.S. after election failure sparks political reactions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
19:14:38 CST
20:14:38 KST

BRASILIA, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- Flavio Bolsonaro, the presidential candidate of Brazil's Liberal Party and son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, reportedly left Brazil for the United States on Tuesday after failing to meet a Supreme Court deadline to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports, which were subsequently canceled amid a money laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing.
Flavio Bolsonaro was defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday's presidential runoff and his reported departure from Brazil has sparked heated reactions.
AFTER ELECTION
Brazil's 2026 general election culminated in a presidential runoff on Sunday, following the first round of voting on Oct. 4. Neither candidate won outright in the closely contested first round. With all votes in the runoff counted, Lula received 51.79 percent of the valid votes, compared with 48.21 percent for Bolsonaro, according to the official tally.
Lula's victory secures him a fourth term as Brazil's president, with his inauguration scheduled for Jan. 5, 2027, for a four-year term.
After Lula's victory, Bolsonaro, speaking in the Brazilian capital of Brasilia, said it is "impossible" to recognize the results and called for the annulment of the election, alleging unequal treatment of voters following a two-hour extension of voting hours at polling stations affected by public transport disruptions and heavy rain.
Bolsonaro argued that the decision had disadvantaged voters in areas where polling stations were not reopened and that his legal team would challenge the results.
However, the Liberal Party, to which Bolsonaro belongs, formally acknowledged Lula's victory on Monday. Other right-wing and center-right parties that had supported Bolsonaro during the election, including the Republicans, the Brazilian Democratic Movement and the Progressives, also acknowledged Lula's victory, making clear that they did not support calls to annul the election results or hold a new election.
PASSPORT OR U.S. VISA
Brazilian media reported Monday that Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports to the Federal Police and barred him from leaving the country.
The ruling is part of an investigation involving Bolsonaro and lawyer Willer Tomaz, according to Brazil's public news agency Agencia Brasil. The probe reportedly involves suspected money laundering and financial links to businesses connected to the sports betting industry.
Additionally, Bolsonaro is under investigation over the financing of a biopic about his father. The probe examines the source of funds for the film's production.
Bolsonaro confirmed on the same day that he intended to comply with a request to surrender his passports and denied plans to flee the country following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, serving a 27-year-and-three-month sentence for plotting a coup after his 2022 election defeat and remains under investigation in related cases.
However, he failed to surrender the documents before the deadline expired on Tuesday, and the passports were subsequently canceled. Bolsonaro was then reported to have left Brazil for the United States, though his exact route remained unclear.
Meanwhile, U.S. media reported Tuesday, citing a senior State Department official, that the department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the United States.
POLITICAL REACTIONS
In response to the news, Lula told supporters who gathered outside the Alvorada Palace: "I regret that he left Brazil ... And his decision to leave Brazil is shameful."
Lula also criticized Bolsonaro for failing to comply with the court order to surrender his passports, saying he should have stayed in Brazil to address the allegations against him. Recalling that he had surrendered his own passport when ordered to do so in 2018, Lula said he had chosen to remain in Brazil to prove his innocence.
Bolsonaro's departure has not been officially confirmed.
Brazilian media reported that there was no record in the country's immigration control system indicating that he had left Brazil through regular border controls. The Federal Police were investigating whether and how he might have left the country.
Argentina's migration department reportedly said on Wednesday that Bolsonaro and his family boarded a private plane bound for Ecuador late on Tuesday, but the Ecuadorian Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to the statement.
The current location of Bolsonaro and his family remains unclear.
Earlier Monday, U.S. President Donald Trump said Brazil's presidential election "looked like another rigged election" and that the decision to extend voting hours was "very strange."
Brazilian Vice President Geraldo Alckmin on Monday rejected Trump's claim that Brazil's presidential election appeared to have been "rigged," saying there was no evidence to support the allegation.
"First, one does not interfere in the politics of another country. That is a fundamental principle," Alckmin said. "Brazil, in fact, is an example to the world in terms of electronic voting and legal safeguards. This is how democracy works: you win an election, you lose an election, and it is the people who decide."
Brazil's Supreme Federal Court ordered the Federal Police on Tuesday to open an investigation into possible foreign interference in the country's electoral process.
The decision issued by the court's Justice Flavio Dino points to signs that algorithms on digital platforms were manipulated to benefit the conservative candidate Bolsonaro. ■

mixes sci-fi horror and small-town politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

John Scalzi has developed a reputation in science fiction for comitting to the bit. Whether with meta-explorations of killable side characters in Redshirts or a world in which the moon literally turns into cheese in When the Moon Hits Your Eye, you can count on Scalzi seeing a concept through to its wildest implications. In his latest romp, corporate greed, lovable cows and hideous monsters converge in Richland, Ohio. It’s a small, exploited town on its last legs—but the first tentacles will be arriving shortly.
Fresh off a red-eye flight after winning his fourth Hugo Award, Scalzi stopped by to chat with us about his newest novel, Monsters of Ohio.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
If you had to pitch Monsters of Ohio to someone who has never read a John Scalzi novel, what would you say?
I describe it as “cozy Cronenberg.” The slightly longer version of that is “Stephen King and Nora Ephron are made to violently kiss.”
When you last sat down with us, you described your niche in contemporary science fiction as taking “a really absurd idea and then [trying] to apply real life to it.” Monsters of Ohio seems to be no exception. How did we get here?
Well, thanks to Stephen King and Stranger Things and all of that sort of stuff, we have all seen the idea of monsters in a small town, right? I thought it would be fun to take a lot of the dressing of that and put a new spin on it, where the idea was not necessarily horror but to see what some of the consequences would be if, all of a sudden, there were monsters in your town and yet you were still trying to get through the rest of your day.
What did your research process look like? How much digging did you do for the more scientific aspects of the book?
A lot of my “research” is not directed research. It is literally “Oh! I remember this one thing I read one time on the internet!” And either that comes in handy while I’m writing, or it will pop up in my head and will keep going around and around and around until I write something about it. My brain is a rat’s nest of judicial decisions, fun facts about small mammals, and lots and lots of astronomy stuff.
I think, in many ways, I was uniquely designed to be a novelist, because when people are like, “When will you ever use that information?” I’ll be like, “Well, as it turns out, I will use it while I’m writing up a book called Monsters of Ohio.” So there you have it.
How important is scientific plausibility to you when writing science fiction?
It’s very important to me that people remember that science fiction has two parts to the phrase. There is the science, but there is also the fiction. I want to get the science at least broadly correct and reasonable so that, when I step into the fiction part, you can see it as a natural extension. Now you may or may not always agree with how I’ve decided to step off into the fiction part, but you can see, at least, [how] I got there.
I am always very hesitant to call myself a hard science-fiction writer because so much of that basically requires an advanced degree—and I have a B. A. in philosophy, so all I know is how to find things. That said, I’ve always also had a real interest in science and a real interest in talking about how science interacts with our lives. And so, when you are writing a story where, you know, [highly unlikely monster shenanigans redacted by editor], you want to be able to do it in a way that is, at least, scientifically plausible. I mean, [a written event] always happens because plot, but mine is rooted in specific things that happened in the natural world, as opposed to “and then magic” or “and then gods and demons.” There’s nothing wrong with gods and demons, but, in my case, I’m a science-fiction writer, so that’s where my brain goes first.
Monsters of Ohio is your 20th novel, and it feels paradoxically cynical and hopeful at the same time.
A lot of that cynicism plus hopefulness comes out of the experience of modern life and day-to-day life.
We live in a world where there is private equity strip-mining small towns. We live in a world where the interests of the moneyed class really are at odds with the interests of the people going day-to-day. [Take] where I live right now. In this moment, we are having a huge discussion about [how] they’re going to put power lines somewhere through Darke County, [Ohio], which is also the county that’s in the book. They swear to us that [the lines] are not to power the huge data centers that are being put up in our state right now, but come on. And part of the problem is that one of the routes is literally my street.
The hopeful part is the part where the people who are dealing with the consequences of that look toward their community, look toward their friends, look toward the people around them for support, for help, for unity—all of those sorts of things. The way that I think the little guy is going to get through this is to look at his neighbors and realize that all the messaging and disinformation that is designed to keep us angry and suspicious at our neighbors is, in fact, designed to keep us angry and suspicious of our neighbors and, in fact, [that] we need our neighbors’ help and that we need to help our neighbors and support them as much as we can during this time.
This is already helping, because I thought the takeaway of the book was that the proverbial little people were going to get through this by exploding.
I mean, why not both?
Getting to the really important questions now: You have often asked musicians to write theme songs for your books. Have you done that here?
I have inquiries out, which is, I think, the only thing that I can say at this time. But it would make sense to do it because the protagonist was very briefly in a very briefly famous emo band. So I would like to have that set up. Unfortunately I may have missed the window for the hardcover release, but there’s always the trade paperback release in about a year.
Chappell Roan would do a great rendition of the protagonist’s signature song, “Red Wine Massacre,” in case you’re taking suggestions.
I think she might be a little bit out of my price range. When you commission something like that, you do have to pay your artists, and I think Chappell Roan might be just a little pricey for a humble science-fiction author.
What would it take to get you to write a book about someone from Michigan?
I would be happy to have a character from Michigan. Will my neighbors burn my house down if I do it? Possibly. But that is the risk one takes for true literature.

Animal-borne Shamonda virus infects and kills a human for the first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:14:22 UTC
20:14:22 KST

A person has contracted and died from the Shamonda virus, a disease-causing microbe that had been thought to only infect animals, for the first time. The incident, while unlikely to herald a more widespread outbreak, is a potent reminder of the potential for pathogens to jump from animals to humans—with deadly consequences.
The Shamonda virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in 1965. Spread by bites from tiny insects called Culicoides midges, it causes several symptoms in the animals, including fever, diarrhea and reduced milk production. The virus has also been known to infect sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. Previously, cases have been detected in some African countries, Japan and—for the first time this summer—Europe. But the virus doesn’t even seem overly contagious and isn’t deadly in adult animals. (Infected pregnant animals can transmit it to their fetus, however, which can result in miscarriage, stillbirth or birth defects.)
Yet for the first time in the more than six decades since it was discovered, Shamonda was detected in humans. A 61-year-old man who was undergoing treatment for leukemia at the Civil Hospital of Lyon in France contracted the disease. According to a case report published in Eurosurveillance, the man had undergone a stem cell transplant and experienced fatal encephalitis, or brain swelling. He showed symptoms, such as blindness and confusion, that the report authors say were likely caused by the virus. The man fell into a coma and succumbed to the disease on October 9, 2026, after life support was withdrawn. He is the first person ever known to have contracted the disease and died as a result. There are no vaccines to protect animals or people from Shamonda infections.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Experts emphasize the need for caution. “At this stage, there is no evidence that the Shamonda virus will become more common in humans,” says clinical virologist Grégory Destras. He is affiliated with the same hospital in Lyon and is a co-author of the report. Destras notes that the virus may have spent several weeks incubating and multiplying in the patient before the neurological symptoms appeared.
In a joint statement, the French Ministry of Health and Ministry of Agriculture said that they suspect the patient contracted the disease from a midge bite in eastern France, where the disease has been found in several animals. Officials have reported their findings to the World Health Organization and the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC).
Shamonda has been found in livestock in 14 European countries. Two new clades of the virus, SHAV-EU1 and SHAV-EU2, were detected earlier this year, and genetic testing revealed traces of the first type in the deceased person’s cerebrospinal fluid, urine and saliva, among other samples.
The Shamonda virus is part of the Simbu serogroup and belongs to the genus Orthobunyavirus—the same serogroup and genus as the Oropouche virus, or sloth fever, which caused 9.4 million human infections in Latin America and the Caribbean regions from 1960 to 2025.
Indiana University School of Medicine virologist Natasha Tilston-Lunel highlights the Oropouche cases, but notes that the Schmallenberg virus, which is closely related to Shamonda, has been found to be widespread in livestock but not humans. She believes that, based on current information, Shamonda may also have limited infectiousness among people. Continued surveillance of livestock and their aborted fetuses, insects and genomic sequencing of human samples, however, will be critical to detecting any changes to Shamonda’s risk in people, she says. Tilston-Lunel was not associated with the new study.
Veterinary virologist Martin Beer of the Friedrich Loeffler Institute in Germany is part of a team that has conducted several studies of the Shamonda virus, including a recent preprint on the first evidence of its presence in European sheep and goats. Beer says that the main transmission route of viruses of the Simbu serogroup are biting midges, which can rapidly spread infections, especially in the summer and autumn. “In winter the transmission cycle stops since the number of biting midges is very low and temperatures below approximately 12 degrees Celsius do not allow efficient virus replication,” he says.
A spokesperson for the ECDC told Scientific American that the agency needs clarity regarding the transmission of the virus and the role of vectors in infecting people. Destras suggests that retrospective analyses of stored samples from immunocompromised people could identify asymptomatic infections and the true scale of Shamonda in France.
Beer points out that novel cases of unexplained encephalitis have occurred in immunocompromised people who were infected with other orthobunyaviruses, such as the Jamestown Canyon virus or the Cache Valley virus. More studies to analyze antibody prevalence against Shamonda in people could give a clearer picture of whether this particular virus made the leap to humans before and we just didn’t realize because no one died.

Jerusalem – Israel’s President Isaac Herzog is known for his unassuming and mild manner, but all eyes will soon be on him as he decides who to task with forming the next coalition government.
The decision is a weighty one, given that partial results show neither the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his rival Gadi Eisenkot securing a majority in Parliament.
After the official announcement of the results, Herzog will consult party representatives and name a candidate who has the best chance of forming a government – not necessarily the one whose party holds the most seats.
Under the law, the president, whose position is otherwise largely ceremonial, is afforded broad discretion, with no guidelines on how to make the choice.
Just ahead of the pivotal vote on Oct 27, Herzog acknowledged there would be tremendous pressure, but vowed not to let outside influence, notably from Donald Trump, sway his decision.
“I don’t think the president of the United States or anybody else can intervene in my discretion,” he told US outlet MS Now.
“It’s Israel’s democracy and Israel’s Constitution, and that’s what counts for me.”
Herzog also told MS Now he would do everything he could to avoid a fresh election – a possibility if neither camp can cobble together a coalition – including backing a unity government between Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
‘Worthy and wonderful man’
Modest, diplomatic and with a strong political pedigree, 66-year-old Herzog was sworn in as Israel’s president in 2021 after being elected by lawmakers in a landslide.
Yair Lapid, now a member of Eisenkot’s bloc, praised Herzog at the time as “a worthy and wonderful man who is always focused on the good of the country and the Jewish people”.
As president, Herzog has faced pressure from Trump to grant Netanyahu a pardon in his long-running corruption trials, which could land him in prison if he loses power.
In April, Herzog invited Netanyahu’s lawyers and prosecutors to his residence for talks on the issue.
Before he served as head of state, Herzog was elected to Israel’s parliament in 2003 and held portfolios including housing, tourism and welfare.
In 2015, as leader of Israel’s centre-left Labour party, Herzog vied to oust Netanyahu as prime minister, presenting himself as a subdued, even-keeled alternative to the bombastic “Bibi”.
Netanyahu, now 77, is Israel’s longest-serving premier, having governed on and off for nearly two decades.
The Oct 27 election was seen as a referendum on the veteran leader’s tenure after he pushed the country sharply to the right and unleashed a wave of wars in response to Hamas’ Oct 7, 2023, attack.
‘Bring a real change’
In an interview with AFP in March 2026, Herzog said the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran marked a “historical juncture”.
“There comes a moment that after well over a generation of endless wars, bloodshed and terror, the root cause of it, which comes from Tehran, will be blocked and stopped, and the whole direction of the region will change,” he said.
“Let’s help us bring a real change so that there will be a different future in the region.”
He also stressed the importance of talks with Lebanon, with the two sides sitting down in April for direct negotiations that are still ongoing.
Herzog’s Irish-born father, Chaim Herzog, served as head of Israel’s military intelligence, then went on to become its ambassador to the United Nations and finally its sixth president, from 1983 to 1993.
Herzog’s grandfather and namesake – Rabbi Yitzhak (Isaac) HaLevi Herzog – was the first chief rabbi for Israel’s Ashkenazis, the branch of Judaism whose roots are in eastern Europe.
At the helm of the Labour party, Herzog worked to steer its focus back to peace with the Palestinians.
He answers to the nickname “Bougie” – reportedly given to him by his Egyptian-born mother, who mixed the French word for doll “poupee” with its Hebrew equivalent “buba”. AFP
