Burnham’s government unveils its first UK budget: What to expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:42:52 UTC
19:42:52 KST

Burnham’s government unveils its first UK budget: What to expect
UK chancellor to present an autumn budget amid rising living costs and energy bills.
British Chancellor John Healey will set out the country’s autumn budget, the government’s tax and spending plans, the first under Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s premiership amid high inflation and government spending levels.
While the budget will be announced in parliament on Wednesday at 12.30 GMT, speculation about what it will lay out has ranged from a series of tax announcements to commitments to defence spending.
But the country continues to deal with a rising cost-of-living crisis and energy bills are expected to see their biggest rise in four years in January due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
As total United Kingdom borrowing broke through the 3 trillion pounds ($3.99 trillion) barrier for the first time in September, the country is already spending 100 billion pounds ($133bn) each year just on servicing that debt.
Despite that challenge, the chancellor has said the budget will move “money and power out of Westminster and into every postcode around Britain”.
In a speech last month, Healey said that he and Burnham were in “lockstep” in meeting fiscal rules, “to balancing the books, with a buffer to protect against uncertainty, to control borrowing to bear down on inflation, and reducing long-term pressures on our public finances”.
Gregory Thwaites, interim chief economist at the British think tank, Resolution Foundation, told Al Jazeera he is expecting a “relatively small budget given the limited room for maneuvre the government has”.
“A bit of action to offset high living costs,” but “most big decisions postponed to next year.”
Following the two budgets from former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which included big tax and spending increases, Healey’s budget is expected to take a more “steady as she goes” line, which some say is the wrong approach.
Here’s how he will be expected to achieve that.
Defence spending
On Monday, Burnham said Healey would set out a plan to fully fund the government’s defence plans and commitments, telling ITV’s Good Morning Britain that his government’s first challenge was financing the already announced defence investment plan.
Announced in June, the plan is backed by 298 billion pounds ($396bn) of investment and will transform the armed forces as the country moves to “warfighting readiness” and stepping up “European security”, according to a government policy paper.
But Burnham said it was “crucial that we have a funded plan that we can then implement, and we will set out more details on Wednesday as to how we’ve done that”.
He added that NATO commitments of spending 3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) on defence spending by 2030 and 3.5 percent by 2035 are included in the pathway, explaining that national security issues were “at the top of the priority list”.
As it stands, Britain spends about 2.6 percent of its GDP on defence.
The Guardian reported that on defence spending, Healey aims to close a 4.7-billion-pound ($6.2bn) funding gap in the government’s plan inherited from the previous Labour Party leader, with cuts to other departmental budgets likely to fund it.
Inflation
Government borrowing and inflation continue to rise, which is a potential spanner in the works for proposed spending.
Last week, UK inflation and government borrowing both hit their highest levels in a year.
According to the Office for National Statistics, borrowing was nearly 25 billion pounds ($33bn) last month alone, “a little higher than a year earlier, as spending, including higher debt interest costs, increased more than government income, partly reflecting the impacts of inflation”.
ONS added that in the financial year to September 2026, borrowing remained below the same period last year, but it was higher than the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecast.
According to Jasper Kenter, a professorial research fellow in ecological economics at Aberystwyth Business School, for the government to grow the economy without raising inflation levels, there needs to be an understanding of what kind of economy is created.
“The strongest policies improve prosperity, resilience and sustainability at the same time,” Kenter said.
“Growth is less likely to be inflationary when it comes from increasing the economy’s productive capacity rather than simply boosting spending. Measures that improve skills, reduce energy dependence, strengthen local economies and regenerate ecosystems are likely to deliver more lasting benefits than short-term stimulus,” he added.
Moreover, Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said in a media release ahead of the budget that Healey “faces a forecast in which borrowing is still expected to fall in coming years, and the fiscal rules are still being met”.
“Despite that, a ‘steady-as-she-goes’ budget is not an option available to the chancellor. Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said.
Tax on banks, online sellers
The budget is also expected to reveal new taxes on banks and online marketplaces such as Amazon, Temu and eBay, as well as a funding boost for mayoralties and local authorities.
The biggest four banks collectively made about profits of 15 billion pounds ($19.9bn) in the first six months of this year. Trade unions are calling for higher taxes on those earnings, the BBC has reported.
According to the BBC, the Treasury is leaning towards changing a 2023 surcharge rate on banks, which would raise about 2 billion pounds ($2.6bn).
On marketplaces such as Amazon, Healey is reportedly looking to crack down on foreign sellers who avoid paying VAT – a UK sales tax – which is expected to raise as much as 1 billion pounds ($1.3bn) and help fund business rate cuts for high street shops, The Times reported.
Paying for social care and benefits
According to The Guardian newspaper, Healey is expected to allocate about 1.42 trillion pounds ($1.8 trillion) this year for day-to-day spending and public investment, with about 100 billion pounds ($132.8bn) going on debt interest.
Kenter, of Aberystwyth Business School, told Al Jazeera that he expects “targeted support rather than large-scale tax cuts or rises” in the budget announcement.
“The government appears keen to signal empathy with the pressures many people are facing. Addressing the harsh cliff edge in carer’s allowance and expanding parental pay are good examples of this,” he said.
Some of the budget’s contents have already been announced, including ending the carers’ allowance limit and removing tariffs on a range of food items, including chocolate and beans, to make them cheaper for shoppers.
Pensioners are also expected to be shielded from income tax through the introduction of a new personal allowance, while Healey is expected to add another 1 billion pounds ($1.3bn) to the 39 billion pounds ($51.8bn) planned for social and affordable housing in England over the next decade.
“Pensioners will benefit from another substantial increase in the state pension, while low-paid workers will benefit from increases in the minimum wage. For most households, the bigger determinants of living standards will remain wages, inflation and energy costs rather than any new tax measures announced in the budget,” Kenter explained.
Last month, Burnham announced a new national care service to provide free personal care for elderly people. As costs of care for the elderly have soared in the UK, this was a major issue from the outset of Burnham’s premiership.
He said the plan would be introduced in phases and would be fully funded from public spending and savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock – an annual increase in state pension that goes up with inflation, wages or a fixed rate of 2.5 percent, whichever is highest.
A report on how this will be implemented is due in summer 2027.
Energy bills
Amid high gas and oil prices as a result of the US-Israeli war with Iran and the subsequent closure of the Strait of Hormuz, energy prices worldwide have increased, with Brent crude futures at $115.90 a barrel on Wednesday.
In the UK, energy prices are predicted to reach nearly 2,000 pounds ($2,655) a year for households in January after energy consultancy Cornwall Insight projected in its latest forecast last month that the government’s cap on energy prices is expected to increase by 16 percent.
On energy bills, reports suggest the chancellor is expected to announce help for households in the budget by scrapping standing charges for energy supply, among other things.

Plato’s Moral Realism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:42:00 UTC
19:42:00 KST

In Plato’s Moral Realism, Gerson defends two connected claims: Plato is a metaethical non-naturalist realist, and his ethical realism necessarily depends on his metaphysics. As quickly emerges, Gerson’s Plato is also a Moorean—after a fashion. Just as Moore used his open-question argument to argue that intrinsic value must be sui generis and unanalyzable lest we fall prey to the naturalistic fallacy, so Plato—on Gerson’s reading—believes the Idea of the Good must have no essential content (it must be “beyond essence”, as Gerson translates ἐπέκεινα τῆς οὐσίας (Republic 509b9)), or else we can always ask why any of its essential properties (or the instantiations of those properties in the world) are themselves good. We might think of Gerson’s Plato as aiming to avoid an essentialistic fallacy—and this Platonic version of the open-question argument serves as an argumentative refrain throughout the book (e.g., 16-19, 33, 49, 66-67, 90, 96, 130, 143, 156, 170, 173, 182). Often explicitly associated with Moore, the argument provides key motivation for Gerson’s central theses: Plato’s superordinate Idea of the Good has no essence, and only such a sui generis metaphysical entity can adequately ground Plato’s normative theory.
After establishing his metaphysical framework at the start of Chapter 2, Gerson draws out its consequences: the identification of the Good with the One means I more fully instantiate the Good the more I realize integrative unity in my life (Chapter 2); the knowledge necessary and sufficient for virtue is a grasp of the Idea of the Good (Chapter 3); that the knowledge relevant to virtuous activity is rooted in Plato’s metaphysics shows the normative theory of the ‘so-called’ early Socratic dialogues is not eudaimonist/prudentialist (Chapter 4); wrongdoing occurs when I fail to act in accordance with my recognition of the Idea of the Good’s normative authority (Chapter 5); the Philebus and Statesman show how the concept of integrative unity provides a contentful normative theory (Chapter 6); and all this has important results for our understanding of Plato’s theology and political philosophy (Chapter 7).
My brief survey risks masking the richness of Gerson’s work, which touches on a staggering array of debates in contemporary Plato scholarship. Given a project this daring—Gerson aims to upend the widely-held assumption that Platonic (and, distinctly, Socratic) ethics can be understood independent of Plato’s metaphysics—it is hardly surprising that some choices in presentation and argument invite objection.
It is often difficult, for instance, to distinguish when Gerson believes he is reconstructing Plato’s own positions using direct textual evidence from when he is ‘filling in the gaps’ in Plato’s theory, whether on the basis of later Neo-Platonism or his own philosophical intuitions. Gerson also makes a number of bold claims without offering the kind of sustained defense one might hope for. For example, Gerson claims that for anyone who believes “the source of all being is no guide to the attainment of the good for human beings…the only possible guide to that which is really good is how that appears to each one” (45)—a striking reductio, but hardly supported by the argument he provides.
Furthermore, when engaging with other perspectives in the secondary literature, Gerson sometimes mistakes the point in dispute. A key example is his engagement with defenders of Socratic eudaimonism (which Gerson calls ‘prudentialism’) in §4.2. Gerson claims that prudentialism reduces to “a probabilistic argument in defense of Socrates” (129); that is, eudaimonist arguments for the life of virtue reduce to virtue being the most likely/reliable way to ensure one’s happiness. However, when scholars like Irwin claim Plato is a rational eudaimonist, they are fundamentally interested not in how we determine whether I have reason to perform this or that action (prudentialist deliberative frameworks might, but need not, involve probabilistic reasoning), but rather in what grounds my reasons (answer: my own good, rather than the Good). By insisting on the non-universal nature of practical maxims derived from probabilistic calculations, Gerson fails to engage with the more fundamental question of the structure of practical reasons—and his criticisms of prudentialist readings miss their mark.
However, because I believe Gerson’s underlying theses are true—Plato is a metaethical non-naturalist realist, and we isolate his normative theory from his metaphysics at our interpretive peril—I want to focus on how Gerson chooses to defend them, namely, by presenting Plato as a Moorean (of a sort) avant la lettre. I have my hesitations about attributing Moore’s open-question argument to Plato some two millennia before Moore, but let us grant that Plato has such an argument available to him and that it structures his conception of the Good throughout the dialogues. We should then ask why, when facing the same theoretical choice points, Gerson’s Moorean Plato opts for such different paths from Moore—which will in turn draw our attention to several key challenges for Gerson’s interpretation.
Moore was an intuitionist, believing we identify intrinsic goodness by employing our innate intuition in conjunction with the Principia’s method of isolation. Importantly, this intuitionism allows us to preserve the unanalyzable character of intrinsic goodness (and thereby avoid the naturalistic fallacy) while still making evaluative determinations.
I found it surprising that Gerson says nothing about the Philebus’ method of isolation (see e.g., 20e-22b) in his chapter on the Philebus and Statesman, especially given the dialogue’s importance for Moore’s own project. More surprising still, while Gerson believes Plato endorses a form of Moorean intuitionism (our vague knowledge of the Good is a “permanent endowment in rational creatures” (166 n.43)), he does not appeal to this intuitionism as the ultimate justification for first-order normative claims. Instead, Gerson attributes several seemingly-essentialist properties to the Idea of the Good, for instance, that it is one, and claims these generate “criteria” or “heuristics” by which we can determine whether the Good is instantiated (43).
Gerson believes that saying “the Good is the One”, or that integrative unity is an ‘index’, ‘criterion’, or ‘heuristic’ for the Good, is different from claiming that “the Form of Justice is part of the Good”. The latter, Gerson claims, is an unacceptable essential predication vulnerable to open-question style objections, whereas the former preserves the essence-less character of the Idea of the Good. It was not at all clear to me by the end of the book that Gerson had earned this distinction—and if he has not, then I find it puzzling why his Plato appeals to such heuristics and identity statements, thereby at least appearing to commit the essentialistic fallacy, when he might instead appeal (like Moore) to direct applications of our valuative intuitions.
Moore also takes the primitive ‘object’ in his axiology to be a form of value—intrinsic value itself is sui generis and unanalyzable. Moore believes the open-question argument applies to what he calls ‘metaphysical ethics’ (turning on non-natural metaphysical objects like Platonic Forms) just as much as to natural properties, because we can still ask why instantiating the Form of the Good is itself good. Of course, this theoretical decision comes with costs—Moore is infamously vague about intrinsic value’s ontological status and chary of questions about its source. Gerson’s Plato, on the other hand, does not take his unanalyzable primitive to be value itself, but rather the source of value. As Gerson repeatedly emphasizes, the Idea of the Good is not itself good, but the source of all goodness (224). This contrast between Moore and Gerson’s Plato raises two issues.
First, it is ultimately unclear how value enters Gerson’s picture. Drawing on Proclus, Gerson distinguishes between the co-ordinate Form of the Good (the genus of all perfections) and the super-ordinate Idea of the Good (the source of all value). When I say that, for instance, ‘justice is good’, I can mean two things: that justice perfects human beings and so participates in the Form of the Good; and that justice is, for human beings, a kind-relative form of integrative unity and thereby a way of instantiating (however imperfectly) the Idea of the Good. Participating in the Form of the Good by being just is a form of self-perfection; instantiating the Idea of the Good by being just (which is, for humans, a form of integrative unity) is good simpliciter and therefore, Gerson’s Plato argues, necessarily also good for me. Gerson believes the former claim is vulnerable to open-question challenges (why is self-perfection good for me?), but the latter is not. Yet it seems to me that these two claims should stand or fall together: I see no principled reason why instantiating the essence-less Idea of the Good through my kind-relative integrative unity is any further removed from the essentialistic fallacy than participating in the Form of the Good by realizing kind-relative perfections. In both cases, we are left asking why such relations are valuable—and merely asserting that the Idea of the Good is the source of value (though not essentially!) cannot resolve this worry.
This raises a second Moorean challenge for Gerson’s account. Precisely because he thought non-natural, metaphysical grounds of value were equally susceptible to naturalistic fallacy-esque objections, Moore deliberately constructed his ethics to be independent of metaphysics: to get his normative theory off the ground, he thought it only necessary to posit an unanalyzable form of value that was intuitively accessible. That Moore built his ethics on such metaphysically-abstemious grounds challenges the stronger of Gerson’s interpretive claims about the relationship between metaphysics and ethics in Plato’s thought, namely, that Plato’s normative theory not only depends on his metaphysics as a matter of historical fact, but that such metaphysical dependence was philosophically necessary—there being no other way, Gerson claims, to construct a robust realist metaethics to undergird the normative theory we find in the dialogues. Couldn’t Plato, like Moore, construct his normative theory by a similar route, avoiding appeal to his metaphysics? He may not in fact have done so—but that does not license Gerson’s bolder claim of theoretical necessity (Gerson calls the Moorean solution “untenable” early in the book (11n.33), but by the end, it was unclear whether his objection amounted to anything more than a question of philosophical taste).
Finally, Moore builds a consequentialist normative theory on the back of his metaethical non-naturalist realism: what makes an action right is that it promotes intrinsic goodness in the world, and our notion of agent-relative value is reducible on analysis to whatever agent-neutral value is found in a particular life. Gerson’s Plato endorses many of consequentialism’s hallmarks (for instance, that the good is prior to the right (§1.4)) and identifies the good-for-me with the Good, but Gerson nevertheless insists that “Plato’s moral realism is unalterably opposed to utilitarianism” (226). His motivating worry is that consequentialist theories (and Gerson here uses ‘utilitarianism’ and ‘consequentialism’ interchangeably) eliminate all universal moral laws except for a principle of maximization, which may require me to sacrifice my own good or harm others for the sake of maximizing overall goodness—both possibilities that Gerson’s Plato would emphatically reject.
This rejection is justified by appeal to the Idea of the Good’s superordinate character, which ensures my good is identical with the Good and consequently will never require my harming others—and Gerson explicitly contends that for Plato “the identity of ‘good’ and ‘good for me’ does not support consequentialism” (19n.51). However, he provides no clear means of resisting Moore’s consequentialist conclusions. Insofar as I aim to ensure (perhaps maximize?) the Idea of the Good’s instantiation in the world and this instantiation is identified with my good, I see no reason to prefer that I instantiate it in my own life rather than the lives of others. The result is ironic: in making Plato a Moorean, Gerson may also have inadvertently made him a utilitarian (insofar as my interest in the Good’s instantiation should not prioritize its instantiation in my life alone)—or, in what would represent an equally repellant conclusion for Gerson, a prudentialist (because the only justification for prioritizing the achievement of my own integrative unity would seem to be pragmatic/probabilistic, insofar as my good is the good I can most effectively or reliably achieve).
All this is not to detract from the accomplishments of Plato’s Moral Realism. Gerson’s magisterial grasp of the ancient commentary tradition and contemporary scholarship is on constant display, and the book serves as a clarion call to re-evaluate our understanding of the relationship between Plato’s ethics and metaphysics. Even if one ultimately decides Plato is no Moorean, Gerson’s arguments deserve careful attention.

Israeli forces continue West Bank raids as Hebron lockdown enters sixth day
UN agency expresses ‘grave concern’ in Hebron and warns of echoes of 2025 ‘Iron Wall’ operation.
The Israeli army has continued its incursions into Hebron as its lockdown of the occupied West Bank’s largest city entered its sixth day.
Israeli forces raided several neighbourhoods in Hebron city as well as towns across the wider governorate on Wednesday, tightening restrictions at the entrances to the city, Anadolu news agency reported.
Troops also raided the Fawwar refugee camp south of Hebron about midnight, searching several Palestinian homes.
The Israeli army carried out raids in other areas across the occupied West Bank, detaining four Palestinians in Tulkarem, the Wafa news agency reported.
Those detained included a journalist and his two brothers, alongside an officer working for the Palestinian General Intelligence Service.
In the town of Beita, south of Nablus, troops fired tear gas at protesters demonstrating against the demolition of two homes belonging to the families of two Palestinian prisoners.
A Palestinian man sustained fractures to his hand after Israeli forces beat him during an attack on the village of Yasid, north of Nablus.
In Burin village, troops raided homes and converted several into military barracks, Wafa reported.
Schools in southern Nablus have been ordered to switch to remote learning to protect students and staff.
‘Alarming echoes’
The raids come a day after the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) expressed “grave concern” over Israel’s continued incursions into Hebron, which have displaced nearly 5,000 Palestinians, warning that “collective punishment” violates international law.
“A near-total lockdown across large parts of Hebron has severely restricted residents’ freedom of movement and their ability to access critical services,” Roland Friedrich, the director of UNRWA Affairs for the occupied West Bank, said in a post on X.
“These developments bring alarming echoes of the massive displacement witnessed in the northern occupied West Bank in early 2025, where more than 34,000 Palestine refugees from Jenin, Tulkarem and Nur Shams camps remain forcibly displaced over a year later.”
Israel’s campaign follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen at a checkpoint last week. The gunmen were later killed by Israeli forces.
Palestinian officials have accused Netanyahu and his hard-right government of exploiting the operation to secure settler votes before Tuesday’s elections in Israel.

Russell Brand says friends abandoned him after 'devastating' sex crime allegations
LONDON, Oct 28 - British comedian and actor Russell Brand, on trial for a string of alleged historical sex offences, told a court on Wednesday that he had dedicated his life to reckless philandering and idiocy but said consent was always non-negotiable.
Brand, once a regular figure on British television and star of a number of Hollywood movies, was giving evidence at London's Southwark Crown Court, where he is accused of three counts of rape, three of sexual assault and an attempted indecent assault involving six women between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old former husband of US singer Katy Perry denies all the allegations.
"I have been persuasive, seductive, begging and flirting, and have dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless philandering and idiocy," he told the court towards the end of about four hours of evidence.
"I was in a position of fame. As I became more successful and famous I was very comfortable allowing that to facilitate sexual access, which I agree was wrong."
The jury has previously been told how all the complainants came forward to detectives after a documentary was broadcast in 2023 along with a number of newspaper articles in which anonymous allegations were made by other women who are not involved in the trial.
Brand, wearing a black suit with an open-neck white shirt and a loose black tie, said the impact had been "devastating". He agreed with his lawyer Ian Winter that his friends would now not "touch you with a bargepole".
Brand, who said his 14-month marriage to Katy Perry in 2010 had brought him "staggering fame," said he had even been barred by a hospital from staying with his son after he had had open heart surgery.
'CONSENT IS FUNDAMENTAL', BRAND SAYS
Prosecutors say Brand raped a woman after meeting her at a fringe event at the Labour Party conference in 1999, forced a woman to give him oral sex in toilets at a London bar in 2004, and molested another woman at a radio station in 2004 or 2005.
He is also accused of trying to pull a woman into the male toilets at MTV Europe, in London, where she was working in 2001, and that in 2009 he anally raped a woman who had agreed to consensual sex at his home.
The final allegation is that he assaulted a woman while they were involved in a recording project.
"Consent is fundamental, essential, necessary and indeed more important than sex itself," Brand told Winter when discussing the first rape allegation.
While he said he did not remember incidents involving three of the complainants, he did recall details about the other alleged rapes, saying both women had either consented or the incident was not as they portrayed.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones queried why he had told police in four interviews between 2023 and 2025 that he had not previously been able to recall any of the women or the incidents.
"You have constructed your account around some of what they said," she suggested.
Brand said there had been "escalating recollection" during the process, saying: "It's been a deeply traumatic episode of my life."
"I've focused on (this) at the expense of my marriage, my children and health ... I recognise that this recollection includes small details that are not consistent and I acknowledge that," he said.
The trial continues, with the jury told it was likely they would be sent out on Tuesday to consider verdicts. REUTERS

Norway’s premier says call with Putin was effort to present European views

Unknown Publisher

11:40:53 CET
19:40:53 KST

OSLO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Norway’s prime minister defended on Wednesday a three-way call with Vladimir Putin and Finland’s president, saying it was intended to ensure the Russian leader heard European as well as US views.
Tuesday’s call between Russia’s Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian premier Jonas Gahr Stoere broke a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin, and was criticised by allies including Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen.
The 90-minute call came ahead of what are expected to be the first face-to-face talks since February between Ukrainian and Russian officials, in Abu Dhabi next month.
“We (Stubb and I) were focused on looking forward, what must happen for this war to not continue endlessly for months, with people dying … and it is even more difficult to find a solution,” Stoere told public broadcaster NRK.
“I don’t think (Putin) will change his mind, but he gets to hear our position very clearly. I am worried that some of these messages do not reach him when the Americans talk to him,” he said.
Norway, said Stoere, was keen to introduce de-escalation steps such as stopping attacks on energy infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine, halting strikes on ships exporting Ukrainian grain and conducting prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Asked whether there could be peace without Ukraine ceding territory, Stoere said: “Today Russia controls nearly 20% (of Ukrainian territory). Ukraine will never sign a deal that recognises that they have lost territory, but whether they can take the current frontline as a reality and as a starting point, that is a different question.”
“And the big question is what kind of security guarantees can there be for the country (Ukraine) after a peace deal? Putin recognises that this is the big question.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov has said Tuesday’s call offered nothing new on the Ukraine conflict, and that European countries were simply seeking a role in the negotiation process.
(Reporting by Gwladys Fouche in Oslo; Editing by Terje Solsvik, Louise Rasmussen, Aidan Lewis)

‘Russia is already part of who I am’: African students in Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:40:52 UTC
19:40:52 KST

‘Russia is already part of who I am’: African students in Moscow
As the Russia-Africa Summit gets under way, students in the capital say education is helping to build ties.
Moscow, Russia – Moscow’s Patrice Lumumba Peoples’ Friendship University – better known as RUDN – offers a view of a relationship often discussed in the language of diplomacy, trade and security.
On the eve of the Russia-Africa Summit, due to begin on Wednesday in the capital Moscow, RUDN’s corridors are crowded with students speaking Russian, English, Arabic and dozens of African languages.
There are national celebrations, cultural showcases, food from across the continent and student clubs that turn the campus into what one graduate calls a “mini-city”.
For Africans who have come to study, work and build careers in Russia, the relationship is not an abstract geopolitical project. It is shaped by friendships, education, professional ambitions and the daily experience of life in Moscow.
Keturah Musonda, a Zambian medical graduate, said she has not regretted coming to Russia.
“I think Moscow is one of the best cities in the world,” she said, praising its transport system, the range of events and the opportunities she found beyond the classroom. Her student years at RUDN were filled with theatre, singing, student unions and medical studies. “My student life was quite colourful,” she said.
But it is Russia’s healthcare system that has left the strongest impression on her. Keturah points to the accessibility of ambulances, the investment in specialised equipment and testing, and the particular attention paid to paediatrics.
“In my country, I have never called an ambulance. No one in my family has ever called an ambulance,” she said.
In Moscow, she was struck by specialised children’s clinics and by a system in which paediatric care is treated as a priority. She hopes African countries can invest more heavily in specialist medicine, rather than relying on overstretched general departments inside large hospitals.
Her own journey was made possible through a Russian government scholarship programme, which allows foreign applicants to apply online, submit documents through Russian cultural centres and national authorities, and compete for university places in Russia.
For Moscow, such programmes are an investment in long-term links. For students like Keturah, they are a route to qualifications and experience they hope to take home.
Chinyama Kazombo, another Zambian medical student, describes Russia as a place where he can realise his potential. Over five years, he has made friends from China, Asia, Russia and across Africa, while participating in student events that introduce Russians to Zambian culture.
Zambia’s independence anniversary, he said, was celebrated in Moscow with dance, exhibitions and national traditions.
The ultimate goal is not simply a Russian diploma.
Zambia needs qualified doctors and other specialists, he said, and the education he receives in Russia could help him serve people back home.
Yet Russia will remain part of his life: “I’ll be working with Russians through my entire life … Russia is already part of who I am.”
For Abobakr Mohamed Abbakar Khussein from Sudan, a lecturer at a Moscow university, relations between Russia and Africa are moving in a pragmatic direction, even if they have not yet reached their full potential.
He sees African governments seeking economic links, security cooperation, energy and agricultural partnerships with countries that respect their sovereignty.
Sudan’s relationship with Russia, he noted, dates back 70 years, beginning shortly after Sudanese independence. He pointed to Russian archaeological work around Sudan’s ancient pyramids, as well as the training of Sudanese specialists in medicine, agriculture, the humanities and linguistics. He also sees potential in mining and nuclear cooperation, including with Rosatom.
But he also highlighted the vulnerability created by the war in Ukraine.
Disruption to Russian and Ukrainian grain and cooking-oil exports threatens food security across Africa, he said. His conclusion is direct: African countries need peace, dependable trade routes and practical partnerships.
Aaron Kasonde, a lecturer and assistant professor at RUDN from Zambia, believes agriculture could become one of the most important areas of Russia-Africa cooperation. Africa has vast arable land and a fast-growing, youthful population – the average age is about 19, he said.
The continent needs fertilisers, irrigation systems, investment and technology, Kasonde added.
Several African states remain net food importers, despite having the land and labour needed to produce more. Russia, one of the world’s major wheat and fertiliser producers, could contribute not only through grain exports but through technologies that help African farmers raise yields and build lasting food security, Kasonde believes.
For Hafi Ahmed from Kenya, the next frontier is broader economic cooperation.
Kenya may be smaller than Russia in territory and population, she said, but it has an educated workforce, skilled doctors and nurses, natural resources and significant growth potential. Cultural exchange also matters. She believes Kenyans and Russians have more in common than many assume – an impression reinforced by her close friendship with a Russian.
What unites these voices is neither blind enthusiasm nor a demand that Africa choose geopolitical sides. They want cooperation to produce measurable benefits: Qualified professionals, modern healthcare, food security, technology, jobs and cultural diversity.
Kasonde puts it simply.
Whether the partner is Russia, China, the United States or Europe, the question for African countries is whether that relationship supports national interests and development. On a campus built around international friendship, that is also the message shaping the future of Russia-Africa ties.

Hungary carries out dawn raids over COVID-era purchase of 17,000 ventilators
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
11:40:27 CET
19:40:27 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Hungary’s tax authority has raided several locations and made arrests in an investigation into COVID-era medical mask and ventilator procurement by the Foreign Ministry.
The raids, announced by the National Tax and Customs Administration late on Tuesday, came after an August 25 report filed with prosecutors by the ministry about suspected fraud in the 2020 purchase of nearly 17,000 ventilators worth a combined 300 billion forints ($910 million) under the previous government led by Viktor Orban.
Foreign Minister Anita Orban said at the time that the ministry had bought thousands of surplus ventilators at inflated prices that could not realistically be used, with most still stored in warehouses.
On Tuesday, the tax agency carried out dawn raids at several locations and questioned 11 suspects, arresting one individual in Austria under a European Arrest Warrant and detaining two others.
An international arrest warrant has also been issued for a suspected leader of the scheme, believed to be residing in Indonesia.
According to the tax authority, the suspects had agreed in 2020 to supply 800 ventilators and 3 million medical masks from China for 15.6 billion forints ($47.31 million).
The group is accused of using a network of shell companies with no real business operations and issuing fraudulent invoices to minimise their VAT obligations, resulting in a 660 million forint ($1.99 million) loss to the state budget.
The tax authority said it was investigating the case for budget fraud, money laundering and other offences.
Separately, the National Bureau of Investigation is conducting its own proceedings relating to mismanagement, including overpricing and questions about the usability of the equipment.
($1 = 329.7200 forints)
(Reporting by Anita Komuves;Editing by Alison Williams)

Documents
Details
Timetables for operational low flying (OLF) training by RAF fast jets and Hercules aircraft. These timetables cover 3 tactical training areas (TTA) only. These are:
- LFA 7(T): central Wales
- LFA 14(T): northern Scotland
- LFA 20(T): the borders of southern Scotland and northern England
When the TTA is not in use, there may be other flying activity in the area. The MOD is unable to provide a timetable for all low flying activity as the information can very quickly become outdated due to weather conditions and training requirements.
Other low flying schedules
Related information
- Low flying military aircraft includes information about how to contact MOD about low flying in your area
- Military low flying includes detailed information about why we carry out low flying in the UK

Lockheed breaks ground on Alabama factory for ARRW hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:37:25 UTC
19:37:25 KST

Lockheed Martin has broken ground on a factory expansion in Troy, Alabama, that will triple the space it uses to build the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, the U.S. Air Force’s first hypersonic missile to enter production.
The company held the groundbreaking for the expansion of its Building P-20 on Oct. 27, the day after the U.S. Air Force disclosed that it had awarded Lockheed a $694 million contract to produce and field the missile. The project adds 4,366 m² (47,000 square feet) of production space and, according to Lockheed Martin’s announcement, will equip the building for ARRW production with advanced manufacturing processes, robotics and digital technologies, while adding jobs over the next four years to the company’s workforce of almost 4,000 in Alabama.
Lockheed said it spent $67 million of its own money on the facility expansion and production equipment before receiving government funding, as part of an $8 billion to $9 billion investment the company plans through 2030 to meet demand for munitions. It also said it funded the work, materials and equipment needed to start ARRW production ahead of the contract award.
“The ARRW production contract award showcases Lockheed Martin’s ability to develop and begin production on cutting-edge systems at unprecedented speed and scale,” said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control.
The U.S. Air Force signed the contract on Sept. 29 and announced it on Oct. 26, moving its first hypersonic missile from flight testing into production. The service did not disclose how many missiles it ordered or when they are due, citing operational security. ARRW is too large for most fighter aircraft and will first be carried by the B-52 Stratofortress bomber, the platform Lockheed says it is integrated on, and it has also been tested on the B-1.
ARRW is a boost-glide weapon. A solid-fuel rocket booster carries it to more than five times the speed of sound, or Mach 5, before the booster drops away and releases a glide vehicle that maneuvers toward its target. That combination of speed and maneuvering makes it harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile. Lockheed says the weapon uses advanced materials to withstand the extreme heat of hypersonic flight and is designed to strike targets from long standoff ranges.
The production order follows a long development path. Lockheed began work on ARRW under an August 2018 Air Force contract, and in June 2019 a B-52 flew the first captive-carry test of the missile out of Edwards Air Force Base, California. In March 2023, the Air Force said it would not pursue follow-on procurement once prototyping ended, but it continued test flights, including a final end-to-end launch from a B-52 flying out of Guam in March 2024, and in 2025 told Congress it intended to buy the weapon. The fiscal 2026 budget provided $362 million to begin procurement, and the fiscal 2027 request seeks $452 million more, along with funding for an Increment 2 version with a terminal seeker and a data link.
Troy is one of Lockheed Martin’s main munitions sites. Earlier this year the company broke ground on a new Munitions Production Center, Building 47, in Troy to support THAAD interceptor production and future work on the Next-Generation Interceptor, and in 2021 it opened a hypersonic missile assembly facility in nearby Courtland, Alabama.

US cruise ship suspends global voyage due to fuel costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:36:53 UTC
19:36:53 KST

A U.S. cruise ship, the MV Odyssey, docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo)
A U.S. cruise ship on a residential world voyage has suspended its operations in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to abandon their floating homes.
The Odyssey set sail two years ago on a three-year voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
The Florida-based company said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 has recently reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia during the war in Iran. Villa Vie Residences said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surge in fuel costs.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” it said. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
Sihanoukville Autonomous Port said in a statement last week that the ship docked on Oct. 23 for a five-day visit. It was to head to Vietnam but remained in the port on Oct. 28.
The ship carried 203 passengers with 15 nationalities, mostly Americans, and 156 crew members. It had a capacity of 650 residents.
Passengers have been told to leave the ship, but the crew’s status was unclear.
The Odyssey had a confirmed itinerary into November 2027. The company planned for a second residential cruise ship to enter service in early 2029, but the statement on the suspension of the Odyssey’s voyage did not address the second ship.

Ireland High Court overturns Gaza student visa refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:36:20 UTC
19:36:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Ireland High Court overturns Gaza student visa refusal
As dozens of Gazan students wait for their chance to study in Ireland, the country's High Court offered a glimmer of hope on Tuesday by overturning the refusal of a study visa to a Palestinian student in Gaza, citing "significant and demonstrable errors".
Student Shaymaa Abudalu was offered a place at University College Cork to study engineering, but her visa was refused in July, on the grounds that she submitted insufficient documents to support her application.
The case is part of a series of similar lawsuits brought by Palestinian students denied visas by the Minister for Justice, Jim O'Callaghan.
The students took the Irish government to court, with their lawyers arguing that the decision to refuse the study visa was unlawful.
"No student trapped in Gaza should have to take the Minister for Justice to the High Court simply to have documents she already submitted properly considered," Sinead Marmion, lawyer at Phoenix Law, told The New Arab.
Abudalu, who has lived in the Gaza Strip amid Israel's ongoing genocide, has lost several family members, including her mother and siblings.
"Today's judgment exposes a serious failure in the way our client's application was handled. While the ruling turns on the particular circumstances of her case, Jim O'Callaghan should not dismiss this as an isolated mistake," Marmion added.
"We have seen strikingly similar refusals affecting other Palestinian students. The Minister should urgently review those cases rather than force students trapped in Gaza to fight his Department one by one through the courts."
While Monday's ruling does not grant Abudalu a visa, it has quashed the refusal and now requires a new, lawful decision.
The court has ordered the Minister of Justice to reconsider Abudalu's application and issue a fresh decision within 10 working days of receiving it.
The judgement also noted that the next assisted evacuation flight from Gaza is scheduled for 23 November, and that a quick visa decision could allow the student to begin her studies this academic year.
The decision comes amid growing public and legal pressure on the Irish government to grant visas to Gazan students.
The Irish government faced intense scrutiny after it was discovered they had rejected visas for Palestinian students over what lawyers describe as "unrealistic" requirements not being met, such as failure to provide documents, insufficient financial evidence or gaps in education and employment.
According to figures cited in Irish reporting, the Department of Justice refused 114 of 138 Palestinian long-stay study-visa applications this year, an 83 percent refusal rate, including 55 students from Gaza, compared to the 13 percent rate in 2025.
Over 40 prominent Irish artists and public figures, including Nicola Coughlan, Hozier, and Kneecap, signed an open letter calling on the Taoiseach and Government to intervene for the 55 students.

Türkiye ready to sign maritime jurisdiction agreement with Egypt: National Defense Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:35:44 UTC
19:35:44 KST

- Ankara welcomes Libyan parliament's approval of 2019 maritime deal
Türkiye is ready to sign an agreement with Egypt on maritime boundary delimitation based on mutual interests, the Turkish National Defense Ministry said Wednesday.
"We once again emphasize that we are ready to sign an Agreement on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas with Egypt in line with mutual interests," it said in a statement.
The potential deal could grant Cairo a larger maritime jurisdiction than a potential agreement with Greece, it added.
"It is assessed that if Egypt signs such an agreement with our country, it would gain more than 15,000 square kilometers (5,792 square miles) of additional maritime jurisdiction compared to a potential agreement it could conclude with Greece."
The ministry stressed that Türkiye would continue protecting its legitimate rights and interests in the Eastern Mediterranean within the framework of international law while contributing to regional peace, security and stability.
The ministry also hailed Libya's approval last week of the memorandum of understanding on the delimitation of maritime jurisdiction signed with Türkiye in 2019.
"The approval by the Libyan House of Representatives on Oct. 20 of the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas, signed between our country and Libya in 2019, is an important development supporting our country's approach based on international law and the principles of equity, which takes into account the legitimate rights and interests of the relevant coastal states," the spokesman said.
Developments in Iraq's Sinjar region
During the weekly press briefing at the ministry, spokesman Rear Admiral Zeki Akturk welcomed efforts by the Iraqi central government to strengthen state authority and normalize conditions in the Sinjar region.
"Ending the presence of terrorist organizations in the region and ensuring security through Iraq's official security forces is an important development for establishing lasting peace and stability in Sinjar and achieving the goal of a terror-free region," the ministry said.
It added that the process is being closely monitored in coordination with relevant Turkish state institutions.
Bilateral defense cooperation, Kosovo mission
The spokesman stressed the Turkish army continues contributing to regional and global peace, security and stability through cooperation with friendly and allied countries, training and advisory activities, and participation in multinational missions.
He said the Türkiye-Albania Naval Forces Cooperation Meeting is scheduled to take place in Türkiye on Nov. 2-5.
"Under the Türkiye-Greece Confidence-Building Measures Implementation Plan, the commander of the Greek Tactical Air Force and an accompanying delegation will visit our Combat Air Force commander on Nov. 3-5," he said.
He further said that Türkiye assumed the deputy command of the NATO-led Kosovo Force (KFOR) for a one-year term during a ceremony held Tuesday.
"As during our country's command of KFOR, we will carry out the deputy command with an understanding of impartiality, transparency and professionalism, continuing to contribute to Kosovo's security and the preservation of regional peace and stability," he said.
Military training, exercises
He said national and international training and exercise activities continue uninterrupted to enhance the Turkish Armed Forces' effectiveness and deterrence across land, sea, air, space and cyberspace.
He said the National Anatolian Phoenix Exercise, named after fallen Air Force pilot Major Ibrahim Bolat, is underway in Konya and will conclude on Nov. 6.
The Crossed Swords Exercise, to be conducted in Estonia remotely, will begin on Nov. 2.
He also announced that the Sea of Friendship-2026 Exercise will take place in Alexandria, Egypt, on Nov. 4-9, with the participation of Turkish and Egyptian naval units and personnel.
The exercise will include surface and anti-submarine warfare, air defense operations and underwater offensive training.
He said the Turkish frigates TCG Gokceada and TCG Yildirim will begin their deployment to Somalia on Oct. 30 to transport supplies by sea and conduct personnel rotations.
On the same day, a Turkish airborne early warning and control aircraft will conduct a mission flight in NATO airspace over Romania as part of assurance measures.
Turkish fighter jets will also participate in the Nexus Ace training in the Mediterranean alongside a NATO Awacs aircraft.
New defense systems enter inventory
The spokesperson said Türkiye's domestic defense industry continues strengthening the Turkish Armed Forces' deterrence and operational capabilities through critical systems developed for land, naval, air and cyber operations.
He announced that the Land Forces Command completed inspection and acceptance procedures for various quantities of Karayel Hull Boats and Kablolu Kamikaze-2 uncrewed ground vehicles over the past week.
Turkish defense manufacturer Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation also delivered various quantities of MAM-15 sniper rifles to defense industry stakeholders.
He added that MKE will participate in Euronaval 2026, one of the world's leading international naval defense and maritime technology exhibitions, scheduled for Nov. 3-6 in Paris, France.

Defence official flagged plans for social media ban request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:33:20 UTC
19:33:20 KST

Defence official who sought to block social media clips claimed she flagged plans with minister
In short:
A senior defence official who sought to block the use of clips from parliamentary hearings on social media claimed in emails she had support from a government minister.
In an email obtained under FOI, Celia Perkins wrote that Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil was "fully supportive" of the plan.
Another government official has since raised concerns that the editing and sharing of social media clips from hearings invited "ridicule and hostility" towards public servants.
A senior Department of Defence official said she had approval from a government minister to try to block the public release of her evidence to a parliamentary hearing due to concerns about "vile" social media commentary.
Deputy secretary Celia Perkins said she had approval from Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil when she told a parliamentary committee hearing last month that she did not "consent" to her evidence appearing on social media.
The request was swiftly rejected by committee chair senator Jess Collins, on advice from parliamentary officials.
"It is our right as senators and members of the public to disseminate the evidence that is provided by the witnesses today in the manner in which we see fit," Senator Collins said.
Emails between Defence officials ahead of the hearing, obtained by the ABC through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request, reveal Ms Perkins told colleagues she raised her plans to make the statement with Mr Khalil and Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles's office two days before the hearing.
"(Department secretary Meghan Quinn) is fully supportive, as is AMINDEF. I discussed today in a meeting with AMINDEF and staff from DPMO and his office," she wrote in the email.
"I'll pass the opening statement to them tomorrow."
AMINDEF refers to Mr Khalil, and DPMO is the Deputy Prime Minister's office.
The ABC understands Mr Marles's office provided no input to Ms Perkins's statement before she made it. Comment has been sought from both Mr Khalil and Mr Marles.
During a Senate estimates hearing this week, Senate Clerk Richard Pye was asked about the advice he provided the committee after Ms Perkins request.
"It's absolutely not something that a witness can do," he said.
"It was profoundly unhelpful, I thought on the day, for the matter to be raised in that way without any notice to anybody, not through the secretariat, not to the chair and not to other members of the committee."
But he added that there were genuine concerns about the effect of footage from committee hearings on social media.
"This is not to minimise the fact that there are some people who have been very bruised by their experiences before Senate and House committees and the treatment of footage that has come out of those," he said.
Concerns over 'vile' commentary
The emails reveal some of the reasoning Ms Perkins put forward before her request.
In an email to Ms Quinn a week before the hearing, she raised her plans.
"You may recall after the last hearing we had some unpleasant social media posts and reactions," she wrote.
"I also want to test with you this idea: I'd like to add an explicit statement that the Defence witnesses appearing do not consent to our evidence being reproduced in edited format on social media platforms."
She said the main argument was that she had to maintain a "safe workplace" for Defence staff, and that online commentary could be "distressing".
"Social media posts using footage from previous hearings in edited and embellished formats had generated significant vile, personal commentary that was distressing for staff and invited online bullying," she said.
Ms Perkins also suggested the posts could raise security concerns, including assisting foreign espionage.
"As senior leaders in Defence — we actively discourage security clearance holders from a social media presence that identifies us and our roles — and these post (sic), designed to invite outraged responses, increase the personal risk from malign online actors, including cyber and foreign intelligence threats."
While Ms Perkins's request was immediately shut down, the Secretaries Board, made up of all federal government departmental secretaries, soon after took up the issue, suggesting new standards were needed to guide the use of evidence given to parliamentary hearings online.
This week Steven Kennedy, head of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, told estimates he did not support censoring footage, but did have concerns.
"Conduct that demeans, intimidates, humiliates or personally targets witnesses is inconsistent with the behaviour code for parliamentarians," he said.

Hong Kong authorities are searching for an elderly man who went missing in a remote rural area of Tai Po three days ago.

French Senate adopts bill requiring protesters to pay for damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:32:20 UTC
19:32:20 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
The French Senate adopted a bill, known as the "rioters-pay," which seeks to hold protesters participating in violent gatherings responsible for damage caused, broadcaster Public Senat reported Wednesday.
The Senate adopted the bill overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday by 229 votes to 105. It seeks "compensation for damage resulting from violence or damage committed in public spaces and the recovery of damages.”
The bill was initially presented as a response to the violence that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s Champions League victory in May and later evolved due to scenes of vandalism and looting during demonstrations that took place on Oct. 17.
The bill reportedly won broad support from the Senate’s right-wing majority but drew criticism from the left, which argued that it undermined several constitutionally protected principles, including freedom of assembly, freedom of expression, and the individualization of penalties.
The bill allows individuals who participated in violent gatherings to be held jointly liable for damages, even if they were not directly responsible for the destruction. The state could seek up to €10,000 ($11,000) in compensation per person.
It also permits the seizure of part of family allowances, housing assistance and France’s minimum-income benefit to recover damages owed.
The Senate also approved an amendment allowing authorities to request the removal of online content likely to cause serious public disorder, particularly material inciting violence, vandalism, or insurrection.
Under the measure, social media platforms would have 24 hours to remove such content or face blocking or delisting.
The Senate further approved tougher security measures, including new administrative bans on demonstrations, additional penalties barring foreign nationals from French territory, harsher sentences, expanded use of judicial drones and algorithmic video surveillance, and evictions from social housing for troublemakers.
The bill will now be examined by the National Assembly, where political divisions could complicate its legislative passage.

Democrats lead national polls as Trump and Obama campaign in key states six days before the US midterm elections.
With six days to go before the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, Democrats are leading Republicans in national polls, but several key Senate races seem too close to call.
President Donald Trump has stepped up his campaigning, holding two Republican rallies in Texas on Tuesday before heading to Ohio on Wednesday. Ex-President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris are also hitting the campaign trail in Georgia for the Democratic Party.
Here is what the latest polls say, what happened on the campaign trail and what to expect on Wednesday.
What do the latest polls suggest?
With less than a week to go before the midterms, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests the Democrats are ahead of the Republicans by nine points.
According to the October 22-26 survey, 47 percent of voters support the Democrats, compared with 36 percent who support the Republicans. When undecided voters’ leanings were taken into account, Democrats lead with 50 percent compared with Republicans’ 41 percent.
Trump’s approval rating improved by a percentage point to 32 percent, with 73 percent of US adults saying the cost of living was going in the wrong direction.

Three brothers, including two prominent luxury real estate agents, were each sentenced to 30 years in prison for operating a yearslong sex trafficking and sexual abuse scheme that targeted women and minors, the US Justice Department said Tuesday.
US District Judge Valerie Caproni sentenced Tal Alexander, 40, and twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 39, in Manhattan federal court following their convictions on multiple federal sex offenses.
Each brother was also sentenced to 10 years of supervised release following his prison term.
The three were convicted on all counts on March 9 following a six-week trial, including on charges of conspiracy to commit sex trafficking.
According to evidence presented at trial, the brothers worked together and with others from at least 2008 until 2021 to drug, sexually assault and rape numerous women.
Oren and Tal Alexander used their prominence in the luxury real estate industry and their social and financial connections in New York and Miami to create opportunities to target women, prosecutors said.
The brothers and their associates recruited women through social media, dating applications, personal encounters and party promoters. Victims were offered luxury travel, accommodations and access to exclusive parties before being taken to private locations.
Prosecutors said the brothers secretly placed sedative drugs in some women’s drinks, leaving them with impaired movement, speech and memory and preventing them from resisting or escaping.
In several cases, the victims were physically restrained while one or more of the brothers assaulted them, despite their cries and explicit demands that they stop.
The scheme also involved women the brothers encountered at bars, nightclubs and social events, according to the Justice Department.
“Alon, Oren, and Tal Alexander are convicted sex traffickers and serial rapists,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement.
McDonald said they had used “their careers and social status to conceal the danger they posed” and praised the victims who came forward.
Alon Alexander was sentenced for crimes including sex trafficking a minor and aggravated sexual abuse. Oren Alexander’s convictions included the sexual exploitation of a minor, while Tal Alexander was sentenced for offenses involving several victims, including a minor.
The three continued to deny drugging, raping or trafficking women during the sentencing hearing.

Diabetes patients in the Gaza Strip are facing growing health risks as shortages of insulin and essential medical supplies continue amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of healthcare materials, Anadolu reports.
Umm Amir Jaha, 39, said she has been unable to find unexpired insulin for her 10-year-old son Amir, who has Type 1 diabetes and requires regular insulin treatment.
She said the family has been forced to use expired insulin pens purchased at high prices after searching across different areas of Gaza.
Amir also needs a blood glucose meter and testing strips to monitor his condition daily, but those supplies have also become difficult to obtain.

READ: Israel obstructs travel of 17,000 Gazan patients for treatment: Health Ministry
Shortages of Type 1 insulin analogues and other diabetes supplies remain severe across Gaza, while access to glucometers and blood glucose test strips is also limited, according to UN humanitarian agencies.
Dr. Rabii Hamdiya, an endocrinology and diabetes specialist at Al Shifa Hospital, said interruptions in insulin treatment can cause dangerously high blood sugar levels and lead to serious complications, including diabetic ketoacidosis and coma.
He said insulin pens used particularly by children are not available in sufficient quantities, forcing some patients to receive insulin by syringe several times a day instead.
The Palestinian Health Ministry said in October that around 71,000 people in Gaza have diabetes, including about 3,500 Type 1 patients who depend entirely on insulin.

Everything you need to know about bats but were too afraid to ask
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:26:28 UTC
19:26:28 KST

Bats are not the world’s most beloved creatures. Mostly night animals, they’ve become a symbol of Halloween—associated with vampires, death and general ghoulishness. Sure, a few bat species do, in fact, feed on animal blood. Some bats have a face only a biologist could love. And yes, bats can be reservoirs of disease. But in their more than 50 million years on Earth, these maligned creatures have developed some admirable qualities, too.
For one, they’re everywhere: bats live on every continent except Antarctica. They echolocate, using sound to navigate their world—and they are the only mammal to evolve true flight. They also eat insects such as mosquitoes—contributing billions of dollars in value annually for the world’s farmers—and are critical pollinators of tropical plants.
“We need them,” says Emma Teeling, a professor and founding director of the Center for Irish Bat Research at University College Dublin.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
So, in honor of spooky season, here are seven bat facts you may not know:
Bats are “super agers.”
In nature, larger animals, such as elephants and whales, tend to live longer than smaller animals, such as mice and shrews, Teeling says. Bats are an exception.
“Bats are some of the smallest mammals in the entire world and can live for this extraordinary long time,” she says. Some of the oldest bats have been known to live for decades.
Teeling and other bat researchers are studying aspects of the animals’ longevity, including bats’ ability to repair their DNA and harbor viruses without getting sick, for clues in order to enhance our own lives.
Vampire bats could help us treat stroke victims.
When vampire bats such as Desmodus rotundus, also known as the common vampire bat, feed on birds and other mammals, they bite their prey and lick the wounds, Teeling says. An anticoagulant in their saliva prevents the blood from clotting up.
Researchers have studied this protein in the hope that it may offer a way to treat blood clots in stroke victims—while lowering the risk of causing brain bleeds. Although drug development stalled a decade ago after lackluster results, the treatment may still have potential, according to a recent review.
There are about 1,500 bat species—and counting.
Bats are incredibly diverse—across all mammals, bats include more species than all but one other group, rodents, says Rachel Page, a scientist at the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute. In fact, there are about 1,500 known bat species worldwide.
Some, such as the vampire bats, drink blood. Others eat nectar, while others still eat insects, fish and even frogs.
Some bats “eavesdrop” on their prey’s mating calls.
For the frog-eating bats, meals can be treacherous. Some frogs are poisonous. Others are so big they could pose a danger. To meet this challenge, the fringe-lipped bat, Trachops cirrhosus, “eavesdrops:” the bats listen for the loud, “conspicuous” nighttime mating calls of their prey and then attack, Page says.
“They exploit those calls. They use them to detect, to locate, and then also to assess those prey” for size and toxicity, she says.
Bats likely evolved in Europe.
In September, Teeling and more than 130 other scientists across the world published a paper in Nature in which they sequenced genomes across all 21 bat families.
By pairing these genetic data with fossil records, they made a breakthrough—bats likely evolved in Europe and then spread to Africa and around the world, they found. Until then, it was thought bats might’ve emerged somewhere in North America, among other theories. “We rewrote evolutionary history,” Teeling says.
Many bats have a signature scent.
Across bat species, 9 percent are known so far to have odor-producing glands and other structures, but research on this is sparse, according to a 2021 paper in Mammal Review co-authored by Page. T. cirrhosus males employ a “pungent” golden crust with a “musky” scent on their forearms, likely to attract females, Page says.
Vampire bats will throw up to feed a friend.
If a vampire bat doesn’t feed for about two nights in a row, it will die, Page explains. “It doesn’t have the energetic reserves to make it beyond that,” she says. But research shows that if a vampire bat comes back to its colony hungry, other bats will step in and regurgitate blood to share—a costly but lifesaving sacrifice.

But just in the more short term, there was one spending bill that got punted to December, and, you know, the new Congress won’t have been sworn in by then. One of the things that got punted was this proposed rule change that was super controversial about how science grants get administered, and that would’ve switched the decision-making from panels of peer-review experts, you know, people who really know this stuff, to political appointees. And scientists were real freaked out about this. I covered this. You had public comments from Nobel laureates saying this would be disastrous for American scientists. So after the election results come in, it’s gonna be really interesting to see how Congress decides to vote on that.
Feltman: Yeah, definitely something we’ll, we’ll have to keep our eye out for. Adam, thanks so much for coming on to chat with us.
Kovac: Rachel, it’s always a pleasure.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. We’ll be back on Friday to talk about vampires. Which frankly are a little less spooky than politics.

U.S. President Donald Trump met with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Türkiye, Wednesday, July 8, 2026. (AP Photo)
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 28 that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelensky, would be set up “very soon.”
The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters.
Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that a trilateral meeting between Kiev, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.
Meanwhile, a local truce aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky appeared to be holding on Oct. 27, with neither side reporting any violations after several hours.
Both sides said they began observing the truce at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT).
The war-ravaged city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region had been caught in the middle of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces at the start of their invasion.
Former residents told AFP last month that those remaining in the city were starving, lacked medicine and could not easily leave.
“The possibility of evacuation from Oleshky is very good news for me and for the people who are trapped there,” Olga, a former resident, told AFP on Oct. 27.
“My acquaintances are ready to leave,” she said.
Announcing the truce last week, U.S. first lady Melania Trump said civilian officials from both Russia and Ukraine would visit residents in their homes and “determine the level of assistance they require.”
“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” she said.
AFP was not able to immediately verify details about the humanitarian mission or whether there had been a decrease in fighting.
The Russian military does not routinely grant international media, including AFP, access to areas under Russian occupation.
Right-leaning U.S. cable network Newsmax said it had been granted “exclusive television access” to accompany observers entering the city.

Organization of Turkic States foreign ministers to meet in Ankara on Thursday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:24:25 UTC
19:24:25 KST

Muhammet Tarhan and Busra Nur Cakmak
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
- Participants expected to approve administrative and financial documents related to the organization’s operations
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host a meeting of the Council of Foreign Ministers of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) on Thursday as part of the organization’s 13th summit.
According to Turkish Foreign Ministry sources, foreign ministers of the member states will convene for the fifth time this year, with one regular and four informal council meetings, at the gathering in Ankara on Oct. 29-30.
The meeting is expected to include consultations on areas of cooperation within the organization and efforts to strengthen its institutional structure.
Participants are also expected to approve several administrative and financial documents concerning the organization’s operations at the end of the meeting.
Fidan is also scheduled to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts on the sidelines of the gathering.
In his address, Fidan is expected to emphasize that political dialogue and the capacity for joint action among Turkic states have been strengthened under the organization's umbrella, while shared historical, linguistic and cultural ties and bonds of brotherhood have been translated into concrete cooperation.
During Türkiye’s chairmanship of the organization, Fidan is expected to underline that priorities will include enhancing the organization’s institutional capacity, improving the human and financial resources and capabilities of its secretariat, and strengthening coordination among Turkic cooperation organizations.
He is also expected to stress the importance of translating economic and strategic cooperation into tangible results, particularly in energy, trade, investment, digital transformation and the defense industry.
Fidan is expected to highlight the importance of strengthening the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor to improve connectivity between Asia and Europe and reinforce economic resilience.
He is also expected to draw attention to developments in Afghanistan and their implications for regional security, stability and connectivity, emphasizing the need to increase consultations and coordination on the issue among member and observer states.
Organization of Turkic States
The organization was established as the Cooperation Council of Turkic-Speaking States under the Nakhchivan Agreement signed on Oct. 3, 2009, by Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan. Its name was changed to the Organization of Turkic States at the Istanbul Summit in 2021.
Its main objectives include strengthening mutual trust and political solidarity among Turkic states, developing and deepening economic and technical cooperation, and documenting and promoting the historical and cultural heritage of the Turkic world.
Headquartered in Istanbul, the OTS has five members -- Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan -- and four observers: Hungary, Turkmenistan, the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) and the Economic Cooperation Organization.
13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States
The OTS’s 13th summit will be held in Ankara on Oct. 29-30, hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Inspired by Erdogan’s vision of the Century of the Turkic World and the motto of Ismail Gasprinski, the summit will be held under the theme Turkish Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Action.
