Please Let the Internet Die
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The internet must be put out of its misery.
Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web—and the social fabric woven there—is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself.
Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements.
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.
In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.
It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”
With this anxiety hammering at my prefrontal cortex day in and out, I was more than intrigued by the absolutist title of technologist and Pulitzer-winning journalist John West’s new book, The Internet Will Die, and So Will You: On Learning to Live in Our Digital Age. In his discerning treatise, West confirms what many have suspected for a good while now: The platforms once seen as enduring archives of knowledge and communication are being cannibalized by ideological warfare and basic greed.
But that’s not the whole story. For one, West argues, people misperceive the “vastness” of the internet, which really amounts to “a vanishing fraction, a rounding error, of the human experience.” Moreover, it is remarkably fragile—West opens with the story of how a 2001 train derailment in a Baltimore tunnel took out a major bundle of fiber-optic cables, leading to internet slowdowns nationwide—and continually undergoes cycles of death and rebirth as a result of this natural instability.
If the internet is much smaller and less solid than imagined, West’s book suggests, then it’s crucial to recognize the forces that determine how those deaths unfold, or which pieces are preserved while others crumble. Because the market has falsely sold us the web as a comprehensive library of accumulated wisdom, each transient phase of this global network comes to define the present, for better and worse. Today we witness a dismal paralysis brought on by algorithmic incentives to churn out inflammatory garbage: Full-time influencers are in a losing arms race for attention with low-effort, high-volume channels that streamline production by delegating the creative process to bleeding-edge software.
West draws a sharp contrast between this holographic environment of monetization and a passionate, personalized internet that spanned from the primordial GeoCities to Tumblr, describing how these innovative communities have been gradually erased. While some endure in half-dead and highly corrupted form, others are lost. In middle school, West maintained a web page devoted to his love of anime; later, he kept a blog documenting his college years. Looking back as an adult, he’s vexed by the fates that have befallen each.
“I really wanted to delete my anime site,” West tells WIRED. “I don't have access to the AOL account anymore, and I couldn't do it.” Instead, it lives on as a zombie page, cluttered with spam ads and dead-end links. As for the college blog, he had neglected to pay domain fees toward the end of his time writing it, and so the final year of posts disappeared. “I kind of got obsessed with this idea that the things we want to last really don't, and then oftentimes the things that we kind of wish would go away hang on for way too long,” West says.
These shifting sands are a far cry from the flawless, collective, permanent memory that internet users originally believed they were building. “‘Forever’ is such a strong word, and it's the wrong word,” West says. Online spaces are memento mori, the same as individuals who self-promote across them (and that includes certain longevity-obsessed biohackers). Sure, there was a time when a celebrity could be “canceled” for tasteless posts unearthed years later, but in 2026, it’s not so easy to surface specific messages when you go hunting for them in your AI-powered Gmail account. Zeitgeist-defining platforms like Vine can be vaporized in an instant, a fact reinforced in January 2025, when Americans posted farewell TikTok videos ahead of an expected US ban on the app.
This random ephemerality, West points out, has eroded any confidence in claims previously backed up by hypertext cross-references, and thus any kind of consensus truth. An analysis of hyperlinks in articles on The New York Times website between 1996 and mid-2019 found that 25 percent of all links were inaccessible. According to a 2016 study, “three out of four citations in scholarly articles have drifted—the websites they purport to cite no longer say what they once did,” he writes. “Over half of Wikipedia’s entries contain at least one link in its references section that goes nowhere, a Pew report found.”
The impulse to drive engagement spreads to users themselves: West noticed, for instance, that when he recently reread a favorite book, Marilynne Robinson’s Gilead, he had the nagging thought that while he loved returning to the novel for the fourth or fifth time, he wouldn’t be able to count it toward his annual Goodreads stats. West says this fixation on the internet’s hollow validations creates “the exact conditions for a space to be filled by something that isn't human.”
Wouldn’t it be liberating, then, to actually deny our attention to astroturfed outrage, engineered virality, and influencer sponcon? To let the mainstream digital economies propped up by AI-enabled surveillance finally fall to ruin? If what the titans of the industry have to offer us these days are “pervert glasses” and the suppression of ads for a probably unflattering documentary, why are we helping them stay in business? Leaving their platforms for dead might be the last lever of power available to the masses.
Doing so could free people to explore dormant corners. West notes that some of the most interesting parts of the internet are the ones that nobody sees, like web portals to streams of YouTube videos that have almost no views. “Some of it’s fucking weird and creepy, but a lot of it’s just people singing a song and having a blast,” he says. West also cites the bustling, zero-revenue, circulation of poetry in web journals as proof that “you can find meaning and make meaning online all the time,” provided there is no financial motivation.
When you eliminate what the platforms want you to fixate on, it’s clear what you’ve been missing, and how you were steered away from it. Your opinions are shaped in a bubble by avatars you’ve never met, weaponized against equally hermetic rival camps. The internet doesn’t really have winners, unless you count the few without the sense to stop chasing relevance at any cost. That’s why the main characters are so malleable in their beliefs; never afraid to pivot, betray, and discard what they once held to be the core of their identity. And that’s when they stood for anything to begin with.
Absent a sudden, lasting outage due to a fresh and severe catastrophe, the internet as it exists won’t perish anytime soon. There are, however, splintering cracks in its facade, which may create room for emergent and strangely evolved life-forms. There’s no reason to assume that the present tech empire will rule the century to come; the organic and anarchic web stands to mount a triumphant renaissance if (or when) it falls.
“Look, the internet is rotting,” West says. “The question is, where are we going to put our energy?” A metaphor he often turns to in his book is compost. “Compost is just rot harnessed for a purpose,” he says. Can a decaying internet be fertilizer for something better? It’s a rosy notion, but speaking as a perennially failed composter—it’s just too gross, and I’m too lazy—I have my doubts about whether enough hardy, patient gardeners can be mobilized to make our digital landscape bloom once more.
Then again, as West’s book sought to remind me, I am destined to die as well. Maybe I’ll be mixed in with the soil.

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

As missiles hit Saudi Arabia, residents insist life goes on — and the show does too
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Despite missile strikes that killed people, disrupted air travel and postponed major events, Riyadh Season opened with thousands attending concerts, comedy and attractions in the Saudi capital.
- Residents say daily life feels largely normal, but renewed Houthi attacks and the Iran war are weighing on the kingdom.
- Government messaging which once touted economic and cultural development, promotes patriotic themes.
RIYADH, Saudi Arabia — The lineup was announced months ago, with top-flight stars in tennis, DJing, comedy and more set to descend on the Saudi capital for a 10-week run of events known as Riyadh Season.
But after successive missile strikes hit Riyadh’s airport this month, killing more than a dozen people, shuttering parts of the country’s airspace and setting off a flurry of cancellations, many wondered if audiences would show up, or if there would be anything to show up for at all.
The answer to both questions came this past weekend, when crowds gathered for Riyadh Season’s opener at Boulevard City, a car-free district in the capital that’s part open-air mall, part amusement park and part entertainment venue.
By the time sunset had turned to dusk, families were milling about a replica of Times Square. Patrons assembled for a sold-out comedy play at one of two theaters, while others went to a 7,000-seat arena, where a famous Lebanese pop star was debuting his comeback tour. It too was sold out.
This is a twilight moment for the Saudi capital. In normal times, October is when the convection-bake temperatures of Riyadh’s ferocious summer give way to a bearable, even pleasant heat, and the city hosts dozens of large-scale events aimed at showcasing Vision 2030, the kingdom’s all-out drive to transform itself into a sporting and entertainment powerhouse.
But between the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and Riyadh’s escalating grudge match with the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels known as the Houthis, these are hardly normal times.
For years, the war with the Houthis — whose official name is Ansar Allah, or Partisans of God — had ebbed and flowed between campaign and ceasefire, but for most Saudis, it had remained background noise. That changed in recent months, with a truce breaking down, and the Houthis lobbing drones, ballistic and cruise missiles across Saudi Arabia.
All of a sudden, the war took on a more present form, unsettling a kingdom unused to conflicts playing out on home turf. Almost every night in Riyadh brings the bass-drum booms and thuds of interceptors launching to destroy incoming projectiles.
Government messaging has turned pugilistic, replacing paeans to Vision 2030 and the country’s leadership with images of Saudi F-15s en route to do battle over Yemen, or commercial billboards declaring “Our bravery brings us together” or “Stable home, reassured hearts.”
In October alone, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi airports have killed at least 21 people and wounded hundreds, forcing authorities to shut down operations in the country’s main international airport in Riyadh and curtailing travel in others. (On Sunday, officials announced some flights at the Riyadh airport had resumed.)
Schools shifted to online-only learning, while many businesses — including Saudi Aramco, the country’s state-owned oil company — were ordered to evacuate headquarters and have all staff work remotely. The U.S. Embassy ordered “non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members” in Saudi Arabia to leave.
The attacks come at an inopportune juncture. Many of the kingdom’s marquee, international-facing gatherings have been affected, including the World Petroleum Congress, a summit between the European Union and Persian Gulf nations, and the government’s flagship investment conference, the Future Investment Initiative.
Though the congress went ahead — with many top oil executives attending virtually — the summit and investment conference were shelved till next year. Also postponed were some of Riyadh Season’s major sporting events, such as the Six Kings Slam tennis tournament.
But other events — including boxing and UFC championships and the WWE Crown Jewel event — remain stubbornly on the calendar. The first few days of Riyadh Season have gone ahead with little incident, even if participants were forced to divert to other cities or even neighboring Bahrain or Kuwait before being ferried back to the Saudi capital.
That shrugging off of the war was a common attitude among visitors to Boulevard City, organizers say.
In the replica Times Square, building-sized screens cast windows of light as people grabbed elaborate drinks made with iced tea, coffee or hibiscus. Trackless trains, their carriages mocked up as reindeer, ferried kids around a giant illuminated orb.
“Between foot traffic in Boulevard City, audiences for the plays and the concerts, we had something like 27,000 people coming in,” said Hassan Albar, Boulevard City’s director, a note of pride — and some relief — creeping into his voice.
“And we’re still at the beginning of the season.”
Despite the daily cellphone alerts that warn residents to remain indoors until danger passes, people interviewed emphasized a show-must-go-on disposition.
“We like to keep it positive, so we’re not going to be staying inside. It’s human nature to feel afraid if you don’t have control, but the situation is fine,” said Neetika Malotra, 33, who was taking pictures of Ankid Abishaikh, 34, before a Boulevard City sign.
Abishaikh said conditions in Saudi Arabia are different from how they’re portrayed online.
“Our parents are outside in India, so when they see news channels or social media, it looks very scary. But we tell them that what they see there is not always right,” he said.
“When you’re here, everything feels normal and we’re doing well.”
Both the U.S.-Israel war on Iran and the Houthis’ campaign have harmed Saudi Arabia’s oil production, with closures of the Strait of Hormuz denying the kingdom its main energy export corridor. In addition to missiles at Riyadh‘s airport, the Houthis over the weekend targeted crude oil pumping stations, an oil refinery, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the East-West Pipeline, which transports oil to terminals on the Red Sea coast.
The Saudi military has struggled to defend against Houthi missiles, hampered by the sheer size of the country — Saudi Arabia’s territory is more than five times the size of California — and a fast-depleting supply of interceptors.
The fighting with the Houthis is compounding the economic headwinds forced on the kingdom by the Iran war and a general economic slowdown; Saudi officials already have had to reassess some of the grander ambitions underpinning Vision 2030.
Contractors, all of whom spoke on condition of anonymity so as not to jeopardize future professional prospects, say that staff working on so-called gigaprojects have been drawn down, reassigned or let go. Ancillary businesses — catering and events organizers — have endured losses of up to two thirds of revenues amid a cost-cutting pullback.
Yet despite those complaints, the consensus among many residents is that the war hasn’t had a drastic impact on their lives, at least in terms of their sense of safety.
“It’s very secure here. I don’t feel anything like what’s said on the news,” said Abdul Rahman Al-Hassan, 38, a dentist who moved to Riyadh nine months ago from Moscow.
He compared the situation here to the Russian capital, which has been the frequent target of a Ukrainian drone campaign.
“Journalists say the same sort of thing about Moscow: That it’s very dangerous and that people are hiding in their basements from the drones,” he said.
“But it’s not true there, and it’s not true here. You can have an attack in one area, but people are still going out normally.”
That may hint at a head-in-the-sand mentality, and it’s hard to gauge public sentiment in a country where openly expressing dissatisfaction with government policies can land you in jail or have you deported. But among Saudis, the conflict with the Houthis appears to have spurred a rally-round-the-flag moment.
“We fully trust the government and the leadership in charge,” said Awatef Mohammad, a 31-year-old English teacher strolling with her partner through Boulevard City.
Similar sentiments emerge even in places more directly in the line of fire. Over the weekend, spectators gathered at Riyadh’s King Abdulaziz Racecourse for an evening of horse racing, despite the fact that the track is barely three miles from the airport.
Jamil Mohammad, a 42-year-old occupational therapist, had his children Jad and Joury in tow. He propped up Joury on a railing to watch the horses saunter past as they prepared for the race. His eyes on his daughter, he expressed a belief in God’s protection that, to many outsiders, can sound like fatalism.
“Look, whether I’m here near the airport, or anywhere else in the world, if God says it’s my time to die, then it’s my time to die. It won’t matter,” he said.
“Death only comes once. I’m not going to let it stop me living my life.”

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Riots across France have left more than 3,000 businesses attacked or looted. Paris shopkeepers have boarded up windows and bought pepper spray and tear gas.
- The unrest has left Paris a city of contrasts: Daily life continues alongside shattered windows, police helicopters and residents’ fear of renewed violence.
- Many residents of Paris, Marseille and other major cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
PARIS — Business is up tenfold at a weapons store near Place de l’Opéra in Paris: Shopkeepers from all over the city have been stocking up on pepper spray and tear gas.
In the nine days since riots erupted in cities across France, thousands of merchants have also boarded up their storefronts, radically altering the Paris streetscape. The screech of electric saws and pounding of nails into plywood are now background noise in the French capital.
“They’re afraid their stores will be attacked and looted,” Yves Gollety, owner of the weapons store, explained.
Adding to the dark mood are police helicopters hovering, with searchlights blazing, to enforce a late-night curfew in the Les Halles and République sections of Paris.
And the city has removed many of the huge street-corner bins where Parisians are accustomed to dropping their empty wine and beer bottles. Rioters had been knocking them over to get glass ammunition against police.
Yet daily life has barely changed in much of Paris, where it can seem like normal times amid the chaos. Friends chat in cafés with shattered windows. Customers ignore plywood covering the front doors of shops.
But the social and economic grievances that boiled over so violently have not gone away, and nobody can escape the dreaded question: What’s next?
More demonstrations, for sure, and a strike planned for Nov. 5, which has left many resigned to toggling, for now, between upheaval and ordinary life.
The contrasts can be jarring.
At Cycles Laurent, a bike store on Boulevard Voltaire, a makeshift wooden window doubles as a spray-painted sign urging people to come on in.
“We remain open,” it says.
The bike shop is one of more than 3,000 businesses attacked or pillaged in France in the aftermath of giant protests against the government of President Emmanuel Macron the weekend of Oct. 17.
Although a tense urban peace has taken hold since then, many residents of Paris, Toulouse, Marseille and other cities beset by riots still feel under siege, much like Los Angeles after the 1992 riots.
“This whole climate is horrible,” said Yolande Montagnac, a retiree who has lived for 45 years near the Gare de Lyon in Paris and was heartbroken by the damage to the city.
Scattered curfews and a police surge to keep nationwide protests under control have helped to stop the looting. More than 400,000 protesters returned to the streets on Saturday, by the police count; closer to double that number, according to unions. Apart from a few tear-gas skirmishes, the demonstrations ended peacefully.
The unrest began after high school students took to the streets last month to denounce poor conditions and resources at their campuses. On Monday, Macron said the government would take “concrete measures” to address those concerns.
As the turmoil has grown, Paris has been the setting of odd contrasts.
As boulevard barricades were burning Oct. 17 in Les Halles, the lilting harmonies of a roving choir singing a peace ballad were soothing passersby shopping for cheese and wine a few blocks away.
Hours later, vandals smashed scores of windows around the corner and ransacked stores as neighbors watched in horror from apartments above. Unchecked by police, looters returned the next night.
Not a week had gone by before a gaggle of fashionistas, testing the limits of decency and humor, gathered on the same stretch of the Rue Étienne Marcel for a riot-porn glamour shot in a wrecked ad-poster frame.
In the distance was a bronze statue of Louis XIV on a rearing horse in the majestic Place des Victoires, its stone pedestal stained by protesters’ splashes of red paint.
On Place de la République, the scene of violent clashes between police and protesters on Oct. 17, the usual skateboarders were back on Sunday morning. By then, graffiti had been scrubbed from the central monument that pays tribute to the French Republic, including its tradition of insurrection.
At Gollety’s weapons store, Armurerie de la Bourse, dozens of guns are on display, but firearm restrictions are so tight in France that merchants were not trying to buy any.
“In France, nobody shoots a robber,” he said. “You go to prison.”
Arnaud, 24, a pastry chef who works at a bakery and declined to share his last name, bought tear gas Friday “to neutralize someone if need be.”
“It’s incredible that it’s come to this,” he said as he left Gollety’s shop. “I think we’ve reached that limit where the French are saying, ‘OK, the state isn’t protecting me, I’m going to try to protect myself until the state protects me.’”
Arnaud supports France’s far right. “There’s no center anymore, no core that can bring everyone together. It’s a loss of bearings, and it’s a mess,” he said.
In the run-up to the protests on Saturday, the Paris police commissioner, Patrice Faure, heightened anxieties by advising merchants to hire security guards, saying police alone could not “guarantee the protection of every business.”
Florence Portelli, the mayor of Taverny, a Paris suburb, was mortified by the call for self-defense.
“The day we start opening the door to that, we end up with what sometimes happens in the United States, in countries where things go absolutely, completely crazy,” she told BFM television.
Since the protests started, they have expanded to cover the high cost of living, aggressive police tactics and other grievances. French police have arrested about 12,000 people.
At the Paris protest on Saturday, a row of police in riot gear led the crowd along the authorized route down boulevards on the city’s outskirts. Just behind them was a group of “black bloc” militants yelling ACAB, the international slogan for “all cops are bastards.”
The sea of 100,000 people marching behind them was a wide mix of union members, students, leftists and others unhappy with Macron.
Chloé Brani, a 21-year-old student from the suburbs, carried a sign that summed it up: “We’re all fed up.”
She blamed inequalities in France on “elites who don’t care.”
If military and police money “were simply put back into the causes we’re asking for — a normal salary, normal living conditions for workers in every possible profession, and high schools in good condition — there actually wouldn’t be a problem,” she said as she marched. “It’s the distribution of wealth that’s unjust.”
Montagnac, a retired executive assistant, sees France’s political leadership in a state of collapse, most evident in its loss of control during the riots. But she also thinks the turmoil is rooted in the decline of human contact in the digital age.
“Everyone is on their phone all the time,” she lamented Sunday morning at the bustling Aligre outdoor produce market, where neighbors were, just like before the riots, buying fruit, vegetables, meat and fish. “There’s no more friendliness. People don’t take the time to stop and chat. It’s always a rush.”
For Montagnac, 69, it was especially painful to see the owner of a furniture store on Boulevard Diderot hauling his sofas and chairs into the back of the shop to deter looters.
“He can’t sleep at night, he’s so scared,” she said.

Commentary: Agitating for attention, Trump and Bill Maher get into it, again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Agitating for attention, Trump and Bill Maher get into it, again
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Soaring gas prices and a war with Iran. Historically low approval ratings. A potential blue tsunami. A new rape allegation.
President Trump has a lot on his plate, and so too does the nation. Sunday, he took to Truth Social to address the people.
“Let’s talk about this COMPLETE AND TOTAL LOSER, Bill Maher,” the president wrote at the top of his longest post ever.
A fireside chat it was not.
The 1,300-word-plus screed was triggered by Friday’s episode of “Real Time With Bill Maher,” a mainstay on HBO since 2003. The comedian referred to Trump as a “lame duck” president with low approval ratings during a segment with his guest, former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.
Trump, 80, likely expected praise from his fellow curmudgeon Maher, 70, since the men had recently dined together at the White House. It was their second such date following a controversial get-together in March 2025, which Maher juiced for all it was worth in an effort to stand out from his fellow late-night hosts.
When Colbert was named the new host of ‘The Late Show’ in 2015, he was considered an unusual choice, but he turned out to be the right fit for these times.
Maher’s chummy relationship with Trump has made him an outlier among his peers, many of whom have been in the president’s crosshairs.
CBS canceled Stephen Colbert’s show after decades on the air following pressure from Trump’s Federal Communications Commission chair. Trump has bitterly complained about being treated unfairly by Jimmy Kimmel and Seth Meyers. They, too, now have targets on their backs.
Maher has avoided the same fate by railing on Trump only half as much as his late-night peers, leaning into various MAGA grievances about the “woke” left and forging a fair-weather friendship with the second-term president.
If the Maher of 2003 could see himself now, he’d likely dedicate a searing monologue to the hypocrisy. The host was once positioned as an irreverent comedian whose political satire was guided by his no-BS take on Capitol Hill and American culture. Common sense over party fealty. Political correctness be damned.
But as the political landscape has shifted, so too has Maher’s approach.
Now he plays the role of a staunchly nonpartisan crank on TV while dining with the president in person.
“Yeah, I did it again, b—!” Maher said to his audience Friday. “I know. I’m the bad guy because I go and say face-to-face to the man the things you write in articles that he’ll never read, but OK. You know what? F— you. I like these dinners.”
So brave. So calculated.
Maher was dipping back into the attention he received in 2025, when he first dined with Trump and described the president as “gracious and measured.”
Their rendezvous was just the sort of thing the comedian would have mercilessly lampooned if he wasn’t in fact part of the joke. Fellow comedians such as Patton Oswalt have criticized the HBO host for placating Trump, while Larry David satirized Maher’s first date with the president in a New York Times essay titled “My Dinner With Adolf.”
The controversy was a boon for “Real Time,” boosting its waning relevance by putting Maher back in the news and reinforcing the tired charade that his fearlessness knows no bounds.
This week’s public skirmish was a repeat performance, if not a somewhat pathetic display of both men’s need to agitate for attention.
Maher told his audience on Friday’s episode that he spoke with the president about deadly ICE incidents, Ukraine and how Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was “dragging” Trump down. In closing, he assured the audience he was no pushover by poking at the president’s recent favorable dealings with Russia (a diesel deal, lifting sanctions), then saying, “I could not have been treated better if I was Russian.”
Given the president’s delicate psyche, Maher knew anything short of absolute praise would be perceived as an insult. As for the knock about Trump’s slumping approval numbers? A sure trigger.
In Sunday’s Truth Social manifesto, Trump referred to Maher as a “biased, dumb SLEAZEBAG” whose program is plagued by low ratings. The president also alleged that the comedian was drunk and had a drink in hand as he toured the White House on Oct. 15, and that Maher is a “major POTHEAD” who “looked like hell this time.”
So much for Trump’s initial comments about their meeting. He had told reporters that it was “a great dinner.”
“Bill Maher, I tell you what, he likes me a lot more than people understand,” Trump said. “And I actually like him.”
Not unlike Trump, Maher also enjoys praise, and blames the “woke left” when he doesn’t get it.
The typically smug host appeared upset earlier this year at the Golden Globes when presenter Wanda Sykes roasted him and another nominee up for best performance in stand-up comedy on television, Ricky Gervais.
“There’s some people pissed off that a queer Black woman is up here doing the job of two mediocre white guys,” Sykes said. “... But first, I want to give them some love.” Addressing Maher directly, she said, “You give us so much. But I would love a little less. Just try less.” The camera panned to a stone-faced Maher, who appeared “butthurt” (a term he likes using to dismiss the gripes of folks he gripes about).
The bruised feelings didn’t stop there. Later, on Maher’s “Club Random” podcast, he vented about being passed over by Hollywood.
“I’ve been nominated for 33 Emmys, and they would never give it to me,” he told his guest Joel Edgerton. “I speak freely, and this woke town f— hates that. That’s OK. I’ve made my peace with that, so I know how this goes.”
If Maher has been “soft-canceled” by the industry, as he claims, then Hollywood has a funny way of showing its disdain: HBO renewed “Real Time” through 2028.
Perhaps he learned from his frenemy Trump that grievance politics sells, and it’s time to cash in.

Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:57:56 UTC
18:57:56 KST

Belgian industry is in the doldrums. Nearly 30% of all the machines in Belgian factories currently stand idle, according to financial dailies De Tijd and L’Echo. The metal and technology federation Agoria describes the industrial slump as “unprecedented”. Sector federations are therefore calling for measures to tackle high costs and are warning of further job losses.
Almost 3 in 10 machines in Belgian factories stand idle
‘In our sector, we have been struggling with a capacity utilisation rate below 80 per cent for four years now. That is unprecedented,’ Patrick Slaets, chief economist at the metal and technology federation Agoria, told VRT NEWS.
“The cause lies in a lack of demand. There is too little investment, due to the high interest rates brought about by inflation and excessively high energy costs resulting from the geopolitical situation.” This is why energy-intensive companies are suffering the most.
A fall in capacity utilisation also means a greater risk of job losses, warns Slaets. “If the machines aren’t running, there’s no need for people to work there. In the technology sector, 20,000 jobs have already been lost over the past three years. That represents a 6 to 7 per cent reduction in capacity compared with pre-crisis levels.”
Chemical sector also reeling from high energy costs
The chemical sector is also facing tough times. According to a study by consultancy firm Roland Berger, European capacity fell by 9 per cent between 2022 and 2025. On top of that, only 69 to 70 per cent of that (reduced) capacity is being utilised.
It’s been announced that chemical company Vynova in Tessenderlo-Ham is temporarily halting production due to high energy prices. 600 employees are at risk of temporary unemployment.
“It is gradually becoming clear that this crisis is more severe than the previous one,” says Gert Verreth, spokesperson for the chemicals’ federation Essenscia.
It is being argued that urgent action is needed to address issues such as high energy costs and bureaucracy. This applies not only to Belgium, as the rest of Europe is also grappling with similar problems.
‘There is political awareness, but progress at European political level is too slow,’ says Verreth. On the one hand, the high costs must be tackled, but on the other, Europe must also send a strong signal on the geopolitical stage.
There is the context of increasingly aggressive industrial policies, with Trump’s tariff war and the mass production being encouraged by the Chinese government. “Europe must act more swiftly and urgently show its teeth.”
It’s being argued that in Belgium, in particular, labour costs must be kept under control. They are already higher than in neighbouring countries and are threatening to rise even further. “If they are not kept in line with our neighbours, we could end up in an industrial recession next year,” Slaets also fears.

Israel’s stock market drops as exit polls show no clear election winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:55:47 UTC
18:55:47 KST

Israel’s stock market drops as exit polls show no clear election winner
Benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index drops more than 3 percent amid uncertainty over who will lead the next government.
Israel’s stock market has fallen sharply amid exit polls showing no clear winner in the country’s parliamentary elections.
The benchmark Tel Aviv 125 index dropped as much as 3.5 percent in early trading on Wednesday as investors weighed the unclear results of Israel’s first election since the start of its genocidal war on Gaza.
Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor the opposition bloc headed by Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot appeared on track to gain a parliamentary majority in the 26th Knesset.
With more than 84 percent of votes counted as of 11 GMT, Netanyahu’s coalition was on course to win 54 seats, while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc was headed for 49 seats, according to tallies published by Israeli media.
Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority in the unicameral parliament.
Israel’s economy has been running hot despite being on a war footing for the past three years amid an influx of investment in the local tech sector.
Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 2.9 percent in 2025 and 3.2 percent in the first half of 2026, according to government figures.
The Bank of Israel last week raised its GDP growth forecast for all of 2026 to 5.6 percent, up from 4 percent, citing ramped-up production by Israeli firms overseas.
The central bank has forecast that GDP growth for 2027 would reach 7.5 percent, far surpassing estimates for advanced economies such as the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany and Japan.

4 in 10 Americans say personal finances worsening: Survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:52:01 UTC
18:52:01 KST

In the NPR/PBS Poll, 40 percent of people said their “personal family finances” have declined in the last 12 months, while 16 percent said the opposite.
Forty-one percent said their personal family finances have “stayed about the same” within the prior year. Less than 1 percent of poll respondents were not sure about the state of their personal family finances within the last year, while three percent didn’t give an answer.
The NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll was conducted two weeks out from Election Day, with the rise in cost of living being a major concern in this election cycle, THE Hill reported.
Democrats have campaigned on targeting the Trump administration’s tariffs and the war in Iran — two factors behind U.S. price hikes. Amid the Iran war, the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, has been closed.
The average price of a regular gallon of gas in the U.S. has risen from about $3.05 last year to about $4.27 as of Tuesday afternoon. The average price of a gallon of diesel has risen in the last year, sitting at about $6.35 as of Tuesday afternoon compared to its $3.66 a gallon price in 2025.
In the NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll, 52 percent of respondents said they would cast their ballot for a Democrat for their congressional district if the election occurred that day, while 42 percent said the same of a Republican.

'Didn't want Mamata to contest another election': Suvendu on why he kept Bhabanipur seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:50:34 UTC
18:50:34 KST

NEW DELHI: Explaining his decision to vacate his Nandigram stronghold and retain Bhabanipur, West Bengal chief minister Suvendu Adhikari said on Wednesday that vacating the Bhabanipur seat would have given his predecessor, Mamata Banerjee, another opportunity to contest the subsequent bypoll and return to the state assembly.Adhikari, who won both seats in the West Bengal assembly elections in April, defeated Mamata Banerjee in Bhabanipur. He had also defeated the then chief minister in Nandigram in the 2021 assembly elections, following which the TMC supremo contested a bypoll from Bhabanipur and won.The chief minister also took a dig at his predecessor, suggesting that she should retire from electoral politics given her age.“Had I vacated Bhabanipur, the person (Mamata Banerjee) I had defeated twice would have got another opportunity to contest an election. I did not want to give her that opportunity. I had trounced her in Bhabanipur, and I would urge her not to contest elections any more. You have already crossed 75 years of age. There is no need to enter the electoral fray any further. You should take rest at home,” PTI quoted Adhikari as saying.He made the remarks after Hasirani Rath and Shakharav Sarkar were sworn in as BJP MLAs following their victories in the Nandigram and Rejinagar bypolls earlier this month.
The BJP leader also sought to reassure people in Nandigram, who he said were “upset” with him for leaving the constituency. He asserted that he would fulfil his commitments to them through Hasirani Rath, the newly elected MLA from Nandigram.“The people of Nandigram were upset with me for leaving the constituency, but I have explained my decision to them. I had to leave Nandigram for this reason. The people have now elected Hasirani Rath with a margin of 1.22 lakh votes. I will fulfil my promise to them through her,” he added.Hasirani Rath is the mother of Chandranath Rath, Adhikari’s aide who was shot dead on May 6, two days after the West Bengal assembly election results were declared. The BJP came to power in the state for the first time, ending the TMC’s 15-year rule.
Turning to the murder of Chandranath Rath, Adhikari alleged that his aide was killed because of his association with him, describing it as a “supari”, or contract killing.“Chandranath was murdered simply because he was my aide. The CBI has arrested seven people, including the shooters and contract killers. What remains to be established is where the Rs 2 crore ‘supari’ for the contract killing came from. Was it Camac Street, Kalighat or Diamond Harbour? Once that is known, the investigation will be complete,” he said.Adhikari appeared to be referring to Camac Street, associated with the office of Trinamool Congress national general secretary and Mamata's nephew Abhishek Banerjee; Kalighat, where Mamata Banerjee resides; and Diamond Harbour, the Lok Sabha constituency represented by Abhishek Banerjee.

At least 39 killed in Spain train collision – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:50:29 UTC
18:50:29 KST

Dozens killed in Spanish high-speed train collision (VIDEOS)
At least 68 people have been killed after two high-speed trains collided near Toledo, Spain, Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page has said, according to Spanish newspaper ABC. More than 179 people have reportedly been injured.
The crash occurred at 8:54 AM local time on Wednesday between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, around 120 km south of Madrid, on the high-speed line linking the Spanish capital with Andalusia. A Renfe AVE train reportedly struck an Iryo train from behind, sending two carriages off the tracks and down an embankment, according to rail infrastructure operator Adif.
WATCH: Dozens confirmed killed as aerial footage reveals devastation after train collision in Toledo, Spain https://t.co/vwdz3IlGlT
— Klaxon Wire (@KlaxonWire) October 28, 2026
The two trains were carrying a combined total of more than 500 passengers, according to Spanish media reports.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has announced three days of national mourning and pledged a thorough investigation into the disaster. Speaking at the crash site, he vowed to establish the cause of the collision and hold anyone responsible for negligence accountable.
Former Spanish Labor Minister Fatima Banez, 59, was among those killed, according to several Spanish media outlets. Banez served under Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy from 2011 to 2018 and was reportedly travelling aboard the Iryo train to attend a business event in Seville.
Spain’s Transport Ministry has identified human error by an operator at rail infrastructure manager Adif as the leading preliminary explanation for the crash. An operator reportedly authorized the Renfe train to pass a red signal despite the Iryo service remaining stationary on the same track.
BREAKING: 🇪🇸 The death toll from the train collision in Spain has risen to 50 At least 50 people were killed and 179 injured when two trains collided in Toledo, Antena 3 reported. The Iryo train was carrying 147 passengers and the AVE train 397. https://t.co/8l4uJI7JgM
— Visegrád 24 (@visegrad24) October 28, 2026
The suspected mistake followed a malfunction of the railway’s automatic safety system, which forced several trains to stop and required traffic controllers to manage movements manually. Investigators are still working to establish the exact cause.
Images shared online show overturned and badly damaged carriages, with emergency crews working at the scene.
Castilla-La Mancha regional President Emiliano Garcia-Page has requested assistance from Spain’s Military Emergency Unit. Adif has suspended high-speed rail traffic between Madrid and Andalusia. Iryo said it activated all emergency protocols.
Iryo confirma el accidente de su tren 6076 en Urda y cancela todos sus servicios hacia el sur Patricia MedjidiJuez | Tribuna Digital7 28 de octubre de 2026 La compañía ferroviaria Iryo ha comunicado la activación de todos sus protocolos de emergencia tras el accidente sufrido este miércoles por uno de sus trenes a la altura de Urda, en la provincia de Toledo. Según el comunicado difundido en sus redes sociales, el convoy afectado es el servicio 6076, que realizaba el trayecto Madrid-Sevilla. La operadora asegura que trabaja en estrecha colaboración con las autoridades competentes para gestionar la emergencia y atender las consecuencias del siniestro. Como consecuencia del accidente, Iryo ha cancelado todos sus servicios con origen en Madrid-Puerta de Atocha hacia el corredor sur. La compañía advierte de que no existe por el momento ninguna previsión de restablecimiento de la circulación ferroviaria y anuncia que continuará informando a los viajeros a través de sus canales oficiales. El accidente ha provocado también la interrupción de la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Andalucía, confirmada por Adif. El comunicado de Iryo no precisa el número de víctimas ni las causas de la colisión, que continúan pendientes de esclarecimiento. Fuentes: Comunicado de Iryo difundido en redes sociales, según el texto facilitado a Tribuna Digital7; InfoAdif; La Voz del Tajo, 28 de octubre de 2026.
— Tribuna Digital7 (@TribunaLibreES) October 28, 2026
Wednesday’s disaster is the latest in a series of serious railway accidents in Spain this year, raising concerns over the safety of the country’s rail network. On January 18, two high-speed trains collided near Adamuz in the southern province of Cordoba, killing 46 people and injuring more than 150. Investigators have identified a broken section of track as the likely cause, although the investigation is ongoing.
WATCH: Sheer force of train collision between Los Yébenes and Urda in Toledo, Spain sends wheels flying far from the tracks; at least 46 killed https://t.co/32RoUdWDLT
— Klaxon Wire (@KlaxonWire) October 28, 2026
Just two days later, a commuter train struck a collapsed retaining wall near Barcelona, killing the driver and injuring dozens. Another passenger train collided with a crane near Cartagena on January 22, injuring six, and a collision at a level crossing in February reportedly left one person dead.
The incidents have fueled concerns over railway infrastructure and maintenance standards, prompting demands for stronger safety measures. The Spanish train drivers’ union (SEMAF) has called a nationwide strike for Thursday, October 29, accusing Renfe and the Transport Ministry of failing to implement safety improvements promised after the disasters in January. Renfe dismissed the accusations, insisting it has fulfilled its commitments.
The full extent of the casualties and the circumstances surrounding Wednesday’s collision remain under investigation.

Como consecuencia del accidente, Iryo ha cancelado todos sus servicios con origen en Madrid-Puerta de Atocha hacia el corredor sur. La compañía advierte de que no existe por el momento ninguna previsión de restablecimiento de la circulación ferroviaria y anuncia que continuará informando a los viajeros a través de sus canales oficiales. El accidente ha provocado también la interrupción de la línea de alta velocidad Madrid-Andalucía, confirmada por Adif. El comunicado de Iryo no precisa el número de víctimas ni las causas de la colisión, que continúan pendientes de esclarecimiento. Iran hasn't tried to repair damaged nuclear facilities: IAEA

2026-10-28

Breadcrumb
Iran hasn't tried to repair nuclear facilities damaged in US strikes: IAEA chief
The head of the UN nuclear agency said Tuesday there has been no indication Iran has tried to repair or reconstruct its nuclear facilities damaged in US and Israeli military strikes this year or last year.
President Donald Trump has said one of the major reasons the US went to war with Iran on 28 February was to deny Tehran the ability to develop nuclear weapons, even as he has insisted that strikes the US carried out on Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 "obliterated" the country’s atomic program.
During a UN Security Council meeting, International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi urged Iran to give inspectors access to all nuclear sites, including those damaged in the military attacks. The IAEA has not been able to verify the status of Iran's stockpile of near weapons-grade uranium since the US bombed its sites last year.
Grossi said that "since June 2025, we have not identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged in the military attacks of 2025 and 2026."
Trump has consistently downplayed the economic impact of the Iran war, which has emerged as a liability for Republicans heading into next week’s midterm elections, and has argued that higher fuel prices are worth paying to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran. The White House didn’t immediately respond Tuesday evening to a request for comment on Grossi's remarks.
Iran insists its nuclear program is peaceful. Meanwhile, the IAEA says the country has a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity—a short, technical step away from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
The UN meeting on Tuesday was called by Bahrain, Denmark, Latvia, France, the United Kingdom and United States after the IAEA referred Iran to the Security Council for failing to comply with its nuclear nonproliferation obligations. Russia and China, allies of Iran, tried unsuccessfully to prevent the meeting.
Under those obligations, which are part of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, Iran is legally bound to declare all nuclear material and activities and allow IAEA inspectors to verify that none of it is being diverted from peaceful uses.
Iran's UN deputy ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi attacked the council for its silence after the US-Israeli attacks, denouncing their "wars of aggression against Iran" and noted the US is committing war crimes against the Iranian people.
He added that "Israel possesses nuclear weapons, yet your concern is the absence of inspectors in Iran."
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz called Iran a "brutal dictatorship" and asked if the Iranian ambassador wanted to apologise to Bahrain's envoy, a council member, for attacking his country.
"We've heard tireless allegations against the United States," he said. "What we have not heard today is an explanation for Iran's continued failure to satisfy its safeguard obligations."
The IAEA asked Iran for answers, Waltz said, and it would be smart for the Iranian representative to start providing some answers.
"Your lies are no good here," he said.

Trump says Putin-Zelenskyy meeting to be arranged 'very soon'

U.S. President Donald Trump said Tuesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could be arranged soon, as Moscow offered to host direct talks in the Russian capital and diplomatic efforts intensified to end the war.
Trump expressed optimism about progress in negotiations but gave no date or location for a potential summit. His remarks came as Russian officials discussed resuming trilateral talks with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi, while European leaders stepped up contacts with Moscow and Kyiv.
“I think with Russia, we’re making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine. There’ll be a meeting set up here soon,” Trump told reporters after returning from Texas, where he had attended midterm election campaign rallies.
Asked about the timing, Trump said the meeting would happen “over the next not too long.” He added that progress could be achieved without a face-to-face meeting between the two leaders.
The comments offered no confirmation that Putin and Zelenskyy had agreed to meet. Neither Kyiv nor Moscow had publicly confirmed an arrangement for a leaders' summit following Trump's remarks.
The latest diplomatic push comes as the war, launched by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, continues to exact a heavy human and economic toll. Trump's administration has pursued negotiations since he returned to the White House in January 2025, but efforts to secure a settlement have yet to produce a breakthrough.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said Tuesday that Putin had invited Zelenskyy to Moscow for direct negotiations, promising that security arrangements would be made for the Ukrainian leader.
According to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, Ushakov said Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb had informed Putin during a recent telephone conversation that Zelenskyy was interested in meeting him directly.
“Our boss reiterated that if Zelenskyy truly wishes to hold direct negotiations, he should come to Moscow, where all necessary conditions, including those regarding his safety, will be provided for him,” Ushakov said, according to TASS.
The invitation leaves a major question unresolved: whether Zelenskyy would accept Moscow as the venue for negotiations with a leader whose forces continue to occupy Ukrainian territory.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly called for direct talks with Putin, arguing that territorial disputes and other fundamental questions about the war's future require decisions at the highest level. He has also insisted that Ukraine must participate in any negotiations affecting its sovereignty and future security.
There was no immediate indication that Kyiv had accepted the Moscow invitation.
Ushakov said the recent 90-minute telephone conversation between Putin, Stubb and Støre focused largely on plans to resume negotiations involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.
The discussions could take place in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, in the first half of November, although a final date and venue had not been confirmed.
“There were many questions on this matter and requests for clarification from our side,” Ushakov said, describing the call as thorough and substantive.
He added that the parties had agreed to speak again if necessary.
Ushakov also said the question of European representation in future negotiations had not yet been addressed, suggesting that Moscow was not currently considering who might represent the continent at the negotiating table.
The position highlights a potential point of friction between Russia and European governments, which have sought a role in shaping any settlement because of its implications for European security.
The latest diplomatic activity follows meetings between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian and European officials in Oslo on Oct. 20, followed by discussions with Putin in St. Petersburg the next day.
Those contacts covered possible peace arrangements, security guarantees and postwar economic issues.
Russian officials subsequently indicated that Moscow was prepared in principle to resume technical-level negotiations with Ukraine and the United States.
Zelenskyy has supported restarting the talks, while arguing that working groups should address technical matters and prepare the ground for a meeting between the leaders.
He has also maintained that any agreement affecting Ukraine must involve Kyiv directly.
Despite renewed diplomatic activity, the prospects for a breakthrough remain uncertain because Moscow and Kyiv continue to disagree over the fundamental terms of a settlement.
Putin has demanded Russian control over occupied Ukrainian territories, including areas Moscow claims but does not fully control. Russia has also opposed a broad cease-fire before an agreement on the main terms of a settlement, arguing that a pause in fighting could allow Ukraine to strengthen its military.
Ukraine has rejected demands to surrender territory and insists that any peace agreement must protect its sovereignty and provide credible security guarantees against another Russian invasion.
Zelenskyy has argued that territorial disputes cannot be resolved by treating occupied land as a matter of geography alone, pointing to the lives lost defending Ukrainian communities.
The Ukrainian president has also warned against easing sanctions on Russia before meaningful progress is made, arguing that doing so would weaken Kyiv's negotiating position.
Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy have been strained by disagreements over the pace and terms of negotiations. Trump has pressed Ukraine to reach a settlement, while Zelenskyy has resisted proposals that could compromise the country's territorial integrity or leave it vulnerable to renewed Russian aggression.
The prospect of a meeting in Moscow could prove particularly difficult given the ongoing war and the two governments' competing demands. Although Ushakov said Russia would guarantee Zelenskyy's safety, no agreement on a venue has been announced.
The renewed push for negotiations comes as fighting and attacks continue across Ukraine, with both countries facing mounting military and economic costs.
Trump's administration has pursued several diplomatic channels, while European leaders have sought to ensure that any settlement accounts for the security of Ukraine and its neighbors.
A separate, limited cease-fire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region has also offered a narrow opening for humanitarian cooperation. The arrangement, reached with the involvement of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, is intended to facilitate aid deliveries and civilian evacuations.
However, local humanitarian arrangements have yet to translate into a broader halt to hostilities.
Trump's latest remarks signal Washington's continued effort to bring the Russian and Ukrainian leaders into direct negotiations. But his prediction that a meeting will take place “very soon” remains an expectation rather than a confirmed diplomatic agreement.

Dozens killed as high-speed trains collide in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:47:00 UTC
18:47:00 KST

The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. (Europa Press via AP)
A collision between two high-speed trains south of Madrid killed 30 people on Oct. 28 and the toll could rise, regional authorities said in Spain’s second such disaster this year.
Images shared by local media showed the wreckage of two trains strewn on the tracks and an embankment as emergency services rushed to the scene, while shocked travellers dragged away their suitcases as they escaped.
The accident in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha comes one month before Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faced heavy criticism for the first disaster, seeks to overturn unfavourable polls in an early general election.
Sources from authorities in Castilla-La Mancha told AFP “at least 30” people had died, raising a previous toll of 10. Authorities have not yet given a toll for any wounded.
Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the government of Castilla-La Mancha, had told local media CMM that “it is possible that the number will increase.”
State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.
A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told AFP the trains collided just before 9 a.m. (0800 GMT) in the municipality of Urda, around 130 kilometres (80 miles) south of Madrid.
“All resources are currently being deployed,” the emergency services spokesperson said, including “several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units.”
Sanchez, who is seeking to extend his eight-year premiership in the Nov. 29 vote, said on X that he was “shocked” by the accident and sent “my love, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”
He cancelled his participation in a summit in Madrid after the news broke, while his Socialist party suspended all its campaign activities.
Condolences flooded in from across Spain and Europe. The Spanish royal household said on X it was “shocked and concerned” by the accident, conveying its support to the victims, their loved ones and the emergency services.
European Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen said “Europe mourns” with the victims after the “devastating news,” while French President Emmanuel Macron expressed his country’s “solidarity.”
Spain’s high-speed rail network has received huge investment in recent years, growing to become the world’s second-largest after China and a source of national pride.
But Oct. 28's accident comes after another collision between two high-speed trains outside the southern village of Adamuz in January left 46 dead, which raised major questions about safety on the country’s railways.
That crash was Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the northwestern city of Santiago de Compostela.
Both of this year’s accidents happened on the line linking Madrid to Seville.

The Men Spending $50,000 Just to Reserve a Tesla Roadster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

In mid-October, CEO Elon Musk sort of made good on a long-standing promise: Tesla’s new second-gen Roadster flew through the air. Technically, the vehicle used compressed air to “thrust” itself—the “flying” lasted mere seconds, and the system takes six to seven hours to refill.
Never mind, though—some buyers were eager to unsheath their credit cards to reserve one of the cars. “I was freaking out,” says Alex Lawrence, the owner of used-electric-vehicle dealership EVAuto, who already had one reservation for a second-gen Roadster and watched the demonstration live online. “I placed another one.”
It’s not a decision most would make lightly. Tesla took years to get the sports car even close to production. The automaker first introduced the vehicle, a successor to its first car ever, as a surprise at a 2017 event, and immediately began taking $50,000 reservations. At the time, the plan was to deliver the cars in 2020; Musk and company now say the vehicle will enter production in 2028, with delivery dates unclear. (If reservation holders had put that money into Tesla stock, they would be up nearly $1 million today.)
The Roadster is also expensive to reserve—and will likely get pricier to buy. The vehicle’s base model, which doesn’t include acceleration thrusters or the flight system, still costs $50,000 to reserve. The second-tier Thrust variant, which comes with the thrusters, requires a $250,000 deposit. The actual flying car, called Rocket, is listed as “invite-only,” and even Musk has acknowledged the vehicle won’t be street legal. Meanwhile, the automaker’s reservation terms note that purchase prices are “only an estimate”—and those estimates don’t even exist yet.
Whatever! “I’m going to do everything in my power to get the flying one,” Lawrence says. When he sees the Roadster, after all, he sees money signs. His EV dealership has a large and growing social media following, and the business, not the man, technically put down the money for the Roadster reservations. “We’re going to put it on the track and use it for marketing content,” he says.
Utah-based tech founder Travis Cook upped his nearly 10-year-old reservation for the base Roadster variant to the Thrust because he actually wants to live with the thing. He calls himself a “car aficionado” and has a dealer’s license so he can buy and sell fun cars. He loves little more than driving an unusual vehicle, he told WIRED from behind the wheel of a Cybertruck as he used the company’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) feature.
“When I roll up somewhere, all the other car aficionados come out, and they're so excited,” he says. “I just get a buzz from that.”
Cook says he has no regrets about his years-old reservation, though he may get frustrated if the price shoots up closer to half a million. “I’m not sure I’m willing to drop too much money on the car—but I probably would,” he says. Close family tolerates his obsession, though his wife doesn’t enjoy going 0 to 60 in his other cars and probably won’t in the Roadster, either. “She’s not going to want to go in it,” he says.
The tech founder has faith in Musk and Tesla. The October demonstration was even crazier than he had expected. “When it launched off the top of the ramp and went and landed, my jaw was on the floor,” Cook says.
Despite the Roadster’s memeable debut, the vehicle doesn’t seem to be a top priority for Tesla. Musk has said for years now that the automaker isn’t really in the business of making cars anymore and instead is focused on robotics, artificial intelligence, and autonomy. He has touted the new Roadster as the company’s last human-driven car ever. The supercar garnered just two mentions in Tesla’s hourlong earnings call with investors this month, with Musk calling it “arguably the coolest demo of any product ever.” Musk, meanwhile, has other preoccupations—he has donated at least $445 million to Republican candidates ahead of the US midterms.
But Lawrence believes Musk will pull off what he says he will and that his own business’s investment in the Roadster will be worth it in the end. The looping, wedge-shaped car demo left him a little nostalgic, a little existential.
“We don’t do crazy stuff like this anymore, like going to the moon. There’s not a lot today that will stop you in your tracks,” he says. “I felt like I was 15, watching that.”

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:43:09 UTC
18:43:09 KST

Mapping the siege of Yemen’s Taiz, and the price families are paying
Three weeks into the siege of Yemen’s third-largest city, prices have doubled, and families are down to the basics.
Taiz, Yemen – In the besieged city of Taiz, Yousef Farhan’s family has run out of choices at mealtime.
“The whole day, we either eat rice or beans, whether in the morning or in the evening,” the 39-year-old father of four told Al Jazeera.
Shelling forced the family from their home years ago, and they have lived in a school in Taiz’s Wadi al-Qadi zone ever since.
Farhan used to sell cucumbers from a small cart in front of the school, earning between 4,000 and 5,000 Yemeni riyals (roughly $2.50 to $3.20) a day. The money was never steady, but it bought a gas cylinder each month and, now and then, a meal with some variety.
Then the siege closed the school, and his trade went with it. The family now cooks over firewood.
“With the suspension of the school due to the shelling and the siege, my source of income stopped, and I was unable to find alternative work since the siege caused many people’s jobs to come to a halt,” he said.
His children, aged five months to five years, depend on whatever he can find. So do his sister and her child, who joined him after their neighbourhood came under fire.
Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, is home to about 1 million of the country’s roughly 43 million people.
The city has been cut off since early October, when it lost both of its land routes. The Houthis took the town of al-Turbah by October 4, severing the Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road, the main artery for goods.
A day earlier, forces loyal to the internationally recognised government closed the eastern al-Houban crossing into Houthi-held territory, citing attempted Houthi incursions.
On October 20, the United Nations warned that road closures and lack of security were blocking vital supplies.
Prices of the food and fuel still available had more than doubled, and Taiz’s water production had dropped by half.
Across Taiz, families like Farhan’s are working out what to eat and whether they can afford to cook it.
The map below shows the main Taiz-Al-Turbah-Aden Road and three other routes out of the city, all now closed.
One day at a time
For weeks, 40-year-old Sayyun Burhan has looked no further ahead than tomorrow.
“We barely live day-to-day, waiting to see how the next day will pass,” she said.
Work is no longer available at the local store where Sayyun’s husband was employed, and his failing health makes it harder for him to find anything else. Meanwhile, the family still needs money for rent, food, water and cooking gas.
Across the city, the cost of water delivered by tankers has roughly tripled since the fighting escalated, according to UN officials.
The strain reaches beyond the kitchen. For Burhan’s children, the siege means missed lessons and long days inside, as she is afraid to let them out.
“They have been deprived of schooling and play,” she said.
Keeping both children safe and fed is becoming harder.
A city running on fumes
Fuel is behind many of Taiz’s civilian emergencies. Diesel keeps water pumps working, hospital generators running and ambulances moving. Petrol enables people can get to work, and patients to treatment. Cooking gas lets families and restaurants prepare food.
But the city’s fuel stations have been closed since October 5.
Prices gathered by Al Jazeera in Taiz show how sharply fuel costs have risen. A 20-litre (5.3-gallon) container of petrol now costs 120,000 riyals ($77), four times last year’s price of 30,000 riyals ($19).
The price of 20 litres of diesel has nearly doubled, from 46,000 riyals ($29) to 90,000 riyals ($58). A cooking gas cylinder has risen from 11,400 riyals ($7) to 40,000 riyals ($26).
Bus fares have risen from 200 riyals (13 cents) to 500 riyals (32 cents), an increase of 150 percent. Every ride now takes a bigger share of household budgets already stretched by rising food prices.
For Farhan, the move to firewood shows how far his family’s spending power has fallen. He once managed with a gas cylinder each month. Now, even a pot of rice or beans depends on what he can burn.
Water shortages are not new in Taiz, but the siege has made them worse. Diesel shortages have disrupted the pumps.
Local authorities say access restrictions are also stopping tankers from the Al-Dhabab basin, an important source of drinking water, from entering the city.
A hospital hall for a home
Fatima Khaled, 55, has kidney failure. She cannot afford repeated trips from her village west of the city to the hospital for treatment, or a room closer to the hospital. She sleeps on the floor of the dialysis hall at Al-Jumhuri General Hospital.
Closed roads and long mountain detours have made every journey for treatment exhausting and expensive.
The hospital itself is under strain. On October 22, the World Health Organization warned that 42 health facilities in Taiz were reporting severe shortages of fuel, oxygen, medicine and medical supplies.
“I feel like I am imprisoned here. We have no housing or shelter here. This hall is our shelter,” Fatima says.

Türkiye’s services producer price index rose 0.17 percent in September from the previous month and 33.23 percent from a year earlier, the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) said on Oct. 28.
The index was 32.88 percent above its level at the end of 2025.
The 12-month average rise stood at 34.31 percent.
All six main service groups recorded price increases compared with September last year.

Prices in the sector also rose 1.78 percent from August.
Annual increases were 32.44 percent in professional, scientific and technical services, 30.17 percent in administrative and support services, 28.09 percent in accommodation and food services and 28.03 percent in information and communication.
Real estate services recorded the smallest annual rise, at 21.93 percent.
On a monthly basis, prices fell 2.53 percent in administrative and support services, 2.51 percent in real estate and 1.16 percent in accommodation and food services.
Professional, scientific and technical services prices rose 0.84 percent from August, while information and communication prices increased 0.37 percent.

Türkiye’s trade deficit narrowed 25.8 percent year-on-year in September to $5.16 billion as exports grew faster than imports, official data showed on Oct. 28.
Exports rose 15.3 percent to $25.97 billion, while imports increased 5.6 percent to $31.13 billion, according to provisional foreign trade figures compiled jointly by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TÜİK) and the Trade Ministry.
Exports covered 83.4 percent of imports, up from 76.4 percent in September last year, when the trade deficit stood at $6.96 billion.
For the first nine months of 2026, the deficit widened 5.7 percent to $70.97 billion from $67.16 billion a year earlier.
Exports increased 5.2 percent to $210.95 billion, while imports rose 5.3 percent to $281.92 billion.
The export-to-import coverage ratio for January-September stood at 74.8 percent, slightly below the 74.9 percent recorded in the same period of 2025.
Excluding energy products and non-monetary gold, September exports rose 10.5 percent from a year earlier, increasing from $21.17 billion to $23.39 billion.
Imports on the same basis grew 6.7 percent, from $22.43 billion to $23.93 billion.
On that basis, the trade deficit stood at $541 million, with exports covering 97.7 percent of imports.
Combined exports and imports excluding energy and gold increased 8.5 percent to $47.31 billion.

Sports events to mark Türkiye’s 103rd Republic Day

2026-10-28
09:37:35 UTC
18:37:35 KST

(AA Photo)
Türkiye will mark the 103rd anniversary of the founding of the republic with cycling events across its 81 provinces, a horseback ride along a historic independence route and an international race on the Osmangazi Bridge, bringing together sports enthusiasts to celebrate the national holiday.
Republic Day, observed on Oct. 29, commemorates the proclamation of the Republic of Türkiye by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923, following the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and the Turkish War of Independence.
The Turkish Cycling Federation’s “Türkiye Pedals” initiative will run from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1, combining Republic Day celebrations with efforts to raise awareness of climate change ahead of the U.N. climate summit COP31, scheduled to take place in the southwestern city of Antalya on Nov. 9-20. The events will be open to licensed athletes, cycling clubs, students, families and other enthusiasts, encouraging bicycle use as a low-emission alternative to motorized transport. In Istanbul, participants will set off from Beşiktaş Square at 10 a.m. on Oct. 31 for a ride covering approximately 10 kilometers.
Meanwhile, 45 riders from across Türkiye have embarked on a two-day horseback journey along the 95-kilometer İstiklal Road, a historic route used during the War of Independence to transport weapons and ammunition from the Black Sea port of İnebolu into Anatolia. Organized for the third time by the Equestrian and Culture Association, the ride commemorates those who supported the independence struggle.
Another major event, the International Osmangazi-Türkiye Century Run, will take place on Oct. 29 on the Osmangazi Bridge, which connects the two sides of the Gulf of İzmit. Organized by Kocaeli Municipality in cooperation with national and local institutions, the event has attracted nearly 8,000 applications, with athletes from 19 countries expected to participate. It will feature a 10-kilometer elite race and a five-kilometer public run.
Kocaeli Mayor Tahir Büyükakın said organizers hope to make the race an annual tradition and eventually establish it as an internationally recognized sporting event, linking the republic’s historical legacy with a vision of a more sustainable future.
