Israeli right makes provocative statements as election votes are counted
Netanyahu and Smotrich incite against Arab voters as rival political camps face an uncertain path to power.
Senior figures on Israel’s right have made a series of provocative statements about Arab voters, alleged attempts to steal the election and plans to establish Jewish settlements in Gaza.
The remarks came during Tuesday’s election and after exit polls suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing alliance had suffered a setback.
With neither major political camp securing a clear majority, Arab-led parties could play an important role in deciding who forms the next government.
Speaking early on Wednesday at his far-right Religious Zionism party’s election headquarters in Jerusalem, Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich dismissed opposition celebrations and promised to preserve the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank, which are considered illegal under international law.
He said his political opponents would not reverse the government’s settlement “revolution”, declaring: “Jewish settlements will be established in Gaza.”
Israel dismantled its settlements in Gaza in 2005.
Earlier on Tuesday, Smotrich warned on Facebook that voter turnout was unusually high in Arab communities and left-wing strongholds, without providing supporting figures.
He claimed that failing to mobilise right-wing voters could allow “terror supporters” to enter government.
Netanyahu, who leads the right-wing Likud party, made similar appeals during voting, warning that Arab voters were rushing to polling stations and that an opposition victory would threaten Israel’s Jewish character.
He also accused three senior figures from Ra’am, an Arab-majority party, of attempting to steal the election.
Police confirmed they arrested three people on suspicion of voter bribery, but there was no indication they held senior positions in Ra’am.
Transportation Minister Miri Regev, also from Likud, echoed the unsubstantiated election theft allegations in a post on X on Tuesday. “They’re trying to steal the elections and the country from us,” she said. “It’s either the right or Palestine.”
British-American political scientist Dov Waxman told Al Jazeera that Netanyahu’s plan after the inconclusive election result will likely be to “hammer home the message” to the Israeli public that a governing coalition that consists of Arab parties is “illegitimate”.
Arab political leaders condemned Netanyahu’s election-day messages as racist and inflammatory.
Al Jazeera correspondent Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, said Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing and religious parties was projected to win 56 seats, with 84 percent of ballots counted, short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat parliament.
She said Mansour Abbas, the leader of Ra’am, claimed he had received approaches from both Netanyahu’s Likud and the opposition camp led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief who heads the Yashar party.

====================================================================================================

ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.
The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.
Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.
Among the records revealed during the discovery process in these cases are dozens of reports, audio transcripts, emails, intercepted Signal chats, photographs, database queries, and more. They reveal the inner workings of the domestic terrorism investigations, running under the names Project Whipple Shield and Operation Puppet Master, authorized by the controversial National Security Presidential Memorandum 7.
Published following Charlie Kirk’s assassination in September of last year, NSPM 7 instructs federal law enforcement to use every tool available against organizations and people who criticize the administration's policies and espouse "anti-Christian" ideas. The full scope and extent of the investigations it authorizes remains unknown.
Defense attorneys for the Minnesota 15 claim that the prosecution stems from a broader nationwide surveillance operation aimed at opponents of the Trump administration’s immigration policies. One attorney in the case directly compares the DHS-run campaign to the FBI’s infamous Counterintelligence Program, or COINTELPRO, which unconstitutionally surveilled, infiltrated, and blackmailed racial justice, civil rights, and anti-war movements from the 1950s through the early 1970s.
Three former law enforcement officials who reviewed filings concur, telling WIRED that the case is almost certainly part of a wider intelligence-gathering operation that began long before the administration invaded Minnesota in December 2025.
Dueling motions in the case over discovery of DHS’s surveillance program reveal that personnel with Homeland Security Investigations—one of ICE’s two components—repurposed funding mechanisms and investigative tools for serious criminal probes and turned them on domestic dissenters. Operation Keyhole, the HSI undercover program that bankrolled the Minnesota 15 prosecution, dates back to 2008. As of June 2026, it was underwriting a half dozen active undercover investigations in the Minneapolis–Saint Paul area.
Around 120 HSI agents, many drawn from specialized units across the country that have served as the leading edge of the administration’s militarized immigration enforcement operations, were assigned to the case—including 11 undercovers. They used highly invasive surveillance techniques, including the deployment of Reaper drones and Patriot Act tools usually restricted to money laundering and terrorism investigations. Undercover operatives also infiltrated churches in apparent violation of a court order.
The Minnesota 15 indictment stems from the Trump administration’s demand that the Justice Department “go big and go loud” to crack down on community response networks during last winter’s Operation Metro Surge. Twin Cities activists organized volunteers to monitor DHS agents and their vehicles using encrypted Signal groups, homebuilt vehicle databases, and a centralized dispatch system. Government prosecutors claim that this amounts to a criminal conspiracy to block immigration enforcement, unlawfully identify and stalk federal agents, and even assault them.
Their defense attorneys say the heavy charges filed against the Minnesota 15 don’t align with their alleged conduct. “This is the first time I’ve had a client who’s accused of a conspiracy and went on a speaking tour,” says Kevin Riach, who represents defendant Isaac Sant.
Peeking Through the Keyhole
An internal ICE document laying out the scope of Operation Puppet Master—which led to the indictment of the Minneapolis 15—ends by noting, “This case has also been accepted under CUC Op Keyhole.” According to prosecutors, Operation Keyhole is a long-standing program created by HSI’s Saint Paul office to fund “undercover activity”—primarily equipment purchases and personnel costs—in a region covering Minnesota, North and South Dakota, Iowa, and Nebraska. The program has funded at least 77 investigations into “narcotics trafficking, child sexual abuse, financial investigations, and counter-proliferation” since it started in December 2008.
The CUC prefix, per an internal 2008 DHS handbook unearthed by the independent media outlet Unicorn Riot, refers to Certified Undercover Operations, a formal designation with clearly defined oversight mechanisms, procedures, and reporting requirements. Operation Keyhole’s parameters are reviewed every six months by a committee comprising senior DOJ and DHS officials. As of June 2026, when it was last renewed, Keyhole funded six active investigations, including Project Whipple Shield, which was initiated in February to probe claims of assault, stalking, and doxing of DHS agents and other federal employees, and underpins the Minnesota 15 indictment.
At least 11 undercover agents working under Operation Keyhole infiltrated Twin Cities anti-ICE activists, participating in martial arts and know-your-rights trainings, marches, general strikes, and community meetings. They also infiltrated activists’ communications network for identifying possible undercover ICE vehicles and dispatching activists to tail them through the Twin Cities, and penetrated several activist group chats on Signal, transmitting their contents back to other HSI colleagues for analysis and eventual inclusion in the indictment.
Activist conferences as far away as Seattle, Michigan, Chicago, and New York City were placed under surveillance as part of the investigation, and HSI teams photographed and ran the license plates of every car parked in the lot of a meeting location or seen transporting activists. There is also drone footage from unarmed Customs and Border Protection Reaper drones of the activists moving around the Twin Cities area.
The undercovers were part of a much broader group of more than 50 HSI agents, including at least two dozen from HSI’s little-known Special Operations Group, that took part in the investigation and surveillance of the defendants, both digital and in-person. Feds with decades of experience on complex financial crimes, drug cartel investigations, human trafficking, and organized crime were pulled into the Minnesota 15 investigation.
Several of the Minnesota 15 case agents are from out of state and appear in court records for the prosecutions of anti-ICE activists in other cities. This includes Los Angeles–based HSI agents Robert Kurtz III, who specializes in financial fraud, and Ryan Ribner, who allegedly assaulted SEIU California president David Huerta at a June 2025 protest of an ICE enforcement operation, arrested him, and then claimed the then 58-year-old Huerta attacked federal law enforcement. (Huerta’s charges were dropped in July after videos contradicting Ribner’s account surfaced.) HSI records show Ribner was also involved in at least two prosecutions of Southern California residents who physically confronted ICE and Border Patrol agents last year.
Other agents from the conspiracy investigation have also been involved in recent high-profile incidents. Tim Gerber, the “team leader” of an HSI Special Operations Group squad, led the investigation of former CNN host Don Lemon for reporting on a protest at a Minneapolis Church where an ICE agent was a pastor. Fellow SOG agent Yue Her was present at the scene of a 2025 incident when Renee Good’s killer, ICE Special Response Team agent Johnathan Ross, was dragged by the car of a man he tried to apprehend.
“This operation does not seem in any way limited to Minnesota,” says Spencer Reynolds, a former DHS attorney and counterterrorism lawyer who now works at the NAACP Legal Defense Fund. “As we saw with the boots on the ground in the streets, with Greg Bovino leading CBP and Border Patrol special forces units on sweeping raids across the country, this is the intelligence and undercover investigative apparatus that is running in parallel to the door-kicking.”
Follow the Money
Mike German, a retired FBI agent who worked undercover domestic terrorism cases for years before becoming a sharp critic of post-9/11 federal law enforcement, likens the Minnesota 15 case to federal law enforcement’s long history of suppressing left-wing social movements, including the CIA’s Operation MH/Chaos, which surveilled the anti-war movement during the Vietnam War for evidence of foreign influence. One difference is the sheer scale—this time, it’s bigger.
According to a 2011 book by former CIA officer Frank Rafalko, the CIA secret investigation into suspected foreign influence on the New Left and anti-Vietnam War movement had 42 officers working the case at its peak. Court records show 119 HSI agents worked on the Minnesota 15 case alone.
“Broad monitoring of social media, communications, and financial transactions are used to link an ever increasing number of people as potential subjects of investigation and prosecution,” German says. “These are exactly the kind of intelligence activities J. Edgar Hoover adopted to suppress the Civil Rights and anti-war movements in the 1960s.”
The key difference today, German says, is the vast pool of data available to the feds.
HSI used highly invasive measures—including scrutiny of wire transfers, PayPal reimbursements, and other financial transactions; forensic digital analysis of website traffic; 15 terabytes worth of infiltrated Signal chats; and information from a commercial data broker—to identify individuals under investigation.
After a local activist uploaded a license-plate search tool on Fly.io, a developer-focused public cloud platform, to an infiltrated Signal chat, HSI agents reviewed website DNS queries and Stripe data along with data purchased from a commercial broker. This gave HSI access to SSH session logs, outbound connection records, the Fly.io account’s signup IP, and a Stripe card fingerprint on an account that had never completed a payment. Agents fused that with Minnesota DVS records and commercial data from the Thomson-Reuters CLEAR platform to produce a driver's license number, Social Security number summary, years of address history, phone numbers, property records, and jointly registered vehicles.
Documents concerning financial records requested through the Treasury Department’s 314(a) suspicious activity reporting program—created by the Patriot Act to enable speedy tracking of finances for terrorism and money-laundering investigations—show that the feds targeted records of 29 “subjects” during queries conducted on March 31, 2026. Emails viewed by WIRED between several HSI agents based in Los Angeles and Arizona show that batches of records were turned over pursuant to those inquiries, including some dealing with SEIU that a senior Minnesota HSI agent sent to a LA-based colleague to be filed “wherever these records are stored.”
HSI investigators used similar workarounds to warrants and grand jury subpoenas to obtain phone records for several journalists who covered Operation Metro Surge, as first reported by The Guardian. Court records show the feds used an administrative summons request reserved for violations of customs and taxation requirements, which does not fit the activity that made up the criminal charges filed by the Minnesota US attorney against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others.
The Minnesota 15 case is the clearest example yet of DHS pursuing the Trump administration’s efforts to crack down on what have long been upheld as First Amendment–protected activities. But it’s unlikely alone.
Riach, the defense attorney, says the HSI reports show the agency is complicit in what he called “the new COINTELPRO.”
“What we saw during the immigration surges last year was that ICE is the administration’s paramilitary force, the projector of strength,” Riach says. “Here, we see that HSI are taking the FBI’s place as the investigative secret police—it’s the classic one-two punch of authoritarian regimes around the world.”

'Nobody heard us': Gen Z ups ante as protests sweep across Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:29:12 UTC
18:29:12 KST

A wave of youth-led protests is sweeping across Europe, with Generation Z demanding better education, affordable housing, economic opportunities and action against corruption, as growing frustration with political leaders fuels demonstrations from France to Serbia and Albania.
In Brussels, 19-year-old student Maya Gourdel writes a slogan that has become a rallying cry for young people challenging those in power: “If we burn, you burn with us!”
Borrowed from the 2012 film “The Hunger Games,” the phrase has been adopted by youth movements worldwide, reflecting the anger of a generation that feels excluded from decisions shaping its future.
From the suburbs of Paris to the streets of Belgrade, thousands of young people have protested deteriorating school facilities, limited job prospects, rising living costs, corruption and a lack of political accountability.
Some demonstrations have turned violent, with thousands of shops damaged or looted in France in recent weeks and police deploying stun grenades and water cannons.
But the protests have also delivered a major political breakthrough. In Serbia, nearly two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and growing authoritarianism culminated in the electoral defeat of longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic this weekend.
“Waking up, the first thing we felt was certainly a sense of relief and freedom,” said Stasa Piletic, a student protester. “Personally, I feel a sense of victory. I feel that we finally moved from protests to responsibility.”
For many young Europeans, the protests reflect a growing belief that traditional political institutions have failed to address their concerns.
Chiara, a 21-year-old student in Milan, said spontaneous demonstrations had created an opportunity for collective action after years of mounting frustration.
“I think the worst damage this ruling class has done to my generation is stealing even the ability to imagine a future, to dream,” she said.
Italian students face schools struggling with teacher shortages and deteriorating buildings, followed by the prospect of poorly paid jobs and increasingly unaffordable housing, she said.
The unrest reflects a broader international trend. Generation Z, generally defined as people born between 1997 and 2012, has mobilized against political and economic grievances in countries including Bangladesh in 2024, Nepal in 2025 and India this year.
Europe has now become a focal point.
Rising prices and the cost of living concern 40% of Europeans aged 16 to 30, according to an EU survey published in 2025.
Of the 92.7 million people in the European Union who faced the risk of poverty or social exclusion in 2025, young adults aged 18 to 24 recorded the highest risk, at 26.3%. The rate among people 65 and older was 18.8%.
Young protesters are also questioning how governments distribute resources between younger and older generations.
In France, people over 60 account for about a quarter of the population but own 60% of the country's wealth, according to the OFCE economic research institute.
Public pensions are France's largest category of government spending and are projected to reach 14% of economic output as the population ages. Efforts to raise the retirement age or reduce benefits have faced strong opposition.
France spends less on pensions than Greece and Italy, which devote about 16% of gross domestic product to public pensions, according to 2025 figures from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. Australia, Chile, Iceland, Ireland and South Korea each spend less than 4% of GDP.
A French government report published in October found that pension spending increased by 2.5 percentage points of GDP between 2000 and 2023, while education spending declined by 0.5 percentage points. Pensions also accounted for 32% of the Education Ministry's budget, limiting resources available for other priorities.
For students facing deteriorating classrooms and staff shortages, the figures reinforce concerns that their needs are being overlooked.
In a suburb north of Paris, 17-year-old high school student Bilal Narjissi has protested what he described as deplorable school conditions and staff shortages.
“There used to be rats,” he said.
Students were evacuated last year after a roof collapsed in the school courtyard, although nobody was injured, he said.
Narjissi said the demonstrations had shown that young people across Europe shared common concerns.
“We all agree on one point: that young people are treated like children, far too much, and that they aren't listened to enough,” he said.
Gourdel, who has also protested for better school conditions in Belgium, said students initially tried peaceful action but struggled to attract attention.
“We tried to do it passively. Nobody heard us. It's only when people started to burn trash or that kind of stuff that the media and cameras started showing us,” she said.
Protests are continuing to spread, with a demonstration planned in Germany this weekend over the cost of living, inequality, war and school conditions.
Albania has also experienced unrest, with student-led demonstrations against Prime Minister Edi Rama's government spreading from Tirana to other cities.
Protesters have voiced anger over perceived corruption, limited employment opportunities and poor education standards.
“Our Prime Minister spent 130 days not listening to us,” said Xyke Kurti, a 19-year-old architecture student.
Kurti said many young Albanians saw emigration as their best chance of securing a future.
“If you ask a student in Albania, 'where do you see your future?' Everyone says 'outside this country',” she said.
She argued that qualifications and talent were often insufficient to guarantee success in a system where personal connections could determine who advances.
Serbia's student movement has achieved what demonstrators elsewhere in Europe are still seeking: an electoral victory after sustained public pressure against an established political leader.
The challenge now is turning protest into effective government. The students and candidates they support have little governing experience, raising questions about their ability to deliver reforms.
Luka Stojakovic, another Serbian protester, dismissed concerns about their inexperience.
“We have seen where people with political experience have brought us,” he said.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a post on X that no embassy personnel were injured and that it was investigating the incident.
Although such attacks are rare in Serbia, the Israeli embassy in Belgrade has been targeted before.
In June 2024, an attacker armed with a crossbow seriously wounded a police officer guarding the embassy before being shot dead by police.
The attacker was identified at the time as a 25-year-old man from a village near Belgrade who had converted to Islam and later embraced extremist views.

Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:26:42 UTC
18:26:42 KST

Russia showcases submarine-launched ballistic missile (VIDEO)
A Russian nuclear-powered submarine has successfully test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile, hitting a target around 6,000 km away on the other side of the country, the Defense Ministry announced on Wednesday.
The Bulava missile was launched from a submerged position by the Generalissimus Suvorov strategic missile submarine in the Far Eastern Sea of Okhotsk, near the Kamchatka Peninsula, as part of a scheduled combat training exercise.
The missile’s warheads reached the designated Chizha test range on the Kanin Peninsula in Russia’s Arkhangelsk Region, 5,500-6,000 km from the launch area. The ministry said monitoring data confirmed that the warheads arrived at their target area on schedule, declaring the exercise a success.
The ministry also released dramatic footage of the launch. The video shows the submarine cruising at sea before cutting to crew members operating control systems inside the vessel. A close-up captures the press of a launch button, followed by a nighttime shot of a blazing missile erupting from the water and streaking skyward.
The R-30 Bulava (NATO designation SS-N-32) is a submarine-launched ballistic missile designed to serve as one of the mainstays of Russia’s sea-based nuclear deterrent. Developed by the Moscow Institute of Thermal Technology and officially adopted into service in May 2024, the solid-fuel missile has a reported maximum range of around 9,300 km.
Weighing approximately 37 tons, the Bulava is designed to carry multiple independently targetable nuclear warheads. It also incorporates measures intended to help it penetrate missile defenses, including a relatively short boost phase and maneuverable reentry vehicles.
The Generalissimus Suvorov is a fourth-generation Project 955A Borei-A nuclear-powered submarine assigned to Russia’s Pacific Fleet and based in Kamchatka. Built at the Sevmash shipyard, the vessel can carry up to 16 Bulava ballistic missiles, alongside torpedo armaments.
The Borei and upgraded Borei-A submarines form a key component of Russia’s strategic nuclear modernization program, replacing aging Soviet-era missile carriers. Russia currently operates eight submarines of the two classes, with additional vessels under construction.
Wednesday’s launch was intended to test the crew’s combat readiness and the submarine’s missile systems, according to the Defense Ministry.

To commemorate the eighth centenary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi, the Italian Embassy in Croatia organized the conference “The Relevance of St. Francis: From Coexistence to Communion and Fraternity” in Zagreb, in collaboration with the Croatian Catholic University, which hosted the event, and the Apostolic Nunciature. The conference was followed by a concert by the Ensemble Micrologus—Giullari di Dio, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute, which offered a musical journey dedicated to the Canticle of the Creatures and the ancient melodies of the Italian lauda tradition. The conference proceedings were opened by the Italian Ambassador to Croatia, Paolo Trichilo; by Monsignor Marco Malizia, ecclesiastical advisor to the Vice President of the Council of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Antonio Tajani; by the Apostolic Nuncio, Monsignor Leopoldo Girelli; and by the rector of the Catholic University of Croatia, Željko Tanjić. Fra Lorenzo Turchi of the Pontifical Antonianum University in Rome served as a speaker, engaging in a discussion with two Croatian professors from the universities of Split and Zagreb—both members of the Franciscan Order— on the Christian experience of St. Francis and how it can offer criteria for discernment in understanding certain dynamics of the present. The event drew a large audience and was attended by several civil and religious authorities, including Cardinal Emeritus of Zagreb Josip Bozanić, Ivan Mašina, advisor to the Croatian Minister of Foreign Affairs; and, representing the Ministry of Culture, Šime Jerčić, Director General of the Office of the Commission for Relations with Religious Communities. In his opening remarks, Ambassador Trichilo highlighted the attention given to St. Francis by Italian institutions and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as evidenced by the establishment of the national holiday on October 4 and the organization of dedicated events by the diplomatic corps. St. Francis, the ambassador emphasized, is a pivotal historical figure for Italian, European, and universal spirituality and culture. His message continues to be a source of inspiration that challenges us to reflect on the future and offers spiritual and ethical guidance for navigating the modern world. He then highlighted how the initiative takes on particular significance in Croatia, given the country’s Catholic tradition. Bishop Malizia conveyed greetings from Minister Tajani, expressing the minister’s satisfaction that the diplomatic network had accepted the invitation to promote initiatives on St. Francis and to focus on a spiritual and human witness capable of speaking to peoples, cultures, and traditions, and to contribute to the promotion of dialogue, peace, and fraternity. He also noted that Italy considers intercultural and interreligious dialogue an essential component of its international vision, emphasizing the important role played by cultural institutions, religious communities, and diplomacy—all united by the responsibility to safeguard peace through mutual understanding, respect, and cooperation. Bishop Malizia then expressed his appreciation for the conference, which represents not only a tribute to St. Francis but also a concrete opportunity to rediscover what unites us and to promote a culture of listening, solidarity, and peace.

Climate change poses ‘global health emergency’ as health risks accelerate: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:25:27 UTC
18:25:27 KST

Merve Berker
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Climate change has become a “global health emergency,” with rising temperatures, extreme drought and other climate-related threats causing increasing harm to human health, according to findings from a new Lancet study, ABC News reported Tuesday.
The 2026 Lancet Countdown report, led by University College London in collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO), found that climate-related health risks are accelerating despite progress since the 2015 Paris Agreement, according to ABC News.
“A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world’s response to them, and in many cases even accelerating,” said Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown.
The study, involving 146 researchers from more than 100 institutions, estimated that heat contributed to more than 540,000 deaths annually between 2016 and 2023, with 68% attributed to climate change.
In 2023 alone, heat was linked to approximately 710,000 deaths, more than 71% of which were attributed to climate change.
Researchers estimated that extreme heat caused more than $1 trillion in lost potential income worldwide in 2025, marking the third consecutive year above that threshold.
The report also found that more than half of the world’s land experienced extreme drought for at least one month in 2025.
Meanwhile, global clean energy investment reached $2.1 trillion in 2025, although fossil fuels continued to account for more than 80% of global energy supply.
The researchers urged governments and international institutions to prioritize climate-related health risks, accelerate emissions reductions and strengthen global cooperation.
“This isn’t a gradual worsening; it’s a step change that must be recognized as the global health emergency it is,” Romanello said.

Mbappé Apologizes After ‘Dictator’ Mao Comment: What to Know About the Chinese Backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

French soccer captain and Real Madrid forward Kylian Mbappé has apologized to China for calling Mao Zedong a “dictator,” a comment that prompted fierce criticism and institutional reprisals.
“My comment was ill-judged,” Mbappé said in a statement in three languages. “I apologize to everyone my words have upset.”
In a video clip from the French talk show “The Bridge” posted on Monday, Mbappé had referred to Mao as “some guy—I think he’s a Chinese dictator” as he described a meme in which his face was photoshopped onto a picture of the late founder and chairman of the Chinese Communist Party. The clip was behind-the-scenes footage from a podcast filmed in March, the podcast said. It has since been removed from the show’s social media accounts. “The Bridge” also apologized to Chinese fans, as well as to Mbappé.
The meme is part of an internet trend where soccer fans have superimposed Mbappé’s face onto pictures of military and political leaders as a play on Mbappé’s nickname “the dictator,” referring to the Real Madrid player’s perceived authority and influence over football clubs and the media. Even Mbappé’s French teammate Ousmane Dembélé made a joke about the moniker during the 2026 World Cup, referring to Mbappé as Mobut after Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo for three decades.
Mbappé told French magazine L’Equipe last month that he found some of the memes funny, but that others demonstrated “a lack of political and human awareness.”
“To be compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions and millions of people miserable … I don’t think I’ve ever done anything like that in my life,” he said.
In the clip shared by The Bridge, Mbappé was asked which meme he finds funniest, and he pointed to the one featuring Mao.
Mbappé’s “dictator” label, however, triggered sharp rebuke in China. Several Chinese broadcasters suspended coverage related to Mbappé and Spanish soccer league LaLiga, while some brands pulled ads that featured the sports star. A spokesperson for China’s Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday, before Mbappé’s apology, that “words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society.”
Parody of Chinese leaders is politically sensitive in China, not least mockery of Mao, who founded the People’s Republic of China in 1949 and ruled the country till his death in 1976.
Many international scholars have described Mao as an authoritarian leader, pointing to his centralized rule, political purges, and aggressive state campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution. Historians estimate that tens of millions of people died during Mao’s rule as a result of famine and violence. But within China, many view him as a revolutionary figure who unified the country and transformed a largely agrarian society into an independent nation. While official accounts have condemned the Cultural Revolution as a “grave blunder,” those same accounts argue that Mao’s lifetime contributions to the Chinese revolution outweighed his mistakes. The Chinese Constitution describes the state as the “people’s democratic dictatorship,” defined as a proletarian dictatorship.
“During a recent interview, I reacted to an image of myself,” Mbappé said in his apology. “I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. … This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry.”
Past sensitivity
Parodies of political figures have incurred anger and sanctions before. In April 2015, CCTV suspended TV presenter Bi Fujian after a private dinner video that showed him mocking Mao while singing a revolutionary opera was leaked online. In July 2017, Chinese social media platforms also restricted references to Winnie-the-Pooh after internet users compared the character to Chinese President Xi Jinping.
In August, artist Gao Zhen was sentenced to three years in prison for “infringing upon the reputation of heroes” because he had made satirical sculptures of Mao, including a 2009 statue called Mao’s Guilt that depicts the late leader kneeling in repentance. Gao, who was based in the U.S., was arrested in August 2024 while visiting family in China.
International sports brands and associations have also come under fire in China over remarks deemed politically offensive.
In October 2019, China paused sponsorship deals with the National Basketball Association after Houston Rockets executive Daryl Morey posted online in support of protests in Hong Kong, which Beijing characterizes as separatist and seditious. CCTV suspended broadcasts of NBA games for a year.
Canceled contracts
Mbappé’s comments may already have cost him.
China’s largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it would cease its partnerships with Mbappé, as did cheesemaker Shanghai Milkground Food Tech and beverage giant Eastroc Beverage, also known as Dongpeng. The companies said they had a “zero-tolerance policy” towards words or behavior that offend the feelings of the Chinese public.
According to French newspaper Le Monde, Mbappé’s Dongpeng and Mengniu contracts were worth approximately 50 million yuan (€6.7 million) combined. Dongpeng had run adverts featuring AI-generated images of Mbappé drinking its sports drink during the 2026 World Cup and sold bottles of its Bushuila electrolyte drink with Mbappé on its packaging. After Mbappé’s comments and prior to their statements, the two consumer brands saw their stock fall.
Global brands including Dior, Rimowa, Nike, Hublot, and On Running also removed promotional content featuring Mbappé from their accounts on Chinese social media platform Weibo, Chinese media reported.
China’s state television CCTV suspended broadcasts of all matches and events involving Mbappé and LaLiga, and pulled advertisements featuring Mbappé, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. The state broadcaster said in a statement after Mbappé’s apology that it hoped he “will genuinely learn a lesson from this” and “thoroughly correct” his mistake.
LaLiga President Javier Tebas said on Tuesday that he met with the Chinese Ambassador in Spain to “seek solutions that allow us to overcome this episode.”
“Our commitment is to keep working together so that an individual episode does not harm the important advances achieved nor affect the millions of Chinese fans who follow our competitions,” Tebas said in a post on X. “A relationship built over so many years cannot be damaged by a single incident,” he added in another post.
Online backlash
Mbappé, once a fan favorite in China where he is affectionately nicknamed “Guigui” after a perceived resemblance to a Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle, now faces a firestorm online.
Calls for brands to terminate partnerships with Mbappé and boycott the player were among the top trending topics on Weibo. Some users accused Mbappé of profiting off the lucrative Chinese sports markets and his millions of fans in the country while disrespecting their national sentiments.
Weibo and Rednote, also known as Xiaohongshu, also appeared to have restricted Mbappé on their platforms, with notices that said his accounts were “banned” or “muted” for violating community guidelines.
In an article titled “Mbappé scores an own goal in China,” state media outlet China Daily reported that the backlash from Chinese fans has “threatened his lucrative commercial relationships and offered a sharp reminder of the limits of celebrity influence.”
Several Chinese news outlets condemned Mbappé’s remarks without restating them. Soccer news outlet Dongqiudi said in a statement, “Kylian Mbappé made inappropriate remarks about China in an interview. As these remarks are likely to hurt China and its people, we cannot translate them.”
“What did he say? Many Chinese would rather not repeat it,” state-linked Global Times said in a video commentary. “The message from Chinese consumers is clear: Respect is not optional; one doesn't get to profit from China while disrespecting it. Not a chance.”
Another article from state-linked newspaper Guangming Daily read, “Insulting China’s late great leader is unacceptable! Eating Chinese food and then smashing the Chinese pot? Mbappe is not worthy!”
“However good your football skills are, you cannot trample on fundamental limits,” it said.
Censorship concerns
Outside of China, some have pushed back against the backlash.
French social media users criticized Mbappé for retreating on his comments. Marc Julienne, director of the Asia Centre at French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), told Le Parisien that describing Mao as a “dictator” reflects a consensus among Western historians, though it is a characterization that remains taboo in China—which, Julienne added, Mbappé may not have realized.
The U.S. House Select Committee on China posted on Tuesday that Mbappé “should not apologize for calling Mao Zedong a dictator. Mao was a dictator, and by orders of magnitude, he did more harm to the Chinese people than a comment from a soccer player ever could.”
“The real disgrace,” the committee said, “is the companies rushing to apologize so they can continue to do business in China.”

At least 10 killed as 2 high-speed trains collide in central Spain

At least 10 killed as 2 high-speed trains collide in central Spain

====================================================================================================

At least 30 killed as 2 high-speed trains collide in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:25:00 UTC
18:25:00 KST

At least 68 people were killed Wednesday when a high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train in central Spain, derailing two carriages and leaving wreckage scattered across a field as emergency crews raced to rescue survivors.
The collision occurred shortly after 9:00 a.m. in Toledo province, on the high-speed rail line connecting Madrid with Seville in southwestern Spain, according to the country's rail infrastructure operator ADIF. Rail services between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia were suspended following the crash.
Officials warned that the number of fatalities could rise as rescue workers reached passengers trapped in the wreckage.
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers were traveling in the same direction when one struck the rear of the other, which had stopped. The impact knocked two carriages off the tracks.
The cause of the collision was not immediately known.
The crash occurred on a relatively flat stretch of railway between the towns of Urda and Los Yebenes, surrounded by open fields. Images from the scene showed a carriage severely mangled, with twisted metal and other debris scattered down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Monica Garcia told state broadcaster TVE that emergency crews were concentrating on recovering survivors and bodies from the two most heavily damaged carriages. Injured passengers were being transported to hospitals across the region.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
The collision involved a train operated by state-owned Renfe and another run by private company Iryo, which is owned by Italian rail operator Trenitalia. Spanish media reported that the Renfe train struck the stationary Iryo service.
Regional authorities said 397 passengers were aboard the Renfe train and 147 were traveling on the Iryo service, bringing the total number of passengers on the two trains to 544.
Iryo said it had activated its safety protocols and was working closely with authorities following the crash.
Emergency responders, including firefighters, police and civil protection teams, were deployed to the scene. A military emergency brigade was also sent to support rescue operations.
Manuel Galan, mayor of nearby Urda, told TVE that civil protection officials had asked the town council to prepare a sports pavilion to receive injured passengers and others affected by the collision.
Emiliano García-Page, president of Castilla-La Mancha, said on X that he was traveling to the crash site as emergency operations continued.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez canceled his scheduled engagements to focus on the disaster, expressing condolences to the victims and their families.
"I am dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo," Sánchez wrote on X. "Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers."
Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia also expressed their sorrow and said they were following developments.
"We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," the royal couple said in a statement posted on X.
The disaster is the second major train accident in Spain this year, renewing concerns about safety on a railway network that has become one of the most extensive high-speed systems in the world.
In January, 45 people were killed in southern Spain when a train derailed near Adamuz in Cordoba province and collided with an oncoming train. The disaster was the country's deadliest rail accident since July 2013, when a train derailed near Santiago de Compostela, killing 80 people.
The January crash shook public confidence in Spain's rail network and prompted renewed scrutiny of railway safety. Investigators examining Wednesday's collision will seek to establish how the two trains came to collide and whether any technical or operational failures contributed to the disaster.
Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail over the past three decades, building a network that connects major cities and serves a population of about 49 million. The country's rail union defines high-speed lines as those designed for trains traveling at 250 kph (155 mph) or faster.
Spain has developed about 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of high-speed track, making it the world's second-largest network after China's, which extends roughly 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles), according to the International Union of Railways.
The network was opened to private operators only in recent years as Spain sought to introduce competition alongside Renfe. Iryo began operating passenger services in the country in 2022.

Pentagon chief proposes ‘ambitious’ defense cooperation with ASEAN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:23:06 UTC
18:23:06 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Wednesday called for an “ambitious” defense cooperation framework with the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Calling the 50th anniversary of US-ASEAN ties next year an “important milestone,” Hegseth told the assembled ASEAN defense chiefs: “And in recognition of this milestone, we propose that we work together to develop a US-ASEAN framework for defense cooperation – a practical framework that guides our cooperation over the next several years.”
He stressed what he called “a critically important next several years,” addressing a joint meeting with defense chiefs of the 11-member bloc in Cebu City, the Philippines, which serves as ASEAN’s current chair.
“The approach we're taking we describe as strong, quiet, and clear. Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics, and to let our actions speak for themselves,” Hegseth said as his Chinese counterpart, Dong Jun, skipped the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus this year.
Beijing instead assigned its military attache at the Chinese Embassy in Manila to represent China at the summit.
“We're not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to,” Hegseth told his ASEAN counterparts.
“But an agreement on the fundamentals is enough to support practical cooperation where our shared interests are overlapping and are clear.”
Hegseth said the US will work with Singapore, as the city-state takes the ASEAN helm next year, for the proposed framework for defense cooperation and “as we look to the future in this region, I'd like us to be even more ambitious.”
The meetings in Cebu City mark the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting and 13th ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting Plus, which also brings together the defense chiefs of China, South Korea, Japan, Australia, and India, although China this year did not send its defense minister.

NEW DELHI: Cyclone ‘Arnab’ has battered India’s eastern coast, uprooting trees and electric poles, damaging roads and bringing torrential rain, with some areas of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha recording up to 30 cm of rainfall. The storm’s impact is now expected to extend to Nepal, which is bracing for several days of rain, thunderstorms and snowfall from Thursday.The Nepal Meteorological Department’s Weather Forecasting Division said the country was currently experiencing the partial influence of westerly winds, with the approaching cyclone expected to bring widespread precipitation and a risk of heavy rain and snowfall through the weekend.
“The country is currently under the partial influence of westerly winds. In addition, the country is expected to come under the influence of Cyclone ‘Arnab’, developed over the Bay of Bengal, from Kartik 12 (Thursday),” the department said in its latest bulletin.Weather conditions remained relatively clear in the Himalayan and hilly regions on Wednesday morning, although fog and mist affected parts of the Terai, valleys and river basins.
The department forecast increasing cloud cover and scattered precipitation from Wednesday afternoon, with conditions becoming more unsettled overnight. Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini provinces are among the areas expected to experience rain, while snowfall is possible in Himalayan regions.The risk is forecast to increase on Thursday night, when thunderstorms and lightning could accompany rain and snowfall. Heavy precipitation is possible in parts of Koshi, Bagmati and Gandaki provinces, while some areas of Lumbini could also receive heavy rainfall.Friday and Saturday are expected to bring the most widespread impacts. The department warned that heavy rain or snowfall could affect several provinces, with isolated locations facing the possibility of very heavy precipitation.
Its Friday forecast states, “Mostly cloudy throughout the country. Light to moderate rain or snowfall accompanied by thunder and lightning is possible at most places in Koshi, Madhesh, Bagmati, Gandaki and Lumbini Provinces and at many places in Karnali and Sudurpashchim Provinces.”The expected combination of westerly winds and moisture associated with Cyclone Arnab could increase the risk of flooding in low-lying areas and landslides in vulnerable hilly regions. Heavy snowfall could also create hazardous conditions in high-altitude areas.
Meanwhile, in India, at least three people died in cyclone Arnab-related incidents in Andhra Pradesh on Wednesday. South Coast Railway (SCoR) cancelled 57 trains and rescheduled 15 others as a precautionary measure. However, officials quoted by ANI said the cyclone had weakened from a very severe to a severe cyclonic storm after moving over land, and was expected to weaken further. Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine's trains keep on rolling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:21:01 UTC
18:21:01 KST

Harassed by Russian drones, Ukraine's trains keep on rolling
ON A TRAIN BETWEEN DNIPRO AND ODESA, Ukraine, Oct 28 - Ukrainian beauty salon owner Antonina Viter is getting used to having her travel plans disrupted by the threat of Russian drone attacks, as she criss-crosses the country by rail to keep her business going.
"Every third trip, we end up evacuating once, twice or even three times," she explained on board a train from the southeastern city of Dnipro to Odesa on the Black Sea.
"What can you do? How else do you get to your client?"
Kyiv has set new rules for rail passengers during air-raid alerts and, sure enough, soon after she spoke, the 36-year-old was standing outside under a pitch-black October sky, wrapped in a blanket, waiting for the "all-clear".
In a country long reliant on its vast rail network, hours-long delays and repeat evacuations when air-raid sirens sound are another way in which Russia's escalating missile and drone attacks are wrecking everyday life for civilians.
New Russian jet-powered drones that are hard to shoot down have attacked everything from shopping centres and filling stations to power plants and other critical infrastructure. And the railways are no exception.
UKRAINIAN RAILWAYS ATTACKED 1,700 TIMES THIS YEAR
The state operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, says Russia has attacked more than 1,700 rail facilities this year, including stations, locomotives and passenger wagons. Russia says its targets are objects used by Kyiv's military.
A trip on the line from Dnipro to Odesa, some 400 km (250 miles) to the southwest, showed how Ukrainians are coping with those disruptions.
The outward journey featured eight evacuations of roughly 30 minutes each, the return journey - one more.
Direct attacks, like the drone strike that killed two train drivers on the Dnipro-Odesa line on August 13, are an ever-present threat.
But air-raid alerts can unexpectedly double the travel time on any route, and some stations in the east and south have been shut indefinitely as fighting creeps closer.
The prospect of being hit is one that 41-year-old IT worker Larysa Konstantynova - who was travelling from Dnipro to Odesa with her teenage son at the start of a holiday trip to Europe - prefers not to think about.
Like Viter, who travels at least six times a month to manage two salons in Kyiv and Dnipro, she says she is adapting.
"It's how your mind works: you just try to be positive and survive with the way things are."
Other attacks have included a strike on a Warsaw-bound train near the Polish border in September.
For some, overnight rail journeys - once opportunities to unwind with few distractions - are now spent in anxious anticipation.
During air raid alerts, passengers can be jolted awake and forced to scramble into fields or up and down embankments, sometimes with children or pets in tow. In the winter, temperatures are often below freezing.
RAILWAY JOURNEYS HAUNTED BY RISK OF RANDOM DEATH
Huddled outside her train with a colleague, Viter tracked a nearby drone on a cell-phone app after hearing its distinctive 'whoosh' overhead.
It was the third evacuation in two hours.
"Better to stand in a field for an hour than to risk never getting to see the next hour," she said, knowing she had to teach a beauty workshop in Odesa the next day.
In fact, although delays of 5 to 12 hours are not unusual on the Dnipro-Odesa route, this train arrived just an hour and 20 minutes late.
Nevertheless, the risk of random death has soared as Russia has broadened its drone and ballistic-missile campaign, exploiting Kyiv's shortage of air defence missiles.
More than 50 railway workers have died on duty this year alone, according to Ukraine's infrastructure minister, and dedicated staff have had to adapt their routines to maintain a network that appears to be close to their hearts.
At the beginning of each journey, conductors sweep through the carriages closing curtains to block out light that might alert a Russian drone.
"They can see us, so we have to hide a bit," said train attendant Olha Boniuk, 49, with the air of a mother soothing her child.
After each evacuation, chief conductor Mykola Zakharchenko, 47, sits in his cramped booth diligently recording the interruption.
All the same, he smiles recalling conversations with passengers, and still enjoys watching dawn break through the carriage window: "Train work, as they say, is romance."
Locomotive driver Mykola Kovalenko put it another way.
"If I quit," he said, "who will drive the trains?" REUTERS

Voters across the U.S. will head to the polls on Nov. 3 for midterm elections that could reshape Congress and determine President Donald Trump's ability to advance his legislative agenda during the final two years of his term.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate's 100 seats – all elected at large – are up for grabs.
In the Senate, Republicans currently hold 53 seats, compared with 45 Democrats and two independents who caucus with Democrats, giving the latter 47 votes. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure a Senate majority.
Polls show close contests in several Republican-held states, while Democrats are also defending seats in states that supported Trump in the 2024 presidential election.
Here are eight Senate races drawing particular attention.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is facing former Republican Congressman Mike Rogers in the contest to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
A Detroit News/WDIV-TV poll done on Oct. 19-22 showed El-Sayed leading Rogers 51.4% to 45.1% among 600 likely voters, with 3.6% undecided. The margin of error was four percentage points.
Michigan's previous Senate election in 2024 was decided by just 19,006 votes out of more than 5.5 million cast, when Democrat Elissa Slotkin defeated Rogers to win the state’s other senatorial seat.
The race has drawn additional attention because El-Sayed, a former public health official, would become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate if he wins.
El-Sayed has hit back hard against claims that his religious faith would somehow amount to “double loyalty,” pointing out that the late John F. Kennedy, a Catholic, faced similar allegations when he ran for president in 1960.
Five-term Republican Sen. Susan Collins faces Democrat Troy Jackson, a former president of the Maine Senate.
A Marist poll released Tuesday showed Jackson with 49% support among likely voters, compared with 47% for Collins. The survey was done on Oct. 22-25 and had a margin of error of 6.6 percentage points.
Collins won her previous election in 2020 with 51% of the vote, defeating Democrat Sara Gideon, who received approximately 42%.
However, Maine supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024 by 52.4% to 45.5% over Trump.
Wooing voters, Collins has touted her status as a powerful centrist who brings lucrative benefits to Maine. Jackson has called her centrism into question, saying that Collins largely supports Trump’s agenda.
Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico for the seat held by retiring Republican Sen. John Cornyn.
Democrats capturing the seat would be a major upset, as they have not won a US Senate election in Texas since 1988.
A Univision/YouGov poll released Tuesday showed Talarico leading Paxton 50% to 45% among 1,000 registered voters surveyed on Oct. 13-21, with a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Unusually for a Democrat, Talarico has made his Christian faith a large part of his campaign, and has also alleged that Paxton is corrupt. Paxton boasts an endorsement from Trump as well as heavy campaign spending by billionaire Elon Musk, who has companies based in Texas.
Texas – the second-largest US state by population – has over 19 million registered voters, up 2.2% from the 2024 presidential election.
In that election, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz defeated Democrat Colin Allred 53.1% to 44.6%.
Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is seeking a return to Congress against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to replace JD Vance, as he gave up the seat when he became vice president.
An InsiderAdvantage poll done on Oct. 21-22 showed Brown leading Husted 47% to 44% among 1,200 likely voters, with a margin of error of 2.8 percentage points.
A Fox News poll done on Oct. 15-19 showed Brown ahead 52% to 47% among 1,592 likely voters.
Brown lost his reelection bid in 2024 to Republican Bernie Moreno, who got 50.1% of the vote against Brown's 46.5%. Trump carried Ohio by approximately 11 percentage points in the same election.
Brown has made his opposition to the building of new data centers a pillar of his campaign, while Husted has blasted Democratic policies on energy and immigration.
Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan faces former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola in a state that uses ranked-choice voting.
A Data for Progress survey done on Oct. 8-16 showed Peltola getting 47% of first-choice support, compared with 44% for Sullivan, among 694 likely voters.
A separate Public Policy Polling survey done on Oct. 14-15 showed Peltola leading Sullivan 48% to 47% among 578 registered voters, within its 4.1-point margin of error.
Sullivan won reelection in 2020 with approximately 54% of the vote, defeating independent Al Gross, who received 41%.
Alaska is a heavily Republican-leaning state, but the high price of gas and diesel fuel – already higher than in the 48 contiguous US states – since the start of the Iran war has squeezed many households, and could cause some voters to rethink their choices.
Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson is facing Democratic state lawmaker Josh Turek for the seat being vacated by Republican Sen. Joni Ernst.
An InsiderAdvantage poll done on Oct. 21-22 showed Hinson leading Turek 47% to 45% among 1,200 likely voters.
A Marist survey done on Oct. 8-11 showed Turek ahead 48% to 45% among likely voters, highlighting differences between recent surveys.
Ernst secured reelection in 2020 with 51.8% of the vote against Democrat Theresa Greenfield's 45.2%.
Trump carried Iowa by approximately 13 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.
Farmers are a large constituency in Iowa, and many who supported Trump two years ago are unhappy about the impact of tariffs and high fuel prices on their wallets.
Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, nearly a century ago.
An InsiderAdvantage poll done on Oct. 13-14 showed Marshall leading Hamilton 48% to 47% among 1,200 likely voters.
An earlier YouGov poll done Sept. 24-Oct. 4 put Hamilton ahead 48% to 45%.
The race has attracted an estimated $71 million in planned political advertising, according to The Associated Press, as both parties invest heavily in a state Trump carried by approximately 16 percentage points in 2024.
Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper faces Michael Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chairman, for the seat being vacated by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.
A Quantus Insights poll done on Oct. 24-25 showed Cooper leading Whatley 51.4% to 42.8% among 722 likely voters, with 3.4% undecided.
A separate Harper Polling survey done on Oct. 20 showed Cooper ahead 49% to 39%.
National Republicans recently pulled their campaign spending from North Carolina, signaling they have conceded the seat as likely lost.
North Carolina was closely contested in the 2024 presidential election, when Trump received 50.86% of the vote against Harris' 47.65%.

Georgia: Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff faces Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a state Trump won in 2024.

New Hampshire: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas faces former Republican Sen. John Sununu for the seat being vacated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen. A Rasmussen Reports poll done on Oct. 20-23 showed Pappas leading 50% to 44% among likely voters.
Nebraska: Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts faces independent candidate Dan Osborn. A GBAO poll done on Oct. 18-22 showed Osborn leading 46% to 45% among 800 likely voters, within the margin of error. Several injured as two trains crash in Spain, authorities say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:17:23 UTC
18:17:23 KST

High-speed train crash in Spain leaves at least 68 dead, dozens injured, officials say
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers continue searching the wreckage for survivors and bodies.
The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Padilla told state broadcaster TVE the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January. Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride.
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focused on rescuing survivors and bodies from the most damaged train cars.
"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Another passenger recounted to Cadena Ser radio how she felt the train slam on the brakes and was thrown forward in her seat, breaking the small table in front of her. She said she saw body parts and trapped people covered in blood.
The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

15,000 skiers and top teams from more than 25 countries train at Snow Valley in Limburg (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:17:07 UTC
18:17:07 KST

During the summer months, around 15,000 skiers come to train at Snow Valley in Peer (Limburg Province). These are not just any skiers; they are members of top international teams. They come from more than 25 countries and every continent, from Africa over Asia to North America and Oceania are represented. On Friday afternoon, the indoor ski centre switches over to the winter season. From Saturday onwards, it will once again be open to the general public for skiing and snowboarding.
15,000 skiers and top teams from more than 25 countries train at Snow Valley in Limburg (VIDEO)
All these nationalities come to Peer for the perfect snow quality. “It’s very close to the quality found at the very highest level, such as in World Cups, European Cups and at the Olympic Games,” says Bart Molin of Snow Valley.
Snow reliability is also a factor. “If you go to a glacier, there’s occasionally bad weather or not enough snow. Then it can happen that you can’t train on some days. In Peer, the weather is stable. It never snows or rains.”
Icy slope
The slope in Peer is made icy, as professional teams seek out those icy conditions. During competitions, organisers treat the snow with water to ensure the conditions are as fair as possible for both early and late starters.
“That’s why we treat the slope with water every week,” Bart continues. “People ski down the slope about 5,000 times a day. That causes it to wear down, and the more it’s skied on, the slipperier it gets. So, we do put a lot of time into it.”
One section of the slope is reserved for youth teams and skiers of a slightly lower standard. There, the snow is natural, just like in the Alps.
Switchover to winter
To prepare for the winter season, all the ice is removed from the slope. The slope closes from Friday afternoon, and the team works late into the night.
The team does not spray new snow onto the layer of ice. “The ice is ground down,” says Bart. “The PistenBully easily takes 6 to 7 hours to do this, until all the ice has turned back into snow. That way, there will once again be snow for recreational skiers from Saturday onwards.”
A PistenBully is a brand of large, tracked vehicle—commonly known as a snowcat. It is used to flatten, compact, and churn snow on ski slopes to create smooth surfaces and the classic "corduroy" look.

Two European leaders called Putin. Why did it cause such a stir?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
09:17:02 UTC
18:17:02 KST

Two European leaders called Putin. Why did it cause such a stir?
The phone call on Tuesday by the leaders of Finland and Norway to Russian President Vladimir Putin caught many by surprise.
Until then, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who took office in early 2024, had never spoken with his Russian counterpart. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, meanwhile, had last spoken with Putin in March 2022 – more than four and a half years ago, when the Ukraine crisis, Russia’s confrontation with the West, and the global geopolitical landscape looked very different.
But the element of surprise was far from the only remarkable thing about this call to the Kremlin.
Equally striking was the pointedly conciliatory tone of Stubb’s statement. Finland joined NATO shortly before he became president, then proceeded on his watch to bury its neutrality and descend into anti-Russian hysteria and paranoia.
This time, Stubb sounded like a different man. He described his conversation with Putin this way: “The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.” Store issued a similar statement, as though the two leaders had copied their carefully chosen words from each other.
The biggest surprise, however – if not an outright bombshell – was Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s revelation that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had no mandate whatsoever to speak on behalf of their European allies.
“I’m very skeptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn’t been coordinated with any of the rest of us,” Frederiksen warned. “I honestly don’t know what those two countries think they can achieve with this,” she added, making little effort to conceal her frustration or irritation.
Store later disputed her criticism, saying that all partners and allies had been informed ahead of the call and given a detailed briefing afterward.
Which raises the question: What was this, really? A mutiny aboard the European ship, with two Nordic leaders breaking ranks with Europe’s consensus-based decision-making and daring to take the initiative in talks with Moscow, going over the heads of the European bureaucracy?
Or was it a coordinated performance, with European leaders deliberately playing good cop and bad cop – keeping tensions with Moscow high while cautiously exploring an exit strategy, as the Ukrainian burden they can neither carry nor abandon falls apart before their eyes?
After all, Europe’s collective budget is coming apart at the seams, with every attempt to plug one hole opening another. Germany, Ukraine’s biggest European donor, is grumbling ever more loudly and trying to shift the burden onto others. So far, no volunteers are in sight.
Still, it is too early to speak of a change in Europe’s mood.
That much was clear from the meeting of E5 defense ministers held in Paris the previous day. The group brings together France, Britain, Italy, Germany, and Poland.
“Our countries share the assessment that Russia represents the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability,” read the E5 communiqué published by the French Defense Ministry.
And yet Stubb and Store’s call to the Kremlin is a wake-up call from Europe for Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky – a loud and unwelcome one.
It is a reminder to Zelensky that metal fatigue is setting in across Europe’s political machinery – and that time is running out for the regime in Kiev.

NATO spots Russian submarine in the High North
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

09:15:36 GMT
18:15:36 KST

A Russian Kilo class submarine has been observed in the High North by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1, according to NATO Maritime Command.
The command said: “SPOTTED: A Russian Kilo-class submarine in the High North, observed by Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 (SNMG1).
“Anti-submarine warfare is a team effort. Ships, submarines, aircraft and helicopters from across the Alliance work together every day to detect, track and, if necessary, counter any threat beneath the surface. Our posture is defensive, our readiness is credible, and our resolve is clear: to deter aggression and keep our one billion people across Europe and North America safe.”
Standing NATO Maritime Group 1 is one of the alliance’s permanently available naval forces, drawing warships from member navies on rotation and operating principally in the North Atlantic and northern European waters. The Royal Navy contributes to it regularly and has commanded it in the past.
The Kilo class is a diesel-electric attack submarine built in large numbers from the 1980s, and the improved Project 636.3 boats are quiet enough on batteries to have earned the nickname Black Hole from American analysts. Russia operates them in the Northern Fleet, the Baltic, the Black Sea and the Pacific, and the type carries torpedoes, mines and the Kalibr land attack cruise missile.
The Defence Committee reported this month that Britain does not have what it needs in the High North, urging ministers to retain Type 23 frigates until the Type 26 arrives and questioning whether the Royal Navy’s attack submarines are putting to sea as often as they should. The committee also called for the return of under-ice submarine skills and warned that Britain sells its nuclear contribution to NATO short.
HMS Prince of Wales is currently in the Arctic and North Atlantic on the second phase of Operation Firecrest with the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless, carrying Merlin Mk2 anti-submarine helicopters among her air group, and RAF Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft operate over the northern approaches from Lossiemouth. NATO warships began the current High North deployment earlier in the year.
