Chalmers lowers hopes for fuel discounts after high inflation result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:12:09 UTC
14:12:09 KST

Jim Chalmers resists blame for another high inflation result
In short:
Jim Chalmers says the government's budget is not the main driver of inflation, but acknowledges today's figures are still "too high".
The treasurer has downplayed the likelihood of further fuel tax discounts, citing budget pressures.
What's next?
The Reserve Bank is considered likely to hike interest rates when its monetary policy board meets on Tuesday.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is urging "perspective", with today's disappointing inflation result making another rate hike a near certainty.
Facing fresh accusations from the opposition that a government "spending addiction" is putting pressure on inflation, Mr Chalmers repeated his longstanding insistence that the government's budget was playing "a helpful role" and was not a "primary driver".
"There are other factors at play," he told reporters today, naming the Middle East war and a surprising burst of private investment in data centres and other areas.
"For every five dollars of demand in our economy, four dollars [are] private and one dollar is public. I think that's an important bit of perspective when it comes to some of the commentary that is around today," he said.
"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … We accept our part in the fight against inflation. We take responsibility for government policy when it comes to the fiscal settings."
Odds of Cup Day rate hike increase
Today's inflation figures confirm the glum prognosis of RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser, who last week warned that inflation was on track to be "materially worse" than the 3.5 per cent the bank forecast in August.
That forecast was for "underlying" inflation for the September quarter, the bank's preferred measure because it is smoother. The actual result was 3.7 per cent.
Economists responded by dialling up their expectations of a rate hike next Tuesday, which KPMG's Brendan Rynne called "locked and loaded" and Deloitte Access Economics' Stephen Smith called the "best bet on Melbourne Cup Day".
Markets also upgraded their expectations of a rate hike to 87 per cent next Tuesday, and fully "priced in" a hike by the end of the year, indicating a belief that a rate hike is a near-certainty in December, if not November.
Another rate hike of 25 basis points would take the rate to 4.85 per cent, its highest level since 2008.
Treasury secretary backs up budget
The Coalition pursued the government over spending levels in Question Time and in Senate estimates today, where Treasury Secretary Jenny Wilkinson backed up Mr Chalmers' assessment that the budget was not a main driver.
"We can only control what we can control," she said, adding that recent budget updates had "taken some pressure from the government out of the economy" by consistently reducing the size of the budget deficits.
"We have seen public demand coming off … The thing that we have been surprised by has been that private demand in the economy has been stronger than we expected."
Pressed by Liberal deputy Jane Hume about the overall level of government spending, which remains at levels rarely seen outside of recessions, Ms Wilkinson said it was important to consider the kind of spending, not just the overall amount.
A similar point was made by RBA Governor Michele Bullock, who maintained her policy of refraining from direct comment on the government's budgets, but named private sector activity, global pressures, and poor productivity as primary drivers of inflation.
"Continued weak productivity growth means that the economy cannot grow strongly without putting pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone's real spending power over the next few years," she said.
Further cost of living relief unlikely
Mr Chalmers downplayed any suggestion that the government would resume its fuel excise discount, despite the continue growth in fuel prices.
"The budget can't afford to do that forever," he said.
"We try to be up front with people and say we need to make sure that when we provide cost of living relief, it's not counterproductive.
"[We must] strike the most effective balance between the pressures on the budget, the pressures on people, and the pressures on our economy."
He labelled the Middle East war "disastrous for Australians, for cost of living, and … around the world" and said it was "absolutely turbocharging" inflation.
"From an economic point of view, the end of the war in the Middle East can't come soon enough."
Speaking in Question Time, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said economic difficulties were "not going to be solved overnight" but that the government would "continue to do everything we can to shield Australians from the worst of the impact."
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said government spending had made Australia "completely vulnerable to international factors" and reiterated calls for a fuel discount offset by further spending cuts.

Netanyahu, Eisenkot deadlocked as Israel election delivers no clear winner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:06:00 UTC
14:06:00 KST

Israel’s election has left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and opposition challenger Gadi Eisenkot without a clear path to power, as exit polls showed their blocs deadlocked despite record turnout and significant gains by Arab Israeli parties.
Eisenkot, a 66-year-old former military chief, vowed Wednesday to move quickly to form a government, saying voters had rejected Netanyahu’s divisive leadership.
Netanyahu, meanwhile, called for a strong right-wing government and highlighted the prospect of renewed military action against Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump.
Neither leader claimed victory. Exit polls from Israel’s three major television networks showed the competing blocs close to evenly matched, with neither securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Kan 11 and Channel 13 projected a 51-51 tie, while Channel 12 gave Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc a narrow 52-49 advantage. Final results were expected Thursday or Friday, leaving the country facing potentially prolonged coalition negotiations or another election.
Speaking to supporters in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said the public had delivered a vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and urged the longtime prime minister to retire from politics.
“The public has voted for change,” Eisenkot said. “A worthy leader would accept the people’s vote of no confidence and announce his retirement from political life today.”
He also warned Netanyahu against using national security to advance his political interests, raising concerns about the prospect of renewed military action against Iran while the government’s future remained uncertain.
“Netanyahu, don’t you dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu did not immediately address supporters after the initial projections. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, an ally of the prime minister, dismissed the opposition’s victory claims as premature.
Arab Israeli parties made some of the strongest gains, with exit polls projecting a combined 17 to 18 seats. Their increased representation could prove decisive in determining whether Netanyahu’s coalition returns to power.
Turnout reached 77.7%, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, the highest in more than two decades and about 7 percentage points above the 2022 election.
The strong participation included a surge among Palestinian citizens of Israel, many of whom voted to prevent Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition from returning to government.
At the headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of Arab parties, supporters celebrated as exit polls were released. Faten Gattas, a candidate for the alliance, pledged continued opposition to occupation and racism.
“We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” she said in Nazareth.
Mansour Abbas, a prominent Arab Israeli political leader, said the right-wing camp had suffered a major defeat and indicated he was open to working with Eisenkot.
However, Eisenkot has largely ruled out forming a government with Arab lawmakers, complicating his route to power. Their parties could still support a minority government in parliamentary votes without formally joining a coalition.
Far-right leader Itamar Ben Gvir warned Netanyahu against forming a unity government with Eisenkot, calling such a move a mistake. Ben Gvir, a prominent supporter of Jewish settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich were projected to win a combined 13 seats, short of the gains some had expected.
Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said Ben Gvir’s polarizing campaign had helped mobilize Arab Israeli voters.
“Even if Netanyahu lost, that doesn’t mean Eisenkot won,” Rahat said.
The election was held in the shadow of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas incursion, which killed about 1,200 people in Israel and saw 251 others taken hostage, according to Israeli figures.
The attack triggered the Gaza genocide and wider regional conflicts involving Hezbollah in Lebanon and Iran.
Netanyahu campaigned on his security record, arguing that Israeli military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iranian targets had made the country safer. He also emphasized his relationship with Trump as an opportunity to confront Iran.
Addressing Likud supporters in Jerusalem early Wednesday, Netanyahu said Israel faced a historic opportunity to eliminate what he described as the Iranian threat.
“Israel faces a singular historical opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat of Iran once and for all,” he said.
Eisenkot, who joined Netanyahu’s wartime government after the Hamas attack before resigning about eight months later, challenged the prime minister’s authority to make major security decisions without a clear public mandate.
He urged the security establishment to resist attempts to put political interests ahead of national security.
Despite presenting himself as a centrist on domestic politics, Eisenkot maintains a hawkish position on Palestinian issues. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas’ military wing must be destroyed or dismantled.
He has described Israel’s campaign in Gaza as a failure because Hamas remains in control. Gaza health authorities have reported more than 74,000 Palestinian deaths during the war.
The exit polls suggested a major setback for Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious coalition, which once held 68 seats but appeared far short of a majority.
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 years across several terms and has repeatedly survived political crises. After four inconclusive elections in two years, his opponents briefly removed him from office in 2021. He returned to power in December 2022.
His latest campaign included sharp attacks on Arab Israeli voters. Netanyahu accused them of trying to “steal the election,” while his Likud party unsuccessfully sought to keep polling stations open beyond their scheduled 10:00 p.m. closing time.
The opposition accused him of seeking grounds to challenge the results. Netanyahu also alleged that three senior officials from the United Arab List had been arrested in southern Israel with envelopes of cash. Election authorities described the incident as an isolated local case.
Netanyahu entered the election facing criticism over intelligence failures that allowed the Oct. 7 attack and longstanding corruption charges, which he denies. He also faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant related to the Gaza war.
His government’s policies have deepened Israel’s international isolation amid the war in Gaza, expanding settlements and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Eisenkot, meanwhile, has drawn public sympathy after losing his son Gal, who was killed fighting in Gaza, and two nephews during the war. Before voting, he privately visited his son’s grave.
The son of working-class Moroccan Jewish immigrants, Eisenkot would become Israel’s first prime minister of Middle Eastern or North African descent if he forms a government.
The election’s outcome remains uncertain as votes are counted and smaller parties prepare to negotiate their role in the next government.
Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, described the exit polls as a major blow to Netanyahu’s coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner.
The deadlock could allow Netanyahu to remain caretaker prime minister during lengthy negotiations. If neither camp can assemble a governing majority, another election may be necessary.
Some Israelis returned from abroad to vote. Eilana Zisblit, 55, who has lived in Canada for nearly three decades, traveled to Israel to support a center-right party in Eisenkot’s bloc.
“The country is going in a really, really bad direction,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP), saying the situation affected Jews and Arabs in Israel as well as Jews abroad.
Eisenkot has urged political leaders to avoid another election, arguing that the record turnout demonstrated the public’s desire for change.

Ex-SC judge Justice Kaul flags ‘punishment’ of prolonged custody before conviction
NEW DELHI: Former Supreme Court judge Sanjay Kishan Kaul has said that the period before conviction or acquittal has become a "punishment" in India, commenting on the denial of bail to Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam. He said that prolonged legal proceedings can themselves become a form of punishment and that bail should generally be the norm.In an interview with news agency ANI, Kaul said he had generally taken a liberal view on bail, but acknowledged that certain laws explicitly restrict the granting of bail in specific cases."I have taken a generally very liberal view on bail. I feel the bail cannot be the punishment. The conviction is the punishment. In our system, unfortunately, the pre-conviction or acquittal period itself becomes a punishment. The process becomes a punishment," former Supreme Court judge said.Kaul said several judges had raised concerns about the issue. He also referred to a judgment written by Justice Sundaresh, with whom he had dealt with the question of bail and the principles governing custody."And many judges have been writing and talking about it. In fact, I, sitting with Justice Sundaresh, had dealt elaborately with the bail itself, trying to say, why are you people under custody? Justice Sundaresh wrote the judgment.
He's, to my mind, a liberal judge on this. And we tried to lay down norms, etc., which were already in existence, but trying to, you know, until this case. So in most cases, our view is, that bail should be the norm. But there are certain acts which prohibit bail," said Kaul.Kaul has co-authored an upcoming memoir, Without Fear or Favour, with Jay Vinayak Ojha. The book is scheduled for release on October 31.Khalid and Imam are accused under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA) in connection with an alleged larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots. According to the prosecution, the violence left 53 people dead and more than 700 injured.The riots broke out amid protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, and the proposed National Register of Citizens.On January 5 this year, the Supreme Court denied bail to Khalid and Imam in the case related to the alleged conspiracy behind the 2020 riots. In its judgment, the court observed that the two accused stood on a "qualitatively different footing" in terms of the prosecution's case and the evidence against them.In September, the Delhi high court had also rejected their bail pleas. The case stems from FIR 59/2020, registered by the Delhi Police Special Cell to investigate the alleged larger conspiracy behind the February 2020 northeast Delhi riots.
‘Met him only a couple of times’: Justice Kaul on Saurav Das
Meanwhile, former Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Kishan Kaul also clarified his association with Cockroach Janta Party activist Saurav Das, saying he had met him only a couple of times when Das was working as a journalist and had advised him to "taper down a little" in his language.Justice Kaul told news agency ANI that a photograph of him with Das, taken at a Diwali gathering about a year ago, was being used to suggest that he shared a particular ideology."So, it was one year ago. He was not even in the news then," Justice Kaul said, explaining how the meeting came about.
"He was a journalist, maybe met me a couple of times. He was insistent that I must, at Diwali time, come. I was going somewhere else. I said, 'Okay, I'll drop in for ten minutes.' I told my wife, 'Have a cup of coffee, I'll drop in for ten minutes, and then we'll go.' That's all that happened," he said.Asked whether he had mentored Das at any point, Justice Kaul denied doing so, while acknowledging that he had advised the activist on his choice of words."I was not mentoring him, but once or twice he met me, I told him that, I will always tell you to taper down a little in your language," he said.Justice Kaul added that differences in language and expression across generations could sometimes cause discomfort, particularly among those accustomed to more civil forms of conversation.

Alishan Forest Railway campaign wins Japan's Good Design Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:01:23 UTC
14:01:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Alishan Forest Railway's campaign celebrating the full reopening of the century-old line has won Japan's 2026 Good Design Award, recognizing its use of contemporary design to promote Taiwan's railway heritage.
The Alishan Forest Railway and Cultural Heritage Office announced the award on Monday, saying the campaign combined visual design, cultural activities, and commemorative merchandise to present the railway's history to a wider audience, per a press release.
Judges praised the campaign for maintaining a consistent visual identity across its events and promotional materials while reinterpreting traditional railway culture through contemporary aesthetics. Elements included original dance performances, Japanese woodblock print-style visuals (ukiyo-e), and specially designed souvenirs.
The railway resumed full-line service on July 6, 2024, after a 15-year interruption caused by typhoon damage. The reopening restored direct train service between Chiayi and Alishan. Celebratory events included a completion ceremony for Tunnel No. 42, a full-line reopening ceremony, and a market combining railway culture, forestry products, and art.
The campaign also extended the railway's identity into everyday life through limited-edition “120,000 Happiness” iPASS cards, commemorative ticket gift boxes, and stamps featuring station landscapes. Searchlight Culture Lab carried out the marketing project, per the press release.
The Good Design Award was established in 1957 and is organized by the Japan Institute of Design Promotion. The 2026 competition received 5,111 entries, according to the railway office.
The Alishan Forest Railway, which has operated for more than a century, is a designated cultural heritage asset in Taiwan. The award highlights efforts to combine heritage preservation, tourism, and contemporary design.

Taiwan economics minister defends energy subsidies to curb inflation

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Economics Minister Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) on Wednesday defended government subsidies for state-owned energy companies, saying that fully passing on higher energy costs to consumers could push Taiwan's annual inflation rate above 3%.
Kung told reporters at the legislature that annual consumer price index growth is about 2%. Citing estimates from the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics, he said a 10% increase in international oil prices would raise the CPI by 0.24% if passed on to consumers, while a 10% increase in electricity prices would raise it by 0.27%, per CNA.
He urged lawmakers to support continued budget allocations to Taipower and CPC Corp. to help stabilize energy prices and protect households and small businesses.
He said the two state-owned companies provide essential electricity and fuel while absorbing costs from rising international energy prices, which have contributed to their financial losses. Government funding has helped shore up their finances and maintain stable domestic supplies, he said.
Kung rejected opposition criticism that Taipower's losses stemmed from flawed energy policies, arguing that surging global energy prices had created similar challenges for other countries.
He said governments have responded in different ways, with some allocating public funds to subsidize state-owned energy providers and others freezing domestic energy prices to shield consumers from higher costs.
According to Ministry of Economic Affairs data, Japan and Indonesia have each allocated more than NT$500 billion (US$15.41 billion) to stabilize domestic energy costs, while South Korea has allocated about NT$130 billion for subsidies, per CNA.
Kung said Taiwan's subsidies were intended to balance the financial stability of state-owned enterprises with the need to keep energy affordable. Without government intervention, higher international prices would be passed on to households and businesses, increasing pressure on living costs and inflation.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said Tuesday that intellectuals with a conscience would support an online appeal reportedly signed by students at more than a dozen Chinese universities calling for an end to Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s indefinite tenure.
The appeal reportedly circulated on university forums, including those at Peking University, as the Chinese Communist Party’s Fifth Plenum opened in Beijing on Monday, per Liberty Times. Posts containing the appeal were quickly deleted, but screenshots later appeared on the dark web and continued spreading on social media platforms outside China.
Radio Free Asia reported that the appeal called for restoring presidential term limits, convening a national constitutional amendment conference, and protecting space for public discussion. The website hosting the letter listed South Korea as its country or region and gave a Singapore mailing address, while the administrator’s email was registered on a Tencent server and the listed phone number and WeChat account were linked to China.
Chiu recalled meeting Chinese intellectuals during the 19th Communist Party Congress in 2017, Liberty Times reported. He said some scholars told him that 95% of Chinese intellectuals would oppose abandoning the leadership succession system and allowing Xi to remain in power beyond the customary transition.
Chiu said intellectuals’ ability to correct the party’s mistakes had disappeared after Xi consolidated power. He added that the appeal reflected the conscience of intellectuals and that, although its authenticity remained uncertain, “any intellectual with a conscience would support the appeal.”

Why Hong Kong developer CK Asset sold a mall at an ‘exceptionally cheap’ price
New owner will struggle to find tenants for shops off the beaten path in Sham Shui Po, analysts say
With the “exceptionally cheap” sale of a vacant Hong Kong shopping mall, developer CK Asset Holdings is freeing up capital for other projects, while the buyer will have to be patient because the location will struggle to attract tenants in the short term, according to analysts.
The developer completed the mall in its residential project Seaside Sonata on Hai Tan Street in Sham Shui Po five years ago but never leased it out. Obra Blanca 2026 brought together more than 23,000 industry professionals in its seventh edition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Direct contact with a material allows one to appreciate textures, compare finishes, and observe how its appearance changes under different lighting conditions. At an exhibition, these possibilities are complemented by exchanges with manufacturers and professionals, helping to understand applications and resolve questions about their use. This relationship between material exploration and architectural practice was one of the central pillars of the seventh edition of Obra Blanca, which drew more than 23,000 professionals to Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
Featuring 190 exhibitors across 13 pavilions and 28,620 m² of exhibition space, the event showcased finishes and products for architecture and interior design. The exhibition was accompanied by a program of conferences, forums, and technical talks, alongside a new digital tool designed to consult and organize product information both during and after the visit.
The exhibition spaces offered diverse ways to engage with the products, ranging from material sample exploration to installations showcasing combinations of colors, textures, and finishes. Their layout provided context for understanding how these elements could be integrated into a project and interact with other components of a space.
"The booths are looking increasingly professional, with highly designed, experiential layouts. So, I think it is highly worthwhile to come and experience it firsthand," commented Nadja Borrás of Gensler.
The event also succeeded in bringing suppliers and professionals together in one place to discuss the featured solutions. For architects and interior designers, this exchange complements the technical information found in catalogs and product spec sheets with discussions tailored to the specific needs of their projects.
Spaces for Professional Exchange
The program brought together 70 specialists and featured three international lectures, four national ones, four forums with international guests, and twelve technical talks. Developed in partnership with 32 strategic allies, the agenda expanded the gathering beyond a simple product showcase, creating spaces to share experiences and discuss industry challenges.
For Christele Harrouk, Editor-in-Chief of ArchDaily, the value of the gathering also lies in this professional dialogue: "Beyond presenting products and innovations, I believe one of the event's greatest strengths is the space it creates to discuss architectural practice and the challenges currently facing the profession."
Harrouk spoke with Paula Villar Pastor, co-founder of the Peruvian association Espacio Común, about the Main Floating Stage of Muyunafest 2025, which won first place in ArchDaily's 2026 Building of the Year Award. Their conversation explored how regional conditions, local knowledge, and community collaboration guide design decisions. "Our conversation addressed a broader challenge that architecture faces today: how to respond to increasingly complex social and environmental realities without losing sight of the practical realities of construction," Harrouk noted.
Fernando Lozano Assad, President of Obra Blanca and Director of TCNA Mexico (Tile Council of North America-Mexico), highlighted the collective effort behind the program: "At Obra Blanca, we have always championed knowledge and community spirit. Building an activities agenda like this is the result of the collaborative drive among our 32 partnerships."
The Espacio Obra Blanca, designed by Augusto Quijano Axle, hosted sixteen expert interviews and showcased the Obra Blanca 2027 CMF Dynamic exhibition, titled La tendencia es emocionar (The Trend is to Emotion). Organized in partnership with La Jabonera Centro de Diseño, this initiative brought together twelve architecture and interior design firms from Guanajuato, Querétaro, and San Luis Potosí to explore color, materials, and finishes.
From Exhibition to Specification
One of the key additions to this edition was OB ESPECIFICA, a free digital tool designed for architects, interior designers, and specifiers. Using QR codes, it allows users to access technical specifications for the exhibited products, save selections, and organize them by project.
The platform also offers options to share these selections with design teams and contact sales representatives. Its purpose is to streamline post-event product research, ensuring that information gathered during the visit remains easily accessible when returning to design and specification work.
In this way, the combination of physical samples, professional dialogue, and technical information formed the backbone of the various activities at Obra Blanca 2026. The next edition will take place from October 12 to 14, 2027, at Expo Santa Fe in Mexico City.
For more information, visit the official Obra Blanca website.

Iran ready to expand electricity connection with reg. states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:57:13 UTC
13:57:13 KST

Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said at the 30th Belarusian Energy and Ecology Forum.
The Iranian energy minister emphasized Iran has established electricity connections with its western neighbors and with Pakistan and Afghanistan to the east, adding that links with Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkey and Iraq are also in place.
Iran is seeking to connect its electricity network to Russia through a neighboring country, Aliabadi stressed.
He said that regional cooperation is increasingly important as electricity demand rises, particularly with the growth of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
He also highlighted the need to expand energy storage and electricity interconnections to balance power generation, distribution and consumption.
The minister said Iran's electricity generation capacity has grown from 7,000 megawatts at the time of the 1979 Islamic Revolution to nearly 97,000 megawatts. He added that Iran manufactures power plant equipment domestically and exports such equipment to regional countries.
Aliabadi said Iran remains committed to developing its electricity industry and is prepared to cooperate with other countries and make use of their capabilities despite sanctions and war.

Elections in Israel: Up to 480,000 ballots remain to be counted, the equivalent of approximately 12 seats in the Knesset
The Israeli Central Elections Commission estimates that between 430,000 and 480,000 so-called "double-envelope" ballots were cast in the parliamentary elections, a figure significantly lower than the 600,000 initially reported. These votes came primarily from soldiers, police officers, prisoners, and diplomats stationed abroad, as well as other voters who cast their ballots outside their usual polling stations. The ballots are counted separately after verification to prevent double voting. According to the Commission, these estimates remain provisional and could still change. With each Knesset seat representing approximately 40,000 votes, these ballots are equivalent to about a dozen seats and could alter the political balance. At this stage, Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is credited with 53 seats, compared to 48 for the predominantly Jewish opposition parties. Neither side has reached the 61 seats needed for an absolute majority. The full count is expected Thursday afternoon, while the final official results are due to be published on November 4.

Centre deputes a high-level team to investigate death of Cheetah, caused by firearm pellet injuries, in Madhya Pradesh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:41:18 UTC
13:41:18 KST

19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25
NEW DELHI: The Centre on Wednesday deputed a high-level team to investigation the death of a 19-month-old male Cheetah of Kuno National Park, Madhya Pradesh, caused by firearm pellet injuries.The team has been tasked with undertaking a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to the death of the Cheetah, examining all available evidence and coordinating closely with the Madhya Pradesh forest department to ensure strict and swift action in the matter.The 19-month-old radio-collared male cheetah, an offspring of Namibia-born Cheetah Nirva, was found injured on Oct 25 in the territorial forests of Morena, outside the protected area of Kuno National Park. Preliminary medical examinations corroborated multiple internal injuries associated with the firearm pellets.The incident, the first reported casualty of a shooting since PM Narendra Modi launched Project Cheetah at Kuno in Sept, 2022, is being viewed quite seriously at the Centre, given the critical importance of Project Cheetah and the need to ensure the highest standards of protection for the reintroduced population of the Big Cat.
“As reported by the MP forest department, the injured cheetah was rescued from the Sheopur Territorial Forest Division the same day and provided intensive veterinary care and emergency surgery at the veterinary facility in Jabalpur. During the surgery, five firearm pellets were recovered from its body. Despite the medical intervention, the Cheetah succumbed to its injuries on Oct 27,” said the Union environment ministry in a statement.It said, “The state govt has already constituted a Special Task Force (STF), comprising forest and police officers, to investigate the incident. The central team deputed by the Union environment ministry would work in coordination with the state machinery. It would also examine the implementation of security protocols, as well as monitoring and protection measures being undertaken to avoid any such incident in future.
“The central team would submit its findings and recommendations to the ministry for further directions to the state govt and field authorities.”The central team comprises the Inspector General of Forests, National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA), Additional Director, Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB), and Regional Deputy Director, WCCB.

China dismisses Taiwan’s accusations of involvement in comedian attack
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:32:45 CET
13:32:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Taiwan is “provoking confrontation” and stirring anti-China sentiment, a Chinese government spokesperson said on Wednesday, after Taiwanese prosecutors indicted five people for plotting to attack a Taiwanese comedian whose shows mocked Beijing.
Taiwan, the democratically governed island that China claims as its own territory, has accused Beijing of trying to use “transnational repression” against people in Taiwan the Chinese government views as separatists or politically suspect.
Taiwan’s government says China was behind last month’s attack on comedian Huang Yi-hao, who satirised Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Speaking at a regular news conference in Beijing and asked about the incident, Taiwan Affairs Office spokesperson Chen Binhua dismissed Taiwan’s accusations as a fabrication by its ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
“The so-called transnational repression narrative is essentially a way of promoting Taiwan independence and peddling a two-state theory, and it is trotted out every time there is an election on the island,” he said, referring to next month’s local elections in Taiwan.
“The DPP fabricates all kinds of pretexts out of thin air, maliciously smears the mainland, stirs up anti-China sentiment, and provokes cross-strait confrontation, all in an attempt to win political power by misleading the Taiwanese public,” Chen said.
This is a “tired routine” repeated year after year, he added.
Taiwan prosecutors said the defendants, whose full names it has not provided, were paid to fake a car accident and “break the arms and legs” of Huang so he could not perform, though in the end he was only lightly injured.
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, in a report delivered to lawmakers earlier on Wednesday, said the case of Huang and others showed what he described as China’s expanding efforts to “challenge people’s personal safety, freedom of expression, and the resilience of democratic society.”
Other China critics in Taiwan have also been attacked, including Hong Kong singer and activist Denise Ho in 2019.
Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.
(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Additional reporting by Ben Blanchard in Taipei; Editing by Kate Mayberry)

Indonesia beefs up security presence to prepare for student protests
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
05:32:30 CET
13:32:30 KST

By Stanley Widianto
JAKARTA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Hundreds of Indonesian students and civil society groups staged protests on Wednesday in cities including the capital Jakarta against President Prabowo Subianto’s policies, including the handling of ongoing forest fires.
Worsened by the El Niño weather pattern that leaves peatland vulnerable to fires, Indonesia has been faced with its worst forest fires, and resulting haze, in 11 years, increasing respiratory illnesses and polluting the air of neighbouring countries Malaysia and Singapore.
Protesters crowded a Jakarta landmark roundabout, with some wearing gas masks, holding up signs protesting over forest fires and demanding the government designate the blazes as a national disaster.
Some carried signs that said “If we burn, you burn with us,” and held up the three-finger sign of protest – references to the The Hunger Games movie that has been adopted as a symbol by many youth protest movements globally.
Anggi Aurien, 28, had been wearing a gas mask for three hours at the landmark, protesting about the forest fires that have killed wildlife.
“Animals don’t have a mind of their own. If we kill them, what’s the difference between us and them?” she said.
Other signs included photos of the orangutan, which bears the brunt of the fires, and a cardboard cutout of Prabowo.
Other students, including from the University of Indonesia, were blocked by dozens of police and military personnel, leading to some scuffles.
“Revolution! Revolution!” protesters chanted.
Ezra Al Barra, a student from the University of Padjadjaran, said the fires were “our collective anger,” adding students came from other regions outside Jakarta.
Students also rallied in Makassar, in South Sulawesi, and Bandung, in West Java, with similar demands. Dozens of them on motorbikes filled the main roads.
Protesters called for the the government halt spending on populist programmes such as Prabowo’s free meals scheme, among other demands.
Syahganda Nainggolan, chief of the government’s communications office, urged calm but said the government welcomed the protests and was open to input.
PRABOWO’S POPULARITY
The protests, the second in a week, came as Prabowo’s approval ratings had fallen steadily since late last year, according to surveys by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, two years into his presidency.
Indonesia has prosecuted companies allegedly linked to the fires and tried methods of modifying the weather to induce rain.
Indonesia’s last major protest took place in August, when hundreds were detained.
In 2025, weeks-long nationwide protests broke out in Indonesia after the police killing of a motorcycle taxi driver, with several more people killed during the unrest.
(Reporting by Stanley Widianto, Johan Purnomo, Heru Asprihanto and Ananda Teresia; Editing by David Stanway and Alex Richardson)

The influential opinion maker, along with many other right-leaning podcasters, was credited by Trump with converting young American men who were once part of the Democratic coalition.
The hunt is ongoing. A US$20 million (S$25.6 million) “Speaking with American Men” project, launched in 2025 by Democratic strategists and donors to bring them back, has one more year to finish the job.
In the meantime, there is Hasan Piker.
The 35-year-old political commentator and live streamer was something of a kingmaker for insurgent left-wing candidates during the Democratic Party primaries earlier in 2026, helping to test and refine the candidates’ messages, driving grassroots campaign donations and providing political visibility.
As the Democrats look to secure a congressional majority in the Nov 3 midterm elections, a left-leaning influencer like him is a source of traction.
On Oct 26, Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar turned to Piker to rev up her re-election campaign in a state that had hit international headlines for its heavy-handed immigration enforcement operations.
Omar is favoured to win, unscathed by investigations into her immigration history and allegations of abuse of welfare funds, charges she calls politically motivated. The congresswoman was born in Somalia in 1982, and her family was admitted to the US as refugees in the mid-1990s after fleeing civil war.
Still, she sought out Piker, calling his massive reach necessary to tackle a decline in early voting among under-40 progressives.
The late evening event in Minneapolis, where she conversed casually with Piker, reportedly sold out within minutes of being announced. The hour-long session, where they bashed the Trump administration and moderate Democrats, was live-streamed over Twitch, the platform where Piker has more than three million subscribers, mostly young, progressive and male.
Bespectacled and clad almost always in formal shirt, jacket and a tie, Piker goes live for around eight hours nearly every day of the week.
Self-declared socialist-Marxist
Born in New Jersey, Piker grew up in Turkey and describes himself as a cultural but not religious Muslim. His break into broadcasting, during the Covid-19 epidemic, came via his uncle Cenk Uygur, a co-founder of The Young Turks, a left-wing YouTube channel.
In between sharing his gym routine, handing out dating advice and discussing gaming, the highly articulate Piker weighs in with unrestrained emotion and expletives on the controversies of the day. The self-declared socialist-Marxist is usually lambasting Wall Street, big banks, defence and pharma companies for everything from inflation to climate change to workplace safety.
He is at his most volatile when it comes to American foreign policy. He has praised Hamas and warned that American Jewish support for Israel could prompt people to “take action” against them. He has also suggested that the US could learn from the Communist Party of China and described the collapse of the Soviet Union as one of the greatest geopolitical catastrophes of the 20th century. He has also walked back his most controversial comments that “America deserved 9/11”.
As with other streamers, outrage is a critical ingredient in his show, creating virality and deep engagement. It is also a rewarding venture, as remuneration runs into millions of dollars for the top streamers, with money coming from paid memberships, platform advertising, sponsorships, merchandise and other audience-supported products. There is a more sensitive source too: funding from advocacy groups and Democratic-aligned intermediary organisations.
To his viewers, Piker is a habit, a screen presence that validates their grievances and gives them a sense of belonging. From there, the flow into politics is seamless.
Traditional Democratic leaders are wary of Piker, but liberals like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, locked in a tight senatorial race, owe him.
During El-Sayed’s primary battle in August 2026 with sitting congresswoman Haley Stevens, Piker was a bridge to young people distrustful of the Democratic Party but amenable to a personality they watch for hours.
“One of the biggest stories of the 2026 election cycle is Hasan Piker,” said Joel Penney, an associate professor at Montclair State University who studies political communication.
The Democratic Party has had many celebrities and liberal advocates, but this turn of events is new, said Penney, the author of a 2022 book titled Pop Culture, Politics, And The News.
“This is much more interactive and more about the ongoing relationship between the fans and the streamers. Piker is responding to fans in real time, I don’t see a lot of other folks who have become famous for that format, the mix of Democratic politics and lifestyle content,” he said.
Other political commentators in the liberal sphere – such as Pod Save America, led by former Obama speechwriter Jon Favreau; MeidasTouch by a former marine and registered Republican Ron Filipkowski; and The Lincoln Project, which features moderate conservatives and former members of the Republican Party – do not command Piker’s massive numbers nor adopt his unscripted, streaming format.
Piker, inevitably, draws comparisons with Rogan and Rush Limbaugh, the conservative talk radio phenomenon who held sway for three decades starting from the early 1990s and drew a weekly audience of around 15 million.
“At their peaks, Rogan and Limbaugh had much greater audiences, in the tens of millions. I don’t think Piker is at that level. But he’s younger, and there’s always room for growth,” noted Aaron Kall, a political analyst at the University of Michigan.
Piker’s extreme views, however, can be a drag for the Democrats. Being linked with him has constrained El-Sayed’s efforts to broaden his appeal. Trump and the Republicans paint the two as fundamentalist, America-hating liberals.
“Piker’s sort of turned into a main character on Fox News reporting and conservative news outlets, which are putting him in the spotlight with the understanding that he would have a negative impact on the campaign,” Montclair's Penney told The Straits Times.
“He might be inspiring more people to vote who wouldn’t otherwise, but he may also be turning off people or encouraging people to vote for the opponent,” he said.
Will moderate swing voters be alienated?
Indeed, for the Democratic leadership, there is a real fear that the polarising Piker will alienate moderate swing voters.
El-Sayed, who is on course to becoming the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has been called to disavow Piker, but he has been reluctant, noted Kall.
“He probably perceives a double standard that right-wing influencers also say controversial things, but the Republicans don’t have to disavow them.”
With Piker by his side, El-Sayed may pick up some voters, but also lose others. In Michigan, with its sizeable Jewish and Arab American communities, that balancing act is especially sensitive.
It is probably the reason the race is very tight and the association with Piker has taken up a disproportionate amount of the campaign, noted Kall.
Penney said it is an open question if Piker can convert his sway with the notoriously unreliable young voters to turnout. “The election day results will be seen as a sort of a verdict on Piker,” he said.
Piker himself sees no risk of attrition of voters because of association with him.
“Getting people to be upset at a Twitch streamer and their affiliation... is going to be very difficult, especially when there are real crises going on in the country,” he said in an Oct 15 interview with National Public Radio, an American public broadcaster.
Democratic Party lacks ‘clear, definable policies’
The Democratic Party stands in its own way, Piker said.
“You can’t podcast your way out of this problem. The problems are with a lack of clear, definable policies that the party represents at the national level.”
The star podcaster claims that this lack of clarity is partly why the Democrats are “still largely very unpopular”.
Even though Trump is the least popular political figure, perhaps in history, Piker said.

Mahmoud Khalil credits Palestinian activism for reshaping US politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:13:28 UTC
13:13:28 KST

Mahmoud Khalil credits Palestinian activism for reshaping US politics
Khalil returned to Columbia University to discuss memoir detailing his arrest and detention by ICE agents.
Pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil says campus advocacy has shifted public perception and encouraged a generation of leaders to question their views on Israel, speaking as he returned to Columbia University for the first time since his arrest on March 8, 2025.
The 31-year-old Columbia graduate, who became a figurehead of the campus movement that swept the United States in 2024, returned to campus on Tuesday to discuss his new memoir, No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention.
“The American public is finally changing, is finally looking at the Palestinian as an equal human,” he told the AFP news agency in an interview.
While Khalil described the event, attended by about 100 people, as a “victory”, he accused university leadership of seeking “to erase me, to erase any Palestinian voices on campus”.
Some Jewish groups on social media opposed his return to campus. In response, a Columbia spokesperson said the university is “committed to rigorous debate, inquiry, and respectful dialogue across differing perspectives”.
“Columbia supports the right of faculty members to organize academic events,” the statement carried by US media read. “An invitation to speak does not signify university endorsement of a speaker’s views.”
Khalil helped lead student demonstrations at Columbia in 2024, which became the epicentre of nationwide campus protests against Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza. He was later arrested by immigration authorities at the height of a federal crackdown on foreign student activists and held for three months without criminal charge, despite holding permanent US residency.
He has repeatedly slammed the university for its handling of the demonstrations, which included authorising the New York Police Department to clear protesters from the Manhattan campus.
“They chose brutality. They chose repression,” Khalil told AFP.
Columbia maintained at the time that the demonstrations presented a safety threat. Khalil also accused the university of failing to protect him from harassment prior to his detention.
Despite the personal toll, Khalil credited Palestinian student advocacy with driving broader political shifts in the United States, pointing to gains by progressive candidates.
“Also, we can see on the ground that we have more progressive candidates being elected into US Congress and positions of power,” he said, citing candidates like Dr Abdul El-Sayed, running for the US Senate in Michigan, and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Khalil was released from immigration custody on June 20, 2025, though the Trump administration continues to seek his deportation.
“A big part of my fight is like fighting for normalcy,” he said. “To go back to being the young father who would go to the park with his son and wife, and no one would bother them.”
Despite the ongoing legal battle, he expressed resolve over his public role.
“My fight is not only about whether I get to stay in this country,” Khalil said. “It is about whether, you know, people in this country can speak their minds.”

Taiwan premier proposes NT$235.7 billion for NT$10,000 cash handout

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:07:48 UTC
13:07:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) has proposed NT$235.7 billion (US$7.4 billion) for NT$10,000 cash payments to eligible recipients under Taiwan’s 2027 central government budget.
Addressing the Legislative Yuan on Tuesday, Cho said central government revenue had exceeded expenditure for nine consecutive years since 2017, per UDN. He said the handout was intended to improve people's livelihoods and ensure that the benefits of AI-driven economic growth were shared more equitably.
Under the Cabinet's proposal, foreign nationals with permanent residency in Taiwan would be eligible for the payment, as would citizens with household registration and nationals without household registration who hold residence permits. Spouses of Taiwanese citizens from China, Hong Kong, Macau, or other countries who hold residence permits would also be eligible.
The eligibility rules generally follow those used for the government’s 2023 and 2025 cash handouts. Taiwanese government employees stationed overseas on official duty, and their dependents who hold Taiwanese nationality, would also qualify.
The 2027 central government budget projects revenue and expenditure of approximately NT$3.927 trillion each, up 13.3% and 31.5%, respectively, from the 2026 statutory budget, UDN reported. The government also plans to repay NT$179 billion in debt through new borrowing, with Cho describing the budget as balanced and requiring no net new borrowing.
Outstanding public debt is projected to reach NT$6.758 trillion by the end of 2027, including supplementary budgets, equivalent to about 23% of average nominal GDP over the previous three years. That ratio would be 2.9 percentage points lower than at the end of 2026 and well below the statutory ceiling of 40.6%, marking the lowest level since Taiwan's provincial government was downsized, Cho said.
Cho urged lawmakers from all parties to support and swiftly pass the 2027 central government budget, per TTV News. He said it would provide the resources needed to care for the public, advance infrastructure projects, maintain Taiwan’s technological lead, and safeguard national security.
In September, KMT Legislative Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) called on the government to distribute NT$20,000 to every citizen this year, arguing that excess tax revenue could cover the cost without borrowing. KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) said on Oct. 8 that the proposed NT$20,000 payment would be separate from the Cabinet's planned NT$10,000 handout next year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — China is stepping up efforts to interfere with Taiwan’s local elections, a National Security Bureau official said on Tuesday.

China’s ultimate goal is to impair people’s ability to make informed judgments and steer them toward Beijing-favored candidates, they said.
The official urged the public to remain vigilant against Chinese misinformation and to recognize that “any candidate favored by an authoritarian state will not be a good choice for a democracy.”

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Independent Legislator Ciwas Ali (高金素梅) denied all charges at her first court hearing Tuesday and asked the judge to clear her name, CNA reported.

She said her aide, Chang Chun-chieh (張俊傑), handled office administration and that she knew nothing about the alleged wrongdoing.

Defense lawyer Cheng Yu-jen (鄭昱仁) cited amendments passed by the legislature concerning public funding for lawmakers' assistants. He argued that the money was intended to help lawmakers hire staff and that Ciwas had no intention of illegally obtaining public funds, per CNA.
The case also involves allegations that Ciwas illegally imported 74,400 COVID-19 rapid test kits from China in 2022 without the required government approval. Prosecutors allege that she authorized Chang to arrange the imports using other people's names to avoid medical device regulations.
Ciwas said Indigenous communities faced severe shortages of medical supplies during the pandemic outbreak, particularly in remote areas with few pharmacies. She said she appealed for donations to help residents obtain urgently needed supplies.

Three Latino Leaders Reflect on Inspiration Across Generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:47:59 UTC
12:47:59 KST

Three leaders within their respective industries gave toasts at TIME’s Latino Leaders celebration on Tuesday night in Miami, where they each honored their cultures and the people who raised them.
Nelson German, a chef, restaurateur, and author; Julián Castro, the CEO of Latino Community Foundation, the largest Latino-serving organization in the U.S.; and actor, singer, and advocate Sofia Carson, all spoke at the event.
German, who was raised in Manhattan’s Washington Heights, reflected on the experience of growing up in a Dominican immigrant family and shying away from his language and culture as a child.
“We wanted to fit in so badly to reach that American dream,” he said. “But now things have changed … We now are embracing those parts of ourselves more fully. We are embracing our cultures, our heritage, our motherlands.”
The act of honoring one’s culture, he said, is about looking both forward and back.
“It's not just about the future; we have to honor the past. The parents and grandparents who work two, three jobs … They gave us a chance to really stand in these kinds of rooms together, so never forget about that.”
For German, who is the executive chef at acclaimed restaurants in Oakland and San Francisco, passing down Dominican culture is done through his work: food.
“The recipes, the stories, they have to stay alive,” he said. “We have to share them with our kids, with our youth … Let's keep creating opportunities for the next generation while giving them the connection to the generation before them.”
Castro also reflected on his childhood, when he was “always on the lookout for Latinas and Latinos doing great things” while growing up in San Antonio, Texas. He would read through the credits of movies, looking for names like “Garcia,” “Hernandez,” and “Rodriguez,” or scan the library for books by Latino authors.
He paid tribute to his grandmother Victoria, who came to the U.S. in 1922 from northern Mexico after her parents passed away and raised Castro’s mother as a single parent. He also honored his mother, who also raised Castro and his brother alone.
“I am sure that if we went around the room tonight, that that is a very common story here, and that each of you, like me, feels very fortunate and very blessed to have been able to achieve their dreams,” he said. “Our families … have always been strivers and hard workers and people of love, of faith, and of family, and we've always driven progress in the United States of America, and that's true today.”
Castro acknowledged what he described as a "cruelty” being aimed at immigrant and Latino families around the country, but stressed that Latinos remained an integral part of the U.S.
“The destiny of the United States and the destiny of Latinos is more intertwined than it ever has been before,” he said. “Only if Latinos succeed can America succeed in the years to come, and vice versa.”
Throughout Carson’s speech, during which she similarly reflected on those who raised and molded her, she repeated the same line several times: “To be a Latin woman is to be hope.”
She stressed the importance of hope, especially in the face of “oppression, plundering, and abandonment,” quoting the words of the Latin-American author and Nobel Prize-winner in literature Gabriel García Márquez.
Carson said that she has spent her entire life admiring her mother, who taught her poems by Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, and read her novels by Chilean-American author Isabel Allende, and sang her songs by Cuban-American singer Celia Cruz.
“To be a Latin woman is to be hope,” she repeated, honoring the crowd’s mothers, grandmothers, sisters, and daughters. “Hope lives in the DNA of who we are. It flows from our bloodstream into everything we touch. It is the beating of our hearts. It is the language of our soul.”
Latino Leaders was presented by PepsiCo.

Netanyahu, Eisenkot stake rival claims to lead Israel after deadlocked vote
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:46:25 CET
12:46:25 KST

By Rami Ayyub, Steven Scheer and Lili Bayer
JERUSALEM, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Benjamin Netanyahu looked set to remain Israel’s caretaker prime minister after unexpectedly strong backing among Jewish voters left his opponents little apparent prospect of unseating him, despite his right-wing bloc losing its parliamentary majority.
With nearly 86% of votes tallied on Wednesday, Israel’s three main broadcasters projected Netanyahu’s bloc of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties would win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, well ahead of the 48 for rival Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
Parties representing Arab Israelis were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot little realistic path to power without their broad backing, which many Jewish political leaders reject.
The results could still change as counting continued, but Eisenkot’s bloc of anti-Netanyahu parties, ranging from the centre-left to the hard right, had fallen short of pre-election polls that forecast a tight race.
Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister during any coalition negotiations and potentially until another election next year. While a caretaker government faces some constraints, experts say it retains powers, including over the war with Iran.
Guy Lurie, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, said a caretaker government formally had the same powers as a regular government, but also “a duty of restraint” and less discretion in some areas.
SECURITY FIGHT SHARPENS
Netanyahu, addressing his Likud party’s faithful after 3 a.m. (0100 GMT), called for the formation of “a strong, right-wing national government.”
He highlighted Israel’s military successes and raised the prospect of renewed joint military action against Iran alongside his ally, US President Donald Trump, saying the two countries had a “singular historical opportunity” to remove what he called the Iranian threat “once and for all.”
Trump, who had urged Israeli voters to keep Netanyahu in power so the two leaders could “finish the job” in Iran, said Netanyahu had done “very well” and claimed his endorsement had “helped him a lot.”
Israel’s high-turnout vote was brushed aside by some in the rest of the Middle East.
In Tehran, banners with images of slain Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei reminded Iranians of US and Israeli strikes launched in February which kicked off the war. Just to the right was a poster of late Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah, who was killed on Netanyahu’s orders in Lebanon.
“I genuinely see the possibility of attack,” said 50-year-old Iranian citizen Abdollah Karimi.
Frustration was also palpable in Egypt, the first Arab country to make peace with Israel in 1979.
Outhman Selim, a 62-year-old lawyer, said his hopes that a Netanyahu defeat would steer the country away from the far right had been dashed.
Eisenkot acknowledged that Netanyahu remained caretaker prime minister but warned that he might use security for political ends.
“I call on the heads of the security establishment and the civil service: Netanyahu is a caretaker prime minister, without a mandate or the people’s trust,” he said. “Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you.”
Netanyahu’s office has previously rejected accusations that he is using the Iran conflict for political gain and did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.
The prospect of a caretaker government without a parliamentary majority weighed on Israeli markets. The shekel currency weakened around 1.6% to 3.10 to the US dollar. Tel Aviv’s key benchmark stock indexes fell more than 3%.
DECISIVE SHIFT IN ISRAELI POLITICS
The result underscored the rightward shift among Israeli Jews during Netanyahu’s years as the country’s dominant political figure. The centre-left that dominated Israel for the first half of its history has been reduced to a small fringe.
Nearly all Jewish parties now share Netanyahu’s rejection of an eventual independent Palestinian state, the basis of internationally endorsed peace efforts since the 1990s.
The election was Israel’s first since Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostages in attacks on October 7, 2023, that plunged the country into wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.
The war in Gaza, which flattened the territory and killed 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities, has left Israel increasingly isolated on the world stage.
Netanyahu himself is wanted by the International Criminal Court in The Hague on war crimes charges he calls absurd, and faces corruption charges in Israel that he dismisses as an establishment plot.
Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest in more than two decades, and was particularly high among Israelis of Palestinian descent, who make up more than a fifth of the population. Many were motivated by what they see as open racism from Netanyahu’s cabinet, which includes a party leader convicted of inciting racial hatred against Arabs.
The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released. “We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Joint List candidate Faten Gattas.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu relied on one small Arab party, but Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Joint List itself. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
(Reporting by Rami Ayyub, Steven Scheer and Lili Bayer; Additional reporting by Lina Obeid, Alexander Cornwell, Sayed Sheasha, Ahmad Al Kerdi and Dawoud Abu Alkas; Writing by Peter Graff and Michael Georgy; Editing by Alex Richardson and Howard Goller)

US judge narrows French President Macron’s defamation lawsuit against podcaster
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
04:46:23 CET
12:46:23 KST

By Jonathan Allen and Jonathan Stempel
Oct 27 (Reuters) - A Delaware judge ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife, Brigitte, may continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of right-wing podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.
The Macrons had sued Owens and two businesses associated with her in July 2025 over what they called her lie-filled “campaign of global humiliation,” including the false claim that France’s first lady was born a male. They said Owens touted false claims and conspiracy theories against them “to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money.”
Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie ruled on Tuesday that he did not have jurisdiction over Owens, who lives in Tennessee, but the Macrons’ case against Candace Owens LLC and Georgetom Inc may continue because those businesses were registered in Delaware.
The decision means Owens would not be personally liable if the Macrons ultimately prevailed.
In rejecting the claims against Owens, Rennie said the Macrons failed to allege that she formed her businesses specifically to defame them.
“The mere fact that Ms. Owens created the entities to publish political commentary and investigative journalism — the broad category of activity giving rise to this litigation — is insufficient,” the judge wrote.
Rennie will review whether to dismiss the lawsuit entirely after the parties brief him on whether France’s statute of limitations required the Macrons to sue within three months or one year of Owens’ alleged defamation. A three-month deadline could lead to a dismissal because the Macrons waited longer.
“We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods,” lawyers for the Macrons said in an emailed statement on Wednesday.
“As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”
In a post on X, Owens thanked the judge and called the case “one of the grossest, legal overreaches by a foreign government leader in human history — a sitting President’s attempt to personally bankrupt a single podcaster from outside the nation in which he governs.”
(Reporting by Jonathan Allen and Jonathan Stempel in New York; Edting by Kate Mayberry and Bill Berkrot)

WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - A federal grand jury has declined to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson who had provided testimony to a congressional panel that probed the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol by President Donald Trump’s supporters, a source familiar with the matter said on Tuesday.

Sanctions equal economic terrorism, Iran tells UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:45:40 UTC
12:45:40 KST

Iran's chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, said unilateral sanctions amount to economic terrorism and that blockades imposed by armed force are acts of aggression under international law.
Speaking at a UN General Assembly meeting on the need to end US economic, commercial and financial sanctions against Cuba, Darzi said it was the 34th time the assembly has declared its firm opposition to unbridled unilateralism, reckless foreign policies and unilateral coercive measures imposed by a government that considers itself above international law while continuing systematic and severe violations.
Darzi said unilateral sanctions, including those states impose independently, are rooted in unilateralism and coercion and therefore endanger multilateralism, destabilize international relations and undermine the UN Charter and international law.
He said the sanctions, as a tool for collective punishment of targeted nations, violate fundamental human rights, obstruct peace, weaken the right to development and block a just, peaceful and equitable international order.
Darzi said more than six decades of unilateral US sanctions and blockade against Cuba are a clear example of coercive pressure against a sovereign state, imposing widespread suffering on its people, undermining their fundamental human rights and hindering their development.
He said the intensification of these measures under the hypocritical pretext of "promoting democracy" reveals the deep contradiction between claimed goals and devastating humanitarian consequences. This approach, he said, instrumentalizes democracy rather than promoting it.
No government has the right to dictate the political future of an independent nation, Darzi said. From any perspective, such policies and actions, including economic warfare, are illegal, immoral and inhumane. The illegal and inhumane blockade that has lasted decades must end immediately, the imposing government must fully compensate the Cuban people for all damages, and all those involved in perpetuating these policies must be held accountable, he said.
Darzi said the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has itself faced aggression and the consequences of US economic pressure and blockades, once again declares its clear and firm opposition to any sanctions against independent and sovereign states, including Cuba.
He said such sanctions harm ordinary people, especially women, children and the elderly, undermine their health, security and welfare and create serious obstacles to development, which is necessary for the full enjoyment of human rights. These measures, by instrumentalizing the "human rights" of a nation, in fact grossly violate the human rights of that same nation. This is not a defense of human rights but blatant hypocrisy, he said.
Darzi recalled the US president's so-called "help" promise to the Iranian people, saying: "Help is on the way," and days later, on his orders, US forces bombed an elementary school in Minab, ruthlessly killing 168 children aged 7 to 12.
He said the UN General Assembly must compel the United States to implement dozens of resolutions adopted with the overwhelming support of the international community that reject the Cuban blockade and call on the US to end its economic, commercial and financial blockade. The serious legal consequences of unilateral coercive measures for the international legal order must not be ignored or underestimated, especially in the current turbulent international environment, he said.
Darzi said the UN Charter, as stated in Articles 1 and 2, is founded on the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and the development of friendly relations among nations. Unilateral coercive measures violate all these principles as well as the principle of non-intervention, especially when their aim is to force states to change their domestic policies, while Article 2(7) prohibits intervention in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of states.
He said invoking human rights can in no way justify measures that impose widespread suffering on innocent people, since sanctions imposed in the name of protecting human rights themselves violate rights such as health, food, development and a dignified life.
These measures target ordinary people and in practice act as a form of collective punishment, hitting the most vulnerable hardest, he said. This is not protection of human rights but denial of human rights through economic pressure, a instrumentalization and weaponization of human rights.
Darzi said that while the Charter considers international cooperation necessary to solve global problems and promote friendly relations among nations, unilateral coercive measures instead strengthen confrontation, deepen divides and weaken the foundations of peaceful coexistence.
He said these measures directly conflict with the text, spirit, subject and purpose of the Charter. Sanctions are a form of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law, he said. Despite differences in form and severity, these measures share a deeply worrying feature: they undermine the sovereignty of states, cause human suffering and substantively violate international law, and are therefore both illegal and illegitimate.
Darzi said a policy that sacrifices the welfare of millions for political ends is incompatible with the principles of humanity, morality and international solidarity.
He reaffirmed Iran's firm solidarity with the government and resilient people of Cuba in their struggle against the blockade and other unjust coercive measures. Iran will continue to support the elimination of unilateral coercive measures and calls on the assembly to intensify efforts to end these measures immediately, including sanctions against Cuba.
The time has come to end these illegal and inhumane measures, Darzi said. Their continuation is not only a failure of international responsibility but a clear manifestation of humanitarian and moral bankruptcy.

meet otter, the portable newborn warmer designed for hospitals with unreliable power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
03:34:24 UTC
12:34:24 KST

meet otter, the portable newborn warmer designed for hospitals with unreliable power
design that matters and MTTS rethink newborn warming with an integrated, heat-conducting bassinet designed for the realities of low-resource healthcare settings.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
otter rethinks medical design for real-world conditions
Otter, a portable newborn warmer developed by Design that Matters and MTTS, is designed to prevent and treat neonatal hypothermia in hospitals with unreliable electricity and limited resources. Awarded the 2026 Seoul Design Award Grand Prize (find top 10 finalists here), the device rethinks newborn warming through an integrated, heat-conducting polycarbonate bassinet, a built-in battery, and an intuitive touchscreen interface. Otter addresses the practical challenges of neonatal care in low-resource settings, where power outages, limited maintenance capacity, and the risk of user error can compromise the reliability of conventional devices.
Newborn incubators and radiant warmers often depend on stable electricity, regular maintenance, and specialized equipment, requirements that can become obstacles in rural hospitals, where power outages and limited technical support complicate the delivery of neonatal care. Otter addresses these constraints through a design developed over eight years of field research, expert interviews, and product reviews across Africa and Southeast Asia. The need is particularly acute for premature and low-birthweight newborns, who are more vulnerable to losing body heat. Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC), which relies on skin-to-skin contact between a newborn and their caregiver, is an established approach to maintaining warmth, but interruptions are sometimes unavoidable. A baby may need to be examined, transferred between departments, or temporarily separated from their mother. Otter provides supplemental warming during these moments, including transfers within hospitals.
seamless bassinet replaces the conventional warming mattress
The central design decision by US-based nonprofit Design that Matters and Vietnamese medical device manufacturer MTTS is to replace the removable water or gel mattress found in many conductive warmers with an integrated, heat-conducting polycarbonate bassinet. The smooth, continuous surface has no fabric, seams, or gaps, making it easier to clean and disinfect between patients. It also prevents direct contact between the newborn and the heating element, reducing the risk of burns associated with conventional systems when a mattress is removed or incorrectly positioned. The heating element and temperature sensors sit within a water-resistant housing beneath the bassinet, protected from rough handling. This integrated construction reduces reliance on consumables and replacement parts. Warming mattresses can be vulnerable to punctures, seam failures, and deterioration, while water-filled systems may require additives that are difficult to source in some settings. Otter simplifies the structure of the product, aiming to reduce the maintenance burden throughout its working life.
Otter weighs 3.6 kg and can be carried between clinical departments without interrupting warming. Its integrated battery automatically takes over when mains electricity is disconnected, supporting continued operation during power failures and patient transfers. The battery provides more than two hours of backup at an ambient temperature of 15°C. The touchscreen displays temperature, heating status, and estimated remaining battery life, while alarms alert staff to problems with the sensor, heating element, or power supply. The interface is designed to make the status of the device easy to assess without requiring extensive technical training. Its physical form follows the same principle. Resembling a familiar newborn bassinet, the open structure allows clinical staff to access the baby while making the device less intimidating for parents. This familiar appearance also supports interaction between mothers and newborns during periods when supplemental warming is needed.
testing the device in clinical settings
Five Otter devices have been operating at Kapiri District Hospital in Zambia since May 2025, where an ongoing implementation study evaluates performance, staff acceptance, and integration with existing care protocols. The devices have been used with low-birthweight newborns, including infants weighing as little as 840 grams, and to maintain warmth during transfers between hospital buildings. The study also takes place in conditions that expose the practical challenges the design is intended to address, including documented power interruptions lasting seven to eleven hours and limited access to biomedical support. The project summary reports successful use during transfers, but the implementation study remains ongoing, and its findings should be understood in that context.
