Global study counts almost 3 million climate change-related deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:52:40 UTC
10:52:40 KST

Global Lancet study counts almost 3 million climate change-related deaths
In short:
A new Lancet report has found the number of heat-related deaths has been growing since the 2015 Paris Agreement, despite real gains from the climate pact.
It says climate action is not keeping pace with increasing health impacts as the world keeps burning fossil fuels.
What's next?
Researchers are calling for climate change to be declared a global health emergency to enable a coordinated global response.
The latest global study on climate change-related health risks has found that 3 million deaths between 2016 and 2023 can be attributed to a warming planet.
Published ahead of the world's COP 31 climate conference in Turkiye, this year's Lancet Countdown report noted significant progress had been made on key climate goals that could reduce heating by 2100 from up to 3.5 degrees Celsius to 2.6C.
It found the growth of energy from renewable sources had "vastly exceeded expectations", but that global action on climate change was "grossly insufficient", and that this had already led to significant harm to human health.
Almost 3 million climate-related deaths
It is the first time the authors of the Lancet Countdown study have quantified heat-related deaths directly due to human-caused climate change.
The authors estimate more than half a million deaths per year between 2016 and 2023 were linked to heat and that 68 per cent of those deaths were caused by climate change.
Developing countries had the highest proportion of heat-related deaths, which the authors found "reflected the disproportionate adverse impacts of climate change on those least responsible for it".
Study co-author and Macquarie University climate health expert Professor Paul Beggs said vulnerable people were most at risk from climate change globally, but no-one was immune.
"Even here in Australia, we know people do die from heatwaves, people do die from bushfire smoke exposure and things like that," he said.
"So I think it doesn't matter where you live; climate change is already having an impact on health, and that's only going to increase."
According to recently released peer-reviewed studies, severe heat killed more than 50,000 people across Europe during this year's Northern Hemisphere summer, which was marred by rolling heatwaves and fires.
The scientists attributed about two-thirds of these deaths to human-caused climate change.
The Lancet report tracks 54 indicators of how climate change and efforts to tackle it affect health, but warns that wider, system-wide risks could be far greater than the individual measures suggest.
"A severe El Niño threatens to compound the impacts of climate change and trigger unprecedented climate-related humanitarian crises globally," the report states.
"Climate change has become a global health emergency. Addressing it requires urgent course correction."
More heatwaves, droughts
The study authors noted that the past 11 years had been the hottest on record, accompanied by more frequent heatwaves and droughts.
Climate change has increased the risk and intensity of droughts, which affected more than 50 per cent of global land in 2025 for at least a month.
At the same time, extreme rainfall has also increased, resulting in a higher flood and landslide risk. The report found the world's exposure to very high or extremely high risk of wildfire had also increased.
Climate change was also affecting productivity, according to the researchers.
"Globally, heat exposure caused the loss of 573 billion potential work hours in 2025, resulting in US $1.07 trillion in income losses," the report found, with low-and middle-income countries most affected.
Western Sydney physician Aditya Vyas co-authored a separate Lancet climate health report due to be released on Oceania.
He said health workers had recorded a 13 per cent increase in emergency presentations during heatwaves, which he described as a "silent killer" in the community.
"The impacts are worse now than they were before, but also they're worsening, and for the next generation this is going to have a real impact on their health status," Dr Vyas said.
'Vested interests' obstructing progress
The Lancet authors found fossil fuels continued to supply about 80 per cent of global energy, pushing energy-related emissions to a record high in 2024.
"Unequal access to clean energy and the persistent use of polluting fuels are not only exacerbating climate change risks, but also directly harming health and increasing vulnerabilities through air pollution," the report states.
The authors also cited "vested interests", in the form of "lobbying and disinformation by fossil fuel interests and political allies", as an obstruction in the effort to transition towards clean energy.
This was "countering the growing body of scientific literature on the links between health and climate change."
The authors singled out the USA for promoting fossil fuel expansion and withdrawing from the Paris Agreement.
"The growing political support for fossil fuels from the USA and other countries threatens to lock the world into a future of irreversible damage and mounting risks to health and survival."
Air quality preventing deaths
The authors also provided cause for hope in the form of growth in renewable energy sources and its effect on human health.
They estimated that 400,000 deaths were prevented in 2023 compared to 2016 due to improved air quality from switching to cleaner energy sources.
Electricity use in transport had increased by 427 per cent from 2016 to 2023 globally, the report's authors noted, which, together with air pollution control and active travel promotion, had "prevented 85,000 deaths across 75 countries".
Scaling up access to off-grid renewables would prevent another 2 million deaths annually, which could be "attributable to household air pollution from solid-fuel use".
Professor Beggs said the report was an urgent call to prioritise human health over fossil fuels.
"Australia is the president of COP this year," he said.
"We're really hoping for big things in terms of progress on mitigating climate change, and that means reducing fossil fuel emissions."

In brief
- Star Entertainment has been fined $260 million over historical money laundering failures.
- The penalty leaves Australia's biggest listed casino operator facing an uncertain future.
Australia's biggest listed casino company is on the brink of administration after being fined $260 million for historical money-laundering violations.
The Star Entertainment Group was fined in the Federal Court on Wednesday, four years after financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC launched legal action against the company.
The agency previously argued a $400 million penalty was necessary to punish what it said were "manifest failures" at Star.
But the stockmarket-listed company, which has a market value of $763 million, argued any penalty over $100 million would send it into liquidation.
Justice Cameron Moore determined a $260 million penalty was appropriate for the significant harm Star's conduct has caused.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"In effect, Star put profit ahead of compliance," the judge said.
Star will have 19 months to pay the fine in four equal instalments.
Shares in the casino giant closed at 13 cents on Tuesday.

The court previously heard that one man was allowed, alongside many other high-risk gamblers, to funnel hundreds of millions of dollars through the casinos, despite his known criminal links.
These concerns fell on deaf ears of senior management, who failed to impose adequate anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism-financing controls, it heard.
Star, which owns casinos in Sydney and the Gold Coast and operates one in Brisbane, has been dealing with a raft of scandals and license suspensions involving years of money laundering, organised crime infiltration and governance failures.

Speaking at the group's annual general meeting on Tuesday, Kim predicted that the "fire is out".
"I didn't come here to say 'mission accomplished'," Kim said.
"I came here to say, the fire is out, and now the rebuilding starts."
The vast majority of customers weren't involved in malfeasance or unwanted behaviour, and the company should welcome them, Kim added.

WELLINGTON, Oct. 28 (Xinhua) -- The number of filled jobs in New Zealand rose 0.3 percent in September from the previous month to 2.36 million, an increase of 7,227 jobs, official data showed on Wednesday.
By industry, public administration and safety recorded the largest annual increase with 6,041 additional filled jobs, up 3.7 percent. Health care and social assistance followed, adding 5,942 jobs, or 2.1 percent. Construction added 2,480 jobs, while education and training gained 2,386 jobs over the year, the agency said in a statement.
By region, Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, recorded the largest increase, with 6,798 additional filled jobs, up 0.9 percent from a year earlier. Canterbury on the South Island followed with an increase of 6,519 jobs, up 2.1 percent, statistics showed.
The number of filled jobs rose by 0.7 percent for both men and women over the year, according to Stats NZ.
Total gross earnings reached 16.1 billion NZ dollars (about 9.15 billion U.S. dollars) in September, up 3.4 percent from a year earlier, it said. ■

US Justice Department sues Maryland school district over transgender policies
WASHINGTON – The US Justice Department sued a public school district in Maryland on Oct 27 over transgender policies that it alleged had violated federal law, the latest attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to limit transgender rights.
The Trump administration has launched federal probes against educational institutions and threatened to freeze their federal funding over transgender policies.
The Justice Department complaint filed in the US District Court for the District of Maryland alleged that Anne Arundel County Public Schools violated the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA) and the Protection of Pupil Rights Amendment (PPRA).
The school district said it “disagrees with the allegations and stands by its compliance with FERPA and PPRA”, saying it has been in regular contact with the Justice Department in “good faith” and found the department’s decision to pursue litigation “regrettable”.
The school system covers 128 schools serving more than 84,000 students, according to its website.
Trump has cast the gender identity of transgender people as a lie, issued a series of executive actions targeting their rights and stated in a directive that the US government will recognise only two sexes: male and female.
The US Education Department previously accused the school district of being in violation of federal law by classifying information about a student’s gender identity as “confidential medical information” that cannot be shared with parents.
“Schools should not discuss preferred pronouns or ‘gender identity’ with a student without parental notification and consent,” Assistant Attorney-General Harmeet Dhillon of the Justice Department’s civil rights division said on Oct 27.
Trump has also targeted educational institutions over other issues like climate initiatives, pro-Palestine protests against US ally Israel’s assault on Gaza and diversity programmes, leading to concerns about academic freedom, free speech and due process. REUTERS

AI generated
TEL AVIV - As the first exit polls arrived in Israel’s election, opposition supporters breathed a sigh of relief.
But as a long night set in, nervousness grew on both sides in a tight race that is pivotal for the country.
At exactly 10pm, exit polls showed a narrow edge for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff and political novice seeking to unseat Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader.
“I feel better,” Kalanit Sharon, 37, told AFP as cheers erupted in the Tel Aviv hall packed with backers of Eisenkot and his Yashar party.
But as the night wore on, exit polls shifted, with major television networks putting the two sides on equal footing – with Arab lists, which could become kingmakers, making strong gains.
The vote, the first general election since Hamas’s unprecedented Oct 7, 2023 attack, drew 77.7% turnout, the highest since 1999.
For Netanyahu, blamed by opponents for the security failures that led to the attack, and for refusing to establish an independent commission of inquiry, his political survival was at stake.
“Three years ago, the government abandoned us,” said Ohad Ben Ami, a former hostage taken to the Gaza Strip by the Palestinian militant group Hamas.
“An Israeli citizen should never have spent a year and a half in Hamas tunnels when deals (with Hamas) were on the table” to secure the hostages’ release, he said at Eisenkot’s event.
Another supporter of the former general, Noa Ayal, a 31-year-old soldier who said she had completed “more than 360 days of reserve duty”, said she had been “waiting for this change for so long”.
“I have a lot of hope, and if Gadi doesn’t become prime minister, it will undoubtedly be very difficult.”
Eisenkot – who swapped his usual plain black shirt for a suit and tie – promised to work swiftly to form a government.
But it will be no small feat with neither side appearing to have secured the votes.
Yaheli Lifshitz, a 23-year-old student, acknowledged the challenge.
“To form a new government, they’ll have to break with established rules and norms and build alliances that have never existed before,” he said.
‘We have to wait’
At a Jerusalem convention centre rented by Netanyahu’s Likud, a sense of uncertainty reigned.
On a giant screen, a video montage celebrated the prime minister, showing hugs with US President Donald Trump alongside footage of military strikes from the assorted wars he has led since the Hamas attack.
When the first exit polls came out, 70-year-old retiree Aliza Schukerman refused to concede defeat.
“We’ll have to wait until tomorrow morning, when they’ve counted all the votes. It will take time,” she said.
“I’m sure that by 10am tomorrow we will know that we’ve won and that Bibi is prime minister again.”
Elie Pieprz, 53, struck a similarly confident note.
“Usually things move more in our favour as the night goes on and as the morning approaches,” he said.
“I’m very optimistic. I feel the prime minister has performed better than some of the pre-campaign polls suggested.”
Asked what might happen if the opposition ultimately prevailed, Pieprz called for a coalition that would still include Likud, citing the conflict with Iran and the need to maintain strong ties with Washington.
“Trying to change course in the middle of the journey is not a good idea,” he said.
Anat Margolin, a 49-year-old engineer, was less confident.
“I don’t know what to hope for because throughout the day you could feel the results were going to be unpredictable, that this wasn’t what we’d prepared for,” she said.
A regular viewer of Channel 14, an outlet supportive of Netanyahu, Margolin said she had mostly heard predictions pointing to a victory for her candidate, not to an opposition lead, however narrow.
“We weren’t hearing about that possibility,” she said. AFP

duyi han installs rain-inspired textile listening garden inside shanghai villa
artist duyi han installs it's raining outside, it's raining inside, pairing rain-ripple carpets, pleated organza sculptures, and embroidered cinematic lyrics to transform the domestic interior into a textile listening garden.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
DUYI HAN turns SHANGHAI RESIDENCE INTO TEXTILE LISTENING GARDEN
Staged within the domestic interior of VILLA tbh in Shanghai, ‘it’s raining outside, it’s raining inside’ is a solo exhibition by designer and artist Duyi Han. Developed following a multi-week residency in the residence, the site-specific installation configures a ‘Listening Garden’ composed of textile sculptures, hand embroidery, objects, and acoustic elements. Drawing visual and atmospheric references from rainfall, cinema, fashion, and pop music, the project investigates how soft furnishings and narrative materiality alter spatial perception within a historic home.
Rain-ripple carpets and embroidered textiles shape the exhibition
At the core of the installation by artist Duyi Han, a custom carpet printed with concentric rain-ripple motifs grounds a cluster of pleated, translucent organza sculptures. The domestic rooms feature varied contextual interventions: a sheer, tailored garment suspended within a timber vitrine, embroidered sneakers arranged as static sculptural accents, resin water droplets suspended over the kitchen sink, and backlit textiles softening the bathroom surfaces. Graphic fragments of song lyrics and film dialogues are embroidered across the woven fabrics, embedding typographic narratives directly into the decorative textiles to link sound, light, and interior form throughout the residence.

US costs of Iran war rise to over $47 billion, according to Pentagon estimate
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
02:16:40 CET
10:16:40 KST

By Phil Stewart
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks.
(Reporting by Phil Stewart; Editing by Tom Hogue and Stephen Coates)

- The Pentagon expects more than US$29 billion to replace munitions and over US$6 billion for lost equipment, while US officials say heavy fighting could restart after the midterms.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US military has spent over US$47 billion (S$60.25 billion) so far to prosecute the war in Iran, more than 25% higher than the Defence Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters.
The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly.
The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the Nov 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years.
The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt US President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress.
The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than US$29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict.
More than US$6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses”, which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war.
Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting that the conflict would last a short time.
Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defences so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs (joint direct attack munitions), which are plentiful.
But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defences, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible.
Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections.
US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so.
The latest Pentagon estimate compares with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth’s July estimate of US$37.5 billion for the cost of the war.
While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks. REUTERS

Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:54:54 UTC
09:54:54 KST

Scientists discover the immune system’s hidden sense of touch
- Date:
- October 27, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising new ability of immune cells that could change how we understand long-term immunity. Researchers found that T cells can actually sense how stiff their surrounding tissues are, using these physical signals to help determine whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells that protect against future infections.
- Share:
Scientists at McGill University have discovered a surprising ability in immune cells that could reshape our understanding of how the body develops lasting protection against infections.
For years, researchers believed that tissue-resident memory T cells, specialized immune cells that remain in the body's tissues after an infection and respond quickly if the same threat returns, were guided mainly by chemical signals.
However, a new study published in Nature Immunology challenges that assumption. Researchers found that T cells can detect how stiff their surrounding tissues are and use this physical information to influence whether they develop into long-lasting memory cells. The findings suggest that adjusting to the stronger mechanical forces within tissues may be important for these protective cells to survive over time.
"This is an exciting fundamental finding that challenges the way we think about immune cells," said lead author Judith Mandl, a professor in McGill's Department of Physiology. "It suggests T cells can 'feel' their surroundings and adapt to them, making the physical environment an active force in shaping their behavior."
The research brought together scientists from McGill's Department of Physiology, the Alan Edwards Centre for Research on Pain, the Department of Bioengineering, and the McGill University Health Centre, along with collaborating institutions in the Netherlands and the United States.
How the Discovery Could Influence Cancer and Immune Treatments
Understanding how T cells respond to physical conditions could eventually open new possibilities for treating diseases in which the immune system mistakenly targets healthy tissue. These include autoimmune disorders, allergies, and complications involving transplant rejection.
The discovery could also have important implications for cancer research, particularly efforts to improve treatments that use the immune system to fight tumors.
"Tumors are often dense and physically difficult for immune cells to penetrate. Understanding how T cells adapt to these environments could help researchers design cancer immunotherapies that are better able to reach and attack tumors," said Mandl.
How Scientists Discovered the Immune Cells' Hidden Sense of Touch
To investigate whether physical surroundings influence T cell behavior, the researchers studied immune cells collected from humans and mice. They placed the cells inside specially designed collagen gels that mimicked tissues with different levels of stiffness.
The experiments revealed a clear pattern. As the gels became stiffer, T cells were increasingly likely to acquire characteristics associated with tissue-resident memory cells, which help provide long-term immune protection.
These results indicate that the physical properties of surrounding tissues can help shape how immune cells develop, adding an important new dimension to scientists' understanding of immune memory.
The researchers now hope to identify the specific molecular sensor that enables T cells to detect their physical environment. Determining how this sensor converts mechanical forces into changes in cell behavior could help explain how the immune system establishes lasting protection.
The study received funding from the Human Frontier Science Program, the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Canadian Foundation for Innovation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada, and the U.S. National Institutes of Health.
Story Source:
Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jérémy Postat, Mauricio Merino, Angela R. Mingarelli, Aysha Cerf, Aanya Bhagrath, Dhanesh Patel, Connie Shen, Johanna Brodbeck, Pouria Tirgar, Dakota Rogers, Jules Blanc, Thiviya Jeyakumar, Caitlin Schneider, Shana Coley, Nadia Giannetti, Taylor A. DePauw, Johannes Textor, Allen Ehrlicher, Stephen C. Jameson, Reza Sharif-Naeini, Abhinav Sharma, Judith N. Mandl. Mechanosensing by T cells promotes a tissue-resident memory transcriptional program. — ONNews (@ONNxews) October 27, 2026
El Paso police said on Monday that they were reviewing the footage and related reports to determine whether any laws had been broken.
“Symbols and language associated with the Ku Klux Klan represent a history of terror, violence and racial hatred,” El Paso Police Chief Peter Pacillas said in a statement on X on Monday. Treating such imagery as “a costume or a joke is unacceptable,” he added.
The incident also drew condemnation from the local branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP).
In a statement cited by local media, the NAACP expressed “utter outrage, disgust and righteous indignation” over the imagery.
Wearing KKK-style clothing is not in itself a crime under US law, although threatening or intimidating conduct may constitute an offense.
Founded after the US Civil War, the KKK became notorious for terrorizing racial and ethnic minorities, primarily blacks, through murder and various forms of intimidation. Membership peaked at an estimated 4 to 5 million people nationwide during the mid-1920s, at a time when only 10-11 million Americans were black.
The incident follows several other recent controversies involving KKK imagery across the US.
Earlier this month, the University of Maryland suspended its club tennis team indefinitely after members circulated tournament materials featuring KKK-style hoods incorporated into the state flag. The images prompted complaints from students at Howard University, a historically Black institution.
In September, a man wearing KKK robes near a Trader Joe’s supermarket in California was arrested for public intoxication. Police said there was no evidence of a hate crime and that wearing the offensive costume was not itself illegal.
Last Halloween, a student in Tennessee was sent home and disciplined after appearing at school dressed as a KKK member. The student had reportedly initially claimed to be wearing a priest’s costume.

Arab parties on course for 17 seats in Israel election, early results show
Record-breaking voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel at about 80 percent, early indicators show.
Israel’s Arab parties are on track to win 17 seats in the Israeli parliament, according to early results and exit polls, after voting among Palestinian citizens of Israel surged to its highest level in decades.
With more than 84 percent of votes counted on Wednesday, the leading Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, were on track to secure a combined 17 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The opposition bloc led by former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party was trailing the coalition led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party. Final results are expected later this week.
Polls estimated voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel at about 80 percent, historic numbers that break 1999 records, Israel’s Channel 12 reported on Tuesday.
The leader of Ra’am, or the United Arab List, Mansour Abbas, said he hopes the final election results will allow the anti-Netanyahu bloc, including his party, to win the 61 seats required to form a government.
“With the numbers we have now, there is no government,” Abbas told Israel’s Channel 12 before preliminary votes began trickling in.
Abbas, whose Ra’am party currently holds five seats in the Knesset and joined the coalition that governed Israel from 2021 to 2022, added that both main blocs reached out to his party before and after the election.
‘Arabs can’t be kept outside’
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Alon Pinkas, a former Israeli ambassador, said creating a government might prove difficult for parties such as Eisenkot’s – which earlier exit polls had put narrowly ahead – because they promised not to form coalitions with Arab parties during the campaign.
“There’s a price to pay,” Pinkas said, because the “Arabs can’t be kept outside and only being considered and co-opted when you need their votes.”
He added that the Arab-led lists will make demands that a Jewish-led coalition government may not support.
Netanyahu and his far-right coalition made last-ditch efforts on Tuesday to get their supporters to the polls, warning of surging voter turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, a tactic Arab politicians denounced as racist and inflammatory.
Cars flying Netanyahu’s Likud party flags drove through Jerusalem blaring the Islamic call to prayer and urging supporters to cast their ballots because “Arabs are voting,” witnesses said.
In social media posts, the embattled prime minister highlighted long queues at polling stations in Arab communities and published an image that he said showed Arab voters, including women wearing the niqab, a veil that covers the lower half of the face, waiting to vote.
“If we don’t wake up now, we’ll find ourselves with a government of Mansour Abbas and Ahmad Tibi,” he said, referring to two leading Palestinian members of the Knesset.
Overall voter turnout was also historic, reaching its highest level since 1999 with 77.7 percent casting ballots in Tuesday’s election, the Central Elections Committee reported. Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 21 percent of the country’s population of 10 million and have traditionally voted at lower rates than Jewish Israelis.
‘Existential moment’
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, called the election “an existential moment for Palestinian-Israelis”.
She noted the record turnout among what has emerged as a key voting bloc, which drew “even [voters] who would usually boycott elections, who didn’t believe it would amount to any kind of influence, that it would change their reality, that it would alter the systemic discrimination that they face”.
The Knesset has passed more than 100 laws discriminating against Palestinian citizens of Israel, who also face discrimination in receiving state funds, Odeh said.

Rights monitors raise concerns over senior UAE diplomat bid for next UN boss
Human rights monitors criticised senior UAE diplomat Lana Nusseibeh's candidacy to be the next UN chief on Tuesday, citing her role in championing the country's foreign policy and denying the UAE's role in fuelling the conflict in Sudan.
Pushback against the prominent Middle Eastern candidate has gathered steam since her late entry last week. Her bid upended the gridlocked race to replace UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year.
Despite months of campaigning by several senior UN figures and former country leaders, the competition has struggled to produce a consensus choice among the Security Council's most powerful nations.
Sudan's war, which erupted in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
"She has been asked about the UAE's role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts, that is not what we need as UN Secretary-General," Kenneth Roth, former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told a webinar organised by online campaigns group Avaaz.
Last month, a UN fact-finding mission said foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks, including individuals and entities in the United Arab Emirates, among others, are helping sustain Sudan's conflict.
"This is the opposite of the kind of moral standing of the human rights leadership that we want from a UN Secretary-General," Roth told the webinar titled "Call To Stop UAE Minister's Bid for UN Top Job Amid Sudan Genocide".
The webinar also featured Sudanese experts, as well as a survivor of the El Fasher massacre, on their concerns about Nusseibeh's candidacy and its implications for the UN's commitment to protect civilians, according to the organisers.
"Electing (the UAE's) senior diplomat as Secretary-General would hand leadership of (United Nations) institutions to that government's chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable," said Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV.
Asked about Sudan during the dialogue with the General Assembly on Tuesday, Nusseibeh said: "If I were to become secretary-general, Sudan would be a number one priority, as one of the most horrific conflicts we have seen in recent history."
"The loss of human life on the ground is a tragedy, the atrocities committed by the RSF are atrocious, and I would support the work of all UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice," she added.
Nusseibeh told the media at the UN after the dialogue that, as a secretary-general, she would work to be a "risk-taker" and "prime mover in mediation efforts."
She has also separately said she would "put the UN's full political and practical support behind ongoing efforts to reach a ceasefire and a credible and inclusive political process that reflects the democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people."
Nusseibeh served as UAE ambassador to the UN for more than a decade. She previously led the UAE's successful campaign to be elected to the Security Council as a non-permanent member in 2022-23. Diplomats working in New York widely describe her as a competent manager, skilled negotiator, and clear communicator.
An informal council poll this month placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the council's five permanent members, Russia, China, the US, France and Britain, who ultimately decided the outcome.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but diplomats are still negotiating the format and exact timing.

Dozens of Former Airmen Are Running in the ’26 Midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:40:57 UTC
09:40:57 KST

More than three dozen former Airmen are running for Congress, including Democrats, Republicans, third-party and independent candidates, Air & Space Forces Magazine has found.
The diverse group includes both former officers and enlisted members whose service spanned the Active, Guard, and Reserve components. They include sitting members as well as newcomers to politics.
Meanwhile, some of Congress’ highest-profile veterans are departing the legislature. They include Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.), a retired brigadier general who has been deeply involved in legislation affecting his former service. Among the issues Bacon championed: recapitalizing Air National Guard fighter squadrons, rethinking pass-through funding in the Air Force budget, and a 2050 force design. Bacon’s district includes Offutt Air Force Base, Neb., home to U.S. Strategic Command.
Bacon is the highest-ranking among 15 Air Force veterans in the current Congress, and not the only one leaving. Also retiring are Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.) and Rep. Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.). Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a “total force Airmen” who served in all three components, died unexpected in July.
Even so, the number of former Airmen in Congress could grow come January, depending on how the election turns out. A crop of new candidates either favored to win election or seen as competitive in their House races include:
- Chris McGowan (R-Iowa), heavily favored in his race, served in the Air Force and Iowa Air National Guard. Having attended Undergraduate Pilot Training, he reclassified as an intelligence officer, according to his official bio.
- Jace Yarborough (R-Texas), also heavily favored, has served on Active Duty and remains in the Air Force Reserve. A lawyer, he touts his legal work challenging the military over past “vaccine mandates, religious discrimination, taxpayer-funded abortion travel, and woke diversity, equity, and inclusion policies.”
- David Flippo (R-Nev.), slightly favored in his race, is a retired USAF lieutenant colonel and former maintenance and logistics officer. His official bio touts his work establishing “three combat bases in Iraq.,” Having said in the past that he received a Bronze Star for valor, he later apologized noting he received a Bronze Star without the valor device.
- Carlos De La Cruz (R-Texas), is competing in a race handicapped by pollsters as a toss-up. He served 20 years in the Air Force as a Military Working Dog handler and an intelligence professional, deploying multiple times to the Middle East.
- Rebecca Bennett (D-N.J.), is locked in a tight race. The former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot now serves in the Air National Guard.
- Eric Conroy (R-Ohio), is seen as a slight underdog in his race. The U.S. Air Force Academy grad, he is a former intelligence officer who worked with Special Operations units and later served in the CIA.
- Kristina Knickerbocker (D-Ohio) is also seen as a slight underdog. The Air Force major, a nurse who has served both on Active-Duty and in the Reserve, is running to represent the district that includes Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio.
Combined with House incumbents running in safe seats and Senators not up for reelection this cycle, these Congressional newcomers could raise the number of former blue-suiters in the Capitol. Among them, former F-22 pilot Rep. August Pfluger is the lone fighter pilot. In September, at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Pfluger called for more “wingmen” to join him as legislators.
“I am the only fifth-generation pilot in Congress,” Pfluger said. “I need some wingmen to come join me. … God bless my Navy SEAL friends, and they are dear friends, but we’ve got a lot of them in Congress. What we don’t have is a lot of air and space expertise.”
Pfluger, facing little challenge, could be up for a leadership position in the Republican conference, depending on how the election goes, according to Punchbowl News.
Another Air Force vet whose leadership position could be affected by the larger midterm results is Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) The former Air Force JAG officer chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, but would become the ranking member if Democrats win the Senate.
Identified Air Force Veterans Running for Congress in 2026*
* Air & Space Forces Magazine made every effort to include all Air Force veterans running for Congress in this list. It is possible that one or more veterans who have not publicized their service may also be among the hundreds of challengers seeking seats in the House and Senate.

Breaking: Inflation surges more than expected ahead of RBA meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:38:39 UTC
09:38:39 KST

Inflation rate rises to 4.3 per cent in September, raising rate hike expectations
In short:
Inflation rose to 4.3 per cent in the year to September, driven by housing and transport costs.
Underlying inflation also edged up, after August's figures were revised lower.
What's next?
Markets now overwhelmingly expect the Reserve Bank to hike interest rates next Tuesday.
Australia's inflation rate rose more than expected in September, raising expectations of an interest rate hike next week.
The consumer price index rose to 0.8 per cent in the month, from 0.4 per cent in August, taking annual inflation to 4.3 per cent, up from 4 per cent a month earlier, the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) said.
"Housing was the largest contributor to annual inflation in September, rising by 5.2 per cent," ABS head of price statistics Rachael McCririck said.
Transport also drove annual inflation higher, largely due to higher fuel prices, which rose 9.4 per cent in September.
The annual trimmed mean, a measure of underlying inflation, also picked up to 3.6 per cent in September. The August trimmed mean was revised lower to 3.5 per cent.
The increase in underlying inflation was despite fuel prices being excluded from the trimmed mean due to their volatility.
Following the CPI release, market pricing for a November interest rate hike surged, putting the chance of a 0.25 per cent increase next week at about 85 per cent, according to Bloomberg data.
KPMG Australia chief economist Brendan Rynne described the inflation figures as "the last data point necessary for the RBA to increase the cash rate for a fifth time this year".
"It is clear pricing pressures in the Australian economy are growing, not weakening, and the upswing in inflation is catching the market off guard," Dr Rynne said.
Betshares chief economist David Bassanese said his base case was the RBA would hike rates next week but then leave them on hold in December in a pre-Christmas reprieve for households.
"The only argument against a rate hike next week is the fact the [RBA] pre-emptively raised rates in September, so may feel it has a little more time to assess economic developments and possibly re-visit the rate hike decision in December," he said.
"Should rates need to rise even further next year, the risk of recession would no doubt intensify."
Inflation 'too high' says RBA
Top Reserve Bank officials appeared at a Senate estimates hearing as the data was released.
Deputy governor Andrew Hauser said inflation was broadly in line with the central bank's expectations, but was too high.
"We have said that repeatedly, and I'm sure that we will say that again today," he said.
The RBA targets inflation between 2-3 per cent.
Last week, Mr Hauser had warned the inflation outlook looked "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike next week.
"Today's data will provide the rationale for acting on these recent tough words next week, and unless we start to see a swing down in inflation over the coming months, then it looks more likely than not another rate rise will be coming at the start of 2027," Dr Rynne said.
The ABS also calculated quarterly inflation figures. The trimmed mean rose 1 per cent in the September quarter.
"Back in August, the RBA forecast a trimmed mean quarterly gain of 0.8 per cent in the September quarter — so today's 1.0 per cent quarterly gain is confirmation that those inflation risks have indeed materialised," Mr Bassanese said.
"Higher underlying inflation reflects several factors, such as the pass through of higher oil prices into wider array of goods and service prices along with still sticky local service sector inflation."
The RBA's interest rate-setting board will kick off its meeting on Monday and hand down its decision on Tuesday afternoon.
It will also release its updated economic forecasts, including for inflation.
What is driving inflation?
In a note to clients, AMP economists described Australia's inflation as coming from "here, there, and everywhere".
"Goods inflation has picked up more since the second half of 2025," AMP's Diana Mousina and My Bui wrote.
"But worryingly, services inflation barely eased post-COVID. It remains stuck around its current rate of 4.1 per cent [year-on-year]."
Health prices rose 3.7 per cent annually, with medical and hospital services (+4.8pc) the main contributor.
Recreation costs rose 4.5 per cent, driven by domestic holiday travel and accommodation (+5.3pc) and games, toys and hobbies (+15.5pc).
The ABS said the games inflation was down to "price increases in memory and storage components being passed on to consumers", as the AI boom lifts demand for components such as chips.
"This is similar to other countries who are also seeing IT prices rise after years of declines. This is concerning for Australia, which imports most of these products," Ms Mousina and Ms Bui wrote.
They noted that about 45 per cent of CPI categories posted price rises above 3 per cent annually, "pretty much unchanged since the beginning of the year".
"Today's data gives them no room to escape from this hawkish sentiment. Inflation is well above target, it has surprised higher and there are no clear signs that it's easing," they said.
"If the RBA doesn't raise rates next week, then their credibility could take a hit and embed higher inflation expectations further."

El Salvador rushes some 1,000 troops to Haiti after gang ambush, source says
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
01:23:24 CET
09:23:24 KST

By Sarah Morland
Oct 27 (Reuters) - El Salvador has sent about 1,000 troops to Haiti after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed security mission went missing in a gang ambush on the outskirts of the capital on October 18, a security official in Haiti told Reuters on Tuesday.
The troops’ arrival aboard flights in recent days dramatically expands the Central American nation’s role in Haiti’s long-standing gang conflict. Yet it remains unclear who will command the new Salvadoran contingent, how long it will stay in Haiti or whether more forces will follow.
Neither the Haitian nor Salvadoran government immediately responded to requests for comment. The official in Haiti spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the security situation.
The deployment comes as the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force has reached about 2,000 personnel, just over a third of its planned strength a year into its mandate, with little improvement in Haiti’s security.
Armed gangs in Haiti have meanwhile expanded their influence over the capital and surrounding regions through extortion and brutal attacks that have displaced nearly 1.5 million people.
Haiti’s leaders have sought international security support since 2022, despite the country’s fraught history of foreign intervention. Gangs’ influence grew rapidly after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moise, deepening an insecurity crisis that has caused authorities to repeatedly delay elections.
Pierre Esperance, head of Haiti’s National Human Rights Defense Network, welcomed the unusually rapid Salvadoran deployment and said he hoped it would help stop gangs from terrorizing civilians. But he warned that any operation must avoid harming residents trapped in gang-held neighborhoods.
“Not everybody living in gang-controlled areas are gangsters,” he said.
President Nayib Bukele last week announced a military operation to recover the missing Salvadorans, who remain unaccounted for since jumping from a burning vehicle during the ambush. He has not said how many troops would be sent.
The US provided C-130 transport aircraft to help move Salvadoran troops to Haiti, a US military official said.
Additional commercial and military flights between San Salvador and Port-au-Prince were visible on flight-tracking site Flightradar24 and were also reported by the Miami Herald.
A photo posted on X on Tuesday by a lawmaker from Bukele’s ruling party showed a plane carrying uniformed soldiers, some taking selfies.
NO CLAIM OF RESPONSIBILITY
Bukele has built strong domestic support through a hardline anti-crime campaign that several right-wing governments in the Americas have sought to emulate. Human rights groups however warn that the crackdown has come at the cost of due process and has been linked to hundreds of deaths in custody.
Bukele said the missing Salvadorans were air force technicians, returning to base from a market, and that he believed they were being held hostage by criminal groups.
No Haitian gang has claimed responsibility for the ambush. Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, has released videos denying that his group is holding the Salvadorans or was involved in the attack.
Before the ambush, El Salvador had deployed at least 124 personnel to the force. Bukele said they were pilots and technicians sent to evacuate wounded personnel, not combatants.
Alongside the international mission, Haiti’s government has also hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince - an ally of US President Donald Trump - which has since 2025 carried out controversial anti-gang drone operations.
Luis Contreras, a Salvadoran security and organized crime analyst, said he expected that at least some of the new troops would operate outside the UN-backed mission’s chain of command and could coordinate with Prince’s firm.
“The UN has lacked the political will to resolve the issue of the gangs in Haiti,” he said. “Once the whereabouts of the four members have been established, they will have to assess whether to engage in a direct and protracted confrontation.”
(Reporting by Sarah Morland in Mexico City, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador and Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince; Editing by Daina Beth Solomon, Bill Berkrot and Jonathan Spicer )

Tarek Chouiref
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
Updated exit polls by Israel’s public broadcaster and Channel 13 put Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc led by former Israeli Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot level at 51 seats each early Wednesday, with 18 seats for Arab parties.
Both projections left the rival blocs short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.
Channel 13 projected that Likud would remain the largest party, with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 23 and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together alliance with 13.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, giving the two Arab lists a combined 18 seats.
The revised projections erased an initial lead for Eisenkot’s bloc. The public broadcaster and Channel 13 had each initially projected 53 seats for his bloc, 50 for Netanyahu’s and 17 for Arab parties.
Earlier, Channel 12 projected 52 seats for Eisenkot’s bloc, 50 for Netanyahu’s and 18 for Arab parties.
Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 election, according to the Central Elections Committee.
Vote counting began after polls closed at 10 pm local time (2000GMT) Tuesday. Exit polls are projections, not official results.
Official results are expected to be announced on Nov. 4.

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to retire from politics, saying voters had rejected his continued leadership and warning him against using Israel’s security for political gain.
Speaking to supporters early Wednesday at his Yashar party’s headquarters in Tel Aviv, Eisenkot said Israelis had voted for change and pledged to work with his partners to form a government representing all sections of society.
“It would be a mistake to hold another election, and it is my duty to do everything possible to carry out the will of the people,” he said.
Eisenkot acknowledged that the final results were still pending but said Netanyahu already faced a larger, stronger “Zionist majority” opposed to his continued rule.
Addressing Netanyahu directly, he said: “Do not dare use Israel’s security for your political needs.”
He also appealed to security chiefs to remember that Netanyahu was heading a caretaker government and that their responsibility was to serve the public.
“Remember that you serve only the interests of Israel’s citizens,” he said, urging them to stand firm against attempts to pressure them and offering his support.
Eisenkot declared that the era of division and incitement was over and pledged to form a Zionist government focused on military conscription.
His speech came as an updated Channel 13 exit poll put Netanyahu’s bloc and the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot level at 51 seats each, with 18 for Arab parties in the 120-seat Knesset.
Earlier, Channel 12 projected 52 seats for Eisenkot’s bloc, 50 for Netanyahu’s and 18 for Arab parties. Neither projection gave either bloc the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Channel 12 also reported that President Isaac Herzog was expected to task Eisenkot with forming the next government, although the decision would depend on the official results and parliamentary parties’ recommendations.
Turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 election, according to the Central Elections Committee.

Iran’s Mojtaba Khamenei reiterates conditions for ending war with US

Iran’s Mojtaba Khamenei reiterates conditions for ending war with US
- Iran says peace talks need the US to end its naval blockade of Persian Gulf ports and lift sanctions, while Washington wants concessions on Iran’s nuclear programme.
- Mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and China are pushing to stop more US-Israeli strikes and ease the Yemen conflict.
- Tehran also wants control of the Strait of Hormuz, and President Pezeshkian told Putin the region can solve its problems without the United States.
AI generated
TEHRAN – Iran’s Supreme Leader reiterated his country’s conditions for ending the war with the US, amid a regional diplomatic push to avert a fresh round of fighting in the Persian Gulf.
Mojtaba Khamenei emphasised the need to implement “the conditions set out by the country’s officials, with the aim of ending the war and the ‘neither war nor peace’ situation” in a meeting with national security chief Mohsen Rezaee, according to a Telegram statement.
Iran has previously said the US must end a naval blockade of its ports on the Persian Gulf and lift sanctions as preconditions for peace talks, while Washington is pushing for Iran to make concessions on its nuclear programme.
Khamenei’s statement comes amid a flurry of diplomatic activity aimed at preventing another round of US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic and resolving the mounting conflict in Yemen between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Since Oct 25, Tehran has hosted a delegation from Qatar – a key mediator with the US – and top security officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.
On Oct 27, China’s Foreign Ministry said it is also dispatching special envoys to the region “to prevent worsening of the situation”.
As well as the war, Khamenei and Rezaee also discussed “protecting national and regional security through the exercise of control over the Strait of Hormuz”, Oct 27’s Telegram statement said.
Disagreements over the strait led to the collapse of the last ceasefire between Iran and the US in June.
Tehran insists that it retain control over the waterway, which is vital for energy supplies, while the US wants to restore freedom of passage.
The countries are also at odds over Iran’s nuclear programme and whether the Islamic Republic should be able to enrich uranium.
Khamenei is Iran’s ultimate decision-maker, but has not appeared in public since the start of the war, sparking speculation about his health and the extent of his control over policy.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Oct 27 that Khamenei was in “complete health and maintains full command of the country’s domestic and international affairs” when he met him last week.
Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has been meeting various senior officials and leaders at a gas summit in Moscow, including Qatar’s Emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Pezeshkian also met his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin on Oct 27. Pezeshkian said that the Middle East can solve its problems without the involvement of the United States.
“I believe we are capable of resolving our problems in the region without relying on the United States,” he said at a meeting with Putin on the sidelines of a summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum in Moscow.
“Our trade is expanding and growing day by day. US actions in the region make it easier for us to move towards greater multilateralism and strengthen our cooperation with you and other countries subject to unilateral US sanctions,” he told Putin.
Putin said he discussed the war with Pezeshkian, expressing hope that the situation would improve.
“We spoke earlier, one-on-one, about the situation in the region – a situation that, undoubtedly, cannot help but cause concern,” he said, adding that he hoped it would “evolve in a positive direction”.
Pezeshkian said he was confident the will existed on both sides to expand cooperation in science, industry, culture, security and military affairs. BLOOMBERG, AFP

- Attorneys for the state and L.A. County said the administration offered no reliable evidence that the voters are noncitizens and no workable way to comply during an ongoing election.
- First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said he had made it ‘abundantly clear that American voters are being disenfranchised in real time.’
A federal judge on Tuesday seemed skeptical of a Trump administration request to immediately block California officials from counting about 20,000 ballots from voters whose citizenship the administration questions, but said he would not issue a ruling until Wednesday.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter questioned how the administration had derived its list of suspect voters, worried about disenfranchising eligible voters, said the demands would represent a “monumental change” to California elections and suggested federal prosecutors bringing the case had other means of holding illegal voters accountable.
But just one day after a federal appeals court rejected the same request, Carter said at the conclusion of a 3½-hour hearing in Los Angeles that he needed more time to rule — except on one related issue.
“This court believes it would be wise — that it would be wise — that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately,” he said — a clear reference to federal authorities threatening elections officials with criminal penalties if they count any of the flagged ballots.
The decision clears the way for the lower court to proceed with hearing the case. A hearing is scheduled Tuesday afternoon before Judge David O. Carter in Los Angeles.
After the hearing, First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles who argued on behalf of the Trump administration, said he had made it “abundantly clear that American voters are being disenfranchised in real time,” and that the administration will wait to see what Carter says Wednesday but was likely to appeal the matter back up to the appellate court.
He also denied threatening state officials, despite the Justice Department having sent formal letters to election officials statewide last week warning them of criminal punishments, and despite Essayli himself having reiterated that position earlier in court Tuesday.
Carter’s hearing came after Monday’s decision from the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals — the reverse of what’s normal — because Justice Department attorneys had tried to go over Carter’s head after he didn’t acquiesce to a deadline they’d set for him to rule on their request for a temporary restraining order against the state last week.
However, when the three-judge appellate panel — composed of two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — ruled 2-1 Monday that it had no jurisdiction to hear the case given Carter hadn’t yet had the chance, the case returned to Carter’s courtroom.
And there, Carter — an appointee of President Clinton — seemed loath to rush to judgment, despite the Trump administration’s claims of urgency. He said the administration’s method for arriving at its list of potential noncitizen voters was unclear and that he would like to develop the record further, including by bringing in an expert for the court.
“What are these systems? What are the algorithms? How was this derived?” he said.
He also seemed unmoved by the Justice Department’s argument that the ballots must be segregated immediately to prevent noncitizen votes from being counted, and more focused on whether noncitizens who illegally vote can be identified and held accountable while avoiding disenfranchising legitimate voters in the process.
For those who do vote illegally, “you’ve got a remedy, for goodness sakes,” he told Essayli. “Go out and indict.”
The Justice Department sued California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan on Oct. 15, two days after Acting Deputy Atty. Gen. Trent McCotter gave Weber and Logan 48 hours to set aside the ballots for the 20,000 flagged voters, whom McCotter described as “likely noncitizens.”
During the hearing, Essayli argued on behalf of the Trump administration that its demands on California and L.A. County were not onerous, could be complied with easily and did not call for ballots to go uncounted. Essayli said the federal government was in court “on a very narrow request for an injunction to separate ballots of those suspected of being noncitizens” only until the state can prove their citizenship.
At 76, Judge David Carter knows he shouldn’t be on skid row exposing himself to the coronavirus. But he wants more for L.A.’s homeless people.
He argued that the “reliability and credibility” of the federal government process for flagging the 20,000 voters is unquestionable — while also telling Carter, “We’re never going to stand here and tell you that everything is 100%.” He said every vote counts, as some elections “are decided by a handful of votes,” and that the federal government is simply asking California not to break existing federal law barring noncitizens from voting.
“We’re not telling California what they have to do. We’re telling them what they can’t do, which is just count these ballots without doing more to ensure whether they’re citizens or not,” Essayli said.
Essayli — who has aggressively sparred with California officials on social media for weeks — also argued to the court that the federal government has maintained a collaborative “tone” since first asking the state to segregate the ballots, and that he was surprised at how “adversarial” state elections officials have been on the issue.
Attorneys for Weber and the state said the Trump administration’s demand on the state “distorts several legal doctrines beyond recognition” and is clearly illegal, particularly during an ongoing election. They said the administration has provided no evidence that the 20,000 voters aren’t citizens, and has used “data and methods known to be unreliable.”
Michael Cohen, a deputy attorney general for the state, said the Trump administration questions California law that allows voters to attest to their citizenship under penalty of perjury, while ignoring the fact that standard was set not by the state but by Congress.
Anne Bellows, another deputy attorney general, said California has an established framework for running elections, and the Trump administration is trying to “sweep it off the table and replace it with a new, unclear procedure in which the federal government can issue a list and require California to change the way a subset of its voters’ ballots are received, and whether or not they are tabulated,” which she said was illegal and a “recipe for disenfranchisement” of thousands of legitimate voters.
“The stakes here are enormous,” she said.
Attorneys for Logan said the Trump administration has made its demands “without any credible argument” as to how it is legal, that the “proposed remedy” it is demanding from the state is “vague and unworkable,” and that if it wants to question California’s existing processes, “the proper audience for that argument” is Congress — not the federal court.
Several attorneys for voting and civil rights groups also argued against the Trump administration during the hearing, including by arguing that its reliance on third-party data sets — including from Lexis Nexis — was not a trustworthy way of identifying whether voters are citizens.
The litigation is just one part of a much wider battle by the Trump administration to intervene in state-run elections nationwide, and particularly in California, including on the notion that state elections have insufficient guardrails to prevent noncitizens from voting. Elections experts say such fraud occurs, but is exceedingly rare.
While the 9th Circuit panel’s unsigned ruling Monday rejected the Trump administration’s appeal for lack of jurisdiction, both judges in the majority — Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote independently to make clear that they would have rejected the case on its merits too.
They said it ran afoul of federal law barring interventions in voting in the immediate lead-up to elections, and the U.S. Constitution, which reserves control of elections for the states and oversight for Congress, not the executive branch.
Judge Patrick J. Bumatay, the other Trump appointee on the panel, also wrote independently in dissent — arguing the federal government must “have the power to stop this potential attack on the integrity of our elections.”
Carter previously rejected an administration lawsuit demanding California’s unredacted voter rolls as “unprecedented and illegal” — a decision similar to those made by dozens of other federal judges in other states. Federal prosecutors recently charged 28 lawful permanent residents in California with election-related crimes, including illegally registering to vote. Some of those charged expressed confusion, said they had no recollection of registering or had never voted.
There are more than 23 million registered voters in California.
Last week, Justice Department officials sent letters to election officials in counties across California demanding they sequester any flagged ballots in their jurisdictions, and warning them that they could face criminal penalties if they don’t. State officials denounced the letters as a legally baseless intimidation tactic.
Federal judges also have slapped back executive orders in which President Trump demanded new nationwide voter ID and citizenship requirements, and blocked a Trump administration plan to empower the U.S. Postal Service to vet mail ballots for the first time.
Beyond the courts, Democrats and voting rights groups have been strategizing for months on how to prevent the Trump administration from interfering in the midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has said it is merely trying to enforce the law and ensure that noncitizens do not illegally vote and negate the ballots of U.S. citizen voters.

German special forces preparing for war with Russia – commander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:07:48 UTC
09:07:48 KST

German special forces preparing for war with Russia – commander
Germany’s elite special forces are preparing for a potential large-scale war with Russia, the unit’s commander told Bild. The remarks come amid tensions between Moscow and NATO over the Ukraine conflict, with German officials warning that the armed forces must be ready for a confrontation by the end of the decade.
The highly secretive unit, known as Kommando Spezialkrafte (KSK), is comparable to Britain’s SAS or the US Green Berets. According to a report from its base in southwestern Germany published on Monday, the commandos are adjusting their training to counter Russian forces equipped with tanks, artillery, drones, and electronic warfare capabilities, including in extreme cold.
“We are orienting ourselves very specifically toward the adversary Russia,” KSK Commander Brigadier General Andreas Kuhne said, adding that his soldiers would have to be prepared to “remain in the field much longer,” potentially “with no end in sight,” if war broke out.
Kuhne also said the unit is preparing to carry out missions before conventional German forces enter combat. “When the 45th Armored Brigade in Lithuania starts its engines in a real emergency, we want to have already completed our job,” he told Bild.
According to the newspaper, only around a third of the KSK’s 1,500 personnel are commandos, while the rest serve in administrative and support roles.
The unit has been rocked by a series of far-right extremism scandals in recent years. In 2017, an investigation was launched following reports that soldiers performed Nazi salutes and listened to far-right music, among other things.
In 2018, investigations exposed an underground far-right network involving German military and security personnel, some of whom allegedly discussed plans to kill political opponents in the event of a breakdown of public order.
In 2020, police discovered a large cache of weapons, ammunition, explosives, and Nazi memorabilia at the property of a KSK sergeant major. Some of the ammunition was suspected of being stolen from German military stockpiles.
The scandals prompted then-Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer to disband one of the KSK’s four commando companies, the 2nd Company, and introduce sweeping reforms. The special forces command itself remained operational.
Speaking to Bild, Kuhne said disciplinary and conduct-related incidents within the unit have become “extremely rare,” but have not disappeared entirely, insisting that misconduct would no longer be tolerated or covered up.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed to transform the German armed forces into Europe’s strongest conventional military force in response to what he describes as threats from Russia. His government has prioritized defense spending and military assistance to Ukraine despite acknowledging that the German economy is in a “structural crisis.”
In July, The Telegraph and Die Welt reported that Berlin was preparing a secret plan to override potential resistance from regional governments to the deployment of NATO troops toward Russia’s borders.
Merz’s military ambitions come amid declining public support for his government. According to an INSA poll published by Bild this week, the chancellor ranked last among 20 prominent German politicians. The surging opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) won state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania in September, while the socialist Left Party (Die Linke) emerged as the largest party in Berlin’s election.
Russia has denied that it plans to attack NATO countries. In August, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed reports that Moscow intends to attack NATO members as “scare stories” that have “nothing to do with reality.”

Giant ball of 2.8 million eels gathers off Tasmania's coast to spawn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
00:02:11 UTC
09:02:11 KST

Australia's giant spawning eel ball estimated to contain 2.8 million eels
In short:
Ocean surveys have revealed that about 2.8 million eels gather for months at an underwater mountain off Tasmania.
The annual aggregation is the only known spawning site globally for purely oceanic eels.
What's next?
Further studies may determine where the eels come from and where their offspring go after spawning.
Millions of eels gather like clockwork each year to make out along a ridge at the bottom of a deep-sea mountain off Tasmania.
About 2.8 million basketwork eels (Diastobranchus capensis) — or 3,500 tonnes' worth — make the pilgrimage to a site next to Patience Seamount in the Huon Marine Park, according to a CSIRO-led study published in Royal Society Open Science.
CSIRO fisheries acoustics researcher and study lead author Ben Scoulding said finding a spawning site for any eel species was unique.
"It's the only known aggregation of … any deep-sea eel anywhere," he said.
Basketwork eels are apex scavengers that grow to about 1.8m in length and get their name from a crosshatch-like pattern on their skin.
"It's like those old woven baskets," Dr Scoulding said.
How do you find a big ball of eels?
Patience Seamount has been a known hot spot for basketwork eels since the 1980s.
Dr Scoulding said fishers had nicknamed the site Eel Hill because they regularly caught the species as bycatch while targeting orange roughy (Hoplostethus atlanticus).
"Then CSIRO conducted some work on the RV Southern Surveyor in the mid 2000s and put a camera down … to confirm the presence of the eels," he said.
But it took until more recent surveys between 2023 and 2025 to determine how many eels were there.
Dr Scoulding said researchers used a combination of techniques to calculate the size of the aggregation and what the eels were up to.
These included hydro-acoustic surveys, which Dr Scoulding described as a "really expensive scientific fish finder", from Australia's flagship ocean science ship the RV Investigator.
"We're essentially pinging sound down into the water column," Dr Scoulding said.
That sound then bounces off different objects and back to the scientists with unique signatures, depending on what is hit.
Dr Scoulding said basketwork eels reflected a lot of sound because they had a big swim bladder (an organ filled with gas to regulate a fish's buoyancy).
"Air is a really good reflector of sound," he said.
Knowing how much sound is reflected by a single eel, and using camera surveys, the researchers estimated the eel aggregation was about 1,000 metres deep and covered an area of about 2 by 3 kilometres.
"The eels are almost touching each other in that centre part," Dr Scoulding said.
"And then the further you get out, it's almost like having one eel in a living room, so every 20 metres cubed."
What are the eels up to?
The eels start gathering at Patience Seamount in December every year.
Dr Scoulding said numbers peaked around May to August before the eels disappeared in October.
"One of the interesting things is the persistence of the aggregation … it is there for the majority of the year," he said.
The researchers caught several eels and found all of them had empty stomachs.
Dr Scoulding said one female had spawned and all the others were close to spawning.
Why exactly the eels chose to gather at Patience specifically was unknown.
"It's one of 120 seamounts within Huon Marine Park … so it's quite unique that all the eels chose Patience to aggregate at," Dr Scoulding said.
Research is ongoing into the connectivity of basketwork eel populations around Australia and New Zealand and whether they all gather at Patience.
Why does it matter how many eels we have?
Basketwork eels are considered vulnerable to extinction on a global list of threatened species.
This is in part because of their status as bycatch in orange roughy fisheries (a popular species on the dinner plate).
Populations of the eel on a particular continental slope in New Zealand have declined 85 per cent in the past 40 years.
Whether similar collapses happened at Patience Seamount in the past was unclear.
Parks Australia island and marine parks branch head Shaun Barclay said the new study helped give a baseline for measuring future change for the eels.
"It's a great example of what marine parks are designed to do, protecting extraordinary places and to let us undertake the science to manage them in the future," he said.
Mr Barclay said Patience Seamount had been protected from the fishing practice of bottom trawling through a new management plan last year.

Israeli election turnout hits 27-year high at 77.7 percent
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
08:01:49 CST
09:01:49 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Voter turnout in Israel's parliamentary election on Tuesday reached 77.7 percent of eligible voters by the time polls closed at 10 p.m. local time, according to the final update from Israel's Central Elections Committee, which oversees the vote.
The turnout was the highest recorded in an Israeli election in 27 years, exceeding the 2022 figure by more than 7 percentage points.
Exit polls by public broadcaster Kan and commercial TV Channel 13 projected 53 seats for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's bloc against 50 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's, while Channel 12 gave Eisenkot's bloc 52 seats and Netanyahu's 50. Neither bloc reached the 61 seats needed for a majority. ■
