FBI agent says he feared case against ex-FBI officials tied to Hunter Biden probes would look political
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 - An FBI agent who helped lead the case against two former senior bureau officials accused of lying to Congress about Hunter Biden investigations testified on Tuesday that he feared the probe would look "political".
The testimony came at a hearing to decide whether the case against Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, both former senior counterintelligence officials, can go forward. It adds to defense claims that the Trump Justice Department brought the case for political reasons, which prosecutors deny.
FBI special agent Bryan Witt said his concerns were based on the fact that the probe began in July, the day after President Donald Trump gave a primetime speech in which he directed the FBI and other agencies to investigate whether the US intelligence community suppressed information about foreign meddling in the 2020 election.
One of the former FBI officials who was charged, Nikki Floris, sought to discredit an FBI intelligence report that said China sought to influence the 2020 election in favor of Biden. FBI Director Kash Patel directed the FBI’s field office in Kansas City, Missouri, where Witt is based, to investigate following Trump’s address, Witt testified.
“I had concerns this would be viewed as political,” Witt said.
The testimony revealed concerns within the FBI about a probe into two of the FBI’s most senior counterintelligence officials whose actions Trump and Republican lawmakers had condemned for years. The case is the latest brought by the Trump Justice Department to face claims of political bias.
Justice Department officials have argued the former FBI officials should be held accountable for misleading a congressional investigation. Spokespeople for the Justice Department and FBI did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Prosecutors called Witt to testify as the agent who outlined the allegations in a criminal complaint.
Asked by Floris’ defense lawyer, Margaret Donovan, if he viewed the investigation as a “witch hunt,” Witt denied making that statement but said “people generally viewed it as that around the office.”
The direction of the probe eventually changed from foreign election influence to 2023 testimony by Floris and Benavides before the House of Representatives Judiciary Committee. Both were charged last week with making false statements about their knowledge and involvement in Hunter Biden investigations.
Hunter Biden was charged during his father's administration with tax and gun crimes. Former President Joe Biden pardoned his son shortly before leaving office.
Floris and Benavides were both supervisors on the FBI’s foreign influence task force ahead of the 2020 election. A criminal complaint accused them of lying to the House panel in denying or downplaying their role in Hunter Biden probes, citing internal FBI records and witness interviews.
JUDGE CRITICIZES PROSECUTORS
Attorneys for Floris and Benavides have disputed the allegations and accused the Trump administration of bringing the case to drive a political narrative.
US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, who presided over the hearing, said their claims had some credibility as he condemned prosecutors for filing a new criminal complaint early on Tuesday that added an obstruction charge against both defendants without seeking a judge’s approval. Faruqui said he was aware of no previous instance of prosecutors filing a criminal complaint that had not been approved by a magistrate judge.
Prosecutors denied doing anything improper and argued they were not legally required to seek a judge’s sign-off.
Faruqui told prosecutors their conduct bolstered defense claims that “everything here is atypical and bizarre and that is because this is not an appropriate case.” REUTERS

No clear mandate projected in Israel election: What’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:06:47 UTC
08:06:47 KST

Israel election results: No clear winner projected, what’s next?
President Isaac Herzog will task the strongest candidate with forming government once results are finalised.
Exit polls from Israel’s legislative elections have come in, with no party or bloc projected to secure a clear mandate to form a new government.
According to The Times of Israel, the partial results give Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc 56 seats and the opposition alliance 48.
That could leave neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat parliament, setting the stage for weeks or months of political jockeying to form Israel’s next government.
The results also show the Arab-led parties, which are not part of either coalition, on course to secure 16 seats. This means the Arab-led parties could emerge as kingmakers if other parties agree to join forces with them.
Here’s what comes next:
What are the exit poll projections for the Israeli parties?
Here’s the breakdown, according to The Times of Israel, with over 66 percent of ballots counted.
Netanyahu’s ruling bloc is leading on 56 seats:
- Likud – 28
- United Torah Judaism – 8
- Shas – 7
- Otzma Yehudit – 7
- Religious Zionism – 6
The opposition alliance is ahead on 48 seats:
- Yashar – 21
- B’Yachad – 11
- Yisrael Beytenu – 8
- The Democrats – 8
Arab-led parties are on course to win 16 seats:
- Joint List – 12
- Ra’am – 4
How have parties reacted?
Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to the incumbent prime minister, said the exit polls show a “lack of confidence” in Netanyahu, while Yair Lapid, the current opposition leader, said the prime minister’s bloc has suffered a “crushing defeat”.
“This is a total collapse, and the public has told them to go home,” Lapid said.
But Gideon Saar, Israel’s foreign minister and a member of Netanyahu’s Likud party, said the opposition’s celebrations were premature.
In a social media post, he said: “Likud is the largest party in Israel. It is always good to learn something from the past.”
Netanyahu, who heads Likud, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises.
Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher based in Israel, told Al Jazeera that early exit poll projections show “a clear weakening of Netanyahu’s bloc” but expressed caution about “declaring either a Netanyahu victory or the end of his political career”.
“The exit polls suggest that his bloc has lost its majority, but they also suggest that his opponents face a difficult task in building one,” he said. “If neither side can form a government, Netanyahu could remain in office as caretaker while the negotiations continue.”
Who will the president nominate to form a government?
It remains to be seen.
Once the final vote tally is announced on November 4, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
That will not necessarily be the leader of the party that won the most seats in the Knesset.
With Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s parties emerging as the strongest, the two are viewed as leading contenders.
How much time will the invited leader have to form a coalition?
Up to 42 days. The candidate initially has 28 days, but the president can extend it by 14 days.
During this time, parties could engage in intensive negotiations and dealmaking, seeking policy concessions or potential ministerial portfolios, as the designated candidate tries to cobble together enough support to govern.
If the candidate cannot assemble a coalition with at least 61 seats, they could also try to form a minority government by relying on support from smaller parties, or negotiate a power-sharing arrangement with alternating prime ministers.
To be sworn in, a new government must win a parliamentary confidence vote by a simple majority, which can be fewer than 61 votes if a number of parties abstain.
What if negotiations fail?
If the first candidate fails to form a government, Herzog has the option of asking another Knesset member to try to do so within 28 days. If that candidate also fails, a majority of Knesset members could put forward a third candidate, who would have a final 14 days to try to assemble one.
If the Knesset remains at an impasse, it would be formally dissolved, and Israelis would return to the polls for another round of elections.
Those elections would have to be called within 90 days. In the meantime, Netanyahu’s government would remain in office as a caretaker government.
Has this happened before?
Yes.
Prolonged gridlock in the Knesset forced Israelis into three rounds of elections between April 2019 and March 2020. The result was a power-sharing agreement between Netanyahu and his then-chief rival, Benny Gantz, under which they were supposed to rotate the prime ministership.
That government collapsed a year later after failing to pass a budget.
Will the opposition form a coalition with the Arab-led parties?
While the exit polls suggest the Arab-led parties could become kingmakers, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with them, citing a lack of shared values.
Asaf Ronel, an Israeli political analyst, said that while exit polls suggest an end to Netanyahu’s “nightmarish government”, there are serious questions about whether other leaders can overcome their “racism and refusal” to collaborate with the Arab-led groups.
“The question now is whether they can let go of their racist election promise, otherwise the most likely scenario is that we are back to another round of elections in the next few months,” he said.
Mohamad Bazzi, director of the Hagop Kevorkian Center for Near Eastern Studies at New York University, said ignoring Arab-led parties will prove a difficult stance to maintain as negotiations continue.
“The numbers are going to make it difficult without that block, that large block, of seats for the Arab parties. It’s going to be difficult to get to that magic number,” he said, referring to the 61 seats required for a majority.
Bazzi also foresees an arrangement where the Arab parties could come to a compromise with Eisenkot’s opposition bloc.
“They could be invited in a form where they don’t actually have any ministries and where they don’t really have power in the governing coalition, but they would provide their support in the Knesset,” he explained.

Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:03:55 UTC
08:03:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel's exit polls show deadlock: What happens next?
Israelis went to the polls on Tuesday in the highest turnout in decades, with initial exit polls showing a slight edge but no majority for the opposition, meaning whoever can cobble together a coalition will form the next government.
The country's main pollsters projected the opposition bloc, led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, to win 52 or 53 seats, and ICC fugitive Netanyahu's bloc to win 50.
Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing they won 17 or 18 seats combined.
Here are four possible scenarios:
Coalition
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority in the 120-member Knesset, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate with the best chance to form a government, not necessarily the party with the most seats, which initial exit polls showed was Netanyahu's Likud.
The Arab parties, particularly Raam, have said they are open to working with Eisenkot's bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm's length, seeing their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu's bloc, however, there is no obvious way to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold to enter parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
After the November 2022 election, Benjamin Netanyahu took 58 days to form his government.
Minority government
If no bloc secures 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority, instead relying on ad hoc support from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab parties, whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian, could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, said it is unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but offered to provide a "safety net" for any one that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said especially high Arab turnout "indicates a strong desire for partnership".
Eisenkot has not publicly even entertained the possibility, and Netanyahu in his campaign relentlessly told Jewish voters that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
"Bottom line, at the moment it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results," Elovitz said.
National unity government
Given Israel's extreme polarisation, a national unity government may seem fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused about a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies and ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu's views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on 16 October found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot, a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the current situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu and casting him as unfit to lead.
Deadlock and new elections
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 because politicians could not forge a lasting coalition.
The president-designated candidate will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although other procedural measures can prevent new elections from being called immediately.

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce

Microsoft moves to shed quarter of workforce
US tech giant Microsoft is moving to shrink its workforce through a buyout program covering some 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global staff, the company has announced.
The move follows thousands of job cuts earlier this year and comes as Big Tech companies seek to slash payroll costs while ramping up AI investment.
Microsoft unveiled the program on Monday, saying that it would cover roughly 27% of its 223,000 employees across selected divisions in the US, Canada, UK, and India, including Xbox, Windows, Copilot, finance, and human resources.
Microsoft has described the initiative as a voluntary exit program, under which employees can leave with severance packages. The company has not disclosed how many workers it expects to accept the offer.
In a memo to employees, Microsoft’s chief people officer Amy Coleman said that the initiative would give eligible staff considering a departure an opportunity to leave with financial support.
The latest move follows several rounds of workforce reductions at Microsoft. In July, the company announced plans to eliminate 4,800 positions, including approximately 3,200 in its Xbox gaming division. It had already launched a voluntary exit program in April covering roughly 8,750 US employees, or about 7% of its American workforce, with around 30% reportedly taking the offer.
The cuts come as Microsoft commits enormous sums to AI infrastructure, including data centers and computing capacity, putting pressure on the company to remove other expenses.
Other Big Tech giants have also been cutting jobs while pouring billions into AI. Amazon announced 16,000 corporate job cuts earlier this year, following another 14,000 layoffs in 2025. Meta has also slashed jobs while ramping up AI investment, while Google has repeatedly launched voluntary exit programs to reduce its workforce.
The trend has fueled concerns that the technology being promoted as a driver of economic growth could also eliminate large numbers of jobs, particularly in administrative, technical, and other white-collar occupations.
The threat extends beyond the tech industry. The Netherlands announced plans on Monday to eliminate around 25,000 government positions by 2035, partly through the adoption of AI, in a drive to save €3.5 billion ($4 billion) annually. The cuts will be phased in over several years, with police and security services exempt.
Denmark has also announced plans to use AI to free up 50 million working hours annually by 2035, equivalent to roughly 30,000 full-time positions, although it has not committed to corresponding layoffs.
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has warned that AI could cause major upheaval in the labor market, while arguing that certain professions, including caregiving, should remain “human reserved” even if machines become capable of performing them.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk warned in July that AI would eventually outperform humans in any job, describing the transition as “a bumpy road.” His warning comes amid growing fears of AI spiraling out of human control following incidents involving systems defying instructions. Musk, whose company xAI develops advanced AI models, also predicted that the technology could surpass humanity’s combined intelligence within five years, potentially escaping human control within a decade.

Trump ally flees to US after Brazil election defeat – media
Right-wing Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has fled to the US following his election defeat to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, Reuters and Brazilian news outlet Jovem Pan reported on Tuesday, citing sources.
A senior US State Department official told AP on Tuesday that Bolsonaro and his family would be granted US visas.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of US President Donald Trump, narrowly lost Sunday’s runoff to Lula despite receiving more votes in the first round earlier this month.
He is under investigation for money laundering and currency evasion involving financial ties to lawyer Willer Tomaz and businesses linked to online gambling. Bolsonaro also faces a separate investigation into suspected irregularities in the financing of ‘Dark Horse’, a biographical film about his father. He denies wrongdoing.
His brother Eduardo, also a politician, moved to the US in February 2025, citing fears of political persecution and arrest. He was subsequently convicted of attempting to interfere with judicial proceedings against his father by lobbying Washington to impose sanctions on Brazilian officials. Eduardo, who remains in the US, was sentenced to four years and two months in prison in June 2026.
Flavio Bolsonaro initially refused to recognize the election results and vowed to seek annulment, citing a two-hour extension of voting.
“They will not silence me. They will not intimidate me. Let’s hold our heads high and keep fighting for our Brazil, whatever happens,” Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Monday, although he later dropped his demand for annulment.
Later on Monday, Bolsonaro was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of the investigation involving Tomaz. The documents were reportedly canceled on Tuesday after he missed the deadline. Bolsonaro, who could face prosecution in lower courts when his Senate term ends on January 31, said on Monday that he had no plans to flee.
Trump also questioned the election results. “It had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated,” he told reporters on Monday. “The extension given was very strange.”
Both campaigns requested a two-hour extension of voting on election day, citing difficulties for voters, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court.
Bolsonaro’s father is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The elder Bolsonaro also traveled to the US following his defeat before returning to Brazil. He denied wrongdoing and argued that the case was politically motivated.
Lula previously served two presidential terms from 2003 to 2010. He was barred from running in the 2018 election after being convicted on corruption charges and imprisoned. Brazil’s Supreme Court later annulled his convictions, restoring his political rights and allowing him to run in 2022, when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro. Lula has also denied wrongdoing and maintained that the corruption case against him was politically motivated.

Ukraine’s Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
23:39:53 CET
07:39:53 KST

Oct 27 (Reuters) - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv’s troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv’s battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
“It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions,” Zelenskiy said.
“Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine’s Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called “fortress belt” of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin’s presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia’s General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow’s forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
Ukraine’s military dismissed the Russian statements.
(Reporting by Ron Popeski and Oleksandr Kozhukhar; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

By Kanishka Singh
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. faced widespread rebuke from civil rights groups, healthcare advocates and Democrats on Tuesday over his anti-Arab comments that the Council on American-Islamic Relations cast as “a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry.”
In his remarks on Monday at a campaign event in Michigan where Republican Mike Rogers is running for the US Senate against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, the US health secretary falsely claimed that Arabs had not won major international awards and “don’t produce” science and literature.
“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” the US health chief said.
Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with the US health chief’s comments.
The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
US rights advocates have raised concerns over escalating rhetoric against Muslims, Arabs, immigrants and ethnic minorities by President Donald Trump and his allies during the ongoing midterm election campaign.
“Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vile anti-Arab rant is a textbook display of unvarnished racism and bigotry,” the Council on American-Islamic Relations, which documents hate against Muslims and Arabs in the US, said on Tuesday.
“His sweeping erasure of Arab contributions to humanity is not only maliciously false, but it also fans the flames of anti-Arab and anti-Muslim hate at a time when communities are already vulnerable to bigoted attacks from other public officials nationwide.”
Kennedy said the rise of the Muslim Brotherhood, one of the Arab world’s oldest and most influential Islamist groups founded almost a century ago, has “created stagnant societies.”
Republicans have claimed, without evidence, El-Sayed has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood even as the Democrat has publicly disavowed the group and denied any connection to it.
El-Sayed, who is Muslim, has faced a host of anti-Muslim attacks during the campaign. Over the weekend, Trump invoked the September 11, 2001, attacks when speaking about El-Sayed, whom he has also repeatedly and falsely called a “jihadist.”
Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy also responded to the US health secretary’s comments.
“I really think everyone needs to pay attention to this coordinated campaign to delegitimize Muslim Americans — not just as citizens but as humans.”
US healthcare advocacy organization and nonprofit Protect Our Care cast Kennedy’s comments as a “wildly racist tirade.”
Kennedy, who has pushed his anti-vaccine views in his role as the top health official, was also in Michigan on Monday to promote funding for Detroit’s health department and touted agreements with hospitals to offer healthier food.
(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; editing by Caroline Humer and Aurora Ellis)

U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., committed Tuesday to a peaceful postelection transfer of power, calling concerns that President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans could contest the results if Democrats win control of Congress "absurd."

Alexander brothers each get 30 years for sex trafficking in US

- Victims said they were drugged and raped at luxury events, while prosecutors said the brothers used wealth and status to lure and abuse women.
- The judge called their conduct “monstrous”, rejected life terms as too harsh, and the brothers said they will appeal.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The Alexander brothers, two of whom were once among the US’ top luxury real estate brokers, were each given 30 years in prison for using their wealth and glamorous lifestyles to traffic women for sex.
Oren and Tal Alexander and their non-broker brother Alon were sentenced on Oct 27 by US District Judge Valerie Caproni. The three were convicted in March of sex trafficking and other charges after a five-week trial in which a number of their victims testified.
Caproni told the brothers: “Your conduct was monstrous.”
Tal, 40, and Oren and Alon, both 39, maintained grim expressions during the sentencing but otherwise had little reaction. The prison terms, while lengthy, were less than the life behind bars prosecutors sought. Lawyers for the brothers told the judge they would appeal.
The prosecution was one of the highest-profile sex-trafficking cases to go to trial in recent years.
Oren and Tal were brokers on some of the most expensive residential property sales ever in New York and Miami, claiming US$8 billion (S$10.26 billion) in sales and dubbing themselves the “0.1% of brokers that really sell to the 0.1% of clients”.
At trial, several women testified that they were drugged and raped after being lured to parties, music festivals and other events in glamorous locations such as the Hamptons and Aspen, Colorado.
In requesting life sentences, prosecutors said the Alexanders “spent years designing, executing and perfecting their playbook of luring victims with promises of luxury, drugging victims so they could not resist, and then forcibly raping them”.
Before sentencing the brothers, Caproni allowed 12 victims to speak. Many addressed the brothers directly, who showed no visible reaction during the statements. One woman said their “wealth, power and social standing cannot shield them from the consequences of their actions”.
Lawyers for the brothers had asked that they be given no more than 15 years behind bars. They claimed that all the encounters were consensual and accused the government of trying to criminalise the behaviour of successful young men seeking to enjoy their lives as bachelors.
The Alexanders also addressed the court. They maintained their innocence and characterised their actions as youthful partying and womanising that often involved recreational drug use and excessive drinking.
Tal described himself as having a “work hard, play hard mentality”.
“I sometimes behaved in ways I’m not proud of,” he told the judge.
Caproni suggested that the brothers might have been better off remaining silent. “You didn’t have to say anything this afternoon. You did not have to stand up and say you never drugged or raped a woman,” she said.
“In my view, that’s entirely a lie.”
But the judge also said she regarded sentencing them to life in prison as a “draconian penalty” and that she did not believe the brothers were “beyond redemption”.
In a statement, Manhattan US Attorney Jamie McDonald, whose office prosecuted the case, said: “Today’s sentence makes clear that this craven, sinister conduct is extraordinarily serious and will be met with serious punishment.”

Porsche posts earnings rebound but expects lower vehicle sales in 2027
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:25:04 CST
07:25:04 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- A senior executive at German sports carmaker Porsche said Tuesday that 2027 was expected to mark a low point for the company, with vehicle sales and operating profit likely to decline, despite a sharp rebound in earnings in the first nine months of 2026.
Porsche chief financial officer Jochen Breckner attributed the expected downturn to gaps in the company's "product portfolio," noting during a quarterly earnings presentation that the combustion-engine Macan was no longer available following the end of its production earlier this year.
According to financial results released Tuesday, Porsche's global vehicle deliveries fell 16 percent year-on-year to 178,532 units in the first nine months, while revenue declined by a smaller 5.9 percent to 25.28 billion euros (28.17 billion U.S. dollars). The company said a higher proportion of high-margin models helped cushion the impact of lower sales volumes.
By contrast, operating profit surged to 1.74 billion euros (1.94 billion dollars) from just 40 million euros (44.6 million dollars) a year earlier, lifting the operating profit margin to 6.9 percent from 0.2 percent.
The Volkswagen-owned carmaker attributed the sharp rebound largely to lower special charges, which fell to around 500 million euros (557 million dollars) in the first nine months from 2.7 billion euros (3 billion dollars) a year earlier.
The charges were mainly related to changes in its electric vehicle strategy and battery operations, alongside workforce restructuring.
In 2022, Porsche announced an ambitious electrification target, aiming for fully electric vehicles to account for more than 80 percent of its sales by 2030.
However, the company revised its strategy late last year amid weaker-than-expected demand for electric vehicles, delaying some electric vehicle projects and extending plans for combustion-engine models. The changes resulted in substantial one-off charges that weighed heavily on last year's earnings.
Alongside the shift in its product strategy, Porsche has also moved to cut costs and reduce its workforce. In July, the company announced plans to cut another 5,000 jobs in Germany by 2035, bringing its planned workforce reductions to around 9,000 positions in the country. ■

New CDC report finds 19 germs cause 50,800 deaths annually in U.S.
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-28
06:24:56 CST
07:24:56 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Nineteen pathogens cause an estimated 9.7 million infections and 50,800 deaths in the United States each year, according to an updated report released by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) on Tuesday.
The 2026 Antimicrobial Resistance Threats Report is the CDC's most comprehensive estimate to date of the impact of drug-resistant bacteria and fungi, as well as Clostridioides difficile, the CDC said.
The report classifies 19 pathogens according to their threat to public health in the United States: four as urgent threats, 13 as serious threats and two as concerning threats.
The four urgent threats are Candida auris (C. auris), carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, and drug-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the report said.
Drug-resistant C. auris infections have increased tenfold since 2019, and some strains are resistant to available classes of antifungal drugs, according to the report.
The report also highlighted the rapid spread of resistance genes, which can make infections harder to treat and more deadly.
"Antimicrobial resistance threatens modern medicine and puts millions of Americans at risk every year," CDC Director Erica Schwartz was quoted as saying by U.S. media outlets. "High-quality data help drive action, and CDC is committed to providing easily accessible information to help protect people from drug-resistant infections." ■

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- U.S. aerospace giant Boeing on Tuesday reported a sharp reduction in its third-quarter net loss, while revenue rose 4 percent year on year to 24.19 billion U.S. dollars, driven by stronger defense and services businesses.
For the quarter that ended Sept. 30, Boeing posted a net loss of 116 million dollars, compared with 5.34 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted loss per share narrowed to 26 cents from 7.14 dollars, while core loss per share, a non-GAAP measure, narrowed to 34 cents from 7.47 dollars.
Operating profit reached 354 million dollars, reversing a 4.78-billion-dollar loss, while operating margin improved to 1.5 percent from negative 20.5 percent.
Commercial airplanes revenue fell 3 percent to 10.7 billion dollars, reflecting a less favorable delivery mix. The division's operating loss narrowed to 697 million dollars from 5.35 billion dollars, while deliveries edged up to 161 aircraft from 160.
Boeing said higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and increased supply chain costs weighed on the division's performance. The year-earlier results were affected by a charge related to the 777X program.
Defense, space and security revenue rose 15 percent to 7.94 billion dollars, with operating profit increasing to 492 million dollars from 114 million dollars, partly reflecting a 252-million-dollar gain from the sale of HRL Laboratories.
Global services revenue grew 4 percent to 5.57 billion dollars, while operating profit reached 1.02 billion dollars.
Operating cash flow rose 33 percent year on year to 1.5 billion dollars, while free cash flow, a non-GAAP measure, reached 464 million dollars. Total order backlog rose to a record 745 billion dollars, including more than 6,300 commercial airplanes.
Boeing also reported progress in its aircraft certification programs. The 737-7 received amended type certification from the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration during the quarter, while the 737-10 obtained certification in October. The company said the 777X program remains on track for its first delivery in 2027. ■

Unknown Publisher

07:24:16 KST

LONDON, Oct. 27 (Xinhua) -- Britain's shop price inflation rose to the highest level in two and a half years amid retailers' limited capability to absorb cost hikes, data from the British Retail Consortium (BRC) showed Tuesday.
Shop prices increased 2.1 percent year on year in October, accelerating from 1.4 percent in September, and well above the 3-month average of 1.6 percent, according to the BRC.
Food inflation accelerated to 2.9 percent from 2.5 percent in September, while non-food inflation rose to 1.7 percent from 0.8 percent.
Mike Watkins, head of retailer and business insight at global marketing research firm NielsenIQ, said global supply chain pressures grew over the last six months, but price cuts by food retailers since the end of summer have delayed some of the impact.
High street retailers will now be more reliant on promotions to drive discretionary non-food spending as consumers are becoming more cautious in the face of higher energy and fuel costs, he added.
Commenting on the record-high shop price inflation, BRC Chief Executive Helen Dickinson said, "The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years."
Although retailers still deliver plenty of promotions on sweet treats ahead of Halloween, price hikes of ambient groceries have driven up food inflation, she noted, emphasizing that non-food inflation climbed to an almost three-year peak as high energy and transport costs pushed up prices.
"The message to the Chancellor ahead of tomorrow's Budget could not be clearer: act now, or prices will keep on rising," Dickinson said, arguing that since retailers cannot endlessly swallow higher business rates, employment costs, energy bills and packaging taxes, October's jump in inflation is only the beginning without a change of course. ■

Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:24:04 UTC
07:24:04 KST

Why Moscow shouldn’t fear a Democratic victory in the US midterms
When Donald Trump returned triumphantly to the White House in January 2025, his supporters believed they could finally finish what he started during his first term and reverse the Democrats’ social engineering agenda, commonly known as ‘wokeism’, curb illegal immigration, accelerate technological development, and above all, ‘make America great again’.
Trump moved quickly on the first two priorities, as he revoked 78 of Joe Biden’s executive orders, tightened border controls and gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) greater resources and powers to conduct raids in sanctuary cities, where the local authorities limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
But Trump’s determination to achieve everything at once, from restructuring the federal government and securing favorable trade deals to pursuing ambitions involving Greenland and Venezuela, has kept American politics in a state of turmoil, while his confrontational approach has also unsettled allies and opponents abroad.
The decision to launch joint military operations with Israel against Iran has proven particularly divisive as it fractured Trump’s conservative coalition, with some supporters accusing him of betraying his promise to end America’s ‘endless wars’, while others fear the political consequences for Republicans in the approaching midterm elections.
The Iran war has also hurt American consumers. Over the past year, gasoline prices have risen by 38% and diesel by 71%, while food prices have increased by 2.5%.
The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz isn’t solely responsible, but Democrats and sympathetic media outlets have made it central to their criticism, while they also point to an increase of $3.8 trillion in the national debt since Trump’s return, allegations of corruption within his administration, and questions about the competence of senior officials, particularly Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
Republicans, including those who oppose the Iran war, are trying to redirect voters towards the administration’s achievements – despite the turbulence, the US economy has grown by 3.2% since the end of 2024, and investment is booming in certain sectors, particularly technology, while illegal crossings at the southern border have reportedly fallen by 95%.
Vice President J.D. Vance, who is increasingly discussed as Trump’s successor, has urged Americans to give Republicans another chance, or at least another two years, to complete what they have begun – but for now, that opportunity appears uncertain. Yet contrary to expectations, losing control of Congress wouldn’t necessarily be a disaster for Trump.
Even with Republican majorities in both chambers, he has preferred to govern through executive orders, issuing more than 290 since January 2025, and this is hardly unprecedented. Bill Clinton issued 364 over his eight years in office, including during periods when Republicans controlled Congress.
For presidents, demonstrating immediate effectiveness and scoring political points often matters more than ensuring continuity.
Democratic threats to impeach Trump and members of his administration may sound formidable, but removing officials from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate, a much higher hurdle, and even if Democrats capture both chambers, converting their numerical advantage into meaningful political influence will not be straightforward.
They could, however, obstruct legislation, block nominations to senior administration positions and the federal judiciary, and subject the White House to sustained congressional scrutiny.
Their minimum objective would be to turn Trump into a lame-duck president for his remaining two years, but this strategy carries risks of its own – in the 2028 presidential campaign, Republicans can argue that the Democrats prevented them from completing their program.
For Moscow, however, the consequences of the midterms could be considerably more serious.
A Democratic-controlled Congress would almost certainly seek to complicate relations with Russia, and there remains a strong desire in Washington to obstruct Trump’s apparent ambition for a new Yalta involving Russia, China, and the US. Equally persistent is the determination among influential American political circles to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia.
This could explain the Trump administration’s intensified diplomatic activity over Ukraine, given whatever opportunities exist for reaching an agreement today could narrow considerably after the new Congress takes office in January 2027.
The urgency could also reflect an attempt to secure lasting advantages for the administration before the political landscape changes.
The argument that there’s little time left, and that Moscow must therefore accept an agreement now or face worse conditions later, shouldn’t be allowed to overshadow Russia’s own interests.
Russia has an objective interest in normalizing relations with the US, but a settlement of the Ukraine conflict must be based on mutually beneficial terms, rather than unilateral concessions extracted under the pressure of America’s electoral calendar.
Ultimately, as Americans prepare to vote in the midterms, Russia should be concerned less with Trump’s political fortunes than with protecting its own interests.
This article was first published by Kommersant, and was translated and edited by the RT team

28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva strongly criticized defeated presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Tuesday, describing the conservative senator’s clandestine departure for the United States as a “shameful” evasion of Brazilian justice.
Speaking two days after winning Brazil's presidential runoff, Lula addressed reports that the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro fled the country to avoid an ongoing money-laundering inquiry.
“He could have stayed and proven that the accusations against him are not true,” Lula remarked. “If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear. A citizen who sneaks out of their own country does so because they have something to hide.”
Confirmation of Bolsonaro’s departure came as a senior US State Department official announced that the US will issue visas to the senator and his family to enter the country.
The flight follows a high-stakes judicial showdown in Brasilia. On Monday, Federal Supreme Court (STF) Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to hand over all travel documents, including his ordinary, diplomatic, and Italian passports, and imposed a strict departure ban over alleged involvement in a money-laundering scheme linked to illegal digital betting platforms.
After the 24-hour deadline expired on Tuesday morning without compliance, the Federal Police formally revoked his Brazilian passports. Just hours before his departure, Bolsonaro publicly insisted he would not flee.
"I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this farce, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me," he said.
Lula sharply criticized Bolsonaro’s failure to abide by judicial commands, contrasting the senator’s actions with his own historical compliance during previous legal proceedings.
“He has proven himself to be the biggest liar I have ever seen on the face of the Earth,” Lula said. “When I was asked to hand over my passport, I did so. He should have surrendered his to the Federal Police given the suspicion that he might flee. But that is the Bolsonaro family for you, Brazil is only his second homeland. His true allegiance lies with the United States.”
Bolsonaro's sudden flight caps a chaotic three-day period following his unexpected loss in Sunday’s runoff election. After leading the first round on Oct. 4 with 47% of valid votes to Lula’s 45%, Bolsonaro had expressed supreme confidence in victory, dropping hints about his future cabinet appointments.
On Sunday, Lula staged a comeback, capturing 51.76% of valid votes to become the first candidate in Brazilian history to reverse a first-round deficit in a presidential runoff.

Ukraine's Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27

Ukraine's Zelenskiy says territory recaptured, forces on the offensive
Oct 27 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Tuesday that Ukrainian forces were retaking territory through a series of offensives, including one operation previously unannounced in which Kyiv's troops used gas pipelines to outflank Russian positions.
Zelenskiy, speaking in his nightly video address, said Kyiv's battlefield position was the strongest in some time in the 4-1/2-year-long war and could be made stronger with more deliveries of air defence systems from its Western allies.
Zelenskiy, citing a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the "Veles" operation using pipelines in Ukraine's northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in eastern Ukraine and the "Vivaldi" operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in key areas.
He said Operation Veles was conducted near Kupiansk, a city in northeastern Kharkiv region recaptured by Ukrainian forces in late 2022, but since under constant Russian pressure.
"It is a strong operation, well planned and technology-driven. The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to advance past our positions," Zelenskiy said.
"Our fighters turned this tactic against the Russians and used the underground infrastructure against the occupiers with extraordinary success," he said.
In the Vivaldi offensive, one senior commander reported last month that Ukraine's Third Army Corps had cleared an area of 75 square kilometres (29 square miles) of Russian infiltration groups and recaptured a further 10 square kilometres.
That operation was focused to the north of the key strongholds in the region — the so-called "fortress belt" of the cities Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Their capture would bring Russia closer to its goal of seizing the entire Donbas region.
Zelenskiy in August spoke of success in an offensive further south, with 26 villages being returned to Ukrainian control.
Russia says it favours an overall resolution of the war rather than a short-lived ceasefire and has pledged to pursue its drive to capture all of Donbas.
Russian commanders repeatedly say, often in announcements in President Vladimir Putin's presence, that their forces are advancing on all sections of the 1,200-km (750-mile) front line.
The chief of Russia's General Staff, Valery Gerasimov, said this month that Moscow's forces had captured 92 Ukrainian settlements, including the town of Dobropillia, since the beginning of September.
Ukraine's military dismissed the Russian statements. REUTERS

Acting oil minister in Moscow: trilateral energy co-op, Iran–Russia gas swap via Azerbaijan

Acting oil minister in Moscow: trilateral energy co-op, Iran–Russia gas swap via Azerbaijan
TEHRAN- Hamid Bovard, caretaker of the Ministry of Oil, on Monday, while announcing the positions of the Islamic Republic of Iran at the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, held bilateral and multilateral consultations aimed at strengthening Iran’s cooperation with other energy-reserve-holding countries.
According to an IRNA report on Monday evening, Hamid Bovard in Moscow continued the thread of contact and trilateral interactions among Iran, Russia, and the Republic of Azerbaijan, which had previously been pursued at the level of the heads of state of these countries in Turkmenistan.
Accordingly, the caretaker of the Ministry of Oil and the energy ministers of Russia and the Republic of Azerbaijan, in a trilateral meeting, discussed strengthening cooperation in the energy sector and effective presence in gas markets.
Bovard, Sergei Tsivilev, Russia’s Minister of Energy, and Parviz Shahbazov, Azerbaijan’s Minister of Energy, exchanged views on ways to develop trilateral cooperation among Tehran, Moscow, and Baku.
In this trilateral meeting, the caretaker of the Ministry of Oil said: “A general agreement for gas exchange between Iran and Russia via the Republic of Azerbaijan has been reached, and the technical stages of implementing this agreement are now being pursued and are on the path to finalization.”
Bovard added: “We hope that with the conclusion of the gas transfer program through the pipeline pursued by the Russian side via the Republic of Azerbaijan, the possibility of gas exchange between Iran and Russia will be provided in the near future.”
In a bilateral meeting with Russia’s Minister of Energy, the caretaker of the Ministry of Oil expressed satisfaction with the process of developing bilateral cooperation and said: “The agreement among Tehran, Moscow, and Baku to finalize the gas trade contract between Iran and Russia will be promising news, and efforts to finalize this contract have accelerated.”
In this meeting, attracting investment by Russian companies for the development of Iran’s oil and gas fields was reviewed.
The two sides also examined the existing obstacles to the implementation of understandings reached at the 19th Meeting of the Iran–Russia Joint Economic Cooperation Committee and exchanged views on solutions to remove these obstacles.
Russia’s Minister of Energy also said that the next meeting of the two countries’ Joint Economic Cooperation Committee will be hosted by Russia.
The Iran–Russia Joint Economic Cooperation Committee is one of the main mechanisms for pursuing and developing cooperation between the two countries in various economic fields, and a significant part of issues related to energy, investment, trade, and the implementation of joint projects between the two countries is pursued within the framework of this commission.
The 19th Iran–Russia Joint Economic Cooperation Committee was held in Tehran in Bahman 1404, and a wide range of issues was reviewed, including the completion of the International North–South Transport Corridor, gas transfer from Russia to Iran, and the development of cooperation in the fields of space industries, nuclear energy, commercial and economic affairs, finance and banking, customs, industry and mining, agriculture, health, culture and tourism, and science and technology.

Iran calls on gas exporters to strengthen cooperation, safeguard energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:16:35 UTC
07:16:35 KST

Iran calls on gas exporters to strengthen cooperation, safeguard energy security
TEHRAN- At the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, Iran’s Acting Minister of Oil, Hamid Bovard, presented a broad strategic vision linking global energy security to peace, regional stability, the security of critical infrastructure, and respect for national sovereignty.
Speaking as the Forum marked its 25th anniversary, Bovard said the global energy system is passing through one of its most complex periods of geopolitical, economic, and technological change. He thanked Russia for hosting the meeting and honored the memory of those killed in the recent war waged by the United States and the Zionist regime against Iran, including Ayatollah Khamenei, civilians, schoolchildren in Minab, and athletes from Lamerd.
Bovard argued that the recent energy crisis caused by the imposed war demonstrated that energy security is not merely an economic or technical issue. It is inseparably tied to peace, regional stability, infrastructure security, and respect for national sovereignty. The consequences of aggression, he said, can extend beyond the region and affect global energy supply, economic growth, and development. He criticized US military interventions in areas including the Persian Gulf and unilateral economic sanctions, saying they not only target Iran’s legitimate rights and interests but also damage trust, investment security, and the predictability of global energy markets. In Iran’s view, world energy security cannot be achieved without the security of energy producers, respect for their sovereignty, sustainable investment, and effective international cooperation.
He said the GECF must become more than ever a platform for convergence, dialogue, and practical cooperation among producing countries, and described the Eighth GECF Summit as a valuable opportunity to strengthen this approach and set a new horizon for strategic cooperation. While the Forum was founded in Tehran in 2001 and is entering a new institutional phase, Bovard said rapid global changes require members to preserve fundamental principles while reconfiguring priorities, tools, and cooperation mechanisms. Iran’s strategic priorities include flexibility toward global energy crises, strengthening natural gas’s role in the future energy mix, and expanding investment, management, and technological cooperation.
Citing the COVID-19 crisis in 2020 and geopolitical developments in 2026, Bovard said global energy markets are more exposed than ever to unpredictable shocks. The GECF should strengthen its capacity for early risk identification, crisis scenario analysis, and coordinated responses. He called for revising the Forum’s long-term strategy with emphasis on strengthening the natural gas value chain. Natural gas, he said, will remain a key pillar of global energy security and economic development because of its reliability, abundance, operational flexibility, industrial applications, and complementary role in renewable energy development. According to the GECF Global Gas Outlook, global gas demand will rise 31 percent by 2055 to more than 5,400 billion cubic meters, and its share of the world energy mix will increase from about 23 percent to 26 percent.
Bovard proposed that the Secretariat, with member participation, study a roadmap to raise natural gas’s share of the global energy mix to an ambitious 30 percent. Such a roadmap should rest on economic studies, long-term demand assessment, investment requirements, and environmental considerations. He also said members should adopt a coordinated approach, based on technical realities and common interests, toward climate regulations and mechanisms that could impose unbalanced restrictions on energy trade and investment, including the possible effects of the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism.
He stressed that huge underground reserves alone do not guarantee supply security. What converts gas resources into energy security is timely investment, access to technology, infrastructure development, and sustainable demand. The GECF outlook estimates that meeting global needs through 2055 will require about $11.6 trillion in upstream investment and $735 billion in midstream investment—more than $12 trillion in total. This makes a stable, predictable environment with appropriate financing mechanisms essential.
Bovard said member cooperation could focus on three areas: first, joint financing and investment mechanisms for gas projects using national, regional, and international financial institutions; second, technological cooperation, knowledge transfer, training, and joint upstream, midstream, and downstream projects, where Iran has extensive experience; and third, structured dialogue between producers and consumers to increase demand security, reduce investment risks, and balance supplier and consumer interests. The Secretariat could play a more active role in identifying opportunities, facilitating contacts among specialized institutions, and following up on practical results.
As a proposer and main founder of the GECF, Iran has consistently emphasized multilateral cooperation, mutual respect, and common capacities for sustainable gas industry development. Bovard said the 14th government, under the Seventh Development Plan, prioritizes cooperation with international energy organizations, especially the GECF. Iran holds the world’s second-largest proven gas reserves and has strategic geography and extensive technical, industrial, and human capacities.
Despite decades of sanctions and imposed wars, Iran’s gas industry has reached annual production capacity of about 300 billion cubic meters, making it one of the world’s three largest producers. Natural gas accounts for about 70 percent of Iran’s energy mix, and the gas network covers about 95 percent of the population. Bovard said Iran is ready to share these experiences through bilateral and multilateral cooperation and to help develop joint projects and strengthen GECF members’ capabilities.
He concluded that the future of the gas industry depends not only on reserves and production capacity but also on the quality of cooperation, policy stability, and the ability to respond jointly to global challenges. The Forum’s 25th anniversary, he said, is an opportunity to begin a new chapter of results-oriented cooperation, joint investment, and strategic convergence. He expressed confidence that collective will and the Secretariat’s capacities can further strengthen the GECF’s role in global energy dialogue and hoped the ministerial meeting and Eighth Summit would strengthen solidarity and realize the common interests of gas producers and consumers.

What Early Voting Data Is Showing About the Midterm Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:15:02 UTC
07:15:02 KST

Election Day is still a week away. But with early voting for the midterms underway in nearly every state, tens of millions of Americans have already cast their ballots, offering an initial glimpse into how the pivotal elections may play out.
With days of early voting left to go before Election Day on Nov. 3, that figure already represents more than a quarter of the roughly 122 million Americans who voted in the 2022 midterms.
Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida who runs the Election Lab, stresses to TIME that early voting data cannot in and of itself be relied on to predict the outcome of the elections. But he says it can reveal other informative aspects of voting behavior.
“Once you start seeing consistency across multiple days of voting and across multiple states, it starts giving us more confidence that whatever we're seeing in terms of relative engagement, that's likely going to carry through to election day,” McDonald says.
Here are some of the notable trends emerging in the early voting data as Election Day nears.
Democrats are outpacing Republicans in early ballots
Registered Democrats so far represent a larger share of early voters in the midterms than Republicans, having cast roughly 45% of early ballots compared to 31% cast by GOP voters, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab data. Another 24% of Americans who have voted early are not registered with either party.
This data is only available for the 27 states that have a formal party registration system, and signifies only the party with which a voter is registered, not the candidates selected on their ballot.
Experts caution that Democrats’ higher turnout in the early vote does not guarantee they’ll maintain that edge, with tens of millions more Americans still expected to show up at the polls.
Republicans are anticipated to make up ground on Election Day, as they have in recent years. A Pew Research survey conducted following the 2024 elections showed that nearly 40% of registered Republican voters cast their ballot in person on Election Day, compared to 28% of registered Democratic voters.
“We expect the Democrats to build up a lead in the early vote, and Election Day tends to be a Republican day, so you can't just look at the early vote as it is now,” McDonald tells TIME.
Polling has shown, however, that Democratic engagement and enthusiasm is higher than it is for Republicans in the lead-up to the elections. According to a PBS News/NPR/Marist poll released on Tuesday, 52% of likely voters said they would back the Democratic candidate in their House district, while 44% would back the Republican candidate. Independent likely voters favored Democratic candidates by 13 points.
More Democrats than Republicans also said in the survey they were very enthusiastic about voting, at 71% and 61% respectively. Another poll from the Pew Research Center earlier this month similarly showed greater engagement and stated motivation from voters backing Democrats: 78% of voters who voiced support for the Democratic candidate in their House district said who controls Congress “really matters,” compared to 69% of voters who backed Republican candidates who said the same. Such polls have suggested a “blue wave” of Democratic support might determine the midterms, but Republicans have pushed back against the numbers.
Bernard Fraga, a political science professor at Emory University, tells TIME that the relative lack of Republican enthusiasm in polls and trailing GOP turnout in early voting shows that support within the party, and for President Donald Trump, has waned.
“This is a story about Democrats who voted in 2024 persisting, and Republicans who voted in 2024 so far at least staying home,” he says.
The midterms come as Trump’s approval rating has hit near record lows amid widespread dissatisfaction with his handling of the war in Iran and the economy. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday put Trump’s approval rating at 32%, up one percentage point from last week, when the same poll recorded the lowest approval rating of his second term.
Fraga says that Republicans are frustrated with what he describes as “failures” of the Trump Administration, which he asserts have decreased GOP voters’ support for their party and led them to stay home rather than casting ballots early.
“Even for steadfast Republican voters, they look at the state of the economy, for example, and say that they're not too enthusiastic about voting,” he says. “Reading the trends, it's clear that Democrats are enthusiastic and mobilized to a much greater degree than even the Republican voters.”
Simon Rosenberg, a long-time Democratic strategist, contends that independents are also more likely to be voting in favor of Democrats, given recent polling, which has shown that more independent likely voters support Democratic candidates. One YouGov poll found that 54% of independents said they’d vote for Democratic candidates, versus 27% who said they’d vote for Republican candidates. Another PBS/NPR/Marist poll showed that independents favored Democrats by a margin of 25 points.
Given such polling, Rosenberg believes that the number of people voting for Democratic candidates is actually higher than the partisan breakdown in early voting data explicitly indicates.
Hispanic voters are turning out early in higher numbers than other recent elections
Rosenberg says that the most significant data coming out of early voting is the number of Hispanic people voting early.
So far, Hispanic early voting participation is outpacing its levels at the same point in the election cycle in 2022 and 2024. Presidential election years such as 2024 typically yield higher voter turnout, which Rosenberg says makes the 2026 figures to date all the more notable and surprising.
“It's almost certain that this heightened performance will carry over through Election Day, and that this will become one of the big storylines of the election,” he says. “It's a universal trend that we're seeing all across the country.”
This trend is most noticeable in states with high Hispanic populations, like Texas.
In one of the most closely watched—and expensive—Senate races this year, James Talarico is vying to become the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Texas since 1988 in a tightly contested battle against the state’s Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Over 4 million votes have been cast early, or an estimated 41% of the total votes expected in the race, according to tracking by VoteHub. As of Monday, Talarico was forecast to hold a narrow two-point lead in the early vote.
The state's Hispanic population, one of the highest in the U.S. per capita, represents 24% of the vote as of Monday, according to VoteHub, a percentage point higher than the share it made up in the final vote tally in the 2024 election. Another analysis reported by The Texas Tribune showed that the Hispanic early vote in Texas has already surpassed the early vote numbers from 2024 and 2022.
“What we can see here is just eye-popping numbers for Hispanics,” McDonald said about the group’s early voter turnout not only in Texas, but around the U.S. “If Hispanics are showing up in force now, it's almost with certainty going to change the overall … diversity of the electorate in this election cycle.”
As a result, McDonald contends that “we're going to see larger swings to the Democrats in more diverse states.”
Polling has indicated that Hispanic and Latino voters, a demographic that helped propel Trump back to the White House two years ago, widely disapprove of the President and the Republican Party heading into midterms. Sixty-six percent of Latino voters surveyed in late September by an NBC News/Telemundo poll said that Trump’s deportation policies have gone too far, while 75% disapprove of his handling of the economy and the cost of living. The poll also found that more Latino voters hold a negative view of the GOP than at any point since 2016.
Another Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Oct. 5 showed that just 24% of Hispanic Americans approved of Trump’s performance in the White House, the lowest such rating the President has received across both of his presidential terms. And just 52% of Hispanic voters who responded to the poll planned to vote Democratic, double the level of support for Republicans among the demographic.
How predictive is early voting data?
Rosenberg cautions that early voting “can tell you a lot, but it can't tell you everything,” and that voter turnout can shift from day to day.
He notes that early voting returns showed Kamala Harris leading in the 2024 presidential election, and that she still lost after a strong gain in Republican turnout for Trump.
But he contends that “the lack of intensity that we're seeing in many rural and Republican counties around the country does not bode well for them for Election Day.”
Fraga says that in general, political scientists are skeptical of using early voting data to predict election outcomes. This has been especially true, he notes, in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw Democrats cast early votes by mail at a significantly higher rate than Republicans, who were more likely to vote early at polls, a dynamic that made it harder to draw on the early vote to confidently predict outcomes on Election Day.
Now, though, “the partisan distribution of voters has become somewhat more stable,” he says. “So we can use that information to now have a better comparison, and as a result, early voting data sheds a lot more light on what's likely to happen in November.”
“It's not determinative. It's not going to predict what's going to happen,” Rosenberg says. “But every campaign in the country right now is living and dying on this early vote data.”
Richard Hall contributed reporting.

Vance calls Alaskan Senate bid by nearly identically named candidate a ‘big fraud’ amid legal challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:04:59 UTC
07:04:59 KST

Diyar Guldogan
28 October 2026•Update: 28 October 2026
US Vice President JD Vance defended the Trump administration’s legal challenge to Alaska’s Senate election, describing the candidacy of a second candidate with a name nearly identical to that of the incumbent as a “big fraud” and arguing that it could confuse voters ahead of next week’s midterm elections.
Speaking to reporters Tuesday as he departed for a campaign rally in Michigan, Vance was asked why Alaskans should not find it "insulting" that the administration appeared to suggest they could not distinguish between the two candidates on the ballot.
“Well, I think the question presumes quite a bit,” Vance responded.
He argued that many voters would recognize the alleged problem but said others might be confused because of competing demands on their time.
"I mean, look, a lot of Alaskans are going to go and look at the ballot and realize exactly what you said, that this is all a big fraud."
“People are busy. People have lives. People have jobs. And when you put a person on the ballot explicitly to try to confuse voters, I think that’s the definition of electoral fraud. And I don’t think that we should endorse it," Vance said.
The comments came after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit last week seeking to prevent Alaska from certifying its Senate election results under certain circumstances if Republican incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses.
The legal dispute centers on Dan J. Sullivan, a second candidate whose name closely resembles that of the incumbent senator. The administration alleges that the challenger's candidacy could mislead voters and affect the outcome of the race.
The filing argues that certifying results affected by the second candidate’s appearance on the ballot would undermine the state’s responsibility to protect election integrity.
Last week, US President Donald Trump accused Democrats of trying to confuse voters in Alaska’s Senate race by fielding a candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Sullivan.
“We have a man named Dan Sullivan. So the Democrats, maybe here they're not so dumb. They put another man also with the name of Dan Sullivan. So we have two Dan Sullivans. How about that?” he said.
The president argued that the presence of two candidates with similar names could create confusion among voters ahead of the November midterm elections.

How Hong Kong went from a yuan gateway to a complete currency ecosystem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
22:00:15 UTC
07:00:15 KST

In FocusHow Hong Kong went from a yuan gateway to a complete currency ecosystem
Yuan can now be used in a wide variety of scenarios in the city, from multi-asset investments to hedging and consumption
In September, Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu unveiled the city’s first five-year plan along with his policy address, highlighting Hong Kong’s strategic role in promoting the greater use of the yuan outside mainland China as a key priority. In the second part of a four-part series on the globalisation of the yuan, Daisy Wu examines Hong Kong’s evolution from an offshore reservoir into a self-sustaining yuan ecosystem.
Of the hundreds of thousands of people who cross the border between mainland China and Hong Kong every day, many pay with the national currency – the yuan, also known as the renminbi – at turnstiles with the tap of a smartphone.
Yet once that currency passes over the same border and into a Hong Kong bank account, it is treated differently from the renminbi on the mainland. As offshore yuan, or CNH, it falls outside mainland China’s capital controls and trades at a market-driven exchange rate, like the US dollar, the British pound and the Japanese yen.

Astronomers may have just discovered our solar system’s sixth dwarf planet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-27
21:50:43 UTC
06:50:43 KST

Congratulations to Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake—there may be a new sibling to welcome into the dwarf planet family.
On Tuesday astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory announced the discovery of a new dwarf planet candidate in a distant part of the solar system beyond Neptune’s orbit. The new object doesn’t have an official name yet and is instead going by its provisional designation—2026 ED138.
The discovery was made by running billions of pieces of data collected by the Rubin Observatory through a search code developed by Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian astronomers Matthew Holman and Kevin Napier.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said in a statement. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”
When Holman and his colleague Mario Jurić of the University of Washington went to double-check, they found 30 more observations of the object by Rubin that dated to between March and July 2026. Looking at other observation tools, the pair found even more sightings going back to 2016. Together, these data allowed the astronomers to begin mapping out 2026 ED138’s orbit.
The suspected dwarf planet is about 46 times as far from the sun as Earth, making it even more remote than Pluto, which is just 40 times as far. The object is also tilted off the solar system’s plane by around 25 degrees, an arrangement that could be linked to disruptions caused by Neptune’s gravitational pull.
Initial measurements indicate that 2026 ED138 has a diameter between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 and 932 miles), which makes it one of the largest dwarf planet candidates yet detected. But size isn’t all that matters: further observations are required to determine if the object has enough mass to be pulled into a round shape, which is a key requirement for a dwarf planet.
Despite its size, 2026 ED138 was able to avoid detection for all these years because it’s located in a part of the night sky that’s crowded with stars whose light drowned it out. The Vera C. Rubin observatory, which is loaded with state-of-the-art, powerful instruments and only recently came online, made the discovery possible. Now that the object has been identified, astronomers can get to work on learning more about it to see if it can join Pluto and the others in the dwarf planet family.
“If confirmed as a dwarf planet, ED138 would join a very small family of worlds,” Holman said. “Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach.”
